case_title: Amit Jain vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Amit Jain, Suspended Director of Mahagun (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, a real-estate development company)[cite: 19]. Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Debenture Trustee)[cite: 19]. Other participants include Aditya Birla Capital Ltd. (secured lender for four separate projects) and Manorialle Social Welfare Society (representing 195 homebuyers of 'Mahagun Manorialle')[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of secured, senior, redeemable non-convertible debentures (NCDs) aggregating up to Rs. 355 Crores pursuant to a Debenture Trust Deed dated 10.12.2020 exclusively secured against the residential project 'Mahagun Manorialle' located at Sector-128, Noida (total saleable area: 13,92,670 sq. ft., 349 residential units)[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed on redemption of Debentures on 30.09.2023; Section 7 petition C.P. (IB) No. 112(ND)/2025 filed for a total default of Rs. 256,48,85,907/-[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recall/default notices issued on 20.02.2024 and 17.04.2024; Section 7 petition filed on 31.01.2025; notice issued by NCLT on 21.02.2025; matter heard and reserved on 18.07.2025; NCLT delivered admission order on 05.08.2025[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Trust Deed dated 10.12.2020 and Schedule VIII restricting security interest solely to 'Mahagun Manorialle'; Status Report dated 04.10.2025 detailing 11 completed projects (over 11.48 million sq. ft. and 9,175 units delivered) and other ongoing, solvent projects financed by independent lenders without default; and a Settlement Agreement dated 21.08.2025 executed between the CD's suspended management and IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd.[cite: 19] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III on 05.08.2025 admitted Section 7 petition against the entire Corporate Debtor without granting time to file a detailed reply[cite: 19]. Interlocutory intervention by Aditya Birla Capital Ltd. (IA No. 53 of 2025) was dismissed on 04.08.2025[cite: 19]. Suspended Director, homebuyer society, and lender appealed to NCLAT[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether the Corporate Debtor was denied natural justice by refusing reasonable opportunity to file a detailed reply to a Section 7 petition; whether CIRP of a multi-project real estate corporate debtor should proceed on a project-specific basis rather than company-wide where debt and default are confined to a single project; and whether an admission order warrants remand in light of a post-admission settlement agreement and binding precedent mandating project-wise resolution[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the residential real estate sector, corporate insolvency resolution under the IBC should, as a general rule, proceed on a project-specific basis confined strictly to the defaulting project rather than encompassing the entire corporate debtor, unless exceptional circumstances justify company-wide insolvency, so as to protect solvent projects and genuine homebuyers from collateral prejudice[cite: 19]. Refusal by the Adjudicating Authority to afford a corporate debtor a fair opportunity to file a detailed reply placing on record the status of distinct operational projects, separate lending structures, and ongoing settlement negotiations violates principles of natural justice and warrants setting aside the blanket admission order for fresh reconsideration[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires the Adjudicating Authority to exercise judicial discretion in real estate matters in harmony with constitutional rights to shelter and recent supreme court jurisprudence mandating project-wise segregation[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete factual proof of multiple independent, solvent real estate projects with distinct lender charges and unbreached credit facilities, coupled with a formal post-admission bilateral settlement agreement[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The blanket admission of the entire Corporate Debtor without evaluating project segregation or granting adequate opportunity to file a detailed reply was unsustainable; petition remanded for de novo consideration[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1186 of 2025 is allowed; the impugned order dated 05.08.2025 is set aside; C.P. (IB) No. 112(ND)/2025 is revived before NCLT New Delhi Court-III for fresh consideration; CD is granted one week to file a detailed reply along with the Status Report and the Financial Creditor one week for rejoinder; Adjudicating Authority directed to determine afresh whether CIRP should be confined to project 'Mahagun Manorialle'; Appeals Nos. 1254, 1258, and 1314 of 2025 disposed of; liberty granted to Aditya Birla Capital Ltd. and homebuyers to file intervention applications; parties to bear their own costs[cite: 19].
summary: NCLAT set aside the order of NCLT New Delhi admitting IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd.'s Section 7 petition against real estate developer Mahagun (India) Pvt. Ltd. and remitted the matter for fresh adjudication[cite: 19]. The debenture default of over Rs. 256 Crores was confined to a single project, 'Mahagun Manorialle', while the CD operated multiple other completed and ongoing solvent projects with thousands of homebuyers and distinct lenders[cite: 19]. NCLAT held that NCLT violated natural justice by refusing the CD time to file a detailed reply and acted contrary to the Supreme Court's mandate in Mansi Brar Fernandes, which dictates that real estate insolvency must proceed on a project-specific basis rather than against the entire company, directing NCLT to consider the project-wise segregation and the parties' post-admission settlement[cite: 19].

case_title: Pankaj Mahajan, RP of Arshiya Limited vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Pankaj Mahajan, Resolution Professional of Arshiya Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 21]. Respondents No. 1 to 8, 11, and 12 are financial creditors comprising the Committee of Creditors (CoC), led by Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company (79.00% voting share)[cite: 21]. Respondents No. 9 and 10 are wholly owned subsidiaries undergoing independent CIRP: NCR Rail Infrastructure Limited and Arshiya Northern FTWZ Limited (ANFL)[cite: 21]. Intervenor Ajay Shankarlal Mittal is the suspended director and personal guarantor of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed private sale under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations of non-core land parcels admeasuring 42.08 acres located at the Free Trade Warehousing Zone (FTWZ) in Khurja, Uttar Pradesh (39.56 acres situated on the site of NCR Rail and 2.52 acres forming part of the spine road on the site of ANFL)[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 7 on 23.04.2024 with total outstanding debt exceeding Rs. 6,600 Crores; the valuation of the subject land parcels was determined at approximately Rs. 32 Crores by two independent registered valuers[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 23.04.2024; CoC approved the two-part sale by 85.46% majority vote in the 7th and 8th CoC meetings (concluded 18.03.2025); RP filed IA No. 1927 of 2025 before NCLT Mumbai Bench seeking approval for the sale under Regulation 29[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports of two independent registered valuers fixing fair market value; CoC meeting minutes establishing that the 39.56 acres are landlocked and non-contiguous within NCR Rail's railway tracks and the 2.52 acres form part of a 6.31-acre spine road vital for FTWZ connectivity; and written consents to the sale by sole charge-holders/mortgagees Edelweiss ARC and SREI Equipment Finance[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench on 16.07.2025 partly allowed IA No. 1927 of 2025, permitting the sale in principle but erroneously directing the RPs of NCR Rail and ANFL to invite independent bids from their respective Prospective Resolution Applicants (PRAs) under Regulation 36A(1A)[cite: 21]. The RP of the CD, along with RPs of ANFL and NCR Rail, appealed to NCLAT[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether the manner and mode of sale of non-core encumbered assets of a Corporate Debtor under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations is a commercial decision within the exclusive domain of the CoC; whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by directing parallel CIRPs of distinct corporate entities to invite bids from their PRAs; and whether Regulation 36A(1A) applies retrospectively to sales approved by the CoC prior to its notification[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mode and manner of disposing of a corporate debtor's non-core assets to achieve value maximization under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations lies within the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors and is non-justiciable absent statutory non-compliance[cite: 21]. Encumbered assets may be validly sold under Regulation 29 where the secured charge-holders expressly consent to the sale, constituting an effective waiver of prejudice[cite: 21]. An Adjudicating Authority supervising the CIRP of one corporate entity lacks jurisdiction to issue directions that make its process contingent upon or interfere with the independent CIRP proceedings of distinct subsidiary companies pending before different benches[cite: 21]. Regulation 36A(1A) is substantive and prospective, having no application to asset sales approved by the CoC prior to its enactment[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 29 permits sale of assets outside the ordinary course of business; while the text refers to unencumbered assets, consensual disposal with mortgagee consent is legally valid[cite: 21]. Regulation 36A(1A) cannot be invoked to compel bidding across separate corporate debtors[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial rationality demonstrated by independent valuation reports, unviability of third-party acquisitions due to landlocked geographic layout in a notified FTWZ, and 85.46% affirmative CoC voting[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC lawfully exercised its commercial wisdom to maximize value by selling the land parcels to the SRAs of the respective subsidiaries; the NCLT's directions mandating competitive bidding among PRAs of other entities were legally unsustainable and quashed[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1450, 1451, and 1452 of 2025 are allowed; the impugned directions in the order dated 16.07.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench are set aside; the sale of the subject land parcels as approved by the CoC in IA No. 1927 of 2025 is allowed as prayed; Intervention Application IA No. 5807 of 2025 is dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeals filed by the Resolution Professionals of Arshiya Limited, Arshiya Northern FTWZ Limited, and NCR Rail Infrastructure Limited against NCLT Mumbai's order modifying a CoC-approved asset sale[cite: 21]. The CoC of Arshiya Limited had approved with 85.46% majority the private sale of 42.08 acres of non-core, landlocked parcels within the Khurja FTWZ to the Successful Resolution Applicants of its subsidiaries to maximize value[cite: 21]. NCLAT held that the mode of sale of assets under Regulation 29 lies within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the CoC, that encumbered assets can be sold with mortgagee consent, that NCLT cannot make a CIRP contingent on parallel CIRPs of separate companies, and that newly inserted Regulation 36A(1A) does not apply retrospectively[cite: 21].

case_title: Anubhav Anilkumar Aggarwal & Anr. vs. Rajendra Kumar Girdhar & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Anubhav Anilkumar Aggarwal and Gokul Anilkumar Aggarwal) are erstwhile directors of Chamber Construction Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 23]. Respondent No. 1 is Rajendra Kumar Girdhar (Resolution Professional/Liquidator)[cite: 23]. Respondent No. 2 is Invent Assets Securitization and Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (ARC)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported assignment of a debt receivable from Mafatlal Engineering Industries Ltd. (a company in liquidation since 1999, with claim admitted at only Rs. 16.68 Crores by its Liquidator)[cite: 23]. Kotak Mahindra Bank assigned the debt to Respondent No. 2 on 29.11.2011; Respondent No. 2 and the CD executed an MOU on 17.12.2011 to assign the debt to CD for an inflated consideration of Rs. 36.90 Crores[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was siphoned of Rs. 38,19,05,000/- paid to Respondent No. 2 between 11.10.2011 and 07.01.2014, including Rs. 36,53,00,000/- paid prior to 28.11.2011[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted to CIRP on 16.07.2019; RP filed IA No. 2853 of 2021 under Section 66 of the IBC in CP No. 3962 of 2018; NCLT passed the contribution order on 07.05.2024[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU terms requiring 99% payment by 28.11.2011—a date prior to Respondent No. 2's own acquisition from Kotak (29.11.2011) and prior to MOU execution (17.12.2011); deliberate payment of only 98.997% to create an automatic artificial default triggering a built-in 'no recourse and forfeiture' clause; failure to execute any assignment deed; and retention by Respondent No. 2 of both the forfeited sums and recoveries from Mafatlal's Liquidator[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 2853 of 2021 held the transaction to be fraudulent, declared the MOU sham and void ab initio, and directed the Appellants under Section 66(1) to contribute Rs. 36.53 Crores to the assets of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 23]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether Section 66(1) of the IBC contains a look-back period limiting the investigation of fraudulent business transactions; whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 66 to examine and treat a fraudulent contract as void ab initio; and whether erstwhile directors are liable to contribute assets for carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors under Section 66(1)[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 66(1) of the IBC prescribes no statutory look-back period; fraudulent trading carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose can be examined irrespective of the time elapsed prior to CIRP commencement[cite: 23]. Section 66(1) and Section 66(2) operate independently in distinct spheres[cite: 23]. While Section 66 does not confer general powers of contractual avoidance as under Sections 43-51, where a contract is per se fraudulent, collusive, and engineered to siphoning assets, it is void ab initio and non est in the eyes of law, and the Tribunal possesses incidental jurisdiction to disregard it and direct restitution[cite: 23]. Directors who knowingly orchestrate transactions designed to forfeit corporate funds under sham arrangements are personally liable to contribute to the corporate debtor's estate[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The legislature deliberately omitted a look-back period in Section 66, unlike Sections 43 and 46[cite: 23]. Fraud vitiates all solemn acts and nullifies contracts ab initio[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Circumstantial proof establishing pre-arranged dates of payment preceding asset acquisition by the assignor, grossly inflated price exceeding admitted liquidation debt, deliberate default of tiny fraction to invite contractual forfeiture, and complete inaction to enforce rights over a decade[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The acquisition and forfeiture arrangement was a fraudulent device to extract corporate funds; NCLT rightly directed the directors to contribute Rs. 36.53 Crores[cite: 23].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 07.05.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 2853 of 2021 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1277 of 2024 is dismissed; pending IAs closed; interim orders vacated; no order as to costs[cite: 23].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by erstwhile directors of Chamber Construction Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Mumbai's order directing them to contribute Rs. 36.53 Crores under Section 66 of the IBC[cite: 23]. The directors had caused the company to pay over Rs. 38 Crores to an ARC for assigning a debt of a company in liquidation worth only Rs. 16.68 Crores, under an MOU structured so that 99% consideration was due before the ARC even acquired the debt, with an artificial default engineered to trigger forfeiture[cite: 23]. NCLAT held that Section 66(1) has no look-back limitation period, that fraud vitiates transactions ab initio allowing the tribunal to treat such sham contracts as non est, and affirmed the personal contribution order against the directors[cite: 23].

case_title: Team Commotrade (India) Private Limited vs. M/s. RG Thermal Solution Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Team Commotrade (India) Private Limited (Operational Creditor, importing and marketing agricultural machinery under brand Zoomlion)[cite: 26]. The Respondent is M/s. RG Thermal Solution Private Limited (Corporate Debtor, appointed as regional sub-dealer for Purba and Paschim Midnapur, West Bengal)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of agricultural machinery, harvesters, and spare parts under a Letter of Intent dated 14.09.2019 and multiple purchase orders, with a security deposit of Rs. 10,00,000/- furnished by the Respondent[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Out of total invoiced value of Rs. 4,04,21,108/-, part payments of Rs. 2,39,31,180/- were made, leaving an unpaid claimed principal balance of Rs. 1,64,89,928/- (claimed total of Rs. 2,37,84,627.60 inclusive of 18% p.a. interest) with default date asserted as 09.08.2021[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form 3 demand notice issued on 11.08.2021; reply to demand notice issued by Corporate Debtor within ten days on 21.08.2021; rejoinder sent on 02.09.2021; Section 9 petition C.P. (IB) No. 211/KB/2022 filed on 07.07.2022[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence establishing pre-existing quality disputes, including a letter dated 10.07.2019 from principal manufacturer Zoomlion Heavy Machinery Co. Ltd. admitting need for machine component upgrades, customer defect complaints from farmers in 2020 leading to exchange of 6 out of 13 harvesters, 2020 consumer litigation before State Commission Cuttack, disputed invoice No. TCIPL/GST/127 dated 09.08.2021 for Rs. 26,00,000/- lacking delivery challans, and 44 invoices aggregating Rs. 45,07,324/- maturing within the Section 10A period[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed Section 9 petition on 25.06.2024 on grounds of pre-existing dispute and threshold bar; Operational Creditor appealed under Section 61(1)[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable when substantial invoices fall within the prohibited Section 10A period and reduce the debt below the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore; whether unilateral interest stipulations in invoices can be clubbed to cross the threshold; and whether customer complaints, manufacturer upgrade letters, and goods returns constitute a plausible pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox doctrine[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor cannot sustain an application under Section 9 of the IBC if, after excluding claims barred under Section 10A and disputed unverified invoices, the net operational debt falls below the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4[cite: 26]. Interest on delayed payments cannot be added to satisfy the threshold unless supported by an express bilateral contract[cite: 26]. A genuine, plausible dispute regarding quality, product defects, and uncertified delivery predating the statutory demand notice completely bars the admission of a Section 9 petition[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A creates an absolute bar against filing CIRP applications for defaults occurring between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021; such invoices must be excised from the operational debt computation[cite: 26]. Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d), receipt of a notice of dispute mandates rejection where the defense is plausible and not spurious or moonshine[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented customer returns, third-party consumer complaints, manufacturer upgrade acknowledgments, and absence of agreed delivery receipts for invoices generated after a 16-month delay[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was mired in bona fide pre-existing disputes and the legally actionable balance of Rs. 93,82,604/- fell below the mandatory Rs. 1 Crore threshold; NCLT rightly dismissed the application[cite: 26].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 25.06.2024 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in C.P. (IB) No. 211/KB/2022 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2272 of 2024 is dismissed; all pending IAs dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 26].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by Team Commotrade (India) Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Kolkata's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC petition filed against sub-dealer RG Thermal Solution Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid harvester supplies[cite: 26]. NCLAT held that the petition was not maintainable as invoices totaling Rs. 45,07,324/- fell squarely within the prohibited Section 10A period and a disputed invoice of Rs. 26,00,000/- lacked delivery challans, which reduced the actionable operational debt to Rs. 93,82,604/-, below the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore (disallowing unilateral interest additions)[cite: 26]. Furthermore, manufacturer letters admitting defects and widespread farmer complaints established a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Mobilox[cite: 26].

case_title: Air Wave Technocrafts Private Limited vs. Voltas Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Air Wave Technocrafts Private Limited (Operational Creditor, providing HVAC operation and maintenance services)[cite: 27]. The Respondent is Voltas Limited (Corporate Debtor, engineering contractor)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of operation and maintenance services for HVAC systems across various client work sites (e.g., Rashtrapati Bhawan, IIT Delhi, Talkatora Stadium) under separate work orders between 2010 and 2019[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 1,20,46,835/- arising out of invoices spanning 2010 to 02.01.2019; default date asserted as 11.08.2022 in Form-3 based on an email denying payments[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last invoice raised 02.01.2019; part payment made 18.02.2021; NeSL information utility registration on 13.02.2023 and 19.06.2023; Section 8 Form-3 Demand Notice issued 17.02.2024; reply to Demand Notice issued 01.03.2024; Section 9 petition C.P. (IB) No. 939/MB/2024 filed on 29.08.2024[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's emails dated 11.08.2022 and 22.12.2022 denying liability for untraceable/unsupported invoices while agreeing to send a settlement proposal of Rs. 15.03 lakhs to management subject to compliance documentation; failure of the Operational Creditor to provide attendance sheets, wage registers, ESIC/PF challans, and certified work orders; and NeSL record of default generated as 'Deemed to be Authenticated' on 04.03.2024 without affirmative confirmation by the debtor[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I dismissed the Section 9 application on 27.05.2025 on grounds of limitation and pre-existing dispute; Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether part-payment on disconnected work-site invoices extends limitation under Section 19 of the Limitation Act for all historical unpaid invoices under a claimed running account; whether a 'deemed authenticated' record of default in an Information Utility constitutes an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18; and whether email exchanges disputing work certification and compliance records establish a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) of the IBC[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Separate invoices issued for disparate work-sites without an overarching master contract cannot be treated as a single continuous running account; part payment mapped to specific verified invoices does not extend the three-year limitation period for other independent, unacknowledged invoices under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act[cite: 27]. Even where part payment is made, a Section 9 petition filed beyond three years from the date of such payment is barred by limitation[cite: 27]. Unilateral registration of debt with an Information Utility, resulting in a 'deemed to be authenticated' status, is an administrative evidentiary entry that does not constitute an express or conscious acknowledgment of liability by the debtor[cite: 27]. Contemporaneous pre-notice communications disputing billing particulars, statutory compliance documents, and certification constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 requires an unequivocal acknowledgment of subsisting liability in writing signed by the debtor prior to the expiration of the limitation period[cite: 27]. Issuance of a Demand Notice under Section 8 is a creditor's act and cannot renew limitation[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of disconnected project invoices, bank statement entries showing lapse of three years from part payment, and email records containing explicit repudiation of unverified claims[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was barred by limitation and clouded by genuine pre-existing disputes; dismissal by NCLT was lawful[cite: 27].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 27.05.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in C.P. (IB) No. 939/MB/2024 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1220 of 2025 is dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 27].
summary: NCLAT affirmed the dismissal of a Section 9 application filed by Air Wave Technocrafts Pvt. Ltd. against Voltas Limited seeking recovery of Rs. 1.20 Crores for HVAC maintenance services rendered between 2010 and 2019[cite: 27]. NCLAT held that the claim was barred by limitation as the last invoice was issued on 02.01.2019 and the petition was filed in August 2024—more than three years even from the last part payment made on 18.02.2021[cite: 27]. The bench rejected the contention of a running account across disconnected sites, ruled that a 'deemed authenticated' status in an Information Utility (NeSL) does not constitute an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and held that pre-notice emails demanding labour compliance records proved a genuine pre-existing dispute[cite: 27].

case_title: Airwill JKM Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. Cadillac Infotech Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Airwill JKM Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and JKM Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (alleged Financial Creditors/Developers)[cite: 28]. The Respondent is Cadillac Infotech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Landowner)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) dated 07.08.2013 entered into between the parties to jointly develop an IT project across plots 1, 2, 11, 12 and adjoining plot 10 in Sector 135, Noida, on a profit/built-up area sharing basis (46.25% owner allocation and 53.75% developer allocation)[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed defaults under Section 7 of Rs. 26,56,25,000/- (Rs. 12.50 Cr principal + interest) by Airwill JKM and Rs. 5,73,75,000/- (Rs. 2.70 Cr principal + interest) by JKM Infrastructure; date of default alleged as August 2014[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU executed on 07.08.2013; Property Development Agreement (PDA) executed on 06.09.2014 with group entity Airwil JKM Infracon Pvt. Ltd.; PDA terminated by CD on 18.06.2015; Arbitral Award delivered on 16.10.2018; Section 34 petition decided by Delhi High Court on 29.11.2021; Section 7 petitions CP (IB) No. 210/ND/2022 and CP (IB) No. 211/ND/2022 filed on 05.03.2022[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses of the MoU dated 07.08.2013 stipulating joint development of an IT park, developer obligation to bear all construction expenses, joint maintenance agency, area allocation of 46.25% to owner and 53.75% to developer, and commercial suit CS(COMM) 277 of 2022 filed by Appellant in Delhi High Court for recovery of the same sums[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-V on 13.06.2025 dismissed both Section 7 petitions, holding that the advances were investments for profit under a joint venture/collaboration agreement rather than disbursements against consideration for time value of money[cite: 28]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether advance funds disbursed by a developer to a landowner under an MoU for land acquisition, amalgamation, and joint construction on an area/profit-sharing basis constitute a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) or Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To determine whether a transaction constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority must examine the real economic nature of the underlying arrangement[cite: 28]. Where funds are advanced pursuant to an MoU or collaboration agreement aimed at joint development of real estate on a shared area or profit-sharing basis, the advance constitutes an investment for profit rather than a loan or borrowing disbursed against consideration for the time value of money[cite: 28]. Joint venture partners and development co-sharers cannot misuse Section 7 of the IBC as a debt recovery forum[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) requires a transaction to have the 'commercial effect of a borrowing' with time value of money; mutual covenants regarding land procurement, construction expense allocation, and profit sharing establish a collaborative business enterprise rather than a debtor-creditor financing transaction[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Analysis of the MoU terms showing developer's allocation of 53.75% built-up area, joint signing of sale deeds with buyers, absence of financial statements depicting loans, and pendency of civil recovery suits[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transaction was a joint venture collaboration; the advance was not a financial debt under Section 5(8), and the Section 7 petition was rightly rejected[cite: 28].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 13.06.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Court-V in CP (IB) No. 210/ND/2022 and CP (IB) No. 211/ND/2022 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1187 & 1188 of 2025 are dismissed, with liberty to pursue pending commercial suits before the Delhi High Court; no orders as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: NCLAT dismissed two appeals filed by Airwill JKM Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and JKM Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. challenging the dismissal of their Section 7 petitions against landowner Cadillac Infotech Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 28]. The Appellants had paid over Rs. 15 Crores under an MoU dated 07.08.2013 to acquire and amalgamate land for developing an IT project in Sector 135, Noida, with built-up space shared at 53.75% for the developer and 46.25% for the owner[cite: 28]. NCLAT held that the real substance of the transaction was a joint venture collaboration and development partnership rather than a financial borrowing with time value of money under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, reaffirming that IBC cannot be used as a debt recovery mechanism[cite: 28].

case_title: Manorialle Social Welfare Society vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Manorialle Social Welfare Society (a registered welfare society representing 195 homebuyers/allottees of the residential project 'Mahagun Manorialle' in Sector-128, Noida)[cite: 29]. Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. (Debenture Trustee/Financial Creditor)[cite: 29]. Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Mahagun (India) Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial facility of Rs. 355 Crores availed through issuance of non-convertible debentures (NCDs) by the Corporate Debtor under a Debenture Trust Deed dated 10.12.2020, exclusively charging the project 'Mahagun Manorialle' (349 residential units)[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 256,48,85,907/- in redemption of debentures on 30.09.2023, triggering Section 7 petition C.P. (IB) No. 112(ND)/2025[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recall notice issued 20.02.2024; Section 7 petition filed 31.01.2025; NCLT passed blanket CIRP admission order on 05.08.2025 without project segregation; Appellant society filed appeal challenging company-wide CIRP[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Trust Deed and Schedule VIII showing debt security was restricted exclusively to 'Mahagun Manorialle'; status reports showing CD possesses 11 completed projects (9,175 units delivered) and multiple ongoing projects involving over 8,500 homebuyers with distinct lenders and no default; and post-admission Settlement Agreement dated 21.08.2025 between CD and Financial Creditor[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III on 05.08.2025 initiated company-wide CIRP against Mahagun (India) Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 29]. Appellant society appealed seeking restriction of CIRP exclusively to 'Mahagun Manorialle' or project-wise segregation[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether CIRP initiated against a multi-project real estate developer for a debt and security strictly limited to one project should be confined to that specific defaulting project to avoid prejudice to solvent projects and homebuyers[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In real estate insolvencies under the IBC, resolution must as a rule proceed on a project-specific basis rather than against the entire corporate debtor, in order to ring-fence solvent projects, prevent collateral prejudice to thousands of uninvolved genuine homebuyers, and protect their fundamental right to shelter[cite: 29]. Where an admission order fails to consider project segregation and the parties enter into a post-admission settlement, the blanket admission order is liable to be set aside and remanded for de novo consideration[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 must be applied in harmony with the Supreme Court's binding mandate in Mansi Brar Fernandes v. Shubha Sharma, requiring project-wise resolution and protection of performing assets[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual demarcation of debenture security in Schedule VIII of the Trust Deed and verified project status records establishing distinct financing and lack of default in other projects[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The blanket admission of the entire Corporate Debtor was unsustainable; the order was set aside and remitted for fresh determination[cite: 29].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 05.08.2025 is set aside; C.P. (IB) No. 112(ND)/2025 is revived before NCLT New Delhi Court-III for fresh consideration; CD granted one week to file a detailed reply along with project status reports and Financial Creditor one week for rejoinder; NCLT directed to consider project-specific CIRP; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1314 of 2025 is disposed of; no order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary: NCLAT set aside NCLT New Delhi's blanket CIRP admission order against real estate developer Mahagun (India) Pvt. Ltd. on an appeal filed by the Manorialle Social Welfare Society (representing 195 homebuyers)[cite: 29]. The financial debt default of Rs. 256 Crores arose exclusively from debentures secured on the 'Mahagun Manorialle' project, whereas the company operated multiple other solvent, independent projects delivering over 9,000 homes[cite: 29]. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Mansi Brar Fernandes, NCLAT held that real estate insolvency must proceed on a project-specific basis to protect solvent projects and genuine homebuyers, setting aside the admission order and remanding the matter for fresh adjudication in light of the project-wise segregation and a post-admission settlement agreement[cite: 29].

case_title: Mr. S. Radhakrishnan & Anr. vs. Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. S. Radhakrishnan and Mrs. V. Thara (minority shareholders/former directors)[cite: 24]. The Respondents are Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company), G. Ravi Sankar and G. Parameswaran (Respondents No. 2 and 3, majority shareholder group), statutory auditors, and company secretaries[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Shareholding, management control, and governance of Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd., involving an Agreement for Transfer of Shares dated 08.04.2010 and board resolutions regarding parity of shareholding[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged siphoning of 25,550 and 37,058 shares by deceit/fraud, non-holding of AGMs, illegal removal of Appellant No. 1 as Whole Time Director, and alleged non-compliance with the NCLT judgment dated 26.10.2017[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Earlier petition CP No. 40/2011 (TP No. 50/HDB/2016) filed under Sections 397/398 of Companies Act 1956; Amendment CA No. 68/2016 filed 06.12.2016; CP No. 40/2011 decided by NCLT on 26.10.2017; fresh company petition CP No. 225/241/HDB/2019 filed in 2019[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operative directions of the judgment dated 26.10.2017 disposing of CP No. 40/2011 and CA No. 68/2016, which granted 50:50 shareholding restoration and directed an EGM, while rejecting all other ungranted reliefs under Clause 5; verbatim identity of the reliefs sought in CP No. 225/2019 with those in dismissed CA No. 68/2016; and Appellant's explicit admission in Para IV of CP No. 225/2019 that the fresh petition was filed due to Respondent's failure to respect and implement the 2017 order[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed CP No. 225/241/HDB/2019 as barred by res judicata and an impermissible substitute for execution; Appellants appealed to NCLAT Chennai under Section 421[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a fresh company petition under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable to execute or redress the non-implementation of an earlier judgment under Section 397/398; and whether re-agitating reliefs previously rejected or disposed of in an earlier petition/amendment application is barred by res judicata under Explanation V to Section 11 and Order II Rule 2 of the CPC[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A fresh company petition under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be utilized as a substitute or device for executing an earlier decree or judgment; non-compliance with an earlier tribunal order must be enforced exclusively through statutory execution mechanisms provided under Section 424(3) of the Act read with Rules 56 and 57 of the NCLT Rules, 2016[cite: 24]. Under Explanation V to Section 11 of the CPC, any relief claimed in an earlier petition or amendment application that is not expressly granted in the final decree is deemed to have been refused, creating a complete bar of res judicata against re-agitating those claims in a subsequent proceeding[cite: 24]. A limited liberty granted to challenge actions arising out of a directed EGM cannot be converted into an unfettered license to reopen settled disputes[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(3) provides a complete, self-contained mechanism for execution of tribunal orders; entertaining a fresh company petition for enforcement of an earlier order constitutes an abuse of process[cite: 24]. Order II Rule 2 bars claims that were available when the first action was instituted[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparative mapping of the prayers in the 2019 petition against the 2016 amendment application and 2011 petition showing substantive identity, along with the petitioner's pleadings admitting that the new action was necessitated by non-enforcement[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The fresh petition was a disguised execution petition barred by res judicata and Order II Rule 2 CPC; NCLT rightly dismissed the petition[cite: 24].
operative_order: The impugned order passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissing CP No. 225/241/HDB/2019 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 89 of 2024 is dismissed; all pending interlocutory applications closed; no orders as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed a company appeal filed by minority shareholders of Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd. against NCLT Hyderabad's dismissal of their Section 241 company petition[cite: 24]. The appellants had previously obtained a partial relief order in CP No. 40/2011 on 26.10.2017, and filed a fresh petition in 2019 asserting identical reliefs regarding balance sheet tampering and director removal on the ground that the company failed to implement the 2017 order[cite: 24]. NCLAT held that under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act read with NCLT Rules 56 & 57, a fresh company petition cannot be used as an execution proceeding, and that ungranted reliefs from earlier proceedings are deemed refused under Explanation V to Section 11 of the CPC, barring the subsequent petition under res judicata and Order II Rule 2[cite: 24].

case_title: Darshan Developers & Anr. vs. Vaishali Patrikar, RP of Satra Properties (India) Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is M/s Darshan Developers (sole proprietorship firm); Appellant No. 2 is Mr. Pravin Viram Satra (sole proprietor and first cousin of the Corporate Debtor's promoter Praful Satra)[cite: 6, 25]. The Respondent is Ms. Vaishali Patrikar, Resolution Professional of Satra Properties (India) Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claimed pre-existing internal accommodation under an MOU dated 17.12.2019 and joint venture agreement between Shreeniwas Developers and the Corporate Debtor for a slum rehabilitation project[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Withdrawal of Rs. 91,00,000/- via two cheques dated 31.07.2020 (Cheque No. 37 for Rs. 50,00,000/- on RBL Bank and Cheque No. 791035 for Rs. 41,00,000/- on IndusInd Bank) cleared during CIRP moratorium[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheques issued 31.07.2020; CIRP initiated and Section 14 moratorium commenced on 03.08.2020; cheques deposited on 04.08.2020; cheques cleared/encashed on 06.08.2020; RP filed IA No. 3921 of 2022 under Section 60(5)[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements establishing that on 31.07.2020, CD had credit balances of only Rs. 8,398/- in RBL Bank and Rs. 9,151.56/- in IndusInd Bank; funds were credited post-moratorium on 04.08.2020 (Rs. 50 lakhs from M&M Legal Ventures and Rs. 41 lakhs from tender deposit); the cheques were encashed on 06.08.2020; and absence of any direct contractual liability or debt owed by CD to Darshan Developers[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 3921 of 2022 held that the post-moratorium encashment breached Section 14 and was an unauthorized accommodation, directing Appellants on 02.01.2024 to jointly and severally refund Rs. 91,00,000/- to the Corporate Debtor; Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether the doctrine of relation back applies to treat cheque encashment as taking effect on the pre-CIRP date of issuance when the corporate debtor's bank accounts had insufficient funds on the issuance date; and whether encashing pre-dated cheques using post-moratorium credits violates Section 14(1) of the IBC[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The doctrine of relation back—holding that payment by cheque relates back to the date of its issuance upon encashment—applies only when the drawer's bank account contains sufficient funds to honor the cheque on the date of issuance and no intervening statutory bar exists[cite: 25]. Where a corporate debtor issues cheques with negligible balances in anticipation of future credits, and the cheques are deposited and encashed post-admission using funds credited after the commencement of CIRP, the transaction constitutes an illegal post-moratorium transfer and dissipation of corporate assets in direct violation of Section 14(1) of the IBC[cite: 25]. Third-party payees who receive such accommodation payments without subsisting underlying debt are jointly and severally liable to refund the full amount to the corporate debtor's estate[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) strictly prohibits transferring, alienating, or disposing of any assets or beneficial interest of the corporate debtor once the moratorium begins, precluding any post-admission bank clearance of pre-dated cheques[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete bank ledger entries confirming negligible funds at issuance, post-moratorium credit infusions, and absence of independent consideration or proven contractual debt[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The encashment on 06.08.2020 was a blatant violation of the Section 14 moratorium; NCLT's direction ordering joint and several restitution of Rs. 91,00,000/- was fully justified[cite: 25].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 02.01.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 3921 of 2022 in C.P. (IB) No. 1632/MB/2019 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 535 of 2024 is dismissed; all pending IAs disposed of; parties to bear their own costs[cite: 25].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by Darshan Developers and its proprietor Pravin Satra against NCLT Mumbai's order directing them to refund Rs. 91,00,000/- to Corporate Debtor Satra Properties (India) Ltd.[cite: 25]. The CD issued two cheques on 31.07.2020 when its accounts held under Rs. 10,000/-, and CIRP commenced on 03.08.2020[cite: 25]. The cheques were deposited and cleared on 06.08.2020 utilizing fresh funds credited post-CIRP[cite: 25]. NCLAT held that the doctrine of relation back cannot apply where funds were insufficient at issuance, that clearing cheques post-admission using post-moratorium credits breaches Section 14(1) of the IBC, and that payees receiving unauthorized accommodation transfers must restore the siphoned sums to the corporate debtor[cite: 25].

case_title: Mr. Ravi Kizhedath & Anr. vs. Hearts Malabar Clinical Solutions Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mr. Ravi Kizhedath and Mrs. Vandana Prabhakaran (petitioners/minority shareholders)[cite: 32]. Respondent No. 1 is Hearts Malabar Clinical Solutions Private Limited; Respondents No. 2 and 3 are Cheriya Kachery Byju and Karuvante Kelappan Valappil (majority shareholders/directors); Respondent No. 4 is Uttam Kumar (Practising Company Secretary); and Respondent No. 5 is A P Vinod Kumar (Chartered Accountant)[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate affairs, governance, and share capital management of Respondent No. 1 Company, involving the issuance and allotment of a Rights Issue of 1,14,20,200 equity shares in 2017, alteration of the register of members, conversion of directors' professional fees into unsecured loans, and shifting of the registered office[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 alleging wrongful exclusion, dilution of shareholding, and fabrication/forgery of statutory corporate records, board meeting notices, attendance sheets, and AGM minutes[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 4/KOB/2020 filed before NCLT Kochi; Interlocutory Application IA No. 96/KOB/2020 filed by petitioners during proceedings; NCLT final order dismissing company petition passed on 25.02.2021; appeal preferred before NCLAT Chennai under Section 421[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Production of 107 disputed documents appended to the Counter Affidavit of Respondents No. 2 and 3; IA No. 96/KOB/2020 filed under Rule 43 of NCLT Rules specifically praying for production of original documents and their transmission to Central Forensic Science Laboratory (CFSL), Hyderabad for signature analysis, carbon dating, and document age analysis[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi dismissed CP No. 40/KOB/2020 on 25.02.2021 without adjudicating IA No. 96/KOB/2020, perversely recording in paragraph 48 that the petitioners had not prayed for forensic examination of the disputed documents; petitioners appealed under Section 421[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority breached Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 43 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 by dismissing an oppression and mismanagement petition based on disputed documents without deciding a pending interlocutory application seeking forensic testing by CFSL; and whether recording a finding that no prayer for forensic analysis was made, contrary to the record, vitiates the final judgment[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 43(3) of the NCLT Rules, 2016, when a party contesting or preferring an oppression and mismanagement petition raises specific allegations of forgery or fabrication regarding core statutory records and files a formal application seeking their referral to the Central Forensic Science Laboratory, the Tribunal is statutorily bound to adjudicate such application on merits before concluding the main petition[cite: 32]. Disposing of the main petition by making passing remarks or recording findings directly contrary to the record—falsely asserting that no forensic examination was sought—violates the fundamental principles of natural justice and renders the adjudication perverse and unsustainable[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 mandates strict adherence to principles of natural justice; Rule 43(3) confers express powers to transmit disputed records to CFSL at the applicant's cost to ascertain truth, which must be judicially exercised when documentary authenticity is challenged[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the explicit prayer in IA No. 96/KOB/2020 vis-à-vis paragraph 48 of the NCLT judgment, establishing an irreconcilable contradiction and total failure to exercise jurisdiction over the forensic plea[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT failed to determine the validity of the underlying documents under Rule 43; the impugned dismissal order was vitiated and required remand for de novo decision after deciding the forensic audit application[cite: 32].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 21 of 2021 is allowed; the impugned order dated 25.02.2021 passed by NCLT Kochi Bench in CP No. 4/KOB/2020 is quashed; the matter is remitted back to NCLT Kochi with a direction to first adjudicate IA No. 96/KOB/2020 on merits and thereafter decide the Company Petition afresh; no order as to costs[cite: 32].
summary: NCLAT Chennai Bench set aside NCLT Kochi's order dismissing an oppression and mismanagement petition filed under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 by minority shareholders of Hearts Malabar Clinical Solutions Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 32] The appellants had challenged a rights issue and loan conversions as fraudulent and filed IA No. 96/KOB/2020 under Rule 43 of the NCLT Rules seeking CFSL forensic examination of 107 documents relied upon by respondents[cite: 32]. NCLAT held that NCLT acted perversely by dismissing the petition while erroneously recording that no prayer for forensic testing was made[cite: 32]. Holding that natural justice under Section 424 requires deciding the forensic application before concluding the lis, NCLAT remanded the matter for fresh disposal[cite: 32].

case_title: Mr. Narappa Manohar Reddy & Ors. vs. Mr. Pankaj Srivastava, Liquidator of M/s. Sagar Power (Neerukatte) Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants No. 1 and 2 are Mr. Narappa Manohar Reddy and Mrs. Narappa Sharada Reddy (shareholders and erstwhile directors of M/s. Sagar Power (Neerukatte) Private Limited); Appellant No. 3 is M/s. New Age Infrastructure Private Limited (shareholder)[cite: 33]. Respondent is Mr. Pankaj Srivastava, Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate operations and financial transactions of the Corporate Debtor subjected to a Transaction Audit during insolvency/liquidation proceedings[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Avoidance application filed by the Liquidator under Section 43 of the IBC alleging preferential transactions and seeking restitution/refund of amounts from the erstwhile directors/shareholders[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP (IB) No. 243/BB/2018 instituted before NCLT Bengaluru; IA No. 499/2020 filed by the Liquidator under Section 43; impugned order passed on 30.11.2022; appeal filed before NCLAT Chennai under Section 61[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants filed a detailed counter-affidavit/reply to IA No. 499/2020 before NCLT Bengaluru controverting the Transaction Audit Report; however, on the final date of hearing, Appellants' advocate was absent without notice after shifting from independent practice to a law firm[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench allowed IA No. 499/2020 on 30.11.2022 directing Appellants to restore amounts under Section 43 without declaring the proceedings ex parte under Order VIII Rule 10 CPC and without evaluating the defences raised in Appellants' written counter-affidavit[cite: 33]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether an order under Section 43 of the IBC passed against respondents whose counsel was absent without declaring them ex parte or evaluating their written counter-affidavit violates the principles of natural justice and Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Adjudicating Authority exercising quasi-judicial powers under the IBC is bound by the fundamental principles of natural justice and audi alteram partem[cite: 33]. Where a party has placed its written counter-affidavit on record but its engaged advocate defaults or fails to appear on the final date of hearing, the litigant cannot be condemned unheard or made to suffer for the lapse or misdemeanour of counsel[cite: 33]. In such circumstances, the Tribunal cannot pass an adverse order without either directing ex parte proceedings under Order VIII Rule 10 of the CPC (allowing time to engage alternative representation) or thoroughly scrutinizing and addressing the specific defences and grounds pleaded in the existing counter-affidavit[cite: 33]. Passing an unreasoned or summary order without adverting to the party's pleaded defences vitiates the proceedings[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 mandates that all adjudications under the IBC must conform to natural justice and procedural fairness; administrative/quasi-judicial orders cannot be sustained where a party is penalized without hearing its defence[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of court order sheets revealing counsel's non-appearance, absence of an ex parte order under Order VIII CPC, and total omission in paragraphs 11-12 of the impugned order to consider the counter-affidavit[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 43 claw-back order was passed in breach of natural justice; the order was quashed and remitted for de novo hearing subject to payment of costs[cite: 33].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 28 of 2023 is allowed; the impugned order dated 30.11.2022 passed by NCLT Bengaluru in IA No. 499/2020 in CP (IB) No. 243/BB/2018 is quashed, subject to payment of Rs. 50,000/- costs to the Prime Minister's Relief Fund within 10 days; NCLT Bengaluru is directed to decide IA No. 499/2020 afresh after giving due opportunity of hearing; all connected IAs disposed of[cite: 33].
summary: NCLAT Chennai Bench allowed an appeal filed by erstwhile directors and shareholders of Sagar Power (Neerukatte) Pvt. Ltd. against NCLT Bengaluru's order under Section 43 of the IBC directing them to restore funds from alleged preferential transactions[cite: 33]. The appellants had filed a counter-affidavit, but their counsel was absent during final hearing due to personal career changes, and NCLT allowed the avoidance application without setting them ex parte or evaluating the defences raised in their reply[cite: 33]. Reaffirming the Supreme Court rulings in Rafiq and Ramesh Chand Ardawatiya, NCLAT held that under Section 424 of the Companies Act, litigants must not suffer for counsel defaults and tribunals must judicially analyze written pleadings before deciding a lis, remanding the matter for fresh disposal[cite: 33].

case_title: Mr. Parvinder Singla, Proprietor of Ganpati Metals vs. M/s J V Industries Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Parvinder Singla, Sole Proprietor of Ganpati Metals (Operational Creditor, trading in copper scraps)[cite: 34]. The Respondent is M/s J V Industries Private Limited (Corporate Debtor, manufacturer purchasing copper scraps)[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of copper scrap under multiple commercial tax invoices raised between July 2020 and July 2021[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Five consignments supplied between 14.06.2021 and 06.07.2021 with an aggregate value of Rs. 3,07,89,249.60/-, against which a part payment of Rs. 50,00,000/- on 17.07.2021 was adjusted, leaving an unpaid principal operational debt of Rs. 2,70,83,131/- (total claim of Rs. 3,76,54,763/- including 18% p.a. interest)[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Written undertaking executed by Operational Creditor on 17.06.2021; Appellant's GST registration cancelled by authorities with retrospective effect on 23.07.2022; Section 8 Form-3 Demand Notice issued on 25.09.2023; Corporate Debtor replied on 04.10.2023 within 10 days; Section 9 petition C.P. (IB)/721(ND)/2023 filed before NCLT New Delhi[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Written undertaking dated 17.06.2021 executed by Appellant undertaking to pay all GST dues, ensure availment of Input Tax Credit (ITC) by the Corporate Debtor, and indemnify the Corporate Debtor in full against any rejection, denial, interest, or penalty imposed by GST authorities; GST Department show-cause notices (Annexures R-2 and R-3) issued to third-party purchasers disallowing ITC on supplies from Ganpati Metals due to fraudulent credit/bogus billing; and corporate debtor's conditional reply demanding a bank guarantee before releasing payments[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bench-V New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 petition on 19.11.2024 on the grounds of a pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox doctrine; Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 34].
legal_issues: Whether a seller's written undertaking to indemnify the purchaser against denial of Input Tax Credit (ITC) under GST laws, coupled with tax authorities' cancellation of the seller's GST registration and issuance of show-cause notices for bogus ITC, constitutes a plausible pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC justifying rejection of a Section 9 application[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, where an operational creditor executes a binding written undertaking promising to ensure the availment of Input Tax Credit (ITC) and to indemnify the corporate debtor against any tax liability, denial, or penalty, and subsequent actions by tax authorities (such as cancellation of GST registration or proceedings for fake ITC) create a genuine, plausible apprehension of financial liability, the dispute over payment withholding pending tax indemnification constitutes a bona fide, non-spurious pre-existing dispute[cite: 34]. Under the rule in Mobilox Innovations, the Adjudicating Authority is only required to determine whether the defence is plausible and not a patently feeble or illusory argument, without resolving complex factual disputes on breach of indemnity which lie strictly within the province of a civil court[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 is designed for undisputed operational debts; where payment terms are tied to statutory tax compliance under a written indemnity, withholding payment due to regulatory investigation represents a bona fide commercial dispute barring CIRP admission[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Existence of an uncontroverted written indemnity undertaking dated 17.06.2021, regulatory cancellation of GST registration on 23.07.2022, third-party ITC disallowance notices, and failure of the creditor to produce proof of actual tax remittance to the exchequer[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor established a plausible pre-existing dispute prior to the Section 8 notice; NCLT rightly dismissed the Section 9 petition[cite: 34].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19.11.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V in C.P. (IB)/721(ND)/2023 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 47 of 2025 is dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 34].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by Parvinder Singla (Proprietor of Ganpati Metals) against NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of his Section 9 IBC petition against buyer J V Industries Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid copper scrap invoices worth Rs. 2.70 Crores[cite: 34]. The Corporate Debtor resisted payment on the ground that the GST authorities had cancelled the supplier's GST registration for fraudulent billing and initiated proceedings for bogus Input Tax Credit (ITC)[cite: 34]. NCLAT held that the supplier had executed an express written undertaking on 17.06.2021 agreeing to indemnify the buyer against any loss or denial of ITC, and because the supplier failed to prove payment of GST to the exchequer, the buyer's apprehension of tax liability was a plausible, bona fide pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox doctrine, barring admission under Section 9[cite: 34].

case_title: Union of India vs. Hari Sankaran
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Union of India (Ministry of Corporate Affairs)[cite: 42]. The Respondent is Hari Sankaran (ex-director/officer facing serious fraud, SFIO, and PMLA prosecutions)[cite: 42]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and oppression/mismanagement proceedings involving IL&FS group companies[cite: 42]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (corporate governance/criminal prosecution and asset-restraint context)[cite: 42]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 3638/2018 filed under Sections 242(4), 246 read with Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013; interim restraint orders passed freezing bank accounts; Respondent filed Company Application No. 538 of 2022 seeking withdrawal of funds for legal fees[cite: 42]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentation detailing extensive ongoing legal proceedings across multiple judicial fora (Supreme Court, Bombay High Court, Chennai High Court, Sessions/Special Courts for SFIO and PMLA complaints, and banking forums for willful defaulter proceedings) and a certificate from bankers confirming that legal expenses amounting to Rs. 3,73,19,080/- were borne by the Respondent's mother and sister[cite: 42]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed an order on 24.02.2023 allowing Rs. 2 Lakhs per month for sustenance[cite: 42]. Respondent filed CA No. 538 of 2022 seeking permission to withdraw Rs. 31,35,000/- for outstanding legal fees and future expenses of Rs. 5 Lakhs per month[cite: 42]. NCLT on 13.06.2024 allowed Prayer A (withdrawal of Rs. 31,35,000/- for outstanding legal fees) and Prayer C (permitting Power of Attorney holder Ms. Deepa Sankaran to withdraw the funds), while refusing Prayer B[cite: 42]. Union of India appealed against the order[cite: 42].
legal_issues: Whether an individual facing severe corporate and criminal fraud prosecutions whose bank accounts are under statutory restraint orders is entitled to withdraw restricted funds to clear outstanding bona fide legal expenses incurred to defend themselves[cite: 42].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of free legal aid services, an individual facing criminal prosecution and corporate fraud complaints possesses a fundamental right to defend themselves, justifying the conditional unfreezing or withdrawal of restrained personal funds to clear actual, outstanding legal fees incurred across active legal proceedings[cite: 42]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal to regulate corporate and personal asset restraints in a manner that balances the enforcement of regulatory claims with the preservation of constitutional rights to a legal defense[cite: 42]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Banker-certified statements proving that third-party family members (mother and sister) had exhausted their personal resources to fund the ongoing litigation expenses of the applicant[cite: 42]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The respondent demonstrated actual outstanding legal liabilities and exhaustion of family resources in defending multiple active proceedings, making the partial withdrawal of restrained funds legally sound and equitable[cite: 42].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 356 of 2024 filed by the Union of India is dismissed; the NCLT order dated 13.06.2024 permitting withdrawal of Rs. 31,35,000/- through the Power of Attorney holder for clearing outstanding legal fees is upheld[cite: 42].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the Union of India's appeal challenging an NCLT order that permitted Hari Sankaran, an accused in IL&FS-related fraud proceedings, to withdraw Rs. 31,35,000/- from his restrained bank accounts to clear outstanding legal fees incurred in defending numerous Supreme Court, High Court, and Special Court prosecutions[cite: 42]. The appellate tribunal held that given the absence of free legal services and the exhaustion of funds advanced by his family members, an individual has a legitimate right to defend themselves, rendering the NCLT's limited release of funds justifiable[cite: 42].

case_title: Workmen of Dunlop Polymers Limited vs. M/s. Miller Trader Private Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Workmen of Dunlop Polymers Ltd., represented by Dunlop Polymers Employees Union (Reg. No. MYS 167/78)[cite: 43]. Respondent No. 1 is M/s. Miller Trader Private Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Dunlop Polymer Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 43]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Labour and workmen employment dues associated with Dunlop Polymers Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (limitation and condonation of delay context)[cite: 43]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench on 29.05.2025 in IA No. 893/2024 in CP(IB) No. 123/BB/2019; free copy made available on 02.06.2025; Company Appeal e-filed on 07.08.2025; delay of 36 days in filing and 58 days in re-filing[cite: 43]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Court records showing that the appeal was filed well beyond the mandatory 30-day period and the absolute 15-day maximum condonable window under Section 61(2) of the IBC, with no application or proof of applying for a certified copy[cite: 43]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed IA No. 893/2024 on 29.05.2025; workmen filed appeal before NCLAT along with IA No. 1564/2025 for condonation of delay and IA No. 1566/2025 for re-filing delay[cite: 43].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the jurisdiction or discretion under Section 61(2) of the IBC or Section 5 of the Limitation Act to condone a delay in filing an appeal beyond the absolute statutory ceiling of 45 days (30 days plus 15 days grace period)[cite: 43].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, every appeal must be filed within 30 days, and the Appellate Tribunal may condone delay for a maximum period not exceeding 15 days upon sufficient cause; this outer limit of 45 days is a peremptory statutory provision, and Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 cannot be invoked to extend limitation beyond this absolute ceiling[cite: 43]. Where an appeal is filed beyond 45 days from the date of the impugned order (or date of receipt of free copy), the delay cannot be condoned[cite: 43]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC limits grace periods strictly to 15 days, rendering any discretion under general limitation laws inapplicable[cite: 43]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Computation of limitation dates from 29.05.2025/02.06.2025 to e-filing date on 07.08.2025, revealing a total lapse exceeding 45 days[cite: 43]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed outside the maximum condonable period permitted by the IBC; the delay condonation application must be rejected and the appeal dismissed[cite: 43].
operative_order: IA No. 1566 of 2025 (re-filing delay) is allowed, condoning the delay of 58 days; IA No. 1564 of 2025 (filing delay of 36 days) is dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 553 of 2025 is dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 43].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by the Workmen of Dunlop Polymers Ltd. against an NCLT Bengaluru order on the ground of limitation[cite: 43]. The NCLT order was passed on 29.05.2025, and the appeal was e-filed on 07.08.2025, incurring a delay of 36 days in filing[cite: 43]. NCLAT held that under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC, the outer limit for filing an appeal is 30 days plus a maximum grace period of 15 days (total 45 days), and Section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot be invoked to condone delays beyond this statutory ceiling[cite: 43]. Consequently, the filing delay application was rejected and the appeal dismissed[cite: 43].

case_title: Shri Rokadoba Maharaj Ginning & Pressing Pvt. Ltd. vs. The Sri Venkatesa Mills Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Shri Rokadoba Maharaj Ginning & Pressing Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 44]. Respondent is The Sri Venkatesa Mills Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 44]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 9 insolvency application (CP No. 605/IB/2017) settled via a joint compromise memo dated 25.09.2018 under which the Corporate Debtor agreed to pay Rs. 25,00,000/- (Rs. 15 Lakhs upfront and remaining Rs. 10 Lakhs in 10 equal installments of Rs. 2.5 Lakhs each)[cite: 44]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in honoring the settlement installments and post-dated cheques issued under subsequent compromise memos[cite: 44]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original Section 9 petition disposed of as settled on 25.09.2018; first MA No. 67/2019 filed under Rule 11 to restore petition; second compromise order passed on 10.12.2019 dismissing petition as withdrawn with liberty to approach afresh; subsequent recall application filed by appellant; NCLAT appeal filed against rejection[cite: 44]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint memo of compromise dated 25.09.2018, subsequent compromise memo and post-dated cheques recorded in order dated 10.12.2019, and repeated invocation of Rule 11 of NCLT Rules for reviving a concluded proceeding upon breach of settlement terms[cite: 44]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed the appellant's applications seeking recall and revival of the closed Company Petition; Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 44].
legal_issues: Whether a party can invoke Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules (inherent powers) to seek the recall of an order and revival of a company petition that was finally disposed of based on a private settlement or compromise, upon breach of the settlement terms, instead of initiating execution proceedings under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act[cite: 44].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A consent order or an order disposing of a company petition on the basis of a joint memo of compromise constitutes a final adjudication of the lis attaching finality, which takes the shape of a binding decree[cite: 44]. In the event of a breach or non-compliance of the terms of a compromise order, the aggrieved party must resort to execution proceedings as mandated by Section 424(3) of the Companies Act read with the NCLT Rules rather than abusing Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules (inherent powers) to repeatedly seek recall and revival of a finally dismissed company petition[cite: 44]. Inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be utilized as a substitute for execution or to circumvent regular procedural laws[cite: 44]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides the specific statutory mechanism for executing tribunal orders; Rule 11 cannot be invoked to revive dead proceedings merely because settlement terms were breached[cite: 44]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of previous order sheets showing repeated compromises, withdrawal orders, and subsequent recall motions[cite: 44]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Filing recurring recall applications for non-compliance of settlement terms represents an abuse of judicial process; NCLT rightly refused to revive the petition via Rule 11[cite: 44].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 424 of 2022 is dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 44].
summary: NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed an appeal filed by Shri Rokadoba Maharaj Ginning & Pressing Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT's refusal to revive a Section 9 company petition that had been withdrawn following a settlement[cite: 44]. The operational creditor had repeatedly invoked Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules (inherent powers) to recall compromise orders and restore the insolvency petition whenever the corporate debtor defaulted on post-dated settlement cheques[cite: 44]. NCLAT held that a compromise order is a final adjudication akin to a decree, and the remedy for its breach lies in execution proceedings under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act rather than abusing Rule 11 to repeatedly revive a concluded winding up/insolvency petition[cite: 44].

case_title: Uday Ved vs. Union of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Uday Ved (independent director); Respondent is Union of India (Ministry of Corporate Affairs)[cite: 45]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and oppression/mismanagement proceedings against IL&FS under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 45]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (corporate governance/impleadment context)[cite: 45]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed impleadment order on 18.07.2019 based on the second SFIO investigation report; NCLAT dismissed Appellant's challenge (Company Appeal No. 215/2019) on 04.03.2020; Supreme Court appeal (Civil Appeal No. 3014/2020) dismissed as withdrawn on 05.04.2021; CA No. 121/2022 filed before NCLT for recall/review; NCLT dismissed CA No. 121/2022 on 20.06.2024[cite: 45]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supreme Court order dated 05.04.2021 permitting withdrawal of Civil Appeal No. 3014/2020 to pursue remedies before NCLT without expressing any opinion on merits; and Supreme Court judgments in separate appeals of co-directors Neera Saggi and Renu Challu (Civil Appeal Nos. 2841 and 3531 of 2020) decided on 15.02.2021[cite: 45]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I dismissed CA No. 121/2022 on 20.06.2024; Appellant appealed to NCLAT Principal Bench[cite: 45].
legal_issues: Whether an application to recall or review an interlocutory impleadment order is maintainable before the Adjudicating Authority after the order has been challenged up to NCLAT and merged into an appellate dismissal, and whether withdrawal of a Supreme Court appeal with liberty to pursue 'appropriate remedies' revives the right to seek recall before the Tribunal[cite: 45].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an interlocutory order passed by the Adjudicating Authority is challenged in an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal and the appeal is dismissed on merits, the original order merges into the appellate order, and the Adjudicating Authority becomes legally incompetent to entertain a subsequent application to review or recall the merged order[cite: 45]. The withdrawal of a Supreme Court appeal with liberty to pursue 'appropriate remedies' does not nullify the doctrine of merger or revive a dead remedy of review before the tribunal of first instance[cite: 45]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Doctrine of merger applies strictly once an appellate court or tribunal disposes of an appeal on merits, extinguishing the lower forum's power to alter its initial order[cite: 45]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of NCLAT's earlier judgment dated 04.03.2019 in Comp. App. No. 215/2019 and Supreme Court's withdrawal order dated 05.04.2021[cite: 45]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The recall application before NCLT was legally barred by merger; the appeal lacks merit and is dismissed[cite: 45].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 254 of 2024 is dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 45].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by Uday Ved (an independent director of IL&FS) challenging NCLT Mumbai's order dismissing his application to recall an impleadment order dated 18.07.2019 based on an SFIO investigation report[cite: 45]. NCLAT held that because the impleadment order had already been challenged in an appeal before NCLAT which was dismissed on merits on 04.03.2020, the order merged into the appellate decision, rendering a subsequent recall application before the NCLT not maintainable[cite: 45]. The bench further noted that the appellant's withdrawal of his Supreme Court appeal with general liberty to pursue 'appropriate remedies' did not revive a review jurisdiction barred by merger[cite: 45].

case_title: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Pancard Clubs Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 5716 of 2025 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1528 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI); Respondents include Pancard Clubs Ltd. and other stakeholders[cite: 46]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Pancard Clubs Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (delay condonation and recall context)[cite: 46]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order passed on 25.04.2024; appeal e-filed on 12.07.2024, beyond the 30-day limitation period and the 15-day maximum condonable grace period under Section 61(2); NCLAT rejected delay condonation on 21.11.2024; Supreme Court dismissed SEBI's civil appeals on 24.01.2025 after SEBI stated intent to seek review before NCLAT; recall application filed subsequently[cite: 46]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supreme Court order dated 24.01.2025 recording that Civil Appeal Nos. 408-409 of 2025 were not pressed as SEBI intended to seek review/recall before NCLAT, without granting any affirmative liberty or remanding the matter[cite: 46]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT on 21.11.2024 rejected IA No. 5536 of 2024 for delay condonation and dismissed CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1528 of 2024 as time-barred[cite: 46]. SEBI filed IA No. 5716 of 2025 seeking recall of the order dated 21.11.2024[cite: 46].
legal_issues: Whether an order rejecting an appeal solely on the ground of delay beyond the absolute statutory ceiling of Section 61(2) of the IBC can be recalled under inherent powers where the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without granting liberty to seek review; and whether grounds like Section 14 limitation exclusion or fraud can be raised for the first time in a recall application against a delay dismissal[cite: 46].
ratio_decidendi: 1.
