ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal's order rejecting an application for condonation of delay because the filing exceeded the absolute statutory ceiling (30 days plus 15 days grace period) cannot be recalled under inherent powers unless recognized grounds for recall (such as procedural fraud on the court or manifest error in the order itself) are established[cite: 46]. A recall application cannot serve as a backdoor mechanism to re-argue a time-barred appeal or introduce new legal grounds (such as Section 14 exclusion) that were never validly before the court during the delay adjudication[cite: 46]. Dismissal of a civil appeal by the Supreme Court as 'not pressed' without granting affirmative liberty or remand confers no fresh legal right to reopen concluded procedural orders[cite: 46]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC is peremptory; inherent powers cannot be invoked to bypass statutory limitation bars[cite: 46]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of filing dates showing a delay exceeding 45 days and absence of recognized recall grounds in the application[cite: 46]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The recall application failed to meet any established ground for recalling an order and was barred by the prior Supreme Court dismissal; application dismissed[cite: 46].
operative_order: I.A. No. 5716 of 2025 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1528 of 2024 is dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 46].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an interlocutory application filed by SEBI seeking recall of an appellate order dated 21.11.2024 which had rejected SEBI's appeal against Pancard Clubs Ltd. as time-barred[cite: 46]. SEBI had filed its appeal beyond the absolute 45-day statutory limit under Section 61(2) of the IBC, and after the Supreme Court dismissed SEBI's civil appeals as 'not pressed' (noting SEBI's intent to seek review), SEBI moved NCLAT for recall[cite: 46]. NCLAT held that the recall application did not disclose any recognized ground for recalling a judgment (such as procedural fraud or manifest error in the delay order), that new legal pleas like Section 14 exclusion cannot be raised to cure a delay dismissal, and that the Supreme Court's dismissal without remand conferred no right to reopen the matter, dismissing the application[cite: 46].

case_title: Equitas Small Finance Bank Ltd. vs. Jumbo Finvest (India) Ltd.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1771 of 2025 & I.A. No. 6926 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant, Equitas Small Finance Bank Ltd., is the Financial Creditor; the Respondent, Jumbo Finvest (India) Ltd., is the Corporate Debtor, a registered Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) authorized as a Financial Service Provider. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant sanctioned a commercial term loan facility to the Respondent on 09.07.2018 for its financial business operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Respondent committed continuous repayment defaults under the term loan facility commencing from 05.01.2019 onwards. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Following an inspection under Section 45N of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 conducted between 11.10.2019 and 17.10.2019 revealing Net NPA at 13.04%, the RBI issued a supervisory directive on 16.01.2020 prohibiting the Respondent from extending new loans, expanding its balance sheet, or accessing public funds; subsequently, RBI formally cancelled Respondent's Certificate of Registration with effect from 14.10.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annexure R-4 RBI letter dated 16.01.2020 directing structured regulatory curbs, the RBI public notice dated 14.10.2025 cancelling registration, and the loan sanction agreement dated 09.07.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a Section 7 petition before the NCLT Jaipur Bench; the Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petition on 22.08.2025 on the ground that the Respondent is a Financial Service Provider under Section 3(17) of the Code, excluded from Section 3(7), and amenable to insolvency solely upon an application filed by the RBI under Section 227 and Rule 5 of the FSP Rules, 2019.
legal_issues: Whether an entity holding a certificate of registration as a Financial Service Provider from the Reserve Bank of India loses its statutory character as an FSP under Section 3(17) of the IBC—thereby becoming subject to Section 7 insolvency proceedings initiated by a financial creditor—by virtue of regulatory supervisory directions prohibiting it from fresh lending, balance sheet expansion, or accessing public funds.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity duly authorized and registered by a financial sector regulator as a financial service provider retains its statutory immunity from standard creditor-initiated corporate insolvency proceedings until its registration is formally cancelled, irrespective of supervisory operational embargoes placed on its lending or borrowing activities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(7) of the IBC explicitly carves out any 'financial service provider' defined under Section 3(17) from the definition of a 'corporate person'. Under Section 227 read with Rule 5 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Insolvency and Liquidation Proceedings of Financial Service Providers and Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2019, CIRP against an FSP can only be initiated upon an application filed by the appropriate financial sector regulator (RBI), and not by an individual financial creditor under Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The subsistence of a valid Certificate of Registration as of the relevant date constitutes conclusive proof of an entity's legal status as an FSP; operational restrictions issued under Section 45N of the RBI Act do not dissolve or strip that legal status prior to de-registration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Respondent's registration as an NBFC subsisted throughout the relevant period until 14.10.2025, it was not a corporate person amenable to a Section 7 application filed by the Appellant, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The rejection of the Section 7 application shall not preclude the Appellant from pursuing remedies available under law against the Respondent, including fresh proceedings post-cancellation of registration.
summary: Equitas Small Finance Bank Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Jaipur Bench rejecting its Section 7 IBC petition against Jumbo Finvest (India) Ltd., an NBFC. The Adjudicating Authority held that the respondent was a Financial Service Provider (FSP) under Section 3(17) and excluded from the definition of a corporate person under Section 3(7). The appellant argued that an RBI directive dated 16.01.2020 prohibiting fresh lending and balance sheet expansion stripped the respondent of its FSP character. NCLAT held that regulatory restrictions do not negate statutory FSP status while registration subsists. As registration was cancelled only on 14.10.2025, CIRP could solely be initiated by RBI under Section 227. The appeal was dismissed with liberty.

case_title: Yusuf Malubhaiwala vs. Mr. Anuj Maheshwari & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Haji Shahadat & Sons (sole proprietorship of Abdul Maaz); Corporate Debtor is Steelexpert Industries (Indore) Ltd., represented by ex-director/Appellant Yusuf Malubhaiwala; Respondent No. 1 is Anuj Maheshwari, IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial trading and supply of iron and steel materials by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor on invoice terms requiring payment within 7 days. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed is Rs. 2,32,98,535/-, comprising Rs. 1,56,44,009/- in principal unpaid invoices and Rs. 76,54,526/- in contractual interest at 24% p.a. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice was issued on 17.10.2019; Corporate Debtor responded by sending a Notice of Dispute on 26.10.2019; Section 9 petition C.P. (IB) No. 29/9/MP/2020 was subsequently filed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor produced commercial invoices, delivery challans, e-way bills, Bank of India certificate, and CA certificate; Corporate Debtor produced three cash receipts totaling Rs. 1,81,84,460/- (one dated 25.04.2017 and two dated 30.04.2019), bank cash withdrawal records, two inconsistent police complaints dated 08.08.2019 and 09.08.2019, and a Civil Suit filed on 25.11.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed C.P. (IB) No. 29/9/MP/2020 before NCLT Indore Bench; on 12.06.2025, NCLT admitted the petition and initiated CIRP, finding the defense of cash receipts uncorroborated and pre-existing disputes unsubstantiated.
legal_issues: Whether uncorroborated cash receipts omitted from the Section 8 reply, pre-notice police complaints concerning personal threats and intimidation, and post-notice civil proceedings establish a plausible, genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9 of the IBC to render a Section 9 application inadmissible.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A pre-existing dispute sufficient to defeat an application under Section 9 of the IBC must be real, bona fide, substantiated by contemporaneous records, and possess a direct nexus to the operational debt; complaints of personal harassment, post-notice civil proceedings, and contradictory claims of cash settlement introduced as afterthoughts fail the Mobilox test. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A 'dispute' within the meaning of Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2)(a) must specifically relate to the existence of the operational debt, quality, or delivery of goods/services. General police complaints alleging coercion do not qualify as disputes concerning operational liability. Furthermore, civil suits or proceedings instituted after the receipt of the Section 8 statutory demand notice cannot constitute a 'pre-existing' dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The defense raised must not be spurious, illusory, or a moonshine defense. Withholding crucial claims of cash discharge in the statutory Section 8 reply and raising them for the first time in reply to the Section 9 petition, especially when contradicted by bank records and mutual inconsistencies in police complaints, destroys the credibility of the defense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed an unresolved operational default above the statutory threshold, and the purported defenses were contrived afterthoughts, justifying the admission of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. The impugned order dated 12.06.2025 passed by NCLT Indore Bench admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP and directing defrayal of the Resolution Professional's fees is affirmed.
summary: Appellant, an ex-director of Corporate Debtor Steelexpert Industries (Indore) Ltd., challenged an order of NCLT Indore Bench admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Operational Creditor Haji Shahadat & Sons for default of Rs. 2,32,98,535/- regarding iron and steel supplies. The appellant contended that the debt was fully settled through cash payments of Rs. 1,81,84,460/-, evidenced by three receipts, and that pre-existing disputes existed via police complaints dated 08.08.2019 and a civil suit. NCLAT held that the cash receipts were an afterthought omitted from the Section 8 reply, the police complaints alleged personal intimidation without nexus to the invoices, and the suit was filed post-demand notice. Applying Mobilox, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Shantilal Javerchand Jain & Ors. vs. Vinodkumar Pukhraj Ambavat & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shantilal Javerchand Jain, Indra Shantilal Jain, and Shirish Shantilal Jain, suspended directors of Corporate Debtor Varsha Corporation Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Vinodkumar Pukhraj Ambavat, Liquidator/former RP; Respondents No. 2 and 3 are purchasers M/s Swastik Diamonds and Maa Kali Jewellers. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants executed 100% unsecured credit sales of 29.885 kg of gold worth Rs. 16,09,74,720/- to Swastik Diamonds between 11.08.2020 and 17.08.2020, followed by another credit sale of Rs. 1,05,67,800/- on 06.06.2022; and credit sales of 560 grams of gold worth Rs. 30,09,290/- to Maa Kali Jewellers on 11.03.2022 and 12.03.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Out of Rs. 17.15 Cr gold sold to Swastik Diamonds, only Rs. 66.10 lakhs was recovered (leaving Rs. 16,49,32,520/- unpaid); out of Rs. 30,09,290/- sold to Maa Kali Jewellers, only Rs. 43,826/- was recovered (leaving Rs. 29,65,464/- unpaid). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition was filed by financial creditor Rajendra Shah on 25.10.2019; NCLT admitted the CD into CIRP on 10.06.2022; final transaction audit report was submitted on 28.11.2022; RP filed IA No. 110 of 2023 on 22.12.2022; liquidation was ordered on 02.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Final Transaction Audit Report by CA Kansal Singla and Associates, ledger accounts revealing that the Swastik Diamonds sale constituted 98% of the CD's total FY 2020-2021 revenue (Rs. 16.48 Cr), executed on 100% credit without security, KYC, or recovery mechanism during the pendency of Section 7 proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 110 of 2023 under Section 66 of the Code; NCLT Mumbai Bench-I partially allowed it on 12.03.2025, holding the transactions fraudulent and directing Appellants No. 1 to 3 to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 16,49,32,520/- and Rs. 29,65,464/- with 12% interest p.a. to the CD.
legal_issues: Whether disposing of substantially the entire inventory and revenue of a corporate debtor by way of unsecured credit sales without security, contracts, or recovery safeguards during the pendency of a Section 7 insolvency petition constitutes fraudulent trading under Section 66(1) and wrongful trading under Section 66(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial transactions carried out by directors outside ordinary trade norms during the pendency of corporate insolvency proceedings that systematically divest the company of valuable assets on uncollateralized credit without realistic recovery mechanisms establish dishonest intent and failure of due diligence, justifying personal contribution to the corporate debtor's estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) and Section 66(2) of the IBC operate independently: Section 66(1) penalizes 'fraudulent trading' carried on by any person with dishonest intent to defraud creditors, whereas Section 66(2) fixes liability for 'wrongful trading' specifically on directors who knew or ought to have known that CIRP could not be avoided and failed to exercise due diligence to minimize loss to creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Fraudulent intent under Section 66 is evaluated on the standard of preponderance of probability; an audit report corroborated by financial statements, abnormal trade patterns (unsecured credit in spot-cash bullion trade), and transactions executed on the eve of CIRP admission establish fraudulent siphoning. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The suspended directors actively transacted to keep gold inventory out of creditors' reach with full knowledge of impending insolvency, affirming their liability to contribute the lost sums.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs. The order dated 12.03.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 110 of 2023 directing Appellants No. 1 to 3 to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 16,49,32,520/- and Rs. 29,65,464/- with interest @12% p.a. from the date of the order until realization is affirmed.
summary: Suspended directors of Corporate Debtor Varsha Corporation Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench-I under Section 66 IBC directing them to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 16,49,32,520/- and Rs. 29,65,464/- with 12% interest p.a. for fraudulent gold transactions. The transactions, involving sales to Swastik Diamonds and Maa Kali Jewellers, constituted 98% of the corporate debtor's annual revenue and were made entirely on unsecured credit without security or formal contracts while Section 7 proceedings were actively pending. NCLAT held that Section 66(1) and 66(2) operate independently and that selling bullion on credit during impending insolvency established clear dishonest intent to siphon assets away from creditors. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s Apex Luminaires Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. G. N. Thirumalesh
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 120/2025 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 121/2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/s Apex Luminaires Pvt. Ltd. and its directors Shringeri Seshagiri, Ajay Gupta, Shringeri Vasundara, and Chaitra Shringeri; Respondent is G. N. Thirumalesh, an alleged former shareholder and director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate equity and governance dispute wherein the Respondent claimed to hold 24,99,000 equity shares (50% shareholding) as an original subscriber, which were allegedly transferred to Appellants No. 3 and 5 on 30.12.2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants asserted that Respondent transferred his entire shareholding for Rs. 5.5 crores received as consideration; Respondent disputed this, alleging fraud, and sought restoration of shares, invalidation of transfer, refund of directors' salaries, and a forensic audit. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting allegedly approving share transfer/resignation took place on 31.12.2021; Form DIR-12 filed on 17.01.2022; Annual Report filed on 31.12.2021; Company Petition C.P. No. 125/BB/2022 filed on 19.09.2022; amendment application CA No. 59 of 2023 filed on 14.04.2023; maintainability objection CA No. 79 of 2023 filed on 08.08.2023; RoC report submitted on 09.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form MGT-7 dated 31.12.2021 showing zero shareholding for Respondent, Form DIR-12 dated 17.01.2022, RoC report Dy. No. 4187 noting omission of the original physical resignation letter, and CA application pleadings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In C.P. No. 125/BB/2022, NCLT Bengaluru Bench passed two orders on 11.07.2025, allowing the amendment application (CA No. 59 of 2023) and dismissing the maintainability objection (CA No. 79 of 2023) on the basis that Respondent's resignation was unverified by an original letter.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can allow substantial amendments introducing new prayers and reject a preliminary challenge to petition maintainability under Sections 241 and 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 via unreasoned orders without adjudicating statutory membership under Section 2(55).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicatory authority cannot grant substantive amendments to pleadings or determine preliminary questions of maintainability through summary, unreasoned orders; a conscious, judicious application of mind evaluating statutory thresholds, cause-of-action transformations, and procedural tests is legally mandatory. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241(1) read with Section 244 requires that a petitioner must qualify as a 'member' under Section 2(55) on the date of presentation of the petition. Where the petitioner admittedly holds zero shares as per statutory filings, the burden of proving member status rests squarely on the petitioner, which cannot be dispensed with by a mere negative inference drawn from an unproduced resignation letter. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Merely extracting party submissions and stating a conclusion without testing whether the amendment satisfies Order VI Rule 17 standards or whether the petitioner has discharged the burden of showing locus under Section 2(55) fails the legal standard of judicial adjudication. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed material perversity by failing to provide analytical reasoning for allowing the amendment and by refusing to decide the preliminary question of maintainability under Section 241/244, requiring both orders to be quashed and remitted.
operative_order: Both Company Appeals are allowed. The impugned orders dated 11.07.2025 in CA No. 59 of 2023 and CA No. 79 of 2023 are quashed. CA No. 59 of 2023 is remitted to NCLT Bengaluru for fresh analytical determination on the merits of the amendment, and the question of maintainability in CA No. 79 of 2023 is directed to be decided afresh as a preliminary issue.
summary: Appellants M/s Apex Luminaires Pvt. Ltd. and its directors appealed against two orders dated 11.07.2025 of NCLT Bengaluru Bench in an oppression and mismanagement petition (CP No. 125/BB/2022) filed by G. N. Thirumalesh under Sections 241-244. The orders allowed the petitioner's amendment application (CA 59/2023) to introduce new prayers challenging share transfers and dismissed the appellants' maintainability objection (CA 79/2023) premised on the petitioner holding zero shares. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority passed unreasoned orders devoid of judicial application of mind, failing to test the amendment under Order VI Rule 17 or evaluate the petitioner's member status under Section 2(55). NCLAT quashed both orders and remitted the matters for fresh adjudication.

case_title: Narayan Maheshwari vs. Kavitha Surana & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Narayan Maheshwari, Promoter and Personal Guarantor of Corporate Debtor M/s Shri Veerganapathi Steels (P) Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Ms. Kavitha Surana, Liquidator; Respondent No. 2 is Bank of India, the sole Financial Creditor holding 100% voting share. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan and credit facilities extended by Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor, backed by promoter personal guarantees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt service resulted in Section 7 admission; during subsequent liquidation, an OTS proposal was sanctioned on 13.09.2022 for Rs. 1,44,40,000/-, satisfied via advance payment of Rs. 17 lakhs on 13.09.2022 and final balance of Rs. 1,27,40,000/- on 15.09.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition CP/229(IB)/2018 admitted on 26.04.2018; liquidation application MA/308/2019 filed upon failure to obtain a resolution plan; liquidation ordered on 19.07.2023; OTS executed on 13.09.2022; Liquidator refused Form FA on 01.11.2022; Appellant filed IA(IBC)/193(CHE)/2023 seeking withdrawal. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank of India OTS approval letter dated 13.09.2022, deposit challans totaling Rs. 1,44,40,000/-, 'No Due Certificate' issued by Respondent No. 2, and email correspondence dated 15.09.2022, 20.09.2022, and 28.09.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA(IBC)/193(CHE)/2023 in CP/229(IB)/2018 seeking directions to permit filing of a withdrawal application under Section 12A during liquidation; NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed the application, holding that Section 12A cannot be invoked post liquidation order.
legal_issues: Whether the provisions of Section 12A of the IBC, located within Chapter II governing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, can be borrowed, extended, or applied to liquidation proceedings under Chapter III to allow withdrawal of an admitted insolvency petition following a post-liquidation One Time Settlement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory withdrawal mechanisms specifically confined by the legislature to corporate insolvency resolution proceedings cannot be extended, borrowed, or applied by exercising inherent powers once a corporate debtor has crossed into statutory liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A was consciously inserted by the legislature into Chapter II of Part II of the IBC, which strictly and exclusively governs CIRP. Upon the passing of a liquidation order under Section 33, the Committee of Creditors ceases to exist in its decision-making capacity, rendering the statutory 90% CoC voting approval requirement impossible to satisfy. Any post-liquidation compromise or arrangement is strictly governed by Regulation 2B of the Liquidation Process Regulations read with Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, to the exclusion of Section 12A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules or Section 60(5) IBC cannot be exercised in conflict with or to circumvent express statutory provisions, nor can they create procedural remedies consciously omitted by the legislature. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following the Three-Member Bench precedent in Asha Chopra vs. Hind Motors, Section 12A is wholly inapplicable at the liquidation stage, rendering the withdrawal application unmaintainable notwithstanding full remittance under an OTS.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 63/2024 is dismissed as devoid of merit. All pending interlocutory applications are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: Promoter and guarantor Narayan Maheshwari appealed an order of NCLT Chennai Bench dismissing his application to withdraw insolvency proceedings against Corporate Debtor M/s Shri Veerganapathi Steels (P) Ltd. under Section 12A IBC. After the corporate debtor was ordered into liquidation, the appellant entered into a One Time Settlement (OTS) with Bank of India (holding 100% voting rights) and paid the entire settled sum of Rs. 1.444 crores, obtaining a No Due Certificate. NCLAT held that Section 12A is strictly confined to Chapter II (CIRP) and cannot be borrowed or applied to Chapter III liquidation proceedings via inherent powers. Following the larger bench decision in Asha Chopra, NCLAT affirmed the dismissal.

case_title: Surinder Arora vs. Nilesh Sharma Resolution Professional Dream Procon Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Surinder Arora, a homebuyer/allottee; Respondent No. 1 is Nilesh Sharma, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Victory Ace Social Welfare Society, Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resale purchase by Appellant from original allottee Anoop Chaudhary of Apartment No. B2-601, Project Victory Ace, Sector 143, Noida, under Builder-Buyer Agreement dated 14.06.2014, transferred on 06.03.2018 with payments made to the CD until January 2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Purchase consideration and maintenance paid by homebuyer/predecessor as reflected in corporate debtor's CRM records and Information Memorandum; claim sought recognition in the resolution plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 06.09.2019; claims submission deadline was 29.10.2019; CoC approved resolution plan with 90.66% vote on 07.05.2021; Appellant submitted claim form via email on 09.06.2021 and speed post on 10.06.2021; RP rejected claim on 15.06.2021; IA No. 3044/2021 filed before NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Information Memorandum dated 17.06.2020 reflecting the unit at Serial No. 57 under list of allottees who had not submitted claims, builder-buyer agreement dated 14.06.2014, transfer letter dated 06.03.2018, and medical evidence of COVID-19 infection. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 3044/2021 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-III; the Adjudicating Authority dismissed the application on 11.08.2023 holding that claims filed after approval of the plan by the CoC cannot be admitted under the Puneet Kaur precedent.
legal_issues: Whether a bona fide homebuyer whose allotment and payments are duly reflected in the books of the Corporate Debtor and the Information Memorandum is barred from having their claim considered in the Resolution Plan merely because the claim was submitted after the Committee of Creditors approved the plan but prior to approval by the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The rights and claims of bona fide homebuyers whose allotments and payments are reflected in the records and Information Memorandum of a corporate debtor do not extinguish upon CoC approval of a resolution plan and must be accommodated via an addendum to the plan before final approval by the adjudicating authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: CIRP Regulation 12 timelines are directory regarding homebuyers whose details are recorded in the CD's records. In terms of Ghanashyam Mishra and Puneet Kaur, claim extinguishment takes place only upon approval of the Resolution Plan by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1), not upon CoC approval under Section 30(4). Under Regulation 36(2), the RP is mandated to include all known liabilities in the Information Memorandum for the Resolution Applicant to address. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The ruling in RPS Infrastructure (which penalizes commercial entities for lack of diligence) is inapplicable to individual homebuyers where the Corporate Debtor's own books and the Information Memorandum unequivocally acknowledge the unit and payments received. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Excluding recorded homebuyers and relegating them to non-claimants causes unfair and inequitable resolution; the RP must supply their details to the resolution applicant to submit an addendum for CoC consideration prior to final plan approval under Section 31.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The order dated 11.08.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi in IA No. 3044/2021 is set aside and the IA is allowed. The RP is directed to furnish the Appellant's details from the CD's records to the Resolution Applicant within one month, who shall prepare an addendum to the Resolution Plan within one month for CoC consideration, to be placed before the Adjudicating Authority within three months.
summary: Homebuyer Surinder Arora appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissing his application for admission of a belated claim for Apartment No. B2-601 in the 'Victory Ace' project of Corporate Debtor Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd. The Resolution Professional rejected the claim because it was submitted on 09.06.2021, after the Committee of Creditors had approved the Resolution Plan on 07.05.2021. NCLAT held that under Puneet Kaur and the Supreme Court ruling in Amit Nehra, homebuyers whose allotments and payments are duly reflected in the Corporate Debtor's books and Information Memorandum do not suffer claim extinguishment prior to plan approval by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31. NCLAT set aside the rejection and directed an addendum to the plan.

case_title: Deepika Bhugra Prasad, Liquidator of M/s Ess Dee Aluminium Ltd. vs. Lucky Holdings Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Deepika Bhugra Prasad, Liquidator of M/s Ess Dee Aluminium Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Lucky Holdings Private Limited, a prospective bidder/H1 auction purchaser. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern under Regulation 32A of the Liquidation Process Regulations pursuant to a sale notice dated 05.04.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent submitted the highest bid of Rs. 124.60 crores, requiring a 25% first instalment payment of Rs. 29.15 crores (after EMD adjustment) within 15 days, which the Respondent failed to pay. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent declared H1 bidder on 26.04.2022 with initial payment deadline of 11.05.2022; interim stay granted by NCLT on 09.05.2022 in IA 397/2022; stay vacated upon unconditional withdrawal of IA on 15.06.2022; Liquidator communicated vacation on 16.06.2022 and 23.06.2022; sale cancelled and EMD forfeited on 01.07.2022; Respondent filed IA No. 800/2022 in August 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of E-auction process document, sale notice clauses, bidder affidavit undertaking dated 13.04.2022, and email correspondence between Liquidator and Respondent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed IA No. 800/2022 filed by Respondent on 17.01.2023, directing refund of the forfeited Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of Rs. 2 crores by applying Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act; Liquidator challenged the order via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 186 of 2023.
legal_issues: Whether a liquidator is legally empowered under the statutory liquidation regulations and binding auction terms to cancel a sale and forfeit the earnest money deposit of a successful bidder who commits default in payment timelines, and whether Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act applies to such statutory forfeiture.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Forfeiture of an earnest money deposit in a public auction conducted under the IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations is a legitimate statutory and contractual remedy for default, and Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act has no application to such statutory forfeiture. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Schedule I read with the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, empowers the liquidator to stipulate strict payment timelines and forfeiture consequences for non-compliance. Bidders who participate voluntarily are bound by the terms of the process document and unequivocal undertakings given via affidavit. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an interim stay is vacated and remaining timelines communicated, a successful bidder's failure to deposit the balance consideration despite having clear notice and opportunities constitutes an unexcused default, rendering cancellation and forfeiture valid. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in applying Section 74 of the Contract Act and overlooking settled precedents; the Liquidator's forfeiture of the EMD was fully justified under statutory auction rules, warranting reversal of the refund order.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 17.01.2023 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in I.A. No. 800 of 2022 is set aside, upholding the Liquidator's action of cancelling the sale and forfeiting the Respondent's EMD. Pending IAs are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: Deepika Bhugra Prasad, Liquidator of Ess Dee Aluminium Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench directing the refund of a forfeited Rs. 2 crore Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) to Lucky Holdings Pvt. Ltd. The respondent had emerged as the H1 bidder in an e-auction for a going concern sale at Rs. 124.60 crores but failed to deposit the 25% first instalment within the stipulated timeline, even after an interim stay by NCLT was vacated. NCLT had ordered a refund by invoking Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act. NCLAT held, relying on Westcoast Infraprojects and subsequent precedents, that Section 74 does not apply to forfeiture under statutory liquidation auctions and that the respondent committed an unexcused default, making the forfeiture valid. The appeal was allowed.

case_title: Bank of Baroda vs. IDBI Bank Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bank of Baroda (Assenting Financial Creditor / Member of Monitoring Committee); Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Bank Limited (Dissenting Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Anish Niranjan Nanavaty (Monitoring Committee Member); Respondent No. 3 is Reliance Projects & Property Management Services Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 4 is Reliance Communications Infrastructure Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Reliance Communications Infrastructure Limited; approval of a resolution plan containing provisions for assigning the Reliance Bhutan Loan (RBL) worth Rs. 195 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor leading to CIRP commencement on 26.09.2019; resolution plan approved by CoC on 05.08.2021 with 67.97% vote share; approved by NCLT on 19.12.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved resolution plan on 05.08.2021; Bank of Baroda filed IA No. 127 of 2022 on 02.01.2022 for reallocation; NCLT directed CoC meeting on 17.10.2023; CoC passed reallocation resolution on 27.10.2023; NCLT approved resolution plan on 19.12.2023; IDBI Bank filed IA(IBC)/2708(MB)2025; NCLT allowed IDBI Bank's application on 10.10.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan provisions (Clauses 1.2.3, 1.2.13, 3.3.20), Form H compliance certificate with Note 10, CoC meeting minutes dated 27.10.2023, and NCLT plan approval order dated 19.12.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IDBI Bank filed IA(IBC)/2708(MB)2025 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-I challenging the CoC's 27.10.2023 reallocation decision; NCLT allowed the application on 10.10.2025, holding that the CoC could not modify the financial layout or assign the Reliance Bhutan Loan to dissenting financial creditors post-approval; Bank of Baroda filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1708 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has the jurisdiction, after approving a resolution plan under Section 30(4) of the IBC, to subsequently pass a resolution altering the financial layout and distribution mechanism—specifically reassigning the Reliance Bhutan Loan from assenting financial creditors to dissenting financial creditors—contrary to the terms of the approved resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved by the Committee of Creditors under Section 30(4) of the IBC, it becomes binding and irrevocable as between the CoC and the successful resolution applicant, and the CoC lacks any legal competence or jurisdiction to subsequently modify, tinker with, or alter its financial layout or distribution mechanism. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(4) requires the CoC to consider the manner of distribution prior to voting. Once finalized and submitted to the Adjudicating Authority, the distribution mechanism is immutable. Furthermore, Clause 3.3.20 of a resolution plan permitting assignment to 'such other entity' cannot be interpreted to include dissenting financial creditors who constitute a distinct statutory class. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The doctrine of commercial wisdom cannot be invoked to validate a post-approval modification of an already finalized resolution plan or distribution framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC's resolution dated 27.10.2023 attempting to reallocate the Reliance Bhutan Loan to dissenting financial creditors was illegal, unauthorized, and contrary to the approved resolution plan, justifying the Adjudicating Authority's decision to set it aside.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The order dated 10.10.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA(IBC)/2708(MB)2025 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Bank of Baroda, an assenting financial creditor, appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench-I allowing an application filed by dissenting financial creditor IDBI Bank Ltd. The NCLT had set aside a CoC resolution dated 27.10.2023 which attempted to reallocate the Rs. 195 crore Reliance Bhutan Loan (RBL)—originally assigned under the resolution plan to assenting financial creditors—to dissenting financial creditors. NCLAT held that once a resolution plan and its distribution mechanism are approved by the CoC under Section 30(4), the CoC cannot subsequently tinker with or modify the financial layout. NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's ruling and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mrs. Kandimalla Gowri Raja Rajeswari & Anr. vs. Geetha Cotton Mills Pvt. Ltd. & 22 Ors. (and connected appeal)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 83/2025 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 86/2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mrs. Kandimalla Gowri Raja Rajeswari & Anr.; Respondents are Geetha Cotton Mills Pvt. Ltd. & 22 Ors. in CA 83/2025, and Green Thumb Agro Pvt. Ltd. & 8 Ors. in CA 86/2025. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate management and oppression disputes arising out of company petitions filed under Sections 59, 241, 242, and 244 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dismissal of company petitions CP No. 179/241/AMR/2019 and CP No. 180/241/AMR/2019 by NCLT on 04.12.2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 04.12.2024; appeals filed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, accompanied by refiling delay condonation applications IA Nos. 796/2025 and 809/2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pleadings and memorandum of terms from related proceedings in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 26/2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CA No. 83/2025 and CA No. 86/2025; during hearings, counsel for all parties made a unanimous statement expressing willingness to resolve their disputes through mediation by a retired High Court judge, similar to an order passed in CA (AT) (CH) No. 26/2025.
legal_issues: Whether company appeals challenging the dismissal of oppression and mismanagement petitions under the Companies Act, 2013 can be disposed of by referring the parties to formal mediation before a designated retired High Court judge.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where parties to corporate management disputes express mutual willingness and unanimity to resolve their controversies through mediation, appellate tribunals can refer the matter to a designated mediator while preserving the parties' statutory rights to judicial remedies if mediation fails. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Section 89 of the CPC and the Companies (Mediation and Conciliation) Rules, 2016, empowers the appellate tribunal to facilitate structured mediation and conciliation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consent of all contesting parties to appoint a specific former judge of a High Court as mediator satisfies the procedural requirements for an amicable settlement framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The company appeals are disposed of by referring the underlying disputes to mediation under the supervision of Hon'ble Justice Mr. M. Satyanarayana Murthy, former judge of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh, with specific financial and procedural directions.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 83/2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 86/2025 are disposed of in terms of the order referring the parties to mediation before Hon'ble Justice Mr. M. Satyanarayana Murthy. Remuneration is fixed at Rs. 1,00,000/- per sitting to be borne equally (50% each), with sittings to be held in Guntur or Hyderabad, and parties directed to appear on 21.12.2025. Liberty is reserved for parties to pursue legal remedies if mediation fails.
summary: Appellants Kandimalla Gowri Raja Rajeswari and Anr. filed two company appeals under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, challenging an order dated 04.12.2024 passed by NCLT dismissing their oppression and mismanagement petitions. During the proceedings, both parties made a unanimous submission agreeing to resolve their disputes through mediation. NCLAT disposed of both appeals by referring the matter to mediation under the supervision of Hon'ble Justice Mr. M. Satyanarayana Murthy, former judge of the Andhra Pradesh High Court, prescribing terms regarding remuneration, sittings, and procedural rules under the Companies (Mediation and Conciliation) Rules, 2016, while keeping judicial remedies open if mediation fails.

case_title: Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes vs. Mr. Mukesh Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1665 of 2024 & I.A. No. 6083 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes (Audit)-3.3, Bangalore; Respondent No. 1 is Mukesh Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Telexcell Information Systems Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Respondent No. 3 is M/s Frans Global Infotech Pvt Ltd., Successful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Outstanding statutory tax dues under the Central Sales Tax (CST) Act for assessment years 2005-06 to 2010-11 and 2013-14. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed statutory dues of Rs. 35,55,420/- (comprising tax of Rs. 12,03,330/-, penalty of Rs. 22,42,558/-, and interest of Rs. 1,09,532/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 05.10.2021; public announcement made on 07.10.2021 with deadline 19.10.2021 (extendable to 03.01.2022); Appellant filed claim on 24.01.2022 (delay of 21 days); CoC approved resolution plan on 15.11.2022; NCLT approved resolution plan on 30.05.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Ex-parte assessment orders, claim submission dated 24.01.2022, and Clause 8.3.3 of the Resolution Plan regarding government dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA (IBC) No. 175/ND/2023 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-III seeking condonation of a 21-day delay in filing its claim; NCLT dismissed the IA on 02.07.2024; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1665 of 2024.
legal_issues: Whether a 21-day delay in filing a statutory tax claim before the Resolution Professional can be condoned, and whether the claim can be settled based on a mutual consensus reached between the statutory tax authority and the Successful Resolution Applicant during appellate proceedings in accordance with the resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where parties reach a mutual consensus during appellate proceedings regarding the settlement of a belated statutory claim in accordance with the provisions of an approved resolution plan, the appeal can be disposed of in terms of such agreed settlement to achieve a pragmatic resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) read with Section 31 of the IBC governs the treatment of government dues in a resolution plan. When a resolution plan provides for a fixed percentage payout for government dues, late-filed claims admitted by consent adjust proportionately within the plan's framework. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A minor procedural delay of 21 days by a public tax authority, when mutually agreed to be resolved based on the financial parameters of the resolution plan, warrants a practical disposal rather than strict technical extinguishment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In view of the mutual consensus arrived at between the Appellant and the Successful Resolution Applicant during the hearing—whereby the SRA agreed to pay 0.5% of the claimed amount (Rs. 17,777/-) as per Clause 8.3.3 of the Plan—the appeal is disposed of accordingly.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of in terms of the mutual consensus between the parties. The Successful Resolution Applicant is directed to pay Rs. 17,777/- to the Appellant within 15 days. No order as to costs. Pending IAs are closed.
summary: The Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Bangalore, appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissing its application for condonation of a 21-day delay in filing a claim of Rs. 35,55,420/- against Corporate Debtor M/s Telexcell Information Systems Ltd. During the hearing before NCLAT, the Successful Resolution Applicant agreed to pay 0.5% of the claimed amount, amounting to Rs. 17,777/-, towards full and final settlement in terms of Clause 8.3.3 of the approved resolution plan, and the appellant consented to this proposal. NCLAT disposed of the appeal directing the SRA to make the payment within 15 days.

case_title: Kaajal Aijaz Ilmi vs. Ram Kumar, Administrator of AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kaajal Aijaz Ilmi, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Ram Kumar, Administrator / Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial service provider insolvency proceedings initiated against AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd. after RBI superseded its Board of Directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial service provider default resulting in RBI supersession under Section 45-IE(1) of the RBI Act, 1934 on 27.01.2025, and CIRP initiation under Section 227 IBC on 20.02.2025. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI notification issued on 27.01.2025; CIRP initiated on 20.02.2025; Administrator issued public announcement and Form-G for Expression of Interest; Appellant filed IA No. 5599/2025; NCLT rejected the IA on 18.11.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RBI supersession notification dated 27.01.2025, NCLT admission order dated 20.02.2025, and Form-G publication. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. No. 5599/2025 before NCLT New Delhi (Court V) seeking copies of resolution plans submitted by Prospective Resolution Applicants; NCLT rejected the application on 18.11.2025 relying on the Supreme Court judgment in Piramal Capital; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1879 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether suspended directors of a financial service provider whose board of directors was superseded by the Reserve Bank of India prior to the commencement of CIRP have the right to attend meetings of the Committee of Creditors and obtain copies of resolution plans submitted by prospective resolution applicants.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the Reserve Bank of India supersedes the board of directors of a financial service provider under the RBI Act, the erstwhile directors are deemed to have vacated their offices, and they have no right to attend meetings of the Committee of Creditors, participate in CIRP proceedings, or obtain copies of resolution plans during the pendency of the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 227 read with FSP Rules, 2019, governs financial service provider insolvencies. Supersession under Section 45-IE(1) of the RBI Act terminates directorship ab initio prior to CIRP commencement, distinguishing such ex-directors from standard suspended directors under Section 24 IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of a specific statutory right under the IBC or FSP Rules, members of a superseded board cannot claim documents during CIRP; they are only entitled to a certified copy of the approved resolution plan after NCLT approval under Section 31 makes it a public document under Section 74 of the Evidence Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following the Supreme Court's binding pronouncement in Piramal Capital and Housing Finance Ltd., the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the suspended director's application for copies of resolution plans.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The order dated 18.11.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi in I.A. No. 5599/2025 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Kaajal Aijaz Ilmi, a suspended director of Corporate Debtor AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi (Court V) rejecting her application (I.A. No. 5599/2025) for copies of resolution plans submitted by Prospective Resolution Applicants. The RBI had superseded the company's board of directors on 27.01.2025 before initiating CIRP under Section 227 IBC on 20.02.2025. NCLAT held, in light of the Supreme Court's ruling in Piramal Capital and Housing Finance Ltd., that supersession by the RBI causes directors to vacate their offices, disentitling them from attending CoC meetings or obtaining resolution plans during CIRP. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Ajay Kumar Bhuwalka & Anr. vs. M/s Bhuwalka Steel Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Ajay Kumar Bhuwalka and Ankit Kumar Bhuwalka, nominal directors/shareholders of Corporate Debtor M/s Bhuwalka Steel Industries Private Limited; Respondent is M/s Bhuwalka Steel Industries Ltd., represented by Resolution Professional Shivadutt Bannanje. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process of Bhuwalka Steel Industries Pvt. Ltd. and avoidance/fraudulent trading proceedings against promoters and nominal directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Resolution Professional filed IA No. 122/2022 seeking contributions of Rs. 154.55 crores under Section 66, Rs. 1.49 crores under Section 44, and a fine of Rs. 1 crore under Section 69 of the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 08.04.2019; IA No. 133/2020 filed under Section 66 disposed of as premature on 10.03.2021 with liberty to revive or file fresh application; IA No. 248/2021 disposed of on 22.02.2022 directing RP to comply within 30 days; IA No. 122/2022 filed on 18.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT orders dated 10.03.2021 and 22.02.2022 granting liberty, forensic audit report, and transaction avoidance filings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants challenged NCLT Chennai Bench order dated 09.07.2025 passed in IA No. 122/2022 which rejected their preliminary objection regarding limitation and held that the avoidance application was maintainable and not time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether an application filed by a Resolution Professional under Sections 43, 44, 66, and 69 of the IBC pursuant to liberty granted by the Adjudicating Authority is barred by limitation, and whether a formal separate application for condonation of delay is mandatory under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Delay can be condoned irrespective of whether there is any formal application, provided there are sufficient materials on record disclosing sufficient cause. Furthermore, an application filed pursuant to express liberty granted by the Adjudicating Authority to revive or file a fresh petition gives rise to a fresh cause of action and is protected by applicable limitation exclusions (such as Supreme Court suo motu COVID-19 orders). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 35A timelines are directory in nature. Avoidance and fraudulent trading applications filed within the framework of liberty granted by prior judicial orders are maintainable and not barred by limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Omission to refer to the correct statutory section or absence of a formal condonation application does not vitiate proceedings when sufficient cause is apparent on record, as established in Sesh Nath Singh. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly held that IA No. 122/2022 was not barred by limitation and was protected by judicial orders and COVID-19 limitation exclusions, rendering the appeal devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 508/2025 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 09.07.2025 holding the application not barred by limitation is affirmed without expressing any opinion on the merits of IA No. 122/2022.
summary: Nominal directors Ajay Kumar Bhuwalka and Ankit Kumar Bhuwalka appealed an order of NCLT Chennai Bench dated 09.07.2025 passed in IA No. 122/2022, which rejected their preliminary objection regarding limitation. The Resolution Professional had filed IA No. 122/2022 under Sections 43, 44, 66, and 69 IBC seeking massive contributions from the directors, pursuant to liberty granted in earlier NCLT orders. NCLAT held, citing Sesh Nath Singh and Supreme Court COVID-19 exclusion orders, that a formal condonation application is not mandatory and that the application was well within extended limitation periods. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Accurate Transheat Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sufi International Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Accurate Transheat Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent is Sufi International Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods by the Appellant to the Respondent under a purchase order during the financial year 2020-2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed unpaid operational debt of Rs. 2,08,68,294/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued on 24.04.2023; Respondent replied denying the claim on 29.05.2023; Information utility (NeSL) filing and authentication completed on 21-10-2023 showing the debt status as 'Disputed'. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NeSL certificate containing Part-B history showing 'Disputed' status with reasons 'No such debt existed. False information & wrong claim. We have already got stay order from honourable high court, Gujarat', and pending criminal complaints under Section 138 of the NI Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed a Section 9 application before NCLT Ahmedabad (Court-2); the Adjudicating Authority rejected the application on 21.07.2025; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1373 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is mandated under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC to reject an application for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process by an operational creditor when there is a record of dispute reflecting in the information utility.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority must reject a Section 9 application if a notice of dispute has been received by the operational creditor or if there is a record of dispute in the information utility. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) provides independent and alternative grounds for rejection: either the receipt of a notice of dispute or the existence of a record of dispute in the information utility (NeSL). When a corporate debtor explicitly registers a dispute upon authentication in the information utility, the statutory condition for rejection is fully satisfied. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: So long as a dispute truly exists in fact and is captured in the information utility records, the Adjudicating Authority cannot entertain a Section 9 application or examine complex contractual disputes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the NeSL record explicitly reflected a pre-existing and authenticated dispute regarding the existence of the debt, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The dismissal of the Section 9 application shall not preclude the Appellant from pursuing other legal remedies available under law.
summary: Accurate Transheat Pvt. Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against Sufi International Pvt. Ltd. for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 2,08,68,294/-. The corporate debtor had disputed the debt upon authentication in the National E-Governance Services Limited (NeSL) information utility and replied to the demand notice citing pending Section 138 proceedings and high court matters. NCLAT held, in accordance with Section 9(5)(ii)(d) and the Supreme Court's ruling in Mobilox Innovations, that a recorded dispute in the information utility mandates the rejection of a Section 9 application. The appeal was dismissed with liberty to pursue other remedies.

case_title: Neeta Saha & Ors. vs. Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 61 of 2025 (with Nos. 649 & 399 of 2025)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Neeta Saha, Aniel Kuumar Saha, and Aunirban Saha (Personal Guarantors of Corporate Debtor M/s Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent is Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Assignee of ECL Finance Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facility of Rs. 90 crores extended by ECL Finance Ltd. to M/s Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd., secured by irrevocable corporate and personal guarantees executed on 22.09.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by principal borrower resulting in default notices on 02.04.2019 and 26.09.2019; personal guarantees invoked on 14.03.2022 for Rs. 189,44,24,774/-; Form-B demand notice issued on 17.11.2022 for Rs. 229,61,30,615/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against corporate debtor commenced on 28.02.2020; loan recall notice issued on 23.03.2020; assignment agreement executed on 27.03.2020; personal guarantee invoked on 14.03.2022; Section 95 applications filed on 02.01.2023; RP report filed on 15.10.2024; NCLT admitted Section 95 applications on 07.01.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantee agreements dated 22.09.2017, default notices, invocation letter dated 14.03.2022, Form-B demand notice, and RP report under Section 99. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) admitted Section 95 applications and initiated personal insolvency resolution process against the Appellants vide common order dated 07.01.2025; Appellants challenged the order through Company Appeals No. 61, 649, and 399 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether initiation of CIRP and moratorium under Section 14 against a principal borrower bars a financial creditor from invoking personal guarantees and filing Section 95 applications against personal guarantors, whether Section 10A bars personal guarantor proceedings for defaults occurring during the 10A period, and whether the quantum of debt claimed can invalidate Section 95 admission when debt exceeds the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 crore.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC applicable to a corporate debtor does not bar a financial creditor from invoking personal guarantees or initiating personal insolvency resolution process under Section 95 against personal guarantors. Furthermore, Section 10A does not apply to proceedings against personal guarantors under Part III of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A is restricted by its terms to Chapter II of Part I (corporate debtors) and was not extended by the legislature to Chapter III of Part III governing individual and personal guarantor insolvencies. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Minor discrepancies or ongoing litigation regarding exact debt quantum do not invalidate a Section 95 application as long as the undisputed default exceeds the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 crore; exact calculations can be addressed during the repayment plan stage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 95 applications were validly filed and processed, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting them upon recommendation by the Resolution Professional.
operative_order: Company Appeals No. 61, 649, and 399 of 2025 are dismissed. The common order dated 07.01.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi in IB-78/ND/2023, IB-79/ND/2023, and IB-82/ND/2023 admitting Section 95 applications is affirmed.
summary: Personal guarantors Neeta Saha, Aniel Kuumar Saha, and Aunirban Saha appealed a common order of NCLT New Delhi admitting Section 95 IBC applications filed by Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd. The appellants argued that the loan recall notice was hit by Section 14 moratorium, that default dates during the COVID-19 period attracted Section 10A bar, and that the claimed debt was inflated. NCLAT held, following Amit Jain, that Section 10A does not apply to personal guarantors under Part III, that Section 14 moratorium does not bar personal guarantee invocation, and that debt exceeding Rs. 1 crore justifies admission, leaving exact calculations for the repayment plan stage. The appeals were dismissed.

case_title: FTI Consulting India Private Limited vs. MGF Developments Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is FTI Consulting India Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent is MGF Developments Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Service agreement dated 26.02.2020 and addendum dated 05.10.2020 whereby the Appellant agreed to provide independent expert services in relation to an arbitration case pending before ICC, London, concerning claims against Emaar MGF Land Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of USD 367,353.29/- (equivalent to Rs. 3,00,94,571/-) arising from four unpaid invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mr. Montek Mayal, primary contact and expert witness for the Appellant, left employment on 14.01.2022; invoices issued between May 2022 and February 2023; Respondent entered into a new agreement with Mr. Mayal via Osborne Partners on 01.06.2023; Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 15.07.2024; Respondent replied with notice of dispute on 25.07.2024; Section 9 application filed on 10.01.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Service agreement dated 26.02.2020, addendum dated 05.10.2020, unpaid invoices, email exchanges, Osborne Partners agreement dated 01.06.2023, and payment details of Rs. 3.88 crores to FTI and Rs. 2.07 crores to Osborne Partners. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court-III) rejected the Section 9 application vide order dated 31.10.2025, holding the dispute to be purely commercial and contractual, and imposed costs of Rs. 25,000/-; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1971 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether a reply to a demand notice raising bona fide contractual disputes regarding the frustration of an expert service agreement following the exit of key personnel and ongoing parallel engagements through another entity constitutes a valid notice of dispute under Section 8(2) of the IBC to warrant dismissal of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor can only trigger the CIRP when there is an undisputed debt and default; if the debt is genuinely disputed under Section 8(2) on plausible contractual grounds requiring investigation, the Section 9 application must be dismissed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates the rejection of a Section 9 application if a notice of dispute has been received by the operational creditor raising plausible contentions that are not patently feeble. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an expert service agreement is premised on specific key personnel (Mr. Montek Mayal) whose departure frustrates the original contract and leads to subsequent direct engagements via another entity (Osborne Partners) alongside substantial payments already made, a genuine pre-existing contractual dispute exists. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Respondent's reply to the demand notice served as a valid notice of dispute raising plausible contentions regarding contractual performance and frustration, justifying the dismissal of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The order dated 31.10.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi in C.P. (IB)-60(ND)/2025 rejecting the Section 9 application is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: FTI Consulting India Pvt. Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against MGF Developments Ltd. for unpaid expert advisory invoices amounting to USD 367,353.29. The corporate debtor defended non-payment by stating that the expert witness (Mr. Montek Mayal) left FTI's employment, rendering the contract frustrated, and that services were subsequently procured directly from Mr. Mayal through Osborne Partners after substantial payments exceeding Rs. 3.88 crores had already been made to FTI. NCLAT held that the corporate debtor's reply to the demand notice raised a valid pre-existing contractual dispute supported by evidence, making the dispute non-frivolous. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Surender Modi & Anr. vs. Mr. Ashish Singh, Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mr. Surender Modi and Primex Estates Private Limited (related parties / former management); Respondent No. 1 is Ashish Singh, Resolution Professional of Vibrant Buildwell Private Limited; Respondent No. 2 is Bishwanath Traders and Investment Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claimed financial debt arising from alleged loan agreements dated 20.12.2007 (for Rs. 30,95,000/- and Rs. 5,10,000/-) advanced to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal and interest totaling Rs. 1,09,33,020/- (Surender Modi) and Rs. 9,43,54,070/- (Primex Estates Pvt. Ltd.). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP on 22.02.2022; public announcement on 24.02.2022; claims submitted on 27.05.2022; rejected by RP on 06.06.2022 and 13.02.2023; IA Nos. 3020 of 2022 and 1950 of 2023 filed by Appellants; NCLT dismissed both IAs on 23.09.2025; resolution plan approved on 04.11.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, addendums with conflicting dates, audited balance sheets for FY 2016-17 classifying amounts under 'Other Advances / Other Long Term Liabilities' rather than long-term borrowings, absence of TDS deductions, and 15 years of uninterrupted silence without demand or interest accrual. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV dismissed IA Nos. 3020 of 2022 and 1950 of 2023 vide orders dated 23.09.2025, rejecting the Appellants' claims; Appellants filed Company Appeals No. 1734 and 1735 of 2025 pursuant to directions of the Supreme Court.
legal_issues: Whether claims submitted by related parties based on 15-year-old loan agreements reflecting suspicious date discrepancies, classified in corporate books as 'Other Advances' rather than borrowings, and unsupported by any demand or interest provisioning over 15 years qualify as genuine financial debt entitled to admission in CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority and Resolution Professional are fully empowered to scrutinize supporting documents to verify the authenticity, accuracy, and tenability of a claim. A claim based on an antedated or fabricated loan agreement, treated as an 'advance' rather than a borrowing in balance sheets, and characterized by 15 years of un-protested silence without demand or interest accrual lacks bona fides and can be lawfully rejected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) of the IBC requires a transaction to have the commercial effect of borrowing. Entries classified under 'Other Long-Term Liabilities' as 'Other Advances' do not partake the character of financial debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contradictory dates on loan agreements (stamped in December 2007, executed in August 2007, disbursal in June 2007), absence of vendor stamp verification, lack of board resolutions, and 15 years of masterly inactivity establish that the claim is an afterthought. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly evaluated the evidence and concluded that the claims were unverified, non-bona fide, and rightly rejected by the Resolution Professional.
operative_order: Company Appeals No. 1734 and 1735 of 2025 are dismissed. The impugned orders dated 23.09.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi in IA Nos. 3020 of 2022 and 1950 of 2023 are affirmed. No costs.
summary: Surender Modi and Primex Estates Pvt. Ltd. appealed orders of NCLT New Delhi dismissing their applications against the rejection of their financial debt claims by the Resolution Professional of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. The claims were based on 2007 loan agreements for Rs. 5.10 lakhs and Rs. 30.95 lakhs along with exorbitant interest. NCLAT held that although the claims were not barred by limitation pursuant to Supreme Court Suo Motu orders, the underlying loan agreements bore glaring date discrepancies and interpolations, the amounts were classified in corporate balance sheets as 'Other Advances' rather than borrowings, and no demands or interest provisions were made for 15 years, establishing that the claims were non-bona fide afterthoughts. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: M/s. Petrofuel (T) Limited vs. M/s. Progressive Constructions Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Petrofuel (T) Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent is M/s. Progressive Constructions Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proceedings under Section 9 of the IBC, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt and default forming the subject matter of the Section 9 petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 04.08.2025; order copy supplied/made available to Appellant on 11.08.2025; Company Appeal e-filed on 06.10.2025 (55 days from receipt of order). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-filing records showing date of order, date of receipt, and date of appeal presentation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed a restoration application seeking recall of the order dismissing the company petition, which was rejected on merits and maintainability on 04.08.2025; Appellant simultaneously invoked Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, and Section 61 of the IBC to challenge the order before NCLAT Chennai.
legal_issues: Whether a company appeal filed 55 days after receipt of the impugned order is maintainable under Section 61(2) of the IBC, given the statutory period of limitation and the maximum condonable period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The general law of limitation does not apply where limitation is self-contained under a special statute like the IBC. The appellate tribunal cannot exercise powers to condone delay beyond the 15-day condonable period provided under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) prescribes an upper limit of 45 days (30 days limitation plus a maximum condonable period of 15 days) for filing an appeal, and any filing beyond this period is barred by a statutory embargo. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Counting from the date of receipt of the order copy (11.08.2025), an appeal filed on 06.10.2025 (55 days later) exceeds the 45-day statutory limit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the company appeal is barred by limitation and falls outside the condonable period, it is liable to be dismissed.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed as barred by limitation.
summary: M/s Petrofuel (T) Limited appealed against an order dated 04.08.2025 rejecting its restoration application in a Section 9 IBC proceeding, simultaneously citing Section 421 of the Companies Act and Section 61 of the IBC. NCLAT Chennai noted that the appeal was e-filed on 06.10.2025, which was 55 days after the order was made available on 11.08.2025. Holding that the delay exceeded the maximum condonable period of 15 days beyond the 30-day statutory limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC, NCLAT dismissed the appeal on the ground of limitation.

case_title: Jitender Kumar Jain (Liquidator of Aaj Ka Anand Papers Ltd.) vs. Aaj Ka Anand Publications LLP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jitender Kumar Jain, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Aaj Ka Anand Papers Limited; Respondents are Aaj Ka Anand Publications LLP & Ors. (Contemnors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of Aaj Ka Anand Papers Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Publication of a series of articles against the liquidator in a newspaper in August 2023 creating alleged obstruction in the liquidation process. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Articles published in August 2023; Contempt Application No. 16 of 2023 filed under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLT order passed on 18.09.2025 rejecting the contempt application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Newspaper articles published in August 2023 and Civil Suit No. 191 of 2024 filed by the Appellant in the Delhi High Court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Contempt Application No. 16 of 2023 before NCLT Mumbai Bench (Court Room No. 1); NCLT rejected the application on 18.09.2025, holding no case for civil contempt was made out; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1911 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting a contempt application filed under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, concerning newspaper publications, when a civil suit on the same matter is pending before the High Court and considerable time has elapsed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Although the Adjudicating Authority possesses powers under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, while exercising jurisdiction under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, it is not bound to initiate contempt proceedings for past publication issues, particularly when alternative civil remedies are already being pursued in a High Court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, empowers the Tribunal to punish for contempt, but its invocation is discretionary and dependent on the factual context of ongoing proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where more than two years have elapsed since the alleged newspaper publication in August 2023 and a civil suit (CS No. 191 of 2024) is already pending in the Delhi High Court, further contempt proceedings before the NCLT are unwarranted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No further proceedings were required with respect to the August 2023 publications, and the contempt application was rightly not entertained, subject to clarifying that observations would not affect the pending High Court suit.
operative_order: The appeal proceedings are closed, with a clarification that any observations made in the order shall have no effect on the pending proceedings initiated by the Appellant in the Delhi High Court.
summary: Jitender Kumar Jain, liquidator of Aaj Ka Anand Papers Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai dismissing his Contempt Application No. 16 of 2023 filed under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, against newspaper publications made in August 2023. NCLAT noted that the appellant had already filed a civil suit (CS No. 191 of 2024) in the Delhi High Court regarding the same articles. NCLAT held that given the lapse of over two years and the pending High Court suit, no further contempt proceedings were warranted before the NCLT, and closed the appeal with a clarification preserving the High Court proceedings.

case_title: Balsam Properties Private Limited & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies, Pune
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Balsam Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.; Respondent is Registrar of Companies, Pune. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company appeal challenging an order passed by the National Company Law Tribunal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Delay of 102 days in filing the company appeal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 17.03.2025 (or 17.05.2025); appeal filed on 12.08.2025; order uploaded on 01.07.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT record and attendance notes showing counsel presence. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA No. 6757 of 2025 seeking condonation of a 102-day delay, arguing that limitation commenced from the date of uploading (01.07.2025) rather than pronouncement, relying on Sanjay Pandurang Kalate v. Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd.; NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the condonation application and the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether limitation for filing a company appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, commences from the date of uploading when the appellant's counsel's attendance is recorded in the impugned order, and whether the tribunal has the power to condone a delay exceeding the statutory condonable period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the record of the Tribunal indicates that counsel was present and the order was pronounced, limitation commences from the date of pronouncement/knowledge, and the principle that limitation starts from the date of uploading applies only when no order was pronounced in open court. There exists a presumption of correctness regarding judicial records. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, prescribes a strict limitation period of 45 days extendable by a further period of 45 days (45 + 45 days). An application for condonation of delay beyond the statutory limit cannot be entertained per the law settled in Bengal Chemists and Druggists Association v. Kalyan Chowdhury. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Because the impugned order recorded the attendance of the appellant's counsel, the contention that the order was not pronounced in open court is contrary to the judicial record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is barred by limitation as the delay of 102 days exceeds the maximum permissible condonable period under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013.
operative_order: The application for condonation of delay (IA No. 6757 of 2025) is dismissed, and consequently Company Appeal (AT) No. 282 of 2025 stands dismissed per law settled in Bengal Chemists. Pending IAs No. 6755 and 6756 of 2025 are disposed of.
summary: Balsam Properties Pvt. Ltd. filed an appeal against an NCLT order dated 17.03.2025 (referred to also as 17.05.2025) with an application for condonation of a 102-day delay, claiming limitation started from the uploading date of 01.07.2025 under Sanjay Pandurang Kalate. NCLAT Principal Bench noted that the impugned order recorded the attendance of the appellant's counsel, establishing that the order was pronounced in open court. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Bengal Chemists and Druggists Association v.
