Kalyan Chowdhury, NCLAT held that the delay exceeded the maximum condonable limit under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Vinod Anand vs. M/s Golden Rolls Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vinod Anand (Financial Creditor / Promoter); Respondent is Golden Rolls Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan of Rs. 2,28,87,885/- extended by the Financial Creditor (promoter) to the Corporate Debtor over a period of time carrying 9% compounded annual interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of the loan extended by the promoter. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP-109(ND)/2023 filed under Section 241/242; IB-125(ND)/2024 filed under Section 7 of the IBC; NCLT dismissed the Section 7 application on 09.10.2025 solely based on the dismissal of the Section 241/242 petition. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 7 application pleadings, loan terms, and NCLT order dated 09.10.2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Section 7 petition (IB-125(ND)/2024) summarily without adjudication by merely citing the dismissal of the oppression and mismanagement petition (CP-109(ND)/2023); Appellant filed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1898 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject an application under Section 7 of the IBC summarily without evaluating its pleadings and merits, merely because a petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, filed by the same financial creditor was dismissed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority is statutorily bound to examine the pleadings, records, and merits of an application filed under Section 7 of the IBC and cannot dismiss it summarily on the sole ground that a separate company petition under Section 241/242 of the Companies Act has been dismissed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC provides an independent and summary remedy for financial creditors upon proof of debt and default, which must be adjudicated on its own merits in accordance with law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An order dismissing a Section 7 application solely by referencing a parallel oppression and mismanagement petition without adverting to Section 7 pleadings is legally unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority failed to consider the Section 7 application, necessitating the setting aside of the impugned order and the revival of the petition for fresh consideration.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of. The impugned order dated 09.10.2025 is set aside. CP (IB) No. 125 of 2024 is revived before the Adjudicating Authority to be heard afresh in accordance with law.
summary: Vinod Anand appealed an order of NCLT dated 09.10.2025 dismissing his Section 7 IBC application (IB-125(ND)/2024) against Golden Rolls Pvt. Ltd. for default on a loan of Rs. 2,28,87,885/-. The NCLT had rejected the Section 7 petition solely because it dismissed a parallel petition filed by the appellant under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority failed to examine the Section 7 application on its own merits. NCLAT set aside the impugned order and revived the Section 7 petition for fresh adjudication in accordance with law.

case_title: Yashdeep Trexim Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Prithvi Devcons Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Yashdeep Trexim Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.; Respondents are Prithvi Devcons Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate petition CP/137(KB)/2025 filed before NCLT Kolkata Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of oppression and mismanagement / corporate disputes. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company petition reserved for ad-interim orders on 02.09.2025; impugned order passed on 24.09.2025 dismissing the petition. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pleadings, cause list, and earlier petitions pending before a collateral/coordinate bench of NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed CP/137(KB)/2025 as infructuous under Section 10 of the CPC on the ground that similar allegations and prayers were sub judice before a collateral bench (Court II); Appellants filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 297 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether Section 10 of the Civil Procedure Code empowers an adjudicating authority (NCLT) to dismiss a company petition on the ground that a previously instituted petition involving similar issues is pending before a coordinate bench.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 10 of the CPC does not contemplate the dismissal of a suit or petition; rather, it mandates that a court shall stay proceedings or not proceed with the trial of a lis when the matter in issue is directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties. Its purpose is to prevent conflicting judgments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10 CPC is a procedural provision for staying trials, not a substantive ground for terminating or dismissing proceedings ab initio. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Dismissing a petition outright under Section 10 CPC instead of staying the trial or considering clubbing is a procedural error. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in dismissing the company petition under Section 10 CPC, requiring the impugned order to be set aside and the matter remitted for examination under proper legal principles or clubbing.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of. The impugned order dated 24.09.2025 is set aside. NCLT is requested to look into the facts of both petitions and proceed in accordance with law per Section 10 CPC ingredients, noting that parties are free to file an application for clubbing of petitions. Pending applications are disposed of.
summary: Yashdeep Trexim Pvt. Ltd. and Anr. appealed against an NCLT order dated 24.09.2025 passed in CP/137(KB)/2025, which dismissed their company petition under Section 10 of the CPC because similar allegations were pending before a collateral bench. NCLAT held that Section 10 of the CPC only empowers a court to stay the trial of a subsequent suit/petition to avoid conflicting judgments, not to dismiss it outright. NCLAT set aside the impugned order and remitted the matter back to the NCLT to proceed in accordance with law or consider clubbing the petitions.

case_title: M/s Singhal Matta & Co. (Chartered Accountants) vs. Track Infoline Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Singhal Matta & Co., Chartered Accountants (Auditor); Respondents are Track Infoline Private Limited & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appointment and rendering of audit and management services by a chartered accountant firm to Respondent No. 1 company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Violation of statutory restrictions under Section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013, by providing prohibited management services alongside auditing services, and tampering with financial records and balance sheets. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed impugned order on 09.05.2025; appeal filed with a 3-day delay; IA No. 5377/2025 filed for condonation of delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 showing management fees charged by the auditor, board resolution dated 31.05.2022, and certificate dated 25.10.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi passed an order on 09.05.2025 removing M/s Singhal Matta & Co. as auditor of Respondent No. 1 company; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 214 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether an auditor appointed under the Companies Act, 2013, can render management services in violation of Section 144, and whether such violation warrants the auditor's removal by the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An auditor appointed under the Companies Act, 2013, is statutorily prohibited by Section 144 from rendering certain non-audit services, including management services, directly or indirectly. Charging management fees alongside audit fees constitutes a clear statutory violation, justifying the auditor's removal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 144 explicitly restricts an auditor from providing specified non-audit services such as internal audit, management services, and accounting. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balance sheets duly audited and signed by the appellant firm for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 explicitly depicted that the appellant had charged management fees during those years, proving a direct breach of Section 144(h). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error in removing the auditor upon finding conclusive documentary proof of statutory violations under Section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013.
operative_order: IA Nos. 5374, 5375, and 5377 are disposed of / allowed. Company Appeal (AT) No. 214 of 2025 is dismissed. Pending applications IA Nos. 5376 and 5333 of 2025 are disposed of.
summary: M/s Singhal Matta & Co., Chartered Accountants, appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated 09.05.2025 removing them as auditors of Respondent No. 1 company. The NCLT found that the appellant firm had provided prohibited management services in violation of Section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013, as evidenced by audited balance sheets for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 showing management fees charged by the auditor. NCLAT condoned the 3-day delay in filing, upheld the findings of the NCLT regarding the statutory violation, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Deepika Bhugra Prasad, Liquidator of M/s Ess Dee Aluminium Ltd. vs. Lucky Holdings Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Deepika Bhugra Prasad, Liquidator of M/s Ess Dee Aluminium Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Lucky Holdings Private Limited, a prospective bidder/H1 auction purchaser. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern under Regulation 32A of the Liquidation Process Regulations pursuant to a sale notice dated 05.04.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent submitted the highest bid of Rs. 124.60 crores, requiring a 25% first instalment payment of Rs. 29.15 crores (after EMD adjustment) within 15 days, which the Respondent failed to pay. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent declared H1 bidder on 26.04.2022 with initial payment deadline of 11.05.2022; interim stay granted by NCLT on 09.05.2022 in IA 397/2022; stay vacated upon unconditional withdrawal of IA on 15.06.2022; Liquidator communicated vacation on 16.06.2022 and 23.06.2022; sale cancelled and EMD forfeited on 01.07.2022; Respondent filed IA No. 800/2022 in August 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of E-auction process document, sale notice clauses, bidder affidavit undertaking dated 13.04.2022, and email correspondence between Liquidator and Respondent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed IA No. 800/2022 filed by Respondent on 17.01.2023, directing refund of the forfeited Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of Rs. 2 crores by applying Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act; Liquidator challenged the order via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 186 of 2023.
legal_issues: Whether a liquidator is legally empowered under the statutory liquidation regulations and binding auction terms to cancel a sale and forfeit the earnest money deposit of a successful bidder who commits default in payment timelines, and whether Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act applies to such statutory forfeiture.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Forfeiture of an earnest money deposit in a public auction conducted under the IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations is a legitimate statutory and contractual remedy for default, and Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act has no application to such statutory forfeiture. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Schedule I read with the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, empowers the liquidator to stipulate strict payment timelines and forfeiture consequences for non-compliance. Bidders who participate voluntarily are bound by the terms of the process document and unequivocal undertakings given via affidavit. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an interim stay is vacated and remaining timelines communicated, a successful bidder's failure to deposit the balance consideration despite having clear notice and opportunities constitutes an unexcused default, rendering cancellation and forfeiture valid. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in applying Section 74 of the Contract Act and overlooking settled precedents; the Liquidator's forfeiture of the EMD was fully justified under statutory auction rules, warranting reversal of the refund order.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 17.01.2023 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in I.A. No. 800 of 2022 is set aside, upholding the Liquidator's action of cancelling the sale and forfeiting the Respondent's EMD. Pending IAs are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: Deepika Bhugra Prasad, Liquidator of Ess Dee Aluminium Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench directing the refund of a forfeited Rs. 2 crore Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) to Lucky Holdings Pvt. Ltd. The respondent had emerged as the H1 bidder in an e-auction for a going concern sale at Rs. 124.60 crores but failed to deposit the 25% first instalment within the stipulated timeline, even after an interim stay by NCLT was vacated. NCLT had ordered a refund by invoking Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act. NCLAT held, relying on Westcoast Infraprojects and subsequent precedents, that Section 74 does not apply to forfeiture under statutory liquidation auctions and that the respondent committed an unexcused default, making the forfeiture valid. The appeal was allowed.

case_title: Bank of Baroda vs. IDBI Bank Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bank of Baroda (Assenting Financial Creditor / Member of Monitoring Committee); Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Bank Limited (Dissenting Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Anish Niranjan Nanavaty (Monitoring Committee Member); Respondent No. 3 is Reliance Projects & Property Management Services Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 4 is Reliance Communications Infrastructure Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Reliance Communications Infrastructure Limited; approval of a resolution plan containing provisions for assigning the Reliance Bhutan Loan (RBL) worth Rs. 195 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor leading to CIRP commencement on 26.09.2019; resolution plan approved by CoC on 05.08.2021 with 67.97% vote share; approved by NCLT on 19.12.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved resolution plan on 05.08.2021; Bank of Baroda filed IA No. 127 of 2022 on 02.01.2022 for reallocation; NCLT directed CoC meeting on 17.10.2023; CoC passed reallocation resolution on 27.10.2023; NCLT approved resolution plan on 19.12.2023; IDBI Bank filed IA(IBC)/2708(MB)2025; NCLT allowed IDBI Bank's application on 10.10.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan provisions (Clauses 1.2.3, 1.2.13, 3.3.20), Form H compliance certificate with Note 10, CoC meeting minutes dated 27.10.2023, and NCLT plan approval order dated 19.12.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IDBI Bank filed IA(IBC)/2708(MB)2025 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-I challenging the CoC's 27.10.2023 reallocation decision; NCLT allowed the application on 10.10.2025, holding that the CoC could not modify the financial layout or assign the Reliance Bhutan Loan to dissenting financial creditors post-approval; Bank of Baroda filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1708 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has the jurisdiction, after approving a resolution plan under Section 30(4) of the IBC, to subsequently pass a resolution altering the financial layout and distribution mechanism—specifically reassigning the Reliance Bhutan Loan from assenting financial creditors to dissenting financial creditors—contrary to the terms of the approved resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved by the Committee of Creditors under Section 30(4) of the IBC, it becomes binding and irrevocable as between the CoC and the successful resolution applicant, and the CoC lacks any legal competence or jurisdiction to subsequently modify, tinker with, or alter its financial layout or distribution mechanism. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(4) requires the CoC to consider the manner of distribution prior to voting. Once finalized and submitted to the Adjudicating Authority, the distribution mechanism is immutable. Furthermore, Clause 3.3.20 of a resolution plan permitting assignment to 'such other entity' cannot be interpreted to include dissenting financial creditors who constitute a distinct statutory class. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The doctrine of commercial wisdom cannot be invoked to validate a post-approval modification of an already finalized resolution plan or distribution framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC's resolution dated 27.10.2023 attempting to reallocate the Reliance Bhutan Loan to dissenting financial creditors was illegal, unauthorized, and contrary to the approved resolution plan, justifying the Adjudicating Authority's decision to set it aside.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The order dated 10.10.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA(IBC)/2708(MB)2025 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Bank of Baroda, an assenting financial creditor, appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench-I allowing an application filed by dissenting financial creditor IDBI Bank Ltd. The NCLT had set aside a CoC resolution dated 27.10.2023 which attempted to reallocate the Rs. 195 crore Reliance Bhutan Loan (RBL)—originally assigned under the resolution plan to assenting financial creditors—to dissenting financial creditors. NCLAT held that once a resolution plan and its distribution mechanism are approved by the CoC under Section 30(4), the CoC cannot subsequently tinker with or modify the financial layout. NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's ruling and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Kaajal Aijaz Ilmi vs. Ram Kumar, Administrator of AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kaajal Aijaz Ilmi, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Ram Kumar, Administrator / Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial service provider insolvency proceedings initiated against AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd. after RBI superseded its Board of Directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial service provider default resulting in RBI supersession under Section 45-IE(1) of the RBI Act, 1934 on 27.01.2025, and CIRP initiation under Section 227 IBC on 20.02.2025. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI notification issued on 27.01.2025; CIRP initiated on 20.02.2025; Administrator issued public announcement and Form-G for Expression of Interest; Appellant filed IA No. 5599/2025; NCLT rejected the IA on 18.11.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RBI supersession notification dated 27.01.2025, NCLT admission order dated 20.02.2025, and Form-G publication. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. No. 5599/2025 before NCLT New Delhi (Court V) seeking copies of resolution plans submitted by Prospective Resolution Applicants; NCLT rejected the application on 18.11.2025 relying on the Supreme Court judgment in Piramal Capital; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1879 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether suspended directors of a financial service provider whose board of directors was superseded by the Reserve Bank of India prior to the commencement of CIRP have the right to attend meetings of the Committee of Creditors and obtain copies of resolution plans submitted by prospective resolution applicants.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the Reserve Bank of India supersedes the board of directors of a financial service provider under the RBI Act, the erstwhile directors are deemed to have vacated their offices, and they have no right to attend meetings of the Committee of Creditors, participate in CIRP proceedings, or obtain copies of resolution plans during the pendency of the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 227 read with FSP Rules, 2019, governs financial service provider insolvencies. Supersession under Section 45-IE(1) of the RBI Act terminates directorship ab initio prior to CIRP commencement, distinguishing such ex-directors from standard suspended directors under Section 24 IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of a specific statutory right under the IBC or FSP Rules, members of a superseded board cannot claim documents during CIRP; they are only entitled to a certified copy of the approved resolution plan after NCLT approval under Section 31 makes it a public document under Section 74 of the Evidence Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following the Supreme Court's binding pronouncement in Piramal Capital and Housing Finance Ltd., the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the suspended director's application for copies of resolution plans.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The order dated 18.11.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi in I.A. No. 5599/2025 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Kaajal Aijaz Ilmi, a suspended director of Corporate Debtor AVIOM India Housing Finance Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi (Court V) rejecting her application (I.A. No. 5599/2025) for copies of resolution plans submitted by Prospective Resolution Applicants. The RBI had superseded the company's board of directors on 27.01.2025 before initiating CIRP under Section 227 IBC on 20.02.2025. NCLAT held, in light of the Supreme Court's ruling in Piramal Capital and Housing Finance Ltd., that supersession by the RBI causes directors to vacate their offices, disentitling them from attending CoC meetings or obtaining resolution plans during CIRP. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Ajay Kumar Bhuwalka & Anr. vs. M/s Bhuwalka Steel Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Ajay Kumar Bhuwalka and Ankit Kumar Bhuwalka, nominal directors/shareholders of Corporate Debtor M/s Bhuwalka Steel Industries Private Limited; Respondent is M/s Bhuwalka Steel Industries Ltd., represented by Resolution Professional Shivadutt Bannanje. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process of Bhuwalka Steel Industries Pvt. Ltd. and avoidance/fraudulent trading proceedings against promoters and nominal directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Resolution Professional filed IA No. 122/2022 seeking contributions of Rs. 154.55 crores under Section 66, Rs. 1.49 crores under Section 44, and a fine of Rs. 1 crore under Section 69 of the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 08.04.2019; IA No. 133/2020 filed under Section 66 disposed of as premature on 10.03.2021 with liberty to revive or file fresh application; IA No. 248/2021 disposed of on 22.02.2022 directing RP to comply within 30 days; IA No. 122/2022 filed on 18.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT orders dated 10.03.2021 and 22.02.2022 granting liberty, forensic audit report, and transaction avoidance filings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants challenged NCLT Chennai Bench order dated 09.07.2025 passed in IA No. 122/2022 which rejected their preliminary objection regarding limitation and held that the avoidance application was maintainable and not time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether an application filed by a Resolution Professional under Sections 43, 44, 66, and 69 of the IBC pursuant to liberty granted by the Adjudicating Authority is barred by limitation, and whether a formal separate application for condonation of delay is mandatory under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Delay can be condoned irrespective of whether there is any formal application, provided there are sufficient materials on record disclosing sufficient cause. Furthermore, an application filed pursuant to express liberty granted by the Adjudicating Authority to revive or file a fresh petition gives rise to a fresh cause of action and is protected by applicable limitation exclusions (such as Supreme Court suo motu COVID-19 orders). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 35A timelines are directory in nature. Avoidance and fraudulent trading applications filed within the framework of liberty granted by prior judicial orders are maintainable and not barred by limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Omission to refer to the correct statutory section or absence of a formal condonation application does not vitiate proceedings when sufficient cause is apparent on record, as established in Sesh Nath Singh. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly held that IA No. 122/2022 was not barred by limitation and was protected by judicial orders and COVID-19 limitation exclusions, rendering the appeal devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 508/2025 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 09.07.2025 holding the application not barred by limitation is affirmed without expressing any opinion on the merits of IA No. 122/2022.
summary: Nominal directors Ajay Kumar Bhuwalka and Ankit Kumar Bhuwalka appealed an order of NCLT Chennai Bench dated 09.07.2025 passed in IA No. 122/2022, which rejected their preliminary objection regarding limitation. The Resolution Professional had filed IA No. 122/2022 under Sections 43, 44, 66, and 69 IBC seeking massive contributions from the directors, pursuant to liberty granted in earlier NCLT orders. NCLAT held, citing Sesh Nath Singh and Supreme Court COVID-19 exclusion orders, that a formal condonation application is not mandatory and that the application was well within extended limitation periods. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Manish Mahendra Somani vs. Bank of Baroda & Anr. (and connected appeal)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 843 of 2025 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 845 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Manish Mahendra Somani and Manoj Mahendra Somani (Personal Guarantors); Respondent No. 1 is Bank of Baroda; Respondent No. 2 is Rajendra Jain (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal guarantees extended by the appellants for loans advanced by Bank of Baroda to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Corporate Debtor leading to personal insolvency proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 94 IBC petitions filed by appellants on 04.10.2023; NCLT appointed an RP and directed service of copies on 16.01.2024; Financial Creditor filed IA Nos. 337 and 336 of 2025; NCLT dismissed Section 94 petitions on 17.04.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing failure of appellants to serve petition copies to the RP as ordered on 16.01.2024, resulting in a 15-month moratorium extension. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed the Section 94 petitions on 17.04.2025 under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules due to non-service of copies to the RP and failure of the RP to file a Section 99 report; Appellants filed Company Appeals No. 843 and 845 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can dismiss a Section 94 IBC petition under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules due to the petitioner's failure to serve a copy of the petition on the appointed Resolution Professional, and whether such dismissal confers an unmerited advantage of an extended moratorium.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While an Adjudicating Authority cannot dismiss a Section 94 petition solely for the failure of a Resolution Professional to submit a Section 99 report, a petitioner's deliberate or negligent failure to comply with a positive order directing service of the petition copies to the RP—thereby unjustly enjoying an extended moratorium—justifies dismissal under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to prevent abuse of process and protect substantive creditor rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules preserves inherent powers to make orders necessary for meeting the ends of justice and preventing abuse of tribunal processes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a procedural default directly results in securing an unmerited 15-month moratorium advantage to the detriment of the financial creditor, the default ceases to be a mere technicality and warrants strict consequences. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority's decision to dismiss the petitions was legally sound and balanced given the appellants' non-compliance and the resulting prejudice to the creditor.
operative_order: Company Appeals No. 843 and 845 of 2025 are dismissed. The orders of the Adjudicating Authority dated 17.04.2025 in I.A. No. 337 of 2025 in C.P. (IB) No. 14 of 2024 and I.A. No. 336 of 2025 in C.P. (IB) No. 13 of 2024 are confirmed.
summary: Manish Mahendra Somani and Manoj Mahendra Somani appealed orders of NCLT Ahmedabad dismissing their Section 94 IBC personal insolvency petitions. The NCLT had invoked Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to dismiss the petitions because the appellants failed to comply with an order dated 16.01.2024 directing them to serve copies of their petitions on the appointed Resolution Professional, thereby enjoying an unmerited 15-month moratorium. NCLAT held that while the RP's failure alone could not ground a dismissal, the appellants' failure to serve the RP coupled with the undue advantage gained warranted dismissal under Rule 11. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: State of Tamil Nadu vs. S. Muthuraju, Liquidator of M/s. Sri Nagananthana Mills Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the State of Tamil Nadu, Commercial Taxes and Registration Dept. (represented by Assistant Commissioner M. Chithradevi); Respondent is S. Muthuraju, Liquidator of M/s. Sri Nagananthana Mills Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tax liabilities under CST assessment orders for assessment years 2003-04 to 2016-17. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim amount of Rs. 1,70,15,094/- raised by the Appellant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate debtor placed into liquidation on 21.06.2018; public notice issued with last date 26.07.2018; claim filed on 12.02.2020 (351 days delayed); claim rejected by liquidator on 17.02.2020; Section 42 application filed on 19.07.2023 (1243 days delayed); NCLT dismissed IA on 20.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator rejection letter dated 17.02.2020, Form C submission, and waterfall distribution status under Section 53. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench rejected the Appellant's Section 42 application and condonation request on 20.03.2024; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 151/2025 with a 30-day re-filing delay.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed under Section 42 of the IBC against a liquidator's rejection of a claim with a delay of over 1,200 days can be entertained after the liquidation process has progressed and asset distribution under Section 53 has been completed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time is the essence of the IBC, and strict limitation periods prescribed under Section 42 (14 days) and liquidation regulations must be enforced. Once a liquidation process has substantially progressed and assets have been distributed under the waterfall mechanism of Section 53, belated claims cannot be entertained or the process reopened. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 42 of the IBC mandates a strict 14-day timeline to challenge a liquidator's decision. Regulation 44(1) of the Liquidation Regulations reinforces the time-bound nature of liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a claimant delays filing a claim by 351 days and delays filing a statutory appeal against rejection by 1,243 days while sleeping over its rights, limitation bars the claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority rightly dismissed the belated Section 42 applications given the massive delay and the completion of asset distribution under Section 53.
operative_order: IA No. 1276/2025 (delay in re-filing) is allowed. Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 151/2025 is dismissed on merits. All pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The State of Tamil Nadu appealed an order of NCLT Chennai dismissing its applications under Section 42 of the IBC. The appellant had submitted a tax claim of Rs. 1,70,15,094/- with a 351-day delay, which the liquidator rejected on 17.02.2020. The appellant then waited 1,243 days before filing an appeal under Section 42 on 19.07.2023. NCLAT Chennai held that the appeal was hopelessly barred by limitation under Section 42 and that reopening the liquidation process after assets had already been distributed under Section 53 would violate the time-bound objectives of the IBC and Regulation 44(1). The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited vs. Kew Precision Parts Private Limited
appeal_number: Review Application (AT) No. 6 of 2025 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1405 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant is Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent in main appeal); Respondent is Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Appellant in main appeal). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 IBC application filed by Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. against Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd., based on an OTS scheme and 10 security cheques given on 02.09.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in honoring the OTS and dishonor of security cheques. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT dismissed Section 7 application on 29.08.2023; NCLAT allowed Kotak Mahindra Bank's appeal and set aside NCLT order on 17.07.2025; Applicant filed civil appeal (not pressed) and a recall application (Review Application (AT) No. 6 of 2025) before NCLAT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: OTS agreement dated 20.12.2018, 10 security cheques dated 02.09.2016, and Supreme Court order dated 17.07.2025 dismissing civil appeal as not pressed. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Applicant moved Review Application (AT) No. 6 of 2025 (treated as a Recall Application) before NCLAT to recall the judgment dated 17.07.2025 passed in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1405 of 2023; NCLAT dismissed the recall application on 12.12.2025.
legal_issues: Whether a judgment of the appellate tribunal can be recalled on the ground of minor narration errors in factual background paragraphs when the substantive findings are based on independent, undisputed conduct and agreements, and whether a recall application is maintainable after an appeal against the same judgment was dismissed as 'not pressed' by the Supreme Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A recall application cannot be maintained as a substitute for an appeal or to reargue merits, particularly when the aggrieved party has already approached the Supreme Court and withdrawn its appeal. Furthermore, narration of facts or observations in introductory paragraphs that have no bearing on the substantive findings and reasoning do not constitute grounds for recall. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Principles governing recall of judgments are restricted to manifest errors or procedural review (such as violation of natural justice), not re-adjudication of substantive issues already addressed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where substantive findings rest upon undisputed facts regarding an OTS agreement and dishonored security cheques, incidental observations in narration paragraphs do not vitiate the final outcome. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The recall application is an impermissible attempt to re-litigate matters already settled before the Supreme Court, warranting dismissal.
operative_order: I.A. No. 7650 of 2025 is disposed of permitting correction of nomenclature to 'recall application'. Review Application (AT) No. 6 of 2025 (Recall Application) is dismissed.
summary: Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd. filed a review (recalculated as a recall) application seeking to set aside NCLAT's judgment dated 17.07.2025 which had allowed Kotak Mahindra Bank's Section 7 IBC appeal. The applicant argued that NCLAT made incorrect observations regarding Section 25(3) of the Contract Act and limitation in its narration paragraphs. NCLAT noted that the applicant had already challenged the judgment before the Supreme Court in a civil appeal which was dismissed as 'not pressed' after being argued at length, and that the narration paragraphs did not form the basis of the substantive reasoning. NCLAT dismissed the recall application.

case_title: Schneider Electric India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sarkun Solar Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1259 of 2025 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1262 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Schneider Electric India Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent is Sarkun Solar Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Execution of solar projects ('Karnataka Project' and 'Punjab Project') completed in 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 8,79,68,530/- for the Karnataka Project and Rs. 20,63,85,616/- for the Punjab Project. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Projects completed in 2017; email exchange on 21.02.2019 and 22.02.2019; Section 8 demand notice issued on 11.07.2022; Section 9 applications filed on 21.08.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Contemporaneous correspondence and emails from 2017 and 2018 regarding project delays, generation losses, defective works, and warranty issues, alongside reply email dated 22.02.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Section 9 applications on the ground of a pre-existing dispute; Appellant filed Company Appeals No. 1259 and 1262 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether contemporaneous correspondence and emails raising issues of project delays, generation losses, defective works, and warranty disputes prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice constitute a valid pre-existing dispute under Section 9(5)(i)(d) of the IBC to warrant dismissal of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where contemporaneous correspondence and emails between parties prior to a demand notice consistently highlight operational deficiencies, project delays, generation losses, and warranty breaches, a genuine pre-existing dispute exists, mandating the dismissal of a Section 9 application under Section 9(5)(i)(d). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(i)(d) requires the adjudicating authority to reject a Section 9 application if a notice of dispute has been received or if a pre-existing dispute is substantiated by evidence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If defenses raised by a corporate debtor are supported by contemporaneous records from 2017 and 2018 and are not mere bluster or moonshine, the dispute is genuine and outside the summary purview of Section 9 IBC proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly identified a robust pre-existing dispute based on contemporaneous records, justifying the dismissal of the Section 9 applications.
operative_order: Company Appeals No. 1259 and 1262 of 2025 are dismissed, with a clarification that dismissal shall not preclude the appellant from pursuing contractual recovery remedies.
summary: Schneider Electric India Pvt. Ltd. appealed orders of NCLT dismissing its Section 9 IBC applications against Sarkun Solar Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid dues of over Rs. 29 crores across the 'Karnataka Project' and 'Punjab Project'. The corporate debtor defended non-payment by citing contemporaneous emails from 2017 and 2018 regarding project delays, generation losses, defective inverters, and warranty issues, as well as a reply email on 22.02.2019. NCLAT held, applying Mobilox Innovations, that the corporate debtor raised genuine pre-existing disputes backed by contemporaneous records, making Section 9 proceedings inappropriate. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Vikas Goel vs. Bank of Baroda & Anr. (and connected appeals)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Vikas Goel, Anil Goel, Sudha Gupta, Vishnu Bhagwan, Devendra, Prateek Gupta, Paras Gupta, and Raj Rani Gupta (Personal Guarantors of M/s. Our Company Infrastructure Developers Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Bank of Baroda / JC Flower Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Bankruptcy Trustee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal guarantees executed by appellants to secure credit facilities extended to M/s. Our Company Infrastructure Developers Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the principal borrower resulting in guarantee invocation and Section 95 applications against personal guarantors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 95 applications admitted post-RP report under Section 99; repayment plans rejected by creditors; NCLT ordered closure of insolvency and directed bankruptcy applications; NCLT allowed bankruptcy applications and appointed bankruptcy trustee; Supreme Court dismissed civil appeals on 05.12.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 95 and 99 reports, repayment plan rejection records, and Supreme Court order dated 05.12.2025 in Civil Appeal No. 13551/2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court-II) allowed bankruptcy applications filed by financial creditors and appointed bankruptcy trustees; Appellants filed multiple company appeals; Supreme Court dismissed parallel civil appeals on 05.12.2025.
legal_issues: Whether an order directing bankruptcy proceedings and appointing a bankruptcy trustee following the rejection of a personal guarantor's repayment plan under Section 95 of the IBC is sustainable, particularly when identical appeals before the Supreme Court have been dismissed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where insolvency proceedings under Section 95 against personal guarantors are validly conducted, repayment plans are rejected by creditors, and parallel challenges before the Supreme Court are dismissed, an order initiating bankruptcy proceedings and appointing a bankruptcy trustee is a valid consequential step that warrants no appellate interference. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Chapter III of Part III of the IBC establishes a seamless progression from insolvency resolution to bankruptcy upon the rejection of a repayment plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Dismissal of parallel civil appeals by the Supreme Court settles the core validity of the underlying Section 95 proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In view of the Supreme Court's binding dismissal of appeals, the bankruptcy orders are unassailable consequential steps, requiring dismissal of the company appeals.
operative_order: Company Appeals No. 1567, 1586, 1629, 1671, 1672, 1673, 1674, and 1675 of 2025 are dismissed. No orders as to costs.
summary: Personal guarantors of M/s. Our Company Infrastructure Developers Pvt. Ltd. appealed orders of NCLT New Delhi allowing bankruptcy applications filed by Bank of Baroda / JC Flower Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. and appointing a bankruptcy trustee after repayment plans were rejected by creditors. During the appellate proceedings, the parties brought to notice that the Supreme Court had already dismissed parallel civil appeals (e.g., Civil Appeal No. 13551/2025) on 05.12.2025. Following the Supreme Court's ruling, NCLAT held that bankruptcy proceedings are a valid consequential step and dismissed all the connected appeals.

case_title: Omkara Asset Reconstruction Private Limited vs. Amit Vijay Karia, Erstwhile Resolution Professional & Anr. (and connected appeal)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 914 of 2025 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 915 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in both appeals is Omkara Asset Reconstruction Private Limited (Financial Creditor / 100% and ~98% CoC voting share); Respondent No. 1 is Amit Vijay Karia (Erstwhile Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Mohd. Raees Sheikh / Mayuri Daga (Liquidators appointed by NCLT). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes of Chinar Realty Private Limited and Chinar Retails and Infrastructure Private Limited failing, leading to liquidation resolutions by the CoC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure of CIRP resulting in liquidation orders under Section 33. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC resolved to send corporate debtors to liquidation and named M/s Stress Credit Resolution Pvt Ltd (SCRIL) as liquidator; NCLT Indore Bench overlooked CoC's choice and appointed separate liquidators vide orders dated 11.06.2025; Omkara ARL filed appeals. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC resolutions nominating SCRIL as liquidator, minutes of meetings, and NCLT appointment orders dated 11.06.2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench appointed independent liquidators of its own choice in I.A. (LIQ) No. 1/MP/2025 and I.A. (LIQ) No. 3/MP/2024 on 11.06.2025; Omkara ARL filed Company Appeals No. 914 and 915 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors (CoC) has the primary authority to select and nominate a liquidator when liquidation is ordered under Section 33 of the IBC, or whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses an independent power to appoint a liquidator of its own choice bypassing the CoC's recommendation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Committee of Creditors possesses the primary authority to select and nominate a liquidator when corporate debtors enter liquidation. While Section 34(1) and Section 34(4)(c) empower the Adjudicating Authority to replace an unwilling or ineligible resolution professional, such replacement must follow the procedure contemplated under Section 27, and the Adjudicating Authority cannot arbitrarily supersede the CoC's choice unless gross statutory fraud or misconduct is established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 22, 27, and 34 of the IBC establish that the selection process of resolution professionals and liquidators rests with the CoC, while the Adjudicating Authority's role is formal appointment subject to board confirmation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An Adjudicating Authority cannot act as an independent selector or veto the CoC's choice of liquidator unless there is tangible evidence of collusion, fraud, or gross misconduct. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in appointing liquidators of its own choice by overriding the CoC's nomination; the CoC's nominated entity (SCRIL) must be appointed subject to IBBI confirmation.
operative_order: Company Appeals No. 914 and 915 of 2025 are allowed. The NCLT Indore Bench orders dated 11.06.2025 in I.A. (LIQ) No. 1/MP/2025 and I.A. (LIQ) No. 3/MP/2024 are set aside. Once the Board confirms M/s Stress Credit Resolution Pvt Ltd (SCRIL), the Adjudicating Authority is directed to appoint it as liquidator.
summary: Omkara Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd., holding 100% and ~98% voting shares in the CoC of two corporate debtors, appealed orders of NCLT Indore Bench dated 11.06.2025 which appointed independent liquidators of the tribunal's own choice, overriding the CoC's nomination of M/s Stress Credit Resolution Pvt Ltd (SCRIL). NCLAT held that the selection of a liquidator rests primarily with the CoC under the scheme of Sections 22, 27, and 34 of the IBC, and the Adjudicating Authority cannot arbitrarily substitute its own choice unless there is proof of fraud or gross misconduct. NCLAT set aside the NCLT orders and directed the appointment of SCRIL subject to IBBI confirmation.

case_title: Nu-World Industries (Pty) Ltd. vs. Veira Electronics Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Nu-World Industries (Pty) Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent is Veira Electronics Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business agreement for purchase, assembly, and distribution of TV and Home-Audio products; goods supplied and invoices raised from 07.03.2019 to 21.05.2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Invoices totaling USD 798,247.40, part-payments of USD 716,421.98, leaving principal outstanding of USD 81,825.42, plus interest of USD 44,151.57 (total USD 125,976.99 / Rs. 1,05,68,291.58). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised from 07.03.2019 to 21.05.2024 (including Section 10A period invoices and part-payments); Section 8 demand notice issued on 26.06.2024; Section 9 application filed on 08.07.2024; NCLT dismissed Section 9 application on 17.04.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices, payment ledgers, interest invoice dated 21.05.2024, and Sino Corp CPA Ltd. auditor communication dated 19.08.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 application on 17.04.2025 holding that excluding Section 10A period invoices and interest rendered the claim below the Rs. 1 crore threshold; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1024 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor can include interest accrued on invoices raised during the Section 10A embargo period to meet the minimum statutory threshold of Rs. 1 crore under Section 4 of the IBC, and whether ambiguous interest computations justify the dismissal of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Invoices raised and interest accruing during the Section 10A period must be strictly segregated and excluded when calculating the minimum statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC. When an operational creditor fails to provide clear, verifiable, invoice-wise interest computations excluding Section 10A periods, the application is liable to be dismissed for failing to meet the threshold. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A bars applications for defaults occurring during the prohibited window, and calculations cannot circumvent this by bulk interest additions on barred invoices. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an invoice levying lump-sum straight-line interest lacks itemized calculations, invoice-wise periods, and clear segregation of Section 10A amounts despite multiple opportunities given by tribunals, the threshold requirement is unsatisfied. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly concluded that the ambiguous interest calculation including Section 10A elements failed to establish satisfaction of the Rs. 1 crore threshold.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The impugned order dated 17.04.2025 rejecting the Section 9 application is affirmed. The appellant is granted liberty to approach a competent court for recovery remedies. No order as to costs.
summary: Nu-World Industries (Pty) Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Veira Electronics Private Limited for an operational debt of Rs. 1,05,68,291.58 (including USD 81,825.42 principal and USD 44,151.57 interest). The NCLT had dismissed the petition holding that once Section 10A period invoices and interest were excluded, the claim fell below the Rs. 1 crore threshold under Section 4. NCLAT held that the appellant's lump-sum interest invoice dated 21.05.2024 lacked itemized clarity and failed to properly segregate Section 10A amounts despite opportunities to produce revised computations. The appeal was dismissed with liberty to pursue other recovery remedies.

case_title: State Tax Officer vs. Nitin Narang, RP of Afcan Impex Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the State Tax Officer, and the Respondent No. 1 is Nitin Narang, the Resolution Professional (RP) of the Corporate Debtor, M/s Afcan Impex Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor was admitted into the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 7 of the IBC based on an application by the Bank of Maharashtra. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant filed a total claim of Rs. 5,80,64,381/-, comprising Gujarat Value Added Tax (GVAT) dues and Central Sales Tax (CST) dues, which were evaluated by the RP and Adjudicating Authority. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The public announcement inviting claims was issued on 23.02.2021; the Appellant filed its claim on 19.04.2021 and subsequently wrote a letter to the RP on 10.03.2023 claiming status as a secured creditor. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan via an order dated 30.09.2025 and partly allowed IA No. 447 of 2025, treating GVAT dues as a secured claim while rejecting the CST dues as a secured claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The State Tax Officer filed Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1804 and 1805 of 2025 before the NCLAT challenging the orders dated 30.09.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench, Court-1) in IA No. 766 of 2021 and IA No. 447 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the dues payable to the State Tax Department under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 (CST Act) qualify as a secured debt or statutory first charge by operation of law under Section 9(2) of the CST Act in a manner similar to Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge or security interest by operation of law requires an explicit substantive provision creating such a charge; machinery provisions governing assessment and recovery cannot independently create a security interest. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(2) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, functions strictly as a machinery and procedural provision for the assessment, collection, and enforcement of tax under general sales tax laws, and does not import or create a substantive first charge on the assets of the dealer equivalent to Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court evaluated whether the statutory framework of the CST Act contains pari materia provisions to Section 48 of the GVAT Act and found an absence of any statutory wording creating a first charge. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in treating the CST dues as unsecured debt and dismissed the appeals.
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1804 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1805 of 2025 are dismissed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: The Appellant, State Tax Officer, filed two appeals against the orders dated 30.09.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority, Ahmedabad, which approved the resolution plan and partly allowed the Appellant's interlocutory application by recognizing GVAT dues as a secured claim while denying the same status to CST dues. The core issue before the NCLAT was whether CST dues enjoy a statutory first charge as a secured debt by virtue of Section 9(2) of the CST Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that Section 9(2) of the CST Act is merely a machinery provision for collection and recovery and does not create a substantive first charge on the assets of the corporate debtor unlike Section 48 of the GVAT Act. Consequently, both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Consortium led by Syonira Invecast Pvt. Ltd. vs. Employees' Provident Fund Organisation & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2319 of 2024 & No. 141 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in the main appeal is the Consortium led by Syonira Invecast Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA), and Respondent No. 1 is the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), with Respondent No. 2 being the erstwhile Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was initiated against the Corporate Debtor, M/s Goa Invescast Ltd., pursuant to an application by Steel and Scrap Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO initially submitted a claim of Rs. 17.90 lakhs in Form-B, which was later revised based on employee claims to Rs. 63.15 lakhs, fully paid by the SRA, following which EPFO subsequently issued notices and summons for fresh dues amounting to Rs. 62,09,154/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 04.07.2019, the resolution plan was approved on 09.11.2021, an order under Section 7A was passed on 06.04.2021 during moratorium, and post-plan notices/summons were issued on 29.04.2022 and 18.05.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assessment and quasi-judicial proceedings under the EPF Act were conducted and orders were passed during the subsistence of the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, without the claims being properly lodged or incorporated into the approved resolution plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The SRA filed I.A. No. 1745 of 2022 before the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench) to set aside post-plan notices and demands, which was partly allowed on 09.10.2024, leading to cross-appeals by both the SRA and the EPFO.
legal_issues: Whether assessment proceedings can be continued by the EPFO under the EPF & MP Act, 1952, after the imposition of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, and whether claims based on such post-moratorium assessments can be enforced against the Successful Resolution Applicant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a moratorium is imposed under Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC, statutory authorities are barred from initiating or continuing assessment or recovery proceedings against the corporate debtor, and claims not part of the approved resolution plan stand extinguished. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'proceedings' under Section 14(1)(a) has a wide and expansive scope covering statutory authorities such as the EPFO, prohibiting any assessment that impacts the corporate debtor's assets during the resolution process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court evaluated whether the assessment orders and demands were finalized during the active moratorium period and found that post-commencement assessments cannot create enforceable pecuniary liabilities against the SRA. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that no assessment proceedings could be continued by the EPFO during the moratorium, and claims arising therefrom cannot be pressed in the CIRP or enforced against the SRA, rendering the cross-appeal by EPFO devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2319 of 2024 filed by the Successful Resolution Applicant is allowed to the extent of prayer (a). The linked appeal filed by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 141 of 2024, is dismissed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: These cross-appeals arose from an order dated 09.10.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in an application filed by the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) challenging post-plan notices and demands raised by the EPFO. The main issue was whether the EPFO could initiate or continue assessment proceedings and raise fresh demands under Sections 7A, 7Q, and 14B of the EPF & MP Act during the subsistence of the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. The NCLAT held that the moratorium bars the continuation or initiation of assessment proceedings by the EPFO against the corporate debtor, and any claims not included in the approved resolution plan stand extinguished under Section 31 of the IBC. Accordingly, the SRA's appeal was allowed, and the EPFO's appeal seeking priority treatment of unsubmitted claims was dismissed.

case_title: Pranav Ansal & Ors. vs. IL&FS Financial Services Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 500 of 2025 & No. 502 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Pranav Ansal (Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, M/s Ansal Properties and Infrastructure Limited) and Gagan Tandon & Ors. (Homebuyers), while Respondent No. 1 is IL&FS Financial Services Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IL&FS granted two rupee term loan facilities totaling Rs. 150 crores to the Corporate Debtor under loan agreements dated 18.03.2016 and 25.11.2016, secured by specific project assets and receivables. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Financial Creditor claimed a default amount of Rs. 2,574,312,692/-, whereas the Corporate Debtor contended that the outstanding amount under a revised settlement agreement was approximately Rs. 83 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The financial facilities were disbursed between 2016 and 2017, a settlement agreement was terminated on 13.05.2024, and Section 7 application was filed on 06.08.2024, leading to admission of CIRP on 25.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor executed multiple real estate and township projects across various states under state policies (such as the UP Hi-Tech Township Policy), with specific land parcels and receivables mortgaged as securities under the loan agreements. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi) admitted the Section 7 application on 25.02.2025 and rejected intervention applications by homebuyers and development authorities, prompting the filing of these appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against a real estate company operating multiple projects across different states should engulf all its projects or be confined strictly to the projects and assets specifically encumbered and provided as security under the loan agreements.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Insolvency resolution of a real estate company should, as a rule, proceed on a project-specific basis or be confined to the specific assets and projects covered under the financing and security agreements to protect solvent projects and genuine homebuyers from collateral prejudice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Adjudicating Authority is required to balance the mechanics of the IBC with the realities of multi-project real estate developments, ensuring that blanket moratoriums do not disrupt unrelated projects or override statutory frameworks governing regional development authorities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court reviewed the specific terms of the loan agreements and security clauses, determining that the securities were restricted to specific township projects at Lucknow and selected assets in Rajasthan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the admission of the Section 7 application based on admitted debt and default was upheld, the NCLAT ruled that the CIRP and its associated moratorium must be confined strictly to the corporate debtor's projects at Lucknow (Mother City and Mother City Extension, including Golf Plots) and the specified built-up properties in Rajasthan, excluding unrelated projects in other states and regions.
operative_order: The order dated 25.02.2025 admitting the Section 7 application is upheld, subject to the direction that the CIRP against the corporate debtor is strictly confined to the projects at Lucknow (Mother City, Mother City Extension, and Golf Plots) and the assets/properties in Rajasthan (Ajmer, Jodhpur, and Jaipur), with specific directions for project-wise resolution and involvement of regulatory authorities.
summary: These appeals challenged an order of the NCLT admitting a Section 7 application filed by IL&FS Financial Services Ltd. against M/s Ansal Properties and Infrastructure Limited. The core question involved the propriety of extending a blanket CIRP across all projects of a real estate developer when the financing agreements and securities were localized to specific projects in Lucknow and Rajasthan. The NCLAT upheld the initiation of CIRP due to admitted debt and default but modified the scope, ruling that the insolvency proceedings and moratorium must be confined strictly to the projects and assets explicitly covered under the loan securities, thereby insulating unrelated projects and safeguarding the interests of homebuyers and statutory authorities.

case_title: Mr. Manoj Seth vs. Larsen and Toubro Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Manoj Seth (Operational Creditor/former employee) and the Respondent is Larsen and Toubro Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/employer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant was appointed as Senior Manager (Mechanical) pursuant to an employment agreement dated 26.03.2013 and was later covered under the ECAL and Retention Pay Scheme, 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed a total operational debt of Rs. 7,04,508/-, comprising salary for June 2018, ECAL and retention pay from July 2017 to June 2018, notice period pay, and interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant resigned on 24.04.2018 (provisionally accepted on 07.05.2018), suspension was ordered and subsequently revoked on 23.06.2018, a legal notice was issued on 05.01.2019, a Section 8 demand notice was sent on 30.01.2019, and replied to on 23.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following workplace incidents in late 2017 and early 2018, the Appellant tendered his resignation, was placed under suspension, and later requested to be relieved while engaging in extensive email correspondence regarding disputed employment dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application under Section 9 of the IBC, which was rejected by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench-VI) via order dated 24.09.2024 on grounds of threshold and pre-existing dispute, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an employment dispute concerning unpaid salary, allowances, and retention pay under a corporate scheme constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute, and whether the Section 9 application was maintainable given the disputed nature and threshold of the claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Summary proceedings under Section 9 of the IBC cannot be utilized as a substitute for debt recovery or for adjudicating complex, contested employment and contractual disputes where claims are un-crystallized and subject to bona fide pre-existing disputes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 15 of an employment contract and specific forfeiture clauses in incentive schemes validly disentitle employees from claiming performance/retention allowances upon resignation or during disputed separation periods. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-existing disputes are adequately established when correspondence prior to the Section 8 demand notice reveals consistent denial of liability and contested entitlements by the employer. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that genuine pre-existing disputes regarding employment entitlements existed between the parties, and the claim fell short of sustainable operational debt under the Code, justifying the dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. Pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The Appellant, a former employee, filed a Section 9 application claiming unpaid salary, ECAL allowances, and retention pay, which was dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority. On appeal, the NCLAT evaluated the employment agreement, incentive scheme terms, and prior email correspondence between the parties. The Appellate Tribunal affirmed that a genuine pre-existing dispute existed regarding the employee's entitlement to allowances post-resignation and that the IBC cannot be invoked as a recovery mechanism for un-crystallized employment dues. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Worldwide Online Services Private Limited vs. Mr. Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Worldwide Online Services Private Limited (WOSPL), and the Respondents include Mr. Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande (Resolution Professional/Liquidator) and suspended directors of the Corporate Debtor, Royal Refinery Private Limited (RRPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor was engaged in bullion trading, importing gold, exporting finished products, and domestic market sales before operations stalled following Department of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) raids in May 2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Resolution Professional identified an outstanding receivable balance of Rs. 98,96,82,438/- due from the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor based on seized DRI records and ledgers. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP of the Corporate Debtor was initiated on 13.11.2019; subsequently, the RP filed IA No. 1624 of 2020 under Section 66 of the Code, which was allowed by the Adjudicating Authority on 29.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Seized DRI documents and ledger accounts demonstrated that millions in receivables were fraudulently wiped out through unilateral journal entries, fake purchase entries, and deletion of sales entries to evade liability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged the Adjudicating Authority's order directing it to refund Rs. 98,96,82,438/- to the Corporate Debtor under Section 66 of the Code.
legal_issues: Whether transactions and book entries that systematically wipe out substantial trade receivables through fictitious adjustments during a period of corporate distress constitute fraudulent trading under Section 66 of the IBC, rendering third-party beneficiaries liable to make contributions to the corporate debtor's assets.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 66(1) of the IBC empowers the Adjudicating Authority to direct any person knowingly party to fraudulent business practices or sham book entries to contribute to the assets of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Fraudulent intent or mental state can be deduced circumstantially from synchronous book alterations, fabricated ledger entries, and the absence of matching physical inventory or genuine commercial documentation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Official records seized by investigative agencies like the DRI override subsequent un-audited, self-serving ledger reversals created by management to shield beneficiaries. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the deletion of valid sales entries and insertion of unverified purchase entries established fraudulent trading designed to defraud creditors, confirming the liability of the beneficiary appellant.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed. No order as to costs. Pending IAs are closed.
summary: The Appellant appealed against an order under Section 66 of the IBC directing it to refund Rs. 98,96,82,438/- to the Corporate Debtor, Royal Refinery Private Limited. The Resolution Professional had discovered through DRI raid records that outstanding receivables owed by the Appellant were fraudulently wiped out using unilateral ledger entries and fictitious purchases after business operations had halted. The NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's findings that the transactions were fraudulent shams intended to defraud creditors, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Jagdish R. Pahuja vs. Punjab National Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Jagdish R. Pahuja (Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, Damara Gold Private Limited) and Respondent No. 1 is Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor sanctioned a Term Loan of Rs. 5.70 crores and Bank Guarantees (BGs) amounting to Rs. 21.50 crores, which were renewed and secured by mortgage of properties in Mumbai. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: BGs were invoked by beneficiaries for Rs. 54.34 crores and debited to the cash credit account; the account became irregular and was classified as NPA on 30.06.2023, with total default claimed at Rs. 39,19,52,518.04/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sanction was initially granted on 17.03.2011 and last renewed on 17.03.2022; SARFAESI notice was issued on 10.08.2023; Section 7 application was filed on 18.12.2024, and admitted on 08.12.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NeSL default records showed authenticated status, and the Corporate Debtor submitted a restructuring proposal letter on 02.09.2024 while failing to cooperate with successive requests for stock audits by the bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench-VI) admitted the Section 7 application on 08.12.2025, leading to the present appeal by the suspended director.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 7 application upon establishing debt and default, and whether the corporate debtor's claim for MSME restructuring under the RBI Circular and Pro Knits precedent barred the admission of CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the existence of a financial debt and a default exceeding the statutory threshold is proven, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to admit a Section 7 application under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While RBI frameworks and guidelines for the revival and rehabilitation of MSMEs are binding on lending institutions, there is a reciprocal obligation on the borrower-Enterprise to actively cooperate and comply with procedural requirements such as stock audits to avail restructuring benefits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A borrower's proposal for loan restructuring acts as a clear acknowledgment of debt and default, and failure to permit mandatory audits nullifies subsequent claims of procedural denial by the lender. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that debt and default were conclusively established, and the Appellant's belated plea of restructuring failed due to lack of cooperation and audit compliance.
operative_order: The appeal, being devoid of merit, is dismissed. No costs.
summary: The Appellant, suspended director of Damara Gold Private Limited, challenged the NCLT order admitting Punjab National Bank's Section 7 application. The Appellant contended that invocation of bank guarantees was unauthorized and that its MSME restructuring proposal under the RBI circular had not been fairly considered pursuant to the Supreme Court's Pro Knits ruling. The NCLAT found that debt and default were clearly proven and that the Appellant had failed to cooperate with multiple requests for stock audits required for restructuring. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Employees Provident Fund Organisation vs. Subhlaxmi Investment Advisory Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Employees Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), and the Respondents are Subhlaxmi Investment Advisory Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA) and Ajay Gupta (Erstwhile Resolution Professional of Metistech Fabrication Private Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the Corporate Debtor, M/s Metistech Fabrication Private Limited, was initiated on 01.11.2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO initially filed an informal claim of Rs. 50,676/-, which was later revised through an ex-parte assessment during moratorium to Rs. 18,33,528/- (including damages and interest), against which a provision of Rs. 5,000/- was made in the resolution plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 01.11.2023; EPFO filed its initial communication on 22.12.2023; the resolution plan was approved by CoC on 21.09.2024, and subsequently approved by the Adjudicating Authority on 28.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: No contemporaneous records or salary deductions reflecting unpaid provident fund liabilities existed in the corporate debtor's books of accounts; assessment proceedings were initiated by EPFO post-commencement of CIRP during moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: EPFO appealed against the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 28.03.2025 approving the resolution plan, challenging the nominal provisioning of Rs. 5,000/- against its crystallized demand of Rs. 18,33,528/-.
legal_issues: Whether assessment proceedings initiated and carried out by the EPFO under the EPF & MP Act, 1952, during the subsistence of the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC are valid, and whether claims arising from such post-moratorium assessments can override an approved resolution plan under the clean slate doctrine.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: After the initiation of CIRP and imposition of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, no assessment proceedings can be initiated or continued by the EPFO, and claims founded on assessments conducted during the moratorium are unenforceable in the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In the absence of contemporaneous records or books of accounts showing actual deductions of employee provident fund contributions by the corporate debtor, unverified assessments conducted during the moratorium do not constitute assets in trust outside the insolvency estate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A resolution plan approved by the CoC and Adjudicating Authority bindingly resolves all claims, protecting the successful resolution applicant from surprise post-plan demands under the clean slate theory. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that post-moratorium assessment claims are barred, and the resolution plan approved in accordance with commercial wisdom cannot be invalidated for lack of full provisioning on unverified statutory claims.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. All interlocutory applications are disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: The EPFO filed an appeal challenging the NCLT's approval of a resolution plan that provided only Rs. 5,000/- against its revised claim of Rs. 18,33,528/- for PF dues. The NCLAT noted that the EPFO had conducted assessment proceedings and raised demands during the active moratorium period under Section 14 of the IBC, without supporting contemporaneous records in the corporate debtor's books. Reaffirming that post-moratorium assessments cannot create enforceable liabilities and upholding the clean slate principle for successful resolution applicants, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Tamil Nadu Power Producers Association vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Tamil Nadu Power Producers Association (TNPPA), representing independent power producers, and the Respondents include the Competition Commission of India (CCI), Chettinad International Coal Terminal Pvt. Ltd. (CICTPL), and Kamarajar Port Limited (KPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Following a Madras High Court ban on coal handling at Chennai Port from June 2011, thermal power producers routed coal imports through CICTPL's common user coal terminal at Kamarajar Port. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CICTPL increased its coal handling charges by 66.67% from Rs. 180 to Rs. 300 per metric tonne in October 2011 and imposed mandatory, unlisted third-party 'Coordination and Liasoning Charges'. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information was filed before the CCI in 2015; CCI issued a prima facie order on 04.01.2016; the DG submitted its main report on 24.03.2018 and supplementary report on 18.10.2019; and the CCI passed the final impugned order on 09.04.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence established that CICTPL was the sole common user coal terminal at Kamarajar Port, and third-party coordination charges were mandatory and managed by entities controlled by the Chettinad Group. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: TNPPA filed an appeal under Section 53B of the Competition Act, 2002, challenging the CCI's impugned order dated 09.04.2021 which had closed the case by holding CICTPL non-dominant.
legal_issues: Whether the CCI erred in defining the relevant product and geographic market by including Krishnapatnam Port and in holding that CICTPL did not hold a dominant position and did not abuse its dominance through mandatory third-party coordination and liasoning charges.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The relevant geographic market for low-value, high-volume commodities like coal must reflect transportation cost realities and consumer proximity, excluding distant ports that are economically non-substitutable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(r) read with Sections 19(6) and 19(7) of the Competition Act, 2002, requires rigorous analysis of consumer preference and hinterland characteristics rather than broad coastal generalizations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proximity constraints and captive transport economics prove that captive users cannot switch to distant ports, making a localized terminal a distinct relevant market where single-player presence constitutes dominance. 4.
