DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the CCI incorrectly included Krishnapatnam Port in the relevant geographic market and erroneously absolved CICTPL, setting aside the impugned order and remanding the matter back to the CCI for fresh adjudication.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 09.04.2021 passed by the CCI is set aside, and the appeal is allowed. The matter is remanded back to the CCI for a fresh decision in accordance with law. Parties are directed to appear before the CCI on 09.02.2026.
summary: The Appellant association challenged the CCI's order closing its antitrust complaint against Chettinad International Coal Terminal Pvt. Ltd. (CICTPL). The CCI had held that CICTPL was not dominant because Krishnapatnam Port exerted competitive constraints. The NCLAT found that the CCI erred in expanding the relevant geographic market to include distant ports, given the heavy transport costs faced by thermal power plants near Chennai. The Appellate Tribunal ruled that CICTPL was dominant in its relevant market and that the mandatory third-party coordination charges constituted an abuse of dominance. Consequently, the CCI's order was set aside and the matter was remanded for fresh consideration.

case_title: Shri Hrushikesh Balkrishna Paranjape vs. Shri Ajay Marathe & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Shri Hrushikesh Balkrishna Paranjape (Promoter Director of the Corporate Debtor), and the Respondents are Shri Ajay Marathe (Resolution Professional) and Canara Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was initiated against M/s Paranjape Agro Products India Pvt. Ltd. on 10.06.2022 pursuant to a Section 7 application by Canara Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: A transaction audit report revealed that stock-in-trade amounting to Rs. 6,56,25,806/- was written off in the books of accounts of the corporate debtor without supporting physical inventory or justification. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 10.06.2022; the transaction audit report was submitted on 12.11.2022; IA No. 1768 of 2023 was filed by the RP; and the Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order on 20.08.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transaction audits and unit visit reports indicated that physical stock was absent at the plant following loan sanction, and inventory write-offs were executed to clean up non-existent book stock as insolvency approached. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench-I) allowed IA No. 1768 of 2023 under Section 66 of the IBC, directing the Appellant to contribute Rs. 6,56,25,806/- to the corporate debtor, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the writing off of substantial inventory in the financial statements of a corporate debtor without physical verification or explanation during impending insolvency constitutes fraudulent trading under Section 66 of the IBC, rendering the promoter-director liable to contribute to the corporate debtor's assets.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 66(1) of the IBC, carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose—such as wiping out non-existent inventory through fictitious write-offs as insolvency looms—attracts personal contribution liability. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Massive write-offs of stock-in-trade that constitute a major percentage of annual income without explanatory notes or supporting physical inventory records are indicative of fraudulent fabrication of accounts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unverified claims of perished perishable goods or uncorroborated procurement from petty farmers fail to displace transaction audit findings that inventory was inflated and non-existent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the inventory write-off was a sham designed to mask non-existent stock and defraud creditors, thereby upholding the contribution order under Section 66.
operative_order: The appeal is devoid of merits and is dismissed with no order as to costs. All pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The Appellant, promoter director of Paranjape Agro Products India Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT order directing him to contribute Rs. 6,56,25,806/- under Section 66 of the IBC. The transaction audit had revealed that stock-in-trade worth over Rs. 6.56 crores was written off without physical inventory or board explanations as the company faced insolvency. The NCLAT affirmed that the write-off was a fraudulent maneuver to conceal non-existent inventory and clean up the books of accounts, and accordingly dismissed the appeal.

case_title: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II vs. M/s. Harshavardhan Cotton and Synthetic Mills Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II (EPFO), and the Respondents are the Liquidator of M/s. Harshavardhan Cotton and Synthetic Mills Private Limited and City Union Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor was covered under the EPF & MP Act, 1952, employing 181 workers; CIRP commenced on 12.03.2018, followed by a liquidation order on 03.12.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO filed a claim of Rs. 6,34,816/- consisting of interest and damages for default in paying EPF contributions for 2007–2015, which the liquidator admitted under Section 40(1) but categorized as government dues under Section 53(1)(e). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced on 03.12.2018; EPFO filed its claim on 01.01.2019; the liquidator realized Rs. 9,20,57,356/- from financial assets and distributed proceeds under Section 53; and the NCLT ordered dissolution of the corporate debtor on 17.11.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The liquidator distributed liquidation proceeds to secured creditors while treating the EPFO claim as general government dues, resulting in a nil payout to the EPFO. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: EPFO appealed against the NCLT order dated 17.11.2023 which had approved dissolution without settling its provident fund, interest, and damages claim in priority.
legal_issues: Whether provident fund dues, including interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B of the EPF Act, fall outside the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC and must be paid in priority over the waterfall mechanism in Section 53.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: All sums due to workmen or employees from provident, pension, and gratuity funds—including interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B—are expressly excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4) takes precedence over the waterfall distribution mechanism in Section 53, requiring third-party trust funds held or due from an employer to be kept outside liquidation estate recovery and paid in full. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The absence of a separate, segregated bank account does not alter the legal character of statutory employee dues; unremitted amounts are deemed to be held in trust and must be satisfied prior to general distribution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the liquidator erred in categorizing PF dues as government dues under Section 53(1)(e), directing the financial creditor who received distribution to remit the admitted sum to the EPFO.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. Respondent No. 2 (City Union Bank) is directed to remit the amount of Rs. 6,34,816/- to the Appellant within 30 days and report compliance to the NCLT. Interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The EPFO appealed against an NCLT order dissolving the corporate debtor after liquidating its assets and distributing proceeds under Section 53 of the IBC without paying the EPFO's claim of Rs. 6,34,816/- (comprising interest and damages). The NCLAT held that provident fund dues—including interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B—stand excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC and must be satisfied in priority over general waterfall distributions. Consequently, the financial creditor who received the proceeds was directed to remit the amount to the EPFO.

case_title: Subhash Chandra Mishra vs. Sunil Kumar, Bankrupt Trustee & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Subhash Chandra Mishra (Bankrupt Personal Guarantor), and the Respondents are Sunil Kumar (Bankruptcy Trustee) and another. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant gave personal guarantees for corporate debtors M/s Niroz Insulations Pvt. Ltd. and M/s Triveni Agrotraders Pvt. Ltd., leading to personal insolvency and subsequent bankruptcy proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The personal insolvency default amount was Rs. 5,35,53,097/-; following the rejection of a repayment plan, a bankruptcy order was passed against the Appellant on 06.11.2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bankruptcy order was passed on 06.11.2024; the bankruptcy trustee issued a debit freeze on the bankrupt's bank account; the bankrupt filed IA No. 585/JPR/2024; and the Adjudicating Authority dismissed the application on 06.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The bankruptcy trustee froze the bankrupt's bank account to secure the bankruptcy estate, while the bankrupt sought unfreezing to meet domestic and medical expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The bankrupt filed an appeal against the NCLT Jaipur Bench order dated 06.06.2025 which had rejected his application to unfreeze his bank account.
legal_issues: Whether funds lying in a bankrupt's bank account constitute part of the bankruptcy estate under Section 155 of the IBC or qualify as 'excluded assets' under Section 79(14)(b), and whether the bankruptcy trustee is legally mandated to release funds for domestic and medical needs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon the passing of a bankruptcy order, all property and bank balances belonging to the bankrupt vest in the bankruptcy trustee as part of the bankruptcy estate for distribution among creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The expression 'provisions' under Section 79(14)(b) of the IBC covers essential household consumables like food grains and edibles housed within a dwelling unit, and does not extend to general bank account balances or cash reserves. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Post-bankruptcy acquisitions and funds received after the bankruptcy commencement date do not vest automatically in the estate unless claimed via statutory notice under Section 159, while pre-existing account funds remain part of the divisible estate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority correctly refused to unfreeze the bank account, but clarified that post-commencement credits are exempt and the bankrupt may apply to the NCLT for specific medical or essential disbursements.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of: (i) The order refusing to unfreeze the bank account is upheld; (ii) Amounts received in the account subsequent to 06.11.2024 without a Section 159 notice must be released to the Appellant; (iii) The Appellant is at liberty to apply to the NCLT for release of funds for specific medical needs. Parties to bear their own costs.
summary: The Appellant, a bankrupt personal guarantor, challenged an NCLT order dismissing his application to unfreeze his bank account. He argued that funds in the account were necessary for domestic and medical needs and qualified as 'excluded assets' under Section 79(14)(b) of the IBC. The NCLAT held that bank balances form part of the bankruptcy estate and do not qualify as excluded provisions under Section 79(14)(b). However, the Appellate Tribunal ruled that funds credited after the bankruptcy commencement date without statutory notice must be released, and granted liberty to the bankrupt to move the NCLT for specific medical expenses.

case_title: Siemens Financial Services Private Limited vs. Ravi Kumar Jain & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1141 of 2025 & No. 1082 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in the primary appeal is Siemens Financial Services Private Limited (Financial Creditor), and the Respondents include Ravi Kumar Jain (Personal Guarantor/Director of RCC Infraventures Ltd.), Gulshan Kumar Gupta (Resolution Professional), and Smt. Sangita Narula (Auction Purchaser). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Siemens Financial Services Private Limited executed a Master Lease Agreement on 28.05.2019 with the lessee, RCC Infraventures Ltd., alongside a personal guarantee and an unconditional demand promissory note issued by Ravi Kumar Jain. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following default in lease rentals, the financial creditor recalled an outstanding amount of Rs. 9,97,31,150/- from both the lessee and the personal guarantor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A legal notice invoking the guarantee and recalling dues was issued on 07.12.2020; a demand notice under Rule 7 of the 2019 Rules was issued on 14.12.2020; Section 95 application was filed on 24.03.2021; an interim-moratorium commenced under Section 96; and the Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order rejecting the application on 04.07.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prior and subsequent to the insolvency filing, Union Bank of India initiated SARFAESI proceedings against the personal guarantor's residential property (Villa Apartment at The Palm Springs, Gurgaon) under a second charge, leading to an auction sale in April 2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Chandigarh Bench) rejected the Section 95 application as non-maintainable on grounds of alleged non-invocation and dismissed related interlocutory applications, resulting in cross-appeals by both the Financial Creditor and the Personal Guarantor.
legal_issues: Whether a legal notice recalling outstanding dues and demanding payment under a master lease and guarantee agreement constitutes a valid prior invocation of the personal guarantee for maintaining an application under Section 95 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 95 of the IBC against a personal guarantor is maintainable provided the personal guarantee has been validly invoked through a prior written demand communication in accordance with the terms of the guarantee deed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A demand notice issued under Rule 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority for Insolvency Resolution Process for Personal Guarantors to Corporate Debtors) Rules, 2019 does not serve as the sole permissible instrument for invocation if a prior written legal notice demanding the recalled debt has already been duly served upon the guarantor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court reviewed the contents of prior legal notices and guarantee clauses to ascertain whether a clear written demand for repayment was communicated to the guarantor prior to initiating insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the guarantee was not invoked, as the legal notice dated 07.12.2020 explicitly satisfied the written communication requirements under the guarantee deed, thereby making the Section 95 petition fully maintainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1141 of 2025 is allowed, and the impugned order dated 04.07.2025 is set aside. Company Petition (IB) No. 178/Chd/Hry/2021 and connected interlocutory applications stand revived for fresh consideration and expeditious disposal under Section 100 within three months. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1082 of 2025 is disposed of accordingly.
summary: Siemens Financial Services Private Limited appealed against an order of the NCLT, Chandigarh Bench, which rejected its Section 95 application against personal guarantor Ravi Kumar Jain on the premise that the personal guarantee had not been validly invoked prior to filing and that the petition lacked certain income tax returns. The NCLAT examined the record and established that a prior legal notice dated 07.12.2020 served as a valid written demand invoking the guarantee under the agreement terms. Finding the Adjudicating Authority's reasoning unfounded, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the dismissal order and revived the insolvency petition for a fresh decision under Section 100.

case_title: Fivebro Water Services Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Bijay Murmuria, Liquidator of Doshion Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1730 of 2025 & No. 1814 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Fivebro Water Services Pvt. Ltd. and Gondwana Engineers Ltd. (subsidiaries/lessees/licensees of the corporate debtor), and the Respondents include Bijay Murmuria (Liquidator of Doshion Pvt. Ltd.) and suspended directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate debtor executed an unregistered lease deed dated 29.09.2020 with Fivebro for its Ahmedabad premises and a license agreement dated 20.07.2021 with Gondwana Engineers for its Mumbai premises. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The liquidator sought possession of the leased/licensed premises and recovery of pending rental and license fee arrears from the subsidiaries following default during CIRP and liquidation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 31.08.2021; a fresh registered lease deed for the Ahmedabad premises was executed on 31.08.2021 (same day CIRP was ordered); liquidation commenced on 21.11.2023; and the Adjudicating Authority passed the common impugned order on 21.06.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The lease agreement for the Ahmedabad premises was registered on 31.08.2021 evening after the admission order was pronounced earlier that day, while the Mumbai license agreement remained unregistered under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench-I) allowed IA Nos. 63 and 94 of 2022 filed by the liquidator, directing the appellants to vacate the premises and pay rental dues, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to order the eviction of occupants from corporate debtor premises and recover rental dues, and whether lease agreements executed after the commencement of CIRP and moratorium are valid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC vests the Adjudicating Authority with wide jurisdiction to entertain and dispose of any question of law or facts arising out of or in relation to insolvency or liquidation proceedings, including the recovery of corporate debtor assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Lease or license agreements executed or registered after the commencement of CIRP and the imposition of moratorium under Section 14 violate statutory prohibitions against alienating or encumbering corporate debtor assets and are void. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The timing of registration of a lease agreement on the exact date of CIRP admission demonstrates an intent to keep assets out of the liquidation estate, rendering the transaction unenforceable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority acted well within its jurisdiction under Section 60(5) in directing the eviction of subsidiaries and the recovery of rent for the liquidation estate.
operative_order: The appeals lack merit and stand dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellants, subsidiary companies of the corporate debtor, challenged an NCLT common order directing them to vacate the Ahmedabad and Mumbai premises and pay pending rental arrears to the liquidator. The NCLAT held that lease agreements executed on the very day of CIRP admission violated the moratorium under Section 14, and that unregistered license agreements were void. Confirming that the Adjudicating Authority possesses residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to recover corporate debtor assets during liquidation, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals.

case_title: Bank of Maharashtra & Anr. vs. Ms. Vandana Garg & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 344 of 2022 & No. 345 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are the Bank of Maharashtra and the Central Bank of India (secured financial creditors who abstained or dissented during voting), and the Respondents include Ms. Vandana Garg (Resolution Professional/Monitoring Committee Chairperson), Sharad Sanghi (Successful Resolution Applicant), and Jyoti Structures Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was initiated against Jyoti Structures Limited, and an amended resolution plan submitted by Sharad Sanghi was approved by the CoC and subsequently by the Adjudicating Authority. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan on 27.03.2019, providing payouts to assenting financial creditors while limiting dissenting/abstaining financial creditors to liquidation value as per Section 30(2)(b)(ii). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 04.07.2017; the resolution plan was approved on 27.03.2019; an application (IA No. 2028 of 2021) seeking equal treatment of all secured financial creditors was filed by the appellant on 09.09.2021; the application was dismissed on 23.12.2021; and the appeal was filed on 04.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The resolution plan was fully implemented by November 2021, with business operations taken over by the new management and payouts under process when the appellants belatedly sought modification. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench) dismissed IA No. 2028 of 2021 on 23.12.2021, prompting the appellants to file these appeals challenging the distribution terms after a delay and long after plan approval.
legal_issues: Whether secured financial creditors who abstained or dissented from voting on a resolution plan can challenge the plan distribution terms long after its approval and implementation, and whether differential payouts between assenting and dissenting creditors violate the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application seeking modification of a resolution plan distribution after it has been approved and fully implemented constitutes an impermissible collateral challenge to the final plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b)(ii) of the IBC mandates that dissenting or non-assenting financial creditors receive an amount not less than their liquidation value, and distribution according to voting stance is permissible under commercial wisdom. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appeals filed years after a resolution plan has been approved, attained finality, and fully implemented are barred by gross delay, acquiescence, and limitation under Section 61(2) of the Code. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the appeals were barred by limitation and laches, and that a resolution plan once approved and implemented cannot be reopened to alter financial payouts.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed as not maintainable. All related interlocutory applications are disposed of. No orders as to costs.
summary: The Appellant banks, which had abstained or dissented during the voting on the resolution plan for Jyoti Structures Limited, filed applications in September 2021 seeking equal treatment with assenting financial creditors regarding plan payouts. Following the NCLT's dismissal of their applications, they appealed to the NCLAT. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals as barred by limitation and laches, noting that the resolution plan had been approved in March 2019 and fully implemented by November 2021, and that reopening it would upset settled corporate revival.

case_title: Ujwal Gupta vs. Union Bank of India Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ujwal Gupta (Personal Guarantor), and the Respondents are Union Bank of India (Financial Creditor, later replaced by CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.) and Vimal Kumar (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: M/s Green World International Pvt. Ltd. availed credit facilities under sanction letters dated 19.02.2013 and 13.03.2015, backed by a personal guarantee deed executed by the Appellant on 01.03.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate debtor's account was classified as NPA on 30.01.2016 following default in loan restructuring terms. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The loan was recalled via Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 29.02.2016; Form-B demand notice under the Personal Guarantor Rules was issued on 14.06.2021; Section 95 application was admitted on 10.09.2024, and the debt was assigned to CFM Asset Reconstruction on 07.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Section 13(2) notice explicitly named the appellant as guarantor/director, demanding repayment of outstanding credit facilities within 60 days, and co-guarantor father had initiated similar personal insolvency proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Bench-III) admitted the Section 95 application on 10.09.2024, prompting the personal guarantor to file the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a demand notice issued under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, addressed to a guarantor who is also a director, constitutes a valid prior invocation of a personal guarantee for maintaining an application under Section 95 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice issued under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act can serve as a valid invocation of a personal guarantee provided its wording and intent clearly demand repayment of corporate debts from the guarantor in terms of the guarantee agreement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where a guarantee deed stipulates general notice requirements without prescribing a rigid format or mandatory procedure, a formal demand notice calling upon the guarantor to discharge co-extensive liabilities satisfies invocation prerequisites. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Sufficiency of invocation is determined by examining whether the notice explicitly notifies the guarantor of the default and requires discharge of the guaranteed sum within a specified timeframe. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the SARFAESI notice dated 29.02.2016 validly invoked the personal guarantee, and affirmed the admission of the Section 95 insolvency application against the personal guarantor.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed. No order as to costs. Pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The Appellant, a personal guarantor, appealed against an NCLT order admitting a Section 95 application filed by Union Bank of India (later replaced by CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.). The Appellant contended that his personal guarantee was never validly invoked because the Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice addressed him as 'Director' rather than 'Guarantor'. The NCLAT held that the notice clearly demanded repayment of the corporate debtor's credit facilities and satisfied the general terms of the guarantee deed. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed and the personal insolvency initiation was affirmed.

case_title: M/s Klassy Enterprises vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Klassy Enterprises (sole proprietorship of Venkatesh Darak), and Respondents include the Competition Commission of India (CCI), Usha International Ltd., Nayan Agencies, Jawahar Brothers, Pune Zila Parishad, and People's All India Anti-Corruption and Crime Prevention Society. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pune Zila Parishad (Respondent No. 5) invited tenders for the procurement of Picofall-cum-sewing machines with ISI marks for distribution among backward classes, women, and disabled persons in rural areas. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Three authorized dealers of Usha International (the appellant, Respondent No. 3, and Respondent No. 4) submitted identical or razor-thin price bids from the same IP address and funded via pooled accounts, resulting in a penalty of Rs. 10,00,000/- imposed on each. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tender was floated on 07.11.2015; information was filed before the CCI in 2016; CCI ordered DG investigation on 22.03.2017; DG submitted reports on 28.03.2018 and 23.10.2019; and the CCI passed the final impugned order on 17.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic investigation established price parallelism, common IP address usage from the appellant's cyber cafe for uploading bids, centralized EMD/tender fee financing through third-party accounts, and heavy pre-bid phone call coordination. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Klassy Enterprises filed an appeal under Section 53B of the Competition Act, 2002, challenging the CCI's order dated 17.03.2021 finding it guilty of bid rigging and cartelization under Section 3(3)(d).
legal_issues: Whether the CCI correctly inferred cartelization and bid rigging under Section 3(3)(d) of the Competition Act based on circumstantial evidence such as price parallelism, common IP address usage, and shared financial arrangements for earnest money deposits.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Direct evidence of cartel formation and bid rigging is rarely available, and horizontal anti-competitive agreements can be legally inferred from a cumulative assessment of strong circumstantial evidence, price parallelism, and digital footprints. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(3) of the Competition Act raises a statutory presumption of appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC) for bid-rigging agreements, shifting the burden to the parties to rebut the presumption. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Simultaneous submission of bids from a single cyber cafe IP address, centralized EMD funding, and narrow price margins without cost justification establish collusive bidding. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the DG's investigation reports successfully established a concerted practice and bid rigging among the competing bidders, affirming the CCI's finding of guilt and proportionate penalty.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the impugned order passed by the Commission is affirmed. No order as to costs. Interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The Appellant challenged a CCI order finding it guilty of cartelization and bid rigging in a government tender for supplying sewing machines, and imposing a penalty of Rs. 10,00,000/-. The NCLAT reviewed the DG's investigative findings, which revealed that competing bidders had used a single IP address from the appellant's cyber cafe, shared EMD funding arrangements, and maintained suspicious telephonic contact prior to bidding. Upholding the CCI's reliance on circumstantial evidence and statutory presumptions under Section 3(3), the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal and affirmed the penalty.

case_title: Sh. Y.Y. Butchi Babu & Sri Surapaneni Ramesh vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 909 of 2024 & No. 936 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Sh. Y.Y. Butchi Babu and Sri Surapaneni Ramesh (Personal Guarantors to the Corporate Debtor, M/s Abir Infrastructure Private Limited), and the Respondents are State Bank of India (Financial Creditor) and M/s Abir Infrastructure Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities from State Bank of India backed by personal guarantees executed by the Appellants, resulting in corporate insolvency and subsequent resolution plan approval. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: State Bank of India filed a total claim of Rs. 3,617.70 crores in the corporate debtor's CIRP, of which Rs. 19.08 crores was admitted, and the approved resolution plan allocated Rs. 13.80 crores to SBI, leaving an unpaid balance of Rs. 5.28 crores plus continuing interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate debtor CIRP commenced on 30.01.2019; resolution plan was approved on 28.10.2021; SBI issued demand notices under Rule 7 on 28.10.2020 claiming Rs. 23.37 crores; Section 95 applications were filed on 09.02.2021; and the Adjudicating Authority admitted the applications on 22.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified bank statements established ongoing outstanding liabilities, while the guarantors relied on self-prepared reconciliation statements and pending DRT recovery proceedings to claim debt extinguishment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Bench-III) admitted the Section 95 applications against the personal guarantors on 22.03.2024, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in admitting Section 95 insolvency applications against personal guarantors when a balance debt remained unpaid post-resolution plan approval, and whether pending DRT recovery proceedings bar personal insolvency admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Approval of a resolution plan for a corporate debtor does not automatically discharge personal guarantors from co-extensive liabilities for unpaid residual debts unless explicitly stated in the plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Contractual clauses making a bank's certified statement of account binding and conclusive against guarantors override unilateral, self-prepared reconciliation statements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pendency of recovery proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) does not oust the jurisdiction of the NCLT or bar the initiation of insolvency resolution processes under Section 95 of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that legally recoverable debt continued to subsist against the personal guarantors, and affirmed the admission of the Section 95 insolvency proceedings.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed. Pending interlocutory applications are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellants, personal guarantors of M/s Abir Infrastructure Private Limited, appealed against NCLT orders admitting Section 95 insolvency applications filed by State Bank of India. They contended that substantial remittances had extinguished their liability and that pending DRT proceedings barred insolvency action. The NCLAT held that the bank's certified statements established a continuing unpaid balance post-resolution plan approval, that contractual terms bound the guarantors to bank computations, and that DRT proceedings do not bar IBC personal insolvency. Accordingly, the appeals were dismissed.

case_title: M/s Cine-Corp Filmdom Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mr. Ashok Kumar Gulla & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Cine-Corp Filmdom Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA), and the Respondents are Mr. Ashok Kumar Gulla (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Carnival Films Pvt. Ltd.) and the Committee of Creditors (through CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor, a cinema theatre operating company, vide order dated 22.03.2024 on an application filed under Section 9 of the IBC by an operational creditor (Amar Construction). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: SRA submitted a revised resolution plan valued at Rs. 23,19,00,000/-, approved by the CoC with a 93.31% voting majority, which contemplated utilizing available current account funds of around Rs. 20 crores (accrued from asset recoveries) for CIRP costs and creditor payouts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 22.03.2024; Form G was re-issued; the CoC approved the final resolution plan on 12.04.2025; and the Adjudicating Authority approved the plan with modifications on 28.08.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority in paragraph 25 of the approval order unilaterally imposed conditions prohibiting the SRA from utilizing the Corporate Debtor's current account funds for creditor payouts, directing that only SRA-contributed funds be used. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The SRA appealed under Section 61 against the Adjudicating Authority's (NCLT, Indore Bench) order dated 28.08.2025 in IA/2 (Plan) (MP) 2025 to the limited extent of modifying paragraph 25 conditions.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction under Section 31 of the IBC to unilaterally modify or impose conditions on commercial terms of a resolution plan approved by the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is non-justiciable and paramount; the Adjudicating Authority has strictly circumscribed jurisdiction under Section 31 to either approve or reject a compliant plan, but lacks jurisdiction to unilaterally modify its commercial terms. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) read with Section 30(2) does not empower the Adjudicating Authority to impose extraneous financial conditions; if a plan is compliant, it must be approved as submitted, or remitted back to the CoC if it fails Section 30(2) parameters. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the Adjudicating Authority expressly records satisfaction that a resolution plan complies with Section 30(2) and CIRP regulations, subsequent imposition of restrictions on the allocation or utilization of corporate funds constitutes an impermissible rewrite of the commercial contract. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the condition restricting utilization of the Corporate Debtor's current account funds was an unlawful interference with the CoC's commercial wisdom, setting aside the condition and remitting the matter for a clean approval order.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 28.08.2025 passed in IA (Plan)/2(MP)2025 is set aside to the extent of paragraph 25, and the application is revived and remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to pass a fresh approval order within 30 days strictly in accordance with law. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicant challenged conditions imposed by the NCLT Indore Bench in paragraph 25 of its order approving the resolution plan for Carnival Films Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had barred the SRA from using around Rs. 20 crores of funds lying in the Corporate Debtor's current account to pay creditors, despite explicit plan terms approved by 93.31% majority of the CoC. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to modify commercial terms or rewrite an approved resolution plan that satisfies statutory requirements. The condition was set aside and the matter remitted for a fresh approval order.

case_title: The State Trading Corporation of India vs. M/s Ganesh Benzoplast Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is The State Trading Corporation of India (Govt. of India Enterprise/Operational Creditor), and the Respondent is M/s Ganesh Benzoplast Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties entered into export credit facilities and domestic raw material procurement agreements supported by Letters of Credit between 2004 and 2007. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred from July 2007 onwards; total aggregate debt claimed under Section 9 petition was Rs. 28,34,13,327/- (comprising export transactions, domestic procurement, and uncollected 'C' Forms plus interest), while the Adjudicating Authority directed payment of Rs. 2,18,88,421/- as 25% principal under a BIFR scheme. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor was declared sick under SICA in 2011; a BIFR revival scheme was sanctioned on 04.12.2015; Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC was served on 20.03.2018; Section 9 petition was filed in 2018; and the impugned rejection order was passed on 13.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: In the BIFR scheme, the Appellant was listed under contingent liabilities rather than as an acknowledged unsecured creditor; the Respondent failed to make five annual equal installments from 2015 to 2020 as contemplated under Option 1 of the scheme. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench) refused to initiate CIRP and instead ordered the Corporate Debtor to deposit Rs. 2,18,88,421/- within 30 days under the BIFR scheme, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exercising jurisdiction under Section 9 of the IBC can decline CIRP admission and enforce a belated partial settlement based on an unfulfilled BIFR rehabilitation scheme where the operational debt was classified as a contingent liability.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is confined to ascertaining the existence of operational debt, default, and the absence of a pre-existing dispute, and cannot exercise equity jurisdiction to force a creditor into accepting a defunct or defaulted BIFR settlement scheme. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A debtor cannot shield itself from CIRP under a BIFR scheme when it has defaulted on the scheme's installment payment timelines and treated the creditor's claim merely as an un-crystallized contingent liability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Directing a corporate debtor to pay a substantial sum demonstrates the admission and existence of an unpaid, overdue debt, disproving the contention that no debt or default existed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in compelling acceptance of a 25% principal settlement instead of adjudicating the petition on statutory merits, setting aside the dismissal and reviving the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal succeeds and the impugned order dated 13.02.2020 is set aside. Company Petition C.P. (IB) 1975/MB/2018 is restored before the Adjudicating Authority for fresh decision strictly in accordance with law. Parties directed to appear on 05.02.2026. No costs.
summary: The State Trading Corporation of India appealed against an order of the NCLT Mumbai Bench which rejected its Section 9 application and instead directed the Corporate Debtor to pay a 25% scaled-down principal amount of Rs. 2,18,88,421/- based on a 2015 BIFR scheme. The NCLAT held that because the Corporate Debtor had failed to abide by the payment schedule prescribed under the BIFR scheme and had categorized the debt as a contingent liability, the Adjudicating Authority could not force an equitable settlement in lieu of determining debt and default under the Code. The dismissal was set aside and the Section 9 petition was restored.

case_title: Ujwal Gupta vs. Union Bank of India Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ujwal Gupta (Personal Guarantor), and Respondent No. 1 is Union Bank of India (whose debt was assigned during the appeal to CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.) with Respondent No. 2 being Vimal Kumar (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities were sanctioned to M/s Green World International Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) on 19.02.2013 and restructured on 13.03.2015, secured by a continuing, on-demand deed of personal guarantee executed by the Appellant on 01.03.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred when the borrower breached restructured loan covenants, leading to NPA classification on 30.01.2016 with total outstanding liability exceeding Rs. 9.85 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A loan recall demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act was issued on 29.02.2016; a demand notice in Form B under Rule 7(1) was issued on 14.06.2021; Section 95 petition was admitted on 10.09.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Section 13(2) notice was addressed directly to the Appellant calling upon him to clear the debt of Rs. 9,85,41,628.10 within 60 days, and his co-guarantor father had initiated insolvency relying on the same notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Bench-III) admitted the Section 95 petition on 10.09.2024, which the personal guarantor challenged on appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, addressed to an individual who is also a director, constitutes a legally valid invocation of a personal guarantee for triggering personal insolvency under Section 95 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The invocation of a personal guarantee is governed strictly by the terms of the guarantee deed; where no specific format is mandated, any clear written demand requiring the guarantor to discharge the principal debt within a stipulated period constitutes a valid invocation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Suffixing the word 'Director' to the name of a personal guarantor in a Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice does not strip the recipient of their legal character as a guarantor or invalidate the demand. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court evaluated the text and substance of the Section 13(2) notice and confirmed that it unequivocally demanded full discharge of the debt within 60 days, satisfying all requirements of an on-demand guarantee. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the personal guarantee was validly invoked through the Section 13(2) notice, and hyper-technical objections regarding authorization letters cannot derail proceedings where debt and default are established.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed. No order as to costs. Pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: The Appellant personal guarantor challenged an NCLT order admitting a Section 95 application filed by Union Bank of India (subsequently assigned to CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.). The Appellant argued that the bank's Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice addressed him as 'Director' and failed to invoke his personal guarantee. The NCLAT held that the deed of guarantee required only written demand and that the Section 13(2) notice clearly demanded discharge of the debt, constituting valid invocation. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the hyper-technical procedural challenges and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Raj Singh Gehlot vs. Anup Kumar, IRP of Aman Hospitality Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Raj Singh Gehlot (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Aman Hospitality Private Limited), and the Respondents are Anup Kumar (IRP) and Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of India sanctioned term loan facilities of Rs. 100 crores (disbursed Rs. 95 crores) and an additional Rs. 38 crores under a consortium arrangement for part-financing a five-star hotel project in Shahdara, Delhi. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was declared NPA on 31.03.2018; Section 7 petition claimed default of Rs. 119,00,94,695.68/- as on 31.03.2025; the Corporate Debtor tendered a demand draft of Rs. 119,00,94,695.68/- in full satisfaction before admission. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SARFAESI recall notice was issued on 22.05.2020; Section 7 application was filed on 08.05.2025; arguments concluded and orders were reserved on 10.12.2025; IA No. 21 of 2026 tendering the full draft was filed on 24.12.2025, in which notice was issued on 07.01.2026 fixing hearing for 02.02.2026; order admitting Section 7 was pronounced on 12.01.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor obtained a demand draft for the exact defaulted amount of Rs. 119,00,94,695.68/-, made it part of an application before the NCLT, and gave an express undertaking before the NCLAT to remit the entire sum directly to the Bank of India. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Principal Bench, New Delhi) admitted the Section 7 petition on 12.01.2026 while IA No. 21 of 2026 was pending for consideration, prompting the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting a Section 7 petition when the Corporate Debtor had filed an application offering to deposit the entire claimed default amount via demand draft and the Adjudicating Authority had issued notice on that application fixing a future hearing date.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The core purpose of Section 7 of the IBC is resolution of insolvency; where a corporate debtor demonstrates solvency and tenders the entire claimed defaulted debt prior to the pronouncement of an admission order, proceeding with insolvency is unjustified. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 does not compel CIRP initiation against an undeniably solvent debtor that tenders full payment of the claimed default amount, as the Code is not an instrument of debt recovery or punitive corporate demise. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: When an Adjudicating Authority enters into and issues notice on an interlocutory application tendering the entire defaulted debt with a scheduled future hearing date, it cannot ignore the pendency of that application and pronounce an admission order beforehand. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the admission order was unsustainable given the tender of the entire Rs. 119.01 crore default amount, setting aside the admission and directing payment to the bank subject to final DRT quantification.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed and the order dated 12.01.2026 admitting Section 7 is set aside. The Appellant is directed to hand over a fresh payment order for Rs. 119,00,94,695.68/- directly to the Bank of India within three days, subject to final adjudication of debt in pending OA No. 258 of 2021 before the DRT. Company Petition CP (IB) No. 276/ND/2025 is disposed of.
summary: The Suspended Director of Aman Hospitality Private Limited appealed against an NCLT order admitting Bank of India's Section 7 petition. Following the conclusion of arguments, the Corporate Debtor had filed an application offering to deposit the full default amount of Rs. 119,00,94,695.68/- via demand draft, in which the NCLT had issued notice and fixed a hearing date. However, the NCLT proceeded to admit the Section 7 petition before that hearing date. The NCLAT held that initiating CIRP against a demonstrably solvent entity that offers the entire claimed default amount defeats the objective of the IBC. The admission was set aside, and the Corporate Debtor was directed to hand over the full amount directly to the bank.

case_title: M/s Apaar Infratech Private Limited vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Apaar Infratech Private Limited (supplier of waterproofing admixtures), and the Respondents include the Competition Commission of India (CCI), Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation Limited (MSRDC), and Penetron India Private Limited along with its overseas parent and affiliates. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MSRDC supervised the construction of the Nagpur-Mumbai Super Communication Expressway (MSM Project) and issued technical specifications and an Identified Vendors List (IVL) for sourcing Crystalline Durability Admixture (CDA). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The informant alleged bid rigging and abuse of dominance under Sections 3 and 4, arguing that mandatory IRC accreditation and inclusion of three related/dummy vendors foreclosed market access for its product (Xypex) in an expressway package. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guidelines and IVL were issued on 19.11.2019; the Appellant filed an information under Section 19(1)(a) in 2022; the CCI considered the matter on 13.07.2022 and 10.08.2022; and passed the impugned order on 24.08.2022 closing the matter under Section 26(2). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Penetron India (R4) and its overseas parent Penetron International (R5) belong to the same corporate group operating at different levels of the supply chain, while MSRDC's infrastructure operations are limited to Maharashtra. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant appealed under Section 53B against the CCI's closure order dated 24.08.2022 which had held that no prima facie case was established under Section 26(2).
legal_issues: Whether the CCI erred in closing the information under Section 26(2) without ordering a Director General investigation, whether related entities in a parent-subsidiary vertical relationship can form a horizontal cartel under Section 3(3), and whether prescribing Indian Road Congress (IRC) accreditation by a regional development authority constitutes abuse of dominance under Section 4.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Entities forming part of the same corporate group operating at different levels of the production and distribution chain have a vertical relationship and cannot be prosecuted for horizontal cartelization or bid rigging under Section 3(3) of the Competition Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 4, assessing abuse of dominance requires delineating the relevant geographic market as the area where conditions of competition are sufficiently homogeneous; for heavy infrastructure procurement across India, a state road authority operating solely within one state is not a dominant buyer. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prescribing technical eligibility criteria, such as industry-standard Indian Road Congress (IRC) accreditation, is an ordinary quality-assurance measure and does not per se demonstrate unfair or discriminatory exclusionary conduct. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no procedural lapse in the CCI's decision to close the information under Section 26(2) without a DG investigation when the information on its face revealed no prima facie contravention.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the order dated 24.08.2022 passed by the Competition Commission of India in Case No. 24 of 2022 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an order of the Competition Commission of India closing its complaint under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act without ordering a Director General investigation. The Appellant alleged cartelization among Penetron group entities and abuse of dominance by MSRDC for mandating Indian Road Congress (IRC) accreditation in an expressway tender. The NCLAT upheld the CCI's closure, finding that parent-subsidiary entities in a vertical relationship cannot form a horizontal cartel under Section 3(3), and that MSRDC was not a dominant player in the pan-India market for heavy infrastructure procurement. Finding no prima facie violation, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. Mrudul Balwant Kulkarni vs. Mrs. Kakumanu Lakshmi & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Mrudul Balwant Kulkarni (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Harihar Infra Venture (India) Pvt. Ltd.), and the Respondents are Mrs. Kakumanu Lakshmi and five other flat allottees (Financial Creditors in a Class). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor entered into registered agreements for sale between 2016 and 2017 to sell fully furnished flats in its project 'Sai Hermitage', followed by Leave and License agreements promising monthly license fees due to delayed possession. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in license fees led to an earlier company petition that was settled via Consent Terms for Rs. 1,96,92,000/- in 12 installments, which the Corporate Debtor subsequently breached through dishonoured cheques. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Flat agreements were executed in 2016-2017; initial CIRP petition was filed in 2019 and settled on 01.12.2019; fresh Section 7 petition (CP (IB) No. 88 of 2021) was filed in 2021; Adjudicating Authority admitted the petition on 15.03.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor contended that the allottees were speculative investors and that the petition failed to meet the statutory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% of total project allottees under Section 7(1), claiming 112 booked units, while the allottees cited Maharashtra RERA data showing zero allotments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench) admitted the Section 7 petition on 15.03.2023 without determining the total number of allottees in the project, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether flat allottees who enter into leave and license agreements and subsequent consent terms for unpaid license fees lose their status as genuine financial creditors in a class, and whether the Section 7 application satisfied the statutory numerical threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The execution of leave and license agreements or subsequent consent terms to compensate allottees for delayed possession does not alter the original nature of the financial debt or strip allottees of their status as financial creditors in a class. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, it is a mandatory statutory requirement that an application by allottees under a real estate project be filed jointly by not less than 100 allottees or not less than 10% of the total number of allottees in the project, whichever is less. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must record a specific, affirmative factual finding on the total number of allotted units in the project to ascertain whether the applicant allottees satisfy the numerical threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the allottees were genuine financial creditors and that breach of consent terms could trigger Section 7, but set aside the admission order and remanded the matter because the Adjudicating Authority had failed to determine whether the six allottees fulfilled the statutory threshold under Section 7(1).
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned admission order dated 15.03.2023 is set aside, and the case is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority to decide afresh whether the application fulfills the threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1). Connected contempt application is closed.
summary: The Suspended Director of Harihar Infra Venture (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by six flat allottees following the breach of settlement consent terms. The Appellant argued that the allottees were speculative investors and that six allottees did not meet the statutory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% of the total project. The NCLAT affirmed that the allottees were genuine financial creditors entitled to invoke Section 7 upon default. However, because the NCLT had admitted the petition without verifying the total number of project allotments to determine whether the statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) was met, the admission order was set aside and remanded for determination of that threshold.

case_title: M/s Canbank Factors Limited vs. Brijesh Singh Bhaduria & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Canbank Factors Limited (an NBFC/Factor), and the Respondents are Brijesh Singh Bhaduria (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s RCI Industries & Technologies Limited) and JTL Industries Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Master Financer Agreement and Master Buyer Agreement on the TReDS 'M1' platform, the Appellant discounted eight invoices raised by trade suppliers on the Corporate Debtor for goods supplied in the ordinary course of business. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to honor the factored invoices upon maturity; the Appellant filed a claim of Rs. 6,35,51,472.63 in Form C asserting status as a Financial Creditor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 25.11.2022; the Appellant submitted Form C on 17.12.2022; the RP advised submission under Form B on 18.12.2022; the Appellant filed IA No. 2208/2023 on 19.04.2023; the CoC approved a resolution plan with 98.05% voting on 05.06.2024; and the NCLT dismissed the IA on 13.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant made payments directly to suppliers for goods delivered to the Corporate Debtor on the TReDS platform; no loan or direct funds were disbursed to the Corporate Debtor for the time value of money. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Bench) dismissed the Appellant's application seeking classification as a Financial Creditor, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether receivables acquired by a factor or financier through invoice discounting on an electronic TReDS platform constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) or retain their character as an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The legal character of a debt under the IBC depends on the substance of the underlying commercial transaction; discounting and assigning trade invoices does not transform an operational debt into a financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, a financial debt requires a disbursement made to the corporate debtor against consideration for the time value of money, whereas Section 5(20) explicitly includes assignees of operational debts within the definition of operational creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a factor pays suppliers directly for goods supplied to a buyer and receives an assignment of receivables without disbursing funds to the corporate debtor, the factor merely steps into the shoes of the suppliers as an operational creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT reaffirmed its precedent in Mudraksh Investfin, holding that invoice discounting on TReDS represents an operational debt and that the RP correctly rejected the financial creditor claim under Form C.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed and the order dated 13.02.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. All related interlocutory applications are disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: Canbank Factors Limited appealed against an NCLT order dismissing its application to be classified as a Financial Creditor in the CIRP of RCI Industries & Technologies Limited. The Appellant had discounted invoices on the TReDS platform for goods supplied to the Corporate Debtor and argued that the assignment of receivables constituted a financial debt. The NCLAT held that because no funds were disbursed to the Corporate Debtor for the time value of money, the underlying transaction remained the supply of goods. Consequently, the assigned debt was operational in nature, and the rejection of the claim under Form C was affirmed.

case_title: Heena Metal Private Limited vs. Global Extrusions Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Heena Metal Private Limited (Operational Creditor), and the Respondent is Global Extrusions Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties engaged in mutual sales and purchases of ferrous and non-ferrous metal products, operating through the Appellant's units in Jamnagar and Mumbai under a running barter arrangement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed an operational debt of Rs. 1,44,39,812/- (Principal: Rs. 1,19,67,353/- and Interest: Rs. 24,72,466/-), which included Rs. 73,59,059/- transferred from its closed Jamnagar unit. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices for the Jamnagar unit were raised between 25.05.2016 and 27.06.2017; a journal entry transferring the Jamnagar balance to Mumbai was made on 31.03.2020; a Demand Notice under Section 8 was issued on 22.11.2021; and the Section 9 petition was filed on 03.05.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The principal claim included four invoices from 2016 totaling Rs. 42,57,226/- where the three-year limitation had expired prior to March 2020, and the signed ledger contained no explicit promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench) dismissed the Section 9 petition on 29.11.2023 on grounds that the enforceable debt fell below the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 crore after excluding time-barred claims, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether unilateral journal entries transferring older balances from a closed unit to another unit revive time-barred claims under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 or Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 to meet the Rs. 1 crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unilateral ledger transfers and internal journal entries cannot revive already time-barred debts to meet the statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act must occur before the expiration of the original limitation period; an acknowledgment made after limitation has lapsed is of no legal effect. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To constitute an enforceable agreement under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a document must contain an express and unambiguous promise to pay a time-barred debt, rather than a mere routine balance entry or internal ledger acknowledgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that deducting the time-barred invoices reduced the surviving operational debt well below the Rs. 1 crore threshold, and affirmed the dismissal of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the order dated 29.11.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. All related interlocutory applications are disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed against an NCLT order dismissing its Section 9 application on the ground that its valid claim fell below the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 crore. The Appellant had merged outstanding invoices from 2016 into its Mumbai accounts via a 2020 journal entry to claim an operational debt of Rs. 1.44 crores. The NCLAT held that internal ledger transfers and routine balance confirmations cannot revive time-barred claims under Section 18 of the Limitation Act or Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. Excluding the time-barred claims brought the default below the Rs. 1 crore threshold, justifying dismissal of the petition.

case_title: Harish Kumar Mittal vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is State Bank of India (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor is Mercator Limited; Personal Guarantor is Harish Kumar Mittal, ex-director of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Resolution Professional is Rajas Shreeram Bodas (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI extended diverse credit facilities including cash credit, working capital, and term loans to Mercator Limited, renewed via Sanction and Revival Letters dated 02.04.2018 and 01.04.2019, secured by an irrevocable and continuing Deed of Guarantee executed by the Appellant on 25.03.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was INR 236,19,05,443.21; the Corporate Debtor's account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset on 23.04.2019, with default formally crystalized on 31.10.2019 and deemed authenticated on the Information Utility on 18.03.2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recall Notice issued on 31.10.2019 demanding payment within 7 days; Form-B Demand Notice issued under Rule 7(1) on 01.06.2021; Section 95(1) petition CP (IB) No. 798/MB/2021 filed on 28.07.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Guarantee dated 25.03.2013, debt acknowledgment letters from 2013 to 2019, Information Utility record dated 18.03.2021, and Section 99 RP Report; Appellant countered with Commercial Suit No. 1353 of 2019 (Suit No. 315 of 2020) claiming damages of Rs. 418.43 Crores against SBI for delay in granting NOC for sale of vessel M/T Nerissa and overcharged SBLC commissions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed CP (IB) No. 798/MB/2021 on 28.07.2021 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV; Appellant e-filed reply belatedly on 01.03.2024 but failed to bring it formally on record; NCLT admitted the petition on 09.12.2024 under Section 100 initiating PIRP.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against an insolvency order under Section 100 in a Section 95 petition is maintainable under Section 61; whether non-consideration of an improperly e-filed reply violates natural justice; and whether pre-existing disputes, allegations of insufficient stamping of a guarantee deed, or defects in recall notices preclude initiation of Personal Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 100.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In personal guarantor insolvency resolution proceedings under Sections 95 to 100 of the IBC, the presence of a pre-existing commercial dispute, unliquidated cross-claims, or technical stamp duty deficiencies on security documentation does not bar admission once the foundational debt disbursement and guarantee default are established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(1) and Section 61(1) read conjointly confer appellate jurisdiction on NCLAT over personal guarantor insolvency orders rendered under Part III; the doctrine of 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) is strictly confined to Section 9 operational debts and has no statutory bearing on Section 7 or Section 95 applications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal applied a summary adjudication standard: proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority are summary in nature where the strict provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Indian Evidence Act, 1872 do not apply, limiting the judicial inquiry strictly to establishing default based on records and the Section 99 report. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that natural justice was observed as the guarantor was heard on merits, the guarantee and default of INR 236.19 Crores were undisputed, subsequent dismissal of the guarantor's civil suit rendered dispute claims infructuous, and the Section 100 admission was fully justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2363 of 2024 is dismissed; all connected Interlocutory Applications are disposed of; no orders as to costs.
summary: State Bank of India filed an application under Section 95 of the IBC against Harish Kumar Mittal, personal guarantor to corporate debtor Mercator Limited, for default of Rs. 236.19 Crores. NCLT Mumbai admitted the petition under Section 100 on 09.12.2024, noting the personal guarantor had failed to place his reply formally on record. The guarantor appealed under Section 61, alleging breach of natural justice, pre-existing commercial disputes pending before the Bombay High Court, insufficient stamping of the guarantee deed, and defects in the loan recall notice. NCLAT affirmed that Section 61 appeals are maintainable, natural justice was satisfied since the appellant was heard on merits, pre-existing disputes and stamp objections are inapplicable to summary Section 95/100 proceedings, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Manoj K. Sheth vs. The Secretary, Competition Commission of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Informant/Appellant is Manoj K. Sheth, an individual securities trader; Respondent No. 1 is the Competition Commission of India; Respondent No. 2 is the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (NSE). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of Co-Location Facilities and Tick-by-Tick (TBT) market data feed dissemination over TCP/IP protocol by NSE to eligible trading members on rack-rental basis commencing August 2009 to facilitate Direct Market Access and algorithmic trading. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Anti-trust complaint alleging market manipulation, front-running, and information asymmetry involving daily trading volumes of Rs. 2-3 lakh crores; underlying SEBI regulatory orders had directed disgorgement of Rs. 624.89 Crores against NSE. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) on 23.09.2019; CCI conducted preliminary conferences on 25.08.2020 and 17.12.2020; impugned closure order passed under Section 26(2) on 28.06.2021; appeal lodged before NCLAT in 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Whistle-blower complaints from 2015, SEBI Technical Advisory Committee Report dated 02.03.2016, Deloitte forensic review dated 23.12.2016, Ernst & Young audit reports, SAT appellate order dated 23.01.2023 overturning SEBI fraud/disgorgement findings, and SEBI order dated 13.09.2024 confirming absence of employee collusion or crowding out. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Manoj K. Sheth filed Case No. 35 of 2019 before CCI alleging abuse of dominance under Section 4; CCI dismissed the information at the threshold stage under Section 26(2) on 28.06.2021 finding no prima facie case of competition contravention.
legal_issues: Whether the CCI erred in closing the information under Section 26(2) without directing a Director General investigation under Section 26(1); and whether NSE abused its dominant position under Section 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(c) through its co-location infrastructure, lack of load balancers and randomizers, and secondary server access.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An enterprise holding a dominant position does not violate antitrust statutes merely by offering specialized, fee-based technological infrastructure on uniform, non-discriminatory terms; establishing abuse of dominance mandates an effects-based analysis demonstrating actionable anti-competitive harm rather than technical imperfections. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4 proscribes abuse of dominance rather than dominance per se, requiring two distinct findings: the practice falls within Section 4(2) and results in, or is likely to result in, an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC); furthermore, forming an opinion under Section 26(1) requires objective prima facie satisfaction, absent which closure under Section 26(2) is statutory. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Effects-based appraisal and sectoral primacy test: the tribunal evaluated technical findings by sectoral regulators and independent forensic auditors (SEBI, SAT, Deloitte, EY), holding that hearsay reports and speculative allegations fail to meet the preponderance of probabilities standard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that NSE offered co-location services on an open first-come-first-served basis without denying market access or creating foreclosure, technical choices were bona fide for a nascent market, and CCI rightly refused to order a DG investigation.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 20 of 2021 is dismissed; all pending Interlocutory Applications stand disposed of; no order as to costs.
summary: Manoj K. Sheth appealed under Section 53B of the Competition Act against CCI's order dated 28.06.2021 in Case No. 35 of 2019, which closed at the threshold under Section 26(2) his complaint alleging NSE abused its dominant position via its co-location facilities and TCP/IP data dissemination architecture favoring select brokers. Appellant alleged violations of Section 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(c). NCLAT affirmed CCI's order, holding that dominance is not per se unlawful without proven anti-competitive abuse and appreciable adverse effect on competition. Co-location was offered uniformly on first-come-first-served terms, technical infrastructure decisions were bona fide, and reliance on SEBI and SAT exonerating findings was lawful, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India vs. Truvisory Insolvency Professionals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI, statutory regulator); Respondent No. 1 is Truvisory Insolvency Professionals Pvt. Ltd.; Respondents No. 2 and 3 are Successful Resolution Applicant/Stakeholders in the CIRP of Township Developers India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), originally initiated by Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Township Developers India Ltd. culminating in approval of a Resolution Plan under IA (IBC) (Plan) No. 53 of 2025 in CP (IB) No. 77/MB/2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount and specific date of default are not specified in the delay condonation proceedings arising out of the approval order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned approval order passed on 13.08.2025; appeal filed on 24.12.2025 alongside IA No. 391 of 2026 seeking condonation of 103 days delay beyond the initial 30 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Official record of limitation reflecting 103 days delay in filing the memo of appeal; Respondent No. 2 filed an affidavit in reply asserting that the delay exceeds the statutory permissible extension of 15 days under Section 61(2). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV allowed IA (IBC) (Plan) No. 53 of 2025 approving the Resolution Plan on 13.08.2025; IBBI filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 110 of 2026 on 24.12.2025 accompanied by IA No. 391 of 2026 praying for condonation of 103 days delay.
legal_issues: Whether Section 198 of the IBC overrides Section 61(2) so as to empower the Appellate Tribunal to condone an appeal filing delay beyond the outer limit of 15 days; and whether the power conferred upon the Adjudicating Authority under Section 198 can be exercised by NCLAT to extend appellate limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The non-obstante clause contained in Section 198 of the IBC applies strictly to the performance of administrative and regulatory duties by the Board within statutorily specified periods before the Adjudicating Authority, and cannot be invoked to override the mandatory, non-extendable appellate limitation period prescribed under Section 61(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) strictly restricts appellate condonation of delay to a maximum period of 15 days upon demonstration of sufficient cause; Section 198 empowers only the relevant 'Adjudicating Authority' to condone delay when the Board fails to perform a specific statutory act (e.g., under Sections 16(4), 27(4), 82(4)), and has no relevance to appellate limitation periods governing the NCLAT. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Textual and contextual statutory interpretation standard (Peerless General Finance principle): the statute must be construed as an integrated whole, precluding courts from reading words into or rewriting rigid statutory limitation limits under the guise of purposive interpretation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that NCLAT has no jurisdiction to condone any delay exceeding 15 days under Section 61(2), Section 198 cannot override appellate limitation, and IBBI's 103 days delay is fatal.
operative_order: I.A. No. 391 of 2026 is rejected and Memo of Appeal in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 110 of 2026 is rejected as barred by time.
summary: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 110 of 2026 challenging an NCLT Mumbai order dated 13.08.2025 approving a Resolution Plan in the CIRP of Township Developers India Ltd. The appeal was filed on 24.12.2025 with a 103-day delay, accompanied by IA No. 391 of 2026 seeking condonation under Section 198 of the IBC. IBBI contended that Section 198's non-obstante clause overrides Section 61(2). NCLAT held that Section 198 applies only to the performance of regulatory and administrative acts by the Board before the Adjudicating Authority and cannot override the rigid 15-day maximum condonation limit under Section 61(2), rejecting both the application and appeal.

case_title: Vinita Agarwala & Ors. vs. Power Pack Steel Industries Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors are Mrs. Vinita Agarwala and 9 other individual lenders (Appellants); Corporate Debtor is Power Pack Steel Industries Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants disbursed short-term business loans to Corporate Debtor between 2015 and 2017 carrying interest @ 15% per annum repayable on demand (e.g., Appellant No. 1 disbursed Rs. 40,00,000/- on 29.06.2017 via RTGS UTR No HDFCR52017062998853644 to Federal Bank). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed financial debt was Rs. 1,73,02,690/- (principal sum of Rs. 1,57,00,000/- plus interest of Rs. 16,02,690/-); Appellant No. 1 claimed Rs. 40,00,000/- with default occurring on 30.06.2018 after demand in March 2018. 4.
