STATUTORY TIMELINES: Repayment demanded in March 2018; Corporate Debtor promised repayment by 30.06.2018; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 150/CTB/2019 filed before NCLT Cuttack in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank transfer records evidencing disbursement, Form 26AS TDS statements for AY 2017-18 reflecting tax deduction on interest, Corporate Debtor's bank transfers of interest @ 18% on 20.10.2018 (Rs. 1,36,110/-) and 01.11.2018 (Rs. 27,221/-), and creditor ledger entries. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed before NCLT Cuttack Bench; dismissed on 07.01.2022 on the ground that borrowing from public violated Section 73(1) of Companies Act, 2013, rendering transactions void under Section 23 of Contract Act and unenforceable under IBC.
legal_issues: Whether an unsecured loan accepted by a corporate debtor in alleged violation of Section 73 of the Companies Act, 2013 renders the underlying transaction void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, thereby precluding admission of a Section 7 petition under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate debtor cannot shield itself from insolvency resolution by pleading its own regulatory infraction in accepting deposits under the Companies Act, as a company cannot take advantage of its own wrong to render a commercial borrowing unenforceable under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Financial debt under Section 5(8) requires disbursement for the time value of money; non-compliance with deposit acceptance conditions under Section 73 or Section 76 of the Companies Act attracts penal liabilities under Section 76A but does not invalidate the debt or interdict its repayment; under Section 238, the IBC overrides provisions of the Companies Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Innoventive Industries standard: the Adjudicating Authority is merely required to satisfy itself that default has occurred based on evidence of disbursement and interest payment, without requiring a formal written contract. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that financial debt and default were conclusively established by bank transfers and Form 26AS TDS deductions, Section 73 does not interdict debt payability, and the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: The order dated 07.01.2022 rejecting Section 7 application is set aside; Adjudicating Authority directed to admit Section 7 application after four weeks; Corporate Debtor granted 30 days to discharge the debt and place proof before NCLT; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: Appellants granted short-term business loans totaling Rs. 1.73 Crores (principal Rs. 1.57 Crores) between 2015 and 2017 to Power Pack Steel Industries Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor paid interest via bank transfers and deducted TDS but defaulted on principal repayment after June 2018. Appellants filed a Section 7 IBC petition, which NCLT Cuttack rejected on 07.01.2022, holding that accepting deposits from public violated Section 73(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, rendering the contracts void under Section 23 of the Contract Act. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that a debtor cannot take advantage of its own wrong, Section 73 does not extinguish commercial debt, IBC overrides the Companies Act under Section 238, and directed admission of Section 7.

case_title: Navin Ashokkumar Aswani vs. Falcon Industries & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Falcon Industries (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor is Geeta Prints Ltd., represented by Suspended Director Navin Ashokkumar Aswani (Appellant); Respondent No. 2 is Rajendra Sanghi (Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of diverse goods/products by Falcon Industries to Geeta Prints Ltd. commencing from May 2002 under various commercial invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed debt was Rs. 4,43,14,429/- comprising principal amount of Rs. 7,62,500/- and unilateral interest @ 24% p.a. compounded quarterly amounting to Rs. 4,35,51,929/-; default arose upon non-payment of invoices within 30 days in 2004. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account confirmation letter dated 03.03.2004; reconciliation letter by Corporate Debtor sent on 24.05.2004; statutory winding-up notice under Sections 433 and 434 of Companies Act, 1956 issued on 09.09.2004; CP No. 240 of 2004 filed in Gujarat High Court in 2004; transferred on 25.11.2021; Form-5 Section 9 petition filed on 24.02.2022 (converted on 04.03.2022). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Signed balance confirmation letter dated 03.03.2004 acknowledging Rs. 7,62,500/-, letter dated 24.05.2004 alleging exaggerated rates, invoice Note 1 stipulating 24% interest if unpaid after 30 days, and interim deposit of Rs. 4.5 Lakhs made by Corporate Debtor before the High Court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Gujarat High Court admitted CP No. 240 of 2004 on 11.12.2006 and transferred it on 25.11.2021 to NCLT Ahmedabad Bench as TP No. 02 of 2022; NCLT admitted the converted Section 9 application on 13.01.2026 holding threshold was Rs. 1 Lakh and disputes were moonshine.
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition admitted by a High Court and subsequently transferred to NCLT under Section 434(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 is automatically admitted under Section 9 of the IBC; whether the enhanced Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore applies to converted petitions; and whether unilateral interest printed on invoices can be included to cross the statutory threshold.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon transfer and conversion of a winding-up petition into an application under Section 9 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority cannot mechanically admit the petition based on a prior High Court admission order and must independently evaluate statutory maintainability, wherein the enhanced monetary threshold applies and unilaterally claimed invoice interest cannot be aggregated absent express agreement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The fifth proviso to Section 434(1)(c) mandates that transferred proceedings be treated as fresh applications under the IBC; when converted after 24.03.2020, the amended Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore strictly governs; unilateral invoice notes charging interest do not constitute a contractual agreement for interest under operational debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual consensus and threshold verification standard: unilateral invoice stipulations charging 24% interest cannot be enforced against a debtor absent an express agreement or course of dealing reflecting payment or written acceptance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that although Corporate Debtor's rate dispute was an afterthought, the operational debt was limited to the principal of Rs. 7,62,500/-, which failed to satisfy the mandatory Rs. 1 Crore threshold applicable to 2022 conversions, invalidating Section 9 admission.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 13.01.2026 admitting Section 9 is set aside; Appellant directed to pay Rs. 4.5 Lakhs with 12% compound interest calculated from 04.04.2006 to Respondent No. 1 within 30 days; Corporate Debtor permitted to withdraw its deposit from High Court; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: Falcon Industries filed a winding-up petition in 2004 against Geeta Prints Ltd. for Rs. 7,62,500/-, which was admitted by the Gujarat High Court in 2006 and transferred to NCLT Ahmedabad in 2021, where it was converted into a Section 9 IBC application claiming Rs. 4.43 Crores (including Rs. 4.35 Crores as 24% interest). NCLT admitted the application on 13.01.2026 applying a Rs. 1 Lakh threshold. On appeal by the suspended director, NCLAT held that transferred petitions converted after 24.03.2020 must satisfy the amended Rs. 1 Crore threshold, unilateral interest in invoices cannot be included without an agreement, and the principal debt of Rs. 7.62 Lakhs fell below the threshold. NCLAT set aside the admission order and directed payment of Rs. 4.5 Lakhs with 12% compound interest.

case_title: Religare Finvest Limited vs. Strategic Credit Capital Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Financial Creditor is Religare Finvest Limited (RFL), an NBFC; Respondent/Corporate Debtor is Strategic Credit Capital Private Limited (SCCPL, formerly Kalinga Finlease Pvt. Ltd.), an NBFC and Financial Service Provider registered under RBI Act whose Certificate of Registration was surrendered/cancelled on 25.01.2019; original lender was Nishu Finlease Private Limited (NFPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 21.07.2015, NFPL disbursed a term loan of Rs. 40,00,00,000/- to SCCPL repayable in 12 months, secured by a pledge over 1,32,33,328 equity shares of ABG Shipyard Limited. On 16.06.2016, NFPL assigned all rights under the loan agreement to RFL for Rs. 45,00,00,000/-. On 01.07.2017, RFL, SCCPL, and Perpetual Capital & Servicing Pvt. Ltd. executed a multi-party Settlement Agreement acknowledging admitted collective dues of Rs. 793,67,20,176/- (subsuming the Rs. 40 Crore loan), obligating SCCPL and Perpetual to realize Rs. 400 Crores on best-efforts basis into an escrow account within 9 months. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount of Rs. 60,97,80,821.86 as on 31.05.2019 (comprising principal of Rs. 40 Crores plus interest at 12% p.a.); date of default was asserted as 24.06.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Termination cum Recall Notice issued on 24.06.2016 demanding Rs. 45,00,00,000/-; Settlement Agreement executed on 01.07.2017; Section 7 petition IB No. 1628 (PB) of 2019 filed before NCLT on 10.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term Loan Agreement dated 21.07.2015, Sale Agreement dated 16.06.2016, Termination cum Recall Notice dated 24.06.2016, Settlement Agreement dated 01.07.2017 (Recital C and Schedule C Part B), audited financial statements of SCCPL for FY 2015-16 reflecting borrowing under other non-current liabilities, and RBI CoR cancellation order dated 25.01.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition filed on 10.06.2019 was dismissed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi on 25.11.2022 on the ground that the loan was subsumed into the all-encompassing Settlement Agreement dated 01.07.2017, which constituted an agreement for recovery rather than establishing a creditor-debtor debt relationship.
legal_issues: Whether a petition under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable against an entity that was a registered NBFC and Financial Service Provider at the time the financial transactions were entered into, notwithstanding the subsequent cancellation of its Certificate of Registration; whether an assigned loan remains an independent, actionable financial debt or becomes subsumed within an all-encompassing multi-party Settlement Agreement operating as a recovery mechanism; and whether the Section 7 petition was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity that operated as a regulated Financial Service Provider at the time the underlying financial borrowing and transactions were executed falls outside the definition of a corporate person under insolvency law, barring insolvency proceedings against it; moreover, where an underlying loan is subsumed within a convoluted, collusive multi-party settlement framework structured for mutual recovery rather than straightforward lending, it ceases to be an independent financial debt establishing a creditor-debtor relationship. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 3(7) and 3(8) read with Section 3(17) of the IBC exclude a Financial Service Provider from the definition of 'corporate debtor'; the status of the entity at the time the financial transaction was undertaken is determinative of whether Section 7 applies. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict threshold scrutiny of the bona fides of the underlying transaction and creditor-debtor jural relationship; where transactions involve circular dealings, price rigging of pledged securities (ABG Shipyard shares), and profit-sharing mechanisms in an escrow recovery structure, the summary test of debt and default fails. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because SCCPL was a Financial Service Provider at the time of the transaction, and the loan was part of a collusive, deep, and convoluted recovery arrangement subsumed under the Settlement Agreement, Section 7 was non-maintainable, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: Appeal is dismissed. All related Interlocutory Applications are also dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: Religare Finvest Limited appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order dated 25.11.2022 dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Strategic Credit Capital Private Limited for default of Rs. 60.97 Crores. The claim stemmed from an assigned Rs. 40 Crore loan from Nishu Finlease secured by ABG Shipyard shares and subsequent multi-party Settlement Agreement dated 01.07.2017. NCLAT held that the Section 7 petition was fundamentally non-maintainable under Section 3(7) read with Section 3(8) of the Code because the Respondent was a registered NBFC and Financial Service Provider at the time of the financial transactions. Furthermore, the underlying transaction was part of a collusive, convoluted recovery structure rather than an independent financial debt. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Rajendra Narayan Panda vs. Shri Mangesh Vittal Kekre & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Omkara Assets Reconstruction Private Limited (assignee of L&T Finance Limited); Corporate Debtor is Panda Technologies India Private Limited; Appellant is Rajendra Narayan Panda, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 is Resolution Professional Mangesh Vittal Kekre. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 17.07.2013, L&T Fincorp Limited (later merged into L&T Finance Ltd.) sanctioned a revolving short-term financing facility of Rs. 1,50,00,000/- with a tenure of 90 days at 13.75% interest p.a., with delayed payment charges of 16% p.a. for 91-120 days and 22% p.a. beyond 121 days; debt was assigned to Omkara ARC on 24.09.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date occurred on 24.04.2017 (NPA declared on 11.06.2016); in Form 1, claimed debt was Rs. 1,40,40,535/- (principal Rs. 64,33,286/- plus interest of Rs. 76,07,249/-); balance sheet acknowledged principal of Rs. 40,06,310/- plus delayed payment charges aggregating over Rs. 1,04,71,252/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 19.04.2017 seeking Rs. 67,19,390/-; loan recall notice issued by assignee on 18.12.2021; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 40 (MP) 2022 filed on 04.04.2022 (registered 06.04.2022). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letter and Facility Agreement dated 17.07.2013, Assignment Agreement dated 24.09.2019, balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor for FY 2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18, 2018-19, and 2019-20 acknowledging subsisting debt, and Information Utility Record of Default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed on 04.04.2022 was admitted by NCLT Indore Bench on 21.01.2025 after setting the Corporate Debtor ex-parte on 23.02.2023 and subsequently recalling it on 16.10.2024 to hear arguments on threshold and limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition fulfilled the statutory threshold limit of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- under Section 4 of the IBC by including delayed payment charges of 22% per annum as stipulated in the loan sanction documents; whether the application was barred by limitation considering NPA classification on 11.06.2016; and whether annual balance sheet entries signed by the Corporate Debtor constitute valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 7 of the IBC, the adjudicating authority is strictly tasked with verifying whether a financial debt and default exist above the statutory minimum threshold, and need not adjudicate the precise quantum of debt; contractually stipulated delayed payment charges and interest form part of the financial debt, and unequivocal acknowledgments in audited balance sheets continuously renew the limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore is satisfied when principal debt combined with contractually agreed delayed payment charges/interest exceeds the threshold; Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to balance sheet entries signed before the expiration of the limitation period, resetting the three-year limitation clock. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Liberal construction of balance sheet acknowledgments as evidence of a subsisting jural debtor-creditor relationship under Section 18; mechanical exclusion of delayed payment charges explicitly mandated by the facility agreement is impermissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The total outstanding debt, including contractual delayed payment charges of 22% p.a., crossed Rs. 1 Crore, and balance sheet entries coupled with the Supreme Court's COVID-19 limitation exclusion saved the claim from limitation, justifying admission under Section 7.
operative_order: The appeal is devoid of any merit and is accordingly dismissed. All related IAs are also disposed of. No orders as to costs. CIRP process stands revived.
summary: Appellant Rajendra Narayan Panda, suspended director of Panda Technologies India Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Indore order dated 21.01.2025 admitting a Section 7 application filed by Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (assignee of L&T Finance). The Appellant argued that the admitted debt fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 and was barred by limitation following a 2016 NPA declaration. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority is only required to ascertain the existence of debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore without determining exact quantum. Contractual delayed payment charges of 22% p.a. were legally includable, and signed balance sheets validly extended limitation under Section 18. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s SSMP Agro Export Private Limited & Ors. vs. Yogesh Sethi & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is M/s SSMP Agro Export Private Limited (promoted by Appellants Nos. 2 and 3, Sagar Kunwar and Shrey Kunwar, sons of Manoj Kunwar); Respondent No. 1 is Yogesh Sethi, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s SSMP Industries Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 Manoj Kunwar is Ex-Director/Promoter of Corporate Debtor; Respondent Nos. 6 and 7 are alleged purchasers A. Ravindra Naidu and V. Kamalapathi Naidu. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unauthorized Agreement to Sell dated 13.12.2019 executed during liquidation by Manoj Kunwar on behalf of Corporate Debtor to sell 9.56 acres of mortgaged liquidation land at Chittoor, Andhra Pradesh for Rs. 6,59,52,000/-, under which an advance of Rs. 1.00 Crore was transferred directly via RTGS into the bank account of Appellant No. 1. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Illegal diversion/receipt of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- belonging to the liquidation estate of the Corporate Debtor; NCLT directed refund with 15% interest per annum. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 27.08.2018; liquidation ordered under Section 33 on 31.07.2019; Agreement to Sell executed and Rs. 1 Crore transferred on 13.12.2019; Liquidator received legal notice from purchasers on 09.06.2022; Liquidator filed IA No. 3827 of 2022 on 11.08.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement to Sell dated 13.12.2019 specifying bank account of Appellant No. 1, RTGS transaction receipts showing two transfers of Rs. 50 Lakhs each on 13.12.2019, audited special audit report dated 18.03.2019 showing diversion of assets, belated police complaint dated 12.12.2023 omitting allegations of forgery of the agreement, and balance sheets of Appellant No. 1. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 3827 of 2022 under Sections 33(5), 33(1), 66, and 60(5); NCLT Delhi Bench-III vide orders dated 14.11.2024 and 20.12.2024 declared the Agreement to Sell void and directed Appellants and ex-directors to deposit Rs. 1 Crore plus 15% interest p.a. into the liquidation estate.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT had jurisdiction under Section 60(5) and Section 66 of the IBC to direct third parties/related entities to refund monies received in connection with an unauthorized sale of liquidation estate property during liquidation; whether allegations of forgery and fraud in respect of the Agreement to Sell ousted the summary jurisdiction of the NCLT requiring relegation to a civil court; and whether the direction to deposit funds with 15% interest per annum was legally sustainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate debtor enters liquidation, its assets form part of the liquidation estate under the statutory custody of the liquidator, and any alienation or receipt of funds arising from an unauthorized transaction of such property during the liquidation moratorium is void ab initio; the adjudicating authority possesses restorative jurisdiction to compel any entity, including related third parties, to disgorge and restore such funds to the liquidation estate without undertaking a full-fledged civil trial for fraud or forgery. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(2) and Section 60(5) read with Section 66 empower the Tribunal to protect the liquidation estate and reverse transactions executed without liquidator authority; the enquiry is restorative in nature to protect creditors, independent of formal avoidance conditions or veil-piercing standards. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective transaction-tracing standard; where bank transfers match the consideration stipulated in an agreement disposing of estate land, belated and uncorroborated pleas of forgery and assertions of unsecured loans lacking contractual documentation are rejected as afterthoughts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 1 Crore was received by Appellant No. 1 pursuant to an illegal sale of estate property during liquidation; the NCLT rightly exercised restorative jurisdiction ordering its deposit into the liquidation estate, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Pending IAs, if any, are closed. There shall be no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants M/s SSMP Agro Export Private Limited and its directors appealed against the NCLT Delhi order directing them to deposit Rs. 1.00 Crore with 15% interest p.a. into the liquidation estate of Corporate Debtor M/s SSMP Industries Ltd. The amount was received via RTGS under an unauthorized Agreement to Sell dated 13.12.2019 executed during liquidation by the promoter (Appellants' father) regarding estate land. Appellants contended that NCLT lacked jurisdiction over third parties and that the agreement was forged. NCLAT held that dealing with liquidation estate property during liquidation is void ab initio, and NCLT has full restorative jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to recover diverted estate funds without conducting a criminal trial. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: IndusInd Bank Limited & Anr. vs. Mrs. Neetu R. Menda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are IndusInd Bank Limited (Appellant No. 1, a scheduled commercial bank) and Link Intime India Private Limited (Appellant No. 2, Registrar and Transfer Agent); Respondent is Mrs. Neetu R. Menda, original registered shareholder; third-party claimant was Navin Amrutlal Chohan. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ownership of 5,000 fully paid equity shares (face value Rs. 10/- each, folio 00916735, distinctive nos. 179891484 to 179896483) in IndusInd Bank held by Respondent since 1994, which were fraudulently transferred to Navin Amrutlal Chohan upon unauthorized issuance of duplicate share certificates in 2015 based on an 11-year-old transfer deed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unlawful transfer of 5,000 equity shares valued at several crores on prevailing market rates; NCLT awarded restoration or alternate damages at closing market value on date of order plus Rs. 25,000/- costs; NCLAT additionally levied Rs. 1,00,000/- legal costs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfer deed dated 04.12.2003 submitted on 05.01.2015; duplicate shares issued and transferred to Chohan on 17.04.2015; Respondent submitted Dematerialisation Request Form on 31.08.2018; RTA rejected demat on 28.09.2018; Respondent filed Section 59 petition CP No. 4770/(MB)/2018 on 23.11.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original physical share certificates retained in custody of Respondent until surrendered for demat in 2018, incomplete indemnity bond by Chohan leaving payment details blank, discrepant Non-Cognizable police report, newspaper advertisement published only in a regional Marathi daily in Mumbai despite shareholder residing in Bangalore, and contradictory reasons for loss across documents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed CP No. 4770/(MB)/2018 under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013; Appellants filed MA No. 2404/2019 challenging maintainability; NCLT Mumbai Court-II allowed CP and rejected MA on 22.12.2023 directing rectification of register or payment of equivalent market value damages.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has summary jurisdiction under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 to adjudicate an open-and-shut case of fraudulent transfer and unauthorized issuance of duplicate share certificates, or whether the aggrieved shareholder must be relegated to a civil court; whether civil court jurisdiction is barred under Section 430; whether the petition was barred by limitation; and whether the NCLT is empowered under Section 59(2) to award compensation/damages equivalent to market value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an open-and-shut case of fraud where a company and its transfer agent unlawfully issue duplicate shares and transfer them to a third party in violation of statutory and regulatory safeguards while the genuine owner retains original share certificates, the company court has exclusive summary jurisdiction under rectification provisions to restore the register or award equivalent compensatory damages, with civil court jurisdiction being completely barred. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59(2) of Companies Act, 2013 explicitly empowers the Tribunal to direct rectification and order the company to pay damages sustained by the aggrieved party; Section 430 ousts civil court jurisdiction on matters within NCLT competence; Section 46 and 56 prohibit issuing duplicate shares or registering transfers without original instruments or mandatory notice to registered holders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective verification of custody of original certificates and non-compliance with SEBI Circular dated 09.05.2001; where procedural requirements of notice, verification, and valid indemnity are blatantly breached, fraud and gross negligence are established on the face of the record without requiring a plenary civil trial. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The fraudulent transfer occurred without sufficient cause due to gross negligence and violation of SEBI guidelines by Appellants; the order directing restoration of shares or payment of market value damages was fully valid, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Appellants directed to pay cost reimbursement of legal expenses of Rs. 1,00,000/- on Appellant No. 1 to the Respondent within two months.
summary: IndusInd Bank Limited and its RTA Link Intime India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 22.12.2023 allowing Mrs. Neetu R. Menda's petition under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLT directed restoration of 5,000 equity shares or payment of equivalent market value damages, finding that duplicate shares had been fraudulently issued to an imposter on an 11-year-old transfer deed while the Respondent retained original certificates. NCLAT held that Section 59 empowers NCLT to rectify registers and award damages in open-and-shut fraud cases without relegating parties to civil courts, whose jurisdiction is barred under Section 430. Finding gross negligence and breach of SEBI transfer guidelines, NCLAT dismissed the appeal with Rs. 1,00,000/- costs.

case_title: J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mr. Vithal M. Dahake, Resolution Professional of Radius Estate Projects Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (assignee of YES Bank Ltd.); Corporate Debtor is Radius Estate Projects Pvt. Ltd. (REPPL, formerly Vishwaroop Realtors Pvt. Ltd.); Principal Borrower is Sumer Radius Realty Pvt. Ltd. (SRRPL); Respondent is Vithal M. Dahake, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: YES Bank sanctioned a Term Loan of Rs. 350 Crores to SRRPL on 31.03.2016 (including Term Loan-I of Rs. 111 Crores for construction and development of the Corporate Debtor's 'Avenue 54' project); REPPL executed a registered Deed of Mortgage dated 12.05.2016 mortgaging its 50% undivided share in land at Bandra (Santacruz SRA Project) with an express covenant to repay the mortgage debt upon borrower default, followed by a Supplemental Deed of Mortgage dated 06.02.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount under Term Loan-I was Rs. 96,92,58,610/- as on 15.07.2019 (account classified NPA on 31.03.2019); total claim lodged by YES Bank was Rs. 184,35,46,857/-, of which Rs. 121,83,22,459/- pertained to the mortgage debt under Term Loan-I. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 13(2) SARFAESI Act issued on 29.07.2019; Possession Notice under Section 13(4) issued on 18.10.2019; CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 06.09.2021; claim submitted on 10.11.2021; RP rejected financial creditor classification on 01.12.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility Letter dated 31.03.2016, Loan Agreement dated 11.05.2016, Deed of Mortgage dated 12.05.2016 containing Clause 3 (Covenant to Pay) and Clause 25 (Liability for Deficiency), Assignment Agreement dated 16.12.2022, and Development Agreements allocating 1,50,000 sq. ft. saleable area to Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: YES Bank filed IA No. 1157/MB/2022 under Section 60(5) in CP No. 380/2021 seeking admission as Secured Financial Creditor; NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the application on 07.08.2024 upholding classification as 'Other Secured Creditor' on the ground that no funds were directly disbursed to the Corporate Debtor.
legal_issues: Whether direct disbursement of funds to the Corporate Debtor is a mandatory sine qua non for classifying a debt as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC; whether a registered Deed of Mortgage containing an express 'covenant to pay' and deficiency liability constitutes an English Mortgage under Section 58(e) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; and whether the mortgagee qualifies as a Secured Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8)(f), (h), and (i) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Direct disbursement of funds into the bank account of the corporate debtor is not a mandatory prerequisite for a debt to qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, provided the disbursement was made for the corporate debtor's benefit with the commercial effect of borrowing; an English Mortgage embodying an explicit covenant to pay and personal liability for deficiencies operates as a contract of guarantee, conferring upon the mortgagee the status of a secured financial creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) does not textually require disbursement 'to the corporate debtor'; read with sub-clauses (f), (h), and (i), an explicit payment undertaking transforms collateral security into a financial debt; Section 58(e) of Transfer of Property Act binds the mortgagor personally to repay mortgage debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual construction test distinguishing pure third-party collateral mortgages (as in Anuj Jain) from instruments containing affirmative covenants to pay and continuing deficiency undertakings (as in China Development Bank). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The mortgage deed was an English Mortgage with an express covenant to pay, securing funds disbursed for the project benefit of the Corporate Debtor, thereby constituting a secured financial debt and entitling Appellant to admission as a Secured Financial Creditor.
operative_order: Appeal succeeds and is allowed; Impugned Order dated 07.08.2024 is set aside. Case remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide in accordance with law; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 19.03.2026. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (assignee of YES Bank) appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its claim of Rs. 121.83 Crores as a Secured Financial Creditor of Corporate Debtor Radius Estate Projects Pvt. Ltd., classifying it as an 'other secured creditor'. The NCLT reasoned that loan proceeds were disbursed to principal borrower Sumer Radius Realty Pvt. Ltd. rather than the Corporate Debtor. NCLAT held that direct disbursement to the debtor is not a sine qua non under Section 5(8) where funds were disbursed for its project benefit. Because the mortgage deed contained an express covenant to pay and deficiency liability, it constituted an English Mortgage and guarantee, establishing a Secured Financial Debt. The appeal was allowed.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. Mr. Anil Tayal, Interim Resolution Professional for M/s Infinia Solutions and Services Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Financial Creditor Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd.; Respondent is Anil Tayal, Interim Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Infinia Solutions and Services Pvt. Ltd. (insolvency initiated by operational creditor Radhika Chatterjee). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by Kotak Mahindra Bank to the Corporate Debtor, secured by personal guarantees/mortgages of third parties/obligors; Corporate Debtor had ceased business operations in 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 4,35,46,467/- via email dated 26.05.2023, which was verified and admitted by the IRP to the tune of Rs. 4,28,73,231/-; claim was subsequently fully satisfied/settled under SARFAESI proceedings on 01.08.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 28.04.2023; Form A public announcement on 06.05.2023; claim submitted on 26.05.2023; first CoC meeting held on 29.05.2023 where Appellant immediately communicated intent to withdraw; formal withdrawal email sent on 29.05.2023; subsequent confirmation emails sent on 31.05.2023 and 05.06.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Withdrawal emails dated 29.05.2023, 31.05.2023, and 05.06.2023 stating commercial wisdom not to participate in CIRP, SARFAESI settlement documentation dated 01.08.2023, and minutes of CoC meetings showing lack of quorum due to Appellant's non-participation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IRP filed IA No. 3965 of 2023 under Section 60(5) seeking directions or permission to reconstitute the CoC and allow Appellant to withdraw its claim; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed the application on 11.03.2024 holding there is no provision in the Code to direct or permit a claimant to withdraw its claim.
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor whose claim has been admitted during CIRP is legally entitled to withdraw its claim under Regulation 12A of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 upon full satisfaction of its debt; whether the phrase 'updation of claim' under Regulation 12A encompasses the complete withdrawal of an admitted claim; and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that there is no provision under the IBC permitting a creditor to withdraw its claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor cannot be compelled to remain a member of the committee of creditors or participate in insolvency proceedings when its claim has been fully satisfied from third-party sources or obligors; statutory provisions governing claim updation encompass complete withdrawal of an admitted claim, subject to judicial determination by the adjudicating authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12A of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016 mandating that a creditor 'shall update its claim as and when the claim is satisfied, partly or fully' textually and purposively includes the right to withdraw a claim that has been satisfied in full, leaving the creditor with zero voting share. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of debt satisfaction; while an IRP/RP possesses only administrative collation powers and lacks adjudicatory jurisdiction to unilaterally delete claims or alter creditor status, the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) must sanction claim withdrawal upon proof of full satisfaction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in concluding that the Code lacks provisions for claim withdrawal; Regulation 12A permits withdrawal upon satisfaction, justifying setting aside the dismissal and remanding the matter for fresh adjudication.
operative_order: The impugned order passed by the Adjudicating Authority is set aside; appeal is allowed. Matter remanded back to NCLT to dispose of IA No. 3965 of 2023 afresh after providing opportunity of being heard. Questions regarding Section 14 applicability and payment of CIRP costs left open for NCLT determination. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 11.03.2024 dismissing an application moved by IRP Anil Tayal seeking permission for the Bank to withdraw its admitted claim of Rs. 4.28 Crores and reconstitute the CoC. The NCLT had held that no provision exists in the IBC permitting a claimant to withdraw its claim. NCLAT set aside the order and allowed the appeal, holding that Regulation 12A of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 mandates updation of claims upon partial or full satisfaction, which encompasses the complete withdrawal of fully satisfied claims. A creditor cannot be forced to participate in CIRP once debt is satisfied. The matter was remanded to NCLT.

case_title: Srei Equipment Finance Limited vs. Roadwings International Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Srei Equipment Finance Ltd. (SEFL) represented through Power of Attorney holder Shri Sohan Kumar Jha; Corporate Debtor is Roadwings International Pvt. Ltd. (RIPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SEFL extended credit and loan facilities to RIPL pursuant to four Financial Agreements executed between 15.04.2017 and 15.07.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by RIPL in repaying the loan facilities under the four financial agreements; existence of debt and default was established and not disputed by RIPL. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI superseded SEFL's board on 04.10.2021; CIRP admitted against SEFL on 08.10.2021 appointing Rajneesh Sharma as Administrator; Administrator executed POA in favor of employee Sohan Jha on 28.03.2023 (valid till 31.03.2024); resolution plan of NARCL approved on 11.08.2023 discharging Administrator and creating Implementation and Monitoring Committee (IMC); IMC ratified POA on 17.08.2023; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 224 (KB)/2023 filed on 04.11.2023; reconstituted Board ratified IMC acts and POA on 26.02.2024; CEO issued fresh POA on 16.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Four Financial Agreements, Power of Attorney dated 28.03.2023, Minutes of IMC meeting dated 17.08.2023 ratifying POA, Minutes and Board Resolution dated 26.02.2024 ratifying acts of IMC and POA, supplementary affidavit dated 18.05.2024, and fresh POA dated 16.04.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 224 (KB)/2023 filed on 04.11.2023 was dismissed by NCLT Kolkata Bench-II on 21.11.2024 on the sole ground that the application lacked subsisting valid authorization because the Administrator who granted the POA stood discharged on 11.08.2023.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by an officer holding a Power of Attorney granted by an Administrator prior to discharge is maintainable when such authorization is subsequently ratified by an Implementation and Monitoring Committee and the reconstituted Board of Directors; and whether the Resolution Professional or IMC can delegate the power to initiate Section 7 proceedings to an employee of the Corporate Debtor under the IBC framework.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: General authorization granted by a corporate entity to its officer or employee via a power of attorney is sufficient to file an application under Section 7 of the IBC, and any purported defect or expiration of authority arising from management transitions is retrospectively validated upon subsequent ratification under the doctrine of relation back ('ratihabitio mandato aequiparatur'). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25(2)(b) read with Sections 17(b), 19(1), and 20(2)(d) of the IBC recognizes the practical necessity of the Resolution Professional utilizing company personnel to institute and continue legal proceedings; the legal maxim 'delegatus non potest delegare' does not bar an RP or monitoring committee from authorizing employees to perform litigious acts to maintain operations as a going concern. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of agency and corporate intent; subsisting and unrevoked agency under Section 201 of the Indian Contract Act substantiated by board minutes and resolutions ratifying prior attorney acts constitutes conclusive proof of authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The POA was valid, unrevoked, and repeatedly ratified by the IMC and the new Board of Directors; the dismissal of the Section 7 petition for lack of authorization was legally erroneous and set aside, with directions to admit the application.
operative_order: Appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 21.11.2024 is set aside. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order of admission of the Section 7 application under the IBC within one month from the date of production of this order and take further steps in accordance with law. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Srei Equipment Finance Limited (SEFL) appealed the NCLT Kolkata order dated 21.11.2024 dismissing its Section 7 petition against Roadwings International Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had dismissed the petition holding that the POA holder, Sohan Jha, lacked subsisting authority because the Administrator who granted the POA on 28.03.2023 was discharged upon approval of NARCL's resolution plan on 11.08.2023. NCLAT set aside the order and allowed the appeal, holding that under IBC provisions (Sections 19, 20, and 25), the RP and IMC can delegate litigious actions to employees. Furthermore, the POA was validly and retrospectively ratified by both the Implementation and Monitoring Committee and the reconstituted Board of Directors.

case_title: Encore Asset Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. vs. Pandhe Constructions Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is Encore Asset Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. (EARC, assignee of DNS Bank Ltd.); Corporate Debtor/Respondent is Pandhe Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor); Principal Borrower is Pandhe Infracons Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: DNS Bank granted a Flexi Overdraft Facility of Rs. 15,00,00,000/- to Pandhe Infracons Pvt. Ltd. secured by a Corporate Guarantee executed by Pandhe Constructions Pvt. Ltd. on 22.03.2014 (renewed on 09.10.2015 and 30.09.2016); facility and security assigned to EARC on 15.05.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal borrower account classified NPA on 30.06.2018; total claimed default in Part IV as on 19.07.2023 was Rs. 35,38,03,129/- with date of default specified as 19.11.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) SARFAESI Act issued on 04.09.2018 demanding Rs. 15,99,70,693.75 within 60 days; notice invoking corporate guarantee issued on 04.11.2019 giving 15 days (expired 18.11.2019); borrower submitted OTS proposal on 10.11.2019; fresh demand notice issued on 18.02.2022 claiming Rs. 28,22,36,755; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 995/MB/2023 filed on 20.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Guarantee deed dated 30.09.2016, Assignment Agreement dated 15.05.2019, Section 13(2) notice dated 04.09.2018, Guarantee Invocation Notice dated 04.11.2019, and OTS proposal letter dated 10.11.2019 from the principal borrower acknowledging debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition filed on 20.08.2023; NCLT Mumbai Bench-VI dismissed the petition on 11.10.2024 as time-barred, reasoning that 3-year limitation from default date 19.11.2019 expired on 18.11.2022 and under the Supreme Court's COVID-19 orders only 411 days from 01.03.2022 were available, expiring on 16.04.2023.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition filed against the corporate guarantor on 20.08.2023 was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963; how the Supreme Court's COVID-19 extension directions in Suo Motu WP (C) No. 3 of 2020 apply to the computation of limitation for defaults occurring prior to or during the pandemic; whether a Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice constitutes invocation of a corporate guarantee; and whether an OTS acknowledgment by the principal borrower extends limitation against the corporate guarantor under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The entire COVID-19 pandemic period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 is statutorily excluded from limitation computations, resulting in an enlargement of the limitation period such that the balance period available as of 15.03.2020 becomes available afresh from 01.03.2022; additionally, an acknowledgment of debt by a principal borrower within limitation binds the guarantor by operation of co-extensive liability and extends limitation against the guarantor under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Direction I and II of the Supreme Court's order in Suo Motu WP (C) No. 3 of 2020 mean limitation stops running on 15.03.2020 and resumes on 01.03.2022, preserving the full unexpired balance; Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act creates co-extensive liability between borrower and guarantor, making written acknowledgments under Section 18 effective against both. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the specific terms and intent of demand notices to establish whether a Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice or a dedicated invocation notice triggered guarantee default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Reckoned from the guarantee default date of 19.11.2019 with the entire COVID period excluded, or considering the OTS acknowledgment of 10.11.2019, the Section 7 petition filed on 20.08.2023 was well within limitation; the dismissal order was set aside and remanded for fresh disposal.
operative_order: Impugned judgment dated 11.10.2024 passed by Adjudicating Authority is set aside. Appeal is allowed. Matter remanded back to NCLT Mumbai to dispose of CP (IB) No. 995/MB/2023 afresh after hearing the parties and tendering fresh evidence. Pending IAs closed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Encore Asset Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of its Section 7 petition against Corporate Guarantor Pandhe Constructions Pvt. Ltd. as time-barred. The NCLT had calculated that limitation from the guarantee default date of 19.11.2019 expired on 16.04.2023 after applying COVID exclusion orders. NCLAT set aside the order and allowed the appeal, holding that the NCLT misapplied the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID limitation orders, which exclude the entire period between 15.03.2020 and 28.02.2022 and preserve the unexpired balance period from 01.03.2022. Additionally, the borrower's OTS acknowledgment extended limitation under Section 18 against the guarantor. The matter was remanded for fresh adjudication.

case_title: Puro Natural Sugars JV vs. Shree Warana Sahakari Bank Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) Puro Natural Sugars JV; Corporate Debtor is Shivaji Cane Processors Limited (an MSME); Dissenting Financial Creditors are Shree Warana Sahakari Bank Ltd. (Respondent No. 1, 11.13% voting share) and Kolhapur Urban Co-operative Bank Ltd. (Respondent No. 2, 10.84% voting share). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium credit facility of Rs. 18.20 Crores sanctioned to Corporate Debtor (Rs. 6.20 Cr from R-1 and Rs. 6.00 Cr from R-2 in January 2017) secured by mortgage deed, personal guarantees, and third-party guarantees of promoters. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default upon CIRP admission; R-1 filed Form-C claim for Rs. 8,94,62,429/- and R-2 filed Form-C claim for Rs. 8,65,70,898/-; resolution plan allocated Rs. 4,34,15,371/- to R-1 and Rs. 4,22,96,889/- to R-2, with Rs. 2,00,00,000/- allocated towards assignment of residual debts and personal guarantees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.02.2021; CoC approved resolution plan on 27.07.2021 (78.03% vote share); NCLT rejected plan approval on 01.05.2023; NCLAT reversed rejection and approved plan on 24.11.2023; Supreme Court dismissed R-1's appeal on 11.03.2024; SRA filed IA No. 4484 of 2024 in August 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan clauses C-3(II) and C-13(7) stipulating irrevocable release of all encumbrances, liens, and attachments over assets of promoters and guarantors; Section 101 recovery certificates and attachments under Section 156 of Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act over un-mortgaged personal properties in Sangli district. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SRA filed IA No. 4484 of 2024 seeking full implementation of plan and release of guarantor properties; NCLT Mumbai Court-V allowed the application on 25.04.2025 holding recovery against guarantors illegal, but added observations in paras 55-57 that personal properties not mortgaged but attached under the MCS Act were not released.
legal_issues: Whether an approved resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC can validly extinguish personal guarantees and release attachments/encumbrances over personal properties of guarantors that were not mortgaged but attached under Section 101 and Section 156 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960; and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in qualifying the approved plan by observing in paras 55-57 that un-mortgaged personal properties remained attached.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan binds all stakeholders including dissenting financial creditors under Section 31 of the IBC, and broad extinguishment clauses releasing all encumbrances, security interests, and attachments over promoter and guarantor assets apply universally, extinguishing statutory recovery attachments levied for the resolved debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 confers absolute binding force on the approved plan; Clause C-13(7) of the resolution plan releasing 'all encumbrances, security interest, liens and/or attachments (including pursuant to applicable Law)' over assets of erstwhile promoters and guarantors encompasses statutory attachments under Section 101 and 156 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960; upon full settlement of debt under the plan, associated recovery attachments cease to have legal basis. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Finality of approved plan terms; where a resolution plan's extinguishment clauses have been affirmed up to the Supreme Court, the Adjudicating Authority cannot retrospectively dilute or carve out exceptions to the scope of release of guarantor assets. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The approved resolution plan settled the entire debt and extinguished all guarantor attachments without exception; paragraphs 55 to 57 of the impugned order impermissibly undermined the plan and must be set aside and deleted.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Observations in paragraphs 55 to 57 of the impugned order dated 25.04.2025 are set aside and deleted; rest of the order remains unaffected. If respondents do not release entire assets within 30 days, Adjudicating Authority shall forward copy of order to IBBI to consider initiating prosecution under Section 74(3) of the IBC. Parties bear own costs.
summary: Appellant Puro Natural Sugars JV, Successful Resolution Applicant of Shivaji Cane Processors Ltd., appealed against observations in paragraphs 55 to 57 of the NCLT Mumbai order dated 25.04.2025 in IA No. 4484/2024. Although NCLT allowed the IA holding that the approved resolution plan extinguished dissenting creditors' rights against personal guarantors, paras 55-57 restricted release only to mortgaged assets, excluding properties attached under Section 101 of Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act. NCLAT held that Clause C-13(7) of the approved plan irrevocably released all encumbrances and attachments over promoter/guarantor assets. Once the underlying debt was resolved under the approved plan (which attained finality before the Supreme Court), creditors had no surviving claim. NCLAT deleted paragraphs 55 to 57 and warned of prosecution under Section 74(3).

case_title: Vinodkumar Nihalchand Parmar vs. Anuj Bajpai & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Private Limited (assignee of Dombivli Nagari Sahakari Bank Ltd. / DNS Bank); Corporate Debtor is Dee Plone Polyster Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant is Vinodkumar Nihalchand Parmar (Suspended Director/Shareholder); Respondent No. 1 is IRP Anuj Bajpai. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: DNS Bank sanctioned loan facilities between 2014 and 2017 (including initial term loan of Rs. 10 Crores, cash credit of Rs. 5 Crores, and fresh term loan of Rs. 6.18 Crores), secured by hypothecation and mortgage deeds over plant, machinery, land, and building; assigned to Pegasus ARC on 31.12.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account classified as NPA on 31.03.2018; total claimed default in Part IV was Rs. 37,35,74,442.07 as of 16.10.2023 comprising principal, interest, and penal charges. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Debt assigned on 31.12.2020 and intimated on 06.01.2021; email acknowledging liability sent by Appellant on 16.02.2024; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 141/MB/2024 filed on 01.11.2023; NCLT reserved orders on 04.06.2025, de-reserved on 23.07.2025 for clarification on Rule 4(3), and admitted petition on 02.09.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements and sanction letters, hypothecation and mortgage deeds, assignment agreement dated 31.12.2020, audited balance sheets for FY 2018-19, 2019-20, and 2020-21 reflecting debt, email admission dated 16.02.2024, and board resolutions empowering the authorized representative. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Pegasus ARC filed Section 7 petition on 01.11.2023; Corporate Debtor opposed on technical grounds (lack of IU certificate, unstamped agreements, non-filing of 65B certificate, non-service to IBBI); NCLT Mumbai Bench-II admitted Section 7 application on 02.09.2025 initiating CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether admission under Section 7 was vitiated by procedural irregularities or natural justice violation when the NCLT de-reserved orders to seek an additional affidavit regarding service on IBBI under Rule 4(3); whether non-filing of an Information Utility default record under Regulation 20(1A) is fatal to a Section 7 petition; whether insufficient stamping of loan agreements under state stamp law bars admission of Section 7; and whether absence of a Section 65B Evidence Act certificate invalidates electronic bank statements.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: At the admission stage of a Section 7 insolvency petition, the inquiry is strictly confined to ascertaining the existence of a financial debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold within limitation; procedural and technical defects such as curable lack of stamping, absence of an Information Utility default record, or omitted Section 65B certificates do not defeat substantive insolvency proceedings where debt and default are independently established through audited balance sheets and admissions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 20(1A) of the IBBI (Information Utilities) Regulations is directory rather than mandatory; Rule 4(3) requiring service on IBBI is a rectifiable procedural requirement; Section 7(5) mandates admission once debt, default, and completeness are satisfied. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Summary verification of debt and default; certified bank records under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 coupled with balance sheet acknowledgments and email admissions provide conclusive evidence, rendering technical evidence objections under Section 65B untenable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Financial debt of Rs. 37.35 Crores and default were undisputed and acknowledged in balance sheets and emails within limitation under Section 18; all procedural defects were cured, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. All related IAs are also disposed of. The IRP shall continue with the insolvency proceedings. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Vinodkumar Nihalchand Parmar, suspended director of Dee Plone Polyster Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Mumbai order dated 02.09.2025 admitting Pegasus ARC's Section 7 petition for a default of Rs. 37.35 Crores. Appellant contended that NCLT violated natural justice by relying on a post-reservation additional affidavit, and raised technical objections regarding lack of an Information Utility record, insufficient stamping, lack of a Section 65B certificate, and non-service to IBBI. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that at Section 7 admission stage, the Tribunal only verifies debt, default, and limitation. Technical defects like IU certificates or stamping are directory/curable and cannot override undisputed financial debt proven by audited accounts and admissions.

case_title: Ganesan Natarajan vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is State Bank of India (lead of consortium including SBH, UBI, IOB); Corporate Debtor is M/s Ennore Coke Limited; Personal Guarantor/Appellant is Ganesan Natarajan (former promoter, CEO, and director); Respondent No. 2 is IRP Manish Jain. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium of lenders sanctioned credit facilities to Corporate Debtor (up to Rs. 110.29 Crores including term loan of Rs. 36.45 Crores); Appellant executed an unconditional, absolute, and irrevocable Deed of Personal Guarantee dated 10.02.2012 guaranteeing repayment on demand upon default by the borrower. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account classified as NPA on 28.10.2015; Demand Notice under Form B issued on 20.01.2020 claiming Rs. 88,34,95,187.40 as of 16.04.2018 (and due as on 19.02.2019) plus future interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee executed on 10.02.2012; Appellant ceased being director on 31.03.2015; NPA on 28.10.2015; Section 13(2) notice on 10.11.2016; Corporate Debtor sent restructuring proposals on 07.12.2016, 23.02.2017, and 15.03.2017; CIRP against Corporate Debtor on 20.06.2017; Form B demand notice issued on 20.01.2020; Section 95 petition CP (IB) 11/CHE/2022 filed on 28.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Personal Guarantee dated 10.02.2012, promissory notes, restructuring letters dated 07.12.2016 and 23.02.2017, letter dated 15.03.2017 marked 'without prejudice' acknowledging debt and proposing OTS, Section 99 report of IRP recommending initiation of IRP, and SARFAESI notice dated 10.11.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed Section 95 petition on 28.11.2021; Appellant opposed on limitation, alleged release/revocation of guarantee on 02.08.2013, and privileged nature of 'without prejudice' letter; NCLT Chennai admitted Section 95 petition on 11.09.2025; Appellant appealed before NCLAT Chennai.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 95 petition filed on 28.11.2021 was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act reckoned from the NPA date 28.10.2015; whether a letter marked 'without prejudice' proposing loan restructuring and debt payment constitutes a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act; whether acknowledgment of debt by the corporate debtor binds the personal guarantor under Section 128 of the Contract Act; and whether an irrevocable continuing guarantee can be unilaterally revoked by the guarantor under Section 130 of the Contract Act upon resigning from directorship.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt by a principal borrower before the expiry of limitation extends the limitation period against the personal guarantor by virtue of the co-extensive liability under contract law; the phrase 'without prejudice' in a settlement or restructuring communication does not negate an unequivocal admission of subsisting liability for limitation purposes under Section 18, and an unconditional, irrevocable guarantee cannot be unilaterally revoked under Section 130 where the right to revoke was contracted out. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to written restructuring proposals acknowledging subsisting jural relations; Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act creates co-extensive liability such that fresh limitation running against the principal debtor applies equally to the guarantor; Section 130 cannot override express contractual waivers of the right to revoke a continuing guarantee. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Holistic construction of correspondence; communications must be read in their entirety to determine whether subsisting liability is admitted, regardless of a 'without prejudice' heading; unilateral revocation letters not properly proven or admitted in evidence cannot displace a registered continuing guarantee. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The letters dated 07.12.2016 and 15.03.2017 continuously acknowledged debt within limitation, and coupled with the Supreme Court's COVID-19 extension, the Section 95 petition filed on 28.11.2021 was well within limitation, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The company appeal lacks merit and is accordingly dismissed. All pending IAs stand closed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Ganesan Natarajan, personal guarantor and former director of Ennore Coke Limited, appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated 11.09.2025 admitting SBI's Section 95 petition for a default of over Rs. 88 Crores. Appellant contended that the petition was time-barred from the 2015 NPA date, that his 2013 resignation revoked the guarantee, and that the debtor's 15.03.2017 restructuring letter marked 'without prejudice' could not extend limitation. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that debtor's successive restructuring letters continuously extended limitation under Section 18, binding the guarantor under Section 128 of the Contract Act. The 'without prejudice' label did not negate the admission of subsisting liability, and an irrevocable continuing guarantee could not be unilaterally revoked under Section 130.

case_title: Vistra ITCL (India) Limited vs. Vithal Madhukar Dahake & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vistra ITCL (India) Limited (acting as Debenture Trustee for debenture holders); Corporate Debtor is Radius Estate Projects Pvt. Ltd. (REPPL, formerly Vishwaroop Realtors Pvt. Ltd.); Principal Borrower is Aaditri Constructions Private Limited (ACPL); Developer is Radius and Deserve Builders LLP; Respondent No. 1 is Resolution Professional Vithal Madhukar Dahake; Respondent No. 2 is Avenue 54 Welfare Association; Respondent No. 3 is Omkara ARC. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debenture Trust Deed dated 03.08.2018 for issuance of 3,95,00,000 secured optionally convertible debentures (aggregating Rs. 395 Crores, Rs. 340 Crores disbursed) by ACPL; Corporate Debtor subsequently executed First Supplemental Indenture of Mortgage dated 29.03.2019 and Second Supplemental Indenture of Mortgage dated 16.04.2019 over its properties in the 'Avenue 54' project, embodying an express 'covenant to pay' (Clause 2) all Secured Obligations and liability for deficiencies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debentures were not redeemed on maturity; Appellant issued Event of Default notice on 28.07.2021; Appellant submitted Form-C claim for Rs. 874,03,27,404/- as of insolvency commencement date. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DTD executed on 03.08.2018; First Supplemental IOM on 29.03.2019; Second Supplemental IOM on 16.04.2019; Event of default notice on 28.07.2021; CIRP admitted against Corporate Debtor on 06.09.2021 (in CP No. 380 of 2021 filed by SBICAP Trustee); claim filed on 02.12.2021; RP rejected financial creditor classification on 06.04.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Trust Deed dated 03.08.2018 (Clause 7 and Clause 24), First Supplemental Indenture of Mortgage dated 29.03.2019 (Clause 2 'Covenant to Pay' and Clause 12), Second Supplemental Indenture of Mortgage dated 16.04.2019, Development Management Agreements, and Event of Default notice dated 28.07.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 2680 of 2023 under Section 60(5) challenging RP's categorization of its claim as 'Other Secured Creditor'; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed the application on 07.05.2024 holding that absence of direct disbursement to the Corporate Debtor precluded financial debt classification under Anuj Jain.
legal_issues: Whether direct disbursement of money to the Corporate Debtor is an indispensable prerequisite for a debt to qualify as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC; whether an express 'covenant to pay' and deficiency undertaking in a supplemental indenture of mortgage securing debentures issued by a third party constitutes a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and financial debt under Section 5(8)(c), (f), and (i); and whether the mortgagee qualifies as a Secured Financial Creditor rather than an 'other secured creditor'.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Direct disbursement of funds into the bank account of the corporate debtor is not a mandatory prerequisite for a debt to qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC; where a corporate debtor executes a mortgage containing an express, unconditional covenant to pay all secured obligations and binds itself not to permit obligations to fall into arrears, the arrangement operates as a contract of guarantee, elevating the debt from pure third-party security to a secured financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) does not textually require disbursement 'to the corporate debtor'; read with Section 5(8)(c), (f), and (i), obligations arising from debenture subscriptions backed by corporate guarantees or payment undertakings fall squarely within financial debt; Clauses 2.1 and 2.2 of the Mortgage Deeds read conjointly create an affirmative obligation beyond mere default interest. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict contractual construction distinguishing pure third-party mortgages lacking payment covenants (as in Anuj Jain) from instruments containing explicit covenants to discharge secured obligations and undertake shortfall liability (following China Development Bank v. Doha Bank). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor undertook an express covenant to pay and assumed co-obligor and surety liability under the DTD and Supplemental Mortgage Deeds; therefore, the debt is a Secured Financial Debt and Appellant is entitled to classification as a Secured Financial Creditor, requiring the impugned order to be set aside.
operative_order: The appeal succeeds and is allowed. Impugned Order dated 07.05.2024 is set aside. Case remanded back to Adjudicating Authority to decide in accordance with law; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 19.03.2026. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Vistra ITCL (India) Limited appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 07.05.2024 upholding the Resolution Professional's decision to treat its claim of Rs. 874.03 Crores as an 'other secured creditor' rather than a 'secured financial creditor' of Corporate Debtor Radius Estate Projects Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT reasoned that debenture proceeds were disbursed to third-party Aaditri Constructions Pvt. Ltd. rather than the debtor. NCLAT set aside the order and allowed the appeal, holding that direct disbursement to the debtor is not a sine qua non under Section 5(8) of the IBC. Because the Corporate Debtor executed Supplemental Mortgage Deeds containing an express covenant to pay all secured obligations and prevent arrears, the arrangement constituted a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Contract Act and a financial debt under Section 5(8). The matter was remanded to NCLT.

case_title: Re Sustainability Limited & Ors. vs. Unknown
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Re Sustainability Limited (Amalgamated/Demerged Company); Appellant No. 2 is Mumbai Waste Management Limited (Amalgamating Company); Appellant No. 3 is Ramky Sustainability Solutions Private Limited (Resulting Company); matter proceeded in rem for sanction of a corporate Composite Scheme of Arrangement. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 18.01.2024, the boards of directors of all three Appellant companies approved a Composite Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013, structured in two interconnected, consecutive steps: first, amalgamation of Appellant No. 2 into Appellant No. 1, followed immediately by demerger of the Demerged Undertaking from Appellant No. 1 into Appellant No. 3 in consideration of compulsorily convertible securities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Matter arises out of corporate restructuring and arrangement; no loan default or financial delinquency involved, and all statutory procedural requirements were fulfilled. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board approvals granted on 18.01.2024; First Motion Petition CA (CAA)/8/230/HDB/2024 filed on 09.02.2024 and allowed on 06.05.2024 (corrigendum issued 09.05.2024); shareholder and creditor meetings convened on 04.07.2024 approving the scheme; Second Motion Petition CP (CAA)/30/230/HDB/2024 filed on 13.07.2024; statutory notices published on 08.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Composite Scheme of Arrangement (Clauses 1.1, 1.2, and Clause 5.1(p) detailing the specific assets, liabilities, properties, and employees of the Demerged Undertaking), voting reports of shareholders and creditors, and statutory reports of the Regional Director, Registrar of Companies, and Official Liquidator raising no objections to the demerger. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II vide order dated 28.04.2025 sanctioned the amalgamation limb but in Paragraph 4 and Paragraph 26 refused to sanction the demerger limb, directing Appellants to file a separate, independent application for demerger on the premise that the demerged undertaking was unspecified.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT, while adjudicating a Second Motion Petition under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, possesses the jurisdiction to unilaterally alter or bifurcate an integrated Composite Scheme of Arrangement approved by shareholders and creditors by sanctioning amalgamation while directing a separate application for demerger; and whether the demerged company and undertaking were sufficiently identified under Clause 5.1(p) of the scheme.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The company court exercising supervisory jurisdiction under corporate arrangement provisions cannot unilaterally alter, modify, or bifurcate the commercial terms of an integrated composite scheme of arrangement approved by shareholders and creditors in their commercial wisdom, provided the scheme is lawful and not objected to by statutory authorities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 2(19AA) of the Income Tax Act empower the Tribunal to sanction composite schemes comprising simultaneous amalgamation and demerger in a single unified proceeding; the jurisdiction of the Tribunal under Miheer H. Mafatlal is supervisory and peripheral, not appellate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Holistic textual construction of scheme documentation; where the scheme explicitly defines the demerged company and categorizes its rights, properties, and liabilities, the adjudicating authority cannot conclude that the undertaking is unspecified. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Composite Scheme clearly identified the demerged undertaking and company, and NCLT erred in carving out an exception directing a separate demerger application; the impugned riders were deleted and the Composite Scheme was sanctioned in its entirety.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 66/2025 is allowed. Paragraphs 4, 26(i), 26(ii), and 26(viii) of NCLT Hyderabad order dated 28.04.2025 are set aside/modified. The Composite Scheme of Arrangement as presented is sanctioned without requiring a separate application for demerger, subject to statutory tax and stamp duty compliances. Connected IAs closed.
summary: Appellants Re Sustainability Limited, Mumbai Waste Management Limited, and Ramky Sustainability Solutions Private Limited appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 28.04.2025 in CP (CAA) No. 30/230/HDB/2024. The NCLT had sanctioned the amalgamation limb of their Composite Scheme of Arrangement but refused to sanction the demerger limb, directing that a separate application be filed because the demerged undertaking was purportedly unspecified. NCLAT set aside the restriction and allowed the appeal, holding that NCLT cannot split a composite scheme approved by shareholders and creditors in their commercial wisdom. Finding that the scheme explicitly defined the demerged undertaking and satisfied all statutory requirements under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, NCLAT sanctioned the Composite Scheme in its entirety.

case_title: Akshay Kumar Bhatia vs. M/s. Cue Learn Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant is Akshay Kumar Bhatia (film actor); Corporate Debtor/Respondent is M/s. Cue Learn Private Limited; third party to contract is Culture Company (P) Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tripartite Endorsement Agreement dated 08.03.2021 for a 2-year tenure (08.03.2021 to 07.03.2023) under which Appellant agreed to make himself available for not more than two days to endorse Respondent's website for a total consideration of Rs. 8.10 Crores plus GST, payable in two equal instalments of Rs. 4.05 Crores (Signing Amount on or before 08.03.2021 or 7 days prior to Day 1 utilization; second instalment on or before 15.04.2022 or 7 days prior to Day 2 utilization, whichever is earlier). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: First instalment of Rs. 4.05 Crores was paid and Day 1 service was rendered; claimed operational debt was Rs. 4.05 Crores plus GST under invoice dated 15.04.2022 for the second instalment, where Day 2 services were neither requested nor rendered; date of default asserted around April/May 2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoice raised on 15.04.2022; Section 8 statutory demand notice issued on 20.05.2022; Respondent replied on 25.05.2022 disputing liability; rejoinder sent on 22.06.2022; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 572 of 2022 filed in 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Endorsement Agreement dated 08.03.2021 (Clauses 3.2, 5, 5.1.1, 5.1.2, 5.2, 7.2), invoice dated 15.04.2022, Section 8 notice and reply dated 25.05.2022 establishing a defense that payment was contingent upon actual rendering/scheduling of Day 2 services and that no invoice was received. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 572 of 2022 was dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-IV on 07.01.2025 holding that a genuine pre-existing dispute existed regarding contract interpretation and that unadjudicated breach/damages fall outside operational debt.
legal_issues: Whether the claim for the second instalment under an executory endorsement agreement where services were not utilized constitutes an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC or merely an unadjudicated claim for damages; and whether the Corporate Debtor raised a plausible, genuine pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox Innovations standard regarding the interpretation of reciprocal contractual obligations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 9 of the IBC, the summary adjudicatory forum cannot interpret ambiguous or disputed reciprocal contractual clauses to determine whether consideration is unconditional or contingent upon actual performance; where a plausible, non-spurious dispute regarding contractual entitlement exists prior to the demand notice, the claim does not qualify as an undisputed operational debt, and parties must be relegated to civil proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Operational debt under Section 5(21) requires an undisputed debt arising out of the actual provision of goods or services; a right to claim damages for breach of contract under Section 3(6) does not ipso facto crystallize into an operational debt enabling initiation of CIRP under Section 9. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Mobilox Innovations plausibility standard; the Adjudicating Authority must only examine whether the defense is not a moonshine or frivolous concoction and is based on a bona fide, plausible construction of the contract, without proceeding to iron out creases or conduct a full trial. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The contract was susceptible to the plausible interpretation that payment was tied to actual utilization of services; hence, a genuine pre-existing dispute existed, justifying dismissal of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The judgment of the Adjudicating Authority in C.P. (IB) No. 572 of 2022 dated 07.01.2025 is affirmed; the present appeal is dismissed. No costs.
summary: Appellant Akshay Kumar Bhatia appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing his Section 9 IBC application against Cue Learn Private Limited for default of Rs. 4.05 Crores. Under a 2021 Endorsement Agreement, Appellant was to provide website endorsement services for up to two days for Rs. 8.10 Crores payable in two instalments. The first instalment was paid and one day of service rendered, but the second day was never scheduled or utilized. When Appellant demanded the balance Rs. 4.05 Crores, the Corporate Debtor disputed liability arguing fees were contingent on services rendered. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a plausible pre-existing dispute existed regarding contract interpretation, and unadjudicated breach claims do not constitute operational debt under Section 5(21).

case_title: Dr. Anita Roy vs. Aquafil Polymers Company Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Dr. Anita Roy is the majority 75% shareholder and director; Respondent No. 1 is Aquafil Polymers Company Private Limited; Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 (Hitesh Shah and Poojan Hiten Shah) are former promoters, directors, and 25% minority shareholders. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Share Purchase and Subscription Agreement (SPA) dated 25.09.2019, Appellant acquired 75% shares for Rs. 1,94,31,510/- and funded an Rs. 18 Crore OTS with SBI; Clause 6 provided that promoters remained liable for past pre-31.03.2019 liabilities and were entitled to Disputed Receivables from arbitrations/litigations, while indemnifying new management. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241-242; Appellant uncovered concealed liabilities exceeding Rs. 30 Crores, revoked promoters' representation powers on 03.12.2022, and issued Section 115 removal notice; promoters filed CP/5(AHM)/2023 alleging oppression. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SPA executed 25.09.2019; OTS settled December 2020; Board resolution revoking authorization passed 03.12.2022; Circular resolution passed 10.01.2023; CP No. 5 of 2023 filed on 16.01.2023; NCLT passed interim order on 15.03.2023; NCLT passed final common order on 18.07.2025. 5.
