FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share Purchase Agreement dated 25.09.2019 (Clause 6), board minutes dated 03.12.2022, arbitral order dated 11.01.2023 in JITF matter, and NCLT common order dated 18.07.2025 appointing an Independent Administrator and forensic auditor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Court-I passed an interim order on 15.03.2023 permitting Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to represent the company in pending proceedings; Appellant appealed under Section 421; during appeal pendency, NCLT on 18.07.2025 passed a final common order disposing of CP No. 5 of 2023.
legal_issues: Whether an interlocutory appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 challenging an interim order of representation under Section 241-242 survives or becomes infructuous upon the Adjudicating Authority passing a comprehensive final order disposing of the company petition; and whether the interim authorization of promoter-directors to represent the company in arbitration concerning pre-SPA disputed receivables was legally valid under the Share Purchase Agreement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against an interim protective order passed in oppression and mismanagement proceedings becomes infructuous when the company court subsequently passes a comprehensive final order under Section 242 regulating the overall management of the company, as the interim directions are overtaken and absorbed by the larger statutory supervisory regime. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 powers to regulate company affairs override internal contractual and managerial arrangements to remedy oppression; an interim arrangement allowing directors who bear past liabilities and hold rights to past receivables under an SPA to represent the company does not violate Section 241. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Doctrine of mootness and merger; appellate courts will not adjudicate interlocutory orders where subsequent final judicial developments render the grant of practical relief impossible or superfluous. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because NCLT passed a final order on 18.07.2025 disposing of CP No. 5 of 2023, appointing an Independent Administrator, and ordering a forensic audit, the challenge to the 15.03.2023 interim order ceased to survive independently, justifying dismissal as infructuous.
operative_order: The appeal has become infructuous in view of the comprehensive directions issued under Section 242 in CP No. 5 (AHM) of 2023 and connected applications. The appeal is dismissed as having become infructuous. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Dr. Anita Roy, majority shareholder of Aquafil Polymers Company Pvt. Ltd., appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act against NCLT Ahmedabad's interim order dated 15.03.2023 in CP No. 5/2023. The interim order permitted minority promoter-directors (Respondents 2 and 3) to represent the company in pending arbitral and judicial proceedings pursuant to Clause 6 of their 2019 Share Purchase Agreement. While the appeal was pending, NCLT passed a final common order on 18.07.2025 disposing of the main petition, removing the Managing Director, appointing an Independent Administrator, and ordering a forensic audit. NCLAT held that the interim order was absorbed by the subsequent final order under Section 242, rendering the appeal infructuous, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Assistant Commissioner of Customs vs. Mr. Renahan Vamakesan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Assistant Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Cochin (statutory operational creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Renahan Vamakesan, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is M/s. Rubberwood India (P) Limited (Corporate Debtor in liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor imported goods under 8 Bills of Entry during 2000-2001 availing duty concessions under Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme; upon failure to fulfill export obligations, customs duty demand of Rs. 14,08,172/- was confirmed vide order dated 25.06.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Customs duty demand of Rs. 14,08,172/-; claim submitted before the liquidator with an admitted, unprecedented delay of 787 days beyond the statutory liquidation period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Duty order passed on 25.06.2009; Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal on 09.10.2013; CESTAT appeal abated/closed on 26.09.2024; CIRP admitted 17.05.2022; liquidation ordered on 15.12.2022 (30-day claim period expired mid-January 2023); Appellant filed Form-B claim on 12.03.2025; Liquidator rejected claim on 19.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EPCG duty demand order dated 25.06.2009, CESTAT abatement order dated 26.09.2024, Form-B claim submission dated 12.03.2025, Liquidator's rejection email dated 19.03.2025 citing 787 days delay, and progress of liquidation asset distribution under Section 53. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed appeal CA(IBC)/6/KOB/2025 under Section 42 of the IBC seeking condonation of 787 days delay and acceptance of claim; NCLT Kochi Bench dismissed the appeal on 30.10.2025 holding the claim hopelessly time-barred without reasonable explanation.
legal_issues: Whether the 30-day timeline prescribed under Regulation 12(2)(b) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 for submission of claims before the liquidator can be extended to condone an inordinate delay of 787 days by a government department; whether statutory authorities enjoy special privilege or exemption from IBC limitation timelines; and whether the pendency and abatement of an appeal under the Customs Act excuses delay in submitting claims during liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate liquidation proceedings where time is of the essence, statutory timelines for submission of claims must be strictly adhered to, and even if claim filing timelines under liquidation regulations are characterized as directory, an inordinate, unprecedented delay cannot be condoned in the absence of a reasonable and satisfactory explanation, especially when the liquidation process has advanced to the distribution stage under waterfall priorities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12(2)(b) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 mandates claim submission within 30 days of the liquidation commencement date; Section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot be imported to bypass special statutory liquidation timelines, and the overriding nature of the IBC under Section 238 bars indefinite extensions for statutory dues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict scrutiny of the explanation for delay; government departments and statutory authorities stand on the same footing as ordinary litigants and cannot claim preferential dispensation or leniency for administrative lethargy. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Customs Department had full knowledge of its demand since 2009 and the CESTAT abatement on 26.09.2024 but failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for the 787-day delay, which would impermissibly disrupt Section 53 asset distributions; hence, the dismissal under Section 42 was justified.
operative_order: The dismissal of the appeal under Section 42 of the IBC on the ground of belated claim with 787 days delay does not suffer from any legal error. The Company Appeal lacks merit and is dismissed. All pending interlocutory applications stand closed.
summary: Appellant Assistant Commissioner of Customs appealed against the NCLT Kochi order dated 30.10.2025 dismissing its appeal under Section 42 of the IBC. The Customs Department sought condonation of a 787-day delay in lodging its claim of Rs. 14.08 Lakhs for EPCG duty defaults with the Liquidator of Rubberwood India (P) Ltd. Customs argued that the claim was delayed due to pending proceedings before CESTAT which abated on 26.09.2024, and relied on Rainbow Papers to contend Regulation 12 is directory. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that time is the essence of the IBC and government authorities enjoy no special privileges. Because the department failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for the inordinate delay and the liquidation had already reached the Section 53 distribution stage, the claim could not be entertained.

case_title: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development vs. SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is National Bank for Agriculture & Rural Development (NABARD), a statutory development bank and refinancing creditor[cite: 24]; Corporate Debtor is SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (SEFL), a notified Financial Service Provider under Section 227[cite: 24]; Respondent No. 2 is Rajneesh Sharma, Administrator/RP[cite: 24]; Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors represented through UCO Bank[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Refinance facility to the extent of Rs. 2,212.5 crores sanctioned by NABARD to SEFL across six sanction letters between 07.05.2016 and 04.03.2019 under six General Refinance Agreements (GRAs) and corresponding Deeds of Assignment of Book Debts (including Deed dated 06.03.2019), wherein SEFL agreed to hold all repayments and recoveries from ultimate borrowers in trust for NABARD under Section 29 of the NABARD Act, 1981[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed outstanding financial debt of Rs. 883,63,31,295/- (comprising principal of Rs. 819,26,16,507/- and interest of Rs. 64,37,14,788/-) as on 08.10.2021[cite: 24]; loan account classified as NPA[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI superseded SEFL's Board on 08.10.2021[cite: 24]; CIRP initiated against SEFL in CP(IB) No. 294/KB/2021 on 08.10.2021[cite: 24]; NABARD issued letters asserting Section 29 statutory priority to the Administrator on 07.10.2021, 14.10.2021, and 20.10.2021[cite: 24]; claim submitted in Form-C on 21.10.2021[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Six General Refinance Agreements containing Clause 10 (statutory trust under Section 29)[cite: 24], Deeds of Assignment of Book Debts[cite: 24], Demand Promissory Notes[cite: 24], MCA charge creation certificates[cite: 24], Administrator's reply admitting Rs. 317.12 crores collected from refinanced accounts (Rs. 197.54 crores pre-CIRP and Rs. 119.58 crores during CIRP)[cite: 24], and Minutes of the 37th CoC meeting dated 03.03.2023 setting aside funds for NABARD pending litigation[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NABARD filed IA(IB) No. 896/KB/2022 on 16.06.2022 seeking directions to ensure priority of repayment and pass on assigned recoveries[cite: 24]; NCLT Kolkata Bench (Court-I) rejected the application on 01.02.2024 holding that NABARD participated in CoC as a secured financial creditor and was bound by the approved resolution plan as a dissenting financial creditor (having received Rs. 122 crores), with further claims barred by res judicata[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether NABARD is entitled to exclusive priority of payment over recoveries and receivables from refinanced loan accounts under Section 29 of the NABARD Act, 1981 read with Rule 10 of the FSP Rules, 2019, treating them as third-party assets held in trust rather than assets of the Corporate Debtor; and whether filing a claim in Form-C and participating in the CoC as a secured financial creditor constitutes a waiver of its statutory trust rights under Section 29[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the insolvency resolution of a financial service provider, funds and receivables collected from ultimate borrowers in respect of refinancing facilities that are statutorily deemed to be held in trust under a governing development bank statute constitute third-party assets under specialized insolvency rules, which do not form part of the corporate debtor's asset pool and must be paid over in priority to the refinancing statutory institution; submitting a claim in standard insolvency forms does not operate as a waiver of overriding statutory trust entitlements[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29(1) of the NABARD Act creates a statutory trust over sums received by a borrowing institution from refinanced loans to the extent of outstanding accommodation; Rule 10 of the FSP Rules expressly excludes third-party assets held in trust from moratorium under Section 14 and CIRP asset pools; Section 227 and Notification dated 30.01.2020 obligate the Administrator to maintain and remit third-party receivables to the statutory beneficiary[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory characterization and tracing of trust funds; where contractual and statutory terms establish an express refinancing arrangement with assigned book debts, and the Administrator's records confirm collections from refinanced accounts, the statutory trust is established and cannot be defeated by general CIRP claim forms[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC having specifically set aside amounts for NABARD in the distribution mechanism of the resolution plan pending judicial determination, NABARD is entitled to the full set-aside amount, with the Rs. 121 crores already received as a dissenting creditor adjusted against it[cite: 24].
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 01.02.2024 rejecting IA (IB) No. 896/KB/2022 is set aside[cite: 24]. IA (IB) No. 896/KB/2022 is allowed[cite: 24]. Appellant shall be entitled to the amount set apart for NABARD as per the distribution mechanism approved in the 37th CoC meeting, with the amount already paid as a dissenting financial creditor adjusted against it[cite: 24]. Parties bear their own costs[cite: 24].
summary: NABARD appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order dated 01.02.2024 rejecting its application in the CIRP of financial service provider SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (SEFL)[cite: 24]. NABARD had extended refinance facilities exceeding Rs. 2,200 Crores with an outstanding debt of Rs. 883.63 Crores, claiming that receivables from refinanced loans were held in statutory trust under Section 29 of the NABARD Act, 1981 and Rule 10 of the FSP Rules, 2019[cite: 24]. The NCLT held that NABARD participated in the CoC and was bound by the resolution plan as a dissenting financial creditor[cite: 24]. NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that statutory trust assets do not belong to the debtor's estate, filing Form-C caused no waiver, and NABARD was entitled to the funds specifically set aside in the resolution plan[cite: 24].

case_title: M/s Pragiti Construction vs. Committee of Creditors of the Corporate Debtor & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Pragiti Construction (Proprietor Renu Verma), an eligible Prospective Resolution Applicant[cite: 25]; Respondent No. 1 is Committee of Creditors of Rancom Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), represented solely by M/s Mahavir Medicare (Operational Creditor holding 100% voting share and competing Resolution Applicant)[cite: 25]; Respondent No. 2 is Rajeev Ranjan Singh, Resolution Professional[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor engaged in trading of generic pharmaceutical and medical products; no financial creditors existed, leaving operational creditor Mahavir Medicare as the sole claimant and sole CoC member[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim of Mahavir Medicare admitted at Rs. 14,99,25,340/-[cite: 25]; Mahavir Medicare submitted a resolution plan of Rs. 12,61,136/- (Rs. 1,00,000/- to operational creditor and Rs. 11,61,136/- CIRP costs)[cite: 25]; Appellant Pragiti Construction submitted a competing resolution plan offering Rs. 20,00,000/- (Rs. 10,00,000/- to operational creditor plus full CIRP costs and Rs. 10,00,000/- for contingencies)[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application admitted on 21.12.2023[cite: 25]; Form A published 23.12.2023[cite: 25]; EOI deadline extended to 04.05.2024[cite: 25]; Mahavir Medicare submitted plan on 04.05.2024 and approved it in 5th CoC meeting via e-voting on 11.06.2024[cite: 25]; Appellant submitted plan on 13.06.2024[cite: 25]; NCLT directed fresh consideration on 10.09.2024[cite: 25]; 6th CoC meeting held on 18.09.2024 rejecting Appellant's plan[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of 6th CoC meeting dated 18.09.2024 showing RP highlighted Appellant's plan was twenty times higher, while sole CoC member rejected it without evaluation matrix citing 99.33% haircut, sector mismatch, and timeline delay[cite: 25]; IA 339/2024 under Section 45 and IA 349/2024 under Section 66 for Rs. 5.65 crores assigned to SRA under approved plan[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench vide orders dated 12.11.2024 dismissed Appellant's IA No. 358 of 2024 seeking plan consideration and allowed RP's IA No. 401 of 2024 approving Mahavir Medicare's resolution plan, holding that CoC exercised commercial wisdom[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether an Operational Creditor who is the sole member of the Committee of Creditors holding 100% voting rights can legally vote upon and approve its own Resolution Plan in light of the express statutory bar in the proviso to Section 30(5) of the IBC; and whether a single-member CoC that is also a competing Resolution Applicant can impartially evaluate competing resolution plans without violating principles of natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua) and the statutory mandate of value maximisation[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the statutory framework of the IBC, a resolution applicant who is not a financial creditor is strictly barred from voting in meetings of the committee of creditors; an operational creditor constituting a sole-member committee cannot exercise voting rights to approve its own resolution plan, and any decision taken in direct conflict of interest to exclude a substantially superior competing offer violates both the express statutory bar and the fundamental principle of natural justice that no entity may be a judge in its own cause[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(5) proviso explicitly restricts the right of a resolution applicant to vote in CoC meetings to cases where such applicant is a financial creditor; an operational creditor resolution applicant has zero voting rights on resolution plans, rendering any approval by it void ab initio; commercial wisdom cannot shield decisions that violate express statutory bars and procedural safeguards under Regulation 39[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance with statutory voting eligibility and procedural natural justice; failure to prepare an evaluation matrix, failure to invite the competing applicant under Section 30(5), and predetermined rejection of a plan offering twenty times higher value establish material irregularity and fatal bias[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The approval of its own plan by the sole operational creditor was void ab initio, and because the current legislative framework contains no mechanism to resolve such a structural conflict of interest, the corporate debtor must be directed into liquidation[cite: 25].
operative_order: Impugned orders dated 12.11.2024 in IA No. 358 of 2024 and IA No. 401 of 2024 are set aside[cite: 25]. Liquidation of Corporate Debtor Rancom Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. is ordered[cite: 25]. CP (IB) No. 31/ALD/2021 is restored to its original position; parties directed to appear before NCLT Allahabad on 18.02.2026[cite: 25]. Matter referred to IBBI for appropriate action against the RP and for initiating statutory amendments[cite: 25].
summary: Appellant Pragiti Construction appealed against NCLT Allahabad orders dated 12.11.2024 approving the resolution plan of M/s Mahavir Medicare and rejecting Appellant's plan for Rancom Healthcare Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 25] In the CIRP, Mahavir Medicare was the petitioning Operational Creditor, the sole claimant, the sole member of the CoC holding 100% voting share, and the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 25]. NCLAT held that under the express proviso to Section 30(5) of the IBC, a resolution applicant who is not a financial creditor has no right to vote on a resolution plan, rendering Mahavir Medicare's self-approval void ab initio[cite: 25]. Further, the rejection of Appellant's plan—offering twenty times the upfront consideration—violated natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua)[cite: 25]. NCLAT set aside the plan approval and ordered liquidation of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 25].

case_title: Baskaran Sathya Prakash & Anr. vs. CS Vasudevan Gopu, Liquidator of M/s. Raaj Internet India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Baskaran Sathya Prakash, former employee/director of Corporate Debtor; Appellant No. 2 is Rathinamala, wife of Appellant No. 1; Respondent is CS Vasudevan Gopu, Liquidator of M/s. Raaj Internet India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant No. 1 claimed unpaid salary and expense reimbursements, while Appellant No. 2 had advanced short-term interest-free loans to the Corporate Debtor, asserting cumulative outstanding dues of Rs. 2.48 Crores upon Appellant No. 1's resignation[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidator categorized loan repayments and service payments to Appellants between 12.10.2017 and 06.02.2018 as preferential transactions under Sections 43 and 44 of the IBC, demanding avoidance and refund of Rs. 2.48 Crores[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidator filed avoidance application MA/653/2018 in CP/185/IB/CB/2018; on 30.10.2023, matter listed for hearing on 14.12.2023; on 14.12.2023, NCLT listed for orders with liberty to argue on 7-day notice; on 13.02.2024, NCLT listed Appellants' IA (IBC)/388/CHE/2024 (seeking to place Board Resolution dated 14.10.2016 on record) along with MA/653/2018 for hearing on 01.03.2024; without notice, NCLT preponed the matter to 19.02.2024 on the cause list and pronounced an ex-parte order in MA/653/2018[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order sheets dated 30.10.2023, 14.12.2023, and 13.02.2024; Cause list of 19.02.2024; undecided IA (IBC)/388/CHE/2024 for bringing Board Resolution dated 14.10.2016 on record; and NCLAT order dated 11.03.2024 in Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 90 of 2024 granting liberty to seek redressal before NCLT[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Pursuant to NCLAT liberty, Appellants filed IA (IBC)/743/CHE/2024 under Section 60(5) read with Rule 11 seeking recall of the ex-parte order dated 19.02.2024; NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed the application on 31.07.2025 holding that it lacked power to review its own order[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 60(5) of the IBC read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules seeking to set aside an ex-parte order passed without notifying a date of hearing or reserving orders constitutes an impermissible application for review or a maintainable application for procedural recall; and whether the Adjudicating Authority violated Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 44 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 by preponing the date of hearing and pronouncing an ex-parte order while leaving an interlocutory application for placing documents on record undecided[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application seeking to recall an ex-parte order passed in violation of mandatory procedural rules of hearing, without prior notice of listing or due adherence to ex-parte procedure, is an application for procedural recall under inherent powers to prevent abuse of process, distinct from a review on substantive merits; adjudicatory tribunals possess inherent jurisdiction to recall orders vitiated by procedural lapses[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(1) and (2) of the Companies Act, 2013 (applicable to IBC proceedings) mandates adherence to principles of natural justice and vests powers of a civil court under CPC; Rule 44 of NCLT Rules, 2016 mandatorily requires notifying parties of the date and place of hearing; Order IX Rule 7 CPC governs proceedings before declaring a party ex-parte; Section 60(5) read with Rule 11 authorizes recall of ex-parte orders rendered without due process[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of tribunal order sheets and cause lists; where the record reveals that a scheduled date was preponed without notice, arguments were never concluded, and a pending document-placement application was left unadjudicated, procedural nullity and violation of natural justice are established on the face of the record[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in mischaracterizing the recall application as a review petition; the dismissal was quashed and the matter remitted for fresh adjudication on merits subject to payment of Rs. 50,000/- costs[cite: 26].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 31.07.2025 is quashed and the appeal is allowed[cite: 26]. Matter is remitted back to NCLT Chennai to reconsider and decide IA (IBC)/743/CHE/2024 after first taking a decision on IA (IBC)/388/CHE/2024, subject to the Appellant depositing costs of Rs. 50,000/- in the Prime Minister's Relief Fund within two weeks[cite: 26]. Pending IAs closed[cite: 26].
summary: Appellants Baskaran Sathya Prakash and Rathinamala appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated 31.07.2025 dismissing their application IA (IBC)/743/CHE/2024, which sought recall of an ex-parte order dated 19.02.2024 in a preferential transaction proceeding under Sections 43-44 IBC[cite: 26]. The NCLT had rejected the recall application on the ground that it had no statutory power to review its own decisions[cite: 26]. NCLAT held that an application to recall an order passed without notice of hearing, after preponing the date from 01.03.2024 to 19.02.2024 and without deciding a pending document application, is a legitimate application for procedural recall under Section 60(5) and Rule 11, not a review on merits[cite: 26]. NCLAT quashed the order and remitted the matter for fresh hearing subject to Rs. 50,000/- costs[cite: 26].

case_title: Malharshanti Enterprises vs. Naresh Sevantilal Shah & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Malharshanti Enterprises (sole proprietorship of Sunil Pande), an Operational Creditor of CAN Enterprises Private Limited. Respondent No. 1 is Naresh Sevantilal Shah, Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) for Corporate Debtor Afcan Impex Private Limited and promoter/director of CAN Enterprises Private Limited. Respondent No. 2 is Nitin Narang, Resolution Professional of Afcan Impex Private Limited. Bank of Maharashtra is the sole Financial Creditor in Afcan Impex CIRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of Maharashtra extended commercial credit facilities to Corporate Debtor Afcan Impex Private Limited. Separately, Malharshanti Enterprises supplied goods and services as an operational creditor to CAN Enterprises Private Limited, giving rise to operational debts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Afcan Impex defaulted on bank credit facilities resulting in Section 7 admission on 17.02.2021. CAN Enterprises defaulted on operational debt of Rs. 1.97 Crores owed to Malharshanti Enterprises, leading to Section 9 admission on 27.01.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 admission of Afcan Impex on 17.02.2021; Form G published on 19.06.2021; CoC approved R1's Resolution Plan on 06.10.2021; Section 29A affidavit filed by R1 on 11.11.2024; R1 settlement offer letter sent on 05.03.2025 and rejected by Appellant on 10.03.2025; NCLT Ahmedabad approved plan on 30.09.2025; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 20.03.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Professional due diligence report verifying R1's Section 29A eligibility; Section 29A affidavit dated 11.11.2024; total lack of RBI NPA classification records regarding R1 or CAN Enterprises; absence of any Registrar of Companies (ROC) disqualification order under Section 164 of Companies Act; evidence of complete plan implementation with disbursements of Rs. 6,51,19,488.68 to all creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of Maharashtra filed CP (IB) No. 289(AHM) of 2020 under Section 7 admitted on 17.02.2021 by NCLT Ahmedabad. NCLT Ahmedabad approved R1's resolution plan in IA No. 766/(AHM)/2021 on 30.09.2025, holding that ongoing proceedings of CAN Enterprises before NCLT Mumbai did not bar approval under Section 29A.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor of a separate corporate debtor has locus standi as a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge the approval of a resolution plan in an unrelated corporate debtor's CIRP, and whether the Successful Resolution Applicant was disqualified under Section 29A(c) or 29A(e) of the IBC due to being a promoter/director of a separate company undergoing CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To qualify as a 'person aggrieved' entitled to maintain an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC, the appellant must be a direct stakeholder in the specific corporate insolvency resolution process suffering direct legal injury; a creditor in a separate, unrelated CIRP lacks locus standi. Furthermore, ineligibility under Section 29A cannot be presumed without satisfying the strict statutory criteria laid down therein, and a fully implemented resolution plan cannot be unsettled belatedly by a non-stakeholder. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'person aggrieved' under Section 61(1) requires deprivation or denial of legal rights within the subject CIRP; Section 29A(c) strictly requires that the person manage, control, or promote a corporate debtor whose account has been classified as an NPA under RBI guidelines for over one year; Section 29A(e) requires an existing, formal disqualification order under Section 164 of the Companies Act 2013 issued by the ROC or MCA, as there is no concept of 'deemed disqualification'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disqualification under Section 29A(c) and 29A(e) demands formal, positive documentary proof of RBI-mandated NPA classification and an operative disqualification order issued by the ROC/MCA; assertions based on mere assumptions or inferential allegations without competent authority declarations are legally unsustainable, and new factual grounds cannot be raised for the first time on appeal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had no claim, participation, or legal stake in Afcan Impex's CIRP, rendering the appeal non-maintainable under Section 61; additionally, the SRA suffered no disqualification under Section 29A(c) or 29A(e), and the fully implemented resolution plan was validly upheld.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 2032 of 2025 as not maintainable and devoid of merit, closed all pending interlocutory applications, and passed no order as to costs.
summary: Malharshanti Enterprises appealed under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code against the NCLT Ahmedabad order approving the resolution plan submitted by Naresh Sevantilal Shah for Afcan Impex Private Limited. The appellant, an operational creditor of CAN Enterprises Private Limited, contended that the resolution applicant was statutorily ineligible under Section 29A(c) and Section 29A(e) due to CAN Enterprises undergoing corporate insolvency. NCLAT held that the appellant, having no claim or financial stake in Afcan Impex, was not a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61. Furthermore, mere corporate insolvency without NPA classification does not attract Section 29A(c), nor can director disqualification under Section 164 be deemed without a formal ROC order. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: SGN Universal Construction Company Private Limited vs. Shailendra Kumar Singh & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors are Shailendra Kumar Singh and 39 other homebuyers (Respondents No. 1 to 40, allottees of Towers 3 and 4). Corporate Debtor is M/s Morpheus Prodevelopers Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 41, through IRP Mr. Shailendra Singh). Appellant is SGN Universal Construction Company Private Limited (contractor claiming exclusive development rights over Tower 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor developed residential project 'Morpheus Bluebell' at Greater Noida (West). Appellant was engaged as contractor in 2014, and in alleged settlement of Rs. 6.92 Crores outstanding dues, Corporate Debtor executed Development Rights Agreement dated 22.02.2017 for Tower 5 for Rs. 7,62,30,333, followed by Power of Attorney dated 16.03.2017 and Addendum dated 15.10.2020 for 18,000 sq. ft. additional FSI. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on its obligation to hand over possession of residential flats to allottees by the scheduled completion date of June 2017, leading 40 homebuyers representing 356 project flats to seek insolvency resolution. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Scheduled possession date June 2017; Corporate Debtor issued notice terminating Development Rights Agreement on 20.06.2022; Appellant replied disputing termination on 27.06.2022; Delhi High Court Section 9 interim orders passed on 04.11.2022 and 16.01.2023, referring disputes to arbitration on 15.03.2024; Section 7 petition filed in February 2024; Arbitrator Section 17 interim order dated 08.06.2024; NCLT Section 7 admission order dated 19.11.2024; NCLAT decision dated 30.03.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Development Rights Agreement dated 22.02.2017 and Addendum dated 15.10.2020; single unified RERA Registration No. UPRERAPRJ11705 reflecting Corporate Debtor as promoter of Towers 3, 4, and 5; site inspection minutes dated 23.11.2024 establishing functionally integrated common facilities (firefighting, STP/WTP, clubhouse, DG sets); termination notice dated 20.06.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Homebuyers filed CP No. (IB) 62(ND)/2024 under Section 7 before NCLT New Delhi (Court-IV). Appellant filed IA No. 2197(ND)/2024 to bring arbitral orders on record. NCLT admitted Section 7 on 19.11.2024, holding that 40 allottees met the statutory threshold across the 356 total units and that Section 238 overrode parallel arbitration.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in taking into account the total units of Tower 5 to determine the statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, whether preliminary observations on the development agreements prejudiced the Appellant, and whether interim arbitral orders can prevent the Resolution Professional from taking custody of project assets under Sections 14, 18(f), and 238 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution by real estate allottees under Section 7 operates against the corporate debtor in rem for the entire real estate project as an integrated whole, and interim orders in personam passed in arbitral proceedings cannot impede the statutory admission of CIRP or restrict an Interim Resolution Professional from discharging statutory asset-custody duties under Section 18(f) in light of the overriding effect of Section 238 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC mandates calculating the minimum numerical threshold of homebuyers based on the denominator of all units within the registered real estate project; development rights constitute 'property' under Section 3(27) and 'assets' under Section 18(f) and Section 25(2)(a); Section 238 ensures that IBC provisions override the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Project integrity is established through common statutory licensing under RERA, shared critical infrastructure (interconnected firefighting, power, and water plants), and physical site verifications, demonstrating that standalone segregation of a tower cannot be sustained against insolvency proceedings in rem. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no illegality in computing the Section 7 threshold across all 356 project units, interim arbitral orders cannot stay CIRP, and non-final observations in the admission order do not prejudice the Appellant's rights which remain open for determination by the RP; hence, the appeal was rejected.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal rejected Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 2207 of 2024, held that observations made were prima facie without expressing any final determination on the substantive rights of the parties, closed all pending interlocutory applications, and made no order as to costs.
summary: SGN Universal Construction Company Private Limited appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by forty homebuyers against Corporate Debtor Morpheus Prodevelopers Private Limited. The appellant, claiming absolute development rights over Tower 5 under agreements executed between 2017 and 2020, challenged the NCLT's inclusion of Tower 5 units to satisfy the Section 7 numerical threshold and contested adverse observations regarding its contractual rights. NCLAT rejected the appeal, holding that the project was functionally integrated under a single RERA registration and the threshold was lawfully computed. Relying on Sections 18(f) and 238, NCLAT affirmed that IBC overrides arbitral interim orders, leaving final ownership claims open for subsequent determination by the Resolution Professional.

case_title: Cosmic CRF Limited vs. Myotic Trading Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 4810, 5965 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 859 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Amzen Transportation Industries Limited. Financial Creditor is IDBI Bank Ltd. Resolution Professional is Deepak Maini. Applicant and Resolution Applicant is Cosmic CRF Limited (managed and promoted by Aditya Vikram Birla and Purvi Birla). Competing Resolution Applicant is Myotic Trading Private Limited (consortium lead). CoC members include Prudent ARC Limited and UCO Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IDBI Bank granted loan facilities to Corporate Debtor Amzen Transportation Industries Limited. Upon default, CIRP was initiated. Cosmic CRF submitted a Resolution Plan on 28.06.2024 pursuant to RFRP dated 20.05.2024 with Rs. 1.50 Crores EMD. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor Amzen to IDBI Bank resulted in Section 7 admission on 04.05.2022. Separately, related company Cosmic Ferro Alloys Limited (CFAL) defaulted on credit facilities of Rs. 178 Crores (including Rs. 13.06 Crores to Citibank NA), declared NPA on 09.12.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Amzen CIRP commenced on 04.05.2022; Form G published on 20.04.2024; Cosmic submitted plan on 28.06.2024; Energy Watchdog complaint dated 20.08.2024; CoC declared Cosmic eligible on 06.03.2025; NCLAT held Cosmic ineligible on 25.07.2025; Supreme Court order in Civil Appeal No. 9900/2025 on 04.08.2025; NCLAT recall judgment on 12.03.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic and due diligence reports by AHSK & Co. and Priyanka Sharma & Associates (PSA) finding Section 29A ineligibility; Business Transfer Agreement dated 19.01.2022 transferring CFAL's Singur unit to Cosmic CRF for Rs. 49 Crores; CFAL approved plan showing retention of Aditya Vikram Birla as Marketing Executive; corporate guarantees executed by Archana Impex Pvt. Ltd. for CFAL debts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted Section 7 CP No. (IB)-3(ND)/2020 on 04.05.2022. On 29.05.2025, NCLT dismissed Myotic's IA No. 1240/ND/2025 for lack of locus. On appeal, NCLAT on 25.07.2025 declared Cosmic ineligible under Section 29A. Pursuant to Supreme Court liberty, Cosmic moved IA No. 4810 of 2025 seeking recall under Rule 11.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal's judgment declaring Cosmic CRF Limited ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC ought to be recalled under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules 2016, and whether a Resolution Applicant whose promoters controlled an NPA corporate debtor (CFAL) resolved through CIRP remains ineligible under Section 29A(c) and Section 29A(j) when it retains operational control and acquires debtor assets without curing overdue debt under the first proviso to Section 29A(c).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 29A of the IBC is a 'see-through' provision requiring the piercing of the corporate veil to examine de facto control and concert of action; erstwhile promoters and connected persons of a corporate debtor whose account was classified as an NPA cannot use corporate restructuring or subsequent third-party resolution to bypass Section 29A(c) and 29A(j) or stage a backdoor entry into insolvency resolution without fully paying all overdue debts, interest, and charges under the first proviso to Section 29A(c). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(c) ineligibility attaches to any person acting jointly or in concert who controlled or promoted an NPA corporate debtor; the clean slate doctrine extinguishes corporate liability upon resolution but does not immunize delinquent promoters from personal statutory ineligibility unless overdue debts are cured pursuant to the first proviso; Section 29A(j) read with Explanation I extends disqualification to connected entities sharing de facto continuity of management and asset control. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: De facto control is determined using the substance-over-form test laid down in ArcelorMittal and Phoenix ARC, evaluating cross-shareholdings, family directorships, post-resolution employment retention, slump sale transfers of core assets, and unresolved guarantee commitments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Aditya Vikram Birla and connected entities exercised de facto management over CFAL when classified as NPA, retained continuous operational ties post-resolution, and acquired CFAL's core assets without paying overdue financial debts under the first proviso to Section 29A(c); therefore, Cosmic CRF Limited is statutorily ineligible under Section 29A(c) and Section 29A(j), and the recall application was dismissed.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed IA No. 4810 of 2025 refusing to recall the judgment dated 25.07.2025, affirmed the Section 29A ineligibility of Cosmic CRF Limited, directed the Resolution Professional to immediately continue the CIRP of Amzen Transportation Industries Limited, directed IBBI to conduct an independent inquiry into the CIRP and stakeholder conduct, and disposed of all pending applications without costs.
summary: Cosmic CRF Limited filed a recall application under Rule 11 before the NCLAT challenging its declaration of ineligibility under Section 29A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code in the corporate insolvency of Amzen Transportation Industries Limited. The applicant contended that the resolution of Cosmic Ferro Alloys Limited extinguished past defaults and severed promoter ties, rendering it eligible. Applying a purposive interpretation and piercing the corporate veil under ArcelorMittal, the NCLAT held that applicant's promoter retained de facto operational association and acquired substantial business assets of the resolved debtor without discharging overdue debts under the first proviso to Section 29A(c). Upholding disqualification under Sections 29A(c) and 29A(j), NCLAT dismissed the recall application.

case_title: BSE Limited vs. Mrudula Brodie & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1786 of 2025 and 1862 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is BSE Limited (Stock Exchange). In CA 1786/2025, Corporate Debtor is Future Corporate Resources Private Limited (under CIRP through IRP Mr. Avil Menezes, Respondent No. 1); other respondents are CDSL, SEBI, and Samurai Securities. In CA 1862/2024, Corporate Debtor is Liz Traders and Agents Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation through Liquidator Ms. Mrudula Brodie, Respondent No. 1); other respondents are NSE, NSDL, IIFL, and SEBI. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtors held listed equity shares and securities in dematerialized format in demat accounts with depository participants (Samurai Securities and IIFL). In CA 1786/2025, the CD held shares in Generali Central Insurance Co. Ltd. and Shendra Advisory Pvt. Ltd. In CA 1862/2024, the CD held shares in Tata Chemicals, Tata Consumer Products, Indian Hotels, Cox and Kings, and Videocon Industries. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In CA 1786/2025, BSE imposed a debit freeze for non-payment of Annual Listing Fees (ALF) of Rs. 15,15,857/- owed by group company Future Retail Ltd. (FRL). In CA 1862/2024, BSE and NSE froze the CD's demat account due to non-compliance with LODR Regulations and non-payment of fines/ALF by listed companies where CD was disclosed as promoter (Cox and Kings Ltd., Cox and Kings Financial Services Ltd., and Tulip Stars Hotels Ltd.). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In CA 1786/2025, CIRP initiated on 24.09.2024 in CP (IB) No. 1113/MB/2022; IRP letters requesting defreeze sent on 25.02.2025 and 19.03.2025; BSE refusal dated 24.03.2025; NCLT order passed on 31.10.2025. In CA 1862/2024, CIRP initiated on 25.02.2022; liquidation ordered on 05.09.2022 in CP IB No. 2941/MB/2019; Liquidator defreeze requests sent in Dec 2022 and Jan 2023; BSE/NSE refusals dated 23.02.2023 and 24.02.2023; NCLT order passed on 31.07.2024; NCLAT final order dated 24.03.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Demat account transaction statements proving undisputed ownership of the subject shares by the respective Corporate Debtors; correspondence and notices from BSE, NSE, CDSL, NSDL, IIFL, and Samurai Securities confirming debit freezes were imposed purely for unpaid ALF and LODR fines; SEBI reply affidavit confirming no-objection to defreezing under Clause 5 of the SEBI SOP Circular dated 11.02.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CA 1786/2025, NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 CP (IB) No. 1113/MB/2022 on 24.09.2024; on 31.10.2025 in IA No. 2590 of 2025, NCLT directed BSE to defreeze the demat account. In CA 1862/2024, NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 CP IB No. 2941/MB/2019 on 25.02.2022; on 31.07.2024 in IA No. 928 of 2023, NCLT directed BSE and NSE to defreeze the demat account to facilitate liquidation estate sales.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to direct stock exchanges and depositories to defreeze demat accounts of corporate debtors frozen prior to CIRP/liquidation for non-payment of Annual Listing Fees and regulatory fines, and whether Section 238 of the IBC overrides the securities regulatory enforcement mechanisms under the SCRA, SEBI Act, and LODR Regulations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 60(5)(c) read with Section 238 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority possesses valid jurisdiction to direct the defreezing of assets undisputedly owned by a corporate debtor where statutory or regulatory dues and penalties have already been fully crystallized, as the recovery of such crystallized dues falls within the collective distribution framework of the Code and cannot be enforced through coercive administrative freezes outside the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) residuary jurisdiction encompasses questions of law or fact arising out of or in relation to insolvency resolution and liquidation; crystallized regulatory fees and penalties constitute 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) making the regulatory authority an 'operational creditor' under Section 5(20); Sections 18(f), 25(2)(a), 35(1)(b), and 36 mandate the IRP/RP/Liquidator to assume custody and control of corporate assets; Section 238 overrides inconsistent recovery mechanisms under Section 28A of the SEBI Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench applies the crystallization test established in Embassy Property Developments: where regulatory proceedings have terminated in crystallized financial liabilities leaving only recovery, and there is no dispute concerning asset title, the matter directly relates to insolvency resolution, distinguishing it from non-crystallized public law adjudications. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Annual Listing Fees and fines were completely crystallized with no ongoing administrative quantification, and the corporate debtors undisputedly owned the shares in the demat accounts; hence, NCLT properly exercised its jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to order defreezing to facilitate CIRP and liquidation, and the appeals were dismissed.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1786 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1862 of 2024, affirmed the NCLT orders directing BSE and depositories to defreeze the Demat accounts of the Corporate Debtors, closed all pending interlocutory applications, and passed no order as to costs.
summary: BSE Limited appealed against two NCLT Mumbai orders directing it to defreeze demat accounts belonging to Corporate Debtors Future Corporate Resources Private Limited and Liz Traders and Agents Private Limited. The accounts had been debit-frozen by BSE for non-payment of crystallized Annual Listing Fees and regulatory fines prior to insolvency. BSE contended that NCLT lacked jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to interfere with the securities regulatory framework. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that since the corporate debtors undisputedly owned the shares and the regulatory dues were fully crystallized leaving only recovery, the matter directly related to insolvency and liquidation. Under Sections 18(f), 35, 60(5), and 238, NCLT possessed valid jurisdiction to order defreezing.

case_title: SPS Steels Rolling Mills Limited vs. Indian Overseas Bank & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 352 of 2024 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 353 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is SPS Steels Rolling Mills Limited[cite: 5]. Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) taking over management is Shakambhari Ispat and Power Limited (operating as the Corporate Debtor)[cite: 5]. Financial Creditors and Committee of Creditors (CoC) members include Central Bank of India (sole respondent in CA 352/2024) and Indian Overseas Bank (Respondent No. 1 in CA 353/2024); Allahabad Bank was the original Section 7 applicant; Assistant Commissioner of Customs and DGFT are statutory beneficiaries[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor obtained Bank Guarantees (BGs) issued in favor of statutory authorities (Customs and DGFT) between 2005-2013 from Indian Overseas Bank and 2012-2014 from Central Bank of India, in lieu of which Corporate Debtor pledged Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs) as margin money[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial Creditors had total admitted claims of Rs. 391.79 Crores following Corporate Debtor's default; all BGs expired uninvoked between 2009 and 24.08.2017[cite: 5]. The FDRs lying with Indian Overseas Bank aggregated Rs. 1,30,00,000/-, and separate undisclosed FDR amounts were held by Central Bank of India[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Allahabad Bank filed Section 7 on 24.08.2017; CIRP admitted on 22.12.2017; public announcement issued on 28.12.2017; SRA submitted Resolution Plan on 09.05.2018; NCLT approved plan on 08.04.2019 in CA(IB) No. 871/KB/2018; SRA took over management on 11.04.2019; FDRs discovered in March 2020; IOB refunded Rs. 79,24,041/- on 18.06.2021; IAs filed in 2021; NCLT dismissal on 21.12.2023; NCLAT decision on 19.03.2026[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: FDR records created in the Corporate Debtor's name as margin money; expired Bank Guarantees; Information Memorandum omitting the FDRs; approved Resolution Plan showing full settlement of Central Bank of India (Rs. 32.50 Crores) and IOB; partial release advice of Rs. 79,24,041/- by IOB on 18.06.2021[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SRA filed IA(IB) No. 500/KB/2021 and IA(IB) No. 501/KB/2021 under Section 60(5) before NCLT Kolkata Bench seeking credit of FDR proceeds[cite: 5]. On 21.12.2023, NCLT dismissed both applications and ordered SRA to refund Rs. 79,24,041/- with interest to be placed before the erstwhile CoC for distribution, holding that had the FDRs been disclosed in the Information Memorandum, the resolution plan value would have been higher[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether Fixed Deposit Receipts created by a Corporate Debtor as margin money for Bank Guarantees that expired uninvoked prior to CIRP constitute assets of the Corporate Debtor that vest in the Successful Resolution Applicant upon plan implementation, or whether such assets omitted from the Information Memorandum belong to the erstwhile Committee of Creditors or can be adjusted by creditor banks towards pre-CIRP claims[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Margin money deposited by a corporate debtor as collateral for bank guarantees remains the property of the corporate debtor once the guarantees expire uninvoked; upon full implementation of an approved resolution plan, all assets of the corporate debtor vest in the corporate debtor under its new management, and any asset inadvertently omitted from the information memorandum does not revert to the erstwhile committee of creditors nor can it be adjusted by creditor banks whose pre-CIRP claims stand extinguished[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted Regulations 36, 37, and 38 of the IBBI CIRP Regulations, 2016 read with Section 31(1) of the IBC; while Regulation 36 requires disclosure of assets and contingent liabilities, it does not mention contingent assets, nor does any provision require a resolution applicant to catalog every acquired asset; Section 31(1) operates to freeze and extinguish pre-CIRP claims on the liability side, while preserving debtor assets in the corporate debtor[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Indian Overseas Bank v. Arvind Kumar, margin money reverses back to the corporate debtor upon expiration of the bank guarantee without invocation; undisputed records showed that all BGs had expired uninvoked prior to CIRP and the banks had received full settlement under the approved plan[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The creditor banks had no legal right to adjust the FDR proceeds towards pre-CIRP debts post-plan implementation, and the NCLT erred in directing the proceeds to be distributed to the erstwhile CoC; the appeals were allowed, the impugned order set aside, and the matter remanded[cite: 5].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 352 and 353 of 2024, set aside the impugned order dated 21.12.2023 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench, remanded the matter back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide in accordance with law, directed parties to appear on 06.04.2026, and closed all pending interlocutory applications with no order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary: SPS Steels Rolling Mills Limited, through Successful Resolution Applicant Shakambhari Ispat and Power Limited, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order denying it proceeds of Fixed Deposit Receipts held with Central Bank of India and Indian Overseas Bank[cite: 5]. The FDRs were pledged as margin money for bank guarantees that expired uninvoked before CIRP, but were omitted from the Information Memorandum[cite: 5]. The NCLT directed the proceeds to be distributed among the erstwhile Committee of Creditors[cite: 5]. Setting aside the order, NCLAT held that margin money for expired guarantees remains the asset of the corporate debtor[cite: 5]. Such omitted assets vest in the resolved corporate debtor and cannot be adjusted by creditor banks whose pre-CIRP claims stand extinguished[cite: 5]. The matter was remanded[cite: 5].

case_title: Phoenix ARC Private Limited vs. Rajendra Himmatlal Salot
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2185 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2186 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor / Assignee is Phoenix ARC Private Limited (Trustee of Phoenix Trust FY 19-21); Original Lender is Janata Sahakari Co-operative Bank; Corporate Debtor is M/s Raj Poly Products Limited; Personal Guarantors are Rajendra Himmatlal Salot (Respondent in CA 2185/2024) and Hema Rajendra Salot (Respondent in CA 2186/2024)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Original Lender sanctioned Cash Credit / Term Loan facilities of Rs. 10 Crores on 19.12.2013 and additional facility of Rs. 4 Crores on 29.09.2014 (total Rs. 14 Crores) to Corporate Debtor, secured by Personal Guarantees executed on 03.12.2014 and extended via Supplementary Agreements dated 11.03.2016 and 31.03.2017[cite: 6]. Credit facility was assigned to Phoenix ARC on 30.03.2019[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted, classified NPA on 28.12.2017; loan recalled on 10.04.2018; outstanding default was Rs. 15,37,21,490.50 as on 31.03.2018, swelling to Rs. 31,95,58,525.47 as on 28.02.2023[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued on 12.04.2018 (received on 18.04.2018); Assignment Agreement executed on 30.03.2019; Form AOC-4 filed with ROC on 31.12.2020; Rule 7(1) demand notices issued on 23.09.2022 and 06.04.2023; guarantee invocation letter dated 14.02.2023; replies received on 04.10.2022, 17.02.2023, and 14.04.2023; Section 95 petition filed on 13.10.2023; NCLT dismissal order on 03.09.2024; NCLAT decision on 24.03.2026[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter of Guarantee dated 03.12.2014; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice dated 12.04.2018; Assignment Agreement dated 30.03.2019; Independent Auditor's Report for FY 2019-20 filed in Form AOC-4 on 31.12.2020 explicitly acknowledging the debt and stating future payments must be made to Phoenix ARC; Section 95 demand notices and replies[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Phoenix ARC filed CP (IB) No. 1174/MB/2023 and CP (IB) No. 1175/MB/2023 under Section 95 against the Personal Guarantors on 13.10.2023[cite: 6]. On 03.09.2024, NCLT Mumbai dismissed the petitions as barred by limitation, computing limitation from 16.06.2018 (expiry of 60 days from Section 13(2) notice) and holding that even with Covid exclusion the period expired on 29.05.2022, without considering the balance sheet acknowledgment[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the issuance of a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act constitutes invocation of a personal guarantee triggering limitation under Section 95 of the IBC, and whether an acknowledgment of debt in the Corporate Debtor's audited financial statements and auditor's report extends limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 against the personal guarantor[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt in the audited balance sheet and auditor's report of a principal borrower constitutes a valid acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 that extends limitation against both the principal borrower and its personal guarantor, giving rise to a fresh three-year limitation period from the date of acknowledgment[cite: 6]. Furthermore, proceedings under the IBC are independent from SARFAESI proceedings, and taking into account Covid-19 limitation exclusions, petitions filed within the extended period are maintainable[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to insolvency petitions under the IBC, resetting limitation upon a written signed acknowledgment in balance sheets or auditor reports; Section 238 overrides inconsistent laws; under the Supreme Court's Covid-19 exclusion order Clause 5(i), the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 stands excluded, making the balance limitation available from 01.03.2022[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd. v. Bishal Jaiswal, balance sheet entries accompanied by auditor notes stating that the corporate debtor must directly deal with and pay the assignee constitute unequivocal, binding written acknowledgments of liability[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The limitation period was refreshed for three years on 31.12.2020 and, following the Covid-19 exclusion period ending 28.02.2022, ran until 01.03.2025; consequently, the Section 95 petitions filed on 13.10.2023 were well within limitation, and the NCLT's dismissal was set aside[cite: 6].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 2185 and 2186 of 2024, set aside the impugned orders dated 03.09.2024, allowed C.P. (IB)/1174/MB/2023 and C.P. (IB)/1175/MB/2023 filed under Section 95 of the IBC, closed all pending interlocutory applications, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: Phoenix ARC Private Limited appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its Section 95 petitions against personal guarantors Rajendra Himmatlal Salot and Hema Rajendra Salot as time-barred[cite: 6]. The NCLT held that limitation began upon expiry of the Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice in June 2018 and expired in May 2022 despite Covid-19 extensions[cite: 6]. Overturning the dismissal, NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor had explicitly acknowledged the debt in its Independent Auditor's Report filed in Form AOC-4 on 31.12.2020[cite: 6]. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, an acknowledgment by the principal borrower binds the personal guarantors, granting a fresh three-year limitation period[cite: 6]. Accounting for Covid-19 exclusion, the petitions filed on 13.10.2023 were well within limitation and were allowed[cite: 6].

case_title: Reliance Realty Limited vs. Altruist Customer Management India Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Reliance Realty Limited (RRL, subsidiary of Reliance Communications Limited)[cite: 7]. Corporate Debtor is Altruist Customer Management India Private Limited (formerly Vertex Customer Management India Private Limited)[cite: 7]. Related entities include Reliance Communications Limited (RCom, undergoing CIRP) and subsidiaries RCIL, RTL, and RWSL[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Reliance Group Companies availed BPO services from Corporate Debtor under Master Services Agreement dated 01.09.2014, accumulating unpaid dues of Rs. 32,86,56,444/-[cite: 7]. To settle these dues, RCom and affiliates entered into a Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) and Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on 20.08.2018, agreeing to let out RRL's Building A-8 in Navi Mumbai on lease for 7 years 4 months, whereby RCom would pay 80% and Corporate Debtor would pay 20% of monthly rent of Rs. 49,77,880/- plus GST[cite: 7]. On 29.03.2019, RRL and Corporate Debtor executed a registered Leave and License Agreement with a lock-in period and an entire agreement clause[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: RRL claimed total outstanding rental dues of Rs. 24,34,59,787/- (including 15% interest) and updated claim of Rs. 25,48,83,305/- as on 15.09.2022 for the default period May 2019 to September 2022[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoS/MoU executed on 20.08.2018; registered License Agreement executed on 29.03.2019 (effective retrospectively from 28.11.2018); default breach notice issued by RRL on 09.01.2020; Corporate Debtor reply denying breach on 28.01.2020; RRL termination notice issued on 21.03.2022; Corporate Debtor protest replies on 25.03.2022, 21.05.2022, and 01.06.2022; Section 8 demand notice issued on 23.08.2022; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 882/ND/2022 filed in late 2022; NCLT dismissal order dated 05.09.2024; NCLAT judgment dated 09.03.2026[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Memorandum of Settlement dated 20.08.2018; tripartite Memorandum of Understanding dated 20.08.2018; undated Letter of Understanding providing that MoS terms prevail in case of conflict; registered License Agreement dated 29.03.2019; correspondence between parties from 2019 to 2022 evidencing disputes over 80:20 rent apportionment, non-payment by insolvent RCom, and eviction suit (Commercial Suit No. 9 of 2020) filed by RRL in Thane Civil Court[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RRL filed CP (IB) No. 882/ND/2022 under Section 9 before NCLT New Delhi Bench[cite: 7]. On 05.09.2024, NCLT dismissed the petition under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) on the ground of a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding whether the rental debt was payable by the Corporate Debtor alone or jointly with RCom under the interrelated settlement agreements[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in rejecting the Section 9 application on the ground of a pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, and whether an operational creditor can enforce 100% of rental dues under a registered license agreement containing an entire agreement clause while disregarding prior interrelated multi-party settlement agreements (MoS, MoU, and LoU) that apportioned liability and predated the statutory demand notice[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC cannot be used as a recovery mechanism or admitted where the operational debt arises from an interconnected web of agreements containing disputed liability apportionments and reciprocal settlement obligations raised prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice; such triable issues constitute a genuine, non-spurious pre-existing dispute requiring comprehensive contractual adjudication rather than summary insolvency proceedings[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC in light of Mobilox Innovations, holding that 'dispute' includes pre-existing controversies over the existence and quantum of debt; where a lease agreement is an offshoot of prior settlement arrangements (MoS and MoU) and the corporate debtor's liability is conditioned upon multi-party adjustments, an operational creditor cannot isolate the license deed to claim an undisputed debt exceeding Section 4 thresholds[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Mobilox Innovations, the Adjudicating Authority must ascertain whether the defense is genuine, plausible, and supported by pre-notice correspondence, without embarking on a full trial of complex evidence; the continuous exchange of objection letters, termination notices, and the pendency of a prior civil eviction suit conclusively established that the dispute was not illusory or moonshine[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liability of the Corporate Debtor was deeply embedded in unresolved contractual disputes over the 80:20 rent apportionment and unadjusted settlement dues of Rs. 32.87 Crores following RCom's CIRP; consequently, the pre-existing dispute barred admission under Section 9, and the appeal was dismissed[cite: 7].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2077 of 2024 with no order as to costs, closed all pending applications, and granted liberty to the Appellant/Operational Creditor to pursue its claims before an appropriate forum in accordance with applicable law[cite: 7].
summary: Reliance Realty Limited appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 application filed against Altruist Customer Management India Private Limited for recovery of alleged rental dues exceeding Rs. 24 Crores[cite: 7]. The appellant claimed debt under a registered 2019 License Agreement containing an entire agreement clause, asserting the corporate debtor admitted 20% liability which crossed the Section 4 statutory threshold[cite: 7]. The respondent demonstrated that the lease was an integral mechanism to settle past dues of Rs. 32.87 Crores under prior settlement agreements apportioning 80% rent to insolvent Reliance Communications[cite: 7]. Affirming the dismissal, NCLAT held that the interrelated agreements and pre-notice correspondence established a genuine, non-spurious pre-existing dispute that cannot be resolved in summary insolvency proceedings[cite: 7].

case_title: Classic Marble Company Pvt. Ltd. vs. Truvisory Insolvency Professionals Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd. Respondent No. 1 is Truvisory Insolvency Professionals Pvt. Ltd. (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor). Financial Creditor initiating CIRP is Srei Equipment Finance Ltd. Appellant is Classic Marble Company Pvt. Ltd. (occupant of premises claiming oral tenancy)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor permitted Appellant (a supplier of marbles and stones) in 2008 to set up a sales office and stock marble on Plot No. 9 at Shree Ram Mills Premises, Lower Parel, Mumbai (measuring 1701.3 sq. mtrs.) to minimise logistical costs, confirmed via permission letter dated 22.12.2008 for VAT registration purposes[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor owed Appellant principal debt of Rs. 1,34,86,201/- for marble supplies delivered between 2006 and 2013; Appellant filed claim before RP for principal and 18% interest totalling Rs. 3,06,51,041/-, which was admitted by the RP[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bombay High Court appointed Provisional Liquidator in Winding Up Petition No. 1066 of 2015 on 05.10.2016; Liquidator took symbolic possession on 04.06.2019 and issued eviction notice on 25.06.2019; Section 7 CIRP initiated on 06.11.2019; RP issued eviction notices on 10.02.2023 and 20.03.2025; RP filed IA No. 1697/MB/2025 on 27.03.2025; Appellant filed civil suit on 01.12.2025; City Civil Court ad-interim order dated 09.12.2025; NCLT order passed on 12.01.2026; NCLAT judgment on 27.03.2026[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter dated 22.12.2008 from Corporate Debtor permitting Appellant to stock marbles for VAT purposes; Provisional Liquidator report dated 04.06.2019 recording symbolic possession; admitted operational debt claim of Rs. 3,06,51,041/- before the RP; Maharashtra Shop and Establishment certificate dated 01.01.2017 stating it confers no property title; complete absence of any written lease or proof of rent payments[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA (I.B.C) No. 1697(MB)2025 in CP(IB) 494/MB/2019 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-I under Sections 18, 25, and 60(5) for eviction of Appellant with police assistance[cite: 8]. On 12.01.2026, NCLT allowed the IA, holding Appellant was in illegal occupation without any tenancy rights and directing vacant possession within 30 days[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 60(5) read with Section 18(1)(f) and Section 25 of the IBC to order the summary eviction of an unauthorized occupant from immovable property owned by the Corporate Debtor, whether the occupant proved a valid oral tenancy, and whether an ad-interim injunction granted by a City Civil Court bars the NCLT from directing possession[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Resolution Professional is statutorily mandated to assume custody and control of all immovable properties owned by the corporate debtor, and the Adjudicating Authority possesses plenary jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to order the summary eviction of unauthorized occupants and licensees without requiring the filing of a separate civil eviction suit. Furthermore, Section 63 of the IBC expressly bars the jurisdiction of civil courts over insolvency assets[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1)(f) and Section 25(2)(a) require the IRP/RP to take custody of assets over which the corporate debtor has ownership rights; Section 60(5)(c) provides residuary jurisdiction to decide questions of fact and law having a direct nexus with corporate debtor's assets in CIRP; Section 63 ousts civil court jurisdiction; an ad-interim civil court order restraining interference 'save and except by following due process of law' does not impede statutory proceedings under the IBC, which constitutes due process of law[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish an oral tenancy under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the claimant must produce concrete evidence of agreed rent, regular payment, and acceptance establishing a landlord-tenant relationship; mere gratuitous permission to stock goods or VAT/shop registrations explicitly stating they confer no property title are wholly insufficient[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was the undisputed owner of the premises, the Appellant failed to produce any evidence of tenancy or rent payment, and the RP had already admitted the Appellant's monetary supply claim; therefore, the Appellant was in unlawful occupation and NCLT correctly ordered eviction with police assistance[cite: 8].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 187 of 2026, affirmed the NCLT order directing the Appellant to handover vacant possession within 30 days, directed that upon failure the Resolution Professional may take possession with police assistance, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Classic Marble Company Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order directing it to vacate and handover possession of commercial premises owned by Corporate Debtor Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd. to the Resolution Professional within 30 days[cite: 8]. The appellant claimed an oral tenancy and permissive occupation since 2008 to settle outstanding marble supply dues of Rs. 1.34 Crores, also citing a civil court injunction[cite: 8]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Sections 18(1)(f), 25, and 60(5) of the IBC, the RP is duty-bound to take custody of corporate debtor-owned properties and NCLT has full jurisdiction to order summary eviction[cite: 8]. The appellant failed to prove any tenancy or rent payment, and Section 63 barred civil court interference[cite: 8].

case_title: Mehsana Urban Co-Operative Bank Ltd. vs. Swastik Ceracon Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Swastik Ceracon Limited (under management of Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 9]. Financial Creditor is Mehsana Urban Co-Operative Bank Ltd. (Multi-State Co-operative Bank, holding 8.9% voting share in CoC)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor held equity shares in Mehsana Urban Co-Operative Bank Ltd., which were reflected as company assets in the Information Memorandum prepared by the RP during CIRP[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on banking credit facilities, leading to CIRP initiation. The Bank submitted a Form-C claim of Rs. 10,43,45,631/- (admitted in CIRP), against which the approved plan allocated over Rs. 5 Crores[cite: 9]. During CIRP and post-plan, the Bank unilaterally adjusted dividends of Rs. 5,25,000/- (2018-19), Rs. 5,25,000/- (2020-21), Rs. 5,25,000/- (2022-23), and Rs. 35,00,000/- (2023-24), along with share value adjustments aggregating Rs. 56,00,000/-[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 15.01.2019; Bank filed Form C claim on 08.02.2019; Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on 20.06.2022; Bank effected unauthorized adjustments on 15.07.2019, 02.08.2021, 18.07.2022, 01.06.2023, and 29.08.2023; SRA filed IA No. 370/AHM/2025 on 04.03.2025; NCLT allowed IA on 30.10.2025; NCLAT judgment dated 12.03.2026[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Information Memorandum reflecting Corporate Debtor's equity shares in Mehsana Urban Co-Operative Bank Ltd. as assets; Form C claim filed by the Bank without disclosing mutual credit set-offs or security interest over the shares; dividend adjustment ledger entries aggregating Rs. 56,00,000/- effected by the Bank across CIRP and post-plan periods; approved Resolution Plan dated 20.06.2022[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SRA filed IA No. 370/AHM/2025 in CP (IB) No. 175/9/AHM/2018 before NCLT Ahmedabad Court-I seeking refund of Rs. 56,00,000/- with interest[cite: 9]. On 30.10.2025, NCLT allowed the application directing refund with 10% interest from respective adjustment dates, holding that set-offs violated Section 14 moratorium and Section 60(5) conferred jurisdiction[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether Section 121 of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 excludes the jurisdiction of the NCLT under Section 60(5) of the IBC over a Multi-State Co-operative Bank, whether Section 238 of the IBC overrides the arbitration provisions under Section 84 of the MSCS Act, and whether a creditor bank can unilaterally adjust or set off dividends and share proceeds of a corporate debtor during and after CIRP in violation of Section 14[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 238 of the IBC, the provisions of the Code prevail over any inconsistent provisions in the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002; consequently, a multi-state cooperative bank that participates in a CIRP as a financial creditor is subject to the jurisdiction of the NCLT under Section 60(5), and any unilateral set-off or appropriation of dividend and share assets of the corporate debtor during the moratorium or post-plan approval is illegal and must be refunded[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 121 of the MSCS Act (which excludes the Companies Act) does not exempt cooperative banks from the IBC, because the IBC defines 'person' under Section 3(23)(g) to include statutory entities and defines Adjudicating Authority under Section 5(1); Section 238 overrides Section 84 of the MSCS Act; Section 14 prohibits any adjustment or recovery against debtor assets during CIRP, and Section 31(1) binds all stakeholders to the approved plan[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court verified from the Information Memorandum that the shares were undisputed corporate debtor assets, and established that the Bank had filed its claim in Form-C without claiming any lien or mutual credit set-off, thereby foreclosing any right to appropriate dividends outside the approved resolution plan[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT had valid jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to direct refund of the Rs. 56,00,000/-, but modified the interest directive so that 10% per annum interest accrues from the date of filing the application (04.03.2025) rather than from respective historical adjustment dates; the appeal was partly allowed[cite: 9].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal partly allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1956 of 2025, modifying Paragraph 25(A) of the NCLT order to direct the Appellant to refund Rs. 56,00,000/- with 10% per annum interest from 04.03.2025 within 45 days, upheld the rest of the impugned order dated 30.10.2025, and directed parties to bear their own costs[cite: 9].
summary: Mehsana Urban Co-Operative Bank Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order directing it to refund Rs. 56,00,000/- with 10% interest to Successful Resolution Applicant Swastik Ceracon Ltd[cite: 9]. The bank had unilaterally adjusted dividends and share proceeds belonging to the corporate debtor against its outstanding credit dues during CIRP and post-plan approval[cite: 9]. The bank contended that under Section 121 of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, NCLT lacked jurisdiction[cite: 9]. Dismissing the jurisdictional challenge, NCLAT held that Section 238 of the IBC overrides the MSCS Act and binds multi-state cooperative banks participating as financial creditors[cite: 9]. Setting off corporate debtor assets violates the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 9]. NCLAT upheld the refund, modifying interest to run from the application filing date[cite: 9].

case_title: S2Tech.Com India Private Limited vs. Birendra Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is S2Tech.com India Private Limited (unsecured Financial Creditor with 3.3% voting share in the CoC of MCL)[cite: 11]. Corporate Debtor is Manjeera Constructions Limited (MCL, Corporate Guarantor)[cite: 11]. Respondent No. 1 is Birendra Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional of MCL[cite: 11]. Respondent No. 2 is Committee of Creditors of MCL represented by lead creditor Catalyst Trusteeship Limited[cite: 11]. Principal Borrower is Manjeera Retail Holdings Private Limited (MRHPL)[cite: 11]. Successful Resolution Applicant is Valentis Laboratories Private Limited (in consortium with Surya Treasure Island Private Limited)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Catalyst Trusteeship Limited and Fedbank Financial Services extended financial facilities to principal borrower MRHPL, secured by a corporate guarantee executed by Corporate Debtor MCL[cite: 11]. 3.
