DEFAULT METRICS: MRHPL defaulted on credit facilities, triggering Section 7 insolvency proceedings against both MRHPL and corporate guarantor MCL[cite: 11]. Valentis offered a resolution value of Rs. 83.54 Crores, whereas competing applicants Boorugu and Gajala offered Rs. 230.12 Crores and Rs. 271.26 Crores respectively[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 against MCL on 18.07.2023[cite: 11]; Form-G published on 22.09.2023 with EOI deadline extended to 16.12.2023[cite: 11]; RFRP issued on 10.01.2024 setting plan submission deadline on 09.02.2024[cite: 11]; Valentis account debited on 09.02.2024 but EMD credited to debtor account on 12.02.2024[cite: 11]; MRHPL resolution plan approved by CoC on 22.03.2024[cite: 11]; Valentis plan approved by MCL CoC on 10.06.2024[cite: 11]; Appellant filed IA No. 1565/2024 on 18.07.2024[cite: 11]; NCLT dismissed IA on 30.07.2024[cite: 11]; NCLAT judgment pronounced on 19.03.2026[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clause 12 of RFRP mandating submission of Rs. 1 Crore EMD along with the plan, non-compliance rendering the bid non-responsive[cite: 11]; bank transaction record proving EMD credit to MCL account on 12.02.2024[cite: 11]; evaluation matrix awarding 5 extra marks to Valentis for upfront recovery[cite: 11]; CoC voting records reflecting 94.25% approval[cite: 11]; MRHPL approved plan ensuring full recovery of dues to Catalyst and Fedbank[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA (IBC) No. 1565/2024 in CP(IB) 320/7/HDB/2022 before NCLT Hyderabad seeking rejection of Valentis plan and evaluation of other bids[cite: 11]. On 30.07.2024, NCLT summarily dismissed the application without assigning detailed reasons[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan is rendered non-responsive under Clause 12 of the RFRP and Regulation 36B of the CIRP Regulations if the Earnest Money Deposit is credited to the corporate debtor account after the submission deadline, whether a dissenting financial creditor has locus standi to challenge CoC approval of an irregular bid, and whether financial creditors who have been assured full recovery from the principal borrower's CIRP can continue to vote and approve a lower-value resolution plan for the corporate guarantor[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Compliance with the mandatory provisions of a Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) and statutory regulations is non-negotiable; receipt of Earnest Money Deposit after the prescribed submission deadline renders a resolution plan non-responsive, and the Resolution Professional possesses no authority to waive or modify such terms to accept a belated deposit[cite: 11]. Furthermore, a dissenting financial creditor possesses the locus standi to challenge commercial actions of the CoC and RP that breach the statutory mandate of value maximization, particularly where majority lenders assured full recovery from the principal borrower force through a non-responsive, low-value bid for the corporate guarantor[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36B of CIRP Regulations read with Clause 12 of RFRP requires actual credit and deposit of EMD within the timeline, as mere debiting of the applicant's account does not satisfy submission; Section 25(1) obligates the RP to preserve debtor value rather than push through non-compliant plans; Section 60(5) and Section 61 empower a dissenting creditor to air grievances against decisions that subvert the statutory objectives of the Code[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict textual compliance governs RFRP clauses; bank records demonstrating that funds were credited into the debtor's account after the cut-off date conclusively establish that the bid was non-responsive[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP acted improperly in accepting Valentis's belated EMD and skewing the evaluation scoring, and the majority CoC acted arbitrarily to the detriment of value maximization; hence, the approval was invalid and the impugned dismissal was set aside[cite: 11].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 456/2024, set aside the impugned order dated 30.07.2024, declared the Resolution Plan of Valentis Laboratories Private Limited invalid, directed the RP to evaluate the remaining compliant resolution plans, directed the RP to examine whether CIRP against MCL subsists in view of full recovery from MRHPL and seek appropriate directions from the NCLT, and closed all pending interlocutory applications[cite: 11].
summary: S2Tech.com India Private Limited, an unsecured financial creditor holding a 3.3% voting share in the Committee of Creditors of Manjeera Constructions Limited (Corporate Guarantor), appealed against the NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing its application to reject the resolution plan of Valentis Laboratories Private Limited[cite: 11]. The appellant contended that Valentis submitted its Earnest Money Deposit past the deadline, violating Clause 12 of the RFRP, and that majority lenders who had already recovered their dues from principal borrower Manjeera Retail Holdings Private Limited acted arbitrarily[cite: 11]. Setting aside the NCLT order, NCLAT held that timely EMD receipt in the debtor's account was mandatory, rendering Valentis's bid non-responsive, and directed the RP to evaluate the remaining compliant resolution plans[cite: 11].

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Sanjay Baleshwar Rai & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 893 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 894, 1280 & 1281 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant / Financial Creditor is State Bank of India (SBI)[cite: 12]. In CA 893 & 894 of 2024, Corporate Debtor is M/s Kandla Energy and Chemicals Ltd. and Personal Guarantors are Sanjay Baleshwar Rai and Kanchan Sanjay Rai[cite: 12]. In CA 1280 & 1281 of 2024, Corporate Debtor is Shri Jalaram Rice Industries Pvt. Ltd. and Personal Guarantors are Jayesh Tribhovandas Ganatra and Bipin Tribhovandas Ganatra[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI extended financial credit facilities to Kandla Energy secured by personal guarantees executed on 21.03.2013, and to Shri Jalaram Rice Industries secured by personal guarantees executed in 2010, 2012, and 2014[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Kandla Energy defaulted on 22.07.2014 (declared NPA), and DRT issued a recovery decree in OA No. 511 of 2015 on 25.06.2018[cite: 12]. Shri Jalaram Rice Industries defaulted on 27.09.2014, and DRT passed a recovery decree in OA No. 207 of 2015 on 19.03.2018[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In Kandla matter, DRT decree on 25.06.2018; 3-year limitation ordinary expiry on 24.06.2021; Rule 7 demand notice issued on 12.10.2022; Section 95 petition filed on 24.01.2023; NCLT dismissal on 18.03.2024[cite: 12]. In Jalaram matter, DRT decree on 19.03.2018; 3-year limitation ordinary expiry on 18.03.2021; Rule 7 notice issued on 10.05.2022; Section 95 petition filed on 25.02.2023; NCLT dismissal on 10.05.2024; NCLAT decision on 12.03.2026[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT recovery decrees dated 25.06.2018 and 19.03.2018 giving fresh 3-year limitation periods; Section 95 filings; Supreme Court orders in Suo Motu WP(C) No. 3 of 2020 dated 08.03.2021, 23.09.2021, and 10.01.2022 excluding 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed Section 95 petitions before NCLT Ahmedabad Court-2[cite: 12]. NCLT dismissed CP(IB)/61(AHM)2023 and CP(IB)/60(AHM)2023 on 18.03.2024 and 19.03.2024, and CP(IB)/100(AHM)/2023 and CP(IB)/101(AHM)/2023 on 10.05.2024, holding that under the Supreme Court's Covid orders, SBI was only entitled to a 90-day extension from 01.03.2022 ending on 30.05.2022[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether under Paragraph 5 of the Supreme Court's Suo Motu order dated 10.01.2022, a creditor whose three-year limitation period under Article 137 expired during the Covid-19 period (15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022) is limited to a flat 90-day extension from 01.03.2022 or is entitled to the greater of 90 days and the actual remaining balance period of limitation computed by excluding the entire Covid eclipse period[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a period of limitation for instituting proceedings under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 would have expired during the Covid-19 period between 15.03.2020 and 28.02.2022, the entire duration from 15.03.2020 until the ordinary expiration date stands excluded from computation; the litigant is entitled to the actual remaining balance period of limitation starting from 01.03.2022, or a minimum period of 90 days, whichever is longer[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Paragraph 5(I) read with Paragraph 5(III) of the Supreme Court's order dated 10.01.2022 in Suo Motu WP(C) No. 3 of 2020, the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 stands excluded for computing limitation under general or special laws; the 90-day provision in Paragraph 5(III) operates as a baseline floor and expressly clarifies that if the actual balance limitation remaining with effect from 01.03.2022 is greater than 90 days, that longer period shall apply[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculation of limitation requires computing the balance period remaining as of 15.03.2020 before normal expiry (1 year, 3 months, 9 days for Kandla, and 1 year, 3 days for Jalaram) and adding that exact balance duration onto 01.03.2022[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The actual balance periods available to SBI from 01.03.2022 extended up to 10.06.2023 and 04.03.2023 respectively, both exceeding 90 days; hence, the Section 95 petitions filed in January and February 2023 were well within limitation, and the NCLT's dismissals were set aside[cite: 12].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed all four appeals (Company Appeal Nos. 893, 894, 1280, and 1281 of 2024), set aside the impugned orders of NCLT Ahmedabad, revived Company Petition Nos. 61/2023, 60/2023, 100/2023, and 101/2023 before the Adjudicating Authority for fresh consideration on merits in accordance with law, and ordered parties to bear their own costs[cite: 12].
summary: State Bank of India appealed against orders of NCLT Ahmedabad dismissing its Section 95 insolvency applications against four personal guarantors (Sanjay Baleshwar Rai, Kanchan Sanjay Rai, Jayesh Tribhovandas Ganatra, and Bipin Tribhovandas Ganatra) as time-barred[cite: 12]. The NCLT held that under the Supreme Court's Covid-19 Suo Motu orders, SBI was only entitled to a 90-day extension from 01.03.2022 expiring on 30.05.2022[cite: 12]. Allowing the appeals, NCLAT held that Paragraph 5(III) of the Supreme Court's order dated 10.01.2022 expressly entitles a litigant to the longer of 90 days or the actual balance period of limitation remaining from 15.03.2020[cite: 12]. Since the balance periods extended until 2023, the applications were within limitation and revived[cite: 12].

case_title: IDFC First Bank Ltd. vs. Seikh Abdul Salam, RP of Jai Gokul Towers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 848 of 2024 & I.A. No. 7183 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1009 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is IDFC First Bank Ltd. (Appellant in CA 848/2024)[cite: 13]. Successful Auction Purchaser is Quest Queen Vista LLP (Appellant in CA 1009/2024)[cite: 13]. Corporate Debtor is M/s Jai Gokul Towers Pvt. Ltd. (holding 1/6th undivided share in the mortgaged property, represented by Resolution Professional Seikh Abdul Salam, Respondent No. 1)[cite: 13]. Principal Borrower is Monotona Tyres Ltd.[cite: 13] Petitioning Creditor initiating CIRP is Miller Traders Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 13] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IDFC First Bank sanctioned a Term Loan of Rs. 25 Crores to Monotona Tyres Ltd., secured by personal/corporate guarantees and mortgage of immovable property (land with B+G+6 building at Mondalghanti, Kolkata) executed on 01.02.2018, wherein Corporate Debtor held 1/6th share[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default led to a consent decree by Bombay High Court on 04.04.2018 for Rs. 30,06,68,557/- principal plus Rs. 1,52,87,671/- interest; execution transferred to DRT Mumbai, which issued Recovery Certificate on 19.02.2021[cite: 13]. Mortgaged property was auctioned on 11.10.2023 for Rs. 32.03 Crores[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recovery Officer issued sale proclamation on 08.09.2023; auction held on 11.10.2023; Quest Queen Vista declared purchaser on 12.10.2023 and deposited full price; Recovery Officer confirmed sale on 20.11.2023; Calcutta High Court stay on sale certificate recalled on 12.03.2024; CIRP admitted against CD on 01.01.2024; Recovery Officer issued ITCP-20 sale certificate on 14.03.2024; purchaser took possession on 16.03.2024; NCLT order dated 24.04.2024; NCLAT decision on 11.03.2026[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT Roznama and confirmation order dated 20.11.2023 recording deposit of full purchase price and poundage fees; absence of setting-aside applications under Rules 60-62 of Second Schedule to Income Tax Act; Form ITCP-18 and ITCP-20 sale certificates; Calcutta High Court vacation order dated 12.03.2024[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 218/(KB)/2023 was admitted against Corporate Debtor on 01.01.2024[cite: 13]. Resolution Professional filed IA (IB) No. 592/(KB)/2024 seeking to declare the sale confirmation and sale certificate null and void under Section 14[cite: 13]. On 24.04.2024, NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed the IA and directed the RP to take back possession[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the confirmation of a statutory auction sale by a DRT Recovery Officer under Rule 63 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Act, 1961 prior to the commencement of CIRP makes the sale absolute and passes title to the auction purchaser, such that the subsequent imposition of a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC cannot invalidate the sale or the subsequent ministerial issuance of the sale certificate[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a statutory auction sale governed by the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Act, 1961 read with Section 29 of the RDB Act, 1993, title to immovable property passes and the sale becomes absolute upon the passing of an order of confirmation of sale under Rule 63 once the entire purchase price has been deposited; the subsequent issuance of a sale certificate under Rule 65 is merely ministerial evidence of title[cite: 13]. Consequently, if confirmation of sale occurs prior to the commencement of CIRP, the asset ceases to be property of the corporate debtor and is unaffected by the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Rule 63 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Act, 1961, when no setting-aside application is pending and the full purchase price is paid, the confirmation order makes the sale absolute; Rule 65 specifies that the sale certificate merely states the antecedent date on which the sale became absolute; this distinguishes RDB Act sales from SARFAESI Rules 8 and 9 where payment can be accepted after moratorium as occurred in IOB v. RCM Infrastructure; Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC only bars enforcement of security interest against property belonging to the debtor[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing transfer of title requires examining whether the full purchase price was deposited and an express order confirming the sale was entered by the competent authority prior to the insolvency commencement date, rendering subsequent physical certificate issuance purely evidentiary[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the DRT Recovery Officer confirmed the auction sale on 20.11.2023 upon full payment and before CIRP commenced on 01.01.2024, title fully vested in Quest Queen Vista LLP prior to the moratorium; hence, the NCLT erred in invalidating the sale, and the order was set aside[cite: 13].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 848 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1009 of 2024, set aside the impugned order dated 24.04.2024 (and corrigendum dated 26.04.2024), dismissed IA (IB) No. 592/(KB)/2024 filed by the Resolution Professional, disposed of pending applications, and directed parties to bear their own costs[cite: 13].
summary: IDFC First Bank Ltd. and auction purchaser Quest Queen Vista LLP appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order declaring the DRT auction sale and sale certificate of immovable property belonging to Corporate Debtor Jai Gokul Towers Pvt. Ltd. null and void under Section 14 of the IBC[cite: 13]. The NCLT held that because the sale certificate was issued in March 2024 post-CIRP admission, the transaction violated the moratorium[cite: 13]. Allowing the appeals, NCLAT held that under Rule 63 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Act, 1961, the sale became absolute upon confirmation on 20.11.2023 when full consideration was deposited, well before CIRP commenced on 01.01.2024[cite: 13]. Consequently, title had already transferred and the sale was valid[cite: 13].

case_title: Tejinder Pal Setia vs. Sh. Arvind Kumar, Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Tejinder Pal Setia, suspended director of Corporate Debtor Chandigarh Overseas Pvt. Ltd. (COPL)[cite: 14]. Respondent No. 1 is Sh. Arvind Kumar, Resolution Professional of COPL[cite: 14]. Respondent No. 2 is M/s Accord Infra Developer Pvt. Ltd. and Respondent No. 3 is M/s Mohali Hi-Tech Builders and Promoters Pvt. Ltd. (both admitted as Financial Creditors in Class / Allottees on the CoC)[cite: 14]. Other respondents include Income Tax Department and ROC[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor developed real estate projects[cite: 14]. In 2009, Corporate Debtor entered into an agreement with Mohali Builders; in 2011 and 2012, it executed Agreements and Agreements to Sell with Accord Infra for block purchases and marketing of multiple commercial and residential units against financial disbursements[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on its project commitments; RP admitted claims of Rs. 9.965 Crores (Accord Infra) and Rs. 7.78 Crores (Mohali Builders) as financial debts from allottees in a class based on allotment documentation and payments[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against COPL on 27.02.2023 (attained finality up to Supreme Court on 06.09.2023)[cite: 14]; CoC constituted on 28.07.2023[cite: 14]; Appellant filed IA No. 2105/2023 in November 2023[cite: 14]; Resolution Plan approved by CoC with 99.21% vote share[cite: 14]; NCLT dismissed IA on 02.07.2025[cite: 14]; NCLAT judgment on 10.03.2026[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreements to Sell dated 29.06.2009, 24.06.2011, and 26.02.2012[cite: 14]; allotment letters and proof of financial consideration payments[cite: 14]; ROC records showing Respondents No. 2 and 3 had been struck off under Section 248 of Companies Act, 2013[cite: 14]; Corporate Debtor's reply in CP No. 210/2020 admitting liability to Respondents[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 2105(CH)/2023 in C.P. (IB) No. 248/Chd/2019 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench-I challenging the constitution of the CoC, seeking exclusion of Accord Infra and Mohali Builders from CoC, and asking to declare all CoC resolutions illegal[cite: 14]. On 02.07.2025, NCLT dismissed the application, upholding the inclusion of Respondents under Section 5(8)(f) and CIRP Regulation 8A[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether commercial entities that purchased multiple units in a real estate project under Agreements to Sell qualify as 'allottees' and Financial Creditors in a class under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC or must be excluded from the CoC as 'promoters' or 'speculative investors' under the RERA Act, whether entities struck off by the ROC retain the right to submit claims under Section 250 of the Companies Act, and whether claims can be admitted under CIRP Regulation 8A without being reflected in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any allottee who disburses funds for the acquisition of units in a real estate project has the commercial effect of a borrowing and qualifies as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, regardless of whether the purchase was for personal consumption, commercial use, or speculative investment; furthermore, companies struck off the register of companies retain the statutory right under Section 250 of the Companies Act, 2013 to pursue and realize outstanding debts[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Explanation (ii) to Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC imports only the definitions of 'allottee' and 'real estate project' from the RERA Act and consciously excludes other RERA definitions such as 'promoter'; speculative investor status is relevant solely at the stage of Section 7 admission to prevent abusive filings, not for claim admission or CoC participation; CIRP Regulation 8A allows proof of debt through sale agreements and payment receipts without requiring reflection in audited balance sheets[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admission of claims by creditors in a class requires documentary verification of sale agreements, allotment records, and consideration receipts establishing disbursement with commercial effect; non-reflection in balance sheets does not invalidate authenticated contractual debts[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondents No. 2 and 3 proved valid payments and agreements for allotment of units and lawfully retained creditor status under Section 250 despite being struck off; therefore, their inclusion in the CoC was valid, and the appeal was dismissed with exemplary costs[cite: 14].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1330 of 2025, affirmed the NCLT order dated 02.07.2025, imposed costs of Rs. 5,00,000/- on the Appellant to be paid to the Prime Minister's Relief Fund within 15 days for pursuing vexatious and obstructive litigation, and disposed of all pending interlocutory applications[cite: 14].
summary: Tejinder Pal Setia, suspended director of Corporate Debtor Chandigarh Overseas Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing his application to remove Accord Infra Developer Pvt. Ltd. and Mohali Hi-Tech Builders and Promoters Pvt. Ltd. from the Committee of Creditors[cite: 14]. The appellant argued that the entities were speculative investors, promoters under RERA, and struck-off companies whose claims lacked balance sheet verification[cite: 14]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that payments made towards unit purchases constitute financial debt under Section 5(8)(f), and the IBC does not import RERA's promoter definition[cite: 14]. Under Section 250 of the Companies Act, struck-off entities retain rights to recover dues[cite: 14]. Finding the litigation vexatious, NCLAT imposed Rs. 5 lakhs costs[cite: 14].

case_title: Mr. Sunil Kumar Jain, RP vs. Employee's Provident Fund Organization & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 701 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 793 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Vas Data Services Private Limited[cite: 15]. Appellant in CA 701/2025 is Sunil Kumar Jain (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor)[cite: 15]. Appellant in CA 793/2025 is Committee of Creditors of Vas Data Services Private Limited[cite: 15]. Respondent No. 1 is Employee's Provident Fund Organization (EPFO)[cite: 15]. Respondent No. 2 in CA 793/2025 is M/s Mansir Dager and Associates (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor employed workers and was subject to statutory provident fund contributions under the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO initiated assessment proceedings claiming default in PF contributions, eventually passing an order demanding Rs. 1,78,18,960/- under Sections 7A, 14B, and 7Q of the EPF & MP Act; initially an unsigned claim of Rs. 3,17,667/- had been submitted[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 09.04.2019; IRP public announcement on 27.04.2019 fixing claim deadline as 10.05.2019; EPFO received intimation on 25.06.2019; CoC approved resolution plan with 100% vote share on 06.08.2020; plan approval application reserved for orders on 25.05.2021; EPFO submitted unsigned Form-B on 11.01.2022 (rejected by RP on 17.01.2022); EPFO finalized assessment order on 21.11.2023; EPFO filed IA No. 470/2024 after 1757 days from CIRP start; NCLT allowed IA on 21.03.2025; NCLAT judgment on 10.03.2026[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Public announcement dated 27.04.2019; Information Memorandum approved by CoC on 20.12.2019 containing litigation disclosures provided by suspended management; assessment order dated 21.11.2023 passed during moratorium; unsigned Form-B dated 11.01.2022; CoC resolution approving plan on 06.08.2020[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: EPFO filed IA No. 470/2024 in C.P. (IB) No. 1683/ND/2018 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-V seeking direction to RP to admit its claim of Rs. 1,78,18,960/-[cite: 15]. On 21.03.2025, NCLT allowed the IA, holding PF dues must be paid in full and made adverse observations against RP for non-disclosure under Regulation 36(2)(h)[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether statutory assessment proceedings under Sections 7A, 14B, and 7Q of the EPF & MP Act can be continued or initiated by the EPFO against a corporate debtor during the subsistence of a moratorium under Section 14(1) of the IBC, whether claims based on such assessments can be admitted after the CoC has approved a resolution plan with 100% vote share, and whether the RP was guilty of non-disclosure under CIRP Regulation 36(2)(h)[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Imposition of a moratorium under Section 14(1) of the IBC creates an absolute statutory freeze prohibiting any authority, including statutory welfare bodies such as the EPFO, from continuing or initiating assessment proceedings that impose fresh pecuniary liability on the corporate debtor during CIRP; any assessment order passed in violation of Section 14(1) is non-est in law[cite: 15]. Furthermore, no belated claims can be entertained after the Committee of Creditors has approved a resolution plan[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'proceedings' under Section 14(1)(a) encompasses statutory assessment proceedings affecting the assets of the corporate debtor, unlike Section 33(5) during liquidation where assessment is not barred; Section 238 gives overriding effect to the IBC over the EPF & MP Act during CIRP; Section 36(4)(b)(iii) applies exclusively to liquidation estates, not to ongoing CIRP where a resolution plan has already received CoC approval[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Claims submitted after a 1757-day delay based on ex-parte assessment orders issued during the moratorium and subsequent to CoC approval of the resolution plan cannot be entertained under the doctrine prohibiting the reopening of finalized resolution processes established in RPS Infrastructure and Essar Steel[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The EPFO assessment order was void ab initio for violating Section 14(1), the claim was hopelessly belated, and the RP committed no regulatory breach because the suspended management never disclosed the proceeding; hence, the NCLT order was set aside and adverse remarks against the RP were expunged[cite: 15].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 701 and 793 of 2025, set aside the impugned order dated 21.03.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V, expunged the adverse remarks recorded against the Resolution Professional in paragraphs 14 and 16 of the impugned order, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: The Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors of Vas Data Services Private Limited appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order directing the admission of EPFO's claim of Rs. 1,78,18,960/-[cite: 15]. The EPFO had finalized its assessment under the EPF & MP Act during the moratorium and filed its claim after a 1757-day delay, long after the CoC had approved the resolution plan with 100% voting share[cite: 15]. Allowing the appeals, NCLAT held that Section 14(1) of the IBC prohibits statutory assessment proceedings against a corporate debtor during CIRP, rendering such assessments void[cite: 15]. Furthermore, belated claims cannot be admitted post-CoC approval under RPS Infrastructure[cite: 15]. NCLAT set aside the order and expunged adverse remarks against the RP[cite: 15].

case_title: Ramachandran Subramanian vs. Anil Kohli, New Liquidator of Tecpro Systems Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ramachandran Subramanian, erstwhile Liquidator of Tecpro Systems Limited[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 1 is Anil Kohli, newly appointed Liquidator[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 2 is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (EARCL), holding 84.82% voting share in the Stakeholders Consultation Committee (SCC)[cite: 16]. Other respondents are Bank of Baroda, ACRE Ltd, and Pegasus ARC Ltd.[cite: 16] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India assigned debt of Rs. 2,200 Crores of Tecpro Systems Limited to EARCL on 03.03.2015 for Rs. 171 Crores, along with assigned pledged shares (30% equity) and mortgage securities; EARCL instituted cash flow monitoring mechanisms and engaged Ernst & Young LLP (EY) on 16.09.2015 for project supervision[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor resulted in Section 7 CIRP initiation on 07.08.2017; approved resolution plan failed implementation, leading to liquidation order on 16.01.2020; in liquidation, an industrial plot was auctioned in September 2022 for Rs. 28.28 Crores, out of which Appellant released Rs. 3,71,06,440/- to HSIIDC towards past dues without SCC approval[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 07.08.2017; liquidation ordered and Appellant appointed Liquidator on 16.01.2020; EARCL filed removal applications in 2020 and on 13.10.2023; Appellant filed IA No. 4269/2024 seeking related-party declaration on 24.08.2024; SCC voted for replacement with 92.25% majority on 17-18.10.2024; EARCL filed IA No. 5798/2024 on 03.12.2024; NCLT order dated 09.01.2026; NCLAT judgment on 10.03.2026[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment Agreement dated 03.03.2015; uninvoked share pledge records of 30% equity; Escrow Agreement dated 08.09.2015; engagement letters with EY; IBBI Disciplinary Committee order dated 05.03.2021 regarding erstwhile RP; SCC voting records of October 2024 showing 92.25% voting share for replacement[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 4269 of 2024 before NCLT Delhi Bench seeking declaration that EARCL was a related party under Section 5(24) and denuded of SCC voting rights[cite: 16]. EARCL filed IA No. 5798 of 2025 for replacement of Appellant[cite: 16]. On 09.01.2026, NCLT dismissed Appellant's IA and allowed EARCL's IA, replacing Appellant with Anil Kohli[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether an erstwhile Liquidator has locus standi as a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge their replacement ordered by the Adjudicating Authority upon recommendation of the Stakeholders Consultation Committee, and whether an Asset Reconstruction Company holding uninvoked pledged shares, escrow monitoring rights, and observer status prior to CIRP constitutes a 'related party' under Section 5(24) or is protected under the second proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Insolvency Professional or Liquidator holds a functional, statutory office of a fiduciary nature and possesses no personal or vested legal right to continue in office; consequently, an outgoing liquidator lacks locus standi as a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61 to challenge a replacement order passed by the Adjudicating Authority based on stakeholder votes[cite: 16]. Furthermore, routine lender-protection mechanisms such as holding uninvoked pledged shares, appointing board observers, establishing escrow monitoring, and supervising pre-CIRP restructuring do not constitute management or policy control under Section 5(24) to classify a regulated secured lender as a related party[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 31A(11) of the Liquidation Process Regulations empowers the SCC by a 66% majority vote to propose replacement, which the Adjudicating Authority may confirm in exercise of its supervisory jurisdiction under Sections 33, 34, and Section 16 of the General Clauses Act; Section 5(24) requires demonstrable de facto corporate policy control, not ordinary creditor oversight; the second proviso to Section 21(2) specifically protects regulated financial entities from related-party disqualification where shareholdings arise from debt security arrangements prior to CIRP[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish related-party control under Section 5(24), positive proof of direct appointment of directors or legal authority over executive board decisions is required; uninvoked share pledges (where voting rights remain with pledgor) and financial advisory monitoring are legally insufficient[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: EARCL did not qualify as a related party under Section 5(24) and was protected by the second proviso to Section 21(2); the SCC lawfully voted by 92.25% majority for replacement; and the Liquidator possessed no locus standi to appeal his removal; hence, the appeal was dismissed[cite: 16].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 267 of 2026, upheld the NCLT order dated 09.01.2026 replacing the Appellant with Respondent No. 1 as Liquidator of Tecpro Systems Limited, closed all pending interlocutory applications, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: Ramachandran Subramanian, erstwhile Liquidator of Tecpro Systems Limited, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order replacing him with Anil Kohli under Regulation 31A(11) of the Liquidation Process Regulations[cite: 16]. The appellant claimed that dominant financial creditor Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (EARCL, 84.82% voting share) was a related party under Section 5(24) due to pre-CIRP share pledges, board observers, and restructuring supervision, invalidating its vote[cite: 16]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that a liquidator has no vested right to continue in office and lacks locus standi under Section 61[cite: 16]. Furthermore, standard lender oversight and uninvoked pledged shares do not constitute management control under Section 5(24), and EARCL was protected under the second proviso to Section 21(2)[cite: 16].

case_title: Akshat Gupta vs. Union Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Personal Guarantor / Bankrupt is Mr. Anil Syal; Bankruptcy Trustee is Mr. Ajay Gupta (Respondent No. 2); Financial Creditor and dominant CoC member (97.27% voting share) is Union Bank of India (Respondent No. 1); Successful Auction Purchaser is Mr. Akshat Gupta (Appellant); Arvind Jain is a minor creditor (2.73% voting share)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bankrupt Anil Syal was personal guarantor for credit facilities extended by Union Bank of India to a corporate borrower, securing the loan by mortgaging residential property at H. No. 117, First Floor, Uday Park, New Delhi-110049, in which the bankrupt held a 50% undivided share and his wife Meenakshi Syal held the remaining 50%[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the borrower and guarantor on debt of Rs. 71,90,78,635/- (admitted claim of Union Bank); Bank claimed property value was Rs. 3.82 Crores (2021) and Rs. 4.5 Crores (2023), whereas Bankruptcy Trustee valued the 50% undivided share at Rs. 90.72 Lakhs; auction sold the 50% share to Appellant for Rs. 91,72,161/-[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bankruptcy process of Anil Syal commenced on 30.09.2022 under Sections 121/122; BT Preliminary Report issued on 23.03.2023; auction notice published on 02.06.2023; e-auction held on 27.06.2023 (25 days after notice); full purchase consideration paid and Sale Certificate issued on 05.07.2023; Union Bank filed IA No. 4421/2023 on 08.08.2023; NCLT set aside sale on 04.07.2024; NCLAT judgment on 25.03.2026[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auction advertisements in Financial Express and Jansatta dated 02.06.2023; Bid Declaration and DD of Rs. 9,07,216/- dated 09.06.2023; balance RTGS payment of Rs. 82,64,945/- on 05.07.2023; Sale Certificate dated 05.07.2023; valuation report of Value Edge Professional Pvt. Ltd. dated March 2023 (discounting value by 40% for indivisibility); earlier bank valuation of Rs. 3.82 Crores; CoC minutes showing key progress reports were shared post-facto[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union Bank filed IA No. 4421/2023 in CP (IB) No. 589/ND/2020 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-III to cancel the auction and sale certificate. On 04.07.2024, NCLT set aside the auction sale and sale certificate, ordered refund to Appellant, and directed fresh valuations and re-auction with at least 30 days notice, holding that Bankruptcy Trustee acted in haste by giving only 25 days notice instead of 30 days[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in cancelling a concluded e-auction sale and setting aside the Sale Certificate of a 50% undivided share in residential property on grounds of procedural irregularities, including providing only a 25-day notice period instead of 30 days, non-consultation and post-facto information sharing with the Committee of Creditors holding 97.27% voting share, and potential undervaluation of an encumbered fractional asset[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In bankruptcy and insolvency asset realizations, statutory sales must strictly conform to principles of transparency, stakeholder consultation, and adequate market exposure to fulfill the paramount objective of value maximization; an auction of a legally complex, fractional, or encumbered asset conducted on a compressed notice period with post-facto reporting to the dominant creditor is vitiated by material procedural irregularities, justifying cancellation even after issuance of a sale certificate[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the IBBI Bankruptcy Process Regulations do not prescribe a rigid timeline, bankruptcy proceedings of personal guarantors under the IBC vest the powers of the DRT in the NCLT; hence, the 30-day notice standard from Rule 8(6) of the SARFAESI Security Interest Rules, 2002 serves as a mandatory benchmark to ensure genuine price discovery[cite: 17]. Regulation 30(3) and Regulation 8(3)(d)(iv) require the trustee to exercise due diligence, disclose mortgages, and consider additional valuations for complex assets rather than unilaterally rushing the sale[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To evaluate procedural fairness in an insolvency auction, the tribunal examines whether the notice period afforded adequate time for prospective bidders to conduct due diligence on title and co-ownership risks, whether the valuation accounted for all encumbrances and was shared in advance with major creditors, and whether the CoC was consulted prior to concluding the sale rather than receiving post-facto reports[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Bankruptcy Trustee committed material procedural lapses by providing only a 25-day notice period, failing to obtain a second valuation under Regulation 30(3), concealing existing SARFAESI encumbrances, and presenting completed sales to the 97.27% CoC as a fait accompli; furthermore, the appellant having accepted refund of the purchase price suffered no adverse injury; thus, the NCLT's cancellation was affirmed and the appeal dismissed[cite: 17].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1577 of 2024, upheld the NCLT order dated 04.07.2024 setting aside the e-auction and Sale Certificate, affirmed the directions for fresh valuation and re-auction with at least 30 days notice, closed all pending interlocutory applications, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: Akshat Gupta, the successful auction purchaser, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order setting aside the completed e-auction and Sale Certificate for a 50% undivided share in residential property belonging to bankrupt personal guarantor Anil Syal[cite: 17]. The NCLT cancelled the sale upon an application by Union Bank of India (holding a 97.27% CoC voting share), holding that the 25-day notice period was inadequate[cite: 17]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that fractional, encumbered assets require sufficient market exposure, adhering to the 30-day notice benchmark[cite: 17]. The Bankruptcy Trustee committed material procedural lapses by failing to disclose bank charges, conducting hasty single valuations, and sharing reports post-facto with the CoC, thereby undermining value maximization[cite: 17].

case_title: Surender Singh vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Surender Singh, suspended director of Corporate Debtor Vatika Limited (real estate developer with 58 projects across Northern India)[cite: 18]. Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited (Debenture Trustee for Indiabulls India Opportunities Fund and Indiabulls High Yield Fund)[cite: 18]. Resolution Professional is Mr. Gaurav Mitra/IRP[cite: 18]. Intervenors include Omkara ARC and homebuyers[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor entered into a Debenture Trust Deed (DTD) on 30.06.2017 with IDBI Trusteeship to issue 1,460 secured non-convertible debentures aggregating Rs. 146 Crores with coupon interest of 11.39% p.a. compounded monthly and payable quarterly, secured by mortgage of 12.212 acres in Sector 88B, Gurgaon, hypothecation of project receivables, and escrow accounts[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debenture Trustee claimed default of Rs. 274,13,45,241/- in Part IV of Section 7 application, including Rs. 146 Crores principal[cite: 18]. However, redemption date of principal was extended by agreement to 30.06.2024[cite: 18]. The actual crystallized default was quarterly interest of Rs. 29,72,29,959/- from 15.03.2022 to 15.12.2023[cite: 18]. Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 37.2 Crores during Section 7 pendency[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DTD executed on 30.06.2017; redemption date extended on 27.06.2023 to 30.06.2024; cure notice for interest issued on 29.12.2023 giving 15 days; NeSL default authentication completed on 14.01.2024; Section 7 petition filed on 24.01.2024; NCLT admission order dated 03.02.2026; NCLAT judgment on 27.03.2026[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Trust Deed dated 30.06.2017; extension letter dated 27.06.2023 extending principal repayment to 30.06.2024; demand/cure notice dated 29.12.2023 demanding Rs. 29,72,29,959/-; NeSL certificate dated 14.01.2024; DTCP License No. 13/2022 for 12.212 acres and HARERA Registration Certificate No. 130/2022 for 'Project Aspirations'; NOC letters issued by Debenture Trustee for sales in 'Project Aspirations'[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IDBI Trusteeship filed CP (IB) No. 45/Chd/Hry/2024 under Section 7 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench Court-I[cite: 18]. On 03.02.2026, NCLT admitted the application against Vatika Limited as a whole, rejected the plea of project-wise insolvency on the ground that IBC only recognizes insolvency of the corporate debtor and not of a project, and appointed an IRP[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether the Debenture Trustee was entitled to claim the un-matured principal amount of Rs. 146 Crores in Part IV of its Section 7 application when redemption was formally extended to a future date, whether payment of Rs. 37.2 Crores during petition pendency cured the default, and whether CIRP against a multi-project real estate company must be restricted on a project-wise basis to the specific project securing the financial facility[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the corporate insolvency resolution of real estate companies developing multiple independent projects, CIRP initiated by a project-specific lender or creditor must, as a rule, be confined strictly to the specific project securing that debt rather than engulfing the entire corporate debtor and its solvent projects[cite: 18]. Furthermore, an applicant under Section 7 cannot claim debt as in default when the contractual maturity date for principal has been mutually extended and no acceleration notice has been issued, though any subsisting threshold default in interest justifies admission[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) mandates admission upon proof of default exceeding Section 4 thresholds, but in the real estate sector, Section 7 must be harmoniously read with CIRP Regulations 4D, 4E, 18(4), and 36A(1) and the doctrine laid down in Mansi Brar Fernandes and Flat Buyers Association Winter Hills; the statutory scheme permits project-specific CIRP to prevent collateral prejudice to solvent projects and bona fide allottees[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To determine whether debt is project-specific, tribunals must examine the underlying contractual financing instruments (e.g., Debenture Trust Deed recitals, project-specific business plans, designated escrow accounts for receivables, and project-specific mortgages), and verify whether the lender issued NOCs and exercised monitoring rights exclusively over an identified licensed/RERA-registered land parcel[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default regarding interest of Rs. 29,72,29,959/- was established and not cured by subsequent pendency payments; however, the NCLT committed a substantial legal error by rejecting project-wise insolvency; hence, the admission of CIRP was modified and strictly confined to 'Project Aspirations' in Sector 88B, Gurgaon[cite: 18].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal partly allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 266 of 2026, upheld Section 7 admission but modified the NCLT order dated 03.02.2026 to confine CIRP strictly to 'Project Aspirations' situated in Sector 88B, Gurgaon, directed the IRP to issue a revised public announcement for claims pertaining solely to Project Aspirations as of 03.02.2026, granted liberty to creditors of other projects to pursue remedies in accordance with law, and disposed of all pending applications without costs[cite: 18].
summary: Suspended director Surender Singh appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited against real estate company Vatika Limited for an alleged default of Rs. 274 Crores under a 2017 Debenture Trust Deed[cite: 18]. The appellant contended that principal redemption was extended to 30.06.2024, interest was paid during pendency, and insolvency should be project-specific[cite: 18]. Modifying the admission order, NCLAT held that while default in quarterly coupon interest exceeding Rs. 29 Crores was established, the NCLT erred in rejecting project-wise insolvency[cite: 18]. Reaffirming Mansi Brar Fernandes, NCLAT held that real estate CIRP must be confined to the specific project pledged ('Project Aspirations'), insulating solvent projects and external homebuyers[cite: 18].

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Think and Learn Pvt. Ltd. vs. Riju Ravindran & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Committee of Creditors of Think and Learn Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Byju's); Respondent No. 1 is Riju Ravindran (suspended director); Respondent No. 2 is BCCI (operational creditor initiating CIRP); Respondent No. 3 is Shailendra Ajmera (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 4 is GLAS Trust Company LLC (dominant financial creditor holding 99.41% voting share in CoC)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: BCCI provided promotional and sponsorship services to Corporate Debtor Think and Learn Pvt. Ltd., giving rise to unpaid operational debt. Separately, GLAS Trust Company LLC extended massive term loan facilities to the Corporate Debtor's offshore parent/affiliates backed by guarantees[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor in paying sponsorship fees to BCCI resulted in Section 9 admission; GLAS Trust claimed financial debt exceeding USD 1.2 Billion (holding 99.41% voting share in CoC), while Aditya Birla Capital held the fractional remainder[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Think and Learn admitted into CIRP under Section 9 in CP(IB) No. 149/BB/2023; RP constituted 4-member CoC on 21.08.2024; RP reconstituted CoC dropping GLAS Trust and ABCL on 31.08.2024; NCLT set aside reconstitution on 29.01.2025 in IA Nos. 660/2025 and 802/2024; Riju Ravindran filed IA No. 466/2025 to remove GLAS Trust; CoC filed impleadment IA No. 495/2025; NCLT dismissed impleadment on 26.08.2025; NCLAT judgment on 03.03.2026[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC constitution order dated 21.08.2024; NCLT orders dated 29.01.2025 and 17.02.2025 restoring GLAS Trust to CoC; CoC resolution dated 30.05.2025 authorizing GLAS Trust to litigate; Special Power of Attorney in favor of Mr. Ramesh verifying the appeal; pleadings in IA No. 466/2025 seeking exclusion of GLAS Trust[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Suspended director Riju Ravindran filed IA No. 466 of 2025 before NCLT Bengaluru to remove GLAS Trust from the CoC[cite: 21]. CoC filed IA No. 495 of 2025 seeking to implead itself as a party respondent[cite: 21]. On 26.08.2025, NCLT dismissed IA No. 495 of 2025, holding that CoC lacks legal juristic personality to litigate in its own name, can only be represented by RP, and is not a necessary party[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors (CoC) constituted under Section 21 of the IBC possesses a legal character and juristic personality entitled to institute or defend legal proceedings in its own name within the framework of the Code, whether the CoC can be represented independently of the Resolution Professional, and whether the CoC is a necessary or proper party in an application filed by a suspended director seeking the removal of a specific financial creditor from the CoC[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a Committee of Creditors does not possess corporate juristic personality under general jurisprudence, pragmatism and functional efficacy under the IBC permit the CoC to litigate in its own name in proceedings arising within the framework of the Code where it acts unanimously or by a single member[cite: 21]. However, a CoC is neither a necessary nor a proper party in a dispute challenging the individual membership or claim of a specific financial creditor, as each member's inclusion depends solely on its distinct contractual relationship with the corporate debtor[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The definition of 'person' under Section 3(23)(g) of the IBC encompasses statutory contrivances, but right to litigate is functionally circumscribed; Section 21 establishes CoC as an independent statutory decision-making body distinct from the RP; hence, RP does not act as agent of the CoC in litigation, and CoC is not mandated to be represented exclusively by the RP; under procedural law (Order I Rule 10 CPC), a party is necessary only if no effective order can be made without its presence[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To determine whether the CoC is a necessary party to a lis, the tribunal assesses whether the relief sought directly infringes the collective statutory functions of the CoC or merely challenges the private contractual debt and individual standing of an isolated constituent member[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Although the CoC has the legal character to litigate in its own name under the IBC without being represented by the RP, it has no collective legal interest in defending the individual inclusion of GLAS Trust in IA No. 466 of 2025; therefore, the CoC was rightly held not to be a necessary or proper party, and the dismissal of its impleadment application was affirmed[cite: 21].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 475/2025, affirmed the NCLT Bengaluru order dated 26.08.2025 dismissing IA No. 495 of 2025 in CP(IB) No. 149/BB/2023, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: The Committee of Creditors of Think and Learn Private Limited appealed against the NCLT Bengaluru order dismissing its application to implead itself in proceedings initiated by suspended director Riju Ravindran to remove GLAS Trust Company LLC from the CoC[cite: 21]. The NCLT held that the CoC lacked juristic personality and could only be represented by the Resolution Professional[cite: 21]. NCLAT held that for the functional efficacy of the IBC, the CoC possesses legal standing to litigate in its own name independently of the RP[cite: 21]. However, because each creditor's membership rests on individual contractual debt, the CoC is neither a necessary nor proper party to defend an isolated member's inclusion[cite: 21]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 21].

case_title: Indu Jain vs. Birla Jewels Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Indu Jain, sole proprietor of M/s IB Jewels (wholesale supplier of rough/uncut diamonds); Corporate Debtor is Birla Jewels Ltd. (manufacturer and retailer operating 'BJEWELZ' stores); related proprietorship of Indu Jain is M/s Brij Ratnam (retail franchisee of Corporate Debtor)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IB Jewels supplied rough and uncut diamond jewellery to Corporate Debtor under a Bill-to-Ship arrangement via manufacturer Jewel Goldi dispatched through Sequel Logistics under three specific invoices (dated 16.06.2019 and 20.06.2019) with a 45-to-60-day credit period[cite: 22]. Separately, Brij Ratnam entered into a Franchisee Agreement dated 05.12.2018 with Corporate Debtor for retailing finished jewellery[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on three invoices totaling Rs. 49,81,921/- (Invoice No. 16 dated 16.06.2019 for Rs. 26,52,781/-, Invoice No. 17 dated 20.06.2019 for Rs. 11,81,272/-, and Invoice No. 18 dated 20.06.2019 for Rs. 11,47,868/-), defaulting on 16.08.2019 and 20.08.2019 upon expiry of credit period[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised on 16.06.2019 and 20.06.2019; Corporate Debtor issued termination notice for Franchisee Agreement to Brij Ratnam on 12.08.2019; Section 8 demand notice issued by IB Jewels on 26.08.2019; Brij Ratnam replied to termination on 27.08.2019; Corporate Debtor replied to Section 8 notice on 05.09.2019; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 3626/MB-VI/2019 filed in 2019; NCLT dismissal on 09.08.2024; NCLAT judgment on 19.03.2026[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three unpaid tax invoices dated June 2019; courier receipts from Sequel Global Critical Logistics with 'payment in favour of Jewel Goldi' endorsement; Section 8 demand notice and reply dated 05.09.2019 showing no denial of delivery of goods; Franchisee Agreement dated 05.12.2018 between Corporate Debtor and Brij Ratnam; termination notice dated 12.08.2019 containing no mention of IB Jewels or the three invoices; separate GST and bank accounts for IB Jewels and Brij Ratnam[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Indu Jain filed CP (IB) No. 3626/MB-VI/2019 under Section 9 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-VI[cite: 22]. On 09.08.2024, NCLT rejected the petition holding that delivery was unproven, a pre-existing dispute existed under the Brij Ratnam franchisee agreement because both entities operated from common premises under Indu Jain, and a sole proprietorship cannot issue a Section 8 notice[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether an individual sole proprietor can issue a Section 8 demand notice through legal counsel and maintain an application under Section 9 of the IBC in light of Section 2(f), whether an operational creditor must produce proof of delivery when the corporate debtor did not dispute receipt in its Section 8 reply, and whether a dispute under a distinct franchisee agreement between the corporate debtor and a sister proprietorship constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' qua unpaid invoices of the operational creditor[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 2(f) of the IBC, a sole proprietorship firm through its proprietor has full legal standing to initiate insolvency proceedings, and a demand notice under Section 8 issued by an authorized advocate on behalf of the proprietor is legally valid[cite: 22]. Furthermore, a contractual dispute arising out of an independent agreement with a distinct proprietorship concern, even if sharing common ownership, address, or management, cannot be imported to manufacture a spurious pre-existing dispute against an undisputed operational debt arising from a separate supply contract[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(f) explicitly extends the application of the Code to proprietorship firms; Section 8 read with Section 30 of the Advocates Act allows authorized legal counsel to issue demand notices; Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandate that a pre-existing dispute must strictly relate to the specific debt, invoices, or goods in question; a corporate debtor cannot introduce post-facto defenses of non-delivery or fraud after failing to dispute delivery in its statutory Section 8 reply[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench applies the Mobilox standard to distinguish plausible, genuine defenses from moonshine afterthoughts; where delivery and debt are not disputed in the statutory Section 8 reply and defenses of forged invoices are raised only before the NCLT, such objections constitute a manufactured afterthought[cite: 22]. Independent GST numbers, bank accounts, and distinct contracts establish legal separability between two businesses run by the same individual[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The supply of uncut diamonds under the three invoices was not disputed in the Section 8 reply, the franchisee dispute with Brij Ratnam was legally extraneous, and the sole proprietor was competent to maintain the action; hence, the NCLT's dismissal was erroneous, the impugned order was set aside, and the Section 9 petition was revived[cite: 22].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1840 of 2024, set aside the impugned order dated 09.08.2024, revived C.P. (IB) No. 3626/MB-VI/2019 on the board of NCLT Mumbai Bench-VI for fresh consideration in accordance with law, directed parties to appear before the Adjudicating Authority on 13.04.2026, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: Indu Jain, sole proprietor of IB Jewels, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order rejecting her Section 9 application filed against Birla Jewels Ltd. for unpaid invoices of rough diamonds amounting to Rs. 49,81,921/-[cite: 22]. The NCLT dismissed the application, holding that a sole proprietorship lacked standing to issue Section 8 notices, delivery was doubtful, and a pre-existing dispute existed with sister concern Brij Ratnam under a franchisee agreement[cite: 22]. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT held that proprietorships can initiate CIRP under Section 2(f) and issue notices through counsel[cite: 22]. Since the debtor never disputed delivery in its Section 8 reply, the dispute with Brij Ratnam under a separate agreement was extraneous[cite: 22]. The petition was revived[cite: 22].

case_title: Sushant Chhabra & Anr. vs. Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 443 of 2026 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 444 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Sushant Chhabra (Appellant in CA 443/2026) and Verinder Kumar Chhabra (Appellant in CA 444/2026), Personal Guarantors of Corporate Debtor M/s UM Autocomp Pvt. Ltd. (later UM Automotive Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 23]. Respondent No. 1 is Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Debenture Trustee); Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional (Anil Kohli); Canara Bank is an earlier petitioning financial creditor[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor issued Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) under a Debenture Trust Deed dated 28.12.2024, secured by an unconditional and irrevocable Deed of Personal Guarantee executed on 28.12.2024 by the Appellants[cite: 23]. Liabilities were novated on 12.05.2025 to UM Automotive Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 23] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on its debenture obligations; Respondent No. 1 issued default-cum-legal notice dated 01.04.2025 demanding payment of Rs. 36,14,50,354/- from the Corporate Debtor and Personal Guarantors[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Canara Bank filed Section 95 petitions CP(IB) No. 122/ND/2025 and CP(IB) No. 121/ND/2025 against the Appellants on 12.01.2025 (triggering interim moratorium)[cite: 23]; RP appointed therein on 27.02.2025[cite: 23]; Respondent No. 1 filed subsequent Section 95 petitions CP(IB) 450/ND/2025 and CP(IB) 446/ND/2025 on 05.08.2025[cite: 23]; Canara Bank petitions withdrawn on 10.11.2025[cite: 23]; NCLT admitted Respondent No. 1's petitions on 17.02.2026[cite: 23]; NCLAT decided appeals on 27.03.2026[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of Personal Guarantee dated 28.12.2024; default notice dated 01.04.2025; record of prior Section 95 filings by Canara Bank on 12.01.2025; withdrawal order dated 10.11.2025 in IA-5449/ND/2025[cite: 23]; RP report recommending admission in IA No. 5571/ND/2025 and IA No. 4652/ND/2025[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed Section 95 petitions on 05.08.2025 before NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II[cite: 23]. Appellants objected to maintainability based on the subsistence of interim moratorium under Section 96 triggered by Canara Bank's prior petitions[cite: 23]. On 17.02.2026, NCLT rejected the objection and admitted the Section 95 applications, holding that the withdrawal of Canara Bank's petitions on 10.11.2025 removed the statutory bar[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency petition filed under Section 95 of the IBC against a personal guarantor during the subsistence of a statutory interim moratorium triggered under Section 96 by an earlier Section 95 petition is void ab initio and non-est in law, and whether the subsequent withdrawal of the earlier petition cures the invalidity of the second petition[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 96(1) of the IBC, filing an application under Section 94 or Section 95 immediately triggers a statutory interim moratorium in relation to all debts of the debtor, creating an absolute bar prohibiting creditors from initiating any legal action or proceedings in respect of any debt[cite: 23]. Any insolvency petition instituted against a personal guarantor during the operation of this interim moratorium is non-est and void ab initio, and the subsequent withdrawal of the prior petition cannot retroactively validate or cure proceedings that were legally non-existent from inception[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory interim moratorium under Section 96(1)(a) attaches automatically on the date of application across all debts; Section 96(1)(b)(ii) mandates that 'creditors of the debtor shall not initiate any legal action or proceedings in respect of any debt'[cite: 23]. Under the scheme of Chapter III, the Code prohibits multiplicity of applications against the same personal guarantor, as all creditors are required to submit claims under Section 102 and Section 103 once admission takes place[cite: 23]. Following the principle in Alchemist Asset Reconstruction, proceedings instituted in violation of a statutory moratorium are non-est in law[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determining statutory compliance requires an objective verification of dates; if a subsequent Section 95 petition was filed prior to the date on which the earlier Section 95 petition was dismissed, admitted, or permitted to be withdrawn, the second application is statutorily barred on the date of its presentation[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Canara Bank's Section 95 petitions were pending and the Section 96 interim moratorium was fully operative on 05.08.2025 when Respondent No. 1 filed its petitions, the filings by Respondent No. 1 were non-est; NCLT erred in admitting them based on the later withdrawal on 10.11.2025, warranting dismissal of the petitions with liberty to file afresh[cite: 23].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 443 and 444 of 2026, set aside the impugned order dated 17.02.2026 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II, dismissed CP(IB)-450/ND/2025 and CP(IB)-446/ND/2025, granted liberty to Respondent No. 1 to file fresh Section 95 applications in accordance with law, and directed parties to bear their own costs[cite: 23].
summary: Personal Guarantors Sushant Chhabra and Verinder Kumar Chhabra appealed against NCLT New Delhi orders admitting Section 95 insolvency applications filed by Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd.[cite: 23] The appellants argued that when Catalyst filed its applications on 05.08.2025, an interim moratorium was already operating under Section 96 due to earlier Section 95 petitions filed by Canara Bank on 12.01.2025, rendering Catalyst's filings non-est[cite: 23]. Catalyst argued that Canara Bank's subsequent withdrawal on 10.11.2025 removed the bar[cite: 23]. Allowing the appeals, NCLAT held that Section 96 creates an absolute statutory bar across all debts, making any proceedings initiated during its currency void ab initio[cite: 23]. A subsequent withdrawal cannot retrospectively validate non-est petitions[cite: 23]. NCLAT dismissed the petitions with liberty to file afresh[cite: 23].

case_title: M/s. Sri Bajrang Wind Park Developers vs. M/s Inox Wind Infrastructure Services Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is M/s. Sri Bajrang Wind Park Developers (registered partnership firm); Corporate Debtor is M/s Inox Wind Infrastructure Services Limited (infrastructure support service provider); Respondents No. 2 to 7 are directors/ex-directors of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor awarded works for a 50 MW wind power project at Sadala, Gujarat (awarded by SJVNL) to the Operational Creditor under an MoU dated 07.01.2016 and multiple Work/Purchase Orders issued in 2018 for WTG foundations, Panther/Dog lines, and USS equipment[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor raised 75 invoices totaling Rs. 111,02,60,040/-; Corporate Debtor made part payments of approx. Rs. 85 Crores (Rs. 59.87 Crores directly and Rs. 25.42 Crores to third-party vendors); unpaid principal claimed was Rs. 25,72,70,275/-, amounting to Rs. 42,49,84,942/- including 24% interest[cite: 24]. Corporate Debtor counter-claimed Rs. 54,50,00,000/- for liquidated damages and project delays[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised between 20.07.2018 and 14.05.2019; Corporate Debtor raised invoice/LD discrepancies via emails on 17.08.2018, 13.11.2018, 22.11.2018, and 05.12.2018; Section 8 demand notice issued on 02.07.2019; reply/notice of dispute issued on 17.07.2019; Corporate Debtor issued arbitration notice on 04.02.2020; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 212/AHM/2021 filed on 21.10.2021; NCLT dismissal on 13.12.2023; NCLAT judgment on 02.03.2026[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Work orders incorporating MoU terms; Clause 38 of Work Orders stipulating default accrues only 365 days after due date; pre-demand notice emails from August-December 2018 calling for reconciliation of disputed invoices and LD deductions; Section 8 reply dated 17.07.2019 detailing liquidated damages; arbitral records before Sole Arbitrator Justice (Retd.) D.K. Jain dismissing appellant's counter-claim[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 212/AHM/2021 under Section 9 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench[cite: 24]. On 13.12.2023, NCLT rejected the petition holding that genuine pre-existing disputes regarding reconciliation, quality, and liquidated damages existed prior to the demand notice, and the demand notice was premature under Clause 38[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application was maintainable in light of pre-existing disputes evidenced by pre-demand notice email correspondence demanding reconciliation of accounts and liquidated damages, whether a demand notice issued prior to the contractual 365-day default cure period under Clause 38 is premature, and whether the appeal should be dismissed despite an unconsummated settlement proposal[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) where the corporate debtor raises a plausible, genuine, and non-spurious pre-existing dispute regarding invoice reconciliation, defective performance, and liquidated damages established through contemporaneous correspondence predating the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 24]. Furthermore, a demand notice issued before the expiry of contractually agreed default credit periods is premature and non-maintainable[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, and following the Supreme Court's rulings in Mobilox Innovations and Sabarmati Gas, repeated requests for reconciliation of disputed ledger anomalies and mutual claims constitute proof of a genuine pre-existing dispute; summary insolvency jurisdiction cannot be used to adjudicate complex cross-claims or breach of contractual performance[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court applies the 'plausible contention' test; series of emails exchanged in 2018 expressly qualifying invoice acceptance as subject to reconciliation of liquidated damages and generation losses conclusively demonstrate that the dispute is not a moonshine or sham defense[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Contemporary communications between August and December 2018 established extensive pre-existing disputes and unfinalized reconciliations, the demand notice was premature under Clause 38, and no finalized settlement was filed; therefore, the NCLT rightly rejected the Section 9 petition, and the appeal was dismissed[cite: 24].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 630 of 2024, upheld the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 13.12.2023, dismissed all related interlocutory applications including the withdrawal-cum-revival application IA No. 1161 of 2026, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: M/s. Sri Bajrang Wind Park Developers appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing its Section 9 application against Inox Wind Infrastructure Services Limited seeking unpaid operational debt of over Rs. 42 Crores[cite: 24]. The NCLT rejected the petition due to pre-existing disputes regarding project delays, liquidated damages, and lack of reconciliation[cite: 24]. During appeal pronouncement, the appellant sought withdrawal based on an incomplete conditional settlement[cite: 24]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that pre-demand notice emails from 2018 established substantial, genuine pre-existing disputes concerning account reconciliations and liquidated damages under Mobilox and Sabarmati Gas[cite: 24]. Furthermore, the demand notice was premature under the contractual payment terms[cite: 24].

case_title: Attluru Sreenivasulu Reddy vs. A.S. Met Corp Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Transfer Appeal (AT) No. 1 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Insolvency) No. 210 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Attluru Sreenivasulu Reddy, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s KLSR Infratech Ltd. (profit-making infrastructure company)[cite: 25]. Respondent No. 1 is Operational Creditor M/s A.S. Met Corp Pvt. Ltd. (supplier of steel coils and strapping seals)[cite: 25]. Other involved persons include Mr. Allu Nagesh (erstwhile Director of CD) and Mr. Piyush Mehta (signatory for OC)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: OC supplied steel goods (CRFH strips/coils) to CD under a commercial practice where payments were settled through 90-day bank Letters of Credit (LCs) discounted by the supplier[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: OC claimed an unpaid default of Rs. 3,79,06,143/- (principal Rs. 2,72,29,416/- plus interest and penalty) under 15 invoices raised between 09.07.2021 and 01.12.2021[cite: 25]. CD maintained that no debt was due, goods under several invoices were rejected and returned, and remaining invoices were fictitious[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD stopped procurement and initiated internal fraud audit on 22.12.2021[cite: 25]; last LC payment made on 20.12.2021[cite: 25]; OC email acknowledging rejected goods on 14.02.2022[cite: 25]; Section 8 demand notice issued on 31.05.2022 (received 14.06.2022)[cite: 25]; CD reply/notice of dispute issued on 15.06.2022[cite: 25]; CD lodged criminal FIR No. 539/2022 on 30.06.2022[cite: 25]; Section 9 petition filed on 24.08.2022[cite: 25]; NCLT admitted petition on 14.07.2023[cite: 25]; Supreme Court transferred appeal on 14.11.2025[cite: 25]; NCLAT judgment pronounced on 23.03.2026[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Detailed reply to demand notice dated 15.06.2022 alleging multi-crore fraud, fake vehicle tracking numbers, and collusion[cite: 25]; FIR No. 539/2022 leading to arrest and chargesheeting of Allu Nagesh and OC officials[cite: 25]; email dated 14.02.2022 by OC admitting rejection and return of goods under Invoice Nos. 227, 228, and 229[cite: 25]; commercial tax GST assessment order dated 02.07.2025 finding duplicate invoices, missing vehicle movement, and non-existent transport vehicles[cite: 25]; audited accounts proving CD's annual turnover exceeded Rs. 400 Crores with substantial profit[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: OC filed CP(IB) No. 263/9/HDB/2022 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench[cite: 25]. On 14.07.2023, NCLT admitted Section 9, holding CD's defense to be a moonshine afterthought because CD allegedly claimed GST input credit and made post-December 2021 payments without demur[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether the Corporate Debtor's reply dated 15.06.2022 constitutes a valid notice of dispute under Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, whether the defenses alleging collusive fake invoices and returned materials were spurious or moonshine, and whether post-initiation GST assessment findings showing non-movement of goods and fraudulent billing can be relied upon to demonstrate pre-existing dispute and malicious initiation under Section 65[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, an application for initiation of CIRP by an operational creditor must be rejected where a timely notice of dispute raising plausible, substantiated contentions supported by pre-existing correspondence is received by the creditor[cite: 25]. Where the operational debt is tainted by serious, documented allegations of fraudulent invoicing, non-delivery of goods, return of materials, and criminal collusion between the supplier and rogue debtor personnel, summary insolvency proceedings cannot be used as an instrument of extortion or to shield a party from criminal liability[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) require the Adjudicating Authority to ascertain whether a genuine dispute truly exists in fact; the tribunal is not required to determine whether the defense will ultimately succeed, but only whether it is not a patently feeble legal argument or bluster[cite: 25]. An acknowledgment obtained from a colluding, chargesheeted director on stamp paper purchased by the creditor carries no legal weight, and clearing bank Letter of Credit commitments does not constitute voluntary payment to the creditor[cite: 25]. Section 65 empowers penalizing fraudulent or malicious filings[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, contemporaneously documented rejections of goods via email, cessation of payments following an internal audit, and statutory GST assessment orders confirming non-movement of vehicles provide conclusive proof that the dispute existed prior to the demand notice and is not a moonshine defense[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CD's reply dated 15.06.2022 was a valid notice of dispute, no payments were made to the OC post-December 2021, and the claims under the subject invoices were fraudulent and heavily disputed; consequently, the Section 9 petition was legally unmaintainable and was dismissed with exemplary costs of Rs. 10 Lakhs[cite: 25].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Transfer Appeal (AT) No. 1 of 2025, set aside the NCLT Hyderabad admission order dated 14.07.2023, dismissed Section 9 petition CP(IB) No. 263/9/HDB/2022 with exemplary costs of Rs. 10,00,000/- to be paid by Respondent No. 1 to the Appellant within 30 days, forwarded a copy of the order to the IBBI for appropriate action, and disposed of all pending interlocutory applications[cite: 25].
summary: Attluru Sreenivasulu Reddy, suspended director of profit-making entity KLSR Infratech Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Hyderabad order admitting a Section 9 application filed by A.S. Met Corp Pvt. Ltd. for alleged unpaid invoices of Rs. 3.79 Crores[cite: 25]. The NCLT had rejected the debtor's defense of fraud and fake invoices as a moonshine afterthought[cite: 25]. Setting aside the admission, NCLAT held that the debtor's reply dated 15.06.2022 constituted a bona fide notice of dispute under Mobilox[cite: 25]. The record, corroborated by pre-notice emails admitting return of goods and a subsequent GST assessment confirming non-movement of transport vehicles, proved the invoices were fabricated[cite: 25]. NCLAT dismissed the petition with Rs. 10 Lakhs exemplary costs against the creditor[cite: 25].

case_title: Bobby Abraham vs. Tata Capital Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 116/2026 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 117, 118 & 119/2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is M/s Tata Capital Limited (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor / Principal Borrower is M/s Simtel Trading Corporation Private Limited; Personal Guarantors are Bobby Abraham (Appellant in CA 116/2026), Jasmine Varghese (Appellant in CA 117/2026), Jossan Varghese (Appellant in CA 118/2026), and Joby Varghese (Appellant in CA 119/2026); Resolution Professional and proposed Bankruptcy Trustee is CA Jasin Jose (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tata Capital sanctioned a Term Loan and Working Capital credit facility aggregating Rs. 39.60 Crores to Corporate Debtor Simtel Trading under a sanction letter dated 13.05.2019 and Channel Finance Agreements, secured by Personal Guarantees executed by the Appellants[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor committed default on 21.11.2018; Tata Capital recalled the entire credit facility demanding Rs. 35,59,75,936/- via Loan Recall Notice dated 13.02.2019[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default occurred 21.11.2018; Loan Recall Notice issued on 13.02.2019; Form B statutory demand notices under Section 95(4)(b) issued on 02.05.2022 (served on 14.05.2022); NCLT Kochi appointed RP under Section 97 on 26.09.2024; RP submitted Section 99 reports on 17.12.2024; Section 95 admitted on 06.05.2025; Section 114(1) order rejecting/closing repayment plan stage passed on 28.08.2025; Tata Capital filed Section 121 bankruptcy application on 28.08.2025; NCLT passed Bankruptcy Order on 14.01.2026; NCLAT decided appeal on 10.03.2026[cite: 26]. 5.
