FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Channel Finance Agreement and Sanction Letter dated 13.05.2019; Loan Recall Notice dated 13.02.2019; Form B Demand Notices dated 02.05.2022; RP Report under Section 99 dated 17.12.2024; un-challenged NCLT order dated 28.08.2025 under Section 114(1) recording absence of any viable repayment plan submitted by Personal Guarantors; Part IV declaration of proposed Bankruptcy Trustee[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench admitted Section 95 petitions on 06.05.2025[cite: 26]. Due to failure of personal guarantors to submit any repayment plan under Section 105, NCLT passed an order under Section 114(1) on 28.08.2025[cite: 26]. Creditor filed applications under Section 121 read with Section 123 of the Code[cite: 26]. On 14.01.2026, NCLT allowed IA Nos. 488, 492, 489, and 490 of 2025, directing the initiation of bankruptcy proceedings and appointing Jasin Jose as Bankruptcy Trustee[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether an order initiating bankruptcy proceedings against personal guarantors under Section 121 read with Section 126 of the IBC is vitiated for lack of prior show-cause notice under Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules 2016 and principles of natural justice under Section 420(1) of the Companies Act, when the prerequisite order under Section 114(1) rejecting or noting non-submission of a repayment plan had attained finality without challenge[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order initiating bankruptcy process and appointing a bankruptcy trustee under Section 121 and Section 126 of the IBC is a natural, consequential statutory corollary following upon an un-challenged order under Section 114 rejecting or recording the failure/non-submission of a repayment plan; personal guarantors who submit to Section 114 proceedings and fail to challenge the adverse Section 114 order are bound by the principles of waiver and acquiescence, and cannot challenge the subsequent Section 121 bankruptcy order on grounds of natural justice or non-issuance of a fresh show-cause notice under general procedural rules[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 115(2) expressly confers entitlement on creditors to file an application for bankruptcy under Chapter IV upon rejection of a repayment plan under Section 114; Section 123 sets out mandatory filing requirements without enacting a requirement for a formal de novo show cause notice before passing an order of bankruptcy under Section 126; Rule 37 of NCLT Rules (Form NCLT-5) applies to ordinary inception proceedings and cannot be invoked to reopen settled issues after exhaustion of Chapter III insolvency procedures[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the record establishes that statutory steps under Sections 95, 96, 99, 100, and 114 were duly conducted with the full knowledge and participation of the personal guarantors, and no viable repayment plan was ever propounded, the pre-conditions for creditor bankruptcy under Section 121(1)(b) stand conclusively satisfied[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Personal Guarantors having waived their right to challenge the Section 114(1) order dated 28.08.2025 could not claim prejudice or violation of audi alteram partem against the consequential bankruptcy order dated 14.01.2026; hence, the appeals lacked merit and were dismissed[cite: 26].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) Nos. 116, 117, 118, and 119 of 2026, affirmed the NCLT Kochi Bench orders dated 14.01.2026 directing initiation of bankruptcy proceedings and appointment of the Bankruptcy Trustee, and closed all connected interlocutory applications[cite: 26].
summary: Personal Guarantors Bobby Abraham, Jasmine Varghese, Jossan Varghese, and Joby Varghese appealed against NCLT Kochi orders initiating bankruptcy proceedings and appointing a Bankruptcy Trustee under Section 121 of the IBC in respect of credit defaults of Corporate Debtor Simtel Trading Corporation Private Limited owed to Tata Capital Limited[cite: 26]. The appellants contended that the bankruptcy orders were passed without issuing a prior show-cause notice under Rule 37 of NCLT Rules, violating principles of natural justice[cite: 26]. Dismissing the appeals, NCLAT held that the initiation of bankruptcy is a natural, consequential statutory corollary under Section 115(2) and Section 121 once an order under Section 114(1) noting non-submission of a repayment plan attains finality[cite: 26]. Having failed to challenge the Section 114 order, the guarantors were barred by waiver and could not claim procedural prejudice[cite: 26].

case_title: Uday Kumar Sahu & Ors. vs. Birendra Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Uday Kumar Sahu and Abhyuday Sahu (purchasers of Unit No. 24 in Manjeera Mall); Respondent No. 1 is Birendra Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (MRHPL); Respondent No. 2 is Monitoring Committee of MRHPL; Respondent No. 3 is M/s Lulu International Shopping Malls Private Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants entered into an Agreement for Sale dated 29.09.2014 with MRHPL and AP Housing Board to purchase commercial retail Unit No. 24 (496 sq. ft. super built-up area) in Manjeera Mall, Kukatpally, paying full sale consideration of Rs. 44,60,000/-, and leased the unit back to the Corporate Debtor under Clause 28 for a 25-year lease rental term[cite: 27]. Formal sale registration was delayed due to disputes between the debtor and the housing board[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Catalyst Trusteeship Limited initiated Section 7 against MRHPL for financial debt default; Appellants claimed their commercial unit had a fully paid purchase consideration of Rs. 44,60,000/- and should be excluded from debtor assets or reflected as a distinct liability in the Information Memorandum[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement for Sale executed on 29.09.2014; Section 7 CIRP admitted against MRHPL on 18.07.2023; RP appointed on 14.09.2023; Form G issued on 21.11.2023; Appellants filed IA No. 314/2024 on 03.02.2024; NCLT directed RP to include debtor liabilities towards Appellants in Information Memorandum on 17.09.2024; Appellants filed Contempt Petition No. 7/2025 alleging willful disobedience; NCLT dismissed Contempt Petition on 26.03.2025; certified copy applied on 28.03.2025, prepared and delivered on 01.04.2025; appeal e-filed on 11.05.2025; NCLAT decided on 24.03.2026[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement for Sale dated 29.09.2014; banking receipts and debtor ledger extracts showing full receipt of Rs. 44,60,000/-; NCLT order dated 17.09.2024 in IA No. 314/2024 directing inclusion of liabilities in the IM; certified copy application receipts confirming 4 days taken in preparation[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed Contempt Petition No. 7/2025 under Section 425 of Companies Act read with Contempt of Courts Act and Section 60(5) of IBC before NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II, alleging non-compliance of order dated 17.09.2024 by the RP[cite: 27]. On 26.03.2025, NCLT dismissed the Contempt Petition, holding that no willful contempt was made out[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC read with Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 is maintainable before the NCLAT against an order of the NCLT dismissing a contempt petition, where no order of punishment for contempt was passed[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, an appeal lies to the appellate forum strictly as of right only against an order or decision passed in the exercise of jurisdiction to punish for contempt (i.e., an order imposing punishment); no statutory appeal is maintainable against an order dropping, rejecting, or dismissing a contempt petition[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 425 of the Companies Act confers power to punish for contempt co-extensive with that of a High Court under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; Section 19(1) of the 1971 Act specifically reserves the right of appeal exclusively against orders imposing 'punishment'; in contempt proceedings, the applicant acts merely as an informer bringing non-compliance to the notice of the court, and once the court declines to punish the contemnor, the applicant possesses no personal right of appeal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Midnapore Peoples Cooperative Bank v. Chunilal Nanda, an appellate tribunal determines maintainability by ascertaining whether the impugned order fastened punitive contempt liability; where the adjudicating authority dropped or dismissed the contempt proceedings without penal sanction, appellate jurisdiction is barred[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the delay in filing the appeal was condonable under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, the appeal was legally non-maintainable under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act because the impugned order merely dismissed the contempt petition without imposing any punishment; the appeal was dismissed[cite: 27].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal condoned the delay in filing the appeal via IA No. 1101/2025, but dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 368/2025 as non-maintainable against an order dismissing a contempt petition, and closed all pending interlocutory applications with no order as to costs[cite: 27].
summary: Commercial unit purchasers Uday Kumar Sahu and Abhyuday Sahu appealed under Section 61 of the IBC against the NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing their Contempt Petition No. 7/2025 filed against Resolution Professional Birendra Kumar Agarwal of Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 27] The appellants alleged willful disobedience of an earlier order directing the RP to record the debtor's registration obligations in the Information Memorandum[cite: 27]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Section 425 of the Companies Act read with Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act and Midnapore Peoples Cooperative Bank, an appeal lies only against an order imposing punishment for contempt[cite: 27]. An order declining or dismissing a contempt petition is not appealable, as the applicant acts merely as an informer and has no right of appeal[cite: 27].

case_title: Subham Capital Private Limited vs. Vedic Realty Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor / Appellant is Subham Capital Private Limited (NBFC); Corporate Debtor / Respondent is Vedic Realty Private Limited (real estate company)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed financial assistance from Appellant under an oral understanding, resulting in multiple loan disbursements aggregating Rs. 22.75 Crores in several tranches between 2011 and 2016 carrying agreed interest[cite: 29]. The transactions were recorded in bank statements, and acknowledged through Demand Promissory Notes, confirmation letters, loan renewal receipts, post-dated cheques, and TDS deduction certificates on interest[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on repayment after making its last partial repayment on 07.04.2021; Appellant issued loan recall notice on 01.03.2022 for outstanding dues exceeding the Section 4 threshold[cite: 29]. Following execution of a Settlement Agreement dated 18.11.2022, Corporate Debtor defaulted on post-dated cheques, remaining in arrears of over Rs. 3 Crores[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursements 2011-2016; last payment 07.04.2021; loan recall notice 01.03.2022; first Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 215 of 2022 filed in 2022; Settlement Agreement executed on 18.11.2022; CP 215/2022 withdrawn; settlement cheques dishonoured; fresh Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 146 of 2023 filed in 2023; NCLT initially admitted ex-parte on 25.01.2024, recalled on 09.02.2024; NCLT dismissed petition on 23.09.2024; NCLAT judgment pronounced on 19.03.2026[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank account statements evidencing loan disbursements; Demand Promissory Notes; signed loan renewal and account confirmation letters from FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18; Form 26AS TDS deduction certificates on interest; dishonoured post-dated cheques; Settlement Agreement dated 18.11.2022 containing Clause 10 revival stipulations[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP(IB) No. 146/KB/2023 under Section 7 before NCLT Kolkata Bench-II[cite: 29]. On 23.09.2024, NCLT dismissed the petition holding that an explicit written loan contract was mandatory for an NBFC under the 2012 RBI Master Circular, and the unconditional withdrawal of the earlier petition CP(IB) No. 215/2022 without court leave barred the fresh petition under principles of res judicata and Order XXIII Rule 1 CPC[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether a formal written loan agreement is a mandatory requirement for an NBFC to establish a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC in light of RBI Fair Practice Master Circulars, and whether the withdrawal of an earlier Section 7 application pursuant to a settlement agreement bars the filing of a fresh Section 7 application upon breach of settlement on principles of res judicata or Order XXIII Rule 1 of the CPC[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, the existence of a financial debt and default does not require a formal written loan agreement as a sine qua non, but may be established through contemporaneous documentary evidence including bank statements, promissory notes, confirmation letters, and TDS deductions on interest[cite: 29]. Furthermore, the withdrawal of a Section 7 petition pursuant to a settlement agreement does not trigger res judicata or bar the institution of a fresh Section 7 application upon subsequent breach of settlement terms, as such default constitutes a distinct, continuing cause of action[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, financial debt means a debt disbursed against consideration for the time value of money; CIRP Regulation 8(2) and Adjudicating Authority Rules 3(1)(d) and 4(1) allow proof of debt through other financial records; Section 238 overrides the pre-existing non-statutory RBI Master Circulars; the procedural bar under Order XXIII Rule 1 CPC cannot be extended to summary IBC insolvency proceedings to permit corporate debtors to evade insolvency via sham settlements[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In Innoventive Industries, the Supreme Court established that the adjudicating authority is merely required to satisfy itself that a default of a financial debt exceeding the statutory threshold has occurred and is due in fact and law[cite: 29]. Signed balance confirmations, promissory notes, and TDS certificates provide sufficient evidence of loan disbursement and time value of money[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and continuing default were fully proved, the lack of a written contract did not vitiate the financial debt, and res judicata did not bar the fresh petition following settlement breach; hence, the NCLT's dismissal was reversed and Section 7 admission was directed[cite: 29].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2068 of 2024, set aside the impugned order dated 23.09.2024 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench-II, directed the Adjudicating Authority to pass an order admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP under Section 7 within one month, and passed no order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary: Subham Capital Private Limited (an NBFC) appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order dismissing its Section 7 petition filed against Vedic Realty Private Limited for unpaid loan disbursements exceeding Rs. 22 Crores[cite: 29]. The NCLT held that an explicit written loan agreement was mandatory for NBFCs under RBI Circulars and that withdrawal of an earlier petition without court leave barred the second petition under res judicata[cite: 29]. Reversing the order, NCLAT held that Section 238 overrides RBI Circulars and a written agreement is not a prerequisite to prove financial debt where bank statements, promissory notes, and TDS certificates establish time value of money[cite: 29]. Furthermore, breach of a settlement agreement creates a fresh cause of action uninhibited by res judicata[cite: 29]. Admission was directed[cite: 29].

case_title: Rashmiben Dineshbhai Lathidadia vs. The Sarvodaya Sahakari Bank Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the personal guarantor, the Corporate Debtor is Palavi Synthetics Pvt. Ltd. (Principal Borrower), and Respondent No. 1 is The Sarvodaya Sahakari Bank Limited (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor granted financial facilities to the Corporate Debtor under various hypothecation agreements, against which the Appellant executed personal guarantee deeds dated 05.09.2012, 21.02.2013, 22.10.2013, and 23.04.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.07.2016. The summary suit claimed repayment of Rs. 2,88,65,468.35/- with 13% compound interest, and the Section 95 application claimed Rs. 44,831,658.35/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The personal guarantee was invoked on 11.08.2016. Summary Suit No. 144 of 2016 was filed on 24.10.2016. Form B demand notice under Section 95(4)(b) was issued on 01.07.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Board of Nominees Surat decreed the summary suit on 15.09.2017. Later, letters dated 17.03.2022 and 12.07.2022 were written by the Appellants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original petition under Section 95 was filed on 14.11.2022, dismissed as defective on 22.12.2023, and a fresh petition was filed on 17.09.2024, which the Adjudicating Authority admitted.
legal_issues: Whether the application filed by the Financial Creditor under Section 95 of the IBC was barred by limitation, and whether a civil court decree provides a fresh starting point of limitation under the IBC framework.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The liability of the principal borrower and the personal guarantor is co-terminus, and the date of default for a personal guarantor arises upon valid invocation of the guarantee. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Issuance of a demand notice under Form-B of the Personal Guarantor Rules cannot be substituted for the actual invocation of the guarantee. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must explicitly evaluate claims of debt acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act and admission of claims in the corporate debtor's CIRP to determine limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Adjudicating Authority failed to consider crucial evidence regarding debt acknowledgment letters and claim admissions, the matter must be remanded back for a fresh decision.
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 25.02.2025 and 21.10.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority are set aside. The appeals are allowed, and the matters are remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority for a fresh decision within two months.
summary: The Appellants, personal guarantors to the corporate debtor, challenged the NCLT orders initiating an insolvency resolution process against them under Section 95 of the IBC. The Financial Creditor had invoked the guarantees, obtained a cooperative court decree, and later filed Section 95 applications. The NCLAT observed that the Adjudicating Authority committed manifest errors in computing limitation, misconstrued the guarantee invocation date as the Form-B notice date, and failed to evaluate crucial evidence regarding debt acknowledgments and claim admissions. Consequently, the appellate tribunal allowed the appeals, set aside the NCLT orders, and remanded the matters back for fresh adjudication.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited vs. IDBI Bank Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. is the Appellant and secured financial creditor, while IDBI Bank Ltd., State Bank of India (SBI), Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. (EARC), and the Liquidator of Gupta Synthetics Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial facilities were extended to the Corporate Debtor under a consortium arrangement starting in 2004, secured by an equitable mortgage and hypothecation of assets recorded via documents on 26.03.2008. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Credit facilities were restructured by lenders during 2009-2010. IDBI and SBI claimed massive outstanding dues, leading to corporate insolvency and subsequent liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor went into liquidation on 14.07.2020. Claims were filed by lenders in August-September 2020, and the Liquidator issued distribution decisions subsequently challenged before the NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original charges were registered with the ROC in 2008, but modifications post-restructuring were not registered. Lenders relied on CERSAI records and original charges. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT allowed applications filed by IDBI and SBI, treating their restructured facilities as secured based on original registrations and CERSAI filings, which Kotak Mahindra Bank challenged in appeal.
legal_issues: Whether failure to register modifications of charges under Section 77 read with Section 79 of the Companies Act, 2013 post-restructuring vitiates the secured status of financial creditors during liquidation under the IBC, and whether Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Regulations allows proof of security via CERSAI.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Restructuring of existing credit facilities into funded interest term loans or working capital term loans does not amount to a material modification of charge requiring fresh ROC registration if the original charge and security remain undisturbed and cover the underlying debt components. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 provides alternative modes of proving security interest (such as CERSAI registration) using the disjunctive 'or', overriding strict technical bars under Section 77(3) of the Companies Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: All consortium lenders had prior knowledge of each other's securities; hence, liberal construction of 'modification' is permitted to protect existing valid security interests. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The restructuring did not create entirely new loans, the original 2008 registered charges subsisted, and CERSAI registration validly proved security interest, upholding the classification of IDBI and SBI as secured creditors.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins) No. 67, 68, and 198 of 2024 filed by Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. are dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank appealed against NCLT orders that classified SBI and IDBI Bank as fully secured creditors in the liquidation of Gupta Synthetics Ltd. The core dispute revolved around whether restructuring credit facilities without registering charge modifications with the ROC stripped the banks of their secured status under Section 77 of the Companies Act. The NCLAT held that loan restructuring under RBI guidelines did not constitute a fresh creation of charge, original charges subsisted, and security interest could be validly proved via CERSAI records under Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Regulations. Consequently, the appeals were dismissed, affirming the lower tribunal's orders.

case_title: Tikkavarapu Venkatram Reddy vs. L&T Finance Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is T. Venkatram Reddy (Personal Guarantor), Respondent No. 1 is L&T Finance Limited (Financial Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Renuka Devi Rangaswamy (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Deccan Chronicle Holdings Limited (Principal Borrower) executed a Facility Agreement dated 13.05.2011 for a term loan of Rs. 25 Crores, backed by a personal guarantee from the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 01.08.2012 after the Financial Creditor invoked call options under the facility agreement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Call option invoked on 24.05.2012 with a 15-day repayment window ending on 08.06.2012 (default date recorded as 01.08.2012). An arbitral award was passed on 15.03.2013. Form B demand notice under Section 95 was issued on 20.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitration proceedings culminated in an award on 15.03.2013, which was upheld by the Bombay High Court on 05.05.2015 and subjected to execution proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Hyderabad) admitted the application under Section 95 of the IBC against the Appellant on 24.06.2022, which was challenged in this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency resolution application under Section 95 of the IBC against a personal guarantor is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act read with Section 238A of the IBC when the default occurred in 2012 and notice was issued in 2020, and whether the concept of 'continuing guarantee' extends limitation indefinitely.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for filing an application under Section 7, 9, or 95 of the IBC is three years under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, starting from the exact date of default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A 'default' under Section 3(12) of the IBC is a singular, definite event of non-payment and cannot be treated as a continuous or recurring event to bypass limitation via Section 129 of the Contract Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The date of default disclosed in the statutory demand notice serves as the binding yardstick, and creditors cannot unilaterally set back or alter the date of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the default occurred in 2012 and the demand notice was issued in 2020 beyond the three-year limitation period, the Section 95 application is time-barred.
operative_order: The company appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 24.06.2022 passed by the NCLT Hyderabad admitting the Appellant to the insolvency resolution process under Section 95 of the IBC is quashed.
summary: The Appellant, personal guarantor of Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd., challenged the NCLT Hyderabad order admitting him to insolvency under Section 95 of the IBC upon an application by L&T Finance Ltd. The NCLAT held that the application was barred by limitation because the default occurred on August 1, 2012, and the demand notice was issued nearly eight years later in January 2020. Rejecting the financial creditor's argument regarding a 'continuing guarantee' under Section 129 of the Contract Act, the appellate tribunal ruled that default is a singular, definite event governed strictly by a three-year limitation period under Article 137. Consequently, the appeal was allowed and the insolvency initiation order was quashed.

case_title: The Peerless General Finance and Investment Co. Ltd. vs. Bhagwati Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is The Peerless General Finance and Investment Co. Ltd. (PGFI), and the Respondents include Bhagwati Developers Pvt. Ltd. (BDPL) and various other shareholders/entities. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In October-December 1987, PGFI passed board and general meeting resolutions to issue 30,000 equity shares at par (Rs. 100 each) via private placement, which were allotted in April 1988. Concurrently, Lodha group members sold their existing shares to Respondent No. 20. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (corporate democracy/oppression dispute involving share allotments and transfers). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 222 of 1991 was filed under Section 397-398 in May 1991 by original petitioners (Chatterjees), who later withdrew their claims, leading to transposition/substitution of BDPL as petitioner after decades of litigation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board meeting minutes showed active participation and consent of Mr. Parasmal Lodha and BDPL in approving the share issuance and transfers without recording dissent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata allowed the company petition after 31 years via order dated 18.07.2022, setting aside share allotments and transfers, which PGFI and other appellants challenged.
legal_issues: Whether shareholders who actively participated, voted in favor, and consented to share issuances and subsequently sold their own shares can maintain a petition under Section 397-398 alleging oppression and mismanagement, and whether private placement share allotments violated Section 77 of the Companies Act, 1956.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Shareholders who have consented to, voted for, or participated in corporate actions without recording dissent, and who have voluntarily exited the company by selling their shares, are estopped from subsequently turning around to challenge those very transactions under Section 397-398 of the Companies Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 77 of the 1956 Act penalizing indirect financial assistance requires strict establishment of statutory ingredients by direct evidence rather than vague presumptions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Silence and lack of recorded dissent in statutory board meeting minutes amount to assent under Section 193(4)(b) of the 1956 Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The substituted petitioner lacked standing to complain of oppression regarding acts they actively facilitated and profited from, and the NCLT erred in setting aside the longstanding share allotments.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) No. 121, 123, and 124 of 2022 are allowed. The common impugned order dated 18.07.2022 passed by NCLT Kolkata is set aside.
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Kolkata order dated July 18, 2022, which allowed a 31-year-old company petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, setting aside private placement share allotments and share transfers. The NCLAT observed that the original promoters (Lodha group/BDPL) had actively participated in board meetings, voted in favor of issuing 30,000 shares at par, and voluntarily sold their own shares at a profit without raising any protest or recording dissent. The appellate tribunal held that such consenting participants were estopped from invoking equitable remedies for oppression and mismanagement. Consequently, the appeals were allowed and the NCLT order was set aside.

case_title: V-Con Integrated Solutions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shreeram Technology Services Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is V-Con Integrated Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and the Respondent is M/s Shreeram Technology Services Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The operational debt arose from telecom/messaging services provided by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor, which formed the basis of an insolvency petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational debt claimed under Section 9 petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition (MP) CP (IB) No. 1 of 2020 was dismissed for non-prosecution on 25.03.2022 after being unattended for multiple hearings. The restoration application (IA No. 195 (MP) of 2022) was filed on 13.08.2022 (with a delay of approximately 5 months/111 days). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Case record showed non-appearance on multiple consecutive dates (31.08.2021, 29.10.2021, 23.12.2021, and 25.03.2022). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Indore Bench rejected the restoration application on 11.12.2024 on the grounds of exceeding the 30-day limitation under Rule 48(2) and failing to show sufficient cause, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an application for restoration of a petition dismissed for default can be entertained beyond the mandatory 30-day period under Rule 48(2) of the NCLT Rules, 2016, by invoking inherent powers under Rule 11 or Rule 15, and whether counsel's negligence constitutes 'sufficient cause' for condoning long delays in IBC proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inherent powers under Rule 11 or general power to extend time under Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules cannot be invoked in contravention of, conflict with, or ignorance of express mandatory provisions such as the 30-day limitation limit prescribed under Rule 48(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where an exhaustive procedure is prescribed for a particular purpose (restoration after default dismissal), no power shall be exercised otherwise than in the prescribed manner. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Condonation of delay requires establishing genuine 'sufficient cause'; gross negligence, repeated non-appearances, and casual reliance on counsel's inaction do not warrant condonation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The restoration application filed after 111 days without meeting statutory requirements was rightly rejected by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 283 of 2025 is dismissed. All related IAs are disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT Indore order dismissing its restoration application filed after 111 days to revive an insolvency petition that had been dismissed for default on March 25, 2022. The NCLAT held that Rule 48(2) of the NCLT Rules strictly mandates filing a restoration application within 30 days, and inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be invoked to override express statutory limitations. Furthermore, the appellant's excuse regarding counsel's negligence did not constitute 'sufficient cause' in time-sensitive IBC proceedings marked by repeated defaults. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Rajeev Vidhyadharan Alias Rajeev Anchal vs. P.J. Mathews & Ors.
appeal_number: IA No. 1812 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 162 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Rajeev Vidhyadharan @ Rajeev Anchal (Managing Director/Promoter), and the Respondents include P.J. Mathews and various other company stakeholders, administrators, and state authorities. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and control dispute concerning M/s Guruchandrika Builders & Property (P) Ltd. and Jatayupara tourism projects. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law dispute arising from NCLT orders regarding contractor dues and project management). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT Kochi Bench passed the impugned order on 22.10.2024. The Appellant pursued writ proceedings before the Kerala High Court until the writ petition was dismissed on 24.03.2025, and subsequent writ appeals and reviews were dismissed by 17.07.2025. The company appeal was filed before NCLAT on 24.06.2025, resulting in a delay of 163 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified copy of the NCLT order was available on 19.09.2025; however, the appellant repeatedly pursued misconceived writ remedies despite judicial warnings about statutory appeal forums. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application for condonation of delay (IA No. 1812 of 2025) in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 162 of 2025 to challenge the NCLT order.
legal_issues: Whether a litigant pursuing misconceived writ remedies before a High Court after being informed of an alternative statutory appeal remedy is entitled to exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, and whether a High Court lacking appellate jurisdiction can direct the appellate tribunal to ignore limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14 of the Limitation Act protects litigants only when prior proceedings were prosecuted with due diligence, in good faith, and bona fide; persistent pursuit of obviously non-maintainable writ remedies after being directed to statutory appeal forums disentitles a party to limitation exclusion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Special enactments like the Companies Act override general laws of limitation, and the mandatory 45-day limitation period under Section 421(3) must be strictly enforced. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once a High Court holds a writ petition not maintainable due to statutory alternative remedies, it becomes functus officio and cannot adjudicate upon or condone delay pertaining to appellate tribunal proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant failed to establish bona fides, good faith, or due diligence, rendering the company appeal hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: IA No. 1812 of 2025 seeking condonation of delay is rejected. Consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 162 of 2025 stands dismissed as barred by limitation.
summary: The Appellant filed a company appeal along with a delay condonation application (IA No. 1812 of 2025) challenging an NCLT Kochi Bench order dated October 22, 2024. Instead of filing a statutory appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act within limitation, the Appellant unsuccessfully pursued writ petitions, writ appeals, and review petitions before the Kerala High Court before approaching the NCLAT. The NCLAT held that the Appellant's conduct in repeatedly pursuing misconceived writ remedies after being informed of the statutory appellate remedy lacked bona fides and due diligence, thereby failing to satisfy the requirements of Section 14 of the Limitation Act. Furthermore, the High Court lacked jurisdiction to issue directions binding the appellate tribunal to ignore limitation. Consequently, the delay condonation application was rejected and the appeal was dismissed as time-barred.

case_title: Durgapur Corporation Private Limited vs. Aryan Ispat And Power Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Durgapur Corporation Private Limited (DCPL) / Operational Creditor, and Respondent is M/s. Aryan Ispat & Power Private Limited / Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An Operation & Management Agreement dated 01.02.2021 was entered between the Owner and Operator for operating a manufacturing plant, where service fees were payable as a share of profits after deducting usage fees and expenses. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: DCPL issued a demand notice dated 12.03.2024 for Rs. 34,12,10,212/-, whereas the Corporate Debtor had earlier issued a demand notice dated 16.12.2023 for Rs. 5,66,26,383/- and filed a Section 9 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: O&M Agreement entered on 01.02.2021; Terminated via Termination Agreement dated 25.11.2022 (effective 01.10.2022); CD's Section 8 notice on 16.12.2023; DCPL's demand notice on 12.03.2024 and Section 9 petition filed on 16.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Termination Agreement dated 25.11.2022 with Balance Settlement Sheet showing Rs. 11,32,24,945/- payable by the Operator to the Owner; prior demand notice and Section 9 petition by Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected DCPL's Section 9 application vide order dated 12.06.2025, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the O&M Agreement created an operational debt within Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether there was a pre-existing dispute between the parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An agreement structured on a profit-sharing basis where payments depend on profits after deducting usage fees and expenses does not create a debt or operational financial liability. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) operational debt contemplates supply of goods or services, not profit-sharing contractual arrangements or joint business operations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prior issuance of a demand notice and filing of a Section 9 petition by the corporate debtor against the operational creditor constitutes a clear pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the O&M agreement did not create an operational debt and there was a pre-existing dispute, the NCLT rightly rejected the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order rejecting Section 9 application.
summary: Durgapur Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) appealed against the NCLT order rejecting its Section 9 petition against Aryan Ispat & Power Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). The NCLAT held that the Operation & Management Agreement was a profit-sharing arrangement rather than a contract for supply of goods or services giving rise to an operational debt. Furthermore, the Corporate Debtor had already issued a prior demand notice and initiated insolvency proceedings against the Operational Creditor, establishing a clear pre-existing dispute. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, confirming the rejection of the Section 9 application.

case_title: GH Energy Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Flovel Hydro Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are GH Energy Pvt. Ltd., Mecamidi HPP India Pvt. Ltd., and its Directors, and Respondent No. 1 is Flovel Hydro Technologies Pvt. Ltd., and Respondent No. 2 is Mecamidi S.A. (France) under liquidation. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Venture and Share Purchase Agreement (JVSPA) and MOU executed in 2010 between Mecamidi HPP India, Mecamidi France (holding 47% shares), and Indian promoters. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law dispute regarding share transfer and non-compete obligations during liquidation). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: JVSPA executed on 15.09.2010; EOGM held on 04.06.2021; NCLT passed common impugned order on 01.02.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Mecamidi France went into liquidation in France; Flovel purchased 47% shares in court auction; EOGM notice sent to liquidator's official email; JVSPA Article 7 contained a non-compete clause, and Articles of Association Article 22/25 governed share transfers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Flovel filed CP No. 35 of 2022 and CP No. 188 of 2021 under Sections 241-242 and 59, which NCLT allowed on 01.02.2024, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether an auction purchaser of shares in a joint venture company during liquidation is bound by the non-compete obligations and charter restrictions under the JVSPA and Articles of Association, and whether the EOGM dated 04.06.2021 was validly convened.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A third-party auction purchaser of shares in a joint venture company steps into the shoes of the transferor and is bound by the restrictive covenants and Articles of Association (such as non-compete obligations and transfer conditions) governing the joint venture. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The expression 'pertaining to' in transfer restriction clauses is expansive, and charter documents permitting transfer only upon agreement to abide by JVSPA obligations operate as a condition precedent. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Service of notice of EOGM on the official email address of a liquidator constitutes valid service under company law without needing notice to the liquidator's secretary. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Flovel is entitled to registration as a shareholder but must sign and be bound by the non-compete clause per the JVSPA and Articles of Association.
operative_order: The appeals are disposed of. The NCLT order is set aside to the extent it held Flovel not bound to sign the non-compete clause; Flovel is directed to sign the non-compete clause per the JVSPA.
summary: Four appeals were filed against the NCLT New Delhi common order dated February 1, 2024, which had directed Mecamidi HPP India Pvt. Ltd. to register 47% shares in favour of Flovel Hydro Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (who purchased them in the liquidation auction of Mecamidi France) and declared an EOGM invalid. The NCLAT upheld the maintainability of Flovel's petition and the validity of the EOGM notice sent via official email. However, the Appellate Tribunal held that Flovel, as an auction purchaser stepping into the shoes of the joint venture partner, was bound by the transfer restrictions and non-compete obligations under Article 22 of the Articles of Association and the JVSPA. Consequently, the appeals were disposed of, directing Flovel to sign and be bound by the non-compete clause.

case_title: Carnet Elias Fernandes vs. Jagdish Kumar Parulkar & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Carnet Elias Fernandes (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor / Promoter of holding company GEI Industrial Systems Ltd.), and Respondent is Jagdish Kumar Parulkar (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of GEI Industries Systems Ltd. / GEI Power Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) commenced on 22.01.2025. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (dispute regarding ineligibility of suspended director/promoter under Section 29A(e) and 29A(f) of the IBC to submit a resolution plan). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 22.01.2025; Form-G published on 21.03.2025; last date for Eol 20.04.2025; final list of PRAs published on 15.05.2025; RP declared appellant ineligible on 11.06.2025; NCLT rejected IA 305 of 2025 on 17.02.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SEBI order dated 26.06.2018 passed for compulsory delisting of GEISL equity shares under Delisting Regulations, barring promoters/directors from accessing securities markets for 10 years. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench rejected IA No. 305 of 2025 filed by the Appellant on 17.02.2026, upholding the RP's letter declaring the Appellant ineligible under Section 29A(e) and 29A(f), leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a promoter/director subject to a SEBI compulsory delisting order barring access to securities markets is ineligible under Section 29A(f) of the IBC to submit a resolution plan, and whether the adjudicating authority can examine or ignore such SEBI orders during CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A person prohibited by SEBI from trading in securities or accessing securities markets by a formal, operative order is ineligible under Section 29A(f) of the IBC to submit a resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: When an operative SEBI prohibition order exists against a promoter or director, the adjudicating authority and resolution professional are not empowered to examine, review, or declare such statutory order void or ignore it during insolvency proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unchallenged statutory orders passed by competent regulatory authorities (like SEBI) holding force of law establish ineligibility under Section 29A(f). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since an operative SEBI order barred the Appellant from accessing securities markets, the RP and Adjudicating Authority correctly declared him ineligible under Section 29A(f).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 487 of 2026 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, suspended director and promoter of the corporate debtor's holding company, challenged the NCLT Indore order rejecting his application to declare himself eligible to submit a resolution plan. The NCLT had upheld the resolution professional's determination that the Appellant was ineligible under Section 29A(e) and 29A(f) of the IBC due to a SEBI order dated June 26, 2018, which compulsorily delisted the company's shares and barred promoters from accessing securities markets for 10 years. The NCLAT held that the adjudicating authority cannot review or ignore operative statutory orders passed by SEBI, and since the prohibition order stood unchalleged and in force, the ineligibility under Section 29A(f) was rightly triggered. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: STCI Finance Limited vs. IMP Powers Limited (Through its Liquidator) & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1019 of 2024, 1657 of 2024 & 893 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is STCI Finance Limited (Financial Creditor / NBFC), Respondent No. 1 is IMP Powers Limited (Corporate Debtor), Respondent No. 2 is Ravindra Kumar Goyal (Liquidator), Respondent No. 4 is Rakesh Ramanlal Shah (Successful Auction Purchaser), and Respondents No. 5 to 10 are State Bank of India and other consortium banks. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: STCI extended term loan facility of Rs. 25 crores in 2017-2018 secured by mortgage/charge on fixed assets, sharing first pari passu charge with SBI. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 29.02.2020; STCI's admitted claim in liquidation was Rs. 39,55,34,828/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 29.03.2022; liquidation ordered on 19.12.2023; STCI claimed on 17.01.2024; e-auction notice issued on 08.03.2024; auction conducted on 21.05.2024 for Rs. 78 crores; NCLT orders passed on 22.04.2024, 20.08.2024, and 05.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Conditional NOCs issued by consortium lenders requiring inter se agreements and reciprocal NOCs which STCI failed to fulfill; STCI failed to pay CIRP costs and workmen dues within 90 days under Regulation 21A; majority secured creditors (>85%) relinquished security interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: STCI filed applications before NCLT Ahmedabad challenging e-auction notice, issuance of sale certificate, and grant of Section 32A immunities, which NCLT dismissed or ruled against STCI, leading to three connected appeals before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a secured creditor claiming first pari passu charge can realize assets independently under Section 52 without fulfilling inter se agreement conditions and mandatory 90-day cost payments under Regulation 21A, resulting in deemed relinquishment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Non-compliance with mandatory requirements under Regulation 21A of the Liquidation Regulations (such as payment of CIRP costs and workmen dues within 90 days) results in automatic statutory relinquishment of security interest and vesting of secured assets in the liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In consortium lending arrangements with joint security, Section 13(9) of the SARFAESI Act operates as applicable law under Section 52(4) of the Code, binding all secured creditors to decisions taken by the statutory majority (60% or more). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Conditional NOCs requiring inter se agreements and reciprocal ceding of charges do not create a valid, perfected pari passu charge if such conditions remain unfulfilled. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since STCI failed to fulfill charge conditions, did not pay CIRP/liquidation costs within 90 days, and majority lenders relinquished security, STCI's security interest stood automatically relinquished, validating the going concern e-auction sale.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1019 of 2024 is dismissed. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1657 of 2024 is disposed of with a direction to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the distribution of sale proceeds under Section 53(1) within 4 weeks. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 893 of 2025 is dismissed as barred by limitation.
summary: STCI Finance Ltd., a financial creditor, filed three appeals challenging NCLT Ahmedabad orders relating to the liquidation sale of IMP Powers Limited as a going concern. STCI claimed an independent right to realize its security under Section 52. The NCLAT held that STCI's alleged first pari passu charge was never perfected due to non-fulfillment of reciprocal NOC and inter se agreement conditions. Furthermore, STCI failed to pay its share of CIRP costs and workmen dues within the mandatory 90-day period under Regulation 21A of the Liquidation Regulations, resulting in automatic deemed relinquishment of its security interest into the liquidation estate. Over 85% of secured creditors had relinquished their security, binding STCI under Section 13(9) of SARFAESI. Consequently, the first appeal was dismissed, the second appeal was disposed of with directions to NCLT to finalize distribution under Section 53 within 4 weeks, and the third appeal was dismissed as time-barred.

case_title: Sanjeev Sangal vs. M/s. Apex Heights Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sanjeev Sangal (Homebuyer / Unsecured Financial Creditor), and Respondent is M/s Apex Heights Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA) / Maple Realcon Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant purchased Flat No. B-0102 in Tower B (Misty Heights project, Greater Noida) for Rs. 47,00,000/-, executing a Builder Buyer Agreement dated 09.03.2018 and paying full consideration via receipts dated 29.07.2016 and 12.08.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor's CIRP commenced on 18.07.2018; Appellant's claim of Rs. 47,00,000/- was fully admitted by the RP on 01.12.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved on 20.02.2020; Appellant filed IA 1929 of 2024 for plan implementation and flat handover; NCLT passed impugned order on 27.11.2024 directing SRA to re-scrutinize claims while keeping the flat on hold. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP admitted the claim in full and incorporated it in the CoC list; BBA and payment receipts furnished; SRA failed to verify documents within the 60-day plan timeline. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi disposed of IA 1929 of 2024 vide order dated 27.11.2024, relegating the homebuyer back to the SRA for re-scrutiny, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a Successful Resolution Applicant can conduct post-approval re-verification or re-adjudication of a homebuyer's claim that was already fully admitted by the Resolution Professional during CIRP and incorporated in the approved Resolution Plan, and withhold flat possession indefinitely.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC, it becomes binding on all stakeholders, and an SRA cannot unilaterally reopen, re-scrutinize, or reject claims that were already duly verified and admitted by the Resolution Professional during CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Resolution plan verification clauses permitting SRA to inspect original documents within specified timelines (e.g. 60 days) are procedural safeguards and do not confer an open-ended, indefinite power to re-adjudicate admitted claims or resile from plan obligations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a homebuyer produces valid allotment agreements and payment receipts and the RP admits the claim in full without keeping it under verification, the claim stands crystallized and must be honored. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in relegating the homebuyer for re-verification after the SRA failed to act within timelines; the SRA must execute conveyance and hand over possession of the flat.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2370 of 2024 is allowed. The impugned order dated 27.11.2024 is set aside, and the Respondent-SRA is directed to execute the conveyance deed and hand over title and physical possession of Flat No. B-0102, Tower-B (Misty Heights, Greater Noida) to the Appellant within two months. Additionally, the matter is referred to IBBI for systemic investigation regarding CIRP conduct.
summary: Sanjeev Sangal, a homebuyer in the Misty Heights project of Maple Realcon Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), filed an appeal against the NCLT New Delhi order dated November 27, 2024. The NCLT had disposed of his application (IA 1929 of 2024) by directing him to approach the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) for re-scrutiny of his claim while keeping his flat on hold. The NCLAT held that the Appellant's claim of Rs. 47 lakhs had already been fully verified and admitted by the Resolution Professional during CIRP, and incorporated in the approved Resolution Plan. The SRA could not use plan verification clauses to conduct open-ended, post-approval re-adjudication or resile from its obligation to deliver flats, especially after failing to act within stipulated timelines. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the NCLT order was set aside, and the SRA was ordered to hand over possession of the flat within two months, alongside an IBBI investigation into CIRP conduct.

case_title: Keshav Bihani & M/s Hari Narayan Bihani vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
appeal_number: Competition App. (AT) No. 44 of 2022 & Competition App. (AT) No. 45 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Keshav Bihani (partner in M/s Hari Narayan Bihani) and M/s Hari Narayan Bihani (partnership firm), and Respondent is the Competition Commission of India (CCI). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of polyacetal protective tubes for axle box guides to Integral Coach Factory (ICF) and Indian Railways. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Penalty imposed under Section 27 on the firm and Section 48 on the active partner (Keshav Bihani) at 5% of average annual income for cartelization/bid-rigging. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CCI passed Section 27 order on 09.06.2022 and Section 48 penalty order on 22.06.2022 in Suo Motu Case No. 06 of 2020; appeals filed in 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Leniency application filed by M/s Jai PolyPan (P) Ltd. disclosing bid-rigging cartel among 7 RDSO Part-I approved vendors; 10 incriminating emails exchanged (8 received by Hari Narayan Bihani) showing tender allocation and price coordination. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI found appellants guilty of cartelisation under Section 3(3) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act and penalized them, leading to appeals before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the CCI can invoke Section 48 of the Competition Act against partners/persons in charge for cartelization violations, and whether receipt of cartel-related emails without protest constitutes participation in bid-rigging.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In cartelisation and bid-rigging cases, receipt of incriminating emails regarding tender allocation and price coordination without protest or dissociation over an extended period constitutes participation through tacit acquiescence and a meeting of minds under Section 3 of the Competition Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 48(1) of the Competition Act prior to amendment, using the words 'punished accordingly', empowers CCI to impose proportionate penalties on individuals (based on average annual income) in the same scale as penalties imposed on enterprises under Section 27. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct documentary evidence in the form of emails establishing tender sharing and price fixing, supported by Section 65B certificates, proves bid-rigging under preponderance of probability standards. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI rightly found the appellants guilty of cartelization and correctly penalized both the firm and its active partner under Sections 27 and 48.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 44 of 2022 and Competition Appeal (AT) No. 45 of 2022 are dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants Keshav Bihani and M/s Hari Narayan Bihani challenged CCI orders dated June 9 and June 22, 2022, which penalized them for participating in a bid-rigging cartel for supplying polyacetal protective tubes to Indian Railways. The NCLAT held that overwhelming direct evidence through emails showing tender allocations and price coordination, which the appellants received without protest or dissociation, established their participation in the cartel through tacit acquiescence. Furthermore, the CCI had correctly invoked Section 48 against the active partner, imposing a proportionate penalty based on average annual income. Consequently, both appeals were dismissed, upholding the CCI orders.

case_title: Consortium of Wafi Investments Ltd. & Suhail Sameer vs. Vishal Jain, RP of Green Soul Ergonomics Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Consortium of Wafi Investments Ltd. and Suhail Sameer (Successful Resolution Applicant), Respondent No. 1 is Vishal Jain (Resolution Professional of Green Soul Ergonomics Pvt. Ltd.), Respondent No. 2 is CoC, and Intervenors/other RAs. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Green Soul Ergonomics Pvt. Ltd. admitted on 01.05.2024; consortium submitted a resolution plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (corporate insolvency resolution plan approval dispute regarding post-approval consortium reconstitution). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 01.05.2024; CoC approved plan on 11.11.2024; email sent on 25.11.2024 seeking to induct OTP Venture Funds Scheme I into consortium; CoC approved reconstitution on 04.12.2024; plan re-approved by CoC on 09.12.2024; NCLT passed impugned remand order on 21.01.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consortium originally comprised Wafi Investments (60%) and Suhail Sameer (40%); after CoC approval on 11.11.2024, OTP Ventures Fund Scheme I was inducted (39%), reducing Suhail Sameer to 1%. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench vide order dated 21.01.2026 held that a resolution plan once approved by CoC cannot be re-approved by adding a new consortium member, and remanded the plan back to CoC, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a consortium whose resolution plan has been approved by the Committee of Creditors can subsequently change its composition or introduce a new member into the consortium before approval by the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan submitted by a consortium is approved by the Committee of Creditors, the composition of the consortium cannot be modified or a new member introduced, as RFRP provisions permitting consortium changes apply only at the pre-approval stage. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1B) of the CIRP Regulations strictly prohibits considering plans from persons not included in the final list of prospective resolution applicants or submitted after deadlines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Permitting post-approval consortium reconstitution alters the implementation entity and evades evaluation criteria and financial strength assessments established during the RFRP stage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since adding a new consortium member post-CoC approval violates the statutory framework and RFRP terms, the NCLT rightly remanded the plan back to the CoC.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 433 of 2026 is dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's remand order.
summary: The Consortium of Wafi Investments Ltd. and Suhail Sameer appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated January 21, 2026, which remanded their approved resolution plan back to the CoC because they had inducted a new member (OTP Venture Funds Scheme I) into the consortium *after* the CoC had already approved their plan on November 11, 2024. The NCLAT held that RFRP clauses permitting consortium changes operate strictly prior to CoC approval. Post-approval introduction of new consortium members violates Regulation 39(1B) and alters the evaluation parameters of prospective resolution applicants. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, upholding the remand order.

case_title: Saurabh & Anr. vs. M/s Apex Heights Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 109 of 2025 & No. 113 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are flat-buyers / homebuyers (Jai Kishore Prasad, Mukta Prasad, Saurabh, Kumari Minakshi), and Respondent is M/s Apex Heights Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA) / Maple Realcon Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants originally booked flats with a sister concern (Mascot Soho Homes Pvt. Ltd.), which were transferred/adjusted into Maple Realcon's Misty Heights project via a settlement deed dated 01.08.2015 and subsequent allotment agreements signed by ex-director B.P. Singh. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor's CIRP commenced on 18.07.2018; Appellants' claims were submitted in Form C and admitted by the RP during CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved on 20.02.2020; Appellants filed IAs (5591 & 5592 of 2024) for flat possession; NCLT passed impugned order on 27.11.2024 directing re-verification by SRA. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP admitted claims and included them in CoC lists; Monitoring Committee verified claims on 02.02.2022; SRA failed to act within the 60-day plan timeline. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi disposed of IAs 5591 & 5592 of 2024 vide common order dated 27.11.2024, relegating homebuyers to the SRA for re-verification, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether an SRA can subject homebuyers' claims that were verified and admitted by the RP and verified by the Monitoring Committee to open-ended, post-approval re-verification and withhold flat possession.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An SRA cannot indefinitely withhold flat possession or reopen claims that have been duly verified and admitted by the Resolution Professional and subsequently verified by the Monitoring Committee. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Resolution plan verification clauses cannot be invoked beyond stipulated timelines (such as 60 days) to undermine crystallized claims or resile from binding plan obligations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where payments, ledgers, settlement deeds, and RP admissions establish valid homebuyer status, further re-scrutiny by the SRA is legally impermissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in directing re-scrutiny; the Appellants are entitled to allotment and possession of their flats.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 109 & 113 of 2025 are allowed. The impugned order dated 27.11.2024 is set aside, and the Respondent-SRA is directed to allot and hand over possession of the flats to the Appellants upon taking differential amounts as noted in the appeals. Additionally, the matter is referred to IBBI for investigation regarding CIRP conduct.
summary: Homebuyers Jai Kishore Prasad, Mukta Prasad, Saurabh, and Kumari Minakshi appealed against the NCLT New Delhi common order dated November 27, 2024, which directed them to approach the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) for claim re-verification. The NCLAT held that the Appellants' claims had already been admitted by the RP during CIRP and explicitly verified by the Monitoring Committee on February 2, 2022. The SRA could not use verification clauses to conduct open-ended re-adjudication beyond stipulated timelines or deny flat delivery. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, the NCLT order was set aside, and the SRA was directed to allot and hand over possession of the flats upon payment of differential amounts, along with an IBBI investigation into CIRP conduct.

case_title: S. Arun vs. M/s. Ambal Agencies & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is S. Arun (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s. Sargam Metals Pvt. Ltd.), Respondent No. 1 is Neeraj Agarwal (Proprietor of Ambal Agencies / Operational Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is K.J. Vinodh (Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of aluminum ingots, sheets, coils, and scrap by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor, leading to unpaid dues of Rs. 265 lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default under MoU dated 21.07.2018 (where balance of Rs. 265 lakhs was converted into a fresh loan repayable in quarterly installments of Rs. 25 lakhs starting 01.07.2018). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU executed on 21.07.2018; part payments made; 5 post-dated cheques issued on 16.06.2021 for Rs. 218.05 lakhs dishonored ('account closed'); Section 8 notice issued on 22.06.2022; Section 9 application filed on 05.09.2022; NCLT admitted application on 28.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU dated 21.07.2018; ledger statements; 5 post-dated cheques issued on 16.06.2021 and bank return memos. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench admitted the Section 9 application vide order dated 28.11.2024, initiating CIRP against the Corporate Debtor, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is barred by limitation when default occurred under an MoU in 2018, and whether the issuance of post-dated cheques in 2021 constitutes an acknowledgment of debt extending limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Issuance of post-dated cheques representing outstanding debt constitutes a clear acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, effectively extending or resetting the limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 applications filed within three years from the date of dishonor of cheques or subsequent acknowledgements are well within limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted issuance of cheques for outstanding dues, subsequent part payments, and bank dishonor memos conclusively establish ongoing debt and default acknowledgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the issuance of cheques in 2021 reset the limitation period and the Section 9 petition was filed in September 2022, the application is not barred by limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 447 of 2024 is dismissed. All interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: S. Arun, suspended director of M/s. Sargam Metals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated November 28, 2024, admitting a Section 9 application filed by Neeraj Agarwal (Ambal Agencies) and initiating CIRP. The Appellant argued that the application was barred by limitation, reckoning default from July 2018 under an MoU. The NCLAT held that although default occurred under the MoU in 2018, the Corporate Debtor subsequently made part payments and issued 5 post-dated cheques on June 16, 2021, for the balance of Rs. 218.05 lakhs, which were dishonored. These cheques constituted a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, resetting the limitation period. Consequently, the Section 9 application filed in September 2022 was within limitation, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mohit Arora vs. PNB Housing Finance Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mohit Arora (Personal Guarantor), Respondent No. 1 is PNB Housing Finance Limited (Financial Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Rakesh Prasad Khandelwal (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facilities totaling Rs. 275 Crores sanctioned on 04.01.2017 to Supertech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) along with co-borrowers (Sarv Realtors Pvt. Ltd. and ASP Sarin Realty Pvt. Ltd.), backed by personal guarantees of Mohit Arora and others. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in monthly installments, leading to SARFAESI notice and Section 95 demand notice dated 09.07.2021 for Rs. 358.91 Crore. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: PNBHFL filed first petition CP(IB) 203 of 2021 on 26.03.2021 (withdrawn on 08.07.2021 with liberty); IFCI filed CP(IB) 428 of 2021 on 02.06.2021; PNBHFL filed second petition CP(IB) 395 of 2021 on 24.07.2021; NCLT admitted PNBHFL's petition on 11.10.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, guarantee deeds, Form-B demand notice, and multiple overlapping Section 95 filings by creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted PNBHFL's Section 95 application against personal guarantor Mohit Arora vide order dated 11.10.2022, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a subsequent Section 95 petition filed by a financial creditor is barred by an interim moratorium triggered by another creditor's petition filed during the pendency/withdrawal of an earlier petition, and whether corporate borrower restructuring discharges personal guarantors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency petition filed under Section 95 of the IBC during the currency of a statutory interim moratorium triggered by a prior petition that was itself filed during an earlier subsisting moratorium is non-est in law and cannot trigger interim moratorium bar against valid prior filings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 96 interim moratorium prohibits initiation of legal actions in respect of a debt, but petitions filed in violation thereof or while prior valid filings are being regularized/re-filed are governed by the overarching principle that fraud or concealment vitiates judicial proceedings and non-est filings do not bar valid substantive applications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Guarantors who conceal prior overlapping insolvency proceedings and attempt to exploit conflicting filings cannot claim protection of interim moratorium to defeat valid creditor claims. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since PNBHFL's first petition was filed in March 2021 (making IFCI's June 2021 petition non-est) and PNBHFL's re-filed petition was validly prosecuted, the admission of Section 95 against the personal guarantor is legally sound.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1284 of 2022 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Mohit Arora, personal guarantor for Supertech Ltd., appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated October 11, 2022, admitting a Section 95 application filed by PNB Housing Finance Limited. The Appellant argued that PNBHFL's second petition was filed during the interim moratorium triggered by another creditor (IFCI)'s petition. The NCLAT held that because PNBHFL had already filed its first petition in March 2021 (which was refiled in July 2021 upon withdrawal with liberty), IFCI's June 2021 petition was filed during an existing moratorium and was thus non-est in law. Furthermore, the Appellant was guilty of material concealment by hiding overlapping proceedings. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, upholding the admission of personal insolvency resolution.

case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner vs. Mr. Vipul Garg, Liquidator & Canara Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Regional Provident Fund Commissioner (EPFO), Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Vipul Garg (Liquidator of M/s Jai Laxmi Lighting Industries Pvt. Ltd.), and Respondent No. 2 is Canara Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor M/s Jai Laxmi Lighting Industries Pvt. Ltd. covered under the EPF Act, 1952. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO claimed Rs. 36,55,290/- towards EPF dues accrued from 05/2012 onwards; liquidation realization was Rs. 1,70,49,610/- distributed under Section 53. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in 2018; liquidation ordered on 21.02.2019; EPFO filed Form B on 02.04.2019; liquidator admitted only Rs. 1,42,463/- and distributed Rs. 6,014/- on pari passu basis; company dissolved on 06.03.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Claims filed in Form B; provisional assessments under Section 7A, 7Q, and 14B; final liquidation report filed on 23.02.2022; NCLT order of dissolution on 06.03.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench approved the final report and dissolved the corporate debtor on 06.03.2023, which led to the present appeal by EPFO.
legal_issues: Whether provident fund, pension, and gratuity dues (including employer contributions, interest, and damages under the EPF Act) are excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC and must be paid in full outside the Section 53 waterfall mechanism, irrespective of whether a separate fund was maintained.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Sums due to workmen or employees from provident, pension, and gratuity funds are statutorily excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC and cannot be pooled into liquidation assets or subjected to the Section 53 waterfall distribution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The absence of a separately maintained designated provident fund account does not deprive workmen/employees of their statutory priority, and PF dues (including employee/employer contributions, interest, and statutory damages under EPF Act Sections 11, 7A, 7Q, 14B) must be paid in full. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory welfare obligations towards social security enjoy overriding priority and cannot be equated with ordinary liquidation claims or distributed proportionally via liquidation percentages. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since PF dues do not form part of the liquidation estate, the adjudicating authority erred in treating them as ordinary liquidation claims and ordering dissolution without ensuring full payment, necessitating a fresh examination.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 840 of 2023 is allowed. The impugned order dated 06.03.2023 is set aside. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to examine the issue fresh in accordance with law. All parties shall appear before the Adjudicating Authority on 12.05.2026.
summary: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner (EPFO) appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order dated March 6, 2023, approving the final liquidation report and dissolving M/s Jai Laxmi Lighting Industries Pvt. Ltd. The EPFO argued that provident fund dues amounting to over Rs. 36 lakhs were incorrectly treated as ordinary liquidation claims and subjected to pro-rata waterfall distribution under Section 53, resulting in a meager payout of Rs. 6,014/-. The NCLAT held that under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC, all sums due to workmen and employees from provident, pension, and gratuity funds are strictly excluded from the liquidation estate, regardless of whether a separate fund account was maintained by the corporate debtor. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the dissolution order was set aside, and the matter was remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority for fresh examination.

case_title: Harti Venkataravanppa Dharmesh vs. Kamalapuri Narasimaih Jayalakshmi & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Harti Venkataravanppa Dharmesh (Managing Director, Shareholder and Promoter of M/s Vistara Media Private Limited / Respondent No. 2 in company petition), and Respondents No. 1 and 2 are Smt. Kamalapuri Narasimaih Jayalakshmi and Sri Krishna Karthik Darshan (Petitioners / Transferees), alongside other company directors and entities. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transfer and transmission of equity shares and optionally convertible preference shares of M/s Vistara Media Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law appeal against condonation of delay in filing a Section 58 petition under the Companies Act, 2013). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Correspondence/email sent in Feb-March 2025; Company Petition CP No. 74/BB/2025 filed under Section 58 on 21.05.2025 with a 36-day delay; NCLT Chennai Bench passed impugned order on 06.02.2026 condoning the delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CA No. 103/2025 filed for condoning 36 days of delay supported by medical certificates and memos; appellant failed to file written objections before NCLT despite opportunities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru / Chennai Bench condoned the 36-day delay vide order dated 06.02.2026 in CA No. 103/2025, which led to the present appeal by the Managing Director.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the power to condone delay in filing an appeal under Section 58(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, by applying Section 433 of the Companies Act read with Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act and Rule 11 of NCLT Rules.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an appeal under Section 58(3) of the Companies Act can be extended or condoned by applying Section 433 of the Companies Act read with Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act and inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, as Section 58 does not expressly exclude the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where special enactments prescribe limitation periods without expressly barring the Limitation Act, provisions of Sections 4 to 24 of the Limitation Act apply via Section 29(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted medical grounds and sufficient cause established via memos warrant liberal construction to advance substantial justice on merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error in condoning the 36-day delay upon uncontroverted medical evidence, and the appeal is without merit.
