operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 28 of 2026 is dismissed. All pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: Harti Venkataravanppa Dharmesh, Managing Director of M/s Vistara Media Private Limited, appealed against the NCLT Chennai bench order dated February 6, 2026, which condoned a 36-day delay in filing a company petition under Section 58 of the Companies Act, 2013. The Appellant argued that Section 58(3) does not permit condonation of delay and that NCLT improperly relied on inherent powers. The NCLAT held that by virtue of Section 433 of the Companies Act read with Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, provisions of the Limitation Act apply to special laws unless expressly excluded, and courts/tribunals can condone delay upon sufficient medical cause. Furthermore, the appellant had failed to file any written objections before the NCLT. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: L & L Partners Litigation vs. Jalesh Kumar Grover, RP of Grandstar Realty Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is L&L Partners Litigation (legal firm claiming as allottee), and Respondent is Jalesh Kumar Grover, Resolution Professional of Grandstar Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: AKME Projects Limited allotted 3 flats to the appellant legal firm on 09.03.2015 in lieu of professional legal fees; later, Yes Bank auctioned AKME's assets under SARFAESI to Grandstar Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) via a sale certificate dated 19.07.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (claim for flat allotment in lieu of legal fees / condonation of delay in filing claim). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Grandstar Realty Pvt. Ltd. on 26.09.2023; public announcement called claims; appellant filed its claim on 09.01.2025 after resolution plan approval in the 15th CoC meeting on 15.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale certificate with Annexure-1 containing a list of 221 valid allottees (appellant's name absent); RP's rejection email dated 13.02.2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed IA No. 1439 of 2025 filed by the appellant for condonation of delay and claim admission on 17.10.2025, leading to the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing to condone delay in filing a claim after resolution plan approval, and whether professional fee adjustments constitute financial debt or valid allottee status.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A commercial entity or legal firm cannot claim condonation of delay or belated admission of claims after the Committee of Creditors has already approved a resolution plan under the time-bound framework of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) Explanation and jurisprudence on financial debt require actual disbursement against time value of money, distinguishing genuine homebuyers from professional service fee adjustments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Omission from the certified encumbrance list (Annexure-1) attached to a SARFAESI sale certificate disproves third-party allottee status. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly dismissed the belated claim application after resolution plan approval, and the appeal is dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1944 of 2025 is dismissed.
summary: L&L Partners Litigation, a legal firm, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated October 17, 2025, which dismissed its application for condonation of delay and admission of a claim for 3 flats allegedly allotted by AKME Projects Ltd. in lieu of legal fees before the property was auctioned under SARFAESI to Grandstar Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). The NCLAT held that the appellant, a commercial entity, filed its claim belatedly after the CoC had already approved the resolution plan, and its name did not figure in the official encumbrance/allottee list attached to the SARFAESI sale certificate. Furthermore, professional fee exchanges lack the essential elements of a financial debt. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: S.M. Kamal Pasha & Anr. vs. S. Rajendran, RP of TD Toll Road Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are S.M. Kamal Pasha and Syed Fahad (Successful Resolution Applicants - SRA), Respondent No. 1 is S. Rajendran (Resolution Professional of TD Toll Road Pvt. Ltd.), and Respondents No. 2 to 7 are CoC members. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of TD Toll Road Pvt. Ltd. admitted on 25.11.2019; SRA submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 172.5 crores, which was unanimously approved by the CoC on 07.05.2021, accompanied by a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of Rs. 8,62,75,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (resolution plan withdrawal/approval dispute). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Plan approved by CoC on 07.05.2021; approval application IA 1505/2021 filed on 29.06.2021; Supreme Court stayed proceedings; appeal dismissed on 09.12.2024; CoC passed resolutions in 22nd/23rd meetings in late 2025 to withdraw plan; NCLT permitted withdrawal on 08.12.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unanimous CoC approval in May 2021; submitted PBG; subsequent cash surplus accumulation in corporate debtor during prolonged litigation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench permitted the RP to withdraw the plan approval application (IA 1505/2021) on 08.12.2025 at the oral mandate of the CoC, which led to the SRA's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors and Resolution Professional can seek withdrawal of a resolution plan that has already been approved by the CoC and pending before the Adjudicating Authority due to efflux of time or cash surplus accumulation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved by the Committee of Creditors, it becomes binding inter se between the CoC and the Successful Resolution Applicant, and neither the CoC nor the RP can renege or seek withdrawal of the plan approval application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 18(2) of the CIRP Regulations strictly prohibits CoC from convening meetings post-approval to decide matters affecting the submitted resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Efflux of time and accumulation of cash reserves during protracted litigation initiated by management do not justify unseating a binding CoC-approved resolution plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in permitting the RP to withdraw the plan approval application, and the impugned order is set aside.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 211 of 2026 is allowed. The impugned order dated 08.12.2025 is set aside, and IA No. 1505 of 2021 is revived for fresh consideration.
summary: Successful Resolution Applicants S.M. Kamal Pasha and Syed Fahad appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated December 8, 2025, which permitted the Resolution Professional to withdraw the plan approval application (IA 1505/2021) at the behest of the CoC. Their plan offering Rs. 172.5 crores had been unanimously approved by the CoC in May 2021, but proceedings were delayed due to litigation by the suspended management. The NCLAT held that under the IBC framework and Regulation 18(2) of the CIRP Regulations, a CoC-approved resolution plan is binding and irrevocable, and the CoC cannot unilaterally seek its withdrawal due to subsequent cash accumulations during delays. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the withdrawal order was set aside, and the plan approval application was revived.

case_title: Narayani Resources Pvt. Ltd. vs. Essar Power Gujarat Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Narayani Resources Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and Respondent is Essar Power Gujarat Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of coal under High Seas Sale / Sale & Purchase Contracts between March 2023 and June 2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Demand notice dated 11.08.2025 claimed an outstanding amount of Rs. 85,04,04,994/- as on 04.08.2025, with default date 25.07.2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 11.08.2025; reply/notice of dispute given on 21.08.2025 detailing settlement of Jan 2025 (Rs. 107 crores settled, principal paid, credit notes issued); Section 9 application filed on 17.05.2025 / 17.10.2025; NCLT rejected application on 04.12.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement discussion on 16.01.2025; WhatsApp communications dated 20.03.2025 showing reconciliation and credit notes; subsequent arbitration application under Section 11 before Bombay High Court, which referred disputes to arbitration on 20.01.2026. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected the Section 9 application vide order dated 04.12.2025 on the ground of a pre-existing dispute regarding financial reconciliation, leading to the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an operational debt application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when there is a pre-existing dispute regarding account reconciliation and a prior settlement agreement, and when disputes have been referred to arbitration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor raises a plausible defense supported by evidence showing pre-existing disputes regarding financial reconciliation and settlement of accounts, a Section 9 application must be rejected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC mandates rejection of an application if a notice of pre-existing dispute has been received and is not spurious, feeble, or illusory. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: WhatsApp chats, settlement negotiations, and credit note exchanges establishing active dispute and reconciliation efforts constitute a valid pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly rejected the Section 9 application due to a pre-existing dispute and ongoing arbitration, and the appeal is dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 158 of 2026 is dismissed.
summary: Narayani Resources Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated December 4, 2025, which rejected its Section 9 application against Essar Power Gujarat Ltd. for coal supplies. The NCLAT held that the corporate debtor had raised a genuine, pre-existing dispute in its reply to the demand notice, detailing a January 2025 settlement, credit note exchanges, and reconciliation discussions. Furthermore, the parties had initiated arbitration proceedings under Section 11 of the Arbitration Act, and the Bombay High Court had referred the contractual disputes to an arbitrator. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, upholding the rejection of the insolvency petition.

case_title: Nimai Gautam Shah (RP of Zep Infratech Ltd.) & Ors. vs. Raj Radhe Finance Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Nimai Gautam Shah (Resolution Professional of Zep Infratech Ltd.), Committee of Creditors (Raj Radhe Finance Ltd. and Rajendra M. Thakkar & Sons Pvt. Ltd.), and Successful Resolution Applicant (Deepvir Enterprise and Kanha Ventures). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Zep Infratech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor - MSME) admitted under Section 7 on 31.07.2023 based on a corporate guarantee given for a loan advanced to Shree Ram Cottex Industries Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debt claims of financial creditors and statutory operational claims (Income Tax Department claim of Rs. 251.79 crores). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 31.07.2023; Form-G issued; CoC approved resolution plan; NCLT remanded plan on 30.04.2024; modified plan approved by CoC on 07.05.2024 (value Rs. 7.75 crores); NCLT rejected plan and ordered liquidation on 23.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Balance sheets showing systematic reduction in tangible assets (property, plant, and equipment) from Rs. 15.06 crores in 2020-21 to Rs. 3.76 crores in 2022-23; disappearance of short-term borrowings of Rs. 443 crores; absence of forensic audit and PUFE proceedings by RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected the CoC-approved resolution plan and ordered liquidation of the corporate debtor on 23.06.2025, leading to three separate appeals by the RP, CoC, and SRA.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can reject a CoC-approved resolution plan and order liquidation when the information memorandum and resolution process are marred by unexplained asset depletion, uninvestigated balance sheet erosions, and inadequate transparency.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority is not a rubber stamp and is duty-bound to probe material irregularities, unexplained asset depletions, and lack of transparency that compromise the integrity and purity of an insolvency resolution process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC requires plans to reflect genuine corporate revival rather than serving as a mask for acquiring assets below fair value and exploiting clean-slate immunities under Section 32A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantial and sequential diminution of balance sheet assets without forensic audits or PUFE proceedings vitiates the quality of the information memorandum and invalidates commercial wisdom. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the resolution plan and ordered liquidation, and all three appeals are dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1061, 1043, and 946 of 2025 are dismissed, confirming the liquidation order.
summary: The Resolution Professional, Committee of Creditors, and Successful Resolution Applicant filed separate appeals against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated June 23, 2025, which rejected a CoC-approved resolution plan for Zep Infratech Ltd. and ordered liquidation. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority correctly noted that the corporate debtor's balance sheets showed unexplained, massive depletions of tangible assets and the disappearance of short-term borrowings exceeding Rs. 440 crores during the lookback period, without any forensic audit or PUFE proceedings initiated by the RP. The resolution process lacked transparency and integrity, and the plan served merely to acquire assets below market value while wiping out massive statutory liabilities. Consequently, all three appeals were dismissed, confirming the liquidation order.

case_title: Maximal Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ganga Ram Agarwal (RP) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Maximal Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (landowner / licensor, formerly Triveni Ferrous Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.), Respondent is Ganga Ram Agarwal (Resolution Professional of PAL Infrastructure & Developer Pvt. Ltd. - Corporate Debtor), along with intervenors (homebuyers) and Parcela Real Estate Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development agreement executed on 15.01.2008 granting development rights over 7.2431 acres (Sector 89, Faridabad) to PAL Infrastructure under license nos. 34-36 of 2007; corporate debtor constructed and allotted units to 664 homebuyers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (dispute over whether development rights constitute assets of the corporate debtor or were terminated in 2009). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Development agreement signed in 2008; alleged termination letter dated 17.06.2009; CIRP against PAL Infrastructure commenced on 05.09.2019; RP filed IA 5134/2020; Appellant filed IA 2729/2021 on 21.06.2021 seeking asset exclusion; Appellant transferred development rights to Parcela on 26.11.2022; NCLT passed common order on 05.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supreme Court order dated 05.05.2015 in Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 5/2015 and subsequent contempt order dated 24.04.2020 recognizing development rights; RERA and DTCP proceedings where appellant admitted transfer of development rights to developer companies; construction records showing 70% completion by corporate debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench disposed of IA 2729/2021 and IA 5134/2020 on 05.06.2025, refusing to exclude the project land from CIRP, leading to appeals by Maximal Infrastructure.
legal_issues: Whether development rights granted to a corporate debtor under a development agreement constitute assets of the corporate debtor under the IBC, and whether an alleged termination letter from 2009 (unproduced until 2024) is valid and effective.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Development rights and a bundle of interests over immovable property created in favour of a corporate debtor for consideration constitute "property" and "assets" under Sections 3(27), 18(1)(f), and 25(2)(a) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC prohibits the corporate debtor and landowners from alienating or disposing of corporate debtor assets during CIRP, rendering post-commencement transfer of development rights void and non-est. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admissions made by landowners before statutory authorities (RERA, DTCP) and the Supreme Court acknowledging continuous development rights estop them from later setting up a belated, unacted-upon 2009 termination claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly held that development rights vest in the corporate debtor as assets, dismissed the exclusion application, and ordered CIRP continuation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 987 & 988 of 2025 are dismissed. The appellant is saddled with a cost of Rs. 25 Lakhs payable to the CIRP account.
summary: Maximal Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated June 5, 2025, which dismissed its application to exclude project land (Sector 89, Faridabad) from the CIRP of PAL Infrastructure & Developer Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). The Appellant argued that development rights granted in 2008 had been automatically terminated via a letter dated June 17, 2009, due to cheque dishonor, and later transferred to Parcela Real Estate in 2022. The NCLAT held that the termination letter was a belated, unacted-upon fabrication, and the appellant had repeatedly admitted before RERA, DTCP, and the Supreme Court that development rights were held by the corporate debtor, which had completed 70% construction for 664 homebuyers. Furthermore, post-commencement transfer of development rights during CIRP was barred by Section 14. Consequently, the appeals were dismissed with costs.

case_title: Consortium of Shantech International Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Amit Chandrashekhar Poddar (RP of Unijules Life Sciences Ltd.) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Dissenting Financial Creditor (Satsai Finlease), Unsuccessful Resolution Applicants (Shantech International, E-hub), and suspended management; Respondents are Amit Chandrashekhar Poddar (Resolution Professional of Unijules Life Sciences Ltd.), S.S. Fabricators and Manufacturers Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA), and CoC members. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Unijules Life Sciences Ltd. admitted on 08.03.2019; second round of Form-G issued on 11.04.2024; resolution plans submitted by multiple PRAs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (resolution plan approval dispute). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved S.S. Fabricators' plan on 24.05.2025 with 98.54% vote share; RP filed plan approval application IA 67 of 2025 on 03.06.2025; NCLT approved plan on 13.11.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 3 rounds of negotiations held in 37th CoC meeting; e-voting extended up to 23.05.2025 within the outer deadline of 31.05.2025 fixed by NCLT on 06.05.2025; EPF dues escrow arrangement in plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the resolution plan submitted by S.S. Fabricators and dismissed objections by DFC and URA on 13.11.2025, leading to six connected appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the approval of a resolution plan by the CoC is vitiated by procedural irregularities such as extending e-voting timelines, escrowing EPF liabilities, capping CIRP costs, or refusing to adopt a Swiss Challenge Mechanism.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan with an overwhelming majority cannot be interfered with on grounds of alleged procedural irregularities unless there is a clear violation of Section 30(2) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Extending e-voting timelines within an overarching outer deadline fixed by the Adjudicating Authority does not vitiate voting results, and post-submission plan modifications are barred under Regulation 39(1A) of CIRP Regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Minority dissenting creditors and unsuccessful resolution applicants cannot challenge CoC-approved plans where statutory majority thresholds and minimum liquidation value entitlements are fully met. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly approved the resolution plan and rejected objections, and all six appeals are dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 02, 69, 71, 73, 89 & 205 of 2026 are dismissed with no orders as to costs.
summary: Multiple appeals were filed by dissenting financial creditors (Satsai Finlease), unsuccessful resolution applicants (Shantech, E-hub), and the suspended director challenging the NCLT Mumbai order dated November 13, 2025, which approved the resolution plan submitted by S.S. Fabricators and Manufacturers Pvt. Ltd. for Unijules Life Sciences Ltd. The Appellants alleged various procedural infractions, including extended e-voting timelines beyond May 20, 2025, capping of CIRP costs, and escrowing EPF dues. The NCLAT held that the e-voting completed within the overall deadline of May 31, 2025, and the CoC exercised its commercial wisdom with a 98.54% majority. The plan fully complied with Section 30(2) of the IBC, and minority dissenters or unsuccessful applicants had no vested right to demand a Swiss Challenge or overturn the CoC's commercial decision. Consequently, all six appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Shri Yarlagadda Krishna Mohan & Ors. vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are personal guarantors (Yarlagadda Krishna Mohan, Yarlagadda Padmavathi, and Yarlagadda Madhu Mohan), Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Shri Sivarama Prasad Bhamidi (Bankruptcy Trustee). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor M/s YKM Entertainment and Hotels Pvt. Ltd. availed financial assistance (totaling enhanced limits of Rs. 138.70 crores) secured by personal guarantees and mortgages executed by the Appellants vide Deed of Guarantee dated 27.10.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 29.11.2016; SARFAESI notices issued; OTS default occurred; Section 95 demand notice issued on 29.04.2022 for Rs. 271,37,80,931/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 95 petitions admitted on 27.02.2024 (appeals dismissed on 06.02.2025); RP filed report under Section 112 on 04.07.2024; NCLT granted liberty on 13.11.2024; Section 123 bankruptcy applications filed; NCLT passed bankruptcy orders on 27.02.2025 / 13.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Executed Guarantee Deed dated 27.10.2015; failure of personal guarantors to submit a repayment plan under Section 105 of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench allowed applications under Section 123 of the IBC on 13.11.2024/2025 initiating bankruptcy proceedings against the personal guarantors, leading to these appeals.
legal_issues: Whether bankruptcy proceedings under Section 123 of the IBC can be initiated against personal guarantors when they fail to submit a repayment plan under Section 105 during the personal insolvency resolution process.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Failure or omission by a personal debtor/guarantor to submit a repayment plan under Section 105 of the IBC during personal insolvency resolution amounts to a deemed rejection under Section 115, legally entitling creditors to file for bankruptcy under Chapter IV (Section 121/123). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Submission of a formal repayment plan under Section 105 is mandatory, and extra-statutory settlement proposals (such as OTS offers) cannot substitute for a statutory repayment plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Co-extensive liability under a continuous guarantee, combined with confirmed default and failure to place a repayment plan on record, justifies the automatic statutory progression to bankruptcy proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the personal guarantors failed to submit a repayment plan, the Adjudicating Authority correctly ordered bankruptcy proceedings, and the appeals are dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 627, 628, and 631 of 2025 are dismissed. All pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: Appellants, personal guarantors for M/s YKM Entertainment and Hotels Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Chennai orders initiating bankruptcy proceedings against them under Section 123 of the IBC. The Appellants argued that their debt computation was inflated and that they had previously engaged in OTS negotiations. The NCLAT held that the Appellants failed to submit a statutory repayment plan under Section 105 of the IBC during their personal insolvency resolution process. Under Section 115, such failure operates as a deemed rejection, automatically enabling creditors to trigger bankruptcy under Section 121. Consequently, the appeals were dismissed, upholding the initiation of bankruptcy proceedings.

case_title: Lorenzo Vitrified Tiles Limited vs. Committee of Creditors of Vrundavan Ceramic Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in CA No. 1950 is Lorenzo Vitrified Tiles Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant) and in CA No. 1952 is Arvind Gaudana (Resolution Professional), while Respondent No. 1 is the Committee of Creditors through State Bank of India (sole financial creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Vrundavan Ceramic Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying matter relates to the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the Corporate Debtor, where a resolution plan submitted by the SRA was approved by the CoC but subsequently rejected by the Adjudicating Authority. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CIRP was initiated upon a Section 7 application filed by the State Bank of India for debt and default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CD was admitted into CIRP on 21.01.2020; the CoC approved the resolution plan on 03.08.2021; the Adjudicating Authority remanded the plan on 08.11.2023 with a deadline of 30.11.2023; and the fresh approval application was filed/refiled after an inordinate delay, culminating in the impugned order dated 27.09.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence showed that the RP and CoC failed to convene meetings or file the revised plan within the timelines stipulated in the remand order, resulting in an 8-month delay before the refiling of the plan approval application. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority rejected the resolution plan and ordered liquidation under Section 33(1)(a) due to non-compliance with timelines, leading to the present appeals before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in rejecting the CoC-approved resolution plan and ordering liquidation due to delays in refiling post-remand, and whether the timelines prescribed in remand orders are mandatory.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The generalized legal principle established is that while revival of a corporate debtor is paramount, endless delays and failure by stakeholders to adhere to statutory or court-mandated timelines cannot be permitted at the cost of asset devaluation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted Sections 12 and 33 of the IBC, holding that expiration of timelines and gross negligence in prosecuting plan approvals warrant liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The legal standard used evaluated whether the delay was attributable to unavoidable litigation or sheer stakeholder lethargy. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals were dismissed, upholding the liquidation order and the adverse remarks against the Resolution Professional's conduct.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1950 of 2024 and 1952 of 2024 are dismissed with no order as to costs, and pending IAs are closed.
summary: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1950 of 2024 and No. 1952 of 2024 challenge the impugned order dated 27.09.2024 passed by the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench, which rejected the resolution plan submitted by Lorenzo Vitrified Tiles Limited and ordered the liquidation of Vrundavan Ceramic Private Limited. The Adjudicating Authority rejected the plan due to an inordinate delay of over eight months in refiling the plan following a previous remand order and strict failure to meet timelines. The NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's findings, emphasizing that endless delays and lackadaisical conduct by the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors cannot be condoned when asset value is rapidly deteriorating. Consequently, both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. vs. Halwasiya Developments Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants include Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor), CIS Infrastructure LLP, Dr. Shravan Kumar Vishnoi (Homebuyers' AR), and Ashok Kumar Gupta (Resolution Professional), while the main Respondent is Halwasiya Developments Pvt. Ltd. (Developer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor (Andes Town Planners Pvt. Ltd.) executed a loan agreement and mortgage deed with DHFL for Rs. 90 crores, and subsequently entered into a Development Management Agreement (DMA) and Consortium Agreement with Halwasiya for constructing the Ananta Residencies project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Piramal Capital and Housing Finance Limited initiated CIRP under Section 7 due to debt and default, with admitted claims totaling Rs. 2,25,04,42,092/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application was admitted on 02.03.2023; the RP filed IA 3739 of 2023 seeking possession and to stop construction; Halwasiya filed IA 5252 of 2023; and the NCLT passed a common order on 17.12.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unregistered DMA and Power of Attorney were executed without lender NOC, though construction was nearly 96% complete and mortgage charge covered the entire land and receivables. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT dismissed the RP's application under Section 19(2)/60(5) and allowed Halwasiya's application, prompting multiple appeals before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 19(2) and 60(5) by the Resolution Professional against a developer is maintainable, and whether a development agreement creates ownership rights or extinguishes the lender's mortgage over the project land.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Development rights acquired through an agreement constitute an asset of the developer, but do not confer ownership rights or extinguish prior registered mortgages and corporate ownership. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 18, 19, and 25 of the IBC empower the RP to take control of assets and demand cooperation and information from third parties associated with the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unregistered agreements cannot transfer immovable property title under the Transfer of Property and Registration Acts, and prior mortgages without NOC remain fully binding. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals were partly allowed, setting aside the NCLT's finding that the project became the developer's asset, upholding the maintainability of the RP's application for information, and confirming that the lender's mortgage remains intact.
operative_order: All appeals are partly allowed; the order dismissing IA 3739 of 2023 is set aside and the application is disposed of directing Halwasiya to provide all details and documents to the RP, while affirming Halwasiya's right to complete construction under supervision and confirming that the CD retains ownership and lenders hold continuing mortgage charges.
summary: These consolidated appeals challenge the common order dated 17.12.2024 passed by the NCLT, New Delhi, regarding the CIRP of Andes Town Planners Pvt. Ltd. The Adjudicating Authority had dismissed the Resolution Professional's application seeking possession and information from Halwasiya Developments Pvt. Ltd., holding that the development agreement made the project an asset of the developer. The NCLAT partly allowed the appeals, ruling that the RP's application under Section 19(2) and 60(5) was fully maintainable. The Appellate Tribunal clarified that while the developer could complete construction to protect homebuyers, it acquired no ownership rights through unregistered documents, prior lender mortgages remained intact, and the developer must provide all project information to the RP.

case_title: Express Resorts and Hotels Limited vs. Amit Jain, Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Express Resorts and Hotels Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant), Respondent No. 1 is Amit Jain (Resolution Professional), and other respondents include financial creditors, RARE Asset Reconstruction Limited, and suspended management. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor (Neesa Leisure Limited) underwent CIRP during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the SRA submitted a resolution plan with a plan value of Rs. 143.83 crores plus Rs. 250 crores in fresh capital expenditure. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CIRP was initiated on 26.04.2019 under Section 7 upon an application by ARCIL. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The EOI was issued in February 2020; the resolution plan was approved by the CoC with a 67.85% voting share on 19.10.2020; an LOI was issued on 07.11.2020; and the plan approval application (IA 851 of 2020) was rejected by the NCLT on 04.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The plan was approved by the CoC prior to the Rainbow Papers judgment, and the SRA voluntarily undertook to pay an additional Rs. 2.33 crores to cover proportionate secured statutory dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After previous rounds of litigation where NCLT remand orders were set aside by the NCLAT, the Adjudicating Authority finally rejected the resolution plan on multiple subjective grounds, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction in rejecting a CoC-approved resolution plan on subjective grounds without identifying any violation of Section 30(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is paramount and non-justiciable unless a clear violation of Section 30(2) is established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) mandates approval if Section 30(2) requirements are met, and subsequent judicial precedents like Rainbow Papers can be implemented without altering the plan's commercial framework when the SRA volunteers compliance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Subjective assumptions by the adjudicating authority regarding valuations, transparency, or negotiations cannot override the collective business decision of the CoC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was allowed, the NCLT's rejection order was set aside, and the resolution plan was approved.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 04.03.2024 is set aside, the resolution plan submitted by the SRA is approved, and the NCLT is directed to pass consequential orders within 15 days.
summary: This appeal challenges the order dated 04.03.2024 passed by the NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench, rejecting the resolution plan submitted by Express Resorts and Hotels Limited for Neesa Leisure Limited, which had been approved by the CoC with a 67.85% voting share in October 2020. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the plan on subjective grounds and assumptions without establishing any violation of Section 30(2) of the IBC. Noting that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is paramount and that the SRA voluntarily agreed to pay an additional Rs. 2.33 crores to cover secured statutory dues in line with the Rainbow Papers judgment, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order, and approved the resolution plan.

case_title: Chandra Shekhar Jha & Anr. vs. Religare Enterprises Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants include shareholders/creditors (Chandra Shekhar Jha and RHC Finance Pvt. Ltd.) and an execution decree holder (Daiichi Sankyo Company Ltd.), while Respondent No. 1 is Religare Enterprises Ltd. (Financial Creditor) and the Corporate Debtor is Ligare Aviation Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Religare Enterprises claimed a financial debt of Rs. 5.87 crores based on an MoU executed in 2009 by RAIML, under which Rs. 3.60 crores was disbursed to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 application was filed for non-payment of the claimed loan amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application was filed on 18.01.2021; the NCLT admitted the application on 18.07.2023; and the NCLAT stayed the order on 28.07.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements demonstrated that the Rs. 3.60 crores received by the Corporate Debtor was immediately transferred on the same day to Religare Finvest Ltd. (subsidiary of the financial creditor), forming part of a series of mirror transactions and financial layering across group entities, which were also the subject of FIR No. 50/2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority admitted Section 7 application, dismissing the corporate debtor's defense as moonshine, which led to appeals by shareholders and Daiichi Sankyo.
legal_issues: Whether a transaction involving immediate onward transfer of funds and financial layering between related group entities constitutes a genuine 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether the adjudicating authority must examine the true nature of the transaction.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transaction that is sham, collusive, or involves mere financial layering and round-tripping of funds without genuine disbursal for time value of money does not constitute a financial debt under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) requires actual disbursal against consideration for time value of money, necessitating a thorough examination of real transaction mechanics. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bank statements showing immediate same-day onward transfer of funds and contemporaneous balance denials rebut claims of genuine financial indebtedness. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals were allowed and the Section 7 application was dismissed because no genuine financial debt existed.
operative_order: Both appeals are allowed, the impugned order dated 18.07.2023 is set aside, and Section 7 application C.P. (IB) No. 2(PB)/2022 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: These appeals challenge the order dated 18.07.2023 passed by the NCLT, Principal Bench, New Delhi, admitting a Section 7 application filed by Religare Enterprises Ltd. against Ligare Aviation Ltd. The Appellants argued that the underlying transaction lacked the elements of a financial debt, as bank statements proved the disbursed amount was immediately transferred on the same day to a subsidiary of the financial creditor as part of round-tripping and financial layering. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority failed to examine the material evidence and true nature of the transaction. Finding that no genuine financial debt existed, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeals and dismissed the Section 7 application.

case_title: J & K Integrated Textiles Park Ltd. vs. Silklon Processors Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is J & K Integrated Textiles Park Ltd. (Financial Creditor) and the Respondents are Silklon Processors Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Corporate Debtors) along with Punjab National Bank and Sunder Lal Aggarwal as interveners. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under the Scheme for Integrated Textiles Parks (SITP), the Financial Creditor leased land and entered into loan agreements providing unsecured loans with 13% interest for building construction to nine industrial units (Corporate Debtors). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtors defaulted on lease rent, interest, and principal repayment towards the unsecured loans, leading to recall notices and dishonoured post-dated cheques. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall notices were issued on 22.04.2020; Section 7 applications were filed in December 2023; and the Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petitions and imposed penalties on 08.01.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, tripartite agreements, and NeSL records established the disbursal and default of financial debt, while Board resolutions authorized filing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the Section 7 applications and imposed a penalty of Rs. 25,00,000/- under Section 65 on both the Financial Creditor and the Corporate Debtors, prompting the present cross-appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 applications filed by the Financial Creditor were maintainable and supported by valid debt and default, and whether the imposition of penalties under Section 65 of the IBC was legally sustainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a financial debt and default are duly established through valid loan agreements and records, and no fraudulent intent is proven, a Section 7 application must be admitted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted Sections 7 and 65 of the IBC, holding that general board authorizations remain valid over time and that routine invocation of remedies cannot be penalized as malicious initiation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented loan agreements specifying unsecured loans with interest constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8), and statutory debt default cannot be overridden by collateral recovery proceedings like SARFAESI. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the dismissal orders, directed admission of the Section 7 applications, and quashed the Section 65 penalties.
operative_order: All 18 appeals are allowed; the impugned orders dated 08.01.2025 dismissing the Section 7 applications are set aside, the Adjudicating Authority is directed to admit the Section 7 applications within 30 days, and the penalties imposed under Section 65 are set aside.
summary: J & K Integrated Textiles Park Ltd. filed appeals against the NCLT Chandigarh Bench orders dismissing its Section 7 applications against nine corporate debtors and imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,00,000/- on each party under Section 65 of the IBC. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the transactions did not involve a financial debt, as the loan agreements explicitly provided for unsecured loans with interest. Furthermore, the appellate tribunal found no evidence of fraudulent or malicious intent to warrant Section 65 penalties and noted that prior SARFAESI proceedings by banks do not bar independent IBC remedies. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the dismissal and penalties, and directed the admission of the Section 7 applications.

case_title: Suraksha Realty Limited vs. Mr. Vithal M. Dahake (RP) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Suraksha Realty Limited (Financial Creditor/Debenture Holder) and Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Vithal M. Dahake (Resolution Professional of Radius Estate Projects Pvt. Ltd., the Corporate Debtor), with promoters as Respondents 2-5. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant subscribed to debentures worth Rs. 1,12,50,00,000/- under a Debenture Subscription Agreement (DSA) dated 18.12.2014, which contemplated creating a first charge over project assets. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to create the security within 30 days and instead created first charges in favor of Yes Bank (2015-2016) and DHFL (2018). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The DSA was executed on 18.12.2014; a registered Deed of Mortgage creating a second charge was executed on 29.07.2021; CIRP commenced on 06.09.2021; and the NCLT allowed the RP's avoidance application on 10.10.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The mortgage of July 2021 was executed barely two months before CIRP for antecedent debt without fresh value, elevating the Appellant from unsecured to secured status. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority held the mortgage to be a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the Code and directed release of the security interest, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a registered deed of mortgage executed within the look-back period for an antecedent debt, transforming an unsecured creditor into a secured creditor, constitutes a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A delayed perfection of security interest executed during the twilight look-back period for an antecedent debt that elevates an unsecured creditor's position under Section 53 constitutes a preferential transaction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 43 of the IBC deems a transfer preferential if it benefits a creditor for an antecedent debt, places them in a better position than under Section 53, and occurs within the look-back period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Seven years' delay in executing a mortgage after a contractual agreement, occurring immediately prior to CIRP without fresh value or ordinary course justification, establishes preference. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order avoiding the preferential mortgage transaction.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, and pending applications are closed.
summary: Suraksha Realty Limited appealed against an order dated 10.10.2025 passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench, which avoided a registered Deed of Mortgage dated 29.07.2021 as a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC. The Appellant had advanced Rs. 112.50 crores under a 2014 Debenture Subscription Agreement, but the mortgage securing the debt was executed only two months prior to the commencement of CIRP, long after the Corporate Debtor had created prior charges in favor of other banks. The NCLAT held that the transaction satisfied all statutory ingredients of a preferential transaction, as it secured an antecedent debt, elevated the Appellant's standing under Section 53, and occurred within the look-back period without being in the ordinary course of business. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Rakesh Dalpatram Panchal vs. Kisaan Steels Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Rakesh Dalpatram Panchal (Ex-Director of Gemini Engi. Fab. Pvt. Ltd., the Corporate Debtor), Respondent No. 1 is Kisaan Steels Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor and Operational Creditor entered into several purchase orders between December 2021 and June 2022 for the supply of forgings and tube sheets totaling Rs. 8.40 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding operational debt of Rs. 6,13,53,270/-, which was subsequently restricted to an undisputed amount of Rs. 3,97,44,173.70/- in the Section 9 petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A demand notice under Section 8 was issued on 01.07.2023; the corporate debtor replied on 14.07.2023; and the NCLT admitted the Section 9 application on 24.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Emails, including an email dated 01.11.2023 from the corporate debtor, acknowledged liability and promised payment subject to a consequence sheet. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 9 application, holding that no genuine pre-existing dispute existed, leading to the present appeal by the suspended director.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting a Section 9 application despite the corporate debtor's contentions of pre-existing disputes regarding delivery delays and defective goods.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an operational debt and default are established and an undisputed amount exceeding the statutory threshold is acknowledged without a bona fide pre-existing dispute, a Section 9 application must be admitted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC require dismissal only when a plausible, bona fide pre-existing dispute exists, rather than manufactured or conditional defenses. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Subsequent written communications acknowledging liability and confirming undisputed sums negate prior generalized claims of defects or delays. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, confirming the admission of the corporate debtor into CIRP under Section 9.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, related IAs are disposed of, and insolvency proceedings shall restart forthwith with no orders as to costs.
summary: Rakesh Dalpatram Panchal, ex-director of Gemini Engi. Fab. Private Limited, appealed against an order dated 24.03.2025 passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench admitting a Section 9 application filed by Kisaan Steels Pvt. Ltd. for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 3,97,44,173.70/-. The Appellant argued that pre-existing disputes regarding delivery timelines and product quality existed prior to the demand notice. The NCLAT held that the corporate debtor had unequivocally acknowledged the undisputed debt through subsequent communications and emails, and that the alleged disputes were spurious and conditional attempts to avoid payment. Consequently, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal and upheld the initiation of CIRP.

case_title: Mr. Rajesh Kaimal vs. Prabhat Ranjan Singh & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Rajesh Kaimal (Suspended Director of Equinox India Developments Ltd., formerly Indiabulls Real Estate Ltd.), and the Respondents are Prabhat Ranjan Singh (RP) and Canara Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Canara Bank extended term loans to the principal borrower (Sinnar Thermal Power Ltd.), for which a corporate guarantee dated 30.06.2010 was executed by the Corporate Debtor requiring timely equity infusion, which was later substituted by a 2012 guarantee. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The principal borrower's account became NPA on 28.09.2017, and the financial creditor issued a loan recall notice invoking the guarantee on 30.09.2020 for Rs. 202,03,39,436/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee invoked on 30.09.2020 with a 3-day payment window; Section 7 application filed in January 2025; and admitted by NCLT on 09.12.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The guarantee instrument obliged the guarantor only to infuse equity rather than repay principal debt, and a parallel Section 7 petition against another guarantor (RattanIndia Enterprises) was dismissed by the same bench on the same date. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted Canara Bank's Section 7 application, prompting the suspended director to file the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate guarantee limited to equity infusion constitutes a financial debt enforceable for principal loan repayment, whether invocation during the Section 10A period bars the application, and whether divergent rulings by the same bench on identical facts are sustainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate guarantee that solely obligates a guarantor to punctually infuse equity share capital upon default does not constitute a direct financial debt for principal loan repayment, and invocation during the Section 10A period bars initiation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A bars applications where default occurs during the prohibited window, and guarantor default arises strictly upon valid invocation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Guarantee terms restricted to equity contribution cannot be expanded to direct debt repayment without specific debt-assumption clauses. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the Section 7 admission order.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 09.12.2025 is set aside, and Section 7 petition C.P. (IB) No. 317 of 2025 is dismissed.
summary: Rajesh Kaimal, suspended director of Equinox India Developments Ltd. (formerly Indiabulls Real Estate Ltd.), appealed against an order dated 09.12.2025 passed by the NCLT New Delhi Bench admitting a Section 7 application filed by Canara Bank. The Appellant argued that the 2010 corporate guarantee only required equity infusion and did not constitute a guarantee for debt repayment, that the guarantee invocation on 30.09.2020 fell squarely within the Section 10A exclusion period, and that the same bench had dismissed a parallel Section 7 petition against another guarantor on the same day. The NCLAT upheld these contentions, holding that the guarantee did not create a direct financial debt for loan repayment and that the petition was barred under Section 10A. Accordingly, the appeal was allowed and the Section 7 application was dismissed.

case_title: State Tax Officer vs. Shri Keyur J. Shah, Liquidator of Gangotri Glazed Tiles Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the State Tax Officer, Gujarat, and Respondents include Shri Keyur J. Shah (Liquidator of Gangotri Glazed Tiles Pvt. Ltd.) and Rajkot Nagarik Sahakari Bank Limited (Secured Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor incurred tax arrears under GVAT and CST Acts for AY 2010-2013, while securing financial credit from the Bank in September 2012 with a registered charge. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Tax dues amounted to over Rs. 31.94 crores, while the bank's secured debt stood at Rs. 9.22 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bank charge registered on 26.09.2012; State Tax lien communicated in August 2019; CIRP initiated on 27.01.2020; liquidation ordered on 02.11.2020; and NCLT Ahmedabad passed the impugned order on 30.07.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The financial creditor registered its charge with ROC in 2012 and elected to realize security under Section 52(1)(b) of the IBC, whereas the State Tax Department's subsequent statutory charge was created in 2019 and not registered with ROC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad Bench allowed the secured financial creditor's application directing the State Tax Department to release its charge, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a subsequent statutory tax charge created by operation of law overrides a prior registered security interest created in favor of a financial creditor under the IBC liquidation framework.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A prior registered security interest created in favor of a financial creditor under the Companies Act prevails in chronological priority over a subsequent statutory tax charge or lien created by operation of law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 52 of the IBC, a secured creditor exercising its right to realize security outside the liquidation estate is entitled to precedence over subsequent statutory claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Chronological priority of charge registration and perfection determines the distribution order among competing secured interests. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT order directing release of the state tax charge in favor of the prior registered secured creditor.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 30.07.2024 is upheld, and the liquidator's bonafide actions are vindicated with adverse observations expunged. No orders as to costs.
summary: The State Tax Officer, Gujarat, appealed against an order dated 30.07.2024 passed by the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench directing the department to release its charge over land belonging to Gangotri Glazed Tiles Private Limited in favor of Rajkot Nagarik Sahakari Bank Limited. The Appellant argued that its statutory first charge under Section 48 of the GVAT Act took precedence. The NCLAT held that while the tax department qualified as a secured operational creditor, its statutory charge created in 2019 could not override a prior registered security interest created in favor of the financial creditor in 2012, particularly when the bank had validly opted to realize its security under Section 52 of the IBC. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed and the NCLT order was upheld.

case_title: The State Tax Officer vs. Jaykumar P. Arlani & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the State Tax Officer, Gujarat, and Respondents include Jaykumar P. Arlani (Liquidator of Shree Raghuvanshi Fibres Pvt. Ltd.), Bank of Baroda, and Rama Agri Enterprise LLP (Auction Purchaser). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor incurred tax arrears under the GVAT Act and CST Act for assessment years 2014-2015 to 2017-2018, while Bank of Baroda held a mortgage security interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total tax claim was approximately Rs. 43.45 crores (comprising VAT and CST components), and assets were sold for Rs. 9.45 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.02.2020; liquidation ordered on 30.08.2022; assets sold on 09.01.2023; sale proceeds distributed to Bank of Baroda on 24.04.2023; and NCLT ordered dissolution on 19.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appellant filed claims in Form B and Form C indicating 'NA' in security columns but contemporaneously requested statutory first charge under Section 48 of the GVAT Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected the appellant's claim to be treated as a secured creditor during dissolution, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether statutory tax dues under the GVAT Act backed by a first charge under Section 48 qualify the state tax department as a secured operational creditor entitled to priority under Section 53 of the IBC, and whether CST dues enjoy similar status.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge created under Section 48 of the GVAT Act operates by law upon assessment, making the state tax department a secured operational creditor for VAT dues, whereas CST dues do not enjoy statutory first charge status. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 48 of the GVAT Act creates a statutory first charge without requiring formal contract or registration, while general common law crown debt principles do not override statutory liquidation waterfalls. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of statutory first charge is established by the assessment order itself under the state enactment, and non-disclosure in claim forms does not waive rights if contemporaneous notices asserting statutory charge were given. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, holding that the appellant is entitled to be treated as a secured operational creditor for its VAT component and directing the liquidator to recall funds from the bank for redistribution.
operative_order: The appeal is partly allowed; the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 19.02.2025 is modified to hold that the appellant is entitled to be treated as a secured operational creditor for its VAT dues (and operational creditor for CST dues), and the liquidator is directed to recall necessary funds from the third respondent bank to satisfy the appellant. Confirmed as to the rest with no costs.
summary: The State Tax Officer, Gujarat, appealed against an order dated 19.02.2025 passed by the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench ordering dissolution of Shree Raghuvanshi Fibres Pvt. Ltd. post-liquidation without recognizing the appellant as a secured creditor. The NCLAT held that by virtue of Section 48 of the GVAT Act, a statutory first charge is created upon assessment, making the appellant a secured operational creditor for its VAT dues (though not for CST dues). The appellate tribunal noted that although the appellant indicated 'NA' in the claim form, it had contemporaneously communicated its claim of statutory charge to the liquidator. Consequently, the NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, directing the liquidator to recall funds from Bank of Baroda to satisfy the appellant's secured VAT dues in accordance with Section 53.

case_title: Shefali Agrawal vs. M/s Stone Age Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Shefali Agrawal (shareholder and former whole-time director) and the Respondents are M/s Stone Age Pvt. Ltd. and its directors/shareholders including Sanjeev Agarwal (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter relates to an enterprise engaged in granite and stone business where the appellant held shares and was removed from directorship followed by share dilution. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Company Law oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant removed from directorship on 25.07.2012; share dilutions occurred in July 2013 and July 2017; company petition filed on 15.10.2018; NCLT judgment rendered on 12.10.2023; and NCLAT judgment pronounced on 14.05.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Legal notices and correspondence from January 2013 established that the appellant had full knowledge of her retirement and share dilution at the relevant time. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Jaipur Bench decided the company petition, holding certain dilutions illegal while ruling that claims pertaining to 2012-2013 were barred by limitation, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the appellant's claims regarding removal from directorship and share dilution occurring in 2012-2013 were barred by limitation, and whether the valuation directions given by the Adjudicating Authority were sustainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Successive violations do not give rise to a fresh cause of action under Article 113 of the Limitation Act, and limitation commences once a party becomes aware of antecedent facts necessary to pursue legal proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are governed by the three-year limitation period under Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented legal notices sent by the appellant in January 2013 conclusively proved her contemporaneous knowledge of the corporate actions complained of. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was dismissed because the challenges to acts occurring in 2012-2013 were barred by limitation and no substantive grounds were raised against the independent valuation mechanism.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed and pending applications are disposed of.
summary: Shefali Agrawal appealed against the order dated 12.10.2023 passed by the NCLT Jaipur Bench in a petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging oppression and mismanagement. The Appellant challenged her removal from directorship in 2012 and subsequent share dilutions in 2013. The NCLAT held that the appellant had full contemporaneous knowledge of these events, as evidenced by her legal notice dated 05.01.2013, making her petition filed in October 2018 barred by the three-year limitation period. Furthermore, the appellate tribunal found no grounds to interfere with the independent share valuation mechanism ordered by the NCLT. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Bindu Kapoor (Suspended Director, Bliss Abode Pvt. Ltd. & Bliss House Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Sapan Mohan Garg (IRP) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Bindu Kapoor (Suspended Director of Bliss Abode Pvt. Ltd. and Bliss House Pvt. Ltd.) and the Respondents include Sapan Mohan Garg (IRP) and JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction Private Limited (Financial Creditor/Assignee of Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate debtors entered into multiple loan agreements totaling hundreds of crores with Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd., secured by personal guarantees of the appellant and her husband Rana Kapoor, hypothecation, and mortgage of properties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following the arrest of guarantor Rana Kapoor, lenders issued loan recall notices on 09.03.2020 demanding over Rs. 388 crores and Rs. 189 crores respectively, which went unpaid. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall notice issued on 09.03.2020; arbitral awards rendered in favor of lenders on 28.02.2023; Section 7 applications filed in July and October 2025; and NCLT admitted the applications on 15.12.2025 and 21.01.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, material adverse effect clauses invoked due to criminal investigations and arrest of the guarantor, and binding arbitral awards established debt and default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted both Section 7 applications, leading to the present appeals by the suspended director.
legal_issues: Whether loan recall notices issued on grounds of material adverse effect following a guarantor's arrest constitute valid defaults, and whether pending Section 34 proceedings against an arbitral award bar the initiation of Section 7 insolvency proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a financial debt and default are established through valid loan agreements and recall notices or arbitral awards, admission of a Section 7 application is mandatory under the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC operates independently of arbitration execution proceedings or pending Section 34 challenges against arbitral awards, which provide a fresh period of limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Material adverse effect clauses validly permit loan recall upon events severely prejudicing the financial capacity or backing of obligors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals were dismissed, upholding the admission of the corporate debtors into CIRP as debt and default were conclusively proved.
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed with parties bearing their own costs.
summary: Bindu Kapoor, suspended director of Bliss Abode Pvt. Ltd. and Bliss House Pvt. Ltd., appealed against orders dated 15.12.2025 and 21.01.2026 passed by the NCLT New Delhi Bench admitting Section 7 applications filed by JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant argued that loans were prematurely recalled following her husband's arrest, that default was un-crystallized due to pending Section 34 petitions against arbitral awards, and that Section 7 was being used for execution. The NCLAT held that loan recall notices were validly issued under material adverse effect clauses, that arbitral awards and default on recall notices provided independent bases and fresh limitation, and that admission under Section 7 is mandatory once debt and default are proved. Consequently, both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: FINVIN Investor Private Limited & Orix Leasing and Financial Services India Limited vs. Palak S. Desai (Liquidator of JSK Marketing Limited) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are FINVIN Investor Pvt. Ltd. (assignee of the CD) and Orix Leasing and Financial Services India Limited (lessor), while Respondents include Palak S. Desai (Liquidator of JSK Marketing Limited), Pratiksha Tradelinks (supplier), and suspended directors (Kunal Jiwarajka & Ors.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Orix Leasing executed a Master Lease Agreement (MLA) on 07.09.2018 financing equipment purchases for JSK Marketing Ltd., backed by a security deposit of Rs. 74,49,947/- and personal guarantees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate debtor defaulted on lease rentals, prompting Orix Leasing to issue a demand notice on 06.08.2019, terminate the lease, and forfeit the security deposit. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MLA executed on 07.09.2018; demand notice on 06.08.2019; CIRP initiated on 23.09.2019; security deposit adjusted during October 2019; and NCLT passed the impugned order on 04.06.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The liquidator filed IA 1319 of 2020 under Sections 43 and 66 alleging missing machinery and fraudulent lease financing, while Orix Leasing produced invoices, delivery receipts, and E-way bills at the appellate stage. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the liquidator's avoidance application but held the MLA to be fraudulent and directed recovery of lease rentals and contributions from Orix Leasing and directors, leading to cross-appeals.
legal_issues: Whether a third-party lessor can be held liable for fraudulent trading under Section 66 of the IBC, and whether an adjustment of security deposits during the moratorium period is void without fresh adjudication on the genuineness of lease transactions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 66(1) of the IBC permits contribution orders against any person knowingly party to fraudulent trading, but third-party liability requires rigorous evaluation of genuine supply documentation and factual context. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Forfeiture or adjustment of security deposits during the operation of the moratorium under Section 14 is prohibited, but consequential restitution requires proper composite proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appellate introduction of foundational supply invoices, E-way bills, and delivery receipts necessitates a remand for de novo adjudication when untested by the adjudicating authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals were allowed, the impugned order was set aside, and the matter was remanded to the Adjudicating Authority for fresh consideration with liberty to tender evidence.
operative_order: Both appeals are disposed of; the impugned order dated 04.06.2024 is set aside, IA No. 1319 of 2020 is revived on the board of the Adjudicating Authority for fresh disposal within two months from appearance on 01.07.2026 with no order as to costs.
summary: FINVIN Investor Pvt. Ltd. and Orix Leasing and Financial Services India Limited filed cross-appeals against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 04.06.2024 passed in IA 1319 of 2020 under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC. The NCLT had rejected the liquidator's application while paradoxically holding the Master Lease Agreement to be fraudulent and directing recovery against Orix Leasing and the directors. The NCLAT noted that new evidentiary documents, such as supply invoices, delivery receipts, and E-way bills, were produced at the appellate stage and had not been considered by the Adjudicating Authority. Consequently, the appellate tribunal set aside the impugned order, remanded the matter back for fresh adjudication, and kept all issues, including third-party liability under Section 66, open.

case_title: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Jyoti Structures Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Lender Banks (SBI, Bank of India, Canara Bank, ICICI Bank, Indian Bank, Union Bank of India) and the Respondents are Jyoti Structures Limited (Corporate Debtor) along with its shareholders (Abhinav Angirish and Sharad Sanghi). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Following the approval of the resolution plan on 27.03.2019 and the NFB Agreement, lender banks were required to roll over and issue non-fund based facilities (Bank Guarantees/Letters of Credit) upon the Closing Date (09.11.2021). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Contempt proceedings arising from alleged non-compliance with NCLT and NCLAT orders directing release of NFB limits). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved on 27.03.2019; Closing Date achieved on 09.11.2021; NCLT order passed on 20.08.2024; NCLAT confirmation on 09.12.2024; contempt applications filed in October 2025; and NCLT passed the impugned contempt order on 16.02.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lender banks issued fresh sanction letters containing standard banking and project appraisal conditions, which the corporate debtor rejected, prompting contempt applications. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench disposed of contempt applications by directing the banks to release rolled-over limits within one month, failing which officers would face one day simple imprisonment, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can impose civil imprisonment for contempt without recording prior prima facie satisfaction, framing precise charges, issuing show-cause notices to specific individuals, and whether issuing conditional sanction letters constitutes willful disobedience.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Contempt proceedings are quasi-criminal in nature and mandatorily require a two-stage process comprising recording of prima facie satisfaction of willful disobedience, framing precise charges against specific named individuals, and issuing show-cause notices before imposing penal consequences. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act and NCLT rules require adherence to principles of natural justice and personal liberty safeguards, barring nameless or composite corporate imprisonment orders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Issuing conditional sanction letters under standard banking norms and project appraisal provisions in the absence of contumacious defiance does not establish wilful disobedience. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals were allowed, the contempt order imposing imprisonment was set aside, and a structured communication mechanism was established for releasing NFB limits.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned contempt order dated 16.02.2026 is set aside, and liberty is granted for formal written communication of requests and responses regarding NFB limit disbursal with a mechanism for reviving contempt applications if necessary.
summary: State Bank of India and five other banks appealed against an order dated 16.02.2026 passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench in contempt applications filed by Jyoti Structures Ltd. and its shareholders directing banks to release rolled-over Bank Guarantee limits within one month or face civil imprisonment. The NCLAT held that the contempt order was vitiated by procedural irregularities, as the Adjudicating Authority failed to record prior prima facie satisfaction, frame precise charges, issue show-cause notices, or identify specific individual contemnors. Furthermore, the banks' issuance of conditional sanction letters under project appraisal clauses did not constitute willful disobedience. Consequently, the appellate tribunal allowed the appeal, set aside the contempt order, and established a procedural mechanism for processing facility requests.

case_title: M/s Dharampal Premchand Ltd. vs. Jitendra Bhandari (SRA) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Dharampal Premchand Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and Respondents include Jitendra Bhandari (Successful Resolution Applicant), Manoj Kumar Mishra (Resolution Professional), and Trimurti Foodtech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant entered into a Contract Manufacturing and Packaging Agreement and an Equipment Lease Agreement with the Corporate Debtor in August 2014, which the appellant prematurely terminated in December 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The appellant claimed Rs. 6,81,21,070/- as an operational creditor during CIRP, while the corporate debtor raised a counter-claim of approximately Rs. 55.68 crores for alleged production breaches. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 11.08.2021; claim filed on 13.09.2021; RP issued legal notice treating claim as contingent in April 2022; resolution plan approved on 31.03.2023; plan successfully implemented and monitoring committee dissolved on 29.08.2024; and NCLT dismissed the recall application on 16.09.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Contemporaneous emails, CoC minutes, information memorandums, and confirmatory letters established that the appellant's claim was consistently classified and disclosed as contingent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dismissed IA 4588 of 2024 filed by the appellant seeking recall of the resolution plan approval order, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor with a disputed and contingent claim is entitled to notice under Section 24(3)(c) of the IBC, and whether an approved and successfully implemented resolution plan can be recalled on the basis of unadjudicated pre-CIRP contractual disputes.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor whose claim is genuinely disputed and classified as contingent pending reciprocal counter-claims is not an admitted operational creditor entitled to CoC meeting notices under Section 24(3)(c), and successfully implemented resolution plans cannot be reopened for pre-CIRP contractual disputes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Claim verification under CIRP permits resolution professionals to classify claims as contingent when substantial unadjudicated cross-claims exist, without constituting procedural fraud or vitiating the process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prolonged silence and acquiescence throughout the CIRP process after receiving explicit notice of contingent classification preclude a creditor from seeking plan recall post-implementation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was dismissed as the appellant failed to establish any fraud, material irregularity, or violation of mandatory provisions warranting interference with a successfully implemented resolution plan.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs and pending IAs are closed.
summary: M/s Dharampal Premchand Ltd. appealed against an order dated 16.09.2025 passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissing its application seeking recall of an order approving the resolution plan for Trimurti Foodtech Ltd. The Appellant argued that its operational claim of Rs. 6.81 crores was wrongfully converted into a contingent claim to deny it CoC notices under Section 24(3)(c), and that its leased machinery was unlawfully absorbed. The NCLAT held that because substantial reciprocal counter-claims exceeding Rs. 55 crores existed, the resolution professional was fully justified in classifying the appellant's claim as contingent. Furthermore, the appellant had full knowledge of this classification during CIRP but remained silent until after the resolution plan was successfully implemented. Consequently, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies & Anr. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are industry associations (Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies and Association of Distillers, Brewers and Vintners of India), and Respondents are the Competition Commission of India (CCI), Kerala State Beverages Corporation (KSBC), and Travancore Sugar and Chemicals Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: KSBC holds a monopsony position in wholesale procurement and distribution of branded alcoholic beverages in Kerala under the Foreign Liquor Rules, 1953, and procures liquor from private and government distillers via rate contracts and tenders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Competition law appeal challenging the closure of information regarding abuse of dominance). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed on 29.04.2020; CCI closed the information under Section 26(2) on 21.10.2021; and NCLAT pronounced judgment on 20.05.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The information alleged unilateral price fixation, arbitrary tender clauses, preferential treatment of state-owned Jawan Rum (Respondent No. 3), discriminatory cash discounts, and unloading charges, but lacked concrete empirical data or cost proof. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The CCI closed Case No. 10 of 2021 at the prima facie stage under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act, leading to the present appeal before the NCLAT.
