legal_issues: Whether the Competition Commission of India erred in closing information under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act without directing an investigation into alleged abuse of dominant position and preferential treatment by a state liquor corporation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To trigger an investigation under Section 26(1) of the Competition Act, an informant must furnish complete information and adequate material establishing a prima facie case of contravention and resultant market harm, rather than speculative or unsubstantiated allegations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 26(2) empowers the CCI to close an information forthwith if no prima facie case is made out after a summary inquiry. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: General sample cost cards and assertions without actual financial data, market exit evidence, or proof of competitive distortion fail to meet the threshold of a prima facie case. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was dismissed as the CCI correctly formed an objective prima facie opinion closing the information due to lack of substantive evidence.
operative_order: The appeal fails and stands rejected with no order as to costs and pending IAs closed.
summary: Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies and another appealed against an order dated 21.10.2021 passed by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) in Case No. 10 of 2021 closing information filed against Kerala State Beverages Corporation (KSBC) and Travancore Sugar and Chemicals Limited under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act. The Appellants alleged abuse of monopsony dominance, unilateral price fixation, and preferential treatment of the state-owned 'Jawan Rum' brand. The NCLAT held that the CCI was fully justified in closing the information at the threshold stage, as the appellants failed to provide concrete empirical data, cost proof, or evidence of market distortion to establish a prima facie case. Consequently, the competition appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Aidem Ventures Pvt. Ltd. vs. News 24 Broadcast India Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Aidem Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and the Respondents are Skyline Radio Network Ltd. (formerly B.A.G. Infotainment Pvt. Ltd.), News 24 Broadcast India Ltd. (formerly B.A.G. Newsline Network Ltd.), and E24 Glamour Ltd. (formerly B.A.G. Glamour Pvt. Ltd.) (Corporate Debtors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreements were entered into on 22.04.2010 appointing the Appellant as the exclusive representative for marketing and selling available advertising airtime options for the television channel 'News24' on a tiered commission structure. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed unpaid operational debt towards accrued commissions amounting to Rs. 43,71,768/-, Rs. 8,69,345/-, and Rs. 23,08,627/- from the respective corporate debtors, which remained unpaid upon collection. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding-up petitions under Sections 433, 434, and 439 of the Companies Act, 1956 were instituted before the High Court of Delhi in 2013 (CP Nos. 451/2013, 429/2013, 450/2013); transferred by the High Court to NCLT on 19.10.2023; and Form 5 was filed following the NCLT order dated 18.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Exclusive representation agreements dated 22.04.2010, billing and collection statements, and lack of any contractual clause or admission supporting the Appellant's claim for 24% per annum interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The High Court of Delhi transferred the winding-up proceedings to the NCLT under Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013; the NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, dismissed the converted Section 9 petitions on 13.02.2026 on the ground of pre-existing disputes, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether winding-up petitions transferred from the High Court to the NCLT and converted to Section 9 applications under Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013 must satisfy the enhanced pecuniary threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC as applicable on the date of consideration, and whether unagreed interest can be added to meet the threshold.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Winding-up petitions transferred from a High Court to the NCLT that are converted into applications for corporate insolvency resolution process must independently satisfy all statutory prerequisites under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, including the prevailing minimum pecuniary threshold under Section 4 on the date of consideration, and cannot be automatically admitted based on pre-transfer status. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Section 434(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that transferred winding-up proceedings shall be dealt with by the Tribunal as applications for initiation of CIRP under the Code, meaning the amended Section 4 threshold (Rs. 1 Crore) applies on the date of adjudication rather than the historical threshold at the time of initial filing before the High Court. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of an explicit contractual agreement or documentary proof evidencing acceptance of interest, unilateral claims of penal interest cannot be clubbed with operational debt to artificially satisfy the statutory threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals were dismissed as the operational debt claimed fell below the mandatory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC, rendering the Section 9 petitions legally unmaintainable.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed as lacking merit, confirming the dismissal of the Section 9 petitions with no order as to costs, and all pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: Aidem Ventures Pvt. Ltd. filed appeals challenging the common order dated 13.02.2026 passed by the NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, which dismissed its Section 9 applications against Skyline Radio Network Ltd., E24 Glamour Ltd., and News 24 Broadcast India Ltd. The proceedings originated as 2013 winding-up petitions before the Delhi High Court for unpaid advertising commissions and were transferred to the NCLT in 2023 under Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLAT held that transferred proceedings treated as Section 9 applications must satisfy the amended Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore. Since the claimed debts were below Rs. 1 Crore and unagreed interest could not be added, the appeals were dismissed as unmaintainable.

case_title: Mr. Rajender Prasad Mittal vs. M/s Jaikrishan Estates Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Rajender Prasad Mittal (erstwhile Director and Shareholder claiming as Financial Creditor), and the Respondent is M/s Jaikrishan Estates Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant advanced funds totaling Rs. 6,86,44,042/- from his Axis Bank personal account to the Corporate Debtor during FY 2014-15 to meet working capital requirements for real estate development projects. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor made partial repayments totaling Rs. 3 Crores, leaving an outstanding principal default balance of Rs. 3,86,44,042/-, with a formal legal demand notice issued on 22.10.2021 demanding repayment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursed in FY 2014-15; demand notice issued on 22.10.2021; Respondent replied on 20.12.2021; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 850/ND/2024 filed in 2024; and NCLT dismissed it on 16.01.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Axis Bank account statements showing fund transfers; Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheets for FY 2016-17, 2018-19, 2020-21, and 2022-23 recording the debt under 'long term borrowings'; reply to demand notice admitting working capital infusion; and a gift deed dated 19.07.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected the Section 7 petition at the threshold without issuing notice to the Respondent, holding that the interest-free working capital advance did not qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8), leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether interest-free advances infused by a director to meet working capital requirements and recorded as long-term borrowings in audited balance sheets constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the Section 7 petition without calling for a reply from the corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Interest-free advances provided by a stakeholder or director to fund working capital requirements have the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, and acknowledgment under long-term borrowings in audited financial statements serves as prima facie evidence of debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) does not mandate that a financial debt must carry interest, as the phrase 'interest, if any' indicates that interest-free loans advanced to sustain corporate operations qualify as financial debt if they possess the commercial effect of borrowing. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where conflicting instruments such as share purchase agreements or assignment gift deeds raise questions regarding the true character of the debt alongside balance sheet admissions, summary rejection without issuing notice and examining the debtor's formal reply is impermissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the Section 7 petition at the threshold without calling for a reply to properly evaluate the nature and enforceability of the debt, necessitating a remand for adjudication on merits.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, the impugned order dated 16.01.2025 is set aside, the matter is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the Section 7 petition on merits after calling for the Respondent's reply, and all pending IAs are disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Mr. Rajender Prasad Mittal, an erstwhile director and shareholder, appealed against an order dated 16.01.2025 passed by the NCLT New Delhi Bench rejecting his Section 7 petition against M/s Jaikrishan Estates Private Limited. The Appellant sought CIRP initiation for an unpaid interest-free advance of Rs. 3.86 Crores for working capital, recorded in the corporate debtor's balance sheets as long-term borrowings. The NCLT dismissed the petition at the pre-notice stage, holding the advance was not a financial debt. The NCLAT held that interest-free director advances can constitute financial debt having the commercial effect of borrowing, and the NCLT erred in dismissing the petition without calling for a reply. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the rejection and remanded the matter for adjudication on merits.

case_title: Ingram Micro India Private Limited vs. Bathla Teletech Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ingram Micro India Private Limited (Operational Creditor and authorised distributor of Apple products), and the Respondent is Bathla Teletech Private Limited (Corporate Debtor and reseller)[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of electronic goods including iPhone 11, iPhone 12, and iPads pursuant to Standard Sales Terms and Conditions accepted on 25.02.2021[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on unpaid invoices dated 03.03.2021 to 16.03.2021 amounting to principal sum of Rs. 5,39,20,029/- plus interest totaling Rs. 5,70,79,189.27/-, with the default date falling due on 11.06.2021[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices issued between 03.03.2021 and 16.03.2021; two post-dated cheques dated 24.05.2021 were returned dishonoured on 28.05.2021; Section 138 NI Act notice issued on 02.06.2021 and replied to on 21.06.2021; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 07.08.2021 (unreplied); Section 9 petition filed on 24.09.2021[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Stamped balance confirmation dated 30.09.2020; dishonoured cheques of Rs. 5.39 crores; emails dated 13.05.2021 and 17.05.2021 acknowledging payables; and unverified counterclaims regarding 2018 iPhone 8 inventory and backend discounts from Apple[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Court V, New Delhi rejected CP IB No. 629/(ND)/2021 on 03.12.2024 on grounds of pre-existing dispute based on reply to Section 138 notice and pending arbitration with Apple[cite: 35].
legal_issues: Whether counterclaims regarding older separate inventory and backend discounts raised for the first time in response to a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act notice constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and 9 of the IBC to bar CIRP admission[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Counterclaims and disputes raised for the first time in response to a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act notice after the dishonour of cheques, absent prior contemporaneous objection to supplies or invoices, constitute a moonshine defence and do not amount to a genuine pre-existing dispute under the IBC[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 8 and 9 require a plausible, bona fide dispute existing prior to the demand notice; the issuance of cheques constitutes an acknowledgment of debt, and disputes with third-party manufacturers cannot be telescoped to create a dispute against an independent distributor[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous email admissions acknowledging liabilities and the issuance of post-dated cheques negate subsequent assertions of defect or dispute relating to separate historical transactions[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in finding a pre-existing dispute; the operational debt and default were conclusively proved, warranting admission under Section 9 failing payment within 30 days[cite: 35].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 03.12.2024 is set aside, and the Respondent is granted 30 days to discharge the debt of Rs. 5,70,79,189.27/-, failing which the Adjudicating Authority shall pass an order admitting the Section 9 application[cite: 35].
summary: Ingram Micro India Private Limited appealed against an order dated 03.12.2024 passed by the NCLT New Delhi Bench rejecting its Section 9 application against Bathla Teletech Private Limited for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 5,70,79,189.27/- arising from supplies of Apple products[cite: 35]. The NCLT had rejected the petition on the ground of a pre-existing dispute based on the corporate debtor's reply to a Section 138 NI Act notice and ongoing arbitration proceedings between the debtor and Apple India[cite: 35]. The NCLAT set aside the rejection, ruling that dishonoured cheques and contemporaneous emails proved an undisputed debt[cite: 35]. Counterclaims raised belatedly in Section 138 proceedings regarding older 2018 stock were held to be moonshine defences[cite: 35]. The appeal was allowed, granting 30 days to pay before CIRP admission[cite: 35].

case_title: Vedanta Limited vs. Bhuvan Madan, Resolution Professional of Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Vedanta Limited (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Bhuvan Madan (Resolution Professional of Jaiprakash Associates Ltd., Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors; Respondent No. 3 is Adani Enterprises Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 36]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Jaiprakash Associates Ltd., where resolution applicants participated in a Challenge Process conducted under RFRP and Process Note terms to submit binding resolution plans[cite: 36]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated under Section 7 by ICICI Bank on 03.06.2024; liquidation value of the CD was Rs. 15,799 crores; Appellant's final plan offered gross value of Rs. 17,926 crores and NPV of Rs. 12,505.85 crores; SRA's plan offered Rs. 14,535 crores with upfront cash of Rs. 6,005 crores[cite: 36]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form G published 10.01.2025; RFRP issued 24.04.2025; Challenge Process held 05.09.2025; final signed plans submitted 14.10.2025; 23rd CoC meeting held 07.11.2025; Appellant submitted Addendum on 08.11.2025; CoC rejected Addendum on 14.11.2025; CoC approved SRA plan with 93.81% votes on 18.11.2025; NCLT approved plan on 17.03.2026[cite: 36]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BDO evaluation report showing SRA scored 89.76/100 while Appellant scored 75.60/100 due to lower upfront cash (Rs. 3,770 cr vs Rs. 6,005 cr); Process Note clauses 13.9, 13.19, and 14.2(xv) barring modifications after challenge closure[cite: 36]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench on 17.03.2026 dismissed Appellant's IA No. 01/2026 challenging the CoC decision and allowed RP's IA (Plan) No. 11/2025 approving Adani's resolution plan, leading to the present appeals[cite: 36].
legal_issues: Whether the CoC's refusal to consider an unsolicited post-challenge addendum modifying payout tranches and equity infusion was valid, and whether the CoC's commercial wisdom approving a plan with higher upfront recovery over an unsuccessful plan with higher gross NPV is subject to judicial review[cite: 36].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsolicited addendum submitted after the closure of a challenge process that alters payment tranches or increases equity infusion constitutes a substantive plan modification rather than a clarification, and the CoC is under no statutory obligation to accept it or rerun the process[cite: 36]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1A) and 39(3) of the CIRP Regulations and Section 30(4) of the IBC empower the CoC to evaluate plans strictly in accordance with the pre-disclosed Evaluation Matrix; the CoC is not mandated to select the highest NPV bidder over a plan offering superior upfront cash and overall feasibility[cite: 36]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Adherence to the procedural rules established in the RFRP and Process Note, coupled with comprehensive quantitative and qualitative scoring by independent advisors, refutes allegations of material irregularity or lack of transparency[cite: 36]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC validly exercised its commercial wisdom in approving the resolution plan of Adani Enterprises Ltd. based on the Evaluation Matrix scoring, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the appellant's challenge[cite: 36].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 552 & 553 of 2026 are dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the approval of the resolution plan and dismissal of IA No. 01/2026[cite: 36].
summary: Vedanta Limited appealed against the orders dated 17.03.2026 passed by the NCLT Allahabad Bench, which dismissed its IA No. 01/2026 and approved the resolution plan submitted by Adani Enterprises Ltd. for Jaiprakash Associates Ltd.[cite: 36] Vedanta argued that its plan offered a higher gross value and NPV, and that the CoC arbitrarily refused to consider its addendum dated 08.11.2025[cite: 36]. The NCLAT held that the addendum was an impermissible post-challenge modification violating the Process Note[cite: 36]. The Appellate Tribunal reaffirmed that the CoC's commercial wisdom is paramount, noting that Adani's plan scored higher on the Evaluation Matrix due to substantially higher upfront cash recovery[cite: 36]. Finding no material irregularity in the process, the NCLAT dismissed both appeals[cite: 36].

case_title: Assistant Commissioner of State Tax, Vapi vs. M/s ARCK Resolution Professionals LLP & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Assistant Commissioner of State Tax, Vapi; Respondent No. 1 is M/s ARCK Resolution Professionals LLP (RP of Corporate Debtor, Vinergy International Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is UV Stressed Assets Management Private Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 37]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tax assessment orders and recovery proceedings under the Gujarat Value Added Tax (GVAT) Act, 2003 and Central Sales Tax (CST) Act, 1956 for unpaid tax liabilities of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 37]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total admitted claim of Rs. 15,65,92,673/- comprising VAT dues of Rs. 3,41,74,431/- and CST dues plus interest[cite: 37]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 on 09.02.2023; claim submitted in Form B on 22.02.2023 and admitted on 03.05.2023; request to treat as secured creditor sent on 05.01.2024; NCLT approved resolution plan on 09.12.2024[cite: 37]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statutory lien notice dated 03.06.2021 under Section 44 of GVAT Act over the corporate debtor's bank accounts; Form B where Appellant marked 'NA' in security column; RP's IA No. 4517 of 2023 for removing the lien where Appellant asserted statutory first charge under Section 48 GVAT Act[cite: 37]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV approved the resolution plan on 09.12.2024 treating Appellant as an unsecured operational creditor, prompting the present appeal[cite: 37].
legal_issues: Whether statutory tax dues under the GVAT Act create a statutory first charge making the department a secured operational creditor under the IBC despite marking 'NA' in Form B, and whether such charge extends to CST dues[cite: 37].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge created by operation of law under state sales tax enactments operates automatically upon assessment, cannot be waived by inadvertent notations in claim forms, and entitles the tax authority to be classified as a secured operational creditor under the IBC, but such charge does not extend to CST dues absent explicit statutory provision[cite: 37]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 48 of the GVAT Act read with Sections 3(30) and 3(31) of the IBC creates an automatic security interest; the maxim ignorantia juris non excusat does not bar the tax department where the resolution professional has actual notice of the statutory lien through judicial filings[cite: 37]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Marking 'NA' in Form B does not constitute an intentional waiver of statutory security when the resolution professional is put on notice via bank lien removal proceedings under Section 17[cite: 37]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant is entitled to secured operational creditor status solely for its VAT component of Rs. 3,41,74,431/-, requiring redistribution under Section 53 without invalidating the approved resolution plan[cite: 37].
operative_order: The appeal is partly allowed; the Appellant is held entitled to be treated as a secured operational creditor for VAT dues of Rs. 3,41,74,431/-; the CoC is directed to undertake redistribution under Section 53; the approval of the resolution plan is confirmed in all other respects with no costs[cite: 37].
summary: The Assistant Commissioner of State Tax, Vapi, appealed against the order dated 09.12.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV approving the resolution plan for Vinergy International Pvt. Ltd., which treated the department's admitted claim of Rs. 15.65 crores as an unsecured operational debt[cite: 37]. The Appellant contended that Section 48 of the GVAT Act creates a statutory first charge as established in Rainbow Papers[cite: 37]. The NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, holding that marking 'NA' in Form B did not waive the statutory charge for VAT dues since the RP had notice through lien removal proceedings[cite: 37]. However, CST dues lacked statutory first charge[cite: 37]. The CoC was directed to adjust distribution under Section 53 accordingly[cite: 37].

case_title: Lyka Labs Ltd. vs. Modi Lifecare Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Lyka Labs Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and the Respondent is Modi Lifecare Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 39]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Technical Guidance Agreement (TG Agreement) executed on 14.09.2012, under which the Respondent agreed to pay royalty fees (minimum Rs. 1 Crore in year 1, Rs. 2 Crores in year 2, or 5% of sales, whichever was higher) for technical guidance and branding[cite: 39]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on accrued royalty fees with demands of Rs. 84,72,740/- and Rs. 5,95,04,537/-, with an admitted pending liability of approximately Rs. 63 Lakhs acknowledged in correspondence[cite: 39]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: TG Agreement executed on 14.09.2012; follow-up letters issued in May-July 2017; Respondent replied on 31.07.2017 acknowledging liability of Rs. 63 Lakhs; Form 3 Demand Notice issued on 10.10.2017 (unreplied); Section 9 petition filed on 27.02.2018[cite: 39]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: TG Agreement dated 14.09.2012; amendment letter dated 02.08.2013; Respondent's admission letter dated 31.07.2017 confirming pending royalty dues of approximately Rs. 63 Lakhs[cite: 39]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected Company Petition No. 141 of 2018 on 22.02.2024 on the technical ground that invoices were not annexed to the Demand Notice, which the Appellant appealed[cite: 39].
legal_issues: Whether a demand notice delivered in Form 3 under Rule 5 of the Application to Adjudicating Authority Rules is defective for non-annexation of invoices where the operational debt arises directly under a contract without an invoicing requirement, and whether admission of liability establishes debt and default above the statutory threshold[cite: 39].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Rule 5 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016, a demand notice in Form 3 is not mandatorily required to be accompanied by invoices if the operational debt arises directly under a contract or document that establishes the liability and default[cite: 39]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) and Rule 5 provide alternative modes for demanding debt (Form 3 demand notice or Form 4 notice with invoice); where a contract creates an independent obligation to pay fixed minimum sums without mandating invoices, non-attachment of invoices does not invalidate the demand notice[cite: 39]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Written communications from a corporate debtor admitting an outstanding liability exceeding the applicable pecuniary threshold defeat claims of a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding quantum[cite: 39]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the Section 9 petition on hyper-technical grounds of missing invoices when debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold were established; hence the rejection was set aside[cite: 39].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 22.02.2024 is set aside, and the Respondent is permitted to deposit the admitted amount of Rs. 63,00,000/- within 30 days, failing which the Adjudicating Authority shall pass an order admitting the Respondent into insolvency under Section 9[cite: 39].
summary: Lyka Labs Ltd. appealed against an order dated 22.02.2024 passed by the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejecting its Section 9 application against Modi Lifecare Industries Ltd. for unpaid royalty fees under a 2012 Technical Guidance Agreement[cite: 39]. The NCLT dismissed the petition on the ground that the Section 8 demand notice was defective because invoices were not annexed[cite: 39]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that under Rule 5, a Form 3 demand notice does not require invoices when the debt arises under a contract providing for fixed minimum royalty payments[cite: 39]. As the corporate debtor had admitted a liability of approximately Rs. 63 lakhs in writing, the debt and default were established[cite: 39]. The corporate debtor was granted 30 days to deposit Rs. 63 lakhs, failing which CIRP would be initiated[cite: 39].

case_title: Paradeep Phosphates Limited vs. State of Orissa & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Paradeep Phosphates Limited (fertilizer manufacturing company), and the Respondents are the State of Orissa and its Commercial Tax Department[cite: 40]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rehabilitation scheme sanctioned by the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) under the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 (SICA), envisaging reliefs and concessions including tax exemptions[cite: 40]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exemption claimed from payment of Orissa Entry Tax on raw material imports under Clause 20(ii)(d) of BIFR Sanctioned Scheme SS-08 for a period of seven years (2007-2014)[cite: 40]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant declared sick on 20.07.2005; Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (DRS) circulated on 03.03.2008; State objected during hearing on 15.05.2008; BIFR sanctioned scheme on 02.09.2008; net worth turned positive on 31.03.2011; BIFR discharged/deregistered Appellant on 16.08.2011; SICA repealed and IBC enacted in December 2016; C.P. No. 342/2017 filed before NCLT on 08.05.2017; NCLT rejected petition on 17.01.2023[cite: 40]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of BIFR hearing dated 15.05.2008 recording State's submission that it had no policy to grant relief to sick companies; BIFR de-registration order dated 16.08.2011 omitting tax directions; Central Government Notification dated 24.05.2017[cite: 40]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed TP No. 99/CTB/2019 (C.P. No. 342/KB/2017) on 17.01.2023, holding that the Appellant had no right to tax exemption after de-registration and that the scheme was not consented to by the State, leading to the present appeal[cite: 40].
legal_issues: Whether a rehabilitation scheme sanctioned under SICA without express consent of a State Government is binding on the State under Section 19(2), whether tax exemptions under a scheme survive de-registration of the sick company, and whether a BIFR scheme can be treated as a deemed approved resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC pursuant to Notification dated 24.05.2017[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Financial assistance, concessions, or tax exemptions envisaged in a rehabilitation scheme under Section 19 of SICA cannot be enforced against a State Government without its express consent, and the deeming fiction of consent under Section 19(2) does not apply when the government's lack of policy or refusal has been actively communicated during hearings[cite: 40]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19(2) and 19(3) of SICA require affirmative consent for financial sacrifices; furthermore, the Central Government Notification dated 24.05.2017 seeking to treat BIFR schemes as deemed approved resolution plans under Section 31 of the IBC is invalid and ultra vires Section 242 of the IBC as held in Spartek Ceramics[cite: 40]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Explicit statements made by state representatives before the BIFR during scheme consideration objecting to concessions rebut any legal presumption of deemed consent[cite: 40]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The sanctioned scheme ceased to be operative upon the company's de-registration in 2011 and expiration in 2014, and could not be enforced under the IBC, justifying the dismissal of the petition[cite: 40].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 17.01.2023 rejecting the company petition[cite: 40].
summary: Paradeep Phosphates Limited appealed against an order dated 17.01.2023 passed by the NCLT Cuttack Bench rejecting its petition seeking to enforce a 2008 BIFR Sanctioned Scheme as a deemed approved resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC to obtain an exemption from Orissa Entry Tax[cite: 40]. The Appellant argued that the State was bound by deemed consent under Section 19(2) of SICA[cite: 40]. The NCLAT held that the State had expressly denied consent during BIFR hearings, precluding any deemed consent[cite: 40]. Moreover, the scheme lapsed upon de-registration in 2011 and expired in 2014, and the Central Government notification deeming BIFR schemes as IBC resolution plans had been declared ultra vires in Spartek Ceramics[cite: 40]. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed[cite: 40].

case_title: Nitin Ramchandra Jadhav & Ors. vs. Vijendra Kumar Jain & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Nitin Ramchandra Jadhav, Bhavrao Gore, and Anmol Kamchandra Jadhav (Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtor Gajanan Solvex Ltd.), Respondent No. 1 is Vijendra Kumar Jain (Erstwhile RP), and Respondent No. 2 is Ram Sethia (Liquidator)[cite: 41]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor held 51% shareholding (19,00,000 shares) in its Singapore subsidiary, Rio Resource PTE. Ltd., which held a USD 3 million fixed deposit with Indian Bank, Singapore; the shares were transferred to Bellwether International Trade PTE. Ltd. under an alleged share purchase agreement dated 31.12.2018 to pay a penalty to Aero Steel Resources Ltd., UAE[cite: 41]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: State Bank of India initiated Section 7 CIRP against the Corporate Debtor for unpaid loan defaults; an avoidance application claimed fraudulent siphoning of share proceeds of Rs. 19.95 Crores and fake sales of Rs. 19,70,000/-[cite: 41]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD account classified as NPA in 2018; SARFAESI notice issued on 29.08.2018; share transfer agreement executed on 31.12.2018; CIRP initiated on 20.07.2022; IA No. 677 of 2023 under Section 66 filed by RP in 2023; NCLT passed impugned order on 07.05.2024[cite: 41]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic audit report by Shambu Gupta and Company; balance sheets of the CD up to FY 2021-2022 continually reflecting Rs. 8,84,91,725/- investment in Rio Resource despite alleged 2018 sale; and lack of banking records showing actual receipt of consideration or legitimate business with Aero Steel[cite: 41]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V allowed IA No. 677 of 2023 under Section 66 directing Appellants to contribute Rs. 9,04,61,725/- and directed an investigation by the SFIO, leading to the present appeal[cite: 41].
legal_issues: Whether the transfer of shares in a subsidiary without routing sale consideration to the Corporate Debtor constitutes fraudulent trading under Section 66(1) of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has statutory jurisdiction to directly order an investigation by the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO)[cite: 41].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Concealing the disposition of subsidiary shares while maintaining fictitious investment entries in financial statements to divert sale proceeds to third parties under sham penalty settlements constitutes fraudulent trading under Section 66(1) of the IBC, but the Adjudicating Authority lacks statutory competence to directly mandate an SFIO investigation without routing through the Central Government[cite: 41]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) applies to any person knowingly party to carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors, requiring contribution to corporate assets; however, Section 212 and 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 restrict the power to direct an SFIO probe solely to the Central Government upon opinion formed by it[cite: 41]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the RP discharges the initial burden via forensic audit and contradictory audited balance sheets, the evidentiary onus shifts to suspended directors to establish bona fide commercial necessity on a preponderance of probabilities[cite: 41]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The finding of fraudulent trading and the order for contribution of Rs. 9,04,61,725/- were affirmed, but the direct SFIO reference was modified to a reference to the Central Government (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) under Section 213[cite: 41].
operative_order: The appeal is partly allowed; the order of the Adjudicating Authority directing the appellants to contribute Rs. 9,04,61,725/- is upheld, while the direction for an SFIO investigation is modified to refer the matter to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs for investigation by inspectors under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013, with no order as to costs[cite: 41].
summary: The Appellants, suspended directors of Gajanan Solvex Ltd., appealed against an order dated 07.05.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-V under Section 66 of the IBC[cite: 41]. The NCLT found the directors guilty of fraudulent trading for surreptitiously transferring 51% shareholding in Singapore subsidiary Rio Resource PTE. Ltd. to Bellwether to settle an alleged commercial penalty with Aero Steel UAE without routing proceeds to the debtor, while falsely continuing to reflect the investment in balance sheets[cite: 41]. The NCLT ordered contribution of Rs. 9,04,61,725/- and directed an SFIO investigation[cite: 41]. The NCLAT upheld the contribution order finding clear fraudulent diversion, but modified the SFIO direction, holding that NCLT cannot directly order an SFIO probe and must refer the matter to the Central Government under Section 213 of the Companies Act[cite: 41].

case_title: Hotel Horizon Private Limited vs. Tea4Health Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Hotel Horizon Private Limited (Operational Creditor/Licensor), acting through its RP, and the Respondent is Tea4Health Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Licensee)[cite: 42]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Registered Leave and License Agreement dated 06.03.2018 granting the Corporate Debtor license to use Unit No. 4 (3500 sq. ft.) in the Appellant's hotel at Juhu, Mumbai, to run a restaurant ('Wine Villa') for 5 years against monthly license fees and common area maintenance charges[cite: 42]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed an operational debt of Rs. 2,62,83,471/- comprising unpaid license fees, CAM charges, HVAC costs, water charges, and interest across invoices issued between July 2018 and December 2019[cite: 42]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Leave and License Agreement executed on 06.03.2018; CIRP initiated against the Appellant-Licensor on 29.01.2019 (later set aside on 07.02.2020); Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 27.12.2019; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 1285/MB-IV/2020 dismissed by NCLT on 31.03.2023[cite: 42]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MA No. 2011 of 2019 filed by Corporate Debtor on 03.06.2019 alleging severe disconnection of water/HVAC, deployment of bouncers, and unadjusted security deposit of Rs. 68.40 Lakhs; NCLT interim orders dated 12.06.2019 and 23.07.2019 ordering police assistance for access[cite: 42]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed the Section 9 petition on 31.03.2023 due to genuine pre-existing disputes regarding unfitness of premises and unadjusted deposits, which the Operational Creditor appealed[cite: 42].
legal_issues: Whether prior disputes concerning disconnection of essential services, premises being rendered commercially unusable during the licensor's own insolvency, and failure to adjust substantial security deposits constitute a plausible pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC[cite: 42].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt claim arising out of a lease or license agreement cannot trigger insolvency when documented disputes regarding breach of essential covenants, failure to provide peaceful commercial enjoyment, and refusal to adjust substantial security deposits predate the statutory demand notice[cite: 42]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC, the adjudicating authority is not an adjudicatory forum for resolving contentious contractual set-offs or damages; the existence of a bona fide, plausible defense supported by contemporaneous records necessitates dismissal[cite: 42]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Mobilox standard applies, requiring the court to verify whether the dispute is not a patently feeble legal argument; formal interlocutory applications and police assistance orders obtained before the Section 8 notice establish a genuine pre-existing dispute[cite: 42]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly rejected the Section 9 application as the dispute regarding the habitability of premises and unadjusted security deposit of Rs. 68.40 Lakhs was authentic and pre-existing[cite: 42].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merit, confirming the impugned order dated 31.03.2023 with no order as to costs, and all pending interlocutory applications are closed[cite: 42].
summary: Hotel Horizon Private Limited appealed against the order dated 31.03.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissing its Section 9 application against Tea4Health Private Limited[cite: 42]. The Appellant claimed Rs. 2.62 crores in unpaid license fees and utility charges under a 2018 leave and license agreement for running a restaurant in its hotel premises[cite: 42]. The Corporate Debtor resisted the petition showing that during the Appellant's prior insolvency, essential water and air-conditioning services were terminated, bouncers obstructed operations, and NCLT had passed police assistance orders on MA No. 2011 of 2019 prior to the demand notice, alongside an unadjusted security deposit of Rs. 68.40 lakhs[cite: 42]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that a bona fide pre-existing dispute barred Section 9 proceedings[cite: 42].

case_title: Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. vs. Union of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. (IL&FS, Core Investment Company), its wholly owned subsidiary IL&FS Financial Services Ltd. (IFIN, NBFC), and intermediate borrower subsidiaries including IL&FS Transportation Networks Limited (ITNL); Respondents include Union of India, contesting Respondent No. 8 SREI Infrastructure Finance Limited (SIFL), and SREI Group borrower entities including Attivo Economic Zone (Mumbai) Pvt. Ltd., Sahaj E-Village Ltd., Giridhan Projects Pvt. Ltd., Bharat Road Network Ltd. (BRNL), and Vistar Financiers Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Following an RBI inspection on 01.11.2017 directing IFIN to run down intra-group exposure and cease fresh lending to group entities, IFIN, SIFL, and their respective group entities engaged in six circuitous round-tripping transactions between March 2017 and March 2018 totaling INR 1,060 Crores; IFIN disbursed loans to SREI Group entities backed by letters of awareness/comfort from SIFL, and SIFL parallelly disbursed equivalent sums to IL&FS subsidiaries (ITNL, FSEL, CNTL, SPPL, GIMCO) backed by letters of awareness from IFIN, routing funds ultimately to ITNL to bypass RBI group lending restrictions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The aggregate value of the 6 transactions was INR 1,060 Crores across multiple tranches (INR 110 Cr, INR 195/200 Cr, INR 205/200 Cr, INR 70/100 Cr, INR 280/250 Cr, and INR 200 Cr); IL&FS Group payment defaults commenced in September 2018, leading to non-repayment and initiation of claims. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI inspection advisory issued on 01.11.2017; Union of India filed petition C.P. No. 3638(MB)/2018 under Sections 241-242 on which NCLT Mumbai reconstituted IL&FS's Board on 01.10.2018; NCLAT stayed creditor coercive actions on 15.10.2018 and approved the resolution framework on 12.03.2020; RBI statutory inspection report issued on 22.03.2019; SFIO submitted report on 28.05.2019; Grant Thornton forensic report issued on 21.04.2019; SEBI order passed on 15.12.2022; IL&FS New Board resolved on 14.03.2023 and 30.05.2023 to collapse circuitous transactions; NCLAT disposed of IA No. 3169/2023 on 16.01.2025 granting liberty to approach NCLT; CA No. 226/2025 filed before NCLT Mumbai on 09.07.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RBI Section 45N Inspection Report dated 22.03.2019 finding both groups acted in concert to bypass group exposure caps; SFIO Report dated 28.05.2019 detailing deceptive routing of INR 2,319.82 Crores to ITNL; Grant Thornton forensic report dated 21.04.2019 classifying disbursements as circuitous; SEBI order dated 15.12.2022; cross-issued Letters of Awareness/Assurance between SIFL and IFIN; and Sahaj End-Use Certificates dated 29.04.2017 and 19.04.2018 confirming onward routing to SIFL. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IL&FS filed CA No. 226/2025 in C.P. No. 3638(MB)/2018 before NCLT Mumbai Bench I seeking declaration of the 6 transactions as sham, fraudulent, and void and for unwinding/collapsing them; SIFL filed CA No. 99/2025 and CA No. 368/2025 seeking distribution of settlement monies. NCLT Mumbai dismissed CA No. 226/2025 and allowed CA Nos. 99/2025 and 368/2025 on 13.04.2026, holding that mutual agreement/consent was mandatory under NCLAT's order and Section 242(2)(f) proviso, RBI reports were merely advisory, and IL&FS was barred by election and approbate-reprobate due to previously filing Section 7 IBC petitions against SREI entities; IL&FS appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the NCLT correctly construed NCLAT's earlier order dated 16.01.2025 by holding that mutual consent is a mandatory precondition for collapsing/unwinding circuitous transactions. 2. Whether for exercise of jurisdiction under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to terminate, set aside, or unwind transactions alleged to be fraudulent and void ab initio, obtaining the consent of the concerned parties under Section 242(2)(f) proviso is a condition precedent. 3. Whether the appellant in CA No. 226/2025 made sufficient pleadings and produced adequate material necessitating examination of fraudulent and void transactions. 4. Whether the unwinding application was barred by the principles of election, estoppel, or approbate and reprobate due to the prior initiation of independent Section 7 IBC proceedings against third parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory powers conferred upon a company tribunal to remedy oppression, mismanagement, and affairs conducted prejudicial to public interest are plenary and overarching; specific statutory clauses illustrating permissible orders do not curtail general remedial powers, and agreements demonstrated to be fraudulent, sham, or collusive devices executed to bypass statutory regulations are void ab initio and can be unwound without the consent of participating wrongdoers, as equitable doctrines like estoppel and election cannot be invoked to perpetuate illegality (ex dolo malo non oritur actio). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal to make any order it thinks fit to bring an end to matters complained of, which general jurisdiction is not restricted by the illustrations in Section 242(2); the proviso to Section 242(2)(f) requiring notice and consent governs only valid and subsisting contracts between a company and third parties, and does not apply to transactions challenged as fraudulent, circuitous, and void ab initio. Furthermore, RBI directions issued under Section 45N of the RBI Act, 1934 are statutory and binding on all NBFCs rather than merely advisory. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To determine whether transactions are sham or fraudulent, the Tribunal must look beyond outward legal form to underlying economic reality, examining concurrent disbursement dates, matching loan amounts, reciprocal letters of awareness, statutory inspection reports (RBI, SFIO), forensic audit findings, and end-use admissions; where substantial documentary evidence demonstrates concerted circuitous fund routing to evade statutory prohibitions, a full merits adjudication is legally warranted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in construing mutual consent under Section 242(2)(f) proviso as an indispensable jurisdictional prerequisite to unwind fraudulent circuitous transactions, misconstrued NCLAT's prior order dated 16.01.2025, and wrongly applied equitable estoppel to defeat inquiry into statutory violations; the dismissal was unsustainable and CA No. 226/2025 was revived for merits determination.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 143-145 of 2026 is allowed with no order as to costs; the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai Bench I dated 13.04.2026 is set aside; CA No. 226/2025 is revived for fresh consideration on merits in accordance with law; CA No. 99/2025 and CA No. 368/2025 are revived for fresh orders; and the funds payable to SIFL from the resolution of IL&FS group entities shall continue to be held in the Escrow Account pending final decision by NCLT.
summary: Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. (IL&FS) appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 13.04.2026 dismissing its application (CA No. 226/2025) which sought to unwind six circuitous, fraudulent loan transactions aggregating INR 1,060 Crores routed via SREI Group entities to circumvent RBI intra-group lending limits, and allowing applications filed by SREI Infrastructure Finance Limited (SIFL). NCLT had held that unwinding required mutual consent under Section 242(2)(f) proviso and was barred by election and estoppel. NCLAT set aside the impugned order and allowed the appeals, ruling that plenary powers under Section 242(1) are not curtailed by Section 242(2)(f) where transactions are alleged to be fraudulent and void ab initio, and equitable estoppel cannot validate statutory illegalities. The proceedings were remanded for adjudication on merits.

case_title: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Manoj Kumar Das & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are State Bank of India (SBI) and 7 other financial creditors of Corporate Debtor Jet Airways (India) Limited (airline operator since 1993); Respondents are Manoj Kumar Das and 295 workmen, S. Gopalkrishnan (workmen/employee representative on the Stakeholders Consultation Committee - SCC), and Mr. Satish Kumar Gupta (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor operated scheduled airline services funded by credit facilities from SBI-led consortium of lenders; Corporate Debtor had statutory employment contracts with workmen and employees obligating payment of salary, provident fund, and gratuity under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 and Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor suffered severe liquidity distress and grounded all flight operations on 17.04.2019, defaulting on credit facilities running into thousands of crores owed to financial creditors, as well as defaulting on workmen salaries, PF contributions (unpaid post-February 2019), and gratuity liabilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SBI filed Section 7 IBC petition admitted on 20.06.2019; CoC approved Jalan Fritsch consortium resolution plan on 03.10.2020; Adjudicating Authority approved plan on 22.06.2021; NCLAT ordered SRA to pay full PF and gratuity dues on 21.10.2022 (affirmed by Supreme Court on 30.01.2023); Supreme Court invoked Article 142 on 07.11.2024 directing liquidation; Adjudicating Authority appointed Liquidator on 26.11.2024; Manoj Kumar Das filed IA No. 3426/2025 on 10.07.2025; S. Gopalkrishnan filed IA No. 4627/2025 on 13.10.2025; SBI filed IA No. 4757/2025 disposed of on 03.02.2026; NCLT decided IA Nos. 3426/2025 and 4627/2025 on 04.02.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's Audited Financial Statements as of 31.03.2019 (Notes 22, 27, 31, and 40 recording employee benefit provisions including Rs. 18,310 lakhs gratuity); Additional Affidavit of RP dated 25.07.2022 confirming Corporate Debtor ceased depositing PF with EPFO after February 2019; Recovery Certificate dated 16.05.2019 issued by Deputy Labour Commissioner for salary dues; and minutes of the 16th SCC meeting dated 18.08.2025 recording disputes over distribution of asset sale proceeds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court I) on 04.02.2026 passed orders directing the Liquidator to pay provident fund and gratuity dues in full as dues outside the liquidation estate pursuant to Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC; SBI and consortium lenders appealed to NCLAT in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 419-420 of 2026 contending that Section 36(4)(a)(iii) exclusion is contingent upon the debtor possessing a segregated fund on the liquidation commencement date, absent which claims must be distributed under Section 53(1)(b) waterfall.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the exclusion of all sums due to any workman or employee from provident fund, pension fund, and gratuity fund from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC is contingent on the physical existence of a segregated or dedicated fund on the liquidation commencement date. 2. Whether the direction of the Adjudicating Authority requiring the Liquidator to pay provident fund and gratuity dues in full outside the liquidation estate is contrary to Section 36(4)(a)(iii) and Section 53(1)(b) of the IBC. 3. Whether workmen dues towards provident fund and gratuity are required to be distributed strictly as per the waterfall mechanism under Section 53(1)(b) of the IBC in the absence of a pre-existing segregated fund.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory social security entitlements of workmen and employees, including provident fund, pension, and gratuity, are constitutionally and statutorily protected property rights that stand completely excluded from the debtor's liquidation estate; their payment in full is an absolute obligation of the liquidator from available assets and is not contingent on the prior maintenance or physical segregation of dedicated funds by the debtor company. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC expressly provides that 'all sums due to any workman or employee from the provident fund, the pension fund and the gratuity fund' shall not be included in the liquidation estate and shall not be used for recovery in liquidation; this provision is due-centric rather than asset-centric. Furthermore, Parliament deliberately omitted the phrase 'maintained by the company' (which appeared in former Section 326 of the Companies Act, 2013), proving legislative intent that non-maintenance of a separate fund does not extinguish the exclusion or push statutory social security dues into the Section 53(1) waterfall mechanism. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An employer's liability for provident fund and gratuity established through statutory provisions, audited balance sheets, financial statements reflecting employee benefit provisions, or admissions by the resolution professional/liquidator is conclusive to mandate payment in full; absence of a separate physical bank account does not alter the character of the statutory debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Exclusion under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) is not contingent upon the existence of a separate fund on the liquidation commencement date, and provident fund and gratuity dues must be discharged in full by the liquidator prior to any waterfall distribution under Section 53(1); the Adjudicating Authority's direction was lawful and the financial creditors' appeals were dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 419-420 of 2026 filed by State Bank of India and other Financial Creditors is dismissed; the direction issued by the Adjudicating Authority in paragraph 20(a) of the order dated 04.02.2026 passed in IA No. 3426 of 2025 and IA No. 4627 of 2025 directing the liquidator to pay provident fund and gratuity dues to workmen and employees in terms of the 1952 and 1972 Acts outside the liquidation estate is upheld; parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: State Bank of India and consortium lenders appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 04.02.2026 directing the Liquidator of Jet Airways (India) Limited to pay provident fund and gratuity dues to workmen and employees in full outside the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. Lenders contended that exclusion requires a dedicated, segregated fund existing on the liquidation commencement date, absent which dues fall under the Section 53 waterfall. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that exclusion under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) is due-centric and not contingent on pre-existing segregated funds, affirming that statutory social security dues must be paid in full prior to any waterfall distribution.

case_title: Sanjeev Chaddha & Ors. vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Sanjeev Chaddha and 351 workmen of Corporate Debtor Jet Airways (India) Limited; Respondents are State Bank of India (lead lender), consortium of financial creditors, and Mr. Satish Kumar Gupta (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contracts of workmen and employees with Corporate Debtor Jet Airways (India) Limited for scheduled airline operations, giving rise to entitlement to wages, provident fund, and gratuity under applicable labour statutes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor ceased operations on 17.04.2019, defaulting on multi-crore credit facilities and leaving unpaid employee salaries from January to March 2019 as well as subsequent statutory termination and retirement dues. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 20.06.2019; resolution plan approved by NCLT on 22.06.2021; protracted appellate litigation between SRA and lenders resulted in CIRP spanning 1,976 days; Supreme Court on 07.11.2024 invoked Article 142 directing liquidation; Liquidator appointed on 26.11.2024 (statutory liquidation commencement date); workmen filed IA No. 3426/2025 on 10.07.2025 seeking exclusion of 1,656 days from CIRP computation for the Section 53(1)(b) 24-month lookback period; NCLT rejected time exclusion prayer on 04.02.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Chronological court records demonstrating CIRP prolonged for 1,976 days due to bona fide appeals up to the Supreme Court; Deputy Labour Commissioner Recovery Certificate dated 16.05.2019 for unpaid salary dues (January-March 2019); and the Liquidator's list of stakeholders artificially reflecting workmen dues under Section 53(1)(b) as NIL because the 24-month lookback preceding 26.11.2024 fell during stalled litigation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai on 04.02.2026 held that Section 5(17) of the IBC strictly defines the liquidation commencement date without any provision for alteration or time exclusion on equitable grounds, and directed the Recovery Certificate claim to be adjudicated under Section 53; workmen appealed to NCLAT in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 551 of 2026 challenging the refusal to exclude 1,656 days and treatment of the Recovery Certificate.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the period of 1,656 days spent in legal proceedings beyond the mandatory 330-day statutory CIRP period can be excluded for computing the 24-month lookback period under Section 53(1)(b)(i) of the IBC. 2. Whether the Recovery Certificate dated 16.05.2019 issued by the Deputy Labour Commissioner for salary dues must be honoured and kept entirely out of the liquidation estate. 3. Whether workmen dues for the period of 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date can be treated as NIL by the Liquidator.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the established legal maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit (the act of the court shall prejudice no person), time consumed in protracted, bona fide legal proceedings before judicial and appellate forums exceeding statutory timelines must be excluded when computing statutory lookback periods for priority entitlements, so that court delay does not annihilate statutory protections granted to vulnerable stakeholders like workmen. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the liquidation commencement date under Section 5(17) of the IBC is a statutorily fixed date that cannot be modified, the 24-month lookback period under Section 53(1)(b)(i) must be interpreted purposively in harmony with Section 12; where the CIRP extends to 1,976 days due to court litigation, time spent beyond the statutory 330-day maximum (namely 1,656 days) must be excluded so that the 24-month window captures the actual operational period preceding insolvency, preventing workmen dues from becoming artificially zero. Conversely, a Recovery Certificate issued for pre-insolvency salary arrears merely quantifies wage claims and remains governed by the Section 53(1)(b) waterfall, rather than being kept outside the liquidation estate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the procedural history unequivocally confirms that the 1,656 days delay was entirely caused by multi-tier litigation between the resolution applicant and financial creditors rather than any default by workmen, judicial equity and the statutory purpose of protecting 24 months of workmen dues demand exclusion of that period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing exclusion of 1,656 days; workmen are entitled to exclusion of 1,656 days from the CIRP period for calculating 24 months dues preceding liquidation commencement date under Section 53(1)(b), rendering their claim active rather than NIL, while the prayer to exclude the Recovery Certificate from the liquidation estate was properly rejected; appeal partly allowed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 551 of 2026 is partly allowed; the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 04.02.2026 is modified to the extent that prayer (iv) in IA No. 3426 of 2025 is allowed, directing the exclusion of 1,656 days from the CIRP period for computing the 24 months' workmen dues preceding the liquidation commencement date (26.11.2024) under Section 53(1)(b) of the IBC; Liquidator directed to re-compute workmen dues accordingly and take consequential action; refusal of prayer (iii) regarding the Recovery Certificate is upheld; parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Sanjeev Chaddha and 351 workmen of Jet Airways (India) Limited appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 04.02.2026, which rejected their prayer to exclude 1,656 days spent in prolonged litigation beyond the statutory 330-day CIRP period for calculating the 24-month lookback period under Section 53(1)(b) of the IBC, and declined to keep salary dues under a Recovery Certificate outside the liquidation estate. NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, holding that under the maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit, the 1,656 days consumed in court proceedings must be excluded so that workmen entitlements are not rendered zero. However, dues under the Recovery Certificate remain workmen dues to be settled under Section 53(1)(b).

case_title: State Bank of India (On Behalf of Financial Creditors) & Ors. vs. Manoj Kumar Das & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are State Bank of India (SBI, representing the Committee of Creditors/Financial Creditors) and seven other financial institutions; Respondents are Manoj Kumar Das and 295 workmen, S. Gopalkrishnan (representative of workmen and employees on the Stakeholders Consultation Committee), and Mr. Satish Kumar Gupta (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Jet Airways (India) Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital and credit facilities extended by SBI and consortium banks to Corporate Debtor Jet Airways (India) Limited; underlying employer-employee contracts governing workmen and flight staff with statutory social security benefits. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Widespread commercial and debt servicing default culminating in grounding of airline operations on 17.04.2019; total default to financial creditors exceeding billions of INR, and unremitted provident fund deductions and unpaid gratuity dues dating back to February 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP initiated on 20.06.2019; resolution plan approved on 22.06.2021; NCLAT ordered payment of full PF and gratuity on 21.10.2022 (affirmed by Supreme Court on 30.01.2023); Supreme Court directed liquidation under Article 142 on 07.11.2024; Liquidator appointed on 26.11.2024; workmen filed IA No. 3426/2025 on 10.07.2025; IA No. 4627/2025 filed on 13.10.2025; SBI filed IA No. 4757/2025 disposed of on 03.02.2026; NCLT passed final impugned order on 04.02.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's Audited Financial Statements as of 31.03.2019 (Notes 22, 27, 31, and 40 detailing employee benefit provisions including Rs. 18,310 lakhs for gratuity); Additional Affidavit of RP dated 25.07.2022 admitting cessation of PF deposits post-February 2019; Recovery Certificate dated 16.05.2019; and minutes of the 16th SCC meeting dated 18.08.2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court I) on 04.02.2026 allowed workmen applications directing the Liquidator to pay provident fund and gratuity dues in full outside the liquidation estate pursuant to Section 36(4)(a)(iii); SBI and financial creditors appealed to NCLAT arguing that Section 36(4)(a)(iii) only applies to existing segregated funds and that in their absence, dues must follow Section 53(1)(b) waterfall priority.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the exclusion of provident fund, pension fund, and gratuity fund dues from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC is contingent upon the debtor having maintained a distinct, segregated fund on the liquidation commencement date. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the Liquidator to pay provident fund and gratuity dues in full outside the liquidation estate. 3. Whether workmen dues towards provident fund and gratuity must be distributed exclusively under the waterfall mechanism of Section 53(1)(b) when no earmarked fund exists.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Social security funds owed to workmen and employees under statutory mandates are excluded in toto from the debtor's liquidation estate and cannot be treated as assets available for creditor distribution; the liquidator is legally obligated to satisfy such claims in full from the general assets of the corporate debtor irrespective of whether the debtor previously maintained an earmarked fund. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC expressly excludes all sums due to any workman or employee from the provident fund, pension fund, and gratuity fund from the liquidation estate; this provision is due-centric, defining the exclusion by the nature and origin of the liability rather than the physical segregation of assets, and Parliament's deliberate removal of the requirement 'maintained by the company' confirms that non-segregation does not extinguish the exclusion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of liability recorded in statutory provisions, audited financial accounts, and admissions of the insolvency professional suffices to establish workmen entitlement; liquidators cannot evade statutory liabilities on the technical ground that the management failed to maintain a separate bank account. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The exclusion under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) is independent of whether a separate fund existed on the liquidation commencement date, and such statutory dues cannot be relegated to the Section 53 waterfall; the Adjudicating Authority's order was upheld and the appeal was dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 419-420 of 2026 is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's direction under paragraph 20(a) of the order dated 04.02.2026 requiring the Liquidator to pay provident fund and gratuity dues to workmen and employees outside the liquidation estate is upheld; parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: State Bank of India and consortium lenders appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 04.02.2026 directing the Liquidator of Jet Airways (India) Limited to pay provident fund and gratuity dues to workmen and employees in full outside the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. Lenders contended that exclusion requires a dedicated, segregated fund existing on the liquidation commencement date, absent which dues fall under the Section 53 waterfall. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that exclusion under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) is due-centric and not contingent on pre-existing segregated funds, affirming that statutory social security dues must be paid in full prior to any waterfall distribution.

case_title: Mr. Gaurav Jaiswal vs. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA, Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor is JHV Sugar Limited (operating an integrated sugar mill and power plant in UP); Appellant is Mr. Gaurav Jaiswal, suspended director of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Alok Kumar Agarwal, Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 03.10.2011, IREDA sanctioned a term loan facility of Rs. 57.10 Crores (comprising Rs. 27.41 Crores Main Loan and Rs. 29.69 Crores Bridge Loan under the Sugar Development Fund) for expanding the Corporate Debtor's sugar mill from 4500 TCD to 6500 TCD and setting up a 20 MW bagasse-based co-generation project, against a Loan Agreement and Deed of Hypothecation dated 03.10.2011[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: IREDA disbursed Rs. 1941.94 Lakhs (approx. Rs. 17.72 to 19.41 Crores) in tranches from 19.12.2012 to 30.11.2015 repayable in 40 quarterly installments starting 30.09.2013[cite: 5, 10]; Corporate Debtor committed recurring defaults[cite: 5, 10]; IREDA issued a loan recall notice on 11.08.2017 demanding Rs. 25,05,26,962/-[cite: 5]; under subsequent OTS-2 dated 31.01.2022/15.05.2021, Corporate Debtor was required to pay Rs. 20,42,49,000/- plus 12.45% simple interest by 25.11.2022[cite: 5]; Corporate Debtor paid principal but admitted an unpaid interest default of Rs. 2,98,85,658/-[cite: 5]; total outstanding claimed by IREDA in Section 7 petition as of 31.03.2023 was Rs. 24,95,05,121/-[cite: 5, 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 16.12.2015[cite: 5, 10]; First Section 7 petition C.P. (IB) No. 153/KB/2018 filed on 18.07.2018 and withdrawn on 17.07.2019 upon approval of OTS-1 dated 15.05.2019[cite: 5]; OTS-2 approved on 15.05.2021/31.01.2022 with deadline 25.11.2022[cite: 5]; IREDA withdrew OTS-2 via email on 12.12.2022 due to non-compliance[cite: 5]; Corporate Debtor replied on 17.04.2023[cite: 5]; IREDA filed fresh Section 7 petition C.P. (IB) No. 131/KB/2023 on 28.04.2023[cite: 5]; NCLT set Corporate Debtor ex-parte on 18.11.2024 after failed post and paper publication[cite: 5, 7]; admission order passed on 07.04.2025[cite: 5, 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NeSL default certificate[cite: 5]; certified loan ledger compliant with Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 confirming outstanding debt of Rs. 25.99 Crores as of 22.03.2023[cite: 5]; emails dated 08.02.2022, 25.11.2022, and 12.12.2022[cite: 5]; Corporate Debtor's letters dated 17.04.2023 and 27.08.2024 explicitly admitting outstanding interest of Rs. 2.98 Crores[cite: 5, 4]; affidavit of service showing petition dispatched to MCA-registered email jhvsugar@gmail.com on 06.06.2023 and paper publications[cite: 5, 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench vide order dated 07.04.2025 admitted Section 7 application C.P. (IB) No. 131/KB/2023 holding debt and default established above the statutory threshold[cite: 5, 2]; Appellant appealed under Section 61 contending violation of natural justice (ex-parte order), non-service at administrative office, and that Section 7 is not maintainable solely for recovery of residual interest when principal is discharged under OTS[cite: 5, 2, 4, 5].
legal_issues: 1. Whether service of a Section 7 petition effected on the registered email address of the Corporate Debtor appearing in MCA portal records and dispatched to its registered office constitutes valid deemed service under Rules 37 and 38 of NCLT Rules, 2016, Section 20(2) of Companies Act, 2013, and Order XXIX Rule 2 CPC. 2. Whether a Section 7 IBC petition is legally maintainable solely for default in payment of an interest component where the principal loan amount has been repaid, provided the defaulted interest exceeds the Rs. 1 Crore threshold. 3. Whether the breach of a conditional One Time Settlement (OTS) entitles the Financial Creditor to revoke the OTS and revive the full underlying contractual debt and default under the original loan agreement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of process upon a corporate debtor effected at its registered email address appearing on the official corporate registry portal and dispatched to its registered office constitutes valid deemed service in law, and a company cannot plead lack of notice by closing its registered office; further, insolvency resolution proceedings are maintainable for default in payment of an interest component alone, provided such interest constitutes a financial debt crossing the statutory threshold, and breach of a conditional settlement agreement revives the entire original contractual claim. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC requires only proof of debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore; the definition of financial debt under Section 5(8) includes interest, and there is no statutory bar to initiating CIRP when default pertains exclusively to interest. Under Section 20(2) of Companies Act, 2013 read with Rules 37 and 38 of NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 12 of Companies Act, 2013, a corporate debtor bears the strict statutory duty to maintain a functional registered office, and transmission to the MCA master data email address amounts to complete legal service. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of a certified statement of account under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, an NeSL record of default, and unequivocal admissions by the corporate debtor in correspondence acknowledging an unpaid interest liability exceeding Rs. 1 Crore constitutes conclusive evidentiary proof of debt and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was validly served, withdrawal of OTS-2 upon breach restored the full contractual debt, and the admitted interest default of Rs. 2.98 Crores crossed the statutory threshold; NCLT's admission order was legally unassailable and the appeal was dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 594 of 2025 is dismissed; the order dated 07.04.2025 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in C.P. (IB) No. 131/KB/2023 admitting the Section 7 petition and initiating CIRP against JHV Sugar Limited is affirmed; all connected Interlocutory Applications are disposed of; no order as to costs.
summary: Mr. Gaurav Jaiswal, suspended director of JHV Sugar Limited, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated 07.04.2025 admitting IREDA's Section 7 IBC petition[cite: 5, 2]. The Appellant contended that the order was ex-parte without proper service and that Section 7 could not be invoked solely for recovering an outstanding interest balance of Rs. 2.98 Crores after principal repayment under OTS-2[cite: 5, 2, 5]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that service on the MCA-registered email and registered office constitutes valid deemed service under NCLT Rules and CPC[cite: 5, 7]. It further held that breach of OTS terms revived the original debt and that a Section 7 petition is maintainable solely on defaulted interest exceeding the Rs. 1 Crore threshold[cite: 5].

case_title: Micro Capitals Private Limited vs. Commissioner of Income Tax & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is KSS Limited (engaged in content distribution and film exhibition, listed on NSE/BSE); Appellant in CA 714/2025 is Micro Capitals Private Limited (NBFC, majority Financial Creditor with 77.97% CoC voting share and sole Resolution Applicant/SRA); Appellant in CA 721/2025 is Mr. Dharmendra Dhelariya (Resolution Professional); Respondents include Commissioner of Income Tax, Principal Chief Commissioner of Customs (statutory claim approx. Rs. 23.14 Cr), and SEBI (statutory penalty claim)[cite: 6, 2, 3, 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unsecured financial credit facilities extended by Micro Capitals Pvt. Ltd. (Rs. 72 Crores) and Axis Bank Limited (holding 22.07% CoC voting share) to Corporate Debtor; statutory customs duties and regulatory penalties owed to SEBI[cite: 6, 3, 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claims exceeded Rs. 106 Crores (including Rs. 95.59 Crores financial debt: Micro Capitals Rs. 74.53 Cr and Axis Bank Rs. 21.06 Cr; and Customs statutory claim of Rs. 23.14 Cr)[cite: 6, 3, 4, 8]; Corporate Debtor suffered insolvency defaults leading to CIRP[cite: 6, 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Micro Capitals filed Section 7 petition admitted on 24.01.2023; public announcement issued 30.01.2023; Form-G published on 25.03.2023 and 17.04.2023; SRA submitted Resolution Plan on 14.06.2023; ED de-sealing application disposed of on 07.09.2023; CoC approved Plan in 7th meeting on 17.10.2023 with 77.97% voting share; RP filed approval application IA No. 04 of 2024; NCLT heard and reserved orders on 29.08.2024 and rejected the Plan on 24.03.2025[cite: 6, 3, 4, 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Valuers assessed Fair Value at Rs. 3.21 Crores and Liquidation Value at Rs. 2.52 Crores; Resolution Plan proposed total payment of Rs. 3.01 Crores (Rs. 2.65 Crores for financial creditors, Rs. 35 Lakhs CIRP costs, Rs. 1 Lakh for operational creditors) plus working capital infusion of Rs. 5 Crores within 6 months and Rs. 5 Crores within 12 months under Clause 2.3(vi) and Rs. 3 Crores SPV equity infusion under Clause 4.20.4(b); Minutes of 1st CoC meeting dated 23.02.2023 confirming registered office was leased premises; Form-H Compliance Certificate item 9[cite: 6, 4, 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V rejected IA No. 04 of 2024 on 24.03.2025 holding that a financial creditor cannot approve its own plan under nemo judex in causa sua, plan lacked genuine fund infusion, feasibility was unexamined, and Customs/SEBI were secured creditors under Rainbow Papers, while making adverse remarks against the RP; SRA and RP appealed to NCLAT[cite: 6, 2, 4, 5].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Financial Creditor who is a member of the Committee of Creditors is legally permitted to submit a Resolution Plan and vote in favour of its own plan under the proviso to Section 30(5) of the IBC, or whether such approval is vitiated by nemo judex in causa sua. 2. Whether statutory dues of Customs under Section 142A of the Customs Act, 1962 and SEBI penalties constitute secured debts ranking equally with secured financial creditors under Rainbow Papers, or whether they rank as operational unsecured debts under Section 53(1)(e)(i) of the IBC. 3. Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction under Section 31(1) by rejecting a CoC-approved resolution plan on subjective grounds of feasibility, viability, and fund infusion, and whether adverse remarks against the RP were justified.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory provisions of the insolvency code expressly authorize a financial creditor to participate as a resolution applicant and vote to approve its own resolution plan, and such legislative dispensation cannot be invalidated by common law natural justice doctrines such as nemo judex in causa sua; furthermore, sovereign statutory claims governed by enactments subordinated to the IBC rank as operational debts under the statutory waterfall mechanism and cannot claim secured creditor status. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proviso to Section 30(5) of the IBC specifically carves out an exception permitting a resolution applicant who is also a financial creditor to vote at CoC meetings on its resolution plan, an express statutory command that Adjudicating Authorities cannot disregard; Section 142A of the Customs Act is expressly made subject to the IBC, and pursuant to Section 238 of the IBC, dues of Customs, Income Tax, and SEBI constitute unsecured operational debts under Section 53(1)(e)(i), rendering Rainbow Papers inapplicable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the record establishes that the plan value (Rs. 3.01 Crores) exceeds the liquidation value (Rs. 2.52 Crores), omitted premises were rented properties, working capital infusions were specifically stipulated, and priority payout was reserved for dissenting financial creditors, the plan complies with Section 30(2) and Regulation 38. 4.
