DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the Resolution Plan and misapplying Rainbow Papers and nemo judex in causa sua; the plan was legally compliant, CoC commercial wisdom was supreme, and adverse remarks against the RP were wholly unmerited; both appeals were allowed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 714 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 721 of 2025 are allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 24.03.2025 is set aside; I.A. (IBC) (PLAN) No. 04 of 2024 is allowed and the Resolution Plan submitted by Micro Capitals Private Limited is approved; Adjudicating Authority directed to pass consequential orders within one month; adverse observations recorded against RP Dharmendra Dhelariya in paragraphs 4 and 12 to 17 are expunged and set aside; parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Micro Capitals Private Limited (majority financial creditor and sole SRA) and Dharmendra Dhelariya (RP) appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 24.03.2025 rejecting the Resolution Plan for KSS Limited and making adverse remarks against the RP[cite: 6, 2, 3]. The NCLT rejected the plan alleging lack of fund infusion, violation of nemo judex in causa sua, and non-treatment of Customs and SEBI dues as secured debts[cite: 6, 4, 5]. NCLAT set aside the impugned order and approved the plan, holding that the proviso to Section 30(5) of the IBC explicitly permits a financial creditor to vote on its own plan, government dues are unsecured operational debts under Section 53(1)(e)(i) overriding Section 142A of the Customs Act, and the RP committed no misconduct[cite: 6].

case_title: Tropical Ventures Company Limited vs. Steering Committee of Incab Industries Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 662 of 2025, 16 of 2026 & 192 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Incab Industries Ltd. (incorporated 1920, manufacturer of basic iron/steel); Tropical Ventures Company Ltd. (Mauritius entity, Appellant in CA 662/2025 & 192/2026, assignee of Leader Universal Holdings Berhad); Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (Secured Financial Creditor/CoC member, Appellant in CA 16/2026); Pankaj Kumar Tibrewal (Resolution Professional); M/s Vedanta Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Naresh Lakhmichand Asrani (ultimate beneficial owner)[cite: 7, 3, 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities between 1997-1999 from resident lenders (ICICI Bank, Citibank, HSBC); Malaysian promoter entity Leader Universal Holdings Berhad (Leader Berhad) executed corporate deeds of guarantee to secure these facilities, and CD registered charges with ROC in 1998-1999; upon invocation, Leader Berhad paid ICICI Bank and Citibank between April 2000 and June 2001, while subsidiary Leader Cable Industry Berhad paid USD 3.75 Million to HSBC on 12.09.2000; on 08.03.2007, Leader Berhad assigned its debt claims to Tropical for USD 1 on as-is-where-is basis[cite: 7, 3, 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Leader Berhad paid actual principal amount of Rs. 85,79,26,944/- to Citibank and ICICI Bank upon guarantee invocation; Tropical filed a claim before RP as secured financial creditor for Rs. 21,52,84,33,946.87 (subsequently admitted by RP at Rs. 19,90,63,12,342/- and later Rs. 17,31,40,02,705/-), including over Rs. 1,646 Crores in interest[cite: 7, 4, 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD declared sick under SICA on 04.04.2000; RBI issued FEMA Notification No. 29/RB-2000 on 26.09.2000; SICA repealed on 01.12.2016; CIRP admitted on 07.08.2019; RP declared Tropical a related party on 17.11.2021; 22nd CoC meeting approved Vedanta's Resolution Plan on 23.06.2022 by 99.37% voting share; NCLT dismissed Tropical's IA 84/2022 on 08.01.2025 and directed RP re-verification; NCLT approved Vedanta's Plan (IA 646/2022) and dismissed Pegasus's IA 1511/2025 on 03.12.2025[cite: 7, 3, 4, 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Shareholding chart showing Naresh Asrani owning 100% of FW Enterprises Ltd., which owns 100% of Tropical, which owns 63% of Leader Universal (Mauritius), which in turn holds 51.2% direct shares in CD and 10% indirect shares via Satyam Incab Holdings; Deed of Assignment dated 08.03.2007; ROC charge registers showing charges only in favour of original resident banks without modification/transfer to Leader Berhad or Tropical; RBI Notification FEMA 29/RB-2000 dated 26.09.2000[cite: 7, 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed Tropical's IA 84/2022 on 08.01.2025 upholding related party status and rejection of HSBC claim; on 03.12.2025 NCLT dismissed Pegasus's IA 1511/2025 challenging Tropical's claim admission and approved Vedanta's Plan allocating Rs. 294.91 Crores to Tropical subject to pending appeals; Tropical appealed in CA 662/2025 and 192/2026; Pegasus appealed in CA 16/2026[cite: 7, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10].
legal_issues: 1. Whether Tropical is a 'related party' of the Corporate Debtor under Section 5(24)(i) and 5(24)(l) of the IBC by virtue of indirect step-down shareholding and common ultimate beneficial ownership. 2. Whether a non-resident guarantor or its foreign assignee can acquire and enforce a security interest in immovable property situated in India by way of subrogation under Section 140 of the Contract Act without prior permission of the RBI under Section 31 of FERA, 1973. 3. Whether the cap on reimbursement under RBI Notification No. FEMA 29/RB-2000 dated 26.09.2000 restricts the claim of a non-resident guarantor's assignee against a resident corporate debtor strictly to the rupee equivalent of the principal amount actually paid to resident lenders, precluding interest claims. 4. Whether CoC's resolution in its 22nd meeting placing disputed claim payouts in an escrow/interest-bearing account pending final judicial determination is valid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate veil and intermediate holding structures must be recognized to determine related party status under insolvency law where a holding entity exercises de facto control over a corporate debtor through multi-tiered step-down subsidiaries and common ultimate beneficial ownership; furthermore, contractual and statutory subrogation under general contract law cannot override mandatory foreign exchange statutory prohibitions requiring prior central bank approval to acquire security interests in domestic immovable properties, nor can an assignee recover amounts exceeding statutory reimbursement ceilings imposed on cross-border guarantee payments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(24)(i) of the IBC read with Section 2(87) Explanation (a) of the Companies Act, 2013, a corporate debtor is a subsidiary of a holding company even where control is exercised through an intermediate subsidiary; Section 31 of FERA, 1973 prohibits non-residents from acquiring any interest in immovable property by mortgage or otherwise without RBI permission, preventing subrogation of immovable charges; and Para 2A of RBI Notification No. FEMA 29/RB-2000 imposes an absolute statutory cap limiting reimbursement to the rupee equivalent of the amount actually paid by the non-resident guarantor, which cannot be relaxed by post-facto approval. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where undisputed shareholding records prove 63% ownership in an intermediate holding entity possessing 51.2% in the debtor, and no RBI permission under Section 31 FERA exists on record, nor is any modified charge registered with the Registrar of Companies under Section 77 of the Companies Act, the claimant cannot be treated as a secured creditor over immovable assets, and claims exceeding actual proof of payment to lenders must be disallowed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Tropical is a related party under Section 5(24); its claim is not secured over immovable properties of the Corporate Debtor; its admitted claim is legally capped at Rs. 85,79,26,944/- under FEMA Notification 29/2000 without interest; and the CoC's conditional plan approval mechanism was lawful; CA 662/2025 and 192/2026 dismissed, CA 16/2026 partly allowed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 662 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 192 of 2026 are dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 16 of 2026 is partly allowed; admission of claim of Tropical Ventures Company Ltd. is confined strictly to Rs. 85,79,26,944/-; Tropical is held not to be a secured creditor with respect to immovable properties of the Corporate Debtor; approval of the Resolution Plan dated 03.12.2025 is affirmed subject to this decision; Monitoring Committee directed to re-determine payouts and distribute escrowed funds within 30 days; parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: These connected appeals arose from the CIRP of Incab Industries Ltd[cite: 7, 3]. Tropical Ventures Company Ltd. appealed against NCLT Kolkata orders declaring it a related party and rejecting its secured claim under an HSBC facility, as well as challenging the payout escrow mechanism under Vedanta's approved Resolution Plan[cite: 7, 4, 5]. Financial creditor Pegasus appealed against the admission of Tropical's claim of over Rs. 1,731 Crores as a secured debt[cite: 7, 4, 7]. NCLAT dismissed Tropical's appeals and partly allowed Pegasus's appeal, holding that Tropical is a related party via step-down subsidiary control, cannot claim secured creditor status over immovable assets without RBI permission under Section 31 of FERA, and its claim is capped at Rs. 85,79,26,944/- (the actual principal paid to lenders) under RBI Notification FEMA 29/2000[cite: 7].

case_title: Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Limited vs. Arena Superstructures Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Arena Superstructures Private Limited (promoter of residential real estate project 'Lotus Arena-I', Sector-79, Noida); Appellant is Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Limited (ACRE, assignee of PNBHFL, sole institutional secured financial creditor holding 28.60% CoC voting share); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Viswanadha Sarma (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Purvanchal Projects Private Limited (SRA); Respondent No. 3 is Real Estate Allottees/Homebuyers (Financial Creditors in Class holding 71.11% CoC voting share); Respondent No. 4 is Dhankalash Distributors Pvt. Ltd. (unsecured financial creditor holding 0.29% voting share)[cite: 8, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Composite Loan Agreement dated 08.03.2017 executed by PNBHFL in favour of Corporate Debtor and co-borrowers (Fest Homes Developers and Villa Stone Propbuild) extending two facilities secured by mortgage over Sector-79 project land (50,000 sq. mtrs) and co-borrower's Sector-150 land (20,863 sq. mtrs), plus hypothecation of project receivables; PNBHFL assigned debt to ACRE on 25.04.2022; Corporate Debtor had entered into Builder-Buyer Agreements with homebuyers for 1,080 flats[cite: 8, 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Facility-I outstanding was Rs. 113,15,56,725.92 and Facility-II outstanding was Rs. 90,84,40,732.48; ACRE's admitted claim was Rs. 200,27,42,110/-; Liquidation value of Corporate Debtor assessed by Registered Valuers was Rs. 151,00,41,336/-; ACRE claimed statutory liquidation entitlement of Rs. 144,91,91,358/- under Section 53(1)(b) after CIRP costs of Rs. 6-13.86 Crores, whereas Approved Plan allocated Rs. 70 Crores in 4 tranches over 42 months[cite: 8, 5, 8, 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 29.10.2020 on Section 7 petition by Dhankalash; RP replaced on 09.06.2021; fresh Form-G issued on 30.06.2021; PNBHFL issued Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 22.02.2022; PNBHFL assigned debt to ACRE on 25.04.2022; CoC approved SRA's Plan on 10.07.2022 with 71.11% majority; RP filed IA 3392/2022 for approval and ACRE filed IA 3556/2022 objecting; NCLT approved Plan and dismissed objections on 19.07.2023[cite: 8, 7, 8, 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: PNBHFL's Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice dated 22.02.2022 expressly describing secured assets as 171 unsold units and excluding 909 sold units; project records proving 806 units (74.36% project area) allotted prior to mortgage creation on 20.03.2017, leaving only 274 units (25.64%) unsold; Registered Valuer reports (Anil Kumar Saxena and Ashish Kumar) determining liquidation value of Rs. 151 Crores after factoring in construction completion costs and receivables; actual CIRP costs of Rs. 13.86 Crores[cite: 8, 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench on 19.07.2023 approved Purvanchal's Resolution Plan in IA 3392/2022 and dismissed ACRE's objections in IA 3556/2022; ACRE appealed in CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 949 of 2023 contending that as sole secured creditor with Rs. 200 Cr debt, it was entitled to the entire net liquidation value of Rs. 145 Cr under Section 30(2)(b) and Section 53(1)(b)[cite: 8, 4, 5, 9, 10].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a dissenting secured financial creditor is entitled to receive the entire liquidation value of the corporate debtor under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53(1)(b) of the IBC, or whether its priority entitlement is limited to the realizable value of its underlying security interest. 2. Whether a mortgage created over a real estate project extends to units already allotted to homebuyers prior to mortgage execution in view of Section 11(4)(h) of RERA, and whether allotted flats form part of the corporate debtor's liquidation assets available for calculating the secured creditor's entitlement. 3. Whether future project receivables from homebuyers can be treated as an independent realizable asset for computing liquidation value payable to a dissenting secured creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate insolvency resolution of a real estate debtor, the statutory minimum liquidation entitlement of a dissenting secured creditor under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53(1)(b) is coextensive with and limited to the actual realizable value of its underlying security interest rather than its total admitted debt; any excess claim beyond the value of security interest falls under the lower priority of Section 53(1)(e)(ii), and units allotted to homebuyers under agreements for sale are statutorily insulated from mortgage encumbrances by virtue of RERA and supreme judicial precedents protecting allottee investments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 30(2)(b), 52(9), and 53(1)(b)(ii) read harmoniously establish that a secured creditor's priority under Section 53(1)(b) is confined strictly to the value of its security interest, while the unpaid balance falls into Section 53(1)(e)(ii); Section 11(4)(h) of RERA contains an overriding non-obstante prohibition against creating charges over allotted units; and liquidation value under Regulation 2(k) of CIRP Regulations is determined on the hypothetical deemed liquidation of the debtor as on the insolvency commencement date, precluding speculation on future customer receivables that depend on ongoing project construction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Predecessor lender's own statutory Section 13(2) SARFAESI demand notice expressly restricting security to unsold flats and excluding sold flats, coupled with project records showing 74.36% area allotted prior to mortgage date, conclusively limits the security interest to 25.64% of the project's liquidation value (Rs. 38.71 Crores). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: ACRE's security interest was restricted to unsold units valued at Rs. 38.71 Crores; the approved Resolution Plan provided ACRE Rs. 70 Crores along with preserved recovery rights against co-borrowers and third-party securities, which substantially exceeded its statutory minimum entitlement; the NCLT's approval order was lawful and CA 949/2023 was dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 949 of 2023 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench dated 19.07.2023 approving the Resolution Plan of Purvanchal Projects Private Limited is upheld against ACRE's objections; parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Limited (ACRE), sole secured financial creditor of real estate developer Arena Superstructures Private Limited, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 19.07.2023 approving Purvanchal Projects' Resolution Plan[cite: 8, 4]. ACRE contended that as a dissenting secured creditor with an admitted claim of Rs. 200.27 Crores, it was entitled under Section 30(2)(b) and Section 53(1)(b) to the entire liquidation value of Rs. 145 Crores rather than the Rs. 70 Crores allocated[cite: 8, 5, 8, 10]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Section 11(4)(h) of RERA, ACRE's security interest was confined only to unsold units (25.64% of the project, valued at Rs. 38.71 Crores) and did not extend to flats allotted to homebuyers[cite: 8]. Because the plan allocated Rs. 70 Crores, exceeding its security value, Section 30(2)(b) was fully satisfied[cite: 8].

case_title: M/s Raghava Square Private Limited vs. M/s IVRCL Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is IVRCL Limited (in liquidation as a going concern); Appellant is M/s Raghava Square Private Limited (successful auction bidder); Respondent No. 1 is Corporate Debtor represented by Chairman of Supervisory Committee; Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Sutanu Sinha (Liquidator); Respondents No. 3 to 29 are financial lenders/secured creditors (ICICI Bank, Union Bank of India, SBI, IDBI, etc.)[cite: 9, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was ordered into liquidation on 26.07.2019; after two failed auction rounds, Liquidator published a 3rd e-auction notice on 20.11.2021 under Regulation 32(e)/32A for the sale of IVRCL Limited as a going concern at a reserve price of Rs. 1,200 Crores on 'as is where is, whatever there is, and without recourse' basis; Appellant submitted a sole bid along with Rs. 50 Crores EMD and a self-styled 'Resolution Scheme' / 'Business Plan' proposing deferred cash payments over 18-24 months and claiming take-over of third-party assets/securities of 100% subsidiaries/joint ventures of the Corporate Debtor (comprising 1,670 acres of land)[cite: 9, 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total sale consideration was Rs. 1,200 Crores; Appellant deposited Rs. 50 Crores EMD on 27.12.2021 and a further Rs. 100 Crores on 26.09.2022; Appellant defaulted on paying the remaining balance consideration of Rs. 1,050 Crores within the schedule fixed by NCLT's order dated 15.06.2022 (requiring payment in six tranches ending 14.06.2023 with 12% interest)[cite: 9, 9, 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: E-auction conducted on 15.12.2021; Appellant declared successful bidder on 27.12.2021; Demand Notice issued on 29.12.2021; 16th SCC meeting held on 31.01.2022 informing bidder that liquidation regulations allow only 90 days for full payment; NCLT passed order in MA No. 2/2022 on 15.06.2022 setting a 12-month payment schedule; NCLT passed order in IA No. 656/2022 on 25.07.2022 directing parties to scrupulously follow business plan; Appellant filed IA No. 357/2023 (restraint on alienation) on 22.02.2023; Appellant filed IA No. 947/2023 (time extension) on 05.06.2023; Liquidator issued cancellation and forfeiture letter on 28.07.2023; Appellant filed IA No. 1314/2023 (challenge to cancellation) on 09.08.2023; NCLT rejected time extensions on 02.08.2024 and dismissed restraint and cancellation challenges on 05.02.2025 (granting 30 days final cure period)[cite: 9, 9, 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 3rd E-Auction Information Process Document dated 20.11.2021 stating sale of IVRCL Limited as a going concern on 'no recourse' basis with no transfer of title beyond company assets; Minutes of 15th, 16th, 18th, 20th, and 22nd SCC meetings confirming lenders' categorical disagreement with inclusion of subsidiary assets and non-concurrence to business plan terms; Virtual Data Room information; Clause 10.5 of E-Auction Document empowering Liquidator to forfeit EMD upon payment default[cite: 9, 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II on 02.08.2024 rejected IA Nos. 947/2023 and 1257/2024 seeking payment timeline extension, and on 05.02.2025 dismissed IA No. 357/2023 (holding subsidiary assets excluded under Section 36(4)(d) and business plan unapproved) and IA No. 1314/2023 (granting 30 days final opportunity to pay Rs. 1,050 Crores failing which cancellation and forfeiture under clause 10.5 stood confirmed); Appellant filed four appeals before NCLAT Chennai Bench[cite: 9, 6, 8].
legal_issues: 1. Whether in an e-auction sale of a corporate debtor as a going concern during liquidation under Regulation 32A of the Liquidation Regulations, the auction purchaser can introduce a unilateral 'Business Plan' to include assets of third-party subsidiaries, joint ventures, or associates of the corporate debtor contrary to Section 36(4)(d) of the IBC. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority's earlier orders dated 15.06.2022 and 25.07.2022 operated as a judicial approval of the bidder's Business Plan and inclusion of subsidiary assets. 3. Whether the auction purchaser was entitled to an extension of time beyond the 12-month period granted by the Adjudicating Authority to deposit the balance sale consideration of Rs. 1,050 Crores. 4. Whether the Liquidator's cancellation of the sale and forfeiture of Rs. 150 Crores deposited by the bidder under Clause 10.5 of the E-Auction Process Document was valid and lawful.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a statutory liquidation sale of a corporate debtor conducted on an 'as is where is and without recourse' basis, the subject matter of sale is strictly circumscribed by the public auction notice and statutory parameters; the assets of independent Indian or foreign subsidiary companies are statutorily excluded from the debtor's liquidation estate by express legislative prohibition, and a successful bidder cannot expand the contractual scope of the purchase to include subsidiary assets under the pretext of an unapproved business plan, nor can it withhold balance sale consideration on that ground. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 36(4)(d) of the IBC and Regulation 21A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary of the corporate debtor are explicitly excluded from the liquidation estate and cannot be used for recovery in liquidation; while shares held by the debtor in a subsidiary form part of intangible assets under Section 36(3)(d), the underlying physical assets of subsidiaries belong to separate legal entities. Furthermore, NCLT orders directing parties to adhere to agreed terms do not constitute judicial sanction of an extra-statutory business plan altering liquidation norms. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unambiguous stipulations in the E-Auction Process Information Document restricting the sale strictly to the corporate debtor on 'no recourse' basis, coupled with SCC meeting minutes establishing that lenders never agreed to the inclusion of subsidiary assets or to the business plan, estop the bidder from asserting that its bid encompassed third-party assets. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bidder's attempt to incorporate subsidiary assets through a business plan was contrary to Section 36(4)(d) and unapproved by lenders; refusal to extend time to deposit balance sale consideration was fully justified; the appeals were dismissed on merits, with the divergence of opinion regarding forfeiture of the deposited Rs. 150 Crores referred to the Hon'ble Chairperson for nomination of a third member.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 93/2025, 96/2025, 309/2024, and 310/2024 are dismissed on substantive merits regarding refusal of asset restraint, denial of time extension, and non-approval of the business plan; on the exclusive issue of the validity of forfeiture of Rs. 150 Crores deposited by the Appellant, the matter is referred to the Hon'ble Chairperson, NCLAT for appropriate nomination of a third member under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 due to a split between Member (Judicial) [upholding forfeiture] and Member (Technical) [ordering refund].
summary: M/s Raghava Square Private Limited, successful bidder in the 3rd e-auction for IVRCL Limited as a going concern for Rs. 1,200 Crores, appealed against NCLT Hyderabad orders refusing to restrain lenders from alienating subsidiary assets, denying extensions to pay balance consideration of Rs. 1,050 Crores, and declining to set aside bid cancellation and forfeiture of Rs. 150 Crores[cite: 9, 6, 8]. The bidder argued that its bid included 1,670 acres of subsidiary lands under an approved Business Plan[cite: 9]. NCLAT held that Section 36(4)(d) of the IBC strictly excludes subsidiary assets from the liquidation estate and that the Business Plan was never approved[cite: 9, 7, 8]. The bench affirmed the dismissal of the substantive prayers, but referred the forfeiture issue to the Chairperson due to a judicial split[cite: 9].

case_title: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority vs. Ayyagari Viswanadha Sarma, Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA, statutory authority and lessor of project land); Corporate Debtor is Arena Superstructures Private Limited (sub-lessee, developer of Lotus Arena-I, Sector-79, Noida); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Ayyagari Viswanadha Sarma (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Purvanchal Projects Private Limited (SRA); Respondent No. 3 is ACRE (Secured Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 4 is Homebuyers in class[cite: 10, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Registered tripartite Sub-Lease Deed dated 19.10.2012 executed between NOIDA (Lessor), M/s Sequel Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. (Lessee/Parent), and Corporate Debtor Arena Superstructures Pvt. Ltd. (Sub-Lessee, 100% subsidiary of Lessee) demising 50,000 sq. meters of commercial plot SC-01/A2, Sector-79, Noida for 90 years for developing a group housing/sports city project; Sub-Lease Deed Clause II(f) explicitly stipulated that NOIDA as Lessor shall have the first charge on the plot towards payment of all dues of Lessor[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on payment of lease premium, annual ground rent, interest, time extension charges, and farmers' compensation; NOIDA filed claim in Form-C for Rs. 84.19 Crores, out of which RP admitted Rs. 68.90 Crores but classified NOIDA as an unsecured 'Operational Creditor'; the approved Resolution Plan allocated only approx. Rs. 7-8 Crores to NOIDA while extinguishing its remaining statutory and leasehold dues[cite: 10, 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tripartite Sub-Lease Deed registered on 19.10.2012[cite: 10]; CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 29.10.2020[cite: 10, 7]; NOIDA submitted Form-C on 12.05.2021 and clarificatory letter on 16.08.2021[cite: 10]; NOIDA filed IA No. 5361 of 2021 challenging classification as operational creditor and reduction of dues, and later IA No. 5979 of 2022[cite: 10, 6]; CoC approved Plan on 10.07.2022[cite: 10, 9]; NCLT approved Plan and dismissed NOIDA's applications on 19.07.2023[cite: 10, 4, 6, 9]; NOIDA appealed under Section 61 on 18.08.2023[cite: 10, 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Sub-Lease Deed dated 19.10.2012, specifically Part II Clause (f) creating an express contractual first charge in favour of NOIDA to secure all dues; layout plans approved by NOIDA in 2014; claims verification list by RP admitting Rs. 68.90 Crores as operational debt; approved Resolution Plan allocating only Rs. 7-8 Crores to NOIDA[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench on 19.07.2023 approved Purvanchal Projects' Resolution Plan and dismissed NOIDA's IA Nos. 5361/2021 and 5979/2022 without examining the contractual first charge under the Sub-Lease Deed; NOIDA appealed in CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 1231 of 2023 contending that it is a Secured Creditor under Section 3(30) & 3(31) of the IBC by virtue of the registered Sub-Lease Deed and Sections 13 and 13-A of the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976[cite: 10, 4, 6].
legal_issues: 1. Whether NOIDA constitutes a 'Secured Creditor' under Section 3(30) read with Section 3(31) and 3(33) of the IBC by virtue of the express first charge created under the registered tripartite Sub-Lease Deed dated 19.10.2012 securing lease dues. 2. Whether the Explanation inserted in Section 3(31) of the IBC by the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 (excluding security interests created merely by operation of law) applies to disentitle a statutory lessor whose first charge is founded upon a bilateral registered contract. 3. Whether the Resolution Plan's classification and treatment of NOIDA as an ordinary Operational Creditor violated Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, requiring modification of the plan's distribution.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a statutory development authority as landowner executes a registered lease or sub-lease deed with a corporate debtor containing an express contractual covenant creating a first charge over the demised land to secure unpaid lease premiums and dues, such charge constitutes a valid 'security interest' created by a 'transaction' under the IBC, elevating the authority to the status of a 'secured creditor'; such consensual contractual charge is not extinguished by legislative amendments that exclude charges arising merely by operation of law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(31) of the IBC defines 'security interest' as any right, title, interest or claim created in favour of a creditor by a 'transaction' securing payment, and Section 3(33) defines 'transaction' to include an agreement or arrangement in writing; a registered tripartite sub-lease deed covenanting a first charge fully satisfies Sections 3(31) and 3(33). Furthermore, the Explanation inserted in Section 3(31) by the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 (notified on 22.05.2026) clarifies that security interests created merely by operation of law are excluded, which does not affect consensual security interests created pursuant to bilateral registered lease agreements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of the registered Sub-Lease Deed containing Clause II(f) declaring a first charge on the plot in favour of the Lessor for all dues conclusively proves the creation of a contractual security interest; non-invocation of statutory penal provisions under Section 13/13A of the UPIADA is immaterial since the contractual charge independently establishes secured creditor status. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan and Adjudicating Authority erred in classifying NOIDA as an ordinary Operational Creditor; NOIDA is a Secured Creditor of the Corporate Debtor; the approval order was set aside to the limited extent of the distribution mechanism, and the RP was directed to propose an addendum treating NOIDA as a Secured Creditor for CoC approval.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1231 of 2023 is disposed of by setting aside the Impugned Order dated 19.07.2023 to the limited extent of the distribution proposed in the Resolution Plan; the Resolution Professional is directed to issue an addendum to the Resolution Plan treating NOIDA as a Secured Creditor and revising the proposed distribution; the CoC shall consider the revised distribution and submit the same before the Adjudicating Authority for final approval; no order as to costs.
summary: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 19.07.2023 approving the Resolution Plan of Purvanchal Projects for Arena Superstructures Private Limited[cite: 10, 4, 6]. NOIDA challenged its classification as an ordinary Operational Creditor and the allocation of only Rs. 7-8 Crores against its admitted claim of Rs. 68.90 Crores[cite: 10]. NCLAT held that Clause II(f) of the registered tripartite Sub-Lease Deed dated 19.10.2012 created an express first charge on the demised land, satisfying the definition of 'security interest' created by a transaction under Sections 3(31) and 3(33) of the IBC[cite: 10]. The 2026 Amendment was held inapplicable to contractual lease covenants[cite: 10]. NCLAT set aside the distribution mechanism and directed the RP and CoC to treat NOIDA as a Secured Creditor under an addendum to the Plan[cite: 10].

case_title: Mr. Raakesh B Kulwal vs. Param Dairy Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Param Dairy Limited (supplier of butter and ghee); Corporate Debtor is M/s Jhandewalas Foods Limited (manufacturer and trader of butter and ghee); Appellant is Mr. Raakesh B Kulwal, suspended director of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Mahesh Chandra Sharma, Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of butter and ghee by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor based on confirmed purchase orders and commercial invoices raised between 01.04.2021 and 28.06.2022[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 3,83,40,235/- (comprising principal amount of Rs. 3,08,07,235/- and compounded interest of Rs. 75.33 Lakhs); default occurred upon expiry of 30-day payment credit periods on unpaid invoices between 2021 and 2022[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued on 02.11.2022[cite: 11]; Corporate Debtor replied on 14.12.2022 disputing liability on account of four alleged defective invoices from February/March 2020[cite: 11]; pre-institution mediation under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act initiated subsequently by Corporate Debtor and ended as a non-starter[cite: 11]; Operational Creditor filed Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 26/9/JPR/2023[cite: 11]; Adjudicating Authority admitted petition on 04.07.2025[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor produced 2021-2022 invoices, proof of delivery, and ledger accounts showing recurring unpaid balances[cite: 11]; Corporate Debtor produced laboratory test reports dated March 2020 from a Delhi lab for perishable goods supplied to Jaipur which covered only three invoices rather than four and showed no contemporaneous dispute communications, rejection memos, or debit notes prior to the Section 8 notice[cite: 11]; Corporate Debtor made part-payments towards outstanding invoices even after receiving the Section 8 Demand Notice[cite: 11]; Corporate Debtor's ledger showed 'stock damages' entries created only from 01.01.2023 onwards[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on 04.07.2025, holding the alleged dispute to be a moonshine defence[cite: 11]; Appellant appealed to NCLAT contending that supply of substandard ghee confirmed by lab reports, return of 67,310 kgs of stock, and Section 12A mediation constituted genuine pre-existing disputes[cite: 11].
legal_issues: 1. Whether laboratory test reports of perishable goods obtained belatedly without contemporaneous protest, rejection memos, or debit notes prior to the Section 8 Demand Notice constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute under the IBC[cite: 11]. 2. Whether pre-institution mediation proceedings under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act initiated subsequent to the service of a Section 8 Demand Notice qualify as a pre-existing dispute[cite: 11]. 3. Whether part-payments made towards outstanding invoices after receipt of a Section 8 Demand Notice constitute an admission of debt and default[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 of the IBC, a dispute must be genuinely pre-existing and supported by contemporaneous documentary evidence brought to the creditor's attention prior to the receipt of the statutory Demand Notice; allegations of defective supplies, unadjusted ledger entries, or subsequent legal proceedings initiated as an afterthought after receipt of the Demand Notice cannot defeat insolvency admission[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d), the existence of a dispute is strictly assessed prior to the delivery of the Section 8 notice; post-notice pre-institution mediation under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act or post-notice civil suits do not qualify as pre-existing disputes[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Mobilox standard, the defence must be plausible and not mere bluster; where a debtor produces inconsistent lab test reports for perishable goods tested in another state without any contemporaneous rejection memos or debit notes, and continues making part-payments post-Demand Notice while inserting ledger damage entries post-notice, the defence is spurious and illusory[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to establish any credible pre-existing dispute prior to 02.11.2022, and the operational debt exceeded the Rs. 1 Crore threshold; NCLT's admission order was affirmed and the appeal was dismissed[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1013 of 2025 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 04.07.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Jaipur Bench) in CP (IB) No. 26/9/JPR/2023 admitting the Section 9 application is sustained; the Interim Resolution Professional is directed to proceed with CIRP in accordance with law; no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: Mr. Raakesh B Kulwal, suspended director of Jhandewalas Foods Limited, appealed against the NCLT Jaipur Bench order dated 04.07.2025 admitting a Section 9 application filed by Param Dairy Limited for an operational debt of Rs. 3.83 Crores[cite: 11]. The Appellant contended that genuine pre-existing disputes existed regarding inferior quality of ghee, return of 67,310 kg of stock, and subsequent commercial mediation[cite: 11]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the alleged quality disputes were not raised contemporaneously prior to the Section 8 demand notice and laboratory reports were inconsistent afterthoughts[cite: 11]. Furthermore, post-notice mediation cannot constitute a pre-existing dispute, and part-payments made after the demand notice confirmed debt and default[cite: 11].

case_title: Rahul Bhakat vs. M/s. Sree UGCL Projects Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is M/s Sree UGCL Projects Limited (subcontractor for mining, crushing, and breaking of ROM); Corporate Debtor is M/s Geosphere Industries Pvt. Ltd. (formerly Godawari Natural Resources Limited, contractor of Jayaswal Neco Industries Limited); Appellant is Rahul Bhakat, Ex-director of Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Ashutosh Khemani, IRP[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Letter of engagement dated 14.03.2019 and Work Order dated 23.03.2019 (amended 14.11.2019 and 26.12.2019) issued by Corporate Debtor to Operational Creditor for screening, crushing, and breaking of run-of-mine ore; Clause 11 stipulated invoice payment within 30 days, while Clauses 19 and 20 provided the Corporate Debtor the contractual right to levy penalties for deficient performance or failure to meet size specifications[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor raised 7 invoices between 17.12.2019 and 31.03.2020 totaling Rs. 15.87 Crores[cite: 12]; claimed default in Section 8 notice was Rs. 18,56,78,817/- (principal Rs. 10.60 Crores + interest Rs. 7.96 Crores)[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor issued 7 contemporaneous letters between 19.08.2019 and 13.03.2020 complaining of excessive fines and low output[cite: 12]; penalty communication of Rs. 11.38 Crores issued on 24.07.2020[cite: 12]; draft settlement MoU executed on 20.12.2021[cite: 12]; credit note for Rs. 10.60 Crores purportedly issued on 30.01.2023[cite: 12]; Work Completion Certificate issued on 15.06.2023[cite: 12]; Demand Notice under Section 8 issued on 19.09.2024[cite: 12]; Corporate Debtor replied on 11.10.2024 disputing liability and asserting pre-existing disputes[cite: 12]; NCLT Cuttack admitted Section 9 petition on 17.10.2025[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Seven contemporaneous letters (19.08.2019 to 13.03.2020) detailing undersized fines (15-20% against 5% contractual cap)[cite: 12]; penalty letter dated 24.07.2020 imposing Rs. 11.38 Crores penalty[cite: 12]; settlement MoU dated 20.12.2021 originated by Operational Creditor expressly acknowledging ongoing quality disputes in Clause 1[cite: 12]; stamped Credit Note dated 30.01.2023 for Rs. 10.60 Crores[cite: 12]; WhatsApp communications demonstrating Work Completion Certificate was issued on creditor's request for income tax purposes[cite: 12]; ledger entries reflecting credit note adjustments[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on 17.10.2025, holding that protest letters were not followed by civil/arbitral suits, the credit note was fabricated, and the completion certificate proved satisfactory performance[cite: 12]; Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 12].
legal_issues: 1. Whether contemporaneous written communications alleging performance deficiencies and levying contractual penalties issued years prior to the Section 8 demand notice constitute a pre-existing dispute under Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC, even absent prior arbitral or civil proceedings[cite: 12]. 2. Whether an Adjudicating Authority in summary Section 9 proceedings has the jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the veracity, authenticity, or alleged forgery of a stamped credit note and settlement MoU[cite: 12]. 3. Whether a Work Completion Certificate issued specifically for tax compliance estops a corporate debtor from asserting pre-existing performance disputes[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an operational insolvency application under Section 9 of the IBC, the adjudicating authority is strictly confined to determining whether a plausible, non-frivolous dispute existed prior to the demand notice; the statute does not require the prior institution of a civil suit, arbitration, or debit note as a condition precedent to establish a pre-existing dispute, nor can summary insolvency proceedings be used to determine allegations of document forgery or adjudicate underlying contractual breaches[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) require rejection of an insolvency petition upon notice of an existing dispute; the standard under Mobilox Innovations is merely whether the defence raises a plausible contention requiring further investigation that is not mere bluster, without requiring proof that the defence will ultimately succeed on merits in civil law[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Receipt of multiple contemporaneous letters regarding substandard execution, a penalty demand notice of Rs. 11.38 Crores, and a draft settlement MoU originated by the creditor acknowledging ongoing quality disputes provide conclusive evidence of a real pre-existing dispute, which cannot be extinguished by a completion certificate shown to have been sought for tax purposes[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor established substantial pre-existing disputes originating between 2019 and 2021, long before the 2024 demand notice; NCLT exceeded its summary jurisdiction by trying issues of forgery and merits; the admission order was erroneous, and the appeal was allowed[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1636 of 2025 is allowed; the impugned order dated 17.10.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Cuttack Bench) in C.P. (IB)/2/CB/2025 initiating CIRP against M/s Geosphere Industries Pvt. Ltd. is set aside; the Corporate Debtor is released from the rigours of CIRP and allowed to function independently through its board of directors with immediate effect; no order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary: Rahul Bhakat, ex-director of Geosphere Industries Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Cuttack order dated 17.10.2025 admitting a Section 9 application filed by operational creditor M/s Sree UGCL Projects Limited for an alleged default of Rs. 18.56 Crores[cite: 12]. The Corporate Debtor contended that the debt was contested through seven contemporaneous letters from 2019-2020 complaining of defective crushing and excessive fines, a penalty notice of Rs. 11.38 Crores, a draft MoU, and a credit note[cite: 12]. Setting aside the admission order, NCLAT held that plausible pre-existing disputes existed long prior to the demand notice[cite: 12]. IBC summary proceedings cannot adjudicate contractual breaches or document authenticity, rendering Section 9 unmaintainable[cite: 12].

case_title: AKJ Metals Private Limited vs. Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is AKJ Metals Private Limited (purchaser/transferee in possession); Corporate Debtor is RCI Industries and Technologies Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya (Resolution Professional); Respondents No. 2 to 5 are suspended directors; Respondent No. 6 is Additional Deputy Commissioner Solan, HP; Respondent No. 7 / R2 in connected appeal are Rikayaa Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. and Rikayaa Greentech Pvt. Ltd. (lessees); JTL Industries Limited is the SRA[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement to Sell dated 24.01.2020 executed between Corporate Debtor and Appellant for Nalagarh property for Rs. 2.29/2.30 Crores (state government permission granted 07.06.2021 and deed of endorsement executed 17.06.2021); Agreement to Sell dated 31.12.2020 for Baddi property for Rs. 3.50/3.53 Crores; full consideration paid and physical possession delivered to Appellant prior to CIRP; Appellant instituted Civil Suit Nos. 755/2021 and 756/2021 before Sr. Civil Judge, New Delhi culminating in Settlement Agreement dated 13.12.2021 and Consent Decrees dated 24.12.2021 appointing a Court Receiver; Appellant subsequently executed 15-year registered Leave and License agreements in early 2022 with Rikayaa entities[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 9 petition against Corporate Debtor initiated on 15.01.2019 and admitted on 25.11.2022; RP claimed properties worth Rs. 4.70 Cr (Baddi) and Rs. 2.29 Cr (Nalagarh) were siphoned off at undervalued consideration[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreements to sell executed on 24.01.2020 and 31.12.2020; Civil Court Consent Decrees passed on 24.12.2021; HP High Court order directing transfer on 10.03.2023; CIRP commenced on 25.11.2022; RP filed IA Nos. 3156 & 3793 of 2023 seeking possession under Sections 18/25; RP filed Section 66 avoidance application IA No. 5153 of 2023 on 22.08.2023; CoC approved JTL Industries' Plan on 17.08.2024; SRA filed affidavit relinquishing rights over both properties on 17.04.2025; NCLT approved Plan in IA 51/2024 and ordered dispossession in IA 3156 & 3793 on 09.10.2025[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreements to Sell dated 24.01.2020 and 31.12.2020; proof of payment of full consideration; certified Consent Decrees dated 24.12.2021 under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC appointing Court Receiver; Himachal Pradesh High Court judgment dated 10.03.2023; registered Leave and License agreements dated 11.02.2022 and 19.04.2022; SRA affidavit dated 17.04.2025 relinquishing all rights/claims to the properties; pending Section 66 avoidance application IA 5153/2023[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi on 09.10.2025 approved the Resolution Plan (IA 51/2024) recording that SRA does not claim the two properties, but simultaneously allowed RP's IA Nos. 3156 and 3793 of 2023 directing Appellant to forthwith hand over physical possession to the RP; Appellant appealed to NCLAT contending possessory rights under Section 53A TPA and finality of Civil Court consent decrees[cite: 13].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional and Adjudicating Authority under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 25 of the IBC can summarily dispossess a third-party purchaser in physical possession whose possessory rights are protected under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and recognized by a final, unappealed Consent Decree of a competent Civil Court[cite: 13]. 2. Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to sit in appeal over, invalidate, or bypass a Consent Decree passed by a competent Civil Court under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC[cite: 13]. 3. Whether the Resolution Professional can seek summary recovery of physical possession under Section 18/25 while a separate application for fraudulent trading under Section 66 of the IBC is pending adjudication[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority exercising summary insolvency jurisdiction under the IBC lacks the legal competence to nullify, override, or sit in appeal over a valid, unappealed Consent Decree passed by a competent Civil Court; the custody and control powers of an insolvency professional under Sections 18 and 25 do not extend to summarily evicting third parties holding lawful physical possession protected by the doctrine of part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, especially where the assets have been expressly excluded from the approved resolution plan[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 18(1)(f) and its Explanation, the insolvency professional is only authorized to take custody of assets over which the debtor has subsisting ownership rights and cannot seize assets owned or held by third parties; Section 66 of the IBC empowers the Tribunal to direct monetary contributions for fraudulent trading but does not authorize the summary dispossession of immovable properties subject to civil court decrees[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the evidentiary record establishes that an agreement to sell was executed, full consideration was discharged, physical possession was transferred prior to CIRP, and a competent Civil Court recognized such possessory rights through a final consent decree appointing a receiver for ministerial conveyance, possessory title is fully established[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the summary handover of the Baddi and Nalagarh properties to the RP; directions for dispossession were set aside, and status quo was directed to be maintained pending adjudication of the Section 66 application; appeals allowed[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1606 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1607 of 2025 are allowed; the impugned orders dated 09.10.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi) in IA-3156/2023 and IA-3793/2023 directing the Appellant to hand over possession of the Baddi and Nalagarh properties to the RP are set aside; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to decide IA No. 5153/2023 under Section 66 expeditiously; status quo regarding possession shall be maintained, and Appellant shall not transfer, alienate, or encumber the properties pending disposal of IA No. 5153/2023; no order as to costs[cite: 13].
summary: AKJ Metals Private Limited appealed against NCLT New Delhi orders dated 09.10.2025 in IA Nos. 3156 & 3793 of 2023 directing it to hand over possession of two industrial properties (Baddi and Nalagarh) to the RP of RCI Industries and Technologies Limited[cite: 13]. The Appellant had purchased the properties under Agreements to Sell in 2020, paid consideration, taken possession pre-CIRP, and obtained civil court Consent Decrees[cite: 13]. NCLAT set aside the eviction directions, holding that NCLT cannot override binding civil court consent decrees or summarily dispossess a third party protected under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act[cite: 13]. Status quo was maintained pending the Section 66 avoidance application[cite: 13].

case_title: Abhishek Singh vs. Tetra-Pak India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is Manpasand Beverages Ltd.; Appellant is Abhishek Singh, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 in CA 1833/2025 is Rajaram Foods Products India Ltd. (formerly Capricorn Food Products India Ltd., supplier of mango and guava pulp); Respondent No. 1 in CA 105/2026 is Tetra-Pak India Private Limited; Respondent No. 2 are respective IRPs (Mr. Pankaj Khetan and Mr. Darshan Bharatbhai Patel)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase orders issued by Corporate Debtor to Capricorn Food Products India Ltd. for supply of fruit pulp against invoices; commercial packaging contracts entered into with Tetra-Pak India Private Limited[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In CA 1833/2025, Rajaram claimed unpaid operational debt of Rs. 5.05 Crores (principal Rs. 4.44 Crores for invoices between 21.03.2018 and 25.03.2019 + interest Rs. 61.72 Lakhs); Corporate Debtor established running account payments of Rs. 7.49 Crores across 80 bank entries between 26.03.2018 and 30.03.2019[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Rajaram issued Section 8 notice on 08.06.2019; Corporate Debtor replied on 13.06.2019 citing GST search/seizures, lack of access, and stating accounts would be settled 'if any payable'; Section 9 CP (IB) No. 595/2019 filed on 17.07.2019 (disposed on 09.03.2021 and later restored); NCLT Ahmedabad admitted CP 595/2019 on 19.11.2025; NCLAT granted interim stay of admission order on 24.11.2025; while stay was operating, NCLT Ahmedabad admitted a second Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 812/2019 filed by Tetra-Pak on 12.01.2026[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Contemporaneous emails (2015-2019) and signed joint inspection minutes dated 10.02.2017 confirming rejected batches of puffed/leaking fruit pulp and quality issues; formal statement of Capricorn's Assistant Manager and MD recorded under CGST investigation on 23.08.2019, 04.10.2019, and 14.10.2019 admitting circular fake invoicing without actual movement of goods and voluntary reversal of Rs. 1.54 Crores ITC; CBI Section 160 CrPC Notice dated 13.07.2023 confirming Capricorn had written off Rs. 4.36 Crores of Manpasand receivables in its books for FY 2019 and 2020; Section 14 moratorium order subsisting from 19.11.2025[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted Rajaram's Section 9 petition on 19.11.2025 holding the reply to demand notice was an admission; NCLAT stayed that order on 24.11.2025; despite the stayed CIRP, NCLT Ahmedabad admitted Tetra-Pak's Section 9 petition on 12.01.2026; Appellant appealed both admission orders[cite: 14].
legal_issues: 1. Whether admissions by an operational creditor's officers before statutory GST authorities of circular invoicing without physical movement of goods, coupled with written-off receivables confirmed by CBI and contemporaneous quality rejection emails, establish a plausible pre-existing dispute barring Section 9 admission[cite: 14]. 2. Whether a qualified reply to a Section 8 demand notice offering to reconcile accounts 'if any payable' due to ongoing search and seizures constitutes an unconditional admission of debt[cite: 14]. 3. Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to admit a subsequent Section 9 insolvency petition and trigger a second, parallel CIRP against a corporate debtor when an earlier CIRP admission order is subsisting, even if the earlier order has been stayed by an appellate tribunal[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt substantiated on paper transactions that statutory investigative agencies have established as circular and sham invoicing without physical movement of goods, combined with contemporaneous quality rejections and book write-offs, presents a genuine pre-existing dispute under Mobilox that cannot be resolved in summary insolvency proceedings; furthermore, the insolvency statutory framework prohibits the parallel initiation of multiple concurrent corporate insolvency resolution processes against the same corporate debtor, and an interim stay of a CIRP admission order keeps the statutory moratorium in abeyance but does not revive the debtor's status to permit a second CIRP admission[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) require dismissal where pre-existing disputes exist; a conditional statement agreeing to settle accounts 'if any payable' is not an admission of liability; Section 14(1)(a) prohibits the institution or continuation of proceedings against a corporate debtor during CIRP, and an interim appellate stay of a CIRP admission order does not extinguish the proceeding in rem so as to confer jurisdiction on an Adjudicating Authority to admit a second overlapping CIRP petition[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Signed minutes of defect meetings, contemporaneous emails rejecting batches, sworn statements of creditor officers before tax authorities admitting fictitious transactions, and formal CBI investigation notices recording write-offs constitute overwhelming evidence of pre-existing dispute[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt claimed by Rajaram was riddled with genuine pre-existing disputes and fraudulent transactions; Tetra-Pak's subsequent CIRP admission during a subsisting stayed CIRP was non-est in law for lack of jurisdiction; both appeals were allowed and the admission orders were set aside[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1833 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 105 of 2026 are allowed; the impugned order dated 19.11.2025 admitting Company Petition No. 595 of 2019 is set aside, CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor is quashed, and Manpasand Beverages Ltd. is released from the rigours of CIRP with immediate effect; the second impugned order dated 12.01.2026 in CP (IB) No. 812 of 2019 is declared non-est in law and set aside, with liberty granted to Tetra-Pak to file afresh if and when situation arises; no order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: Abhishek Singh, suspended director of Manpasand Beverages Ltd., appealed against two NCLT Ahmedabad orders: an order dated 19.11.2025 admitting Rajaram Foods' Section 9 petition (Rs. 5.05 Cr default), and an order dated 12.01.2026 admitting Tetra-Pak's Section 9 petition[cite: 14]. NCLAT allowed both appeals and quashed the CIRPs[cite: 14]. It held that Rajaram's debt was plagued by pre-existing disputes, evidenced by contemporaneous quality rejections, CBI-confirmed write-offs, and sworn admissions before GST authorities of circular invoicing without physical delivery[cite: 14]. Regarding Tetra-Pak's petition, NCLAT ruled that admitting a parallel CIRP during the subsistence of an earlier stayed CIRP is jurisdictionally impermissible and non-est in law[cite: 14].

case_title: Calcutta Pinjrapole Society vs. Pratap Mukherjee, Resolution Professional of RSI Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Calcutta Pinjrapole Society (registered society, owner/landlord); Corporate Debtor is RSI Private Limited (formerly R.S. Iron Industries Private Limited, former contractual lessee); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Pratap Mukherjee (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Merc Infra India Private Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Registered lease deed dated 05.01.1958 executed by Appellant leasing immovable property comprising a two-storied building, structures, and 14 bighas of land at 30, Goshala Road, Mauza Lillooah, Bally, Howrah to the Corporate Debtor for 21 years at a monthly rent of Rs. 675/-; lease expired by efflux of time on 31.12.1978; Corporate Debtor failed to vacate and continued in unlawful possession for 48 years[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor suffered civil eviction decree on 21.05.2005; Appellant submitted Claim Form B before RP for Rs. 68,72,94,678/- towards arrears of rent and mesne profits/occupier charges from 01.01.1979 to 2024, which RP rejected on 22.10.2024[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease ended on 31.12.1978; Title Suit No. 101/2004 decreed eviction on 21.05.2005; First Appellate Court affirmed eviction on 30.06.2010 (remanding mesne profits quantum); High Court dismissed second appeal SAT No. 431/2010 on 17.10.2012; Supreme Court dismissed SLP (C) No. 19628/2013 on 12.08.2013 directing execution; Executing Court dismissed Section 47 CPC objections on 21.02.2014; High Court in WPLRT 160/2014 on 14.09.2023 directed execution within 6 months; Corporate Debtor filed Section 10 IBC petition in 2019 admitted on 24.04.2024; Appellant filed IA No. 198/KB/2025 on 09.12.2024; NCLT rejected exclusion on 22.01.2026[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Lease Deed dated 05.01.1958; Trial Court judgment and eviction decree dated 21.05.2005; Supreme Court order dated 12.08.2013 affirming eviction; Calcutta High Court order dated 14.09.2023 setting aside Land Tribunal order and directing eviction handover; interim status quo order dated 12.05.2023 passed by Land Tribunal in favor of Appellant against State of West Bengal; Information Memorandum prepared by RP reflecting the property and pending litigations[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-II rejected Appellant's IA No. 198/KB/2025 on 22.01.2026 holding ownership was in dispute and Appellant failed to produce title deeds, while admitting contractual rent only; Appellant appealed to NCLAT seeking exclusion of the property from CIRP[cite: 15].
legal_issues: 1. Whether immovable property occupied by a corporate debtor as an unauthorised occupant following expiry of its lease and against whom a final decree of eviction has been affirmed up to the Supreme Court constitutes an 'asset' of the corporate debtor under Section 18(1)(f) of the IBC[cite: 15]. 2. Whether an Adjudicating Authority in Section 10 CIRP proceedings has the jurisdiction to question the ownership title of a landlord whose eviction decree against the debtor has attained judicial finality before the Supreme Court[cite: 15]. 3. Whether the Explanation to Section 18(1) of the IBC mandates the exclusion of third-party immovable property from the Information Memorandum and the resolution process[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Immovable property in which a corporate debtor holds no subsisting proprietary, contractual, or lawful possessory right on the insolvency commencement date cannot be categorized as an 'asset' of the corporate debtor under the IBC; the unauthorized and wrongful possession of an erstwhile tenant whose contractual lease has expired by efflux of time and who has suffered an eviction decree confirmed by the highest appellate court cannot be treated as a corporate asset, included in the Information Memorandum, or transferred to a resolution applicant[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 18(1)(f) and its Explanation, the interim resolution professional is only empowered to take custody of assets over which the debtor has ownership rights, and 'assets' expressly exclude assets owned by a third party in possession of the corporate debtor under contractual arrangements or otherwise; the statutory protections of the IBC and Section 14 moratorium protect only existing, subsisting, and enforceable rights, and cannot be leveraged to perpetuate unlawful occupancy or illegality[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A final civil court eviction decree affirmed by the High Court and Supreme Court, coupled with an expired lease deed, constitutes indisputable conclusive evidence that the debtor has no subsisting right or title in the property; the Adjudicating Authority committed patent error in demanding registered conveyance deeds from the landlord in summary proceedings[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had no subsisting right in the 14-bigha property; the NCLT's refusal to exclude the property was wholly unsustainable; the appeal was allowed and the property was excluded from CIRP, declaring all actions taken regarding the asset non-est[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 474 of 2026 is allowed; the impugned order dated 22.01.2026 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench) in I.A. (IB) No. 198/KB/2025 is set aside; prayer (i) of I.A. (IB) No. 198/KB/2025 is allowed, and the property measuring 14 Bighas and 1 Cottah at 30, Goshala Road, Mauza Lillooah, Bally, Howrah is excluded from the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor; all subsequent actions taken with respect to the said asset are declared non-est; Appellant is granted liberty to execute its eviction decree and pursue mesne profits before the civil court; parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 15].
summary: Calcutta Pinjrapole Society appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order dated 22.01.2026 rejecting its application (IA No. 198/KB/2025) to exclude its 14-bigha property in Howrah from the CIRP of RSI Private Limited[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor was an erstwhile lessee whose 21-year lease expired in 1978 and against whom an eviction decree had been affirmed up to the Supreme Court[cite: 15]. Setting aside the NCLT order, NCLAT held that under Section 18(1) of the IBC, property in which the debtor has no subsisting right and is in unauthorized, wrongful possession cannot constitute a corporate asset or be included in the resolution process[cite: 15]. The property was excluded from CIRP, and subsequent actions regarding it were declared non-est[cite: 15].

case_title: Sri. K.M. Abdulla vs. Kerala Chamber of Commerce & Industry
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sri K.M. Abdulla (former shareholder, Director, and Chairman of Respondent company between 2009-2011); Respondent is Kerala Chamber of Commerce & Industry (a Section 8 non-profit company under the Companies Act, 2013)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent Company, in a joint venture arrangement with Cherupushpam Films Pvt. Ltd., floated a special purpose vehicle project to construct a commercial multi-storied complex named 'Kerala Trade Centre' (KTC) at Marine Drive, Kochi; Appellant purportedly deposited funds in five instalments by cheques totaling Rs. 30,00,000/- upon an alleged oral offer of 18% interest per annum and space booking in the project[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed was non-refund of deposit of Rs. 30,00,000/- (out of which Rs. 25,00,000/- was captured under 'advance for space (booking charges)' in KTC's audited accounts for FY 2013-14) along with accrued interest at 18% per annum[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant issued statutory repayment demand notice on 12.06.2019 to the Chairman and Board of Directors of Respondent Company; Respondent replied denying deposit liability; Appellant filed Company Petition CP/30/KOB/2020 under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Kochi; NCLT dismissed petition on 06.10.2021; Appellant appealed to NCLAT; during pendency, Respondent was admitted into CIRP under Section 7/9 IBC in CP(IB)/33/KOB/2021 on 21.02.2022 and moratorium was declared[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited financial statements of Kerala Trade Centre for FY 2013-14 showing Rs. 25 Lakhs as advance for space booking in the name of Appellant; bank account records proving that funds were credited directly into the account of Kerala Trade Centre and not the Respondent company; advance deposit receipt dated 14.09.2013 issued by Kerala Trade Centre; Form TM-1 under Trade Marks Act, 1999 establishing Kerala Trade Centre as an independent commercial entity; branch audit report[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench dismissed CP/30/KOB/2020 on 06.10.2021 holding that monies were paid to Kerala Trade Centre, a separate entity, and not to the Respondent Company, leaving remedies open against KTC; Appellant appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLAT heard the appeal on 02.06.2026[cite: 16].
legal_issues: 1. Whether advances paid towards commercial space booking in a joint venture project (Kerala Trade Centre) and credited into its bank account constitute an accepted company 'deposit' with the parent Section 8 company (Kerala Chamber of Commerce & Industry) under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 16]. 2. Whether an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 for refund of company deposits survives or is rendered infructuous upon the initiation of CIRP and declaration of moratorium under Section 14 read with Section 238 of the IBC against the respondent company[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application seeking directions for the repayment of an alleged company deposit under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be sustained unless the claimant discharges the evidentiary burden of proving that the funds were actually accepted by and credited into the bank accounts of the respondent company itself; monies credited to a separate joint venture entity or special purpose vehicle for real estate booking do not constitute company deposits, and subsequent admission of the respondent into corporate insolvency resolution process interdicts independent recovery appeals by virtue of the overriding statutory moratorium under Section 14 and Section 238 of the IBC[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 applies strictly to defaults in repayment of deposits accepted under Section 73(2); commercial advances for space booking do not fall within the statutory remit of Section 73 deposits where the company never received the funds. Furthermore, Section 238 of the IBC accords overriding effect to the Section 14 moratorium, rendering parallel recovery appeals infructuous and reserving rights to file claims before the Resolution Professional under Sections 30(2) and 53(1) of the IBC[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish liability under Section 73(4), direct banking proof and ledger evidence demonstrating deposit into the respondent's books must be produced; where audited accounts, bank statements, and receipts demonstrate that funds were deposited with an independent third-party entity (KTC), the claim against the respondent company fails[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to establish that any deposit was made with the Respondent Company, and the Respondent's subsequent admission into CIRP rendered the appeal infructuous; the appeal lacked merit and was dismissed[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 57/2021 is dismissed as lacking merit and having been rendered infructuous in view of the subsequent admission of the Respondent Company into CIRP and declaration of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, reserving liberty to the Appellant to pursue remedies under the IBC or against Kerala Trade Centre in accordance with law; no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: Sri K.M. Abdulla appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against the NCLT Kochi order dated 06.10.2021 dismissing his petition under Section 73(4) which sought repayment of Rs. 30 Lakhs allegedly deposited with Kerala Chamber of Commerce & Industry with 18% interest[cite: 16]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Appellant failed to discharge the burden of proving that the deposit was made into the Respondent's accounts, as bank records and receipts showed the monies were credited to a separate joint venture entity, Kerala Trade Centre, for space booking[cite: 16]. Additionally, the subsequent initiation of CIRP and moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC against the Respondent rendered the appeal infructuous[cite: 16].

case_title: The Income Tax Department vs. The Registrar of Companies & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 150/2025 (with Restoration Nos. 06, 07, 08 & 09 of 2026 in Comp. App. Nos. 150, 151, 152 & 153 of 2025)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Income Tax Department (statutory revenue department of the Government of India); Respondent No. 1 is The Registrar of Companies (RoC); Respondent No. 2 in each connected appeal are struck-off corporate entities whose names had been removed from the register of companies by the RoC[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory assessment, reassessment, and tax recovery proceedings initiated by the Income Tax Department against Respondent No. 2 companies under the Income Tax Act, 1961, necessitating restoration of the companies' names on the register under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pending statutory tax liabilities against struck-off companies; NCLT Amaravati ordered restoration but imposed a cost of Rs. 25,000/- in each case on the Income Tax Department payable to the RoC towards Gazette publication charges and counsel fees[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Petitions filed by the Income Tax Department in C.A. Nos. 1/252/AMR/2025, 2/252/AMR/2025, 3/252/AMR/2025, and 4/252/AMR/2025; NCLT Amaravati passed common restoration orders on 17.07.2025 imposing costs; certified copies received by Appellant on 08.08.2025; appeals filed on 16.09.2025 (16 days delay); Registry reported defects on 02.10.2025; appeals dismissed under Rule 26 NCLAT Rules on 23.01.2026; Restoration Applications filed and allowed on 17.06.2026[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Restoration orders dated 17.07.2025 showing that NCLT Amaravati imposed costs of Rs. 25,000/- upon the Department solely on a passing oral prayer of the RoC without recording any finding of bad faith, frivolous litigation, or actual itemized expenditure; proofs of payment showing costs deposited under protest by the Department with RoC; medical and administrative records explaining the 16 days delay in filing[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravati Bench restored Respondent No. 2 companies to enable the Department to recover legitimate taxes, but ordered the Department to pay Rs. 25,000/- costs in each case to RoC under Rule 87A(4)(c) of NCLT Rules, 2016; Department appealed under Section 421 challenging solely the cost imposition; NCLAT recalled earlier dismissal orders, condoned 16 days delay, and adjudicated the merits of the cost orders[cite: 17].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has the authority under Rule 87A(4)(c) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 read with Section 35 CPC to mechanically impose costs upon a statutory authority, such as the Income Tax Department, when it applies under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 for the restoration of a struck-off company in discharge of sovereign revenue recovery functions[cite: 17]. 2. Whether an order imposing costs under Rule 87A(4)(c) can be sustained in the absence of a judicial determination and objective quantification of the actual expenses 'occasioned by' the application[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory powers to award costs under company tribunal procedural rules are compensatory and penal in nature, requiring strict judicial justification and quantification of expenses actually occasioned by the litigation; costs cannot be routinely or arbitrarily imposed upon a sovereign statutory department performing public duties to recover government revenue, as transferring costs between statutory arms of the government to cover ordinary administrative publications and counsel fees is unnecessary and superfluous[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 87A(4)(c) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 provides that the applicant shall pay to the RoC costs 'of, and occasioned by, the appeal or application, unless the Tribunal directs otherwise'; the term 'occasioned by' read with Section 35 CPC requires a judicious determination based on evidence of actual expenses incurred, while 'unless the Tribunal directs otherwise' vests discretion to exempt statutory authorities acting in good faith from paying costs[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An award of costs requires concrete evidence establishing that the litigation was frivolous, vexatious, or caused quantifiable extraordinary expenditure; a mechanical direction based solely on a passing request by the RoC without examining itemized expenses fails the test of judicial determination[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Income Tax Department initiated restoration proceedings bona fide to recover public taxes; NCLT erred in imposing costs without justification or quantification; the cost orders were unsustainable and quashed with a direction for refund[cite: 17].
operative_order: Restoration Applications (AT) (CH) Nos. 06, 07, 08 & 09 of 2026 are allowed and the dismissal order dated 23.01.2026 is recalled; 16 days delay in filing the appeals is condoned; Company Appeals (AT) (CH) Nos. 150, 151, 152 & 153 of 2025 are allowed; the impugned orders dated 17.07.2025 passed by NCLT Amaravati to the extent of imposing costs of Rs. 25,000/- on the Appellant in each case are quashed, and RoC is directed to refund the costs deposited under protest within 4 weeks; all pending IAs closed[cite: 17].
summary: The Income Tax Department appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against four orders dated 17.07.2025 passed by NCLT Amaravati which, while restoring four struck-off companies under Section 252(3) to enable tax assessments, directed the Department to pay Rs. 25,000/- costs in each case to the Registrar of Companies (RoC)[cite: 17]. Recalling an earlier procedural dismissal and condoning 16 days delay, NCLAT allowed the appeals on merits, holding that under Rule 87A(4)(c) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 read with Section 35 CPC, costs cannot be imposed arbitrarily without quantifying actual expenses occasioned[cite: 17]. Imposing costs on a sovereign authority discharging statutory tax recovery functions to fund another state arm was held superfluous; costs were quashed and refund ordered[cite: 17].

case_title: Bhawarlal Bhagrajji & Ors. vs. Jindutt Safe Vaults Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mr. Bhawarlal Bhagrajji, Mr. Babulal K Jain, Mr. Ghewarchand B Jain (Appellants 1 to 3, who did not press the appeal), and Mr. Tarun Kumar and Mr. Rahul Kumar J Jain (Appellants 4 and 5, legal heirs of Late Jayanthilal M Jain and Late Mrs. J. Lalitha Bai), holding 33.56% direct equity and 58.29% family majority shareholding; Respondents are M/s Jindutt Safe Vaults Private Limited (Respondent No. 1 company), four directors Mr. Nathmal Jain, Mr. Mukesh Kumar Bhandari, Mr. Himmatmal Bhandari, Mr. Dhanraj Bhandari (Respondents 2 to 5, holding 41.7% shares), and statutory auditor CA Rahul M Jain (Respondent 6)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operation and management of a private family safe-deposit vault company; underlying disputes regarding transmission of shares of deceased family members and operation of corporate bank accounts[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants alleged diversion of company funds to individual director accounts under guise of expenses without board approval, sharp unexplained increases in profit and loss expenditure, and an unauthorized loan of Rs. 40 Lakhs obtained from an ex-director without Board Resolution[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellants filed petition CP/124(CHE)/2022 on 20.04.2022 under Sections 59, 241, and 242 alleging oppression and mismanagement; during pendency, Appellants filed IA(CA)/96(CHE)/2023 on 19.05.2023 under Section 242(4) seeking directions for production of eight years of company bank statements and individual ledgers; NCLT Chennai dismissed the IA and disposed of the CP on 04.06.2026 granting liberty; Appellants filed Company Appeal on 02.07.2026 along with IA No. 134/2026 seeking condonation of 28 days delay[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share registers establishing Appellants and family hold 58.29% of company shares, forming an absolute majority against Respondents' 41.7%; absence of tangible documents attached to the CP proving fund diversion; audited balance sheets and profit and loss accounts of Respondent No. 1; IA filed by Appellants seeking tribunal discovery orders for eight years of bank statements across all company accounts[cite: 18]. 6.
