PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench on 04.06.2026 disposed of IA(CA)/96(CHE)/2023 and CP/124(CHE)/2022 without adjudicating merits, holding that Appellants holding 58.29% majority have the corporate power to inspect books, replace the board, and take over management, and cannot use Section 242(4) to fish for evidence, reserving liberty to re-approach if unresolved issues remain; Appellants appealed to NCLAT; Appellants 1 to 3 withdrew; NCLAT heard Appellants 4 and 5 on merits[cite: 18].
legal_issues: 1. Whether shareholders possessing an aggregate majority of 58.29% equity in a company can invoke Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to compel respondent directors to produce eight years of bank statements and individual ledgers to fish for evidence of oppression and mismanagement, rather than exercising their majority voting rights to inspect books or replace the board[cite: 18]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority committed an error in disposing of a petition under Section 241 and 242 without determining allegations on merits when the petitioners failed to produce prima facie evidence, while reserving liberty to pursue fresh proceedings after exhausting majority corporate remedies[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings alleging oppression and mismanagement under Section 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, petitioners must stand on their own legs and place sufficient credible evidence on record to substantiate their allegations; majority shareholders controlling more than 50% of the equity cannot utilize interim discovery applications under Section 242(4) as a fishing expedition to compel the company to produce historical banking records, but must exercise their statutory corporate majority powers to inspect accounts, replace management, or conduct internal inquiries[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241(1) requires a foundational showing of oppressive or prejudicial conduct before a tribunal can intervene; interim powers under Section 242(4) read with Rule 32 of NCLT Rules, 2016 are intended to grant urgent protective relief, primarily to oppressed minority shareholders excluded from corporate management, and cannot be invoked by majority shareholders who already possess corporate control to bypass ordinary company procedures[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a petition contains only vague, conjectural assertions of fund diversion and the petitioners holding 58.29% equity fail to show that they are incapacitated or powerless against the respondents, no case for judicial direction to compel production of eight years of bank statements is made out[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly declined to order production of documents and properly closed the petition leaving all issues open for the majority shareholders to exercise their corporate rights; the appeal was devoid of merit and was dismissed[cite: 18].
operative_order: IA No. 134/2026 for condonation of delay is allowed; the statement of Appellant Nos. 1, 2, and 3 withdrawing the appeal is recorded and the appeal is dismissed as not pressed qua them; Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 8 of 2026 is dismissed on merits as against Appellant Nos. 4 and 5; the impugned order of NCLT Chennai Bench dated 04.06.2026 is affirmed; all pending Interlocutory Applications stand closed[cite: 18].
summary: Bhawarlal Bhagrajji and family shareholders holding 58.29% majority equity appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated 04.06.2026 which disposed of their oppression and mismanagement petition (CP/124/2022) and rejected their interim application (IA/96/2023) seeking production of eight years of bank statements from Jindutt Safe Vaults Pvt. Ltd. and its directors[cite: 18]. Appellants 1-3 withdrew, while Appellants 4-5 pursued the appeal[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Section 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, majority shareholders cannot use Section 242(4) as a fishing expedition to gather evidence through tribunal orders when they possess the corporate power to inspect records and replace management through majority voting[cite: 18]. Closing the petition with liberty to re-approach was affirmed[cite: 18].

case_title: Value Wise Consultancy Private Limited vs. The Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is M/s Siddhi Vinayak Logistics Ltd. (in liquidation); Appellant is Value Wise Consultancy Private Limited through Liquidator Mr. Sumit Binani; Respondent No. 1 is The Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement (ED, under PMLA); Respondents No. 2 to 5 are corporate debtors/customers of Corporate Debtor (Ashok Leyland Ltd., Haldia Petrochemicals Ltd., Sonalika International Tractors Ltd., Hindustan Coca Cola Beverage Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial logistics and fleet transportation contracts executed by Corporate Debtor funded through multi-bank consortium credit facilities; parallel CBI FIRs registered alleging Rs. 1,600 Crores bank fraud, criminal conspiracy, and fund diversion leading to PMLA proceeds-of-crime attachment proceedings[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank fraud exceeding Rs. 1,600 Crores; ED provisional attachment of movable/immovable assets on 08.06.2017; during CIRP moratorium on 02.08.2018, ED withdrew Rs. 2,29,10,131.06 from Corporate Debtor's ICICI Bank account; during liquidation on 18.06.2019, ED provisionally attached 6,170 commercial vehicles (confirmed for 1,344 vehicles)[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ED issued Section 50 PMLA restraint notices to debtors on 24.04.2017; Provisional Attachment Order issued on 08.06.2017; CIRP initiated on 12.09.2017 in CP (IB) No. 89 of 2017 triggering Section 14 moratorium; PMLA Adjudicating Authority confirmed attachment on 24.10.2017; ED debited Rs. 2.29 Crores on 02.08.2018; Appellate Tribunal for PMLA set aside attachment on 12.12.2018 (ED appealed to Bombay High Court without stay); liquidation ordered on 19.11.2018; ED issued fresh provisional attachment of 6,170 vehicles on 18.06.2019; Liquidator filed IA 453/2019 and IA 773/2021; NCLT dismissed applications on 19.07.2022[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Provisional Attachment Orders dated 08.06.2017 and 18.06.2019; confirmation orders under Section 8(4) PMLA; ICICI Bank statement confirming withdrawal of Rs. 2,29,10,131.06 by ED on 02.08.2018; Section 50 PMLA communications dated 24.04.2017 restraining customers from releasing admitted dues; IBBI Circular No. IBBI/CIRP/87/2025 dated 04.11.2025 advising resolution professionals to seek restitution of attached assets before the Special Court under Sections 8(7) or 8(8) of the PMLA[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 19.07.2022 dismissed Liquidator's IA Nos. 453/2019 and 773/2021 under Section 60(5) holding that NCLT lacks jurisdiction to interfere with criminal attachment proceedings under PMLA; Liquidator appealed to NCLAT contending that ED's withdrawals and attachments violated Section 14 moratorium and depleted the insolvency estate[cite: 19].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(a) or Section 33(5) of the IBC applies to interdict, override, or invalidate attachment, seizure, and withdrawal of bank funds and assets by the Directorate of Enforcement under the PMLA, 2002[cite: 19]. 2. Whether the National Company Law Tribunal exercising jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC possesses the subject-matter jurisdiction to quash attachment orders or Section 50 notices issued by the Enforcement Directorate under the PMLA or direct refund of funds withdrawn by the ED[cite: 19]. 3. Whether the ED is legally permitted to retain funds withdrawn during the moratorium when the underlying attachment order was subsequently set aside by the Appellate Tribunal for PMLA without an operating stay from the High Court[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory moratorium under insolvency law is designed to freeze civil liabilities and preserve the legitimate assets of a corporate debtor to ensure a smooth resolution, but it does not operate as an omnibus shield to immunize proceeds of crime or stay penal and criminal proceedings under special anti-money laundering statutes enacted in the national interest; the adjudicating tribunals under insolvency legislation lack subject-matter jurisdiction to interfere with, review, or reverse attachment orders, seizures, or notices issued by criminal authorities under anti-money laundering law, and aggrieved parties must exclusively pursue statutory remedies before designated special courts under the penal enactment[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(a) and Section 33(5) of the IBC apply only to civil proceedings that threaten to add to the debt liability of the corporate debtor or dissipate legitimately acquired assets, and do not encompass public law criminal proceedings under the PMLA; the Enforcement Directorate is not a 'creditor' under Section 5(20)/(21) of the IBC, and Section 60(5) does not confer jurisdiction over criminal attachments[cite: 19]. Section 41 of the PMLA bars civil courts and authorities from entertaining matters within the competence of PMLA forums, and restitution of attached assets must be sought under Sections 8(7) or 8(8) of the PMLA[cite: 19]. Section 32A of the IBC protects assets only upon approval of a successful resolution plan, not during ongoing liquidation[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the Enforcement Directorate produces records showing scheduled predicate offences (FIRs of bank fraud and diversion) giving rise to proceedings regarding 'proceeds of crime', the statutory presumption of tainted property applies under PMLA, completely displacing insolvency jurisdiction regardless of whether an appellate order setting aside attachment is under challenge before the High Court[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly held that it lacked jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to interfere with PMLA attachments, Section 50 notices, or fund withdrawals by the ED; the Liquidator must seek relief before the PMLA authorities or the High Court; appeals dismissed[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1226 and 1227 of 2022 are dismissed; the Common Order dated 19.07.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad) in IA No. 453 of 2019 and IA No. 773 of 2021 in CP (IB) No. 89 of 2017 is affirmed; all pending Interlocutory Applications stand disposed of; no order as to costs[cite: 19].
summary: The Liquidator of Siddhi Vinayak Logistics Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 19.07.2022 dismissing his applications under Section 60(5) of the IBC which sought withdrawal of ED provisional attachments over vehicles, quashing of Section 50 PMLA notices issued to debtors, and refund of Rs. 2.29 Crores debited by the ED from the debtor's bank account during the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 19]. Dismissing the appeals, a three-judge bench of the NCLAT held that the IBC moratorium applies solely to civil liabilities and legitimately acquired assets, and cannot shield proceeds of crime or interdict criminal confiscation proceedings under the PMLA[cite: 19]. The NCLT lacks jurisdiction to review PMLA actions; remedies lie exclusively before PMLA special courts or the High Court[cite: 19].

case_title: Krihaan Texchem Private Limited vs. UPL Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor is M/s S. Kumars Nationwide Limited (in liquidation); Appellant in CA 811/2025 is Krihaan Texchem Private Limited (formerly Reid & Taylor International Pvt. Ltd., successful auction purchaser); Appellant in CA 1106/2025 / Respondent No. 1 is UPL Limited (purchaser of Lot 2 assets in prior auction and competing bidder); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Om Prakash Agarwal (Liquidator)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor held 99-year leasehold rights over Plot No. 825 at Jhagadia Industrial Estate, Bharuch, Gujarat; Liquidator issued e-auction notice on 12.12.2019 in two lots; Lot 2 (leasehold land 1,15,632 sq. mtrs. plus freehold land 81,326 sq. mtrs., totaling 1,96,958 sq. mtrs.) was sold on 16.01.2020 to UPL Limited for Rs. 43.43 Crores; subsequent GIDC sub-division order dated 15.12.2020 created an Additional Land parcel (Plot 825/3) admeasuring 12,981.64 sq. mtrs[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor under liquidation; Liquidator issued e-auction notice on 30.03.2021 for Additional Land (Plot 825/3) with a reserve price of Rs. 2.90 Crores; in the e-auction on 16.04.2021, Krihaan Texchem emerged as the highest bidder at Rs. 4.58 Crores against UPL's bid of Rs. 3.99 Crores; Krihaan paid 10% deposit of Rs. 74.80 Lakhs (or 45.8 Lakhs plus balance); UPL subsequently offered Rs. 4.87 Crores orally during court hearings[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Prior e-auction held on 16.01.2020; GIDC final sub-division order issued on 15.12.2020; Liquidator issued e-auction notice for Plot 825/3 on 30.03.2021; UPL filed IA 847/2021 on 05.04.2021; E-auction held on 16.04.2021 wherein Krihaan emerged successful bidder; Liquidator issued Letter of Intent to Krihaan; Krihaan filed IA 1189/2021; NCLT Mumbai set aside auction on 02.05.2025 ordering fresh auction; Krihaan and UPL filed cross-appeals[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: GIDC sub-division order dated 15.12.2020 sub-dividing Plot 825 into 825/1 (158,541.89 sq. m), 825/2 (112,742.20 sq. m), and 825/3 (12,981.64 sq. m); Certificate of Sale and Deed of Assignment dated 10.02.2021 in favour of UPL confirming sale of only 1,15,632 sq. m; official e-auction logs of 16.04.2021 confirming Krihaan's bid of Rs. 4.58 Crores and UPL's bid of Rs. 3.99 Crores; Liquidator's mathematical computation showing reserve price of Rs. 2.90 Crores was derived from consolidated Lot 2 rate (Rs. 43.43 Cr / 1,96,958 sq. m x 12,981.64 sq. m = Rs. 2.86 Cr, rounded up to Rs. 2.90 Cr), exposing NCLT's calculation of Rs. 4.87 Crores as a mathematical error excluding freehold land[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-III on 02.05.2025 allowed UPL's IA 847/2021 in part, set aside the e-auction notice dated 30.03.2021 and e-auction dated 16.04.2021, and ordered a fresh auction with refund of Krihaan's deposit, holding that reserve price was undervalued based on an erroneous calculation of Rs. 4.87 Crores; Krihaan appealed in CA 811/2025 to uphold the sale and UPL appealed in CA 1106/2025 seeking direct transfer at Lot 2 rates[cite: 20].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the legal jurisdiction to set aside a concluded, valid public e-auction and direct a fresh auction merely on the expectation of obtaining a higher price or on the basis of a higher post-auction oral offer made by an unsuccessful bidder who was outbid during the auction[cite: 20]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority committed a patent mathematical and factual error in calculating the reserve price for the additional land by excluding the freehold land area from the consolidated Lot 2 asset purchase[cite: 20]. 3. Whether an additional sub-divided land parcel created post-auction by industrial development authorities automatically forms part of an earlier auction lot sold on tentative measurements[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In statutory liquidation sales under the IBC, a public e-auction that has been transparently conducted without fraud, collusion, or fundamental procedural irregularity cannot be set aside by the adjudicating authority merely on the speculative expectation of fetching a higher price or because an unsuccessful bidder offers a higher price outside the auction process; the sanctity and finality of public auctions must be protected to prevent commercial uncertainty and abuse of judicial processes[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 33 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 establishes public auction as the mandatory norm and private sale as a narrow exception requiring prior permission; a liquidator acts lawfully in refusing private negotiation and subjecting newly discovered assets to open competitive e-auction[cite: 20]. Furthermore, under Section 61(1) of the IBC, a successful auction purchaser whose confirmed bid is cancelled is a 'person aggrieved' with undeniable locus standi to appeal[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Judicial interference with an auction is restricted to proof of grave irregularities going to the root of the sale; where the record proves that the reserve price was mathematically derived from the actual rate paid for the parent lot including both leasehold and freehold land, and the auction was publicly advertised, open, and competitive, an oral post-auction bid by an outbid participant provides zero legal foundation to annul the sale[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's decision directing a fresh auction was based on an arithmetic miscalculation and impermissible post-auction interference; the e-auction won by Krihaan Texchem at Rs. 4.58 Crores was valid, and UPL's claim to direct transfer was untenable; CA 811/2025 allowed and CA 1106/2025 dismissed[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 811 of 2025 is allowed and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1106 of 2025 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 02.05.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-III in IA-1189 of 2021 and IA No. 847 of 2021 is set aside; the Liquidator (Respondent No. 2) is directed to issue the Sale Certificate for Plot No. 825/3 admeasuring 12,981.64 sq. mts. in Jhagadia GIDC, Bharuch in favour of Krihaan Texchem Private Limited and take all consequential steps to register the sale; all pending IAs disposed of; no order as to costs[cite: 20].
summary: Krihaan Texchem Pvt. Ltd. and UPL Limited filed cross-appeals against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 02.05.2025 which set aside the public e-auction dated 16.04.2021 for an additional 12,981.64 sq. m. land parcel (Plot 825/3) of Corporate Debtor S. Kumars Nationwide Limited and ordered a fresh auction[cite: 20]. Krihaan had won the auction with a bid of Rs. 4.58 Crores, outbidding UPL (Rs. 3.99 Crores), but NCLT annulled the sale based on an arithmetic miscalculation of the reserve price and UPL's post-auction oral offer of Rs. 4.87 Crores[cite: 20]. NCLAT allowed Krihaan's appeal and dismissed UPL's appeal, holding that under Eva Agro Feeds and Celir LLP, a valid public auction cannot be cancelled on the mere expectation of a higher price or post-auction offers[cite: 20]. The Liquidator was directed to issue the sale certificate to Krihaan[cite: 20].

case_title: Dr. Badri Prasad vs. Tata Capital Financial Services Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Dr. Badri Prasad (promoter, director, and personal guarantor of Corporate Debtor M/s Furnace Fabrica (India) Limited); Respondent No. 1 is Tata Capital Financial Services Limited (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Rajesh Ramani (Resolution Professional)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial Creditor extended a term loan and working capital credit facility totaling Rs. 39.60 Crores to Corporate Debtor on 13.05.2019, secured by an irrevocable and unconditional personal guarantee executed by the Appellant and co-guarantors (Mr. Riaz Basheeruddin, Mr. Abdul Basheeruddin) alongside corporate guarantees and hypothecation; Appellant personally signed the loan sanction letter dated 13.05.2019 and the Letter of Guarantee dated 13.05.2019 as 'Guarantor No. 1'[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on loan repayments, resulting in the account being classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 16.12.2022; statutory demand notice issued on 19.12.2022; loan recall notice issued on 10.01.2023; total outstanding default claimed as on 16.02.2023 was Rs. 18,95,48,246.53 plus interest and costs[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Credit facilities sanctioned on 13.05.2019; NPA classification on 16.12.2022; loan recall notice on 10.01.2023; statutory Form B demand notice issued to personal guarantor under Section 95(4)(b) on 16.02.2023; Financial Creditor filed Section 95 petition CP(IBC)/32/KOB/2023 before NCLT Kochi on 18.04.2023; Appellant subsequently filed RoC complaint on 18.07.2023, Section 241-242 CP No. 18/2023 on 15.07.2023, and Bombay High Court commercial suit on 10.11.2023; NCLT Kochi admitted Section 95 petition on 14.08.2024[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan Sanction Letter dated 13.05.2019 signed by Appellant as 'Guarantor'; Loan Agreement Document dated 13.05.2019 with Clause 8 guarantee covenants; Letter of Guarantee dated 13.05.2019 executed by Appellant as Guarantor No. 1 containing Clauses 16 and 17 undertakings; NPA classification certificate dated 16.12.2022; internal MoU dated 01.03.2014 between promoters purporting to oust Appellant from management (which was never communicated to the lender prior to default)[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench admitted Tata Capital's Section 95 application CP(IBC)/32/KOB/2023 on 14.08.2024; Appellant appealed to NCLAT contending that admission without a Resolution Professional report under Section 99 was void, that he had resigned executive roles under a 2014 MoU, and that guarantee documents were signed under duress[cite: 21].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the admission of an insolvency application against a personal guarantor under Section 100 of the IBC without obtaining a prior recommendation report from the Resolution Professional under Section 99 of the IBC vitiates the admission proceedings when the existence of debt, default, and execution of guarantee documents are admitted on record[cite: 21]. 2. Whether an ex-director who signs a loan sanction letter and a letter of guarantee as a personal guarantor can escape statutory liability under Section 95 of the IBC by relying on an undisclosed internal promoter MoU or a belated defence of signing under duress[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In personal insolvency resolution proceedings under Part III of the IBC, the primary function of the Resolution Professional's report under Section 99 is recommendatory to assist the adjudicating authority in ascertaining debt and default; where the factum of financial advance, default through NPA classification, and execution of guarantee documentation are uncontroverted and admitted on record, the absence or non-submission of an RP report does not cause prejudice or jurisdictional invalidity so as to vitiate an admission order under Section 100[cite: 21]. Furthermore, an internal management ouster MoU or unproven, belated claims of execution under duress cannot extinguish a personal guarantor's independent statutory and contractual liability to the creditor[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 99 of the IBC prescribes a procedural, recommendatory mechanism designed to facilitate the Adjudicating Authority's decision-making under Section 100; it does not confer a substantive right on the guarantor to contest debt and default de novo when such elements are already admitted[cite: 21]. Notice under Section 95(4)(b) followed by petition under Section 95 fully satisfies statutory prerequisites[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted signatures on the loan sanction letter and letter of guarantee, combined with the NPA classification of the debt, establish conclusive evidentiary proof of debt, default, and guarantee obligations; collateral civil suits and complaints initiated after the Section 95 demand notice constitute afterthoughts that do not impeach the guarantee[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt, default, and personal guarantee were fully proved; procedural omission regarding the Section 99 report was immaterial in light of admitted facts; the NCLT's admission order was affirmed and the appeal dismissed[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 401 of 2024 is dismissed; the order dated 14.08.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kochi Bench) in CP(IBC)/32/KOB/2023 admitting the Section 95 application against the Appellant is affirmed; all pending Interlocutory Applications stand closed; no order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: Dr. Badri Prasad, promoter and personal guarantor of Furnace Fabrica (India) Limited, appealed against the NCLT Kochi order dated 14.08.2024 admitting Tata Capital's Section 95 IBC application for a default of Rs. 18.95 Crores[cite: 21]. The Appellant contended that the admission was void because no Resolution Professional report was submitted under Section 99, and argued he had exited management under a 2014 MoU and signed guarantee papers under duress[cite: 21]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the Section 99 report is merely recommendatory to ascertain debt and default; where the loan sanction letter, guarantee letter, and default (NPA) are admitted, non-receipt of the report does not vitiate admission[cite: 21]. Claims of duress and internal MoUs were dismissed as unsubstantiated afterthoughts[cite: 21].

case_title: Manjeera Construction Limited vs. Manjeera Hospitality (Rajahmundry) Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Manjeera Construction Limited, acting through its authorized director Sh. Sandip Omprakash Agrawal; Respondents in CA No. 53/2026 are Manjeera Hospitality (Rajahmundry) Pvt. Ltd. and its directors (Gajjala Yoganand, Gajjala Veena, Venkata Satyanarayana Murthy Nagavarapu); Respondents in CA No. 54/2026 are Manjeera Hospitality (Amravati) Pvt. Ltd., its directors (Gajjala Veena, Gajjala Padmaja), Manjeera Hotels and Resorts Pvt. Ltd., and the Registrar of Companies, Vijayawada[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate investment and equity holding; Appellant instituted two separate company petitions under Section 241 and Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the Respondent companies[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: At the filing and scrutiny stage, NCLT Registry raised defect objections regarding failure to establish qualifying membership and requisite shareholding thresholds under Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, refusing to number or register the company petitions[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company petitions presented before NCLT; Registry raised scrutiny defect objections; Registrar declined registration; Appellant filed appeals under Rule 63 of NCLT Rules, 2016; Single Member Bench dismissed appeals on 27.02.2026; Appellant filed Company Appeals before NCLAT Chennai on 09.06.2026[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Scrutiny defect memos issued by the NCLT Registry; impugned orders dated 27.02.2026 passed by the Single Member Bench affirming refusal of registration; pleadings in company petitions seeking adjudication of oppression and mismanagement and statutory waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1)[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Single Member Bench, acting on appeals preferred under Rule 63 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, affirmed the Registrar's decision declining registration and dismissed the appeals on 27.02.2026 on the ground of non-maintainability for lack of proof of qualifying shareholding under Section 244; Appellant appealed to NCLAT Chennai Bench[cite: 22].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Registrar of the NCLT or an officiating officer under Rule 17 and Rule 28(3) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 possesses the statutory or adjudicatory competence to decide substantive legal questions regarding the maintainability of a company petition under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 at the scrutiny stage and decline registration[cite: 22]. 2. Whether the question of maintainability of an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241, including the grant of waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1), is exclusively a judicial function that must be adjudicated by a regularly constituted Division Bench of the Tribunal[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The authority vested in a tribunal's registry to scrutinize pleadings is strictly administrative and ministerial, restricted to verifying formal compliance and pointing out clerical or procedural defects; the registry cannot usurp judicial authority by adjudicating substantive legal questions of maintainability or declining to register a petition on the ground that statutory eligibility criteria are not met, as the determination of maintainability is an un-delegable judicial function[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 17 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 exhaustively enumerates the administrative functions of the Registrar, which contain no grant of judicial power to decide legal questions affecting the merits of a petition; Rule 28(3) and Rule 63 authorize refusal to register only when a party fails to cure administrative or clerical defects within the prescribed time[cite: 22]. Furthermore, non-holding of the requisite qualifying shareholding under Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 is not an absolute bar because the proviso to Section 244(1) empowers the Tribunal on the judicial side to grant waiver, which requires judicial appreciation by a Division Bench[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where scrutiny objections reveal that the refusal to number and register a petition was predicated upon legal questions of maintainability and lack of threshold shareholding rather than clerical or ministerial defects, the action of the Registry and the Single Member Bench acting under Rule 63 is ultra vires and invalid[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Registrar and Single Member Bench lacked jurisdiction to reject the company petitions on maintainability; the Registry must number the petitions, record objections, and place them before a judicial bench; appeals allowed[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (CH) Nos. 53 & 54 of 2026 are allowed; the impugned order dated 27.02.2026 passed by the Ld. NCLT (Single Member) is quashed; the matter is remitted to the Registry of Ld. NCLT with directions to raise maintainability objections, number the petitions, and place them on the regular judicial side before the competent bench to decide maintainability under Section 241 and waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013; no order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: Manjeera Construction Limited appealed against the NCLT Single Member Bench order dated 27.02.2026 which dismissed its appeals under Rule 63 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and upheld the Registry's decision declining to number and register two company petitions filed under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 on grounds of non-maintainability under Section 244[cite: 22]. Allowing the appeals, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the scrutiny powers of the Registrar under Rule 17 and Rule 28(3) are strictly ministerial, administrative, and limited to clerical defects[cite: 22]. The Registrar cannot adjudicate questions of maintainability or Section 244 waiver, which belong exclusively to a judicial division bench[cite: 22]. The matter was remitted for numbering and judicial adjudication[cite: 22].

case_title: Devakonda Sunil Kumar vs. M/s. Arvensis Energy Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Devakonda Sunil Kumar (unsuccessful resolution applicant who did not participate in liquidation auction); Respondent No. 1 is M/s. Arvensis Energy Private Limited (sole successful auction purchaser); Respondent No. 2 is M/s. Aegis Resolution Services Private Limited represented by Liquidator Mr. Avil Menezes of Corporate Debtor Pioneer Gas Power Limited[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Following the liquidation of Pioneer Gas Power Limited, Liquidator issued a process memorandum on 12.12.2025 for public e-auction of corporate debtor assets; e-auction held on 08.01.2026 wherein Arvensis emerged successful bidder for Rs. 204.02 Crores; Letter of Intent issued on 15.01.2026 stipulating balance payment of Rs. 183.82 Crores (post Rs. 20.20 Cr EMD) within 90 days, expiring 15.04.2026[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Arvensis deposited Rs. 70 Crores but faced delay in paying the remaining balance of Rs. 113.82 Crores; applied for extension till 25.06.2026 agreeing to pay 12% p.a. interest for the delayed period under Clause 12 of Schedule I[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC rejected Appellant's CIRP plan on 08.06.2025; NCLT ordered liquidation on 11.11.2025; auction held on 08.01.2026; LoI issued on 15.01.2026; Arvensis filed IA(IBC)/609/2026 on 09.04.2026 seeking extension; NCLT granted extension on 11.05.2026; Appellant appealed on 22.06.2026[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Process Memorandum dated 12.12.2025; Letter of Intent dated 15.01.2026; proof of deposit of Rs. 20.20 Crores EMD and Rs. 70 Crores part-payment; SCC minutes recording creditors' unanimous consent to extension; records proving Appellant never challenged rejection of his resolution plan, the liquidation order, or the auction terms, and never submitted a bid[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 11.05.2026 allowed Arvensis's IA(IBC)/609/2026 based on the Liquidator's no-objection, extending the balance payment deadline till 25.06.2026 with interest; Appellant appealed under Section 61 contending the 90-day period under Clause 12 of Schedule I is mandatory and cancellation was required[cite: 23].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant who did not challenge the rejection of its CIRP plan or the order of liquidation, and who failed to participate in the liquidation auction, has the locus standi as a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge an extension of time granted to the successful auction bidder[cite: 23]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 35 of the IBC read with Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, 2016 and Regulation 31A(1)(h) of the Liquidation Regulations to extend the 90-day balance payment period under Clause 12 of Schedule I with interest upon consent of the stakeholders[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity that did not participate in a statutory liquidation auction and failed to challenge the tender process possesses no actionable legal right or grievance, and cannot claim status as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61 of the IBC based on a speculative expectation of participating in a hypothetical future auction if the sale were cancelled; furthermore, the 90-day payment timeline in liquidation process regulations does not disable the adjudicating authority from granting reasonable time extensions on terms of interest where creditors consent and substantial consideration has been deposited[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) of the IBC requires an appellant to be directly and prejudicially affected in its existing legal rights; a former resolution applicant or outside bystander is not a 'person aggrieved'[cite: 23]. While Clause 12 of Schedule I of the Liquidation Regulations prescribes payment within 90 days, it must be read with Regulation 31A(1)(h) and Section 35 of the IBC, which empower the Tribunal under its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to grant extensions of time for balance sale consideration beyond 90 days with compensatory interest[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the record establishes that the successful bidder paid Rs. 70 Crores, the liquidator and lenders consented to the extension, and the appellant was a complete stranger to the auction process, no statutory contravention or prejudice to the insolvency resolution framework is demonstrated[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant has no locus standi, and the NCLT acted within jurisdiction under Section 35 and Rule 11 in extending the payment deadline till 25.06.2026 with interest; appeal dismissed[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 302 of 2026 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 11.05.2026 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in IA(IBC)/609/2026 in CP (IB)/164/7/HDB/2021 permitting Respondent No. 1 to deposit the balance sale consideration on or before 25.06.2026 with interest is affirmed; all pending Interlocutory Applications stand closed; no order as to costs[cite: 23].
summary: Devakonda Sunil Kumar, a former resolution applicant of Pioneer Gas Power Limited whose plan was rejected during CIRP, appealed against the NCLT Hyderabad order dated 11.05.2026 granting successful auction bidder Arvensis Energy an extension till 25.06.2026 to pay balance sale consideration with interest[cite: 23]. The Appellant contended that the 90-day timeline under Clause 12 of Schedule I of the Liquidation Regulations is mandatory and the sale should have been cancelled[cite: 23]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT Chennai held that having neither challenged the liquidation order nor participated in the auction, the Appellant lacked locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61[cite: 23]. Furthermore, NCLT possessed inherent powers under Section 35 and Rule 11 to extend payment timelines with interest upon creditor consent[cite: 23].

case_title: M/s. LIC Housing Finance Ltd. vs. Mr. Ramakrishnan Sadasivan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. LIC Housing Finance Ltd. (financial creditor/intervener); Respondent is Mr. Ramakrishnan Sadasivan (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s. Lokaa Developers Private Limited)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by LIC Housing Finance Ltd. to Corporate Debtor Lokaa Developers Private Limited; Corporate Debtor entered CIRP in CP(IB)/124/2023; Appellant filed Intervention Petition Inv.P/IBC/6/2025 objecting to the Resolution Plan[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arising from credit facility non-repayment; intervention petition seeking protection of financial claims and exclusion from the resolution plan was dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority on 28.10.2025[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order pronounced on 28.10.2025; order uploaded on 31.10.2025; certified copy applied on 30.10.2025 and obtained on 31.10.2025; Company Appeal filed on 15.12.2025 without any condonation of delay application; Registry reported 16 days delay on 19.12.2025; Appellant filed IA No. 1830/2025 for condonation of delay on 20.12.2025; NCLAT heard and decided on 16.06.2026[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Impugned order dated 28.10.2025; certified copy dated 31.10.2025; Registry defect report dated 19.12.2025 noting 16 days delay; filing fee receipt dated 20.12.2025 establishing the belated institution of IA No. 1830/2025[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench on 28.10.2025 dismissed Appellant's Intervention Petition Inv.P/IBC/6/2025 in CP(IB)/124/2023; Appellant filed CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 658/2025 on 15.12.2025 and subsequently filed IA No. 1830/2025 on 20.12.2025 seeking condonation of delay; Respondent opposed on grounds of limitation under Section 61(2)[cite: 24].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal preferred under Section 61 of the IBC filed beyond the statutory 30-day period without an accompanying application for condonation of delay is validly instituted on the initial filing date or only on the date when the condonation application is filed[cite: 24]. 2. Whether the period of limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC commences from the date of pronouncement of the order or from the date of uploading, and whether delay exceeding the statutory maximum condonable period of 15 days can be condoned[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the statutory limitation period of 30 days and the maximum condonable period of 15 days under the proviso are rigid and jurisdictional; where an appeal is presented beyond 30 days without an accompanying application for condonation of delay, the appeal cannot be deemed validly instituted until the delay application is formally filed, and if that date falls beyond the 45-day outer limit, the tribunal possesses no statutory power to condone the delay[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC mandates that every appeal shall be filed within 30 days, and the proviso limits the discretion of the Appellate Tribunal to extend time strictly to a period 'not exceeding fifteen days'; unlike Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, limitation under Section 61(2) commences from the date of pronouncement of the order in open court and not from the date of uploading, subject only to exclusion under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act for the time taken to obtain a certified copy applied for within limitation[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculating limitation from the date of pronouncement (28.10.2025) and excluding time for obtaining the certified copy, the 30-day period expired on 27.11.2025 and the 15-day condonable period expired on 12.12.2025; since the condonation application was filed on 20.12.2025 (47th day), the delay was legally fatal[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was presented beyond the non-extendable statutory period of 45 days; IA No. 1830/2025 was rejected and the appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 24].
operative_order: IA No. 1830/2025 for condonation of delay is rejected; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 658/2025 is dismissed as barred by limitation under Section 61(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; no order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: LIC Housing Finance Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated 28.10.2025 dismissing its intervention application (Inv.P/IBC/6/2025) in the CIRP of Lokaa Developers Private Limited[cite: 24]. The appeal was filed on 15.12.2025 without an accompanying condonation of delay application, which was subsequently filed as IA No. 1830/2025 on 20.12.2025 after registry objections[cite: 24]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT Chennai held that an appeal filed beyond 30 days without a delay application is not validly instituted until the application is filed[cite: 24]. Computing limitation from the date of pronouncement under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the outer 45-day condonable limit expired on 12.12.2025[cite: 24]. The tribunal lacked jurisdiction to condone delay beyond 15 days, rendering the appeal time-barred[cite: 24].

case_title: Mr. A. Joseb Raj vs. Mr. P.R. Raman, Liquidator & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. A. Joseb Raj (shareholder, suspended director, and personal guarantor of Corporate Debtor Oceanic Edibles International Limited, who was subsequently adjudicated bankrupt); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. P.R. Raman (Liquidator); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Casurina Bay Farms Private Limited (successful auction purchaser)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed financial credit facilities from ICICI Bank; admitted to CIRP on 12.09.2017; liquidation ordered on 10.12.2018; Liquidator invited compromise schemes under Section 230 of the Companies Act (rejected by SCC on 14.11.2019 due to Section 29A disqualification); Liquidator conducted multiple e-auctions to sell the Corporate Debtor's assets on 'as is where is and without recourse' basis[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation value assessed at Rs. 24,84,33,000/-; reserve price in 1st auction was Rs. 28.50 Crores (no bids received); after 4 failed auctions with progressive reductions, 5th e-auction on 24.11.2023 was held at reserve price of Rs. 20,77,65,000/-; Casurina Bay Farms emerged successful bidder at Rs. 20,79,65,000/- and deposited full sale consideration with interest[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 12.09.2017; liquidation ordered on 10.12.2018; compromise scheme rejected on 14.11.2019; failed auctions held on 04.10.2021, 23.11.2022, 15.09.2023, and 11.10.2023; 5th auction notice published on 06.11.2023; auction concluded on 24.11.2023; sale certificate issued; Central Bank of India filed personal insolvency CP(IB)/169(CHE)/2025 wherein Appellant was declared bankrupt under Sections 121/123 on 31.10.2025; NCLT Chennai dismissed Appellant's challenges in IA 777/2024 and IA 283/2025 on 23.07.2025; NCLAT heard appeal on 25.06.2026[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auction notice dated 06.11.2023 published in 'Trinity Mirror' (English), 'Dinaboomi' (Tamil), and IBBI website; valuation reports assessing liquidation value at Rs. 24.84 Crores; 5th e-auction logs dated 24.11.2023; Sale Certificate issued upon receipt of full sale consideration; order dated 31.10.2025 in CP(IB)/169(CHE)/2025 declaring Appellant bankrupt and appointing Bankruptcy Trustee[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 777(CHE)/2024 and IA No. 283(CHE)/2025 before NCLT Chennai challenging the 5th auction alleging fraud, wide circulation defects, lack of registration of sale certificate, and reserve price reduction; NCLT dismissed applications on 23.07.2025; Appellant appealed to NCLAT Chennai[cite: 25].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a shareholder and personal guarantor who has been subsequently adjudicated bankrupt under Sections 121 and 123 of the IBC retains the locus standi to maintain an appeal under Section 61 challenging the sale of corporate debtor assets in liquidation[cite: 25]. 2. Whether a concluded liquidation e-auction can be set aside on unsubstantiated allegations of fraud, procedural irregularity in newspaper circulation under Regulation 12(3), or non-registration of a sale certificate issued under Clause 12 of Schedule I of the Liquidation Regulations[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a personal guarantor is adjudicated bankrupt under the insolvency code, all rights and standing to litigate in respect of the debtor's estate vest in the bankruptcy trustee, divesting the individual of locus standi to maintain an appeal as an aggrieved person; furthermore, a public auction concluded in compliance with statutory liquidation procedures upon deposit of full consideration and issuance of a sale certificate cannot be invalidated on bald, unsubstantiated allegations of fraud, nor does a sale certificate require compulsory registration under registration law[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 121 and 123 of the IBC, bankruptcy administration deprives the debtor of independent standing to litigate corporate asset disposals[cite: 25]. Under Regulation 12(3) of the Liquidation Regulations, publication in widely circulated regional newspapers enlisted by statutory bar councils constitutes sufficient public notice; under Schedule I Clause 12, confirmation of sale and issuance of the sale certificate finalizes the auction process[cite: 25]. As held in *Esjaypee v. Canara Bank*, a sale certificate issued by an authorized officer does not require compulsory registration under the Registration Act[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Fraud is a serious factual plea requiring strict proof; where the record establishes that four prior auctions failed, the reserve price was reduced in accordance with statutory guidelines, public notice was duly published in recognized dailies, full price was deposited, and the appellant produced no tangible evidence of collusion, the auction is legally unassailable[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant lost locus standi upon bankruptcy adjudication, and the challenge to the auction sale lacked merit; NCLT order affirmed and appeal dismissed[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 457 of 2025 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Chennai Bench dated 23.07.2025 dismissing IA No. 777(CHE)/2024, IA No. 283(CHE)/2025, and IA(IBC)/1045(CHE)/2025 is affirmed; all pending Interlocutory Applications stand rejected; no order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: Mr. A. Joseb Raj, suspended director and personal guarantor of Oceanic Edibles International Limited, appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated 23.07.2025 dismissing his applications (IA Nos. 777/2024 and 283/2025) which sought to set aside the 5th e-auction of corporate debtor assets sold to Casurina Bay Farms Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 20.79 Crores[cite: 25]. The Appellant alleged fraud, inadequate newspaper circulation, and non-registration of the sale certificate[cite: 25]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT Chennai held that the Appellant lost locus standi upon being adjudicated bankrupt under Sections 121/123 of the IBC[cite: 25]. Furthermore, four previous auctions had failed, publication in regional dailies complied with Regulation 12(3), and a sale certificate requires no compulsory registration under Esjaypee v. Canara Bank[cite: 25].

case_title: ARC Research and Development Centre Limited & Anr. vs. Liquidator of Adya Oils and Chemicals Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Adya Oils and Chemicals Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (in liquidation, represented by Liquidator Truee IPE LLP); ARC Research and Development Centre Limited and ARC Fintube Technologies Pvt. Ltd. are the Appellants/adjacent landowners whose promoters/directors are related parties to the Corporate Debtor's suspended promoters. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor owns non-agricultural land in New Block No. 83 (Old Block No. 87), Village Manglej, Taluka Karjan, District Vadodara, Gujarat, purchased to establish a castor oil plant. Appellants own adjacent New Block Nos. 90 and 92 (Old Block Nos. 94 and 96), purchased in July 2007 from Jord Engineers India Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 16.09.2019 and ordered into liquidation on 04.03.2020 due to insolvency default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Taluka Panchayat Kacheri, Karjan issued Non-Agricultural (NA) Order dated 04.11.1999 granting right of access from National Highway 8 through Block Nos. 94 and 96 based on an undertaking dated 20.09.1999; obstruction wall was erected by Appellants during COVID-19 lockdown in 2020-2021; Liquidator's police complaint was closed on 09.06.2021; Liquidator filed IA No. 2658 of 2021 under Section 60(5) in November 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NA Order dated 04.11.1999 backed by clearances from 13 statutory authorities; satellite imagery of 2020 and 2025 showing historical access roads subsequently blocked by Appellants' factory construction and mud filling; MCA records establishing Appellants and Corporate Debtor shared related-party promoter relationships. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 2658 of 2021 before NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-V in C.P. (I.B.) No. 2392/MB/2019; on 22.01.2025, NCLT allowed prayers (b) to (h), holding Corporate Debtor established prescriptive easement under Section 15 of the Indian Easements Act and that jurisdiction lay under Section 60(5)(c) because obstruction directly depressed liquidation asset value.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC has jurisdiction to adjudicate and protect a prescriptive easementary right of way over adjacent third-party land or whether the Liquidator must be relegated to a civil court; and whether the Corporate Debtor had a subsisting right of way over New Block Nos. 90 and 92 with sufficient nexus to the liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency adjudicating authority possesses summary jurisdiction under insolvency law to protect and enforce an established, recorded access pathway to an asset of the liquidation estate where post-commencement obstruction by related entities directly impairs asset value maximization and realization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC is couched in expansive language empowering the tribunal to determine questions of fact and law arising out of or in relation to insolvency/liquidation; recognizing and enforcing an existing right of access documented in an unchallenged 1999 public statutory order does not equate to impermissibly creating a new civil easement or encroaching on civil court jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unbroken, peaceful, and open use for over twenty years pursuant to an official administrative order, corroborated by comparative satellite imagery and uncontroverted related-party ties, establishes an existing right of way and mala fide post-CIRP obstruction designed to devalue estate assets. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT properly assumed jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) as the post-CIRP obstruction had a proximate nexus with the liquidation process, justifying the dismissal of the appeal and the protection of the right of way.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed in terms of the majority judgment (2:1). Liquidator is granted liberty to seek the assistance of local administration and police to ensure the right of way through New Block Nos. 90 and 92 remains free, unobstructed, and of adequate width. Both Appellants are directed to pay costs of Rs. 5 Lakhs each, to be deposited in the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund. All pending interlocutory applications disposed of.
summary: ARC Research and Development Centre Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order declaring an easementary right of way under Section 15 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 over its lands in favour of Corporate Debtor Adya Oils and Chemicals Ltd. (in liquidation). The Appellants contended that NCLT lacked jurisdiction to decide civil easement disputes under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC. By a 2:1 majority, NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the post-CIRP obstruction of access granted via a 1999 statutory NA order was a mala fide effort by related parties to depress liquidation value. The Tribunal affirmed NCLT's jurisdiction and imposed Rs. 5 Lakhs costs on each Appellant.

case_title: Santosh R. Shetty vs. Rajan Deshraj Agarwal (RP of Sristi Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1378 of 2024 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1383 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Santosh R. Shetty is the Appellant (Suspended Director/Promoter and Personal Guarantor); Sristi Hospitality Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (MSME hospitality entity); Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd. is the sole unrelated Financial Creditor/CoC member (Respondent No. 2); Rajan Deshraj Agarwal is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Consortium of Admas Industries Pvt. Ltd., Subh Ashish Exim Pvt. Ltd., and Amit Jatia is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed a Term Loan and Overdraft facility aggregating Rs. 21.50 Crores in 2017 secured by mortgage over 'Liberty Lodge', Vile Parle West, Mumbai, with personal guarantees executed by Appellant and family members. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 30.03.2019; Section 7 petition claimed default of Rs. 28,30,42,444.42 as on 31.03.2022; total admitted financial debt of Rs. 29,78,73,126, with overall admitted creditor claims amounting to Rs. 32,41,10,546. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued on 11.04.2019; symbolic possession taken on 17.06.2019; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 518 of 2022 filed on 31.03.2022 and admitted on 27.02.2023; Form G published on 16.05.2023; CoC approved resolution plan with 100% vote on 05.08.2023; Plan approval IA filed on 10.08.2023; Appellant filed objection IA No. 2141 of 2024 on 24.04.2024, after orders were reserved on 05.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuations conducted post-admission by two independent IBBI-registered valuers under Regulations 27 and 35; Appellant relied on historic pre-CIRP valuations of 2017 (Rs. 57.65 Cr) and 2020 (Rs. 76.72 Cr); IBBI order dated 04.02.2025 confirming that non-supply of 7th CoC minutes to Appellant was a mere procedural lapse. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V admitted Section 7 application on 27.02.2023. By order dated 07.05.2024, NCLT dismissed Appellant's IA No. 2141 of 2024 seeking revaluation on grounds of gross delay and laches. By order dated 12.07.2024 in IA No. 3612 of 2022, NCLT approved Respondent No. 3's resolution plan offering Rs. 32.41 Crores.
legal_issues: Whether a suspended director and personal guarantor possesses locus standi under Section 61(1) of the IBC; whether an application challenging valuation and CIRP validity filed after CoC approval and reservation of orders can be dismissed for delay; whether pre-CIRP valuations can challenge post-CIRP valuations conducted by IBBI valuers; and whether the commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving a resolution plan is open to judicial review regarding consideration adequacy.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application challenging CIRP proceedings or seeking re-valuation filed at the final approval stage after the CoC has approved a resolution plan and orders have been reserved is barred by delay and laches; moreover, the commercial wisdom of the CoC regarding the viability and consideration adequacy of a resolution plan is non-justiciable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) of the IBC confers locus standi on a personal guarantor as a 'person aggrieved'; however, appellate review under Section 61(3) is confined strictly to violations of Section 30(2) or material irregularity, excluding assessments of commercial adequacy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Only valuations conducted by IBBI-registered valuers appointed post-admission under Regulations 27 and 35 of the CIRP Regulations are legally relevant for the CoC, and historical pre-CIRP valuations or bare allegations of undervaluation cannot displace statutory valuations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly dismissed the belated objection application and approved the statutory resolution plan, as the Appellant failed to participate in the CIRP or prove any material irregularity.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1378 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1383 of 2024 are dismissed. All pending interlocutory applications in these appeals stand disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: Suspended Director and Personal Guarantor Santosh R. Shetty challenged NCLT Mumbai orders dismissing his belated application (IA 2141/2024) for fresh valuation and approving the Resolution Plan of Respondent No. 3 for Sristi Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant alleged gross undervaluation of prime property 'Liberty Lodge', lack of notice, and suppression of CoC minutes. NCLAT held that while the Appellant had locus standi as a personal guarantor, his application was rightly rejected for gross delay after orders were reserved. Further, pre-CIRP valuations cannot displace post-CIRP statutory valuations by IBBI valuers, and the commercial wisdom of the CoC approving the plan with 100% voting is non-justiciable. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Uttar Pradesh Housing and Development Board vs. K.S.N. Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1581 of 2023, 820 of 2025 & 926 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Uttar Pradesh Housing and Development Board / UPAVP is the Appellant/Lessor and statutory development authority; K.S.N. Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Joint Allottee; Ramesh Kumar Prasad is the Original Allottee; Omkara Assets Reconstruction Company Ltd. is the petitioning Financial Creditor; Jayanti Jain is the Authorized Representative of Homebuyers/Allottees (Financial Creditors in Class); Bhati Associates is the Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial Plot No. 16, Vasundhara, Ghaziabad was auctioned to Ramesh Kumar Prasad in 2006 for Rs. 25,62,67,693; CD was added as joint allottee in 2010; Hire Purchase Agreement executed on 30.03.2010 providing 21 quarterly instalments of Rs. 1,68,71,406 at 18% interest, with legal title reserved in UPAVP until full payment. CD undertook housing construction, creating third-party interests in favour of 144 flat buyers and 44 shop buyers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in instalments led UPAVP to issue a recovery certificate for Rs. 81,62,95,193 on 22.01.2021; UPAVP filed Form B claim in CIRP for Rs. 1,39,47,89,026; Omkara ARC claimed financial debt of Rs. 32,15,72,653; admitted claim of homebuyers was Rs. 78,26,16,253. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demolition notice issued on 10.11.2017; property sealed under Section 51(2) of UP 1973 Act on 27.08.2019; property confiscated on 20.07.2021; Section 7 CIRP admitted on 11.10.2022 (moratorium declared from 13.05.2022); NCLT ordered de-sealing on 17.10.2023; NCLT remanded the Resolution Plan to CoC on 27.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Hire Purchase Agreement dated 30.03.2010; show cause notice dated 28.10.2017 and demolition order dated 10.11.2017 for constructing 5 unauthorized floors; sealing memo dated 27.08.2019; UPAVP Form B claim demanding land dues and compounding fees; Resolution Plan proposing Rs. 20 Crores to UPAVP with mandatory regularisation of unauthorized structures without statutory compounding. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 CIRP initiated on 11.10.2022. RP filed IA No. 5536 of 2022 for de-sealing, which NCLT allowed on 17.10.2023 under erroneous belief that sealing occurred during moratorium. On 27.03.2025, NCLT disposed of IA Nos. 3259 and 5187 of 2023 by remanding the Resolution Plan to CoC because third-party public land owned by UPAVP was impermissibly dealt with in the plan.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority could order de-sealing under Section 14 when property was sealed by a statutory authority years prior to CIRP for unauthorized construction; whether contractual and development rights under a Hire Purchase Agreement constitute 'assets' under Sections 18 and 25 of the IBC; and whether a Resolution Plan can compel transfer of ownership of public land and force compounding of illegal constructions without statutory approval.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency resolution plan cannot compulsorily divest a statutory development authority of its ownership in public land or compel compounding of building violations contrary to town planning statutes; however, subsisting contractual and development rights of the corporate debtor constitute intangible assets under Sections 18 and 25 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(27) read with Sections 18(1)(f) and 25(2)(a) includes contractual development rights within 'assets'; however, Explanation (a) to Section 18 excludes third-party owned land from the debtor's estate, and Section 238 does not override municipal planning statutes governing public regularisation powers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where sealing and confiscation were executed years prior to CIRP under building planning laws rather than for recovery of dues, Section 14 moratorium cannot operate retrospectively to invalidate completed administrative actions; furthermore, title remaining with a statutory authority bars treating public land as debtor property. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The de-sealing order was unsustainable as the sealing occurred long before CIRP, but the remand of the Resolution Plan to CoC was valid because the plan unlawfully attempted to transfer title in third-party public land and force regularisation without statutory compounding.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1581 of 2023 filed by UPAVP is allowed, and the NCLT order dated 17.10.2023 directing de-sealing is set aside. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 820 of 2025 and 926 of 2025 are dismissed, affirming the remand of the Resolution Plan to the CoC. UPAVP is directed to maintain status quo over the subject land and constructed structures, subject to further orders of NCLT. No order as to costs.
summary: UPAVP appealed against the NCLT order directing de-sealing of a commercial-residential project in Ghaziabad, while the RP and Homebuyers appealed against the remand of the Resolution Plan for K.S.N. Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. The property had been sealed in 2019 for unauthorized construction before CIRP commenced in 2022. The NCLAT held that de-sealing could not be ordered under Section 14 as lawful statutory sealing preceded moratorium. Furthermore, while the Corporate Debtor possessed contractual development rights constituting 'assets' under Sections 18 and 25, the Resolution Plan impermissibly treated the statutory authority's land as debtor property and forced building regularisation without statutory compounding. The remand to CoC was upheld.

case_title: Maharashtra Airport Development Company Ltd. vs. Vinod Kumar Kothari & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1355 of 2023 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 939 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Maharashtra Airport Development Company Ltd. / MADCL is the Appellant (Government SPV, Project Owner, Lessor, and 26% equity shareholder); Abhijeet MADC Nagpur Energy Pvt. Ltd. / AMNEPL is the Corporate Debtor/Project SPV; Vinod Kumar Kothari is the Liquidator (Respondent No. 1); Successful Auction Purchaser of the slump sale undertaking and standalone corporate entity is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Concession Agreement dated 07.11.2007 granted Corporate Debtor an exclusive license to develop, design, construct, operate, and maintain a coal-based thermal power plant at MIHAN SEZ Nagpur on BOT basis for 33 years; MADCL leased 6.2654 ha inside SEZ and 35.03 ha outside SEZ on 26.11.2008 and 16.06.2010 for 33 years in exchange for 26% equity shareholding in CD as lease premium under a Shareholders Agreement dated 02.04.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt servicing led to CIRP under Section 7; in liquidation, MADCL filed claims of Rs. 41,22,71,985 as unsecured financial creditor and Rs. 8,66,13,84,438 as operational creditor, both rejected by the liquidator and affirmed by NCLT without further appeal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted to CIRP on 06.10.2017; liquidation ordered on 31.08.2018; public auction for slump sale of undertaking conducted on 21.10.2020; sale certificates issued on 19.12.2020 and 21.12.2020; sale agreement executed on 24.12.2020; Liquidator filed IA No. 2504 of 2020 on 26.12.2020; MADCL filed intervention IA No. 147 of 2023 on 18.12.2022; NCLT approved sale closure on 28.04.2023 and granted concessions in IA No. 3985 of 2023 on 13.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Concession Agreement dated 07.11.2007; Indentures of Lease dated 26.11.2008 and 16.06.2010; Shareholders Agreement dated 02.04.2009; MERC regulatory orders; asset sale report dated 24.12.2020 showing realization distributed to secured creditors under Section 53. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CIRP initiated under Section 7 on 06.10.2017 in CP No. 1315/I&BP/2017; liquidation initiated on 31.08.2018. Liquidator filed IA No. 2504 of 2020 to take completion of sale/liquidation on record, allowed by NCLT on 28.04.2023. Auction Purchaser filed IA No. 3985 of 2023 for reliefs and concessions, granted by NCLT on 13.03.2024 subject to protection of MADCL's BOT rights.
legal_issues: Whether 33-year leasehold and operational rights under a BOT concession agreement constitute liquidation estate assets saleable via slump sale; whether the standalone legal entity shell of the Corporate Debtor can be auctioned; and whether an equity shareholder holding 26% shares in lieu of lease premium can obstruct liquidation sales or claim proceeds contrary to the Section 53 waterfall.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Leasehold and operational rights arising under long-term BOT concession agreements constitute intangible commercial assets that form part of the corporate debtor's liquidation estate and can be auctioned by the liquidator; moreover, equity shareholders rank last under Section 53 and cannot block asset realization or resist clean-slate extinguishment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1)(f) and Section 25(2)(a) read with Section 3(27) encompass leasehold interests within 'property' and 'assets'; Section 35 empowers the liquidator to execute slump sales and sell the corporate shell to maximize value; Section 238 overrides inconsistent contractual transfer restrictions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the concession agreement was never terminated pre-CIRP, and the auction purchaser explicitly admits that it acquires no superior rights and remains bound to revert the project upon expiration of the concession term, the grantor suffers no actionable legal prejudice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidation slump sale and entity transfer were lawful as they transferred only leasehold operating rights rather than land ownership, preserved the grantor's reversionary BOT entitlements, and properly extinguished liabilities under Section 53.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1355 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 939 of 2024 are dismissed. The NCLT orders are affirmed, confirming that MADCL's rights under the BOT agreements remain protected and the Successful Auction Purchaser is bound to revert the facility to MADCL at the end of the concession term. No order as to costs.
summary: MADCL appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders recording the completion of the liquidation sale and granting concessions to the Auction Purchaser of Abhijeet MADC Nagpur Energy Pvt. Ltd. (AMNEPL). MADCL contended that the CD held only a BOT license and leasehold rights for a 33-year power project in MIHAN SEZ, prohibiting sale of assets or dilution of MADCL's 26% shareholding. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that leasehold and BOT operating rights constitute intangible liquidation assets under Sections 18, 25, and 35. As MADCL never terminated the concession agreement and equity ranks last under Section 53, the sale with clean slate protections was valid, while MADCL's ultimate reversionary rights at term-end remained protected.

case_title: CA Som Prakash Aggarwal & M/s S. Prakash Aggarwal & Co. vs. National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) No. 200 of 2022 & Comp. App. (AT) No. 177 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: CA Som Prakash Aggarwal is the Engagement Partner / Appellant in CA 200/2022; M/s S. Prakash Aggarwal & Co. is the Statutory Audit Firm / Appellant in CA 177/2024; National Financial Reporting Authority / NFRA is the statutory disciplinary regulator (Respondent); Vikas WSP Limited is the audited listed Public Interest Entity; PNB, UBI, and BOI are the consortium lender banks. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory audit of listed entity Vikas WSP Limited for FY 2019-20 conducted by M/s S. Prakash Aggarwal & Co. through Engagement Partner CA Som Prakash Aggarwal pursuant to Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Auditee held borrowings of Rs. 135.65 Crores classified as NPA by lenders in 2015/2016; auditee reduced finance costs from Rs. 21.08 Crores in FY 2018-19 to Rs. 4.16 Crores in FY 2019-20, understating interest by at least Rs. 16.91 Crores, which constituted 88% of reported Profit Before Tax of Rs. 19.20 Crores; in subsequent CIRP on 02.02.2022, RP admitted bank interest claims of Rs. 124.28 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Audit report issued with unmodified opinion on 26.06.2020; SEBI flagged accounting distortion on 25.08.2021; NFRA issued production notice on 11.11.2021; SCN issued to EP on 29.06.2022; NFRA penalty order against EP passed on 12.09.2022; SCN issued to Audit Firm on 04.12.2023; NFRA penalty order against Firm passed on 23.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Note 33(a)(i) of VWL's financial statements disclosing non-provision of interest citing RBI NPA norms and OTS negotiations; unauthenticated, defective Management Representation Letter dated 24.06.2020 citing future inventory as of 30.09.2020; complete absence of external bank confirmations or working paper documentation challenging interest suppression; admitted failure to appoint an Engagement Quality Control Reviewer (EQCR). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Disciplinary proceedings initiated by NFRA under Section 132(4) of Companies Act, 2013 culminated in Order NF-23/46/2021 dated 12.09.2022 imposing Rs. 3 Lakhs fine, 3-year debarment, and mandatory training on EP, and Order 009/2024 dated 23.04.2024 imposing Rs. 5 Lakhs fine on the Audit Firm.
legal_issues: Whether RBI IRACP prudential norms prohibiting banks from recognizing income on NPA accounts extinguish a borrower's legal obligation to accrue interest expense under Ind AS 109; whether unapproved OTS talks permit substituting contractual cash flows under the Effective Interest Rate method; whether Standards on Auditing are mandatory statutory requirements; and whether penalizing an audit firm under SQC 1 after penalizing the engagement partner constitutes impermissible double jeopardy.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Prudential guidelines governing income recognition for banks do not extinguish or modify a borrower's legal and accounting obligations to accrue contractual interest on amortized cost under Ind AS 109; moreover, an audit firm is independently and primarily accountable under SQC 1 for systemic quality control failures separate from the engagement partner's individual liability under Standards on Auditing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 143(9) and (10) of the Companies Act impose mandatory statutory duties to comply with Standards on Auditing; Ind AS 109 permits derecognition of a financial liability only upon legal discharge or extinguishment; Section 132(4) empowers NFRA to discipline both individual auditors and audit firms without offending the rule against double jeopardy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Speculative, unapproved settlement proposals and an internally contradictory Management Representation Letter do not constitute sufficient appropriate audit evidence under SA 500 and SA 580 to justify omitting contractual liabilities or expressing an unmodified audit opinion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The EP and the Audit Firm committed gross professional misconduct across multiple auditing and accounting standards, rendering the monetary penalties, professional debarment, and training orders fully justified and proportionate.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) No. 200 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 177 of 2024 are dismissed. Sanctions imposed by NFRA (Rs. 3 Lakhs penalty, 3-year debarment, and mandatory training for CA Som Prakash Aggarwal; Rs. 5 Lakhs penalty for M/s S. Prakash Aggarwal & Co.) are affirmed. Penalty amounts deposited pursuant to the appeals shall be adjusted against outstanding liabilities. No order as to costs.
summary: Statutory Auditor CA Som Prakash Aggarwal and his firm M/s S. Prakash Aggarwal & Co. appealed against NFRA orders penalizing them for professional misconduct in the FY 2019-20 statutory audit of listed entity Vikas WSP Limited. The auditor issued an unmodified opinion despite the auditee omitting Rs. 16.91 Crores in accrued interest on NPA borrowings (overstating PBT by 88%) based on RBI NPA norms and unapproved OTS negotiations. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, ruling that RBI lender norms do not relieve borrowers from accruing interest under Ind AS 109, Standards on Auditing are statutory mandates, EQCR appointment is mandatory under SA 220, and the audit firm bears independent liability under SQC 1.

case_title: Nakul Gupta vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 6]; Technofab Engineering Limited is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]; Nakul Gupta (erstwhile director who resigned on 08.03.2018) is the Personal Guarantor/Appellant[cite: 6]; Rajesh Mittal is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital consortium credit facilities aggregating Rs. 907 Crores granted to the Corporate Debtor by Bank of India consortium, including Rs. 117 Crores sanctioned by SBI (Rs. 10 Cr fund-based and Rs. 107 Cr non-fund based) under Letter of Arrangement dated 11.10.2017, secured by Working Capital Consortium Agreement and Deed of Guarantee dated 17.10.2017 executed by Appellant[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 15,61,66,989 claimed following NPA classification; initial overdue of Rs. 2,72,00,999 recorded on 22.05.2019; specific date of default was 27.06.2019[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee executed on 17.10.2017; Appellant resigned on 08.03.2018; BOI renewed consortium facilities to Rs. 1075 Crores on 24.10.2018; SBI issued renewal sanction letter on 01.01.2019; account classified as NPA on 27.06.2019; Demand Notice issued on 13.05.2022; Loan Recall Notice issued on 15.11.2022; CIRP against CD initiated on 18.11.2022; Section 95 petition filed in 2022; RP submitted Section 99 report on 26.12.2022[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Guarantee dated 17.10.2017 containing Clauses 1, 3, 7, 8, 11, 14, 18, and 19 establishing an irrevocable and continuing guarantee with waiver of discharge; absence of written notice of revocation to SBI under Section 130; Information Utility NeSL default records[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed Section 95 application CP (IB) No. 769/2022; RP filed recommendation IA No. 593/ND/2023 under Section 99; NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the application under Section 100 on 27.02.2024, holding the continuing guarantee remained operative for pre-variance liabilities[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the resignation of a director revokes an irrevocable and continuing personal guarantee under Section 130 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 without formal written notice to the creditor; and whether subsequent renewal or enhancement of consortium credit facilities without the guarantor's consent constitutes novation under Section 62 or variance under Section 133 discharging the guarantor from liabilities incurred under the original facility[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An irrevocable continuing guarantee given by a director is not discharged by the director's mere resignation from the corporate debtor without an express written notice of revocation served on the creditor; nor does a renewal of credit facilities that does not increase the creditor's specific sanctioned exposure constitute novation or variance discharging the surety[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 129 and 130 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 require strict written notice to the creditor for revocation of a continuing guarantee, which only operates prospectively; Section 62 requires bilateral consent to substitute a contract, and Section 133 discharges a surety only for subsequent transactions, preserving liabilities accrued under pre-variance terms[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Express contractual terms of a personal guarantee deed creating continuing, joint and several liability on demand and explicitly waiving rights to claim discharge under the Contract Act override unilateral assertions of resignation or unexecuted renewal letters[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Appellant never served a written revocation notice on SBI and SBI's sanctioned facility remained at Rs. 117 Crores under the 2017 loan documents, the personal guarantee remained fully enforceable, justifying initiation of insolvency proceedings under Section 100 of the IBC[cite: 6].
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 494 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 6]. The order dated 27.02.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench in CP (IB) No. 769/2022 admitting personal insolvency proceedings against the Appellant is affirmed[cite: 6]. All related interlocutory applications are dismissed[cite: 6]. No order as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: Nakul Gupta, erstwhile director of Technofab Engineering Limited, appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order admitting a Section 95 petition filed by State Bank of India to initiate personal insolvency proceedings against him[cite: 6].
