The Appellant contended that his resignation as director in March 2018, coupled with the consortium's subsequent renewal and enhancement of credit facilities in 2018-2019 without his consent, discharged his personal guarantee under Sections 62, 130, and 133 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 6]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the guarantee was continuing and irrevocable, mere resignation does not effect revocation without written notice to the creditor under Section 130, and renewal without increasing SBI's limit did not constitute novation[cite: 6]. The admission was upheld[cite: 6].

case_title: Metamorphosis Trading LLP vs. Kumar Motors Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Metamorphosis Trading LLP is the Appellant/Financial Creditor (assignee of Innoventive Industries Ltd.)[cite: 8]; Kumar Motors Private Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 8]; Innoventive Industries Ltd. is the original investor (under liquidation)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Subscription and Shareholders Agreement (SSA) executed on 06.09.2011 between Innoventive Industries Ltd., promoters, and Corporate Debtor, whereby Innoventive agreed to invest in equity shares and convertible warrants to acquire at least 51% shareholding, nominate 50% directors, and control fundamental corporate governance issues[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed debt of Rs. 8,70,03,275/- (disbursed between 08.09.2011 and 09.05.2012); specific date of default alleged in Section 7 petition was 21.07.2021 (date of assignment deed)[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SSA executed 06.09.2011; Innoventive issued breach letter 04.03.2013 and demand notice claiming 24% interest on 21.03.2013; Company Petition No. 468 of 2013 for winding up filed 20.06.2013 (admitted 04.08.2015); Innoventive entered liquidation on 08.12.2017; debt assigned to Appellant on 21.07.2021; High Court transferred winding up petition to NCLT on 27.07.2022; NCLT granted liberty on 11.09.2023 to file Section 7 petition; CP(IB)/7(MB)/2024 filed thereafter[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SSA clauses 2.1, 2.5, 4A.1, 4A.2, 8.1, 9.1, 18.11, and 18.12 establishing equity investment and exit through IPO/strategic sale with no repayment clause; audited balance sheets showing corresponding increase in share capital from Rs. 5.50 Cr to Rs. 14.20 Cr in FY 2012-13[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed Section 7 petition CP(IB)/7(MB)/2024 on 08.04.2024, holding that advances paid towards subscription of shares and warrants do not constitute financial debt[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether funds advanced under a Subscription and Shareholders Agreement for the acquisition of equity shares and convertible warrants constitute a 'financial debt' having the 'commercial effect of a borrowing' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC; and whether failure to allot shares converts share subscription money into a financial debt under Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Amounts invested in a company for the acquisition of equity shares or convertible warrants to attain controlling shareholding and management participation do not possess the commercial effect of a borrowing and do not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC in the absence of an express obligation for repayment, assured returns, or time value of money[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC requires an initial existence of a debt disbursed against consideration for time value of money; equity share capital and warrant subscription amounts do not partake of the character of debt; Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be applied retrospectively to agreements executed under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the terms, intent, and substance of the investment agreement demonstrates whether the transaction was an equity participation arrangement bearing entrepreneurial risk rather than a loan transaction[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the SSA contained no covenant for repayment of principal or payment of interest, and the consideration was 51% equity control, the claim was not a financial debt, rendering the Section 7 petition unmaintainable[cite: 8].
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1083 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 8]. The impugned order dated 08.04.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP(IB)/7(MB)/2024 is upheld[cite: 8]. Liberty is granted to the Appellant to pursue appropriate remedies before other competent judicial forums[cite: 8]. Pending applications closed[cite: 8]. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Metamorphosis Trading LLP, assignee of Innoventive Industries Ltd. (in liquidation), appealed against NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of its Section 7 petition seeking CIRP against Kumar Motors Private Limited for an alleged default of Rs. 8.70 Crores[cite: 8]. The claim arose from funds advanced by Innoventive in 2011-2012 under a Subscription and Shareholders Agreement (SSA) to acquire 51% shareholding and board control[cite: 8]. The Appellant contended that non-allotment of shares transformed the investment into a financial debt under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC and Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 8]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, affirming that equity subscription funds lacking any repayment stipulation or time value of money do not constitute financial debt[cite: 8].

case_title: Sturdy Industries Limited vs. Surya Irrigation Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sturdy Industries Limited (acting through its Resolution Professional) is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Surya Irrigation Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of goods by Operational Creditor to Corporate Debtor during FY 2014-2015 pursuant to invoices, with accounts running and reconciled until 23.02.2015[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Date of default specified in Part IV of Section 9 petition was 07.03.2015; operational debt claimed varied across balance confirmations (Rs. 4,73,31,706, Rs. 3,05,58,222, and Rs. 2,44,46,578)[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised in 2014-2015; date of default 07.03.2015; courier disputing accounts sent 19.01.2017; emails raising disputes sent February-August 2018; Section 8 demand notice issued 10.03.2021 (served 12.03.2021); Section 9 petition filed on 23.09.2021; NCLT dismissed petition on 06.11.2024 (rectified on 12.02.2025); appeal filed after admitted delay of 125 days[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three balance confirmation letters dated 14.12.2017, 30.05.2018, and 22.05.2019 showing contradictory, shifting amounts; Operational Creditor's letter dated 25.11.2019 showing a credit balance of Rs. 1,61,37,994; pre-notice dispute communications dated 19.01.2017 and July-August 2018 detailing ledger differences and group company set-offs[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench dismissed Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 79/9/JPR/2021 on 06.11.2024 (rectified for date of pronouncement on 12.02.2025) as barred by limitation under Article 137 and on ground of pre-existing dispute[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC filed beyond the condonable period of 45 days can be entertained on the ground that limitation runs from a subsequent clerical rectification order; whether balance confirmation letters reflecting contradictory amounts constitute valid acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act; and whether pre-notice correspondence disputing ledger accounts and claiming set-offs constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 9[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal lacks statutory jurisdiction to condone delay beyond the outer limit of 45 days under Section 61(2) of the IBC, and an order rectifying a mere clerical typographical error does not reset limitation; moreover, inconsistent and unproved balance confirmations cannot extend limitation under Section 18, and genuine pre-notice disputes regarding account reconciliation bar Section 9 admission[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) proviso strictly caps condonable delay at 15 days; Section 60(6) moratorium exclusion applies exclusively to original suits/applications and not to appeals under Section 61; Article 137 of the Limitation Act imposes a strict 3-year limitation from the date of default for Section 9 petitions[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, pre-notice written communications asserting specific discrepancies, ledger challenges, and set-offs establish a plausible pre-existing dispute; balance confirmations recording materially shifting figures do not establish an unequivocal admission of debt[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is barred by limitation as the 125-day delay is non-condonable, and the Section 9 petition was independently barred by limitation and defeated by a bona fide pre-existing dispute[cite: 9].
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 607 of 2025 is dismissed as barred by limitation and on merits[cite: 9]. The order dated 06.11.2024, as rectified on 12.02.2025, passed by NCLT Jaipur Bench in C.P. (IB) No. 79/9/JPR/2021 is upheld[cite: 9]. Pending interlocutory applications stand disposed of[cite: 9]. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: Sturdy Industries Limited, through its Resolution Professional, appealed against NCLT Jaipur's order dismissing its Section 9 petition against Surya Irrigation Private Limited for alleged operational dues from 2014-2015[cite: 9]. The stated default occurred on 07.03.2015, while the Section 9 petition was filed in September 2021[cite: 9]. The Appellant sought to extend limitation via three balance confirmations, and argued that the appeal was timely reckoned from a clerical rectification order dated 12.02.2025[cite: 9]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a 125-day delay cannot be condoned beyond Section 61(2)'s 45-day cap as clerical corrections do not reset limitation[cite: 9]. On merits, shifting balance confirmations did not satisfy Section 18, and pre-notice communications revealed a genuine pre-existing dispute under Mobilox[cite: 9].

case_title: Brajesh Kumar Tripathi & Anr. vs. Hastimal Kachhara (RP of Pushp Ratna Realty Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 938 of 2026 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 939 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Brajesh Kumar Tripathi and Abhishek Tripathi are Landowners/Appellants[cite: 10]; Pushp Ratna Realty Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 10]; Hasti Mal Kachhara is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 10]; Rajendra Hirani is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3)[cite: 10]; 43 Homebuyers are Financial Creditors in Class[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Registered Development-cum-Collaboration Agreement dated 29.01.2010 (amended 21.07.2010) executed between Appellants and Corporate Debtor for construction of residential project on Survey No. 388/2/17 (0.112 ha) at Village Khajrana, Indore, entitling Appellants to 37% and Corporate Debtor to 63% of developed saleable area; Corporate Debtor integrated land into composite township project 'Lush by Pushpratna'[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor failed to complete construction within 5 years plus 18-month grace period (expired July 2019)[cite: 10]; CIRP initiated on 16.10.2024 on application by homebuyers whose claims were admitted[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed 29.01.2010; layout sanctioned 2013; building permission revoked 04.07.2023; RERA registration expired 31.12.2019; Appellants issued termination notice on 06.08.2024; Section 9 Arbitration status quo order obtained 06.09.2024; CIRP admitted 16.10.2024; NCLT approved Resolution Plan on 09.03.2026[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Development Agreement containing express non-termination clause; sanctioned master layout covering contiguous parcels; public RERA portal records (p-ind-17-1023); Commercial Court status quo order dated 06.09.2024[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA No. 260(MP)/2025 seeking exclusion of land; RP filed IA(Plan)/3(MP)/2025 for plan approval; NCLT Indore Bench on 09.03.2026 dismissed Appellants' exclusion application and approved the Resolution Plan supported by 100% CoC voting[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether private land contributed under a development agreement forming part of a sanctioned integrated real estate project can be excluded from CIRP following unilateral termination by landowners; whether landowners contributing land for development are 'promoters' under Section 2(zk) of RERA bound to project completion; and whether an interim status quo order under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act survives CIRP admission and plan approval[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Development rights acquired by a corporate debtor under a registered collaboration agreement for a composite township project constitute insolvency estate assets, and landowners who acquiesce in statutory layout approvals and creation of third-party homebuyer interests cannot unilaterally terminate the agreement or isolate their land parcel to defeat CIRP[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Landowners contributing land to a residential project qualify as 'promoters' under Section 2(zk) of the RERA Act, 2016, and cannot alter approved project layouts without two-thirds allottee consent under Section 14 of RERA; Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC protects properties in possession of the debtor, and pre-CIRP arbitral status quo orders yield to clean-slate vesting under Section 31[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Decade-long acquiescence, inclusion of contiguous land in public town planning sanctions, and crystallization of third-party allottee rights estop landowners from asserting unilateral termination on the eve of CIRP[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The subject land was an inseparable component of the composite project, rendering the belated contract termination legally ineffective and justifying dismissal of the exclusion application and approval of the resolution plan[cite: 10].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 938 of 2026 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 939 of 2026 are rejected and dismissed[cite: 10]. The impugned orders dated 09.03.2026 passed by NCLT Indore Bench approving the Resolution Plan and dismissing IA No. 260(MP)/2025 are affirmed[cite: 10]. All pending interlocutory applications closed[cite: 10]. No order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary: Landowners Brajesh Kumar Tripathi and Abhishek Tripathi appealed against NCLT Indore orders approving a Resolution Plan for Pushp Ratna Realty Private Limited and dismissing their application to exclude their 0.112-hectare land parcel[cite: 10]. The Appellants contended that their 2010 Development Agreement was terminated on 06.08.2024 prior to CIRP admission, that a pre-CIRP arbitral status quo order was in force, and that third-party land could not be included in the resolution estate[cite: 10]. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that the land formed an integral part of the sanctioned composite project 'Lush by Pushpratna'[cite: 10]. Having acquiesced for a decade while homebuyer rights crystallized, the landowners acted as promoters under RERA and could not unilaterally terminate the agreement to derail CIRP[cite: 10].

case_title: Gursimran Kaur Mann vs. Oriental Bank of Commerce (Now Punjab National Bank) & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1404 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1405 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Oriental Bank of Commerce (now Punjab National Bank) is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1[cite: 11]; Simbhaoli Sugars Limited is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 11]; Gursimran Kaur Mann (suspended director) is the Appellant[cite: 11]; State Bank of India is the lead bank of the Joint Lenders' Forum (intervenor)[cite: 11]; sugarcane farmers and Cane Commissioner UP are statutory stakeholders[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities aggregating Rs. 110 Crores extended by OBC to Corporate Debtor vide sanction letter dated 29.01.2016 and loan agreement, forming part of total consortium debt of Rs. 1,436.92 Crores[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of principal and interest; total outstanding debt claimed by OBC in Form 1 was Rs. 103.61 Crores plus interest as of 31.07.2018; account classified as NPA on 30.11.2016[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account slipped to NPA on 30.11.2016; legal notice issued 29.10.2017; loan recall notice issued 01.11.2017; DRT recovery filed 23.11.2017; RBI circular issued 12.02.2018; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 331/ALD/2018 filed on 05.09.2018 / 17.09.2018; NCLT admitted CIRP on 11.07.2024[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement dated 29.01.2016; recall notice dated 01.11.2017; NeSL Record of Default; Supreme Court order dated 18.03.2024 in SLP (C) No. 4092/2024 upholding rejection of OTS; absence of any approved or pending debt restructuring proposal[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: OBC filed Section 7 petition in September 2018; NCLT Allahabad Bench admitted the Corporate Debtor into CIRP on 11.07.2024, holding that debt and default were conclusively established and the Dharani Sugars ruling did not apply as the loan recall preceded the struck-down RBI circular[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition filed after the issuance of the RBI Circular dated 12.02.2018 is rendered non-est under the Supreme Court's ruling in Dharani Sugars when the financial creditor initiated loan recovery and recall prior to the circular; and whether potential receivables from a State Government or claims under the UP Sugarcane Act warrant discretionary rejection of Section 7 admission under the Vidarbha Industries doctrine[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency petition under Section 7 of the IBC initiated by a financial creditor independently of the quashed RBI circular of 12.02.2018 is valid and maintainable where loan recall and default preceded the circular; once debt and default are established, CIRP admission is mandatory, and the Vidarbha Industries exception applies only where an adjudicated and realizable claim in favor of the corporate debtor exceeds the debt owed[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proceedings under Section 7 are not vitiated by the Dharani Sugars judgment unless the action was triggered solely by operation of the quashed RBI circular; Section 7 admission cannot be stalled by speculative claims or unapproved OTS proposals[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Entry of default in NeSL records, accompanied by an unanswered loan recall notice predating the circular, conclusively establishes default; unliquidated assertions of dues owed by state authorities do not satisfy the evidentiary threshold required to withhold CIRP admission[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The financial debt and default being undisputed and independent of the RBI circular, the NCLT correctly admitted the Corporate Debtor into CIRP, while directing the IRP to adhere to statutory tagging orders for farmers' sugarcane dues[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1405 of 2024 is dismissed, upholding the NCLT order dated 11.07.2024 admitting Simbhaoli Sugars Limited into CIRP[cite: 11]. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1404 of 2024 is disposed of with directions to the Resolution Professional to consider sugarcane farmers' claims and adhere to statutory tagging orders issued by the District Magistrate[cite: 11]. Interim orders vacated[cite: 11]. All pending IAs closed[cite: 11]. No costs[cite: 11].
summary: Gursimran Kaur Mann, suspended director of Simbhaoli Sugars Limited, appealed against the NCLT Allahabad order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by Oriental Bank of Commerce (now PNB) for a default of Rs. 103.61 Crores[cite: 11]. The Appellant argued that the petition was non-est under the Supreme Court's Dharani Sugars judgment striking down the RBI Circular of 12.02.2018, and that the petition should be deferred under Vidarbha Industries due to dues owed by the UP Government[cite: 11]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the loan recall in November 2017 preceded the circular, rendering the petition independent and valid[cite: 11]. Furthermore, unadjudicated claims cannot defer mandatory Section 7 admission once debt and default are proved, while safeguarding farmers' statutory cane dues[cite: 11].

case_title: Mega Mall Management Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ajay Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional of Avani Projects & Infrastructures Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Avani Projects & Infrastructures Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Ajay Kumar Agarwal is the Resolution Professional (Respondent); Mega Mall Management Services Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant (Mall Management Company, step-down subsidiary, and related party of the Corporate Debtor); Aster Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. is the third-party parking assignee[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor developed Avani Riverside Mall[cite: 12]. Under Agreement dated 01.06.2011, Appellant was appointed maintenance agency to maintain common areas and parking, collect revenues/charges for a monthly fee of Rs. 50,000/-, and remit collections to Corporate Debtor; on 31.01.2018, parties executed a Supplemental Agreement granting operational surplus/deficit to Appellant and a Tripartite Agreement assigning parking operations to Aster Buildtech for Rs. 10 Lakhs[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on financial debts resulting in Section 7 CIRP admission on 13.03.2019; Transaction Audit quantified diverted mall revenues at approximately Rs. 117 Crores and Rs. 1.94 Crores, leading to avoidance application IA No. 591 of 2025[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court admitted winding-up petition against Corporate Debtor on 01.12.2017 (presented in 2016); Supplemental and Tripartite Agreements executed on 31.01.2018; Section 7 petition admitted on 13.03.2019; RP filed Section 19(2) IA No. 395 of 2020 on 06.03.2020 (disposed 13.06.2022); RP sent information requests on 25.06.2022, 02.07.2022, and 29.02.2024; RP filed IA (IBC) No. 910 of 2024 on 19.04.2024[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Maintenance Agreement dated 01.06.2011; Supplemental and Tripartite Agreements dated 31.01.2018; lease deeds with anchor tenants Reliance Footprint and PVR Ltd.; audited balance sheet for FY 2016-17 showing mall income of Rs. 307.56 Lakhs and fixed assets of Rs. 97.39 Crores; Transaction Audit Report dated 16.12.2024 by S.K. Agarwal & Co.[cite: 12] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA (IBC) No. 910 of 2024 under Section 60(5) in CP (IB) No. 378/KB/2018 seeking disclosure of rent and parking collections for FY 2021-22 and 2022-23; NCLT Kolkata Bench-II allowed the application on 18.06.2025, directing Appellant to furnish complete details within 30 days[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional under Section 60(5) read with Section 19 of the IBC can legitimately compel disclosure of rent and parking collection records from a mall management company and related party without first conclusively establishing the Corporate Debtor's subsisting ownership in the underlying mall units; and whether agreements executed after the presentation and admission of winding-up proceedings insulate a third party from disclosure[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Directing production of financial and operational information is a preliminary facilitative step rather than an adjudication of proprietary title, and a related entity or contracted manager possessing relevant records cannot withhold disclosure by asserting defenses that themselves require investigation[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19(2) and Section 60(5) of the IBC empower the adjudicating authority to compel cooperation and disclosure from any person associated with the corporate debtor's business or assets to enable the resolution professional to discharge statutory duties of asset verification and value preservation; separate legal personality cannot shield disclosure where direct transactional nexus exists[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where commercial rights and revenue streams were transferred away under agreements executed during the pendency of winding-up proceedings (subject to Sections 441(2) and 531 of the Companies Act, 1956) and avoidance applications under Section 66 are pending, the threshold of legitimate inquiry is satisfied, rendering the request for information bona fide and necessary[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in ordering disclosure of rent and parking collections as the direction was narrow, did not adjudicate substantive title, and was necessary for the CIRP, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1236 of 2025 is dismissed[cite: 12]. The impugned order dated 18.06.2025 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Kolkata Bench-II in I.A. (IBC) No. 910 of 2024 in CP (IB) No. 378/KB/2018 directing the Appellant to furnish complete details of rent and parking collections from Avani Riverside Mall for Financial Years 2021-22 and 2022-23 and thereafter within thirty days is affirmed[cite: 12]. No order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary: Mega Mall Management Services Pvt. Ltd., an entity managing Avani Riverside Mall and a related party of Corporate Debtor Avani Projects & Infrastructures Ltd., appealed against NCLT Kolkata's order directing it to disclose rent and parking revenues collected for FY 2021-22 and 2022-23 to the Resolution Professional[cite: 12]. Appellant argued that 2018 supplemental agreements novated earlier contracts and transferred revenues to third parties, making it an unconnected entity[cite: 12]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that compelling disclosure does not adjudicate substantive title and that related entities cannot withhold financial records concerning transactions entered into during the shadow of winding-up, affirming the RP's statutory right to obtain information under the IBC[cite: 12].

case_title: Hannu Steels Private Limited vs. Rathi Powertech Global Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hannu Steels Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Appellant; Rathi Powertech Global Private Limited is the Operational Creditor/Respondent[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: License User Agreement dated 01.03.2022 and Addendum dated 28.02.2023 under which Respondent granted Appellant a license to use the trademark 'POWERTECH' for manufacturing and marketing TMT Bars for a monthly royalty of Rs. 30,00,000/- plus GST, with Clause 20 providing a 3-month written termination right[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default in payment of royalty/licence fee for part of September 2024 and October 2024 to February 2025[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CAQM ordered closure of manufacturing unit on 03.06.2024; Appellant issued Clause 20 termination notice on 10.06.2024 effective 10.09.2024; Operational Creditor served Section 8 demand notice; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 567/ND/2025 filed on 19.10.2025 (registered 29.10.2025)[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: License User Agreement and Addendum; CAQM statutory closure order under Section 12(2)(xi); termination notice dated 10.06.2024; proforma invoices challenged by Corporate Debtor; website tracking records by Appellant[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Notice accepted on 19.11.2025 with one week granted to file reply; on 08.12.2025, NCLT Delhi Bench-IV closed Appellant's right to file reply and on 05.01.2026 reserved orders; Appellant filed appeal with an admitted delay of seven days[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether a delay of 7 days in filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC can be condoned due to advocate's failure to communicate the impugned order; and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in closing the Corporate Debtor's right to file a reply to a Section 9 petition after a single default, in violation of natural justice[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating authority should not prematurely forfeit a litigant's right to place its substantive defense on record in summary insolvency proceedings where the procedural default is attributable to counsel's lapse rather than deliberate contumacy and a prima facie plausible defense exists[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) proviso confers discretion to condone up to 15 days delay for 'sufficient cause', which must receive a liberal, justice-oriented construction; the summary nature of IBC proceedings cannot override the fundamental requirement of audi alteram partem[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the litigant demonstrates bona fide diligence by monitoring case status independently and acting promptly upon discovering counsel's default, and where the defense (statutory factory closure and contract termination) is prima facie substantial rather than sham, procedural defaults should not preclude adjudication on merits[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order closing the right to file reply deprived the Corporate Debtor of natural justice; the order is set aside and one final opportunity is granted to file a reply[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 124 of 2026 is allowed[cite: 13]. The delay of seven days in filing the appeal is condoned[cite: 13]. The impugned order dated 08.12.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV in CP (IB) No. 567/ND/2025 closing the right to file reply is set aside[cite: 13]. Appellant is granted one final opportunity to file its reply before the Adjudicating Authority within a time-bound schedule[cite: 13]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 13].
summary: Corporate Debtor Hannu Steels Pvt. Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV closing its right to file a reply to a Section 9 petition filed by Rathi Powertech Global Pvt. Ltd. over disputed trademark royalties[cite: 13]. The Appellant explained that its previous counsel failed to file the reply or inform it of the proceedings, and asserted a bona fide defense based on statutory factory closure by CAQM and a 3-month contract termination notice[cite: 13]. NCLAT condoned a 7-day delay under Section 61(2), held that procedural dispatch under the IBC must not eclipse audi alteram partem when serious civil consequences follow, set aside the closure order, and granted one final opportunity to file a reply[cite: 13].

case_title: The South Indian Bank Ltd. vs. Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya, Resolution Professional for RCI Industries and Technologies Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The South Indian Bank Ltd. is the Scheduled Commercial Bank/Financier/Appellant; RCI Industries and Technologies Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Buyer; Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Successful Resolution Applicant is Respondent No. 2; Mynd Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is the TReDS platform host ('M1 Exchange')[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant provided credit facilities including CCOL exposure of Rs. 20,62,76,197 and TReDS reverse factoring facility of Rs. 17,92,08,473 pursuant to Master Financier Agreement dated 07.04.2018 and Master Buyer's Agreement dated 21.12.2018, whereby Appellant discounted suppliers' invoices on the M1 platform and took assignment of trade receivables[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor account became NPA on 15.11.2019 following NACH auto-debit bounces; Appellant filed total claim of Rs. 38.54 Crores (CCOL: Rs. 20.62 Cr; TReDS: Rs. 17.92 Cr)[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted to CIRP on 25.11.2022 under Section 9; Appellant filed Form C on 13.12.2022; RP rejected TReDS claim as financial debt on 18.12.2022 directing filing under Form B; Appellant filed IA No. 3206 of 2023 on 05.06.2023; CoC approved resolution plan on 05.06.2024; NCLT dismissed IA on 13.02.2025; Appellant filed Form B on 12/13.03.2025; NCLT approved plan on 09.10.2025[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Master Financier Agreement and Master Buyer's Agreement; digital Deeds of Assignment executed by MSME suppliers under Clause 4.3.3; NACH auto-debit bounce notices; RP's communication dated 18.12.2022[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 3206 of 2023 under Section 60(5) seeking reclassification of TReDS dues as financial debt; NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissed IA on 13.02.2025 relying on Mudraksh Investfin Pvt. Ltd. v. Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether credit facilities extended by a scheduled commercial bank on the TReDS platform on a reverse-factoring basis constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) or an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC; and whether an approved and fully implemented resolution plan can be unsettled to reclassify an omitted claim[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Invoice discounting and reverse-factoring transactions on a TReDS platform constitute an assignment of operational trade debts where funds are disbursed to suppliers to discharge trade payables rather than placed at the debtor's disposal, thereby rendering the discounting financier an operational creditor under Sections 5(20) and 5(21) of the IBC[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The core touchstone running through all limbs of Section 5(8) is disbursal against consideration for the time value of money to the corporate debtor; discounting margin earned by a financier is compensation for early payment of trade receivables, not loan consideration; an assignee of an operational debt remains an operational creditor under Section 5(20)[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Looking at the true economic substance under the Global Credit Capital test, the obligation of the corporate debtor remains an existing trade payable for goods supplied, unaffected by the regulatory status of the financier as a bank[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The TReDS claim was properly classified as an operational debt; furthermore, the resolution plan having been approved and fully implemented, completed CIRP proceedings cannot be reopened[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 597 of 2025 is dismissed[cite: 14]. The impugned order dated 13.02.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench in IA No. 3206/2023 in IB No. 2688/ND/2019 is affirmed[cite: 14]. Appellant is not precluded from pursuing its claim before any other appropriate forum in accordance with law[cite: 14]. All related IAs disposed of[cite: 14]. No order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: The South Indian Bank Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of its application seeking reclassification of Rs. 17.92 Crores extended to RCI Industries and Technologies Ltd. under the TReDS reverse-factoring platform from 'operational debt' to 'financial debt'[cite: 14]. The Bank argued that as a scheduled commercial bank providing buyer-led financing with interest, its disbursals had the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(e)/(f)[cite: 14]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that discounting invoices on TReDS is an assignment of trade payables where no loan disbursal is made directly to the corporate debtor, maintaining its operational character under Sections 5(20) and 5(21) per Mudraksh[cite: 14]. The full implementation of the approved resolution plan further barred reopening the claim[cite: 14].

case_title: Uniworth Enterprises LLP vs. Starco Metaplast Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Uniworth Enterprises LLP is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Starco Metaplast Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of pharmaceutical packaging materials by Operational Creditor to Corporate Debtor on running account basis between August and November 2021; POs placed for 2,21,573 kgs (Rs. 4,07,63,236); supplies made of 1,35,567 kgs (Rs. 2,53,88,620) across multiple invoices[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed of Rs. 2,83,84,205/- (principal of Rs. 2,32,60,608/- and interest of Rs. 51,23,597/- @ 15% p.a.); Corporate Debtor expressly admitted liability of Rs. 1,91,80,733/- in reply to demand notice[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised 05.08.2021 to 09.11.2021; reconciliation meeting November 2022; email demanding PDCs sent 04.01.2023; Section 8 demand notice issued 23.01.2023; CD replied on 09.02.2023 offering monthly instalments of Rs. 15 Lakhs; Section 9 petition filed 22.02.2023 (registered 24.03.2023); CD filed IA No. 4625/2024 for additional documents on 11.09.2024; NCLT dismissed petition on 09.05.2025[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 8 reply dated 09.02.2023 admitting running account and offering to pay Rs. 1,91,80,733/-; debit notes dated 01.12.2021 for Rs. 40,84,275/- for short supply of 85,250 kgs; payment records showing ad-hoc RTGS transfers and Oxyzo Financial Services disbursements appropriated by Creditor on FIFO basis under Section 60 Contract Act; NeSL authenticated record of default dated 12.02.2024[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV dismissed Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 176 of 2023 on 09.05.2025, holding that FIFO adjustments against older/Section 10A invoices were improper, reducing outstanding debt below Rs. 1 Crore threshold and disclosing pre-existing disputes[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether a creditor in a running account is entitled under Section 60 of the Indian Contract Act to appropriate unallocated payments on a FIFO basis; whether an admitted debt of Rs. 1.91 Crores satisfies the Section 4 threshold notwithstanding unissued credit notes; and whether short-supply debit notes and a belated Section 10A defense constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute under Mobilox[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of specific appropriation instructions from a debtor in an ongoing running account, the creditor is entitled under Section 60 of the Indian Contract Act to apply payments on a FIFO basis to older lawful debts; furthermore, where the debtor unequivocally admits a liability exceeding the statutory threshold in its Section 8 reply, disputed debit notes or unliquidated damage claims do not constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A of the IBC bars initiation of CIRP for defaults occurring during the suspension period, but does not invalidate the underlying debt or prohibit voluntary payment and lawful contractual appropriation toward pre-existing dues; Section 4 threshold is satisfied if the admitted debt net of disputed debit notes exceeds Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, a defense that shifts from an admitted running account in the Section 8 reply to an invoice-by-invoice theory in court constitutes an impermissible approbation and reprobation and is a spurious, moonshine dispute[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default exceeded the statutory threshold and were admitted, and the alleged disputes were illusory, warranting reversal of the NCLT order and conditional admission under Section 9[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1056 of 2025 is allowed[cite: 15]. The impugned order dated 09.05.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV in C.P. (IB) No. 176 of 2023 is set aside[cite: 15]. Respondent Corporate Debtor is granted 15 days from the date of this order to pay Rs. 2,83,84,205/-, failing which the Corporate Debtor shall stand admitted into CIRP and the Adjudicating Authority shall pass an order of admission under Section 9[cite: 15]. All related IAs disposed of[cite: 15]. No order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Uniworth Enterprises LLP appealed against NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of its Section 9 petition against Starco Metaplast Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid pharma packaging supplies amounting to Rs. 2.83 Crores[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor claimed that payments had discharged the subject invoices, that older dues were barred by Section 10A, and that debit notes for short supply established a pre-existing dispute under Mobilox[cite: 15]. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that the Corporate Debtor had admitted running account status and liability of Rs. 1.91 Crores (above the Section 4 threshold) in its Section 8 reply[cite: 15]. The Creditor rightfully appropriated payments on a FIFO basis under Section 60 of the Contract Act[cite: 15]. The defenses were held to be spurious, and the CD was directed to pay within 15 days or face CIRP admission[cite: 15].

case_title: M/s Assam Power Distribution Company Ltd. vs. Mrs. Meena Sureka, Liquidator of Brahmaputra Rolling Mills Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Assam Power Distribution Company Ltd. (APDCL) is the State Power Utility/Operational Creditor/Appellant; Brahmaputra Rolling Mills Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (in liquidation); Mrs. Meena Sureka is the Liquidator (Respondent); BISCON Group includes separate affiliated companies (Brahmaputra Galvochem, Brahmaputra Iron & Steel, Brahmaputra TMT Bars, Brahmaputra Tubulars)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of electricity by APDCL to the Corporate Debtor until disconnection on 31.12.2014, against separate load security deposits and independent consumer connections maintained for each group company[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Upon reconciliation of accounts following disconnection, the load security deposited by Corporate Debtor exceeded unpaid electricity charges, leaving a net refundable surplus of Rs. 37,66,906.80 payable by APDCL to the Corporate Debtor; APDCL claimed parallel dues of Rs. 9,07,03,124 across other BISCON group companies[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Electricity disconnected on 31.12.2014; CIRP of CD initiated on 18.11.2022; APDCL filed Form B on 08.12.2022 for Rs. 21,61,779.88; RP informed APDCL on 06.01.2023 that Rs. 37,66,906.80 was refundable to CD; liquidation ordered on 13.10.2023; APDCL filed Form C on 02.12.2023 for Rs. 28,39,285.24 (rejected); APDCL admitted Rs. 37.66 Lakhs liability in letter dated 06.02.2024 but sought group set-off; other group entities dissolved on 13.12.2024; Liquidator filed IA No. 119/GB/2024; NCLT allowed IA on 27.05.2025[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: APDCL's claim form recording 'N/A' under mutual dealings/set-off; APDCL admission letter dated 06.02.2024 admitting liability of Rs. 37,66,906.80; separate electricity meters, bills, and load security ledgers for each group entity; NCLT dissolution orders dated 13.12.2024 for group entities[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA(IBC)/119/GB/2024 in CP(IB)/16/GB/2022 under Section 60(5) read with Section 35 to recover refundable load security; NCLT Guwahati Bench on 27.05.2025 directed APDCL to pay Rs. 37,66,906.80 with applicable interest from 31.12.2014, rejecting group set-off[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor under Regulation 29 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 can invoke the 'Group of Companies Doctrine' to set off its admitted liability toward a corporate debtor against claims owed to it by separate, affiliated companies of the same promoter group[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory insolvency set-off under Regulation 29 of the Liquidation Process Regulations requires strict mutuality of dealings between the identical legal entities; an operational debtor cannot invoke the group of companies doctrine to adjust liabilities owed to a corporate debtor against cross-claims pending against distinct, legally incorporated group companies[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 29 applies strictly to mutual credits and mutual debts between the specific corporate debtor and the other party; Section 35(1)(b) mandates the liquidator to realize all assets and actionable claims; Section 53 waterfall cannot be bypassed through unauthorized multi-entity set-offs; Section 238 of the IBC overrides inconsistent provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Separate contracts, distinct consumer connections, individual billing accounts, and separate load security deposits confirm distinct legal identities, precluding consolidated economic treatment; furthermore, claims against entities already dissolved under Section 54 cannot be revived for set-off[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because mutuality was lacking across separate juristic persons, APDCL was legally obligated to refund the surplus load security to the liquidation estate without set-off, justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1205 of 2025 is dismissed[cite: 16]. The impugned order dated 27.05.2025 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Guwahati Bench in IA(IBC)/119/GB/2024 in CP(IB)/16/GB/2022 directing the Appellant to pay Rs. 37,66,906.80 along with applicable interest to the Liquidator is affirmed[cite: 16]. All related IAs disposed of[cite: 16]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 16].
summary: State power discom Assam Power Distribution Company Ltd. (APDCL) appealed an order of NCLT Guwahati directing it to refund Rs. 37,66,906.80 in excess load security with interest to the Liquidator of Brahmaputra Rolling Mills Pvt. Ltd[cite: 16]. APDCL sought to set off this refund under Regulation 29 of the Liquidation Regulations against unpaid electricity dues of Rs. 9.07 Crores owed by other companies in the BISCON Group, invoking the group of companies doctrine[cite: 16]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that insolvency set-off requires strict mutuality between the same corporate debtor and creditor[cite: 16]. Since each group entity had distinct contracts, meters, and separate liquidation proceedings, cross-entity set-off was impermissible under Section 53 and Regulation 29[cite: 16].

case_title: Kavish Gupta vs. Yes Bank Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kavish Gupta is the Suspended Director of KKSPUN India Limited (Corporate Debtor/Appellant in connected appeals); Yes Bank Limited is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Harvinder Singh is the IRP (Respondent No. 2); State Bank of India is the Lead Consortium Bank (Respondent No. 3); IndusInd Bank is a Consortium Member (Respondent No. 4)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned by Yes Bank since 2016 (Cash Credit, Bank Guarantee, and GECL facilities); parallel consortium credit facilities led by SBI amounting to Rs. 169.88 Crores renewed on 18.02.2022 to finance infrastructure precast concrete manufacturing operations[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities; Yes Bank classified loan account as NPA on 05.08.2022 with outstanding default of Rs. 32,57,29,534.01 as of 01.06.2023; SBI loan account classified as NPA on 10.08.2022 with default of Rs. 190.49 Crores[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Yes Bank issued loan recall notice on 07.03.2023 for Rs. 32.13 Crores; Yes Bank filed Section 7 CP (IB) No. 36/ND/2024 on 14.12.2023 (registered 24.01.2024); CD filed Section 230 scheme application CA (CAA) No. 114/ND/2024 on 07.12.2024; JLM rejected OTS proposal on 10.02.2025; NCLT closed right to argue on 19.03.2025 and reserved orders on 02.04.2025; NCLT admitted Section 7 petition on 11.07.2025[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements and sanction letters; NeSL default authentication dated 05.08.2022; Corporate Debtor's debt acknowledgment letters dated 24.11.2021; Balance Sheets for 2022 and 2023; rejected OTS proposals dated 08.01.2024, 06.07.2024, 24.09.2024, and 30.01.2025; pending DRT Counterclaim of Rs. 817 Crores[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Yes Bank filed Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 36/ND/2024; SBI filed CP (IB) No. 326/ND/2024; NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV admitted Yes Bank's petition under Section 7 on 11.07.2025 and disposed of SBI's petition; CD's recall and restoration applications (IA 1913/2025, RA 37/2025, IA 1916/2025, RA 36/2025) were dismissed[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether the pendency of a Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 or active OTS negotiations legally bar the Adjudicating Authority from admitting a Section 7 IBC application; and whether an unadjudicated counterclaim before the DRT or commercial viability under Vidarbha Industries can prevent CIRP admission once financial debt and default are established[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of compromise proceedings under Section 230 of the Companies Act, ongoing settlement negotiations, or unadjudicated counterclaims before a recovery tribunal do not operate as a legal bar to the admission of a Section 7 petition once the jurisdictional facts of financial debt and default are conclusively established[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC mandates CIRP admission upon proof of default; the discretion recognized in Vidarbha Industries is a narrow exception applicable only where an adjudicated and realizable claim exceeding the debt exists; statutory timelines cannot be subordinated to speculative restructuring schemes[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: NeSL certificates of default, balance sheet debt acknowledgments, and repeated written OTS proposals conclusively prove default; closure of oral arguments after multiple unutilized adjournments does not violate natural justice when written submissions are considered[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The financial debt exceeding Rs. 32 Crores and continuous default were undisputed, rendering Section 7 admission legally unimpeachable and dismissing all procedural and substantive appeals[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1015 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the admission of KKSPUN India Limited into CIRP[cite: 17]. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 815 of 2025 and 816 of 2025 are dismissed as challenging procedural orders in the same petition[cite: 17]. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 812 of 2025 and 813 of 2025 are dismissed as infructuous[cite: 17]. All pending interlocutory applications disposed of[cite: 17]. No order as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: Kavish Gupta, suspended director of KKSPUN India Limited, appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by Yes Bank Ltd. for a default of Rs. 32.57 Crores, alongside appeals challenging procedural orders closing the right to argue[cite: 17]. The Appellant contended that NCLT violated natural justice and erred in initiating CIRP while a Scheme of Compromise under Section 230 of the Companies Act was pending, OTS talks were ongoing, and an Rs. 817 Crore counterclaim was pending before the DRT[cite: 17]. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that Section 230 schemes and unadjudicated DRT counterclaims cannot stall Section 7 admission once financial debt and default are established through NeSL records and repeated OTS admissions[cite: 17].

case_title: Allcheckdeals India Private Limited & Ors. vs. Info Edge (India) Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Allcheckdeals India Pvt. Ltd. (Transferor Co. 1), Axilly Labs Pvt. Ltd. (Transferor Co. 2), Diphda Internet Services Ltd. (Transferor Co. 3), and Zwayam Digital Pvt. Ltd. (Transferor Co. 4) are wholly owned subsidiaries/Appellants 1 to 4; Info Edge (India) Limited is the listed holding Transferee Company/Appellant 5[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Scheme of Amalgamation under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 for the merger of four wholly owned subsidiaries into their parent holding company, wherein no shares are to be issued by the Transferee Company and no compromise or arrangement is proposed with its members or creditors[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Matter does not involve debt default; all applicant companies maintained positive net worths as on 31.03.2025 (Transferor Co. 1: Rs. 13.08 Cr; Transferor Co. 2: Rs. 58.78 Cr; Transferor Co. 3: Rs. 2,621.42 Cr; Transferor Co. 4: Rs. 18.26 Cr; Transferee Co.: Rs. 27,701.31 Cr)[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respective Boards approved Scheme on 05.02.2025; joint First Motion Application CA (CAA) No. 62/ND/2025 filed on 15.07.2025; matter reserved on 18.11.2025; NCLT pronounced impugned order on 07.04.2026[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited financial statements as on 31.03.2025 showing asset base far exceeding liabilities; 100% share ownership certificates; consent affidavits from shareholders/creditors of Transferor companies; absence of debt restructuring or capital reduction under Section 230(2)[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court IV on 07.04.2026 dispensed with meetings of stakeholders of Transferor Companies, but directed Transferee Company to convene meetings of its 1,93,534 equity shareholders (quorum 96,770), 3 secured creditors, and 37 unsecured creditors without assigning any reasons[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has discretion under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 to dispense with meetings of equity shareholders, secured creditors, and unsecured creditors of a holding Transferee Company in a merger of wholly owned subsidiaries where no new shares are issued and no rights of stakeholders are affected; and whether directing such meetings without assigning any reasons or finding of prejudice is sustainable in law[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a scheme of amalgamation of wholly owned subsidiaries with their holding company where no shares are issued, no capital reorganization occurs, and no compromise is offered to creditors or members whose rights remain unaffected, convening meetings of the transferee company's stakeholders may be dispensed with[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 232(1) uses the word 'may', conferring judicial discretion to dispense with stakeholder meetings when statutory conditions are satisfied; such discretion must be exercised on intelligible criteria and cannot be exercised arbitrarily without recorded reasons[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where audited balance sheets demonstrate an overwhelmingly positive net worth and asset sufficiency to meet all liabilities, and the scheme involves no dilution or variation of stakeholder rights, imposing procedural meetings represents an onerous and unnecessary burden devoid of protective value[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in directing meetings of the Transferee Company without assigning reasons or identifying prejudice, justifying the setting aside of the directions and granting dispensation of meetings[cite: 18].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) No. 243 of 2026 is allowed[cite: 18]. The impugned order dated 07.04.2026 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench Court IV in CA (CAA) No. 62/ND/2025 is set aside to the limited extent it directed convening and holding of meetings of the equity shareholders, secured creditors, and unsecured creditors of Info Edge (India) Limited, and the requirement of convening such meetings is dispensed with[cite: 18]. Remaining portions of the order concerning transferor companies remain undisturbed[cite: 18]. No order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: Allcheckdeals India Pvt. Ltd., three other wholly owned subsidiaries, and their listed parent Info Edge (India) Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi directing Info Edge to convene meetings of its 1.93 lakh shareholders and creditors under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, despite dispensing with meetings for the subsidiaries[cite: 18]. The Appellants contended that no fresh shares were being issued, no compromise was proposed, and Info Edge had a positive net worth exceeding Rs. 27,700 Crores[cite: 18]. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that where a merger involves wholly owned subsidiaries without altering stakeholder rights, meetings of the transferee company can be dispensed with[cite: 18]. The unreasoned direction was set aside[cite: 18].

case_title: Vivid Solutions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Mukesh Jain & Ors.
appeal_number: COMPANY APPEAL (AT) NO. 125 OF 2021 & IA No. 538/2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vivid Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is Appellant No. 1; Rajendra Tulsidas Katore and Anita Katore are Appellants No. 2 and 3 (alleged transferees); Ukay Metal Industries Pvt. Ltd. is Appellant No. 4; Mukesh Jain, Sushil Jain, and Sonu Jain are Respondents No. 1 to 3 (original 100% shareholders/promoters); Federal Bank Ltd. is Respondent No. 4[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants claimed that under an MOU dated 21.12.2012, Respondents agreed to transfer 100% shareholding in Appellant No. 1 and its sole industrial land (E-74, MIDC Ambad, Nashik) to Appellants No. 2 and 3 for Rs. 3 Crores and Rs. 1 Lakh share face value, following which Appellants altered balance sheets to reflect transfer of property to Appellant No. 4 against an unsecured loan[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over alleged transfer of 100% shares and immovable property valued at over Rs. 10.62 Crores (per bank valuation) against an unsecured loan entry of Rs. 3 Crores without consideration finalization[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MOU executed 21.12.2012; payments made through March 2014; resignation letters purportedly executed 31.03.2014; Company Petition No. 1841/2019 filed under Sections 241-242 on 06.05.2019 after Respondents discovered shareholding deletion via letter dated 25.03.2019; retrospective revised ROC filings lodged by Appellants on 07.04.2019[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unchallenged MCA records and MGT-7 returns from 2014 to 2017 reflecting Respondents as 100% shareholders; original share certificates remaining in possession of Respondents without transfer endorsement; complete absence of stamped Form SH-4 share transfer deeds; absence of registered conveyance deed under Section 54 TP Act for the MIDC plot; rental payments continuing from Appellant No. 4 to Appellant No. 1[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed CP No. 1841/2019 alleging oppression and mismanagement before NCLT Mumbai; on 08.10.2021, NCLT declared Respondents to be 100% shareholders, holding the share transfer and property transfer illegal, null, and void due to non-compliance with Section 56 Companies Act and Section 54 TP Act[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether 100% shareholding in a company can be transferred by unilateral retrospective book entries and revised ROC filings without executed share transfer deeds (Form SH-4) or share certificate endorsements under Section 56 of the Companies Act, 2013; and whether corporate immovable property can be transferred to an affiliate through balance sheet entries adjusting unsecured loans without a registered conveyance deed under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Title to shares cannot pass without strict compliance with mandatory statutory transfer mechanisms, and ownership of corporate immovable property cannot be divested through accounting balance sheet adjustments absent a registered instrument of conveyance[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 56 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires delivery of a duly stamped, executed transfer form (SH-4) along with certificates; Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act read with Section 17 of the Registration Act mandates a registered conveyance deed for immovable property transfer; Section 130 of the Companies Act prohibits reopening accounts without tribunal sanction[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous statutory annual returns filed under Section 92 enjoy a presumption of correctness that cannot be displaced by unilateral retrospective revisions filed years later as an afterthought to criminal complaints; possession of unendorsed original share certificates conclusively refutes completed share transfer[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The purported transfer of shares and stripping of the company's sole asset through fictitious journal entries constituted oppression and mismanagement of the gravest kind, warranting dismissal of the appeal and affirmation of the NCLT order[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 125 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 19]. The impugned order dated 08.10.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai in Company Petition No. 1841/2019 declaring Respondents No. 1 to 3 as 100% shareholders and invalidating the transfer of shares and immovable property is affirmed[cite: 19]. Pending applications are disposed of[cite: 19]. No order as to costs[cite: 19].
summary: Appellants Rajendra Katore and associates appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order declaring Respondents Mukesh Jain and family to be 100% shareholders of Vivid Solutions Pvt. Ltd. and setting aside the transfer of the company's shares and its sole MIDC industrial property[cite: 19]. The Appellants claimed to have acquired 100% equity and the property pursuant to an MOU dated 21.12.2012 for Rs. 3 Crores, reflecting the transfers via balance sheet entries[cite: 19]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that no valid share transfer occurred due to non-execution of Form SH-4 under Section 56 of the Companies Act, 2013, and the property transfer without a registered deed violated Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, constituting oppression and mismanagement[cite: 19].

case_title: M/s. Shree Dhanvantari Pharmaceuticals vs. M/s. Konkan Ayur Pharma Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Shree Dhanvantari Pharmaceuticals is a partnership firm/Financial Creditor/Appellant; M/s. Konkan Ayur Pharma Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1; Respondent No. 2 (partner) and Respondent No. 3 (legal representative of deceased partner) are dissenting partners/intervenors[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial advances aggregating Rs. 2,26,45,568/- made by the Appellant partnership firm to Corporate Debtor across financial years closing 31.03.2015 to 31.03.2019, claimed with 18% interest p.a. totaling Rs. 3,55,54,900/-[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal debt of Rs. 2,26,45,568/- claimed; date of default originally stated as 31.03.2019 (last transaction date), subsequently altered via affidavit to 30.05.2022; default claimed upon non-payment after demand notice[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last ledger transaction dated 31.03.2019; Demand notice issued 14.05.2022 (dispatched 17.05.2022); Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 1309/MB-IV/2022 filed in August 2022; amendment affidavit filed 13.07.2023; NCLT dismissed petition on 07.02.2024[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor balance sheets for FY 2015-16 and 2016-17 reflecting Appellant as sundry creditor under current liabilities; ledger accounts covering 12.06.2010 to 31.03.2019 showing absence of interest debits; Partnership Deed dated 14.07.1992 Clauses 13, 14, 29, and 31[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 7 petition; Respondents No. 2 and 3 filed Intervention Petitions INVP 44/2023 and 46/2023 challenging authorization; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed the petition on 07.02.2024 citing lack of clarity regarding date of default, lack of loan agreement, and internal partnership disputes[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether a majority of surviving partners in a partnership firm has statutory authority under Section 12(c) and 18 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 to institute a Section 7 IBC petition in the firm's name despite objection by a minority partner; and whether an artificially altered date of default can revive a debt where the three-year limitation period from the last transaction date has expired[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a majority of surviving partners possesses legal authority under partnership law to institute legal proceedings in the name of the firm for ordinary business recovery, an insolvency application under Section 7 is barred by limitation if filed beyond three years from the actual date of default, and an artificial date cannot be created by issuing a belated demand notice[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12(c) and 18 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 authorize majority partners to bind the firm in business matters; under Section 3(12) of the IBC read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period runs from the date debt becomes due and payable and cannot be extended by an unsubstantiated date of default inserted via affidavit[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of a written loan agreement specifying a future due date, the ledger's last transaction date constitutes the nearest ascertainable terminus a quo for limitation; altering the date of default without factual foundation fails the test of legal certainty[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The majority partners held valid authorization to file the petition, but because the last transaction occurred on 31.03.2019 and the petition was filed in August 2022, the debt was time-barred, justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 988 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 20]. The order dated 07.02.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV in CP (IB) No. 1309/MB-IV/2022 is affirmed[cite: 20]. No order as to costs[cite: 20].
summary: M/s. Shree Dhanvantari Pharmaceuticals appealed against NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of its Section 7 petition against Konkan Ayur Pharma Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 2.26 Crores[cite: 20]. The NCLT dismissed the petition on grounds of partnership authorization disputes, lack of a loan agreement, and uncertainty regarding the date of default[cite: 20]. NCLAT held that majority surviving partners had valid legal authority to file the petition under Section 12(c) of the Partnership Act, and formal loan agreements are not mandatory to establish debt[cite: 20]. However, because the last transaction occurred on 31.03.2019 and the Section 7 petition was filed in August 2022, the debt was barred by limitation under Article 137[cite: 20]. The dismissal was affirmed[cite: 20].

case_title: UCO Bank vs. Subrata Das & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 451 of 2025 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 452 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: UCO Bank is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; M/s Haridra Vintrade Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Principal Borrower; Subrata Das and Rahul Gupta are former Directors and Personal Guarantors (Respondents in CA 451/2025 and 452/2025 respectively)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sanction of Cash Credit Facility of Rs. 250 Lakhs by UCO Bank to the Principal Borrower vide Sanction Letter dated 15.07.2022, secured by personal guarantees executed by the Respondents via Letters of Guarantee[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account irregular and classified as NPA on 30.03.2023 for default in debt servicing under RBI guidelines; total outstanding debt of Rs. 250 Lakhs plus accrued interest[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Credit facility sanctioned 15.07.2022; account classified as NPA on 30.03.2023; Demand Notices issued invoking guarantees; Demand Notice in Form B served on Respondents on 20.06.2024; Section 95(1) petitions C.P. (IB) Nos. 286/2024 and 285/2024 filed in 2024; NCLT dismissed petitions on 17.12.2024 and 08.01.2025[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction Letter dated 15.07.2022; executed Letters of Guarantee; NPA classification records; Form B demand notices served on 20.06.2024; IRP recommendations in Section 99 report recommending admission[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: UCO Bank filed Section 95(1) applications against the personal guarantors; NCLT Kolkata Bench (Court II and Special Bench Court I) dismissed the petitions on 17.12.2024 and 08.01.2025, holding that NCLT lacks jurisdiction over personal guarantors unless CIRP or liquidation is pending or concluded against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 95(1) of the IBC against a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor is maintainable before the NCLT when no CIRP or liquidation proceeding is initiated, pending, or concluded against the principal corporate debtor; and whether a financial creditor can proceed directly against a personal guarantor under Section 60(1) of the Code[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency resolution application under Section 95(1) of the IBC can be instituted directly against a personal guarantor before the NCLT irrespective of whether corporate insolvency resolution or liquidation proceedings have been initiated, are pending, or have concluded against the principal corporate debtor[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(1) vests general territorial jurisdiction in NCLT as the adjudicating authority for corporate debtors and their personal guarantors; Section 60(2) is an enabling provision ensuring consolidation when CIRP is pending, but does not restrict or condition Section 60(1) jurisdiction; Section 179(1) is expressly subject to Section 60[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liability of a surety is co-extensive and concurrent with that of the principal debtor; requiring creditors to first litigate against the debtor defeats the statutory character of financial debt under Section 5(8)[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT Kolkata Bench erred in holding that Section 95 applications lie only before the DRT in the absence of debtor CIRP; the decisions were per incuriam binding precedent, requiring the orders to be set aside and remanded[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 451 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 452 of 2025 are allowed[cite: 21]. The impugned orders dated 17.12.2024 and 08.01.2025 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench are set aside[cite: 21]. The original Section 95 petitions are restored to the file of the Adjudicating Authority for disposal in accordance with law[cite: 21]. Parties directed to appear before NCLT on 27.07.2026[cite: 21]. Pending IAs closed[cite: 21]. No costs[cite: 21].
summary: UCO Bank appealed against orders of NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissing its Section 95(1) applications filed against Subrata Das and Rahul Gupta, personal guarantors of Haridra Vintrade Pvt. Ltd., for a default of Rs. 2.50 Crores[cite: 21]. The NCLT had held that applications against personal guarantors are not maintainable before NCLT unless CIRP or liquidation is pending or completed against the corporate debtor[cite: 21]. NCLAT set aside the orders and allowed the appeals, ruling that under Section 60(1) of the IBC and Section 128 of the Contract Act, a creditor has a concurrent right to proceed directly against a personal guarantor before NCLT without first exhausting remedies against the corporate debtor[cite: 21].

case_title: Sachin Naveen Sinha vs. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
appeal_number: I.A. No. 4537 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1165 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sachin Naveen Sinha is the Appellant (Insolvency Professional / Erstwhile IRP/RP); Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) is the statutory disciplinary regulator (Respondent)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Professional engagement of Appellant as Resolution Professional across four separate CIRP assignments under the IBC framework[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disciplinary proceedings initiated against Appellant for failing to constitute a Committee of Creditors for approximately two years in a single CIRP (CP(IB) 63/9/JPR/2020) despite the existence of a secured financial creditor (SBI)[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Jaipur Bench removed Appellant and ordered refund of Rs. 2 Lakhs on 26.09.2025; IBBI initiated inspection/investigation and passed disciplinary order dated 08.06.2026 suspending registration for 3 years effective 08.07.2026; Parliament enacted Section 220(7) via Act 6 of 2026 on 22.05.2026; Appellant filed appeal and stay IA No. 4537 of 2026 before NCLAT[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Disciplinary Committee order dated 08.06.2026; absence of charges or show cause notices concerning Appellant's conduct in the three other active CIRPs; Regulation 13(7) mandate requiring intimation of disciplinary orders to CoCs[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority recommended disciplinary action in IA 382/2025; IBBI Disciplinary Committee suspended registration for 3 years; Appellant appealed under Section 220(7) and sought stay in IA No. 4537 of 2026; NCLAT adjudicated the stay application on substantive interpretations of Section 220(2) versus Section 220(7) and Regulation 13(7)[cite: 22].
legal_issues: What is the scope and extent of appellate jurisdiction exercised by NCLAT under the newly inserted Section 220(7) of the IBC; and whether the IBBI can, under Section 220(2), impose a blanket 3-year suspension barring an IP across all ongoing assignments without hearing or notice regarding other assignments, thereby superseding CoC authority and rendering Regulation 13(7) otiose[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A regulatory disciplinary authority cannot exercise its statutory powers disproportionately or in violation of natural justice by imposing a blanket suspension across multiple independent assignments where the alleged misconduct is confined to a single assignment, without affording the professional a hearing regarding the other assignments[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 220(7) vests unbridled first appellate jurisdiction in NCLAT without limiting language; Section 220(2) disciplinary powers must be read harmoniously with Regulation 13(7) of the Inspection Regulations (passed pursuant to Section 241), which contemplates informing other CoCs to decide on replacement under Section 27 rather than automatic blanket disqualification[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the doctrine of audi alteram partem, penalizing an individual in relation to matters where no charges were framed or heard constitutes an ultra vires and disproportionate exercise of regulatory power[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A strong prima facie case of disproportionate punishment and procedural overreach was established, justifying the interim suspension of the IBBI's blanket debarment order qua other CIRP assignments[cite: 22].
operative_order: I.A. No. 4537 of 2026 is allowed[cite: 22]. The order of suspension dated 08.06.2026 imposed by the IBBI is suspended with regard to other assignments in which the Appellant is appointed as a resolution professional[cite: 22]. IBBI is granted liberty to communicate the disciplinary order to the respective CoCs of those assignments to take an independent call on retaining the Appellant[cite: 22]. No order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: Insolvency Professional Sachin Naveen Sinha appealed against an IBBI Disciplinary Committee order suspending his registration for three years for failing to constitute a CoC for two years in a single CIRP[cite: 22]. The Appellant filed IA No. 4537/2026 seeking a stay, arguing that IBBI lacked authority to impose a blanket ban across three other ongoing CIRP assignments where no complaints existed[cite: 22]. NCLAT held that its newly conferred appellate jurisdiction under Section 220(7) is plenary[cite: 22]. Interpreting Section 220(2) harmoniously with Regulation 13(7) and audi alteram partem, the Tribunal ruled that IBBI overstepped by penalizing the IP across assignments without hearing him, and suspended the debarment order qua other assignments[cite: 22].

case_title: Mathew C.K. & Ors. vs. Kumar Rajan, Resolution Professional of Hindustan Newsprint Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mathew C.K. and 27 other former/current employees and workmen (or legal representatives) are the Appellants; Hindustan Newsprint Limited (HNL) is the Corporate Debtor; Kumar Rajan is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); RBL Bank Ltd. is the petitioning Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 2); Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (KINFRA) is the Successful Resolution Applicant / Monitoring Committee (Respondents No. 3 & 4)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment relationships under which workmen and employees earned statutory retirement benefits including Provident Fund and Gratuity during operation of HNL's newsprint manufacturing unit in Kerala[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Commercial crisis forced plant closure on 01.01.2019; total admitted claims included Rs. 6,404.12 Lakhs for workmen and Rs. 3,190.48 Lakhs for employees, with admitted PF claims of Rs. 3,046.32 Lakhs and gratuity claims of Rs. 2,961.46 Lakhs for workmen and Rs. 1,410.75 Lakhs for employees[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 28.11.2019; public announcement 04.12.2019; Form G published 05.06.2020; CoC approved KINFRA's revised plan on 22.12.2020; NCLT approved plan on 29.01.2021 in IA(IBC)/21/KOB/2021; appeal preferred in 2021[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocating only 35.13% toward workmen's PF/gratuity and 16.31% toward employees' retirement dues; binding precedent of coordinate bench in Mrs. C.G. Vijayalakshmi (08.02.2023) and Supreme Court affirmance in Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench approved KINFRA's resolution plan on 29.01.2021 in IA(IBC)/21/KOB/2021 in TIBA/03/KOB/2019; Appellants appealed challenging the plan's failure to provide 100% payment for PF and gratuity dues[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether statutory provident fund and gratuity dues owed to workmen and employees of a corporate debtor can be subjected to percentage haircuts (35.13% or 16.31%) under a Resolution Plan or whether Section 30(2) read with Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC and special labor enactments mandate payment in full[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Provident Fund and Gratuity dues owed to workmen and employees are statutory trust entitlements excluded from the liquidation estate and waterfall distribution, and must be paid in full under any resolution plan to comply with Section 30(2) of the IBC[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(e) requires resolution plans to comply with all laws in force, including the EPF Act, 1952 and Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972; Section 36(4)(a)(iii) excludes employee welfare funds from estate assets; treating such statutory dues on par with secured or unsecured financial creditors violates Section 30(2)[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where claims towards PF and gratuity are admitted by the resolution professional, any provision in a resolution plan proposing partial payout (such as 35.13%) demonstrates an ex-facie contravention of statutory mandates[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is squarely covered by the coordinate bench rulings in Mrs. C.G. Vijayalakshmi and Jet Airways, requiring the Successful Resolution Applicant to satisfy admitted PF and gratuity dues in full[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 40 of 2021 is allowed in part on the same terms as Mrs. C.G. Vijayalakshmi[cite: 23].
