Successful Resolution Applicant (KINFRA) is directed to pay the eligible Provident Fund and Gratuity amounts due to the Appellants in full, after adjusting payments already made, while the remaining admitted dues shall be paid as proposed in the approved Resolution Plan[cite: 23]. Pending IAs closed[cite: 23]. No costs[cite: 23].
summary: Twenty-eight former and current employees and workmen of Hindustan Newsprint Limited appealed against NCLT Kochi Bench's approval of KINFRA's Resolution Plan under Section 31 of the IBC[cite: 23]. The Appellants challenged the plan for paying only 35.13% of workmen's admitted gratuity and PF claims and 16.31% of employees' claims[cite: 23]. NCLAT Chennai allowed the appeal in part, holding that under Section 30(2) of the IBC read with the EPF Act, 1952 and Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, provident fund and gratuity dues are excluded from the liquidation waterfall and must be paid in full, following the binding ratio in Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers[cite: 23]. The SRA was directed to pay the balance in full[cite: 23].

case_title: Deepti Pankaj Chugh vs. The State Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deepti Pankaj Chugh is the Personal Guarantor/Appellant; State Bank of India (SAMB, Ahmedabad) is the Financial Creditor/Respondent; M/s Aditya Prints Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (in liquidation); Saurabh Premprakash Chugh is a co-personal guarantor[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor from State Bank of India, secured inter alia by personal guarantees executed by the Appellant and other guarantors, and mortgages over immovable properties[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 28.07.2016 with retrospective effect from 28.10.2013; Section 13(2) SARFAESI demand notice issued on 20.03.2017 claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 49,76,13,119.38[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account NPA w.e.f. 28.10.2013; Section 13(2) notice issued to CD and Appellant on 20.03.2017; possession notice under Section 13(4) issued on 27.01.2022; Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP on 10.05.2022 and liquidation ordered on 20.07.2023; Appellant filed first Section 94 petition CP(IB) 55/2024 on 11.01.2024 (dismissed with liberty on 01.02.2024); Appellant filed second Section 94 petition CP(IB) 147/2024 on 19.03.2024 (dismissed on merits as time-barred on 01.05.2024); Appellant filed third Section 94 petition CP(IB) 76/2025 on 31.01.2025; NCLT dismissed it on 24.02.2025[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Demand Notice dated 20.03.2017 issued directly to the Appellant under Section 13(2); dismissal order on merits in CP(IB) 147/2024 dated 01.05.2024 suppressed by Appellant; repeated successive Section 94 filings timed to coincide with SARFAESI physical possession and auction measures to invoke Section 96 interim moratorium[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed CP (IB) No. 76/AHM/2025 on 24.02.2025 with Rs. 1 Lakh cost, holding that successive petitions after earlier dismissals on merits are unmaintainable and an abuse of process[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a personal guarantor can repeatedly file applications under Section 94 of the IBC to trigger interim moratorium under Section 96 after an earlier identical petition was dismissed on merits as time-barred, or whether such successive proceedings are barred by res judicata and constitute an abuse of process; and whether limitation runs from a Section 13(2) demand notice or subsequent Section 13(4) possession notices[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The repeated filing of insolvency applications under Section 94 of the IBC by a personal guarantor following the dismissal of an earlier petition on merits is barred by the doctrine of res judicata and constitutes an abuse of process when initiated to subvert recovery under the SARFAESI Act by taking unfair advantage of the statutory interim moratorium[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 94 is intended for genuine personal insolvency resolution and cannot be deployed as an obstructionist device; Section 238A bars claims filed beyond three years from the date of default/demand notice; Section 96 interim moratorium cannot be invoked through non-maintainable successive petitions[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Suppressing prior dismissal orders on limitation and misrepresenting procedural history demonstrates lack of clean hands and constructive fraud on the court, warranting dismissal with exemplary costs[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition was time-barred reckoned from the 20.03.2017 demand notice and hit by res judicata following the unappealed order of 01.05.2024, fully justifying dismissal of the appeal and imposition of Rs. 2 Lakhs costs[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 646 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT order dated 24.02.2025[cite: 24]. Costs of Rs. 2 Lakhs are imposed on the Appellant, to be deposited in the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund within one month[cite: 24]. All related IAs disposed of[cite: 24]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 24].
summary: Deepti Pankaj Chugh, personal guarantor of Corporate Debtor Aditya Prints Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation), appealed against NCLT Ahmedabad's dismissal of her Section 94 petition (CP (IB) No. 76/2025) with costs of Rs. 1 Lakh[cite: 24]. The Appellant argued that limitation ran from the SARFAESI Section 13(4) possession notice of 27.01.2022 rather than the 2017 Section 13(2) notice[cite: 24]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, finding that the Appellant had concealed a prior dismissal on merits of an identical petition (CP (IB) No. 147/2024) as time-barred[cite: 24]. Holding the subsequent petition barred by res judicata and a mala fide tactic to abuse the Section 96 interim moratorium against bank auctions, NCLAT affirmed the order and imposed Rs. 2 Lakhs in costs[cite: 24].

case_title: Sukhbir Singh vs. Verbio India Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sukhbir Singh is the Suspended Director and Shareholder of Farm2energy Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Appellant); Verbio India Private Limited is the Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Harish Malhotra is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 19.07.2022 and Deed of Hypothecation for supply of 20,000 tons of Biomass Bales by Corporate Debtor to Operational Creditor for total consideration of Rs. 4,40,00,000/-, against which Operational Creditor paid 35% advance aggregating Rs. 1,54,00,000/- (Rs. 77 Lakhs each on 20.07.2022 and 18.08.2022)[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor supplied goods worth only Rs. 34,46,136/-; default amount claimed for refund of unadjusted advance was Rs. 1,19,53,864/- along with interest @ 9% p.a., with date of default stated as 16.01.2022/15.12.2022[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Supply period expired 15.12.2022; Legal notice issued 06.01.2023; Section 8 Demand Notice dated 17.01.2023 served on 19.01.2023; 10-day statutory period expired without dispute notice or payment on 29.01.2023; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 80/CHD/PB/2023 filed in 2023; NCLT admitted CIRP on 09.09.2024[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement dated 19.07.2022; Deed of Hypothecation; postal proof of delivery of Section 8 notice on 19.01.2023 supported by affidavit; Corporate Debtor email dated 27.12.2022 expressly admitting liability to refund balance advance by 31.03.2023; absence of supply bills or dispute notices prior to demand notice[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 petition; NCLT Chandigarh Bench Court-I admitted the petition on 09.09.2024, holding that unrefunded advance for supply of goods constitutes an undisputed operational debt in default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether an unrefunded advance paid for the procurement and supply of goods constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC; whether failure to deliver a formal reply to a Section 8 demand notice bars raising disputes post-facto; and whether pre-CIRP emails admitting liability and promising repayment defeat a defense of pre-existing dispute under Mobilox Innovations[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance payment made for the supply of goods constitutes an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and the recipient's failure to either supply the contracted goods or refund the unadjusted advance amounts to an operational default entitling the creditor to initiate CIRP under Section 9[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) covers claims having a direct nexus with the provision of goods, encompassing advance payments made by a purchaser; under Section 8(2), the debtor must communicate a pre-existing dispute within 10 days of notice; absent a bona fide dispute, admission under Section 9(5)(i) is mandatory[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, written email admissions by the corporate debtor promising to arrange funds and return the balance advance establish the absence of a genuine pre-existing dispute, rendering subsequent allegations of selective rejection spurious and an afterthought[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because service of the Section 8 notice was proven, the debt and default exceeded Rs. 1 Crore, and liability was admitted in writing without pre-existing dispute, Section 9 admission was legally sound, justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 26].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the NCLT order dated 09.09.2024 admitting Farm2energy Private Limited into CIRP[cite: 26]. The interim order dated 06.02.2025 restraining consideration of resolution plans stands vacated[cite: 26]. The IRP/RP is directed to proceed with the CIRP, and the Appellant is directed to extend full cooperation under Section 19 of the Code[cite: 26]. All pending IAs are disposed of[cite: 26].
summary: Sukhbir Singh, suspended director of Farm2energy Private Limited, appealed against NCLT Chandigarh's order admitting a Section 9 petition filed by Verbio India Private Limited for default in refunding an advance of Rs. 1.19 Crores[cite: 26]. The Operational Creditor had paid Rs. 1.54 Crores advance for supply of 20,000 tons of biomass bales, but the Corporate Debtor supplied only Rs. 34.46 Lakhs worth of goods and failed to refund the balance[cite: 26]. The Appellant alleged improper service of the Section 8 notice and pre-existing quality disputes[cite: 26]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that an unreturned advance for goods constitutes operational debt, proof of notice delivery was on record, and the Corporate Debtor had admitted its refund liability in contemporaneous emails, leaving no plausible pre-existing dispute under Mobilox[cite: 26].

case_title: Tech Lads India Private Limited vs. Satnam Global Infraprojects Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tech Lads India Private Limited is the Operational Creditor/Appellant (Lead Consortium Bidder); Satnam Global Infraprojects Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent (Consortium Partner)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium Agreement dated 29.05.2020 to jointly bid for Telecommunications Consultants India Ltd. (TCIL) tender for Meghalaya Multi-Lane Free Flow Vehicle Monitoring System (awarded for Rs. 41,06,40,000/-); Agreement Clause (k) expressly provided that Appellant shall make payments to Corporate Debtor for supplies and services rendered as per scope of work; on 20.04.2021, Appellant paid Rs. 8,00,00,000/- via RTGS as advance for material supplies[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 6,20,00,000/- principal plus 18% interest totaling Rs. 9,29,55,562/-, after adjusting partial refunds; date of default specified as 18.06.2021[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Advance of Rs. 8 Cr paid 20.04.2021; partial refunds received through March 2022; Corporate Debtor issued four settlement cheques on 05.09.2023; CD uploaded e-invoice on GST portal on 26.03.2024; Section 8 Demand Notice issued 08.04.2024 (served 15.04.2024); CD sent reconciliation email on 24.04.2024; Section 9 petition CP(IB) No. 329/ND/2024 filed in 2024; NCLT dismissed it on 24.09.2025[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consortium Agreement Clauses (i) and (k) establishing inter se supply and payment obligations; bank statements proving Rs. 8 Cr RTGS transfer; copies of four cheques of Rs. 2 Crores each dated 05.09.2023 drawn on Canara Bank; fake GST invoice for Rs. 4,72,66,500/- uploaded by CD and withdrawn after Appellant's GST complaint; CD email dated 24.04.2024 citing only account reconciliation without denying debt[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-V dismissed Section 9 petition CP(IB) No. 329/ND/2024 on 24.09.2025, holding that the Consortium Agreement contained obligations only toward the third-party client (TCIL) and lacked inter se commercial transactions constituting operational debt[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether advance payments made by a lead consortium member to a consortium partner for the supply of project materials pursuant to express inter se contract clauses constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC; and whether the issuance of settlement cheques and uploading of GST invoices establish debt and negate a defense of security deposit or pre-existing dispute[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance payment made for the supply of goods under an agreement containing reciprocal commercial supply obligations constitutes an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and the recipient is an operational debtor irrespective of whether the parties jointly formed a consortium to bid for an external project[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines operational debt broadly as a claim bearing nexus with the provision of goods or services, covering situations where the claimant is the purchaser/receiver of goods; Section 8 does not mandate an invoice if debt is evidenced by demand notice, bank statements, and dishonored/returned cheques under Consolidated Construction Consortium[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsubstantiated oral defenses that an advance was a 'security deposit' cannot stand when the agreement contains no such clause and the debtor uploaded supply invoices on the GST portal and issued settlement cheques; an email merely stating 'accounts are under reconciliation' does not constitute a pre-existing dispute under Mobilox[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The existence of an operational debt of Rs. 6.20 Crores in default was conclusively established, rendering the NCLT's dismissal erroneous and requiring revival of the petition for admission[cite: 28].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1751 of 2025 is allowed[cite: 28]. The impugned order dated 24.09.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V in CP (IB) No. 329/ND/2024 is set aside[cite: 28]. CP (IB) No. 329/ND/2024 is revived before the NCLT for passing an admission order within three months, during which time the Corporate Debtor is granted liberty to liquidate the operational debt and avoid CIRP admission[cite: 28]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 28].
summary: Tech Lads India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of its Section 9 petition against consortium partner Satnam Global Infraprojects Ltd. for default on an unrefunded advance of Rs. 6.20 Crores plus interest[cite: 28]. Under a Consortium Agreement for a Meghalaya vehicle monitoring project, Tech Lads paid Rs. 8 Crores as advance for materials, but Satnam Global failed to supply goods, issued four cheques of Rs. 2 Crores each which were not cleared, and uploaded then withdrew an invoice on the GST portal[cite: 28]. The NCLT held that consortium partners had no inter se commercial operational debt[cite: 28]. NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that Clause (k) created express supply and payment obligations, and following Consolidated Construction Consortium, an advance for goods constitutes operational debt[cite: 28]. The petition was revived for admission unless paid within three months[cite: 28].

case_title: Ammeet Kumar Agarwal vs. Ssarvi Resolution Services LLP
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ammeet Kumar Agarwal is the Suspended Director of Supreme Transport Organisation Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Axis Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Ssarvi Resolution Services LLP (through partner Prashant Jain) is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities were extended by Axis Bank Ltd. to the Corporate Debtor, which subsequently defaulted. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted dues leading to an interim deposit order were Rs. 10,49,26,262/-; an aggregate sum of Rs. 8,05,11,748/- was withdrawn/appropriated from the Corporate Debtor's Bank of Baroda account during the moratorium. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated on 08.09.2023 under Section 7; interim protection staying the CoC was granted on 15.09.2023 conditioned on deposit, extended on 16.10.2023, and vacated on 06.12.2023; unencumbered Panvel property was sold on 02.11.2023; IA No. 3653 of 2024 was instituted on 10.05.2024; impugned order was passed on 19.12.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale proceeds from the Panvel property were deposited into the Bank of Baroda account during moratorium and subsequently withdrawn/disbursed; the appellant failed to produce contemporaneous bank instructions, records, or cheques establishing the defence of legitimate pre-CIRP liabilities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Axis Bank initiated Section 7 proceedings in CP (IB) No. 368(MB)/2023, admitted by NCLT Mumbai on 08.09.2023. In IA No. 3653 of 2024, NCLT directed the appellant and respondents to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 8,05,11,748/- to the Corporate Debtor and recommended IBBI/MCA prosecution under Section 74.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority had the jurisdiction under Section 14 read with Section 60(5) of the IBC to direct restoration of funds alienated during the moratorium without conclusively determining fraudulent or wrongful trading under Section 66.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory power to direct the refund and restoration of corporate debtor funds dissipated in breach of the statutory moratorium independently of any formal adjudication or establishment of fraudulent intent under avoidance provisions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) read with Section 14 confers wide residuary jurisdiction to protect and preserve the insolvency estate for resolution; merely citing Section 66 in an application does not restrict the court from granting relief flowing from violations of the moratorium under Section 14. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden is on the suspended management to provide tangible documentary proof that post-commencement withdrawals represent bona fide pre-CIRP commitments; in the absence of verified records, an adverse inference is warranted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT acted within its jurisdiction by directing the restoration of Rs. 8,05,11,748/- under Section 14 read with Section 60(5), while directions referable to Section 74 were rendered infructuous upon its omission by the IBC Amendment Act, 2026.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 86 of 2025 is dismissed, confirming the NCLT Mumbai direction ordering the joint and several contribution of Rs. 8,05,11,748/- to the account of the Corporate Debtor; directions regarding Section 74 held infructuous; no order as to costs.
summary: Ammeet Kumar Agarwal, suspended director of Supreme Transport Organisation Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Mumbai order directing him and others to contribute Rs. 8,05,11,748/- back to the Corporate Debtor's account for unauthorized withdrawals during the CIRP moratorium and referring the matter to IBBI/MCA under Section 74. The appellant argued that the application was under Section 66, which required proof of fraudulent intent. The NCLAT held that the NCLT exercised valid jurisdiction under Section 14 read with Section 60(5) to preserve the debtor's estate independently of Section 66. As Section 74 was omitted by the IBC Amendment Act, 2026, those directions became infructuous. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Catalyst Trusteeship Limited & Anr. vs. Suman Kumar Verma
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1539 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1555 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Catalyst Trusteeship Limited (Debenture Trustee for SWAMIH Investment Fund-I) and DCB Bank Limited are Financial Creditors; Swastik Homebuild Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Suman Kumar Verma is the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP); Homebuyers represent Financial Creditors in a class. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Priority debt financing/interim finance extended under SWAMIH fund and loan facility extended by DCB Bank for affordable housing development. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Catalyst Trusteeship claimed Rs. 27,68,79,224/- (Rs. 26,77,93,424/- admitted); DCB Bank claimed Rs. 10,99,85,312/- (Rs. 10,21,62,738/- admitted). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP initiated on 19.12.2024; public announcement made on 23.12.2024 with claim cutoff on 06.01.2025; CoC reconstituted on 08.03.2025 following homebuyer claim verification; IA Nos. 434 and 476 of 2025 dismissed by NCLT Chandigarh on 08.08.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants' combined voting share dropped from an initial majority to 32.43% as 134 homebuyer claims were verified and admitted; IRP had engaged an IPE where one director faced since-stayed IBBI suspension. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Homebuyers filed CP No. 134 of 2021 admitted on 19.12.2024. Appellants filed IA No. 434 of 2025 seeking IRP replacement under inherent powers and IA No. 476 of 2025 seeking stay of CoC meetings; NCLT Chandigarh dismissed both applications on 08.08.2025.
legal_issues: Whether a minority member or group of the Committee of Creditors can seek judicial replacement or removal of an Interim Resolution Professional under inherent powers absent the requisite 66% majority vote prescribed under Sections 22 and 27 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The replacement, appointment, and continuation of an IRP or RP falls strictly within the commercial wisdom and statutory governance of the Committee of Creditors under Sections 22 and 27; adjudicating tribunals cannot intervene using inherent powers unless extraordinary bad faith or statutory illegality is established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 22 and 27 are exhaustive codes for the removal and replacement of resolution professionals requiring a 66% voting share; individual or minority creditors have no independent right to seek replacement before the Tribunal outside this mechanism. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Allegations of loss of trust or grievances over partial claim collation and resulting dilution of voting shares do not meet the legal threshold of proven misconduct warranting judicial intervention dehors Section 27. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The reduction of appellants' voting share stemmed from the legitimate statutory collation of class creditors' claims under Section 18(b), and the NCLT rightly dismissed the applications for IRP replacement.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1539 and 1555 of 2025 are dismissed, affirming the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 08.08.2025; pending interlocutory applications disposed of without costs.
summary: Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. and DCB Bank Ltd., holding 32.43% combined voting share in the CoC of Swastik Homebuild Pvt. Ltd., appealed the dismissal of their applications seeking removal of the IRP and stay of CoC meetings. The appellants alleged bias, improper collation of claims, and loss of confidence after their voting shares were diluted by the admission of 134 homebuyer claims. The NCLAT held that under Sections 22 and 27 of the IBC, replacement of an IRP/RP rests exclusively within the commercial wisdom of the CoC by a mandatory 66% majority vote. Because minority creditors cannot bypass this statutory process absent extraordinary circumstances, the appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Gondwana Engineers Limited vs. Bijay Murmuria & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gondwana Engineers Limited is the Appellant (borrower entity); Doshion Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (guarantor-mortgagor); Bijay Murmuria is the Liquidator; IDBI Bank, Bank of Baroda, Bank of Maharashtra (BOM) are lenders; Areion Finserve and Raj Radhe Finance are assignees. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan against property originally sanctioned to Corporate Debtor by BOM in 2010 over Sigma-9 Property; IDBI and Dena Bank (BOB) were granted a second pari-passu charge via BOM NOC in 2012; BOM closed the 2010 loan on 20.03.2015 and executed a fresh mortgage to secure Appellant's separate loan facilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Facilities of IDBI Bank and Dena Bank aggregated approx. Rs. 140 crores (restructured to Rs. 93.48 cr and Rs. 87.77 cr respectively); BOM's separate claim against Appellant was Rs. 67,35,15,663.64. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 31.08.2021; Liquidation ordered on 03.10.2023 with claim deadline 08.11.2023; BOM assigned debt to Areion on 27.10.2023 (regd. 30.11.2023); Areion submitted Form D belatedly on 06.07.2024; Areion assigned to Raj Radhe on 02.05.2025; impugned NCLT order passed on 30.06.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BOM issued a No Due Certificate on 20.03.2015; neither BOM nor its assignees submitted a Section 52 intimation to realise security outside liquidation within the mandatory 30-day window under Regulation 21A(1). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted CIRP in CP (IB) No. 59 of 2019 on 31.08.2021 and ordered liquidation on 03.10.2023. In IA Nos. 440/2025, 1137/2025, and 525/2026, the Adjudicating Authority held on 30.06.2026 that Sigma-9 Property formed part of the liquidation estate, BOB/IDBI held first priority, Raj Radhe's security lapsed under Regulation 21A(3), and ordered title deeds surrendered.
legal_issues: Whether the second pari-passu charge holders automatically assumed first charge priority under Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act upon discharge of the original first mortgage, and whether a secured creditor's failure to exercise the Section 52 option within 30 days under Regulation 21A causes the asset to lapse into the liquidation estate.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon full repayment and discharge of a senior mortgage, a subsisting subordinate encumbrance automatically elevates to first priority; any subsequent mortgage executed thereafter secures only a subordinate rank, and failure to timely elect realization under Section 52 results in the asset statutorily lapsing into the liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, priority is governed by temporal creation; Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC expressly empowers the Adjudicating Authority to decide questions of priorities, while Regulation 21A(3) of the Liquidation Regulations operates as a mandatory deeming fiction vesting the asset in the liquidation estate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Registration of a subsequent modification under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot confer priority over an earlier created, subsisting equitable mortgage of which the parties had actual or constructive notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: IDBI Bank and BOB's charge elevated to first priority upon discharge of BOM's 2010 facility; because BOM's assignees failed to exercise the Section 52 option within 30 days, the security interest lapsed into the liquidation estate under Regulation 21A(3).
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1276 of 2026 is dismissed, upholding the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 30.06.2026 directing the Sigma-9 Property to remain in the liquidation estate and requiring delivery of original title deeds to the Liquidator; no order as to costs.
summary: Gondwana Engineers Ltd. appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order declaring that House No. 9, Sigma Corporate Park (owned by the Corporate Debtor, Doshion Pvt. Ltd.) formed part of the liquidation estate and that IDBI Bank and Bank of Baroda held first charge priority. The appellant asserted priority based on a 2015 mortgage in favor of Bank of Maharashtra (BOM), later assigned to Areion Finserve and Raj Radhe Finance. The NCLAT affirmed that upon BOM's discharge of its 2010 loan, the consortium's second charge automatically ascended to first priority under Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act. Furthermore, because the assignees failed to elect realization outside liquidation within the 30-day timeline under Regulation 21A, the property statutorily lapsed into the liquidation estate under Regulation 21A(3).

case_title: Vinay Gupta & Anr. vs. Oswal Minerals Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1038 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1032 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vinay Gupta and Niharika Goel are Suspended Directors of Satellite Cables Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Oswal Minerals Limited is the Operational Creditor; Suraj Garg is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA); Bank of Baroda is the sole Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational credit default resulting in Section 9 admission; resolution applicant Suraj Garg submitted a resolution plan of Rs. 5.85 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CoC approved SRA plan of Rs. 5.85 crores by 100% vote; a rival applicant belatedly offered Rs. 6.00 crores via email; CGST confirmed a tax demand of Rs. 17,47,70,663/- via Order-in-Original dated 20.12.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition admitted on 03.01.2023; hybrid challenge conducted on 21.11.2023; CoC approved plan on 06.12.2023 (voting concluded 22.12.2023); CGST order passed 20.12.2023; NCLT New Delhi approved plan on 23.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants claimed non-receipt of plan copies and asserted an unexecuted OTS under which Rs. 2.50 crores was deposited; SRA is a practicing CA who undertook not to become a Whole-Time Director (appointed non-executive director). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP (IB) No. 1185/(ND)/2019 was admitted on 03.01.2023; RP filed IA (PLAN) No. 5 of 2024, which NCLT New Delhi approved on 23.04.2024 over suspended directors' oral objections.
legal_issues: Whether non-supply of a resolution plan copy to suspended directors absent a confidentiality undertaking vitiates plan approval, whether a practicing Chartered Accountant is disqualified under Section 29A from acting as a Resolution Applicant, and whether post-closure revised bids or unassessed government dues invalidate a CoC-approved resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a compliant resolution plan by a 100% majority is non-justiciable and cannot be set aside on the grounds of procedural non-supply of documents without proof of real prejudice, post-bidding revision offers, or unprovided statutory taxes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A does not bar a practicing Chartered Accountant from acting as a Resolution Applicant provided they do not assume the role of a whole-time director; furthermore, by virtue of the Explanation to Section 3(31) inserted in 2026, security interests exclude statutory operational liens, ranking government tax dues below secured debt under Section 53. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mere allegations of procedural irregularities or unconsummated Section 12A OTS discussions do not satisfy the specific vitiating grounds under Section 61(3) of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan complies with Section 30(2); non-supply of the plan to suspended directors who failed to furnish confidentiality undertakings caused no prejudice, and the plan approval by NCLT was valid.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1032 and 1038 of 2024 are dismissed, confirming the NCLT New Delhi order dated 23.04.2024 approving Suraj Garg's resolution plan; each appellant is assessed costs of Rs. 1,00,000/- for abusing process; pending IAs disposed of.
summary: Suspended directors of Satellite Cables Pvt. Ltd. challenged the approval of Suraj Garg's resolution plan, asserting natural justice violations due to non-receipt of the plan, ineligibility of the SRA as a practicing Chartered Accountant under the Chartered Accountants Act, an unaccepted OTS, refusal to accept an unsolicited higher email bid, and non-provision of Rs. 17.47 crore in CGST dues. The NCLAT rejected all grounds, finding that the appellants refused to submit a confidentiality undertaking and showed no prejudice. It held that practicing CAs are not barred under Section 29A provided they do not act as Whole-Time Directors, post-closure bids were properly ignored to preserve CIRP finality, and statutory dues are governed by Section 53. The appeals were dismissed with costs of Rs. 1 lakh each.

case_title: Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation & Ors. vs. Zaveri & Co. Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1557 & 1684 of 2023 and 626-628 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gujarat Hydrocarbons and Power SEZ Limited (GHPSL) is the Corporate Debtor; SREI Infrastructure Finance Limited is the sole Financial Creditor; Assam Company India Limited (ACIL) is the Corporate Guarantor; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) is the lessor/regulator/Operational Creditor; Zaveri & Co. Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rs. 100 crore credit facility extended by SREI in 2011 to GHPSL, guaranteed by ACIL, to develop a sector-specific SEZ on GIDC leasehold land in Bharuch, Gujarat. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: SREI's claim of Rs. 648.80 crores was reduced by NCLT Guwahati in ACIL's CIRP to Rs. 241.27 crores, where SREI received Rs. 38.87 crores; despite this, RP in GHPSL admitted SREI's claim at Rs. 1,885.08 crores and ranked ACIL's subrogated claim at nil. SRA offered Rs. 135 crores (Rs. 125 crores to SREI). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ACIL plan approved on 20.09.2018; GHPSL CIRP admitted 18.11.2020; plan approved by CoC 30.08.2021; GIDC terminated lease 13.12.2021; NCLT approved plan on 19.09.2023 and 19.02.2025 after remand. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Information Memorandum failed to disclose that SEZ de-notification was pending and incomplete without the Development Commissioner's certificate; SRA's plan contained non-public knowledge assuming conversion to non-SEZ industrial use without GIDC's mandatory prior consent under Lease Clause 3.3(v). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP (IB) No. 571 (ND)/2020 admitted on 18.11.2020. NCLT dismissed applications challenging SREI's claim inflation (IA 1764/2021, IA 596/2022) and GIDC's objections (IA 136/2022, IA 5224/2024), approving Zaveri & Co.'s plan on 19.02.2025.
legal_issues: Whether an Information Memorandum containing an inflated, unverified claim violating a prior binding judicial determination and omitting regulatory land status vitiates the CIRP, whether a corporate guarantor paying under a resolution plan subrogates as a secured creditor under Section 140 of the Contract Act, and whether a resolution plan premised on unobtained regulatory de-notification and unauthorized change of land use is viable under Section 30(2).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan founded upon a materially inaccurate Information Memorandum that incorporates judicially rejected debt claims, misranks statutory subrogation rights, and presumes unobtained statutory conversion consents for leased public land is fundamentally non-viable and must be quashed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory duty under Section 29 and Regulation 36 mandates the presentation of true and accurate facts in the Information Memorandum; commercial wisdom cannot validate a plan built on false information. Under Section 140 of the Contract Act, a surety discharging guaranteed debt is invested with creditor security rights pro tanto as a secured creditor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plans utilizing land owned by statutory authorities bound by special regulations require strict scrutiny of regulatory feasibility; bare presumptions of regulatory clearance render the plan impermissibly conditional. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SREI's admissible claim is limited to Rs. 241.27 crores less Rs. 38.87 crores; ACIL is subrogated as a secured creditor to the extent of Rs. 38.87 crores; Zaveri & Co.'s plan is infeasible for lack of regulatory approval, requiring CIRP recommencement with a new RP and fresh Form G.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins) Nos. 626-628 of 2025 and Nos. 1557 and 1684 of 2023 are allowed in part; composite order dated 19.02.2025 and plan approval of Zaveri & Co. are set aside; Rs. 50,000 cost on appellant quashed; ACIL recognized as secured financial creditor for Rs. 38.87 crores; SREI claim restricted to Rs. 241.27 crores less credit; CIRP to restart from fresh Form G with a new RP; period excluded under Section 12.
summary: Appeals were filed by the suspended director, corporate guarantor (Assam Company India Ltd./BRS Ventures), and the land regulator/lessor (GIDC) challenging the approval of Zaveri & Co.'s resolution plan for Gujarat Hydrocarbons and Power SEZ Ltd. Appellants argued that SREI's claim was improperly inflated to Rs. 1,885.08 crores despite prior binding judicial reduction to Rs. 241.27 crores, ACIL's subrogated secured rights were ignored, and the plan assumed unauthorized conversion of leasehold SEZ land to general industrial use without GIDC's mandatory consent. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the plan approval, recognized ACIL as a secured creditor for Rs. 38.87 crores, corrected SREI's claim, and directed the CIRP to be re-run from the Form G stage under a newly appointed RP.

case_title: Mr. Satya Prakash Bagla & Anr. vs. Mrs. Kanta Agarwala & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) No. 161 of 2024 and Comp. App. (AT) No. 162 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Satya Prakash Bagla (90% shareholder, MD), Achal Kumar Jindal, and Johnson Abraham are Appellants; Kanta Agarwala and Suresh Kumar Agarwala (10% equity holders) are Respondents/Original Petitioners; Exclusive Capital Limited (ECL) is an RBI-registered NBFC. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of Rs. 315 crores in Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) to Teesta Retail Pvt. Ltd. and their conversion into Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares (CCPS) with a 20-year conversion tenure, alongside related-party transactions including a Rs. 9.09 crore purchase of a Bentley motor vehicle from Luxus Retail Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: ECL's net owned funds were Rs. 2.34 crores, but it raised Rs. 315 crores in debt, causing its leverage ratio to spike to 117.77 (statutory ceiling: 7). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ECL registered as NBFC on 16.12.2021; OCDs issued between Oct 2021-Mar 2022; Respondents acquired shares on 05.09.2022; CCPS conversion ratified on 27.09.2022; Bentley purchased 16.12.2022; RBI approved share allotment on 30.05.2023 (lapsed 30.11.2023); KMPs resigned en masse on 10.12.2023; CP No. 48/ND/2024 filed Feb 2024; NCLT passed interim orders in March-April 2024 and final impugned order on 15.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RBI imposed a monetary penalty of Rs. 10.30 lakhs on 27.03.2026 for leverage ratio breaches; multiple related-party loans (e.g. Rs. 14 crores to Luxus) lacked loan documentation or hypothecation and breached internal tranche limits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Minority shareholders filed CP No. 48/ND/2024 under Sections 241-242 alleging oppression and mismanagement. On 15.05.2024, NCLT New Delhi appointed an Administrator (retired High Court Judge), suspended the Board for 180 days, ordered cancellation of OCDs/CCPS and refund of Rs. 315 crores, and ordered a forensic audit.
legal_issues: Whether raising debt exceeding statutory leverage ratios by 117 times, converting OCDs to long-term CCPS, executing undocumented related-party loans, and removing independent directors during pending oppression proceedings constitute acts prejudicial to public interest and the company under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Continuous regulatory violations of binding prudential norms by an entity dealing with public funds, coupled with circular and undocumented related-party transactions, mass resignations of compliance personnel, and removal of independent directors during litigation, constitute a consecutive story establishing oppression and mismanagement prejudicial to public interest. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241(1)(a) incorporates 'prejudicial to public interest' as an independent ground; the existence of a statutory penal remedy under Section 58G of the RBI Act does not oust or curtail the Tribunal's wide equitable remedial jurisdiction under Section 242 to rectify corporate mismanagement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Events must be evaluated not in isolation but cumulatively as a continuous course of conduct demonstrating lack of probity; the fact that subsequent members acquired shares after initial transactions does not bar them from challenging ongoing, persistent governance failures. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The prima facie evidence of gross leverage ratio breaches, self-dealing transactions exceeding share capital, and dismantling of corporate governance safeguards fully justified interim management intervention by an independent Administrator.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 161 and 162 of 2024 are dismissed; matter is remanded to NCLT New Delhi to finally adjudicate CP No. 48/ND/2024 and pending IAs in accordance with law; the Tribunal is directed to consider the Observer's reports and settle outstanding Observer remuneration; parties directed to appear on 10.09.2026; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants appealed an NCLT New Delhi order passed in an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 concerning Exclusive Capital Ltd. (an NBFC). The NCLT suspended the Board for 180 days, appointed an independent Administrator, directed cancellation and refund of Rs. 315 crore in OCDs/CCPS, and ordered a forensic audit following severe leverage ratio breaches (117 times the limit) and questionable related-party transactions. The NCLAT held that the cumulative course of conduct—including serious prudential violations confirmed by RBI penalties, mass resignations of KMPs, and the purchase of an extravagant vehicle from an insider entity—demonstrated clear lack of probity prejudicial to the company and public interest. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT remanded the petition to the NCLT for final adjudication while directing that the court-appointed Observer's fees be settled.

case_title: Titus Babu vs. Sintex Industries Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Titus Babu is the Appellant (minority shareholder/member); Sintex Industries Limited (SIL) is the Corporate Debtor and Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Acquisition of 1,35,000 equity shares of SIL by the Appellant between October 31, 2017, and January 30, 2023, prior to corporate delisting under an approved Resolution Plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pre-existing equity share capital comprising 59,92,49,762 equity shares extinguished without payment under the approved Resolution Plan due to inadequate liquidation value. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by NCLT Ahmedabad on 10.02.2023; shares delisted from BSE and NSE on 10.03.2023; Appellant sent clarification email on 10.04.2023; Company Appeal No. 31 of 2025 filed before NCLT Ahmedabad on 09.12.2025; NCLT passed impugned order on 06.03.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SIL's communications dated 11.04.2023 and 13.06.2024 confirming that the Appellant's 1,35,000 equity shares stood cancelled pursuant to the capital reduction mandated by the approved Resolution Plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed Comp. Appeal No. 31 of 2025 on 06.03.2026 as not maintainable under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, holding that the approved Resolution Plan bound all members and extinguished pre-existing equity capital.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-CIRP equity shareholder whose shares were cancelled pursuant to an approved Resolution Plan under the IBC can invoke Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 to claim rectification, fresh share issuance, or monetary compensation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved Resolution Plan under Section 31 of the IBC binds all stakeholders, including members, and operates with overriding effect under Section 238 to extinguish pre-existing equity capital without consideration where liquidation value is nil, barring subsequent company-law rectification or compensation claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 is a summary rectificatory provision that cannot be used to revive extinguished share capital or adjudicate speculative monetary claims, while Sections 31 and 238 of the IBC ensure that successful resolution applicants take over corporate debtors on a clean slate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Omission of a member's name from the register resulting directly from a court-sanctioned insolvency resolution plan is not 'without sufficient cause'. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant's pre-CIRP shareholding and membership rights lawfully stood extinguished by the approved Resolution Plan, rendering rectification and compensation proceedings under Section 59 unsustainable.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) No. 168 of 2026 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 06.03.2026; no order as to costs; pending IAs closed.
summary: Titus Babu, who held 1,35,000 equity shares in Sintex Industries Limited, appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing his company appeal under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013. The appellant sought Rs. 82.3 crores in compensation, interest, and fresh shares after discovering his shareholding was cancelled pursuant to capital reduction under the approved Resolution Plan. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 59 cannot be used to reopen or challenge a concluded insolvency resolution. Under Sections 31 and 238 of the IBC, the approved Resolution Plan is binding on all members, extinguishes pre-existing equity capital where liquidation value is nil, and ensures the clean-slate acquisition of the corporate debtor.

case_title: BSR & Associates LLP vs. Serious Fraud Investigation Office & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 182 of 2026 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 183 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: BSR & Associates LLP and N. Sampath Ganesh are Appellants (statutory auditors/auditor partner); Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) is Respondent No. 1; IL&FS Securities Services Limited (ISSL) is Respondent No. 2; Union of India through Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) is Respondent No. 18[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory audit of IL&FS Securities Services Limited (ISSL, a subsidiary of IL&FS) for FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18 in connection with management operations, Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs), and Term Money Deposit Receipts (TMDRs)[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory audit failures involving omission to report placement of ICDs in distressed group companies, failure to assess impairment, and non-compliance with F&O Regulations and SCRR, giving rise to fraud allegations under Section 447[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Central Government ordered SFIO investigation on 30.09.2018; SFIO submitted Investigation Report under Section 212(12) on 14.07.2023; MCA issued authorization letter on 26.09.2023; NCLT Mumbai passed the impugned order on 17.03.2026[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SFIO Investigation Report dated 14.07.2023 concluding fraud under Section 447; MCA letter dated 26.09.2023 signed by Deputy Director conveying approval of competent authority directing SFIO to place report before NCLT Mumbai and seek attachment/disgorgement proceedings[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No. 3638 of 2018 was filed by Union of India under Section 241(2); SFIO filed CA No. 234 of 2025 in CA No. 396 of 2021 in the name of Union of India seeking disgorgement/attachment under Section 212(14A)[cite: 19]. Appellants challenged maintainability arguing SFIO lacked locus and Section 458 delegation notification was absent, which NCLT Mumbai rejected on 17.03.2026[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) has the locus or power to file an application before the NCLT for attachment and disgorgement under Section 212(14A) of the Companies Act, 2013 on behalf of the Central Government, and whether such authorization requires a gazetted notification laid before Parliament under Section 458[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An administrative authorization issued by the Central Government permitting an attached investigative agency to institute or prosecute proceedings in the name of the Union of India represents an execution of a ministerial act to enforce a governmental decision, which does not constitute a statutory delegation of discretionary power requiring gazetted notification or parliamentary tabling[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 212(14A) vests discretionary power in the Central Government to apply for disgorgement and personal liability; under the Allocation of Business Rules and Transaction of Business Rules framed pursuant to Article 77(3) of the Constitution, such power is exercised by the Minister-in-charge through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, distinct from statutory delegation under Section 458[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The distinction between the delegation of core statutory discretion and the administrative authorization of an officer to execute or file legal proceedings (as established in Sidhartha Sarawgi v. Board of Trustees for the Port of Kolkata)[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Central Government independently considered the SFIO report and took the decision to apply for disgorgement, and the application was formally filed in the name of the Union of India, the administrative authorization to the Director of SFIO to present the petition was legally valid and maintainable[cite: 19].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 182 of 2026 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 183 of 2026 are dismissed, upholding the NCLT Mumbai order dated 17.03.2026 in CA No. 234/2025; all pending applications are disposed of without costs[cite: 19].
summary: BSR & Associates LLP and its partner appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting their maintainability objection to an application filed by the SFIO under Section 212(14A) of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking attachment and disgorgement[cite: 19]. The appellants contended that Section 212(14A) vests power exclusively in the Central Government and that authorising the SFIO without a gazetted notification under Section 458 was illegal[cite: 19]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the application was filed in the name of the Union of India following an independent decision by the Central Government[cite: 19]. The direction to the SFIO Director was a valid administrative authorization under the Allocation of Business Rules rather than a statutory delegation[cite: 19].

case_title: Titus Babu vs. Sintex Industries Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Titus Babu is the Appellant (pre-CIRP shareholder/member); Sintex Industries Limited (SIL) is the Corporate Debtor and Respondent; Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) is the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase of 1,35,000 equity shares of SIL by the Appellant in tranches between 31.10.2017 and 30.01.2023 via Geojit Financial Services depository[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In CIRP of SIL, pre-existing equity share capital comprising 59,92,49,762 equity shares of Re. 1/- each was cancelled and extinguished at NIL liquidation value under Clause 6.1 of the approved resolution plan[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by NCLT Ahmedabad on 10.02.2023 in IA 275 of 2022; shares delisted from BSE and NSE on 10.03.2023; Appellant sent query emails on 10.04.2023 and received confirmation of cancellation on 11.04.2023 and 13.06.2024; Company Appeal No. 31 of 2025 filed before NCLT on 09.12.2025; NCLT passed impugned order on 06.03.2026[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Depository and company records confirming cancellation and delisting of shares pursuant to capital reduction under the approved resolution plan; Appellant produced correspondence with NSDL, NSE, RBI, SEBI SCORES, and annual returns for FY 2022-23[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CIRP was admitted in CP (IB) No. 848/NCLT/AHM/2019 and plan approved on 10.02.2023[cite: 21]. Appellant filed Comp. Appeal No. 31 of 2025 under Section 59 of Companies Act, 2013 seeking Rs. 82.3 crores compensation (total ~Rs. 110 crores with interest) and share restoration[cite: 21]. NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the petition on 06.03.2026 as not maintainable[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether a pre-CIRP shareholder of a corporate debtor whose shares were cancelled without consideration under an approved and implemented resolution plan retains independent membership rights capable of enforcement, rectification, or compensation under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a company limited by shares, the terms 'member' and 'shareholder' are legally co-extensive, and the complete extinguishment of equity share capital under a sanctioned insolvency resolution plan simultaneously terminates membership status, precluding any subsequent claim under company law for register rectification or compensation[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 is a summary rectificatory remedy limited to correcting entries made or omitted without sufficient cause; an omission flowing directly from an approved resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC is backed by legal cause, and by virtue of Section 238 of the IBC, the approved plan overrides inconsistent provisions of the Companies Act[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The clean slate doctrine established in Essar Steel and Ghanashyam Mishra bars any collateral attack or revival of extinguished pre-CIRP claims and rights against a successfully resolved corporate debtor[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant ceased to be a member upon lawful cancellation of his shares under the approved plan; Section 59 cannot be converted into an action for damages or share revival, and the appeal was properly dismissed[cite: 21].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) No. 168 of 2026 is dismissed, confirming the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 06.03.2026; no order as to costs; all pending interlocutory applications stand closed[cite: 21].
summary: Titus Babu appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing his petition under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 21]. The appellant held 1,35,000 equity shares in Sintex Industries Limited, which were completely cancelled and extinguished without consideration under an approved CIRP Resolution Plan due to nil liquidation value[cite: 21]. The appellant claimed that his statutory membership rights survived share extinguishment and claimed Rs. 82.3 crores in compensation[cite: 21]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that membership is legally synonymous with shareholding in a company limited by shares[cite: 21]. Under Sections 31, 32A, and 238 of the IBC, an approved plan binds all members and extinguishes all pre-CIRP claims on a clean slate, rendering Section 59 inapplicable[cite: 21].

case_title: Ashutosh Majumdar vs. Omkara Asset Reconstruction Private Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 351 of 2025 & I.A. No. 3064 of 2025, 536 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashutosh Majumdar is the Appellant (Suspended Director of Chemstar Organics India Limited); Chemstar Organics (India) Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Omkara Asset Reconstruction Private Limited is the Financial Creditor (assignee of GIIC); Indrajeet Mukherjee is the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facility of Rs. 625 lakhs sanctioned and disbursed by Gujarat Industrial Investment Corporation Limited (GIIC) under Loan Cum Agreement backed by Deed of Hypothecation and joint equitable mortgage for setting up an expansion project at Vadodara[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount in Part-IV of Section 7 petition was Rs. 11,87,21,370/- as on 28.06.2022; default originated in 2002 with continuous failure to pay installments and interest, leading to possession notices in 2002 and 2004[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BIFR proceedings pending till dissolution on 30.11.2016; GIIC approved OTS on 15.02.2018; GIIC assigned debt to Omkara on 14.08.2018; Omkara approved fresh OTS on 03.04.2019 extended till 31.03.2020 at 24% p.a. interest; Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 21.20 lakhs on 28.08.2019; Omkara revoked OTS on 08.01.2020 demanding full payment within 10 days; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued on 22.06.2021 demanding Rs. 10,51,18,900/-; Section 7 petition filed on 30.06.2022[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, assignment deed dated 14.08.2018, OTS sanction letters dated 03.04.2019 and 19.04.2019, demand emails dated 03.10.2019, 14.10.2019, 26.11.2019, 10.12.2019, 21.12.2019, and revocation notice dated 08.01.2020[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP (IB)-1028(MB)/C-III/2022 admitted on 06.12.2022, remanded on appeal on 01.09.2023, and re-admitted by NCLT Mumbai on 20.02.2025 holding that debt and default exceeded the threshold and continued beyond Section 10A[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition is barred by Section 10A of the IBC where a default originating prior to the protected period continues thereafter, whether an unfulfilled OTS constitutes novation under Section 62 of the Contract Act, and whether an Adjudicating Authority must ascertain the exact quantum of interest and debt before admitting a Section 7 application[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an admitted financial debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold under Section 4 are established, the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily required under Section 7 to admit the corporate debtor into CIRP without needing to adjudicate the precise quantum or interest disputes, and a continuous default extending beyond the Section 10A period is not immune from insolvency proceedings[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A of the IBC temporarily suspends CIRP initiation only for defaults arising strictly between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021, and its proviso does not bar applications where defaults commenced earlier or continued thereafter; under Section 62 of the Contract Act, failed or conditional settlement agreements that do not explicitly rescind the original loan documents do not operate as novation[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The rule established in Innoventive Industries and Indus Biotech that the Adjudicating Authority merely has to satisfy itself of the existence of a debt and default above the statutory threshold from the record[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default in respect of the assigned loan continued post-moratorium, the debt was not novated, the appellant's unilateral deposit of Rs. 4 crores could not stall CIRP against an admitted claim of Rs. 11.87 crores, and the admission order was valid[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 351 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai order dated 20.02.2025 admitting Chemstar Organics (India) Limited into CIRP; all interim orders vacated; pending applications closed with no order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: Ashutosh Majumdar, suspended director of Chemstar Organics (India) Ltd., challenged an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Omkara Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 11.87 crores[cite: 22]. The appellant contended that the default fell within the Section 10A period under an extended OTS, that the debt stood novated under Section 62 of the Contract Act, and that his deposit of Rs. 4 crores before the tribunal discharged the liability[cite: 22]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 10A does not protect continuing defaults, conditional unfulfilled OTS agreements do not novate original loan liabilities, and admitted debt and default exceeding Section 4 mandate CIRP admission[cite: 22].

case_title: Aditya Vivek Kawade vs. Bank of Maharashtra & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 499 of 2026 & I.A. No. 1935, 1936, 1937 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Aditya Vivek Kawade is the Appellant (Personal Guarantor); Aniirudh Civil Engineers and Contractors Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Bank of Maharashtra is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Anil Kashi Drolia is the Resolution Professional/Bankruptcy Trustee (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities (Cash Credit Limit Rs. 300L, Term Loan Rs. 190L, WCTL Rs. 200L, PBG Rs. 279.5L, totaling Rs. 969.5 lakhs) sanctioned between 2012 and 2013 by Bank of Maharashtra to the Corporate Debtor, secured by personal guarantees of the Appellant and his father[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on 29.05.2014; outstanding debt was Rs. 35,69,35,879/- as of 28.02.2023; total admitted claims in PIRP were Rs. 90,74,96,492/-; Appellant submitted an unviable repayment plan proposing Rs. 2,00,000/- against CIRP costs exceeding Rs. 4,00,000/-[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued 31.01.2015; Form B Demand Notice under Personal Guarantor Rules issued 28.06.2022; Section 95 petition CP (IB) 296/2023 filed 31.03.2023; Appellant set ex parte 05.04.2024; PIRP admitted 22.08.2024; PIRP closed under Section 115(2) on 26.06.2025; Bankruptcy petition CP (IB) 75/MB/2026 filed 23.01.2026 and allowed on 03.02.2026[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of guarantee dated 17.02.2012, 28.03.2012, 30.03.2013, 15.05.2013; RP emails seeking repayment plan; CoC minutes of 26.12.2024 rejecting repayment plan and resolving closure; NCLT dismissal of recall and rectification IAs on 07.01.2026 and 27.02.2026[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted PIRP on 22.08.2024, closed PIRP on 26.06.2025 in IA 572/2025 due to lack of viable repayment plan, and initiated Bankruptcy Process under Section 121(1) on 03.02.2026 in CP (IB) 75/MB/2026, condoning 118 days delay on Rs. 25,000 cost[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether initiation of bankruptcy process under Section 121(1) of the IBC requires prior service of notice upon an ex-parte personal guarantor after closure of PIRP, and whether the guarantor can collaterally challenge the underlying PIRP admission and closure orders on grounds of limitation and lack of guarantee invocation[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order initiating bankruptcy process under Section 121 of the IBC is a natural statutory sequel to an unchallenged PIRP closure order, and an ex parte debtor who participated in meetings and allowed antecedent admission and closure orders to attain finality cannot raise collateral attacks against bankruptcy initiation[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 121 does not mandate service of prior notice upon the bankrupt before passing a bankruptcy order upon failure of the repayment process; the statutory right to object under Section 99 does not extend to closure orders under Section 115(2)[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Principles of res judicata, finality of judicial orders, and bar against raising new factual and limitation pleas for the first time in appeal; suppression of material dismissal orders constitutes abuse of process[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The personal guarantee was lawfully invoked in 2022 within limitation, the closure of PIRP was justified due to an absurd repayment plan, and the bankruptcy order was unassailable[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 499 of 2026 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai order dated 03.02.2026; cost of Rs. 5,00,000/- is imposed on the Appellant for misleading the Tribunal, payable to Prime Minister National Relief Fund; pending IAs closed[cite: 23].
summary: Aditya Vivek Kawade, personal guarantor of Aniirudh Civil Engineers and Contractors Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Mumbai order initiating bankruptcy proceedings against him under Section 121(1) of the IBC upon an application by Bank of Maharashtra[cite: 23]. The appellant challenged the order citing natural justice violations, limitation based on a 2015 SARFAESI notice, and dismissal of an identical petition against his co-guarantor father[cite: 23]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that bankruptcy is a natural statutory sequel to the final and unchallenged PIRP closure order triggered by an absurd Rs. 2 lakh repayment plan against Rs. 35.69 crore dues[cite: 23]. For concealing prior recall dismissals and misleading the court, Rs. 5 lakh cost was imposed on the appellant[cite: 23].

case_title: Mr. Balendra Choudhury & Ors. vs. Assam Medical Corporation Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Balendra Choudhury and SMB Baruah are Original Petitioners/Shareholders/Appellants; Assam Medical Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (AMC) is the Company; Dr. Kalicharan Das Trust is the promoter Trust; Agarwal and Khemani groups are Incoming Shareholder Transferees[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Private sale and transfer of 117 equity shares of AMC held by Dr. Kalicharan Das Trust and 85 equity shares held by individual shareholders to outside third-party entities and individuals (Agarwal and Khemani groups) at Rs. 4,00,000/- per share[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Illegal transfer of 202 total equity shares out of 500 total equity shares in a private company to non-members in breach of pre-emptive transfer restrictions, altering control and board directorships[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share Transfer Agreement executed on 28.12.2017; Board meetings approving share transfers held on 03.01.2018 and 24.01.2018; EOGM confirming new directors held 24.01.2018; objection letters issued 12.04.2018 and 05.05.2018; Company Petition filed June 2018; NCLT Guwahati passed impugned order on 03.06.2020[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Articles of Association of AMC, specifically Article 15 requiring written notice to Board, Board agency, and fair valuation by auditor; Board minutes dated 03.01.2018 and 24.01.2018 showing transfers to strangers without offering pre-emption to existing members; letters of protest[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Petitioners filed CP No. 16/59/213/241/244/GB/2018 before NCLT Guwahati alleging oppression and illegal share transfers[cite: 24]. NCLT Guwahati set aside the transfer of 117 Trust shares but upheld transfer of 85 individual shares on 03.06.2020[cite: 24]. All aggrieved sides appealed[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether the transfer of shares of a private limited company to outsiders without complying with the pre-emptive rights mechanism mandated under Article 15 of the Articles of Association is ultra vires and void, and whether the law permits applying different standards to transfers made by a Trust versus individual shareholders[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Articles of Association of a private company constitute a statutory contract binding the company and its members inter se; any transfer of shares to non-members executed in disregard of mandatory pre-emptive rights contained in the Articles is ultra vires and void ab initio, and the law applies uniformly to all shareholders regardless of whether shares are held individually or by a trust[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(68) of the Companies Act, 2013 (and Section 3(1)(iii) of the 1956 Act) mandates that a private company's articles must restrict the right to transfer shares; Article 15 embodies this statutory restriction, requiring notice to the Board and pre-emptive offering to members, breach of which cannot be cured by majority board acquiescence[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Doctrine of ultra vires in corporate actions (Claude-Lila Parulekar v. Sakal Papers and Sangramsinh P. Gaekwad); waiver of statutory pre-emption cannot be presumed without conscious, intentional abandonment with full knowledge[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Article 15 was violated in toto and no pre-emptive offers were made to existing members, all transfers of both the Trust shares and individual shares are illegal and void; the company must rectify its register and remove resultant directors[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 102, 103, 104 and 113 of 2020 are disposed of; NCLT order dated 03.06.2020 is modified; transfers of shares held by both individual shareholders and the Trust are set aside as void; Assam Medical Corporation Pvt. Ltd. is directed to undo all transfers in its registers and file statutory declarations; directorships of transferees are terminated; no order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: Four connected appeals were filed against an NCLT Guwahati order that set aside the transfer of 117 shares held by Dr. Kalicharan Das Trust in Assam Medical Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (a private company) to outside purchasers, but upheld the transfer of shares by individual shareholders[cite: 24]. The original petitioners contended that all transfers violated the mandatory pre-emption procedure in Article 15 of the Articles of Association[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that the Articles of Association form a binding contract and transfers violating pre-emption restrictions are ultra vires and void[cite: 24]. Holding that company law does not distinguish between trust and individual shareholdings, the NCLAT set aside all share transfers and unseated incoming directors[cite: 24].

case_title: Kanta Gupta vs. Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kanta Gupta is the Appellant and personal guarantor of the principal borrower/Corporate Debtor, M/s OSIL Exports Limited; Bank of India is the lead bank and Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1) representing a consortium of five banks (Bank of India, State Bank of India, State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur, State Bank of Patiala, and Oriental Bank of Commerce); the Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor is Respondent No. 5. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by OSIL Exports Limited from the five-bank consortium, secured by personal guarantee deeds executed by the appellant on 21.05.2014 and 21.02.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted and loan account was declared NPA on 31.12.2015; personal guarantee was invoked under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act on 10.09.2019 for total consortium outstanding; guarantors submitted OTS proposals offering Rs. 22 crores to settle liabilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted into CIRP under Section 7 on 31.01.2018; liquidation of CD ordered under Section 33 on 17.10.2019; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice invoking personal guarantee issued on 10.09.2019; Section 13(4) symbolic possession taken on 25.11.2019; OTS proposal submitted by guarantors on 16.04.2021 and revised on 03.04.2023; Section 94 petition CP No. 295/2025 filed on 18.12.2025; Adjudicating Authority dismissed petition on 26.05.2026; Liquidator published auction notice for leasehold rights of subject property on 30.06.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of guarantee dated 21.05.2014 and 21.02.2015; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice dated 10.09.2019; written OTS proposals dated 16.04.2021 and 03.04.2023 relied upon by appellant as acknowledgement under Section 18 of Limitation Act; Resolution Professional report dated 05.02.2026 recommending admission; objections by Bank of India showing OTS was never accepted. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed petition CP No. 295/2025 under Section 94 of IBC on 18.12.2025; NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the petition on 26.05.2026 holding it barred by limitation under Article 137 of Limitation Act and Section 238A of IBC, as the three-year period from guarantee invocation expired on 09.09.2022 and could not be extended by debtor's own unilateral OTS.
legal_issues: Whether an application filed by a personal guarantor under Section 94 of the IBC is governed by the Limitation Act, 1963, whether limitation commences from the invocation of personal guarantee, and whether a personal guarantor can rely on their own unilateral, unaccepted OTS proposals to extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for filing an insolvency application by or against a personal guarantor commences from the date of invocation of the personal guarantee, and a debtor cannot rely upon their own unilateral acknowledgement of liability or unaccepted settlement offer to extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act against a creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1) of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires an acknowledgement of liability to be made in writing and signed by the party against whom the property or right is claimed; the benefit of an acknowledgement can only be claimed against the party that made it, meaning a debtor cannot use their own admission to renew limitation in their own favor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unaccepted OTS proposal constitutes merely an admission of liability provable against the debtor, not a bilateral acknowledgment signed by the creditor; applying Section 18 to debtor's unilateral acts to extend limitation for Section 94 petitions would enable wide abuse to scuttle SARFAESI recovery proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Bank of India invoked the personal guarantee on 10.09.2019, the three-year limitation period under Article 137 expired on 09.09.2022 without valid acknowledgment from the creditor; hence, the Section 94 application filed on 18.12.2025 was patently barred by limitation, and the NCLT properly dismissed the petition without staying the SARFAESI auction.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1058 of 2026 and IA No. 4477 of 2026 are dismissed, affirming the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 26.05.2026; pending IAs disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Smt. Kanta Gupta, personal guarantor of OSIL Exports Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Chandigarh dismissing her Section 94 IBC petition as time-barred and filed IA No. 4477 of 2026 to stay an auction notice issued by the liquidator. The appellant argued that OTS proposals submitted in 2021 and 2023 extended limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act following guarantee invocation in 2019. The NCLAT held that limitation runs from the date of guarantee invocation and expired on 09.09.2022 under Article 137. A debtor cannot utilize their own unilateral, unaccepted OTS admission to extend limitation in their own favor under Section 18. The appeal and stay application were dismissed without costs.

case_title: Mr. Babu Manoharan Jaikumar Christhurajan vs. Mr. Umesh Garg & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Babu Manoharan Jaikumar Christhurajan is the Appellant and Suspended Director/Personal Guarantor; M/s Jeppiaar Cements Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (corporate guarantor); M/s Jeppiaar Power Corporation Ltd. is the Principal Borrower; Umesh Garg is the Resolution Professional/Liquidator (Respondent Nos. 1 & 2); Indian Bank (96.65% voting share) and HDFC Bank (3.35% voting share) are Financial Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loans of Rs. 92.50 crores (sanctioned 27.06.2013) and Rs. 48.50 crores (sanctioned 05.08.2016) availed by the Principal Borrower from Indian Bank, secured by corporate guarantees of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the principal borrower led to Section 7 CIRP against the corporate guarantor; Indian Bank subsequently sanctioned an OTS to the personal guarantors, who made partial payment of Rs. 66.75 crores before liquidation, and fully paid the entire settlement dues on 15.09.2022, obtaining a No Objection Certificate. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 10.10.2019; initial 180 days ended on 07.04.2020; exclusion of 737 Covid days sought via IA No. 656 of 2022; OTS sanctioned on 30.03.2022; 11th CoC meeting held on 13.06.2022 with voting on liquidation closing 04.07.2022; RP filed IA No. 800 of 2022 under Section 33(1) on 14.07.2022; NCLT ordered liquidation on 26.08.2022; entire OTS paid on 15.09.2022; Indian Bank filed Section 12A withdrawal application IA No. 512 of 2023, dismissed on 20.04.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 11th CoC meeting showing neither financial creditor voted in favour of liquidation; RP emails dated 12.07.2022 and 14.07.2022 showing RP intended to file Section 60(5) application but switched to Section 33(1) upon tribunal registry's insistence and Indian Bank's informal instruction; Indian Bank's OTS sanction, extension letter dated 28.07.2022, and final NOC dated 15.09.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application IBA/685/2019 admitted on 10.10.2019. In IA No. 800 of 2022, NCLT Special Bench II Chennai ordered liquidation of the Corporate Debtor on 26.08.2022 under Section 33(1) for expiry of CIRP timelines, which the suspended director appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation passed under Section 33(1) of the IBC can be set aside and CIRP revived to accommodate a withdrawal application under Section 12A where financial debts have been settled under an OTS and the CoC did not vote for liquidation under Section 33(2).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Liquidation is a measure of last resort, and where the financial debts of a corporate debtor have been resolved or are being actively settled via an OTS with the creditors, an order of liquidation passed mechanically upon expiration of directory timelines without an objective assessment by the resolution professional or a CoC vote must be set aside to enable exit via Section 12A. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A forms an integral part of the insolvency resolution framework alongside Section 31 and Section 33; statutory timelines under Section 12(3) are directory rather than mandatory when a viable resolution or Section 12A exit is in sight. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A resolution professional's decision to file for liquidation under Section 33(1) must be based on independent, objective assessment and proper CoC deliberation; acting under perceived Registry advice and ex-committee informal bank instructions renders the action arbitrary. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Indian Bank and HDFC Bank debts were fully satisfied through the OTS and neither creditor voted for liquidation, the liquidation order dated 26.08.2022 was unsustainable and set aside, restoring CIRP to explore the Section 12A withdrawal route.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 358 of 2022 is allowed; the NCLT Chennai order dated 26.08.2022 in IA No. 800/2022 in IBA/685/2019 ordering liquidation is set aside; CIRP is restored; the Resolution Professional is directed to explore the Section 12A route; pending IAs closed without costs.
