summary: Suspended director of Jeppiaar Cements Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chennai order directing the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under Section 33(1) of the IBC. The appellant contended that an OTS had been sanctioned by Indian Bank, substantial payments were made before liquidation, and neither member of the CoC voted in favour of liquidation at the 11th meeting. The RP nonetheless applied for liquidation following registry objections. The NCLAT held that liquidation is a remedy of last resort and timelines are directory. Because the financial debts were settled under the OTS, destroying a solvent company was contrary to IBC objectives. The liquidation order was set aside and CIRP restored to explore Section 12A withdrawal.

case_title: Naresh Chand vs. Mani Mahesh Ispat Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1217 of 2026 & I.A. No. 4705 of 2026
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Naresh Chand is the Appellant (Suspended Director of Ashiana Ispat Pvt. Ltd.); Ashiana Ispat Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Mani Mahesh Ispat Private Limited is the Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Prashant Agarwal is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regular supply of mild steel ingots and mild steel billets by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor in the ordinary course of business. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of Rs. 5,73,65,819/- against 27 unpaid invoices raised between 29.04.2023 and 12.09.2023 and two debit notes dated 23.09.2023, after adjusting a lump sum payment of Rs. 45 lakhs made on 30.09.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: FIR lodged under Sections 420/406 IPC on 13.12.2023; settlement agreement and agreement to sell executed on 14.02.2024; addendum executed on 12.09.2024; three post-dated cheques issued in October 2024 and dishonoured on 10.01.2025; Section 8(1) demand notice issued on 10.01.2025; Section 9 petition filed on 25.02.2025; Civil Suit (OS) No. 320/2025 filed before Delhi High Court by OC director on 14.05.2025; NCLT Jaipur admitted Section 9 petition on 03.07.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Confirmed ledger accounts from 01.04.2023 to 31.10.2023 acknowledging Rs. 5,73,65,819/- liability; TDS deductions reflected in Form 26AS; settlement agreement admitting debt; three dishonoured cheques dated 21.10.2024, 22.10.2024, and 23.10.2024; absence of ledger reversal entries discharging debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP IB No. 25/9/JPR/2025 under Section 9 of IBC. NCLT Jaipur Bench admitted the petition and initiated CIRP on 03.07.2026, holding that debt and default were acknowledged, no quality dispute was raised, and the conditional agreement to sell did not discharge the operational debt.
legal_issues: Whether the execution of a conditional settlement agreement and agreement to sell an immovable property constitutes novation of contract under Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 converting operational debt into advance sale consideration, and whether a subsequent civil suit for specific performance constitutes a pre-existing dispute barring Section 9 admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A conditional settlement agreement intended to secure payment of an existing debt does not operate as a novation of contract under Section 62 of the Contract Act unless the parties intend to completely extinguish the original obligation; a subsequent civil suit filed after the Section 9 application does not establish a genuine pre-existing dispute under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Novation under Section 62 requires complete substitution of the old contract with terms so inconsistent that both cannot stand together; where a settlement agreement expressly stipulates that the agreement to sell cancels upon payment, the underlying operational debt remains alive. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, a pre-existing dispute must be real and supported by contemporaneous evidence prior to Section 8 notice; a moonshine defence or subsequent collateral litigation does not defeat an admitted debt confirmed by dishonoured cheques. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default of Rs. 5,73,65,819/- were admitted, no dispute regarding goods quality existed, the agreement to sell was mere security, and the Section 9 petition was rightly admitted.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1217 of 2026 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Jaipur judgment dated 03.07.2026 admitting Ashiana Ispat Limited into CIRP; pending IAs disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Naresh Chand, suspended director of Ashiana Ispat Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Jaipur order admitting a Section 9 IBC petition filed by Mani Mahesh Ispat Pvt. Ltd. for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 5,73,65,819/-. The appellant argued that the operational debt had been novated under Section 62 of the Contract Act into advance consideration under an agreement to sell property owned by a director's wife, and that a pending specific performance suit in the Delhi High Court constituted a pre-existing dispute. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the agreement to sell was conditional security that kept the original debt alive. Dishonoured cheques confirmed continuing default, and the defence was a moonshine.

case_title: M/s Posco International Corporation vs. M/s Mohana Cotton Ginning Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Posco International Corporation (formerly Posco Daewoo Corporation) is the Appellant/Operational Creditor; M/s Mohana Cotton Ginning Private Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: International shipment contract dated 16.12.2016 executed between the parties for supply of 300 Metric Tonnes of Indian raw cotton Grade SLM valued at USD 453,177.57 to M/s Ada Fios in Portugal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of USD 74,342/- agreed to be paid under a settlement agreement dated 01.09.2017 to resolve quality issues, which fell due on 20.09.2017 along with 15% per annum default interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Debit note raised 30.06.2017; settlement agreement executed 01.09.2017 with payment due 20.09.2017; default reminders sent 03.11.2017, 07.11.2017, and legal notice sent 22.01.2018; Section 8 demand notice issued 12.02.2018; reply to demand notice sent 22.02.2018; Section 9 petition filed 04.04.2018; NCLT rejected petition on 11.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 28.07.2017 and emails dated 07.12.2017 from Corporate Debtor admitting liability to pay USD 73,000 plus amendment charges; executed Settlement Agreement dated 01.09.2017; debit note countersigned; reply to Section 8 notice dated 22.02.2018 raising belated counter-allegations of direct solicitation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed TCP(IB) No. 50/9/AMR/2019 (CP(IB) No. 285/9/HDB/2018) under Section 9 of IBC. NCLT Amaravati Bench rejected the petition on 11.09.2019, holding that the dispute should be resolved via arbitration, the appellant was not an Operational Creditor because it did not supply goods directly to the CD, and a pre-existing dispute existed.
legal_issues: Whether the existence of an arbitration clause bars the maintainability of a Section 9 petition under the IBC, whether a purchaser/trader claiming refund under a settlement agreement arising from supply transactions qualifies as an Operational Creditor under Section 5(20) and 5(21), and whether a dispute raised for the first time in response to a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Mobilox.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory remedies provided under the IBC override private contractual arbitration clauses by virtue of Section 238; claims arising out of transactions in respect of goods qualify as operational debt, and disputes raised for the first time in reply to a Section 8 demand notice do not constitute pre-existing disputes barring Section 9 admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) must be interpreted purposively where the phrase 'in respect of' goods covers amounts due under a settlement agreement resolving commercial supply transactions; Section 238 gives IBC overriding effect over arbitration clauses and Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Mobilox Innovations, a pre-existing dispute cannot be a patently feeble legal argument; disputes never agitated before an adjudicatory forum prior to the Section 8 notice and contradicted by written acknowledgements of debt cannot bar admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt of USD 74,342/- was an operational debt, default was established, the arbitration clause was no bar, no genuine pre-existing dispute existed, and the petition ought to be admitted.
operative_order: TA (AT) No. 205/2021 is allowed; the impugned order dated 11.09.2019 passed by NCLT Amaravati is quashed; NCLT is directed to admit the application under Section 9 of the IBC and proceed in accordance with law after imposing a moratorium.
summary: Posco International Corporation appealed an NCLT Amaravati order rejecting its Section 9 IBC petition against Mohana Cotton Ginning Pvt. Ltd. for default of USD 74,342/- due under a settlement agreement. NCLT had rejected the petition on grounds of an arbitration clause, holding appellant was not an operational creditor, and finding a pre-existing dispute. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that statutory IBC remedies override contractual arbitration clauses by virtue of Section 238. It held that claims in respect of goods under a settlement agreement constitute operational debt under Section 5(21) and that unadjudicated claims raised after demand notices do not constitute pre-existing disputes. The NCLT was directed to admit the petition.

case_title: Prabhaben Ravjibhai Harkani vs. Bank of Baroda & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prabhaben Ravjibhai Harkani is the Appellant (Personal Guarantor of Corporate Debtor M/s Shubham Ginning Pressing Pvt. Ltd. and borrower in individual capacity); Bank of Baroda (formerly Dena Bank) is Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Axis Bank is Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned to the Corporate Debtor by Bank of Baroda on 26.10.2013 for Rs. 15 crores, secured by personal guarantee deeds executed by the appellant on 30.10.2013 and 19.03.2015; and credit facilities sanctioned by Axis Bank on 06.01.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dues claimed were Rs. 20,57,98,655.77/- (Bank of Baroda) and Rs. 45,17,882.90/- (Axis Bank); date of default for Bank of Baroda was 29.07.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 29.07.2016; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued on 19.09.2016; OA No. 813 of 2016 filed before DRT; possession taken in 2018; first Section 94 petition filed 08.06.2023 and dismissed 20.11.2023 with liberty; fresh SARFAESI auction held on 24.12.2024; second Section 94 petition CP IB No. 38 of 2025 filed on 03.01.2025; NCLT dismissed petition on 21.04.2025; sale certificate issued 17.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of guarantee dated 30.10.2013 and 19.03.2015; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice dated 19.09.2016; DRT possession orders; successful auction records showing 25% purchase price deposited by auction purchaser M/s Pramukh Developers prior to second Section 94 filing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed second petition CP IB No. 38 of 2025 under Section 94 of IBC. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-II dismissed the petition on 21.04.2025 as barred by limitation under Article 137 and Section 238A without appointing a Resolution Professional, finding it was an abuse of process to gain an interim moratorium and stall concluded SARFAESI auctions.
legal_issues: Whether the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to an insolvency application filed by a personal guarantor under Section 94 of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority can dismiss an ex-facie time-barred Section 94 petition at the threshold without appointing a Resolution Professional under Section 97.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Limitation Act, 1963 applies to debtor-initiated insolvency applications under Section 94 of the IBC by virtue of Section 238A, and the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to dismiss a Section 94 application at the threshold on grounds of limitation or abuse of process without mandatorily appointing a Resolution Professional under Section 97. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A makes the Limitation Act applicable to proceedings under the IBC; the limitation for initiating proceedings against a personal guarantor runs from the date of default/guarantee invocation under Article 137; Dilip Jiwrajka's ruling on RP appointment applies strictly to creditor applications under Section 95 and does not preclude threshold dismissal of time-barred debtor petitions under Section 94. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where recovery proceedings under SARFAESI have substantially matured, auctions are concluded, and third-party rights are created, a belated Section 94 petition is deemed a non-bona fide abuse of process filed solely to trigger Section 96 interim moratorium. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The guarantee was invoked on 19.09.2016 and limitation expired on 18.09.2019; the application filed in 2025 was ex-facie time-barred and constituted an abuse of process, justifying threshold rejection without appointing an RP.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1002 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 21.04.2025 in CP(IB) No. 38 of 2025; pending IAs disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Prabhaben Ravjibhai Harkani, personal guarantor of Shubham Ginning Pressing Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing her Section 94 IBC petition as barred by limitation. The appellant contended that the Limitation Act does not apply to debtor petitions under Section 94 (drawing parity with Section 10) and that the NCLT violated mandatory procedure under Dilip Jiwrajka by failing to appoint a Resolution Professional under Section 97. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 238A applies the Limitation Act to Section 94, and limitation expired three years after guarantee invocation in 2016. An ex-facie time-barred application filed to obstruct concluded SARFAESI auctions can be rejected at the threshold without appointing an RP.

case_title: Exclusive Capital Limited & Ors. vs. Mrs. Kanta Agarwala & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Exclusive Capital Limited (ECL) is an RBI-registered NBFC (Appellant No. 1); Satya Prakash Bagla (MD) and Achal Kumar Jindal (Director) are Appellants Nos. 2 & 3; Mrs. Kanta Agarwala and Suresh Agarwala are minority shareholders holding 10% equity (Respondents Nos. 1 & 2); Justice R.K. Gauba (Retd.) acts as court-appointed Observer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance and conversion of Rs. 315 crores Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) to Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares (CCPS) and related party transactions in an NBFC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Regulatory breach of leverage ratio (exceeding 117 times the ceiling of 7); undocumented loans of Rs. 55 crores; Rs. 16 crore luxury car transactions; and non-finalized financial statements for FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 48/ND/2024 disposed of with interim directions on 15.05.2024; Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 161 & 162 of 2024 filed; Supreme Court passed order on 24.02.2025 granting liberty to parties to move NCLT/NCLAT; Respondents filed IA No. 115/2025; NCLT passed impugned interim order on 16.04.2025 deferring 29th and 30th AGMs scheduled for 18.04.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Observer Reports Nos. 1 to 5 recording non-cooperation and unilateral appointments of statutory auditor and CFO; MCA records reflecting appointments based on unapproved Board minutes of 20.06.2024; RBI status report and order dated 27.03.2026 imposing Rs. 10.30 lakhs penalty. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following Supreme Court's order dated 24.02.2025, Respondents filed IA No. 115 of 2025 in CP No. 48/ND/2024. NCLT New Delhi Bench-II passed an interim order on 16.04.2025 restraining the company from convening its 29th and 30th AGMs pending reply and further hearing, which Appellants challenged alleging NCLT was functus officio.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal becomes functus officio upon passing an interim/disposal order under Section 242 when appellate proceedings remain sub-judice and the Supreme Court expressly grants liberty to seek directions, and whether the NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 242(4) to defer Annual General Meetings pending scrutiny of disputed financial statements.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The doctrine of functus officio does not bar a company tribunal from entertaining ancillary protective applications where the underlying dispute remains live under pending appellate scrutiny and a superior court has expressly granted liberty to seek directions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 confers continuing jurisdiction on the Tribunal to pass interim orders regulating corporate affairs; the doctrine of functus officio applies to final concluded decrees, not to orders of an interim or interlocutory character under appellate review. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appellate courts will not interfere with discretionary ad-interim status-quo orders designed to preserve the subject matter and prevent irreversible corporate actions unless the discretion was exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal acted within its jurisdiction and in compliance with the Supreme Court's mandate by deferring the AGMs to prevent the premature adoption of clouded financial statements, leaving all substantive contentions open.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) No. 112 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT New Delhi interim order dated 16.04.2025 in I.A. No. 115/2025 in C.P. No. 48/ND/2024; all contentions left open for final adjudication before the Tribunal; no order as to costs.
summary: Exclusive Capital Limited and its promoter-directors appealed an NCLT New Delhi interim order passed in IA No. 115 of 2025 in CP No. 48/ND/2024, which restrained the company from holding its 29th and 30th AGMs. The appellants contended that the NCLT became functus officio after disposing of the main petition on 15.05.2024. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the doctrine of functus officio did not apply because the previous order was under active appellate review and the Supreme Court had expressly granted liberty to seek directions. The NCLT properly exercised its interim powers under Section 242(4) to prevent adoption of disputed financial statements.

case_title: M/s. Pearl City Marine Products Private Limited & Ors. vs. Mr. Hiras K. M. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Pearl City Marine Products Private Limited (Appellant No. 1 Company), Mr. Velliyattil Alikutty Abubacker (Chairman/Shareholder/Appellant No. 2), Mr. Abdul Rahiman Pullat (Director/Appellant No. 3), and Mr. Ahmed Uwaiz Velliyattil Abubacker (Additional Director/Appellant No. 4); Mr. Hiras K.M. (MD and Shareholder/Respondent No. 1), Mr. Shurooq Shanavas (Additional Director/Respondent No. 2), and removed directors Mr. Velliyattil Muhammed Haneefa Abuthahir and Mr. Velliyattil Muhammed Haneefa (Respondents Nos. 3 and 4); Registrar of Companies Kerala (Respondent No. 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate governance and Board management of a private limited company comprising seven original directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate governance impasse following the removal of Respondents 3 and 4 from the Board for proven misconduct at an EGM held on 10.11.2025; subsequent requisition by Respondent No. 1 on 20.01.2026 under Section 100 to convene an EGM to re-induct Respondents 3 and 4, which the Board rejected by a 3:2 majority vote on 09.02.2026. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EGM removing directors held on 10.11.2025; Section 100 requisition notice issued on 20.01.2026; Board resolution rejecting requisition passed on 09.02.2026; Company Petition CP No. 04/KOB/2026 filed under Section 98 on 05.03.2026; NCLT Kochi Bench passed impugned order on 22.06.2026. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Requisition notice dated 20.01.2026; Board minutes dated 09.02.2026; absence of any attempt by requisitionists to convene the meeting under Section 100(4); withdrawal of Section 241/242 petition CP No. 37/2026 by Respondents 3 and 4 on 05.03.2026 upon filing of Section 98 petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP No. 04/KOB/2026 under Section 98 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Kochi Bench seeking an order directing the convening of an EGM. NCLT Kochi allowed the petition on 22.06.2026 and directed the EGM to be held, which the Appellants challenged under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether Section 100(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides an exclusive remedy precluding resort to Section 98, and whether the NCLT can exercise exceptional discretionary jurisdiction under Section 98 to direct the convening of an Extraordinary General Meeting without the requisitioning member establishing that it was impracticable to hold the meeting under Section 100(4).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory power of the Tribunal under Section 98 to intervene in internal corporate management and direct the convening of an extraordinary general meeting is an exceptional jurisdiction that must be exercised sparingly, conditional upon proof of the statutory prerequisite that it has become impracticable to convene or conduct the meeting in the manner prescribed by the Act or Articles. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Calling an EGM by requisitioning shareholders under Section 100(4) and seeking a tribunal-directed meeting under Section 98 are mutually exclusive remedies; however, while the requisitionist's right under Section 100(4) is absolute, invocation of Section 98 is qualified and strictly dependent on proving impracticability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the principles established in Re: Ruttonjee and Co. Ltd., impracticability must be evaluated from a commonsense and prudent business viewpoint, requiring proof of an irremovable deadlock; a bare 3:2 Board refusal where the company has over 110 shareholders and no attempt was made to convene under Section 100(4) does not satisfy the test. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the requisitionist failed to plead or establish foundational facts demonstrating that convening an EGM under Section 100(4) was impracticable, the NCLT erred in usurping domestic corporate democracy under Section 98, and its order must be set aside.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 76 of 2026 is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Kochi Bench dated 22.06.2026 in CP No. 04/KOB/2026 is set aside; all pending interlocutory applications stand closed with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants appealed an NCLT Kochi order passed under Section 98 of the Companies Act, 2013, which directed the convening of an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) to consider re-inducting two directors previously removed for misconduct. The company's Board had rejected the requisition under Section 100 by a 3:2 majority. The NCLAT held that while remedies under Section 100(4) and Section 98 are mutually exclusive, Section 98 is an exceptional power that can be invoked only upon establishing that holding the meeting without tribunal intervention is impracticable. Because the company had over 110 shareholders and the requisitionist made no attempt to convene the meeting under Section 100(4), impracticability was not established. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the NCLT order.

case_title: Renu Lalit Agarwal vs. Small Industries Development Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Renu Lalit Agarwal is the Appellant (Suspended Director of AS Infracon Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor); Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Ajit Gyanchand Jain is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2); Kosas Exports Ltd. is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Secured Business Loan facility of Rs. 7,00,00,000/- sanctioned by SIDBI to Kosas Exports Ltd. under Sanction Letter dated 24.02.2014 and Loan Agreement dated 26.02.2014, secured by an unconditional and irrevocable Deed of Corporate Guarantee executed by the Corporate Debtor on 26.02.2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan disbursed on 11.03.2014; borrower account classified as NPA on 08.11.2015; loan recall notice issued on 08.03.2016; guarantee invoked on 27.07.2016 demanding Rs. 7,28,75,463/- plus interest; Principal Borrower submitted written OTS proposals offering Rs. 12 crores on 08.06.2019 and Rs. 7.50 crores on 05.11.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recall notice issued 08.03.2016; invocation notice issued 27.07.2016; OTS proposals submitted 08.06.2019 and 05.11.2020; Section 7 petition filed on 12.05.2023; NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted petition on 30.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Corporate Guarantee dated 26.02.2014, including Clause 3 (guarantee on demand) and Clause 22 (acknowledgment of debt by borrower binds guarantor); written OTS proposals acknowledging subsisting debt; NCLT order sheets spanning seven hearings between 07.02.2024 and 18.09.2024 showing repeated postal and email notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SIDBI filed CP No. IB 21/KB/2024 under Section 7 of IBC. Following repeated non-appearance, NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the petition ex parte on 30.10.2024 and initiated CIRP, which the suspended director appealed alleging non-service of notice and limitation bar.
legal_issues: Whether the ex parte admission of a Section 7 petition violates principles of natural justice when postal and email notices were repeatedly issued to the registered office and updated particulars, and whether an acknowledgment of debt in OTS proposals by the principal borrower extends limitation against a corporate guarantor under Section 18 of the Limitation Act pursuant to Clause 22 of the guarantee deed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of statutory notice by speed post and email at the registered office and furnished particulars across multiple hearings satisfies the requirement of natural justice under Rule 38 of the NCLT Rules, and a corporate debtor cannot plead denial of hearing caused by its own failure to maintain a functional registered office; furthermore, a contractual stipulation in a guarantee deed providing that an acknowledgment of debt by the borrower binds the guarantor operates under Section 18 of the Limitation Act to extend limitation against the corporate guarantor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 128 of the Contract Act read with Section 5(5A) and Section 7 of the IBC and the rule in Laxmi Pat Surana, the liability of a corporate guarantor is coextensive with the principal debtor; written acknowledgments of liability in OTS proposals restart the three-year limitation period under Article 137. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A party cannot rely on a default of its own making under Section 12 of the Companies Act to impeach valid postal and electronic service; written OTS proposals placed on record by the borrower operate as binding acknowledgments of a subsisting debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed on 12.05.2023 was well within limitation due to the OTS acknowledgments of 08.06.2019 and 05.11.2020, service was legally sufficient, financial debt and default were undisputed, and CIRP admission was valid.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 2264 of 2024 is dismissed, confirming the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated 30.10.2024 in CP No. IB 21/KB/2024 admitting AS Infracon Pvt. Ltd. into CIRP; all pending interlocutory applications stand closed with no order as to costs.
summary: Renu Lalit Agarwal, suspended director of AS Infracon Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor), appealed an NCLT Kolkata order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by SIDBI for default of Rs. 7.28 crores on a loan sanctioned to Kosas Exports Ltd. The appellant contended that the ex parte order violated natural justice as the registered office was closed, and that the petition was time-barred since the 2016 guarantee invocation notice was never served. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that service by post and email across seven months satisfied Rule 38, and a company cannot plead lack of notice caused by its own failure to maintain a registered office under Section 12 of the Companies Act. Moreover, OTS proposals sent by the principal borrower extended limitation against the guarantor under Clause 22 of the guarantee deed and Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

case_title: Sumit Bansal & Ors. vs. Rajeev Lochan, Resolution Professional of M/s RG Residency Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Sumit Bansal, Ms. Monica Bansal, Ms. Parul Bansal, and LR of late Prem Bansal are Appellants (flat purchasers/claimants); Mr. Rajeev Lochan is the Resolution Professional (Respondent); M/s RG Residency Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking and allotment of residential flats (Nos. B-1603, B-2601, B-2602, and H-2406) measuring approx. 6599 sq. ft. in the project 'RG Regency Pvt. Ltd.' under unregistered agreements for sale dated 24.11.2015 for total consideration of Rs. 1,35,00,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Consideration of Rs. 1,35,00,000/- paid in full; symbolic possession given with promised physical delivery by 30.09.2018; Corporate Debtor failed to complete construction and issued appreciation/refund cheques (e.g. Cheque No. 969845 dated 30.09.2018 for Rs. 9,11,250/-) which were dishonoured upon presentation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreements for sale executed on 24.11.2015; promised completion date 30.09.2018; appreciation cheques handed over 31.03.2019; CD status of claims email dated 26.04.2024; Appellants filed IA No. 2471 of 2024 (and connected IAs) on 25.04.2024/02.05.2024; NCLT Principal Bench dismissed IAs on 13.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unregistered agreements for sale dated 24.11.2015 containing Clause 7(d) for appreciation cheques and Clause 10 arbitration clause; dishonoured cheques; criminal complaints filed under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act; statement of claim in arbitration seeking refund of entire investment with 12% interest from 01.10.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In insolvency proceedings CP (IBPP) No. 01/PB/2023, Appellants filed IA Nos. 2471/2024, 2432/2024, 2465/2024, 2527/2024, and 2531/2024 under Section 60(5) seeking admission of full claims and declaration of their status as Financial Creditors in the class of allottees under Section 5(8)(f). NCLT Principal Bench directed remittance of Rs. 1.35 crores but rejected Financial Creditor status on 13.05.2025, which Appellants challenged under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether real estate purchasers who have invoked arbitration seeking refund of their entire investment with interest, accepted refund/appreciation cheques, and initiated Section 138 NI Act proceedings continue to retain the status of allottees entitled to be classified as Financial Creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Real estate flat purchasers who elect to seek full monetary refund of consideration with interest through arbitration, accept refund/appreciation cheques, and prosecute cheque-bouncing proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act renounce their status as continuing allottees under a real estate project, disentitling them from claiming classification as financial creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8)(f) and Section 3(11) of the IBC, a financial debt requires a subsisting and continuing liability or obligation owed to an allottee; the deeming fiction under the Explanation to Section 5(8)(f) applies strictly to amounts raised from a continuing allottee and cannot be invoked where the claimant has elected to treat the transaction as a terminated borrowing seeking refund. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The ruling in Vishal Chelani v. Debashis Nanda applies to RERA decree-holders who remain home buyers within the class; it does not extend to claimants whose own pleadings and parallel proceedings establish that they no longer seek allotment of property but recovery of money. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants ceased to be allottees by seeking money recovery in parallel arbitration and Section 138 proceedings; the NCLT rightly refused to accord them Financial Creditor status in the CoC, and the appeals must be dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins) Nos. 858, 873, 874, 875 and 821 of 2025 are dismissed, affirming the NCLT Principal Bench order dated 13.05.2025; all pending interlocutory applications stand closed; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants who booked flats in RG Residency Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order that declined to recognize them as Financial Creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC. The appellants paid Rs. 1.35 crores under unregistered agreements for sale, but when construction was delayed, they accepted appreciation cheques, initiated Section 138 NI Act proceedings when the cheques bounced, and commenced arbitration seeking full refund with 12% interest. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT order, distinguishing Vishal Chelani and holding that the deeming fiction under Explanation to Section 5(8)(f) applies only to continuing allottees. By pursuing parallel proceedings for monetary refund, the appellants renounced their allottee status and could not claim financial creditor classification.

case_title: Kalidindi Venkateswara Raju vs. Sri Yadadri Lifesciences Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kalidindi Venkateswara Raju is the Appellant (alleged Financial Creditor/arranger); Sri Yadadri Lifesciences Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (bulk drug manufacturing company)[cite: 38]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) dated 25.01.2021 under which the Appellant agreed to arrange and provide an unsecured loan facility aggregating approx. Rs. 8 crores through self and known third-party sources at 24% interest p.a. to assist the Corporate Debtor in settling its OTS with State Bank of India[cite: 38]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed total outstanding debt of Rs. 11.30 crores (principal Rs. 7,46,89,001/- plus interest Rs. 3.83 crores) as per a consolidated receipt dated 30.11.2023; demand notice issued on 05.12.2023 demanding interest within 7 days, which Corporate Debtor failed to pay after seeking time till January 2024[cite: 38]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU executed on 25.01.2021; consolidated receipt issued on 30.11.2023; demand notice issued on 05.12.2023; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 22/7/HDB/2024 filed on 23.01.2024; NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the petition on 24.10.2024[cite: 38]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU dated 25.01.2021; individual receipts and consolidated receipt dated 30.11.2023 reflecting funds from 9 individuals; absence of assignment deeds from third parties; records showing Appellant personally disbursed Rs. 1,17,14,001/-, of which Rs. 3,00,000/- was repaid and Rs. 43,50,000/- was an unverified cash entry in an expenses account violating Section 269SS of the Income Tax Act[cite: 38]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad rejected the Section 7 petition with Rs. 1 lakh cost on 24.10.2024, holding that Appellant cannot claim financial creditor status for third-party loans without assignments, permissible direct debt was below Rs. 1 crore, and the petition was collusive[cite: 38].
legal_issues: Whether an individual who mobilizes funds from third parties under an MoU without formal deeds of assignment qualifies as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) of the IBC for the aggregate amount, and whether unverified cash loans violating Section 269SS of the Income Tax Act can be counted to satisfy the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 crore[cite: 38].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An arranger of loans who mobilizes funds from third parties cannot maintain an application under Section 7 of the IBC as a Financial Creditor for the aggregate debt in the absence of a legally valid assignment or transfer of debt under Section 5(7), and uncorroborated cash entries violating statutory banking requirements cannot be recognized to meet the Section 4 monetary threshold[cite: 38]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) and Section 3(11) of the IBC, a financial debt must be directly owed to the claimant or legally assigned to them; the definition of consideration under Section 2(d) of the Contract Act cannot override or dilute the specific statutory criteria required to establish financial creditor status under the IBC[cite: 38]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consolidated receipts issued by a corporate debtor cannot substitute for demonstrable banking transactions; cash transactions recorded without banking trails are legally impermissible and cannot establish disbursed financial debt[cite: 38]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: After excluding third-party funds and impermissible cash entries, the Appellant's direct loan fell below the mandatory threshold of Rs. 1 crore, rendering the Section 7 petition non-maintainable[cite: 38].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 450/2024 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Hyderabad order dated 24.10.2024 rejecting the Section 7 petition; cost of Rs. 1,00,000/- imposed on the Appellant is waived; pending IAs closed[cite: 38].
summary: Kalidindi Venkateswara Raju appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order rejecting his Section 7 IBC petition against Sri Yadadri Lifesciences Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 11.30 crores[cite: 38]. Under an MoU, the appellant had mobilized unsecured loans from nine individuals to fund the debtor's bank settlement[cite: 38]. The NCLAT held that an arranger cannot claim financial creditor status under Section 5(7) for funds provided by third parties without formal assignment deeds[cite: 38]. Furthermore, after excluding uncorroborated cash entries that violated Section 269SS of the Income Tax Act, the appellant's direct loan fell below the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 crore[cite: 38]. The dismissal of the Section 7 petition was affirmed, while the cost was waived[cite: 38].

case_title: Asif Ahmed Siddique vs. UCO Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Asif Ahmed Siddique is the Appellant (Personal Guarantor); UCO Bank is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Atul Narayan Naik is the Resolution Professional of the Personal Guarantor (Respondent No. 2); Avil Jerome Menezes is the Resolution Professional of Nyka Steel Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 3)[cite: 39]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital and term loan facilities sanctioned to Nyka Steel Private Limited in 2013 and 2017, renewed and enhanced via Sanction Letter dated 12.04.2018, secured by continuing personal guarantee deeds executed by the Appellant on 15.07.2013 and 12.12.2017[cite: 39]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor resulted in account classification as NPA on 18.01.2020 (w.e.f. 30.09.2019); recall notice issued on 18.01.2020; demand notices dated 12.09.2023 and 27.11.2024 issued demanding Rs. 51,76,09,050.43 and Rs. 96,23,11,185.08 respectively[cite: 39]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 18.01.2020; recall notice issued on 18.01.2020; Section 95 petition CP(IB)/184(MB)/2025 filed on 22.12.2024; RP appointed on 26.03.2025; NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 95 petition on 03.02.2026[cite: 39]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Guarantee dated 12.12.2017 stipulating continuing liability capped at Rs. 40 crores plus interest at 12.70% p.a. from demand date; credit facility renewal letter dated 12.04.2018 signed by Appellant; postal dispatch receipts proving delivery of recall notice dated 18.01.2020; RP report under Section 99 recommending admission[cite: 39]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: UCO Bank filed CP(IB) No. 184(MB)/2025 under Section 95 read with Section 60(2) against the Personal Guarantor[cite: 39]. NCLT Mumbai admitted the petition on 03.02.2026, declared moratorium under Section 101, and appointed RP, which the Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 39].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 95 petition against a personal guarantor is maintainable when credit facilities were renewed without a fresh guarantee deed, whether the guarantor's liability is strictly capped at Rs. 40 crores excluding interest, and whether proof of dispatch of a recall notice constitutes valid guarantee invocation[cite: 39].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A continuing personal guarantee remains enforceable across subsequent renewals and enhancements of credit facilities signed by the guarantor, and a contractual clause stipulating a principal limit plus interest allows total enforceable liability to exceed the nominal principal ceiling[cite: 39]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 95 read with Section 60(2) of the IBC, personal insolvency proceedings lie before the same bench where CIRP against the corporate debtor is pending; under Sections 99 and 100, proof of dispatch of a recall notice to the guarantor's recorded address satisfies the requirement of guarantee invocation[cite: 39]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Express terms of a continuing guarantee deed and signed renewal letters demonstrate that liability covers renewed facilities; postal dispatch receipts establish valid service in the absence of a notified change of address[cite: 39]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The guarantee was continuing and covered renewed facilities, liability legitimately exceeded Rs. 40 crores due to interest at 12.70% p.a., default was established, and the Section 95 petition was properly admitted[cite: 39].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 489/2026 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai order dated 03.02.2026 in CP(IB) No. 184(MB)/2025; pending applications disposed of without costs[cite: 39].
summary: Asif Ahmed Siddique, personal guarantor of Nyka Steel Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 95 IBC petition filed by UCO Bank for default of Rs. 96.23 crores[cite: 39]. The appellant argued that no fresh guarantee was executed for the 2018 renewal, his liability was capped at Rs. 40 crores, the recall notice was not served, and NPA classification was improper[cite: 39]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the guarantee deed dated 12.12.2017 was a continuing guarantee expressly covering Rs. 40 crores plus interest at 12.70% p.a., and the 2018 renewal was signed by the appellant[cite: 39]. Proof of dispatch established valid invocation, justifying admission[cite: 39].

case_title: Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Limited vs. Vs.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Limited is the Applicant/Transferee Company; M/s Dipesh Mining Pvt. Ltd., Jiwanjyoti Traders Pvt. Ltd., Paramount Dealcomm Pvt. Ltd., Premsagar Merchants Pvt. Ltd., and Splendor Distributors Pvt. Ltd. are the 5 wholly owned subsidiary Transferor Companies[cite: 40]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: First motion application under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 for a scheme of amalgamation of five wholly owned subsidiary transferor companies into the listed parent transferee company[cite: 40]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Transferee Company has authorized share capital of Rs. 20,00,00,000/- and issued/paid-up capital of Rs. 13,39,75,120/-; sought dispensation from convening meetings of its equity shareholders, secured creditors, and unsecured creditors without furnishing 90% consent affidavits[cite: 40]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appointed date of scheme fixed as 01.04.2026[cite: 40]; NCLT Kolkata Bench dispensed with meetings of Transferor Companies via order dated 23.04.2026 in CA (CAA) No. 31 of 2026[cite: 40]; NCLT New Delhi Bench-III passed the impugned order on 05.06.2026 in Company Application (CAA) No. 12(ND) of 2026[cite: 40]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transferee company shares are listed on BSE and NSE[cite: 40]; reliance placed on SEBI Master Circular dated 20.06.2023 for wholly owned subsidiary mergers[cite: 40]; absence of consent affidavits from at least 90% in value of creditors/shareholders of the Transferee Company as required under Section 230(9)[cite: 40]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In first motion Company Application (CAA) No. 12(ND) of 2026, NCLT Delhi Bench-III declined to dispense with meetings of equity shareholders, secured creditors, and unsecured creditors of the Transferee Company due to lack of consent affidavits under Section 230(9), directing meetings via video conferencing[cite: 40]. Appellant appealed under Section 421[cite: 40].
legal_issues: Whether the requirement of convening meetings of equity shareholders and creditors of a listed parent transferee company can be dispensed with under Section 230(9) of the Companies Act, 2013 in a merger with its wholly owned subsidiaries without furnishing consent affidavits of at least 90% in value[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a scheme of amalgamation under Sections 230-232, the statutory power of the Tribunal to dispense with the convening of meetings of creditors or shareholders under Section 230(9) is strictly conditional upon furnishing consent affidavits from at least ninety percent in value, and no implied exception exists for listed holding companies amalgamating with wholly owned subsidiaries[cite: 40]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230(9) of the Companies Act, 2013 unambiguously mandates that dispensation from calling meetings can only be granted where creditors or class of creditors having at least 90% value confirm by affidavit; the statute carves out no exemption for holding companies absorbing wholly owned subsidiaries[cite: 40]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where public interest and substantial public shareholding are involved in a listed company, compliance with statutory procedural requirements of Section 230(9) is mandatory; parity cannot be claimed with unlisted subsidiary transferor companies that furnished 100% consent affidavits[cite: 40]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Limited failed to place on record consent affidavits of 90% in value from its shareholders and creditors, the NCLT rightly exercised its judicial discretion in refusing dispensation and directing meetings to be convened[cite: 40].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) No. 310 of 2026 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Delhi Bench-III order dated 05.06.2026; appellant permitted to proceed with convening meetings via video conferencing and apply afresh[cite: 40].
summary: Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Limited, a listed parent company, appealed an NCLT Delhi order refusing to dispense with meetings of its equity shareholders, secured creditors, and unsecured creditors in a first motion application under Sections 230-232 for amalgamation with five wholly owned subsidiaries[cite: 40]. The appellant argued that since it holds 100% shares of the transferor companies and no new shares are issued, Section 230(9) consent affidavits were unnecessary[cite: 40]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 230(9) contains no statutory exemption for parent-subsidiary mergers and mandates affidavits from 90% in value to dispense with meetings, especially for listed companies with public shareholding[cite: 40].
